<meta>This is the opening page of the Preface to the modernized edition of the Félire Óengusso (The Martyrology of Oengus).</meta>

## PREFACE.

The first edition of the metrical Martyrology <note>A calendar of saints and martyrs.</note> called in Irish *Félire Óengusso Céle Dé* <note>The Calendar of Oengus, the Servant of God.</note> was published in 1880 by the Royal Irish Academy. It was presented in parallel columns from four corrupt and uncorrected texts, hereafter referred to as R¹, R², L, and *LB*. In the preface to that edition, I argued—for reasons that then seemed conclusive to me—that the poem could not have been composed much before the end of the tenth century. Further study, along with the arguments of Professors Strachan¹ and Thurneysen,² have convinced me that I was wrong.³ I now believe that its composition may, in accordance with Irish tradition, be safely assigned to the year 800 or thereabouts. 

An Irish metrical martyrology of such antiquity deserves the attention of all who are interested in religious history, liturgical books, Celtic philology <note>The study of language in historical sources.</note>, or poetic art. The Council of the Henry Bradshaw Society is surely justified in attempting to provide its members with a critical text of this unique poem, including various readings from the ten manuscripts in which it is wholly or partially preserved.

In forming the text, as well as in making the translation and glossary, I have used to the best of my power the discoveries in Old-Irish grammar and etymology <note>The study of the origin of words.</note> achieved during the last twelve years by Ascoli, Windisch, Thurneysen, Zimmer, Zupitza, Osthoff, Sommer, Rozwadowski, Pedersen, Sarauw, Strachan, and Lidén. I am far from regarding the present edition as definitive. I know too well that I have not realized my ideal; but, remembering the story told of Thorwaldsen in his old age,⁴ I cannot say that I am therefore discouraged.

<margin>¹ *Deponent verb*, p. 110.</margin>
<margin>² *Journal of Celtic Philology* <note>original: "ZCP"</note> i. 345.</margin>
<margin>³ I especially regret that my error should have misled the Rev. F. E. Warren in *Liturgy and Ritual of the Celtic Church*, p. xvi, and Professor Bury in *Life of St. Patrick*, p. 343, note 4.</margin>
<margin>⁴ 
> “A friend found him unhappy before a finished statue and asked if he was discouraged because he had not been able to realize his ideal. The sculptor responded that, on the contrary, he *had* realized his ideal, and therefore he was downcast; for the first time, his hand had been able to accomplish all that his mind had planned.” 
—*North American Review*, June 15, 1905, p. 873.</margin>

<summary>The author retracts his previous dating of the Félire Óengusso, now placing its composition around 800 AD, and introduces this new edition as a product of recent advancements in Celtic philology.</summary>
<keywords>Félire Óengusso, Martyrology of Oengus, Celtic philology, Old Irish, Henry Bradshaw Society, historical linguistics, hagiography</keywords>

<page-num>viii</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

### PREFACE.

I now propose, first, to describe the ten <term>MSS.</term> <note>abbreviation for manuscripts</note> on which the present edition is founded; secondly, to notice the author of the <term>Martyrology</term> <note>a catalog or list of saints and martyrs</note>, <term>Oengus the Culdee</term> <note>an 8th-9th century Irish monk and saint</note>; thirdly, to consider some of the characteristics of the language of the poem, especially as bearing on the date of its composition; fourthly, to explain the metre in which it is written; fifthly, to give some account of its contents; and lastly, to notice the passages in the Irish prefaces and <term>scholia</term> <note>ancient grammatical or explanatory notes</note> which seem to throw light on early Irish religious practices, superstitions, folklore, and legal antiquities.

---

### I. DESCRIPTION OF THE MANUSCRIPTS.

The <term>MSS.</term> on which the present edition is founded will be respectively denoted by the following signs, here arranged in alphabetical order: *B, C, E, F, H, L, LB, P, R¹, R²*.

->*B* = Brussels MS. 5100-4.<-

As this <term>codex</term> <note>an ancient manuscript in book form</note> has been fully described in the preface to the *<term>Martyrology of Gorman</term>, London, 1895*, it will be enough here to say that it is a small paper manuscript in the Royal Library, Brussels, almost wholly in the handwriting of <term>Michael O'Clery</term>, one of the <term>Four Masters</term> <note>authors of the Annals of the Kingdom of Ireland</note>, who died about 1644. The copy of the <term>Martyrology of Oengus</term> which it contains is in Michael's handwriting, and was transcribed from a book written by <term>Siodrach Ua Maelconaire</term> in the year 1533. It begins on folio 94a and ends on folio 119b. It omits lines 393-396 and lines 543-546 of the epilogue, as well as the first two lines of the <term>quatrain</term> <note>a four-line stanza</note> for October 8; the latter omission is supplied in the margin by a recent hand. All its important readings are, in the present work, marked *B*, and are given in the footnotes.

<margin>¹ For example: <term>noemanim</term> (Prologue 99), <term>ainim</term> (123), <term>na betha</term> (156), <term>itaimne</term> (162), <term>uarilius</term> (Jan. 22), <term>da shinchell</term> (March 26), <term>Ambifani</term> (April 2), <term>Anterini</term> (May 4), <term>pro pace</term> <note>original Latin: "for peace"</note> (May 13), <term>dia</term> (May 31), <term>do dofarnic</term> (June 10), <term>Treofonia</term> (Oct. 18).</margin>

It seems to me on the whole to come closer to the copy in the <term>Lebar Brecc</term>¹ <note>The "Speckled Book," a famous 15th-century Irish manuscript</note> than to those in the other <term>MSS.</term> But there are often variances, some—such as, in the prologue, *<term>rith roreith</term> (28), <term>n-oidhidh</term> (49), <term>riaghaib</term> (52), <term>gerat</term> (90), <term>a dun</term> (130), <term>ro sretha</term> (138), <term>bertair</term> (175), <term>dilsiu</term> (185), <term>as nesa</term> (217), <term>slebe</term> (240), <term>gruidiu</term> (265), <term>sluinnfid</term> (300), <term>trib</term> (328)*—which are decidedly better than the readings of the <term>Speckled Book</term>. So at January 18, *B* has *<term>tasc</term>* <note>report/announcement</note> while *LB* has *<term>bás</term>* <note>death</note>; at February 6, *B* has *<term>Mel</term>* while *LB* has *<term>Moel</term>*. See also February 15 (*<term>i feil Beraig badhaig</term>* <note>"on the feast of victorious Berach"</note>); February 28, April 30 (*<term>forcennat</term>* <note>"they end"</note>); June 15 (*<term>mórgail</term>* <note>"great valor"</note>); July 10 (*<term>carcar</term>* <note>"prison"</note>); July 15 (*<term>cach n-arim</term>* <note>"every number"</note>); August 3 (*<term>noeibi</term>* <note>"of holiness"</note>); August 5 (*<term>comarc</term>* <note>"protection"</note>); August 7 (*<term>coecdaib</term>* <note>"in fifties"</note>); August 19 (*<term>raithe</term>* <note>"of the quarter/season"</note>).

September 11 (<note>original Old Irish: imbliuch</note> "at the lake-shore"); November 3 (<note>original Old Irish: lith cain Corcunutan</note> "the fair festival of Corcunutan"), 7 (<note>original Old Irish: fofuair</note> "he found"), 22 (<note>original Old Irish: immartrai</note> "about martyrdom"): December 26 (<note>original Old Irish: atneocham</note> "we beseech him"), Epilogue 32 (<note>original Old Irish: riga</note> "kings") 226 (<note>original Old Irish: ronnain</note> "may he protect us"). Readings which deserve consideration, though they have not been adopted in the text, are Epilogue 43 (<note>original Old Irish: i conair Crist credail</note> "in the path of pious Christ"), 70 (<note>original Old Irish: thair tiar</note> "in the east, in the west"), 129 (<note>original Old Irish: roat</note> "a long road," derived from <note>original Old Irish: ro-fot</note> "great length"), 175 (<note>original Old Irish: dna</note> "moreover").

### C = The Cheltenham MS.

This is a parchment manuscript now containing 48 pages. It formerly belonged to the lexicographer <term>Edward O'Reilly</term> <note>An Irish scholar and author of an Irish-English dictionary (1765–1830)</note>, by whom it was sold to the late <term>Sir Thomas Phillips</term>. When I examined the manuscript, it was in the library of the <term>Rev. John F. A. Fenwick</term>, Thirlstane House, Cheltenham. The extravagant date, "as old as the tenth century," which <term>Dr. Petrie</term> (in his work *On the History and Antiquities of Tara Hill*, p. 71) ascribed to this codex, was probably due to the seller's ignorance or greed. Paleography <note>the study of ancient writing systems</note>, grammar, and spelling show that it can hardly be older than the fifteenth century. As it is now unknown to <term>Celtists</term> <note>scholars of Celtic languages and culture</note>, the following brief list of its contents may be welcome:

**P. 1.** Illegible.
**P. 2.** Begins: <note>original Old Irish: et ni derna failti friu</note> "and he did not make them welcome," etc., a passage relating to the creation of <term>Eve</term> from <term>Adam</term>'s seventh rib.
**P. 3.** Poem beginning:
<note>original Old Irish: Athair caich, coimsid nime. in ri uasal ainglighe</note> "Father of everyone, ruler of heaven, the noble, angelic king," and ending (p. 4): <note>original Old Irish: rucad Gaoideil ar n-at[h]air</note> "<term>Góidel</term> <note>The legendary ancestor of the Gaelic people</note>, our father, was born."¹
**P. 4.** <note>original Old Irish: Ro aitreph tra Nell mac Feniusa Fairsaid theas i n-Eigipt</note> "Now Niall, son of Fenius Farsaid, dwelt in the south, in Egypt."
**P. 5.** <note>original Old Irish: Imtusa cloinne Danaine et cloinne Deirgthinedh et cloinde Luighdech meic Ithe</note> "Adventures of the Children of <term>Danann</term> and the Children of <term>Dergthene</term> and the Children of <term>Lugaid</term>, son of <term>Ith</term>."
**P. 9.** <note>original Old Irish: Imtussa Mog[a]Nuadat</note> "Adventures of <term>Mugh Nuadat</term>."
**P. 12.** A scribe's note beginning: <note>original Old Irish: Misse in Dubaltach mac Semuis do graiph in beag sin</note> "I am <term>Dubaltach</term>, son of <term>James</term>, who wrote that little bit," etc.
**P. 13.** Story beginning with a description of a combat between the King of <term>Erin</term> <note>Ireland</note> and the King of <term>Ulaid</term> <note>Ulster</note>.
**Pp. 20–45** contain an imperfect copy of the <term>Martyrology of Oengus</term>. Missing are the lines from the quatrain for March 13 to the second line of the quatrain for November 21; and page 19, which probably contained a prose preface, is now illegible.
**P. 20.** <note>original Old Irish: IMrordus in rigraid</note> "I have commemorated the king-folk," Prologue 21.

¹ Also in the <term>Book of Lecan</term>, folio 267 (<term>Plummer</term>).

## PREFACE.

**Page 22.** *Bless us, O Christ.* <note>original: "Sén a Crist"</note> Beginning of the invocation prefixed to the prologue.

**Page 24.** *Before the assembly of the world's people* <note>original: "Re sil dálach dained"</note>, first line of the quatrain for January 1.

**Page 27.** *The Kalends of February magnify* <note>original: "Morait kl. Febrai"</note>, first line of the quatrain for February 1.
The poem continues to the end of the quatrain for March 12. There is then a gap <term>lacuna</term> in the text down to page 35, which begins with *the son of Coman from Aran* <note>original: "mac Comain a hAraind"</note>, the third line of the quatrain for November 21.

**Page 36.** *Announce the Kalends of December* <note>original: "Sluind Decimbir kalaind"</note>, December 1.

**Pages 41–45.** *From one Kalends to another* <note>original: "On kaland cu araile"</note> etc. The epilogue.

**Page 45.** *The three cries of the world* <note>original: "Tri gairi in domain"</note>. See *Lives of the Saints from the Book of Lismore* <note>original: "Lism. Lives"</note> xxxi., where they are said to be:
1. The cry of the Israelites when they entered the Red Sea; 
2. The cry of Hell when Christ carried off his prey from it; 
3. And the cry of Doomsday when the righteous separate from the sinners. 
See also the manuscript *Egerton 1782*, folio 49b, cited in *Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie* <note>original: "Celt. Zeits."</note> iv. 237.

" Poem ascribed to Comghall of Bangor <note>original: "Bennchor"</note>, beginning: *I am alone in my little oratory, without anyone in my company* <note>original: "Maonuran imm aruclan gan duine imm gnais"</note>.

**Page 46.** *Concerning the words of Colmán son of Beona* <note>original: "De uerbis Colmain macoBeonae"</note>, that is, *concerning the vices* <note>original: "de uitiis"</note> lurking in the shadow of good works, etc., see the *Martyrology of Gorman* <note>original: "Mart. Gorm."</note> viii. For this Colmán’s *Alphabet of Devotion* <note>original: "Apgitir Crábaid"</note>, see *Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie* <note>original: "ZCP."</note> i. 496; iii. 447.

**Line 25.** *The gift of wisdom makes a king of a pauper, makes a landholder of a landless man, and makes a sage of a fool.* <note>original: "Dán ecnaig dogni rig do pauper, dogni coairt di eissirt, dogni gaoth do baoth."</note>

**Line 28.** Legend of saints Secundinus and Patrick beginning: *Once upon a time Seachnall went to Armagh, and Patrick was not there, and he saw two chariot-horses* <note>original: "Feacht n-aile luidh Seachnall do Ardmacha, 7 ni raibi Patric hifus, conaccai dá ech carpuitt"</note> etc.

**Page 46a, line 44.** *Let everyone take heed, before abandoning God’s commandments, how in his hardships he will look for God, and how in want or in need he will pray to the mighty Lord, and how God will hear his piteous cry or his fervent prayer.* <note>original: "Tabradh nech dá uidh re n-aithnedaib Dé do dibirt cinnus déchfus ina deccraib ar Dia, 7 cindus guidhfes in Cuimdhe cumachtach inn airc no a n-éiccin, 7 cindus doclúinfi Dia a donuall nó a dibregóit."</note>

The long vowels are sometimes marked. Here and there, too, there is a valuable gloss <note>interlinear or marginal explanation</note>, for example *immídchuairt* <note>original: Ep. 94</note>, interpreted as *i. í medoncuairt* <note>meaning: "in the middle circuit"</note>. This proves the error of translating *Tech Mídchuarda* as "mead-circling house" in O'Curry's *Manners and Customs*, III. 600.

It is unnecessary to cite many of the Middle Irish corruptions <note>linguistic deviations from Old Irish forms</note> such as *lithdath* (Prologue 19), *ritroith* (28), *morrigu* (61), *riglad* for *rigrad* (278), and *dáined* for *dóine* (January 1).

The note at the end (below, page 288) regarding the number of quatrains <note>four-line stanzas</note> in the Martyrology is more accurately given below, page xvii, from the *Leabhar Breac* <note>The "Speckled Book," an important medieval Irish manuscript</note> 105, upper margin.

### E = Egerton 88.

Egerton 88, hereafter referred to as *E*, is a small-folio parchment manuscript in the British Museum. It was written by Domnall O’Davoren <note>original: O Duibh-dá-bhoireann</note> and his pupils in the latter half of the sixteenth century. Its contents are catalogued in the introduction to *Three Irish Glossaries* (London, 1862, pp. lix–lxii) and much more elaborately in S. H. O'Grady's *Catalogue of Irish Manuscripts in the British Museum* (pp. 85–141). The portion containing parts of our Martyrology is the so-called O'Davoren's Glossary (folios 80a–93a), which has been edited twice: first in the *Three Irish Glossaries* mentioned above, and secondly in the *Archive for Celtic Lexicography* <note>original: Archiv für Celtische Lexicographie</note> II. 198–504. A paper copy of this glossary (unfortunately imperfect) by Dudley MacFirbis is preserved in H. 2. 15 (a manuscript in the library of Trinity College, Dublin) and is cited here as *MacF*.

The various readings of the fragments of the Martyrology contained in O'Davoren's Glossary are generally not important; however, some are worth citing, such as *ciabtar* (Prologue 74), *o luid* (128), *ciatcois* (182), *ciarbo ligdha* (214), *menann* (285), *dodonfairci* (January 26), *Ain* (January 29), *armuinnter* (September 2), *atroeris* (December 16), *a lere* (December 20), *decmaic* (Epilogue 172), and *ciabdar bailc a mbresa*—"though mighty were their battles" (Prologue 75)—which may be the true reading. We may also cite *Domrairbera* (Epilogue 65), *ro drebraing* (August 26), and *cachain* (December 8).

### F = The Franciscan Manuscript.

This is a beautifully written parchment manuscript in small folio. It was formerly at Louvain <note>in modern-day Belgium</note>, where it was used by Father John Colgan, author of the *Acts of the Irish Saints* <note>original: Acta Sanctorum Hiberniae, published in Louvain, 1645</note>. It was afterwards kept in the Irish monastery in Rome and is now in the Franciscan monastery at Merchants' Quay, Dublin. It contains ninety-nine pages in double columns. Long vowels are rarely marked, but the aspirated <note>original: infected</note> consonants *g, d,* and *b* are often furnished with a sign.

# DESCRIPTION OF THE MANUSCRIPTS.

The scribe's note at the end of the epilogue is difficult to read, but it seems to say:
"It ends, amen, it ends. I, Rory O'Luinin <note>original: Ruaidhri hua Luinin</note>, son of Matthew, son of S...h Luinin, wrote this calendar <note>original: feilire</note> for the son of Maguire (?)—that is, for Cathal the Younger, son of Cathal, son of Gilla Patrick, the victualler <note>term: victualler; a provider of food and supplies</note> of the synod."

Therefore, the manuscript appears to have been written by Rory O'Luinin for Cathal Maguire, a canon of Armagh and Dean of Clogher, who died in 1470, and is referred to here as the "victualler of the synod."

Manuscript F provides some good readings <note>referring to specific linguistic forms or word choices in the text</note>, such as: *andorogbus* (Prologue 18), *a ngretha* (154), *bertair* (175), *Noois* (184), *tathunn* (217), *thuirter* (230), *doine* (340), *estecht* (Jan. 8, 19), *nad cumscaigset* (Feb. 6), *retglaind* (March 3), *airdirc* (March 21), *feil in tSincill* (26), *Pollionis*, *rindnim* (May 29), *dodafarnaic* (June 10), *Oendruim* (23), *Albbae* (25), *noib* (Aug. 12), *dorime* (Sep. 5), *arsil* (29), *frem* (Oct. 10), *coair* (26), *rerta* (Dec. 26, likely intended as *rerthae*), *atnecham* (Dec. 26), and *fomruirmius* (Epilogue 38). 

However, it also contains some exceedingly poor readings, such as: *righaib* (Prologue 52), *sluinnfet* (320), *rochaemhnacar* (Jan. 4), *snaithsium* (Jan. 30), *Pauli* (Feb. 19), *cinn indis* (27), *crich* (28), *lighaib* (March 30), *bladach* (April 7), *Epectini* (May 23), *toirm* (July 7), *Aplenoir* (22), *Lumbus* (29), *concatail* (Aug. 8), *Agatha* (30), *sotbotha* (Nov. 15), *diruirmisem* (Epilogue 6), *riagail* (32), *rorach* (129), *roguide* (364), *coisced* (393), *firt* (534), and *promsat*, *lobsat* (Epilogue 219, 220).

Manuscript F is heavily annotated with interlinear explanations <note>term: glossed; provided with brief explanatory notes</note> and contains numerous scholarly commentaries <note>term: scholia; ancient or medieval grammatical, critical, or explanatory notes</note>. Most of these agree in substance with those in the other manuscripts. Others, added with the phrase "on this day" <note>original: in hoc die</note> at the end of the entry, provide the names of certain saints omitted by Oengus. Because of these additions, this copy is called by Colgan "The Augmented Oengus" <note>original: Aengusius auctus</note>, and it seems to have been used extensively by the compilers of the *Martyrology of Donegal*.

->*H* = *H*. 3. 18.<-

This is a collection of manuscripts in the library of Trinity College Dublin, where it is (or was recently) marked H. 3. 18. These manuscripts are of various dates and sizes and are now divided into two parts: Part I contains pages 1–457, and Part II contains pages 458–875. It formerly belonged to Edward Lhuyd, the author of the *Archaeologia Britannica* (Oxford, 1707). The page numbers are in his handwriting, and two Welsh notes by him on pages 459 and 585 record the dates when he purchased parts of the collection.

->L = Laud 610.<-

This is a double-columned parchment folio in the Bodleian Library. ## DESCRIPTION OF THE MANUSCRIPTS.

The diverse contents of the codex <note>original: "codex"; a manuscript volume</note> are described by Dr. Todd (*Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy II. 336*) and Dr. O’Donovan (*Book of Rights, Dublin, 1847, pp. xxviii–xxxiii*). The date (1453) and one of the scribes’ names are mentioned in the concluding note <note>original: "colophon"</note> to the fragment of *Cormac’s Glossary* contained in folios 79ª–86ª:

> This is the year of the Lord when this little glossary of the Psalter [of Cashel] was written: namely, one thousand years, four hundred years, thirteen years, and two score [1453]; the fifth day of the month of February and the eighth day of the moon. I am Yellow John O’Clery <note>original: "Seaan Buidhi ó Cléirig"</note> who wrote it; and for Edmund Butler, son of Richard <note>original: "Émann Bvillter mac Risterd"</note>, this little glossary of Cormac’s Psalter has been written. <note>original: "IS hé annala in Tigerna..."</note>

The history of the manuscript is continued by the following entry on the lower margin of folio 110ᵇ:

> This Psalter was the Psalter of Mac Richard Butler, namely Edmund Butler, until the defeat at Baile in Phoill <margin>Now Piltown in the county of Kilkenny. The battle was fought in 1462, and there is an account of it, by Dubhaltach Mac Firbisigh, in the *Miscellany of the Irish Archaeological Society*, p. 247.</margin> was inflicted on the Earl of Ormond and on Mac Richard by the Earl of Desmond <margin>The eighth Earl, who was beheaded at Drogheda in 1467. He was, according to the O’Clerys, ‘learned in Latin, English, and ancient Irish writings.’</margin>, namely Thomas. And this book and the *Book of the Rock* were taken as a ransom for Mac Richard; and it is that Mac Richard who had these books written for himself, and kept them until Thomas, Earl of Desmond, took them away. <note>original: "Salttair maic Ruisderd Buitiler..."</note>

“Thus,” says Dr. Todd (*Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy, Dublin, 1841, p. 338*), “it appears that this book and the *Book of Carrick* (now unknown) were in the fifteenth century considered a sufficient ransom for the person of a great chieftain—a remarkable proof of the preservation of a love of literature among the native Irish nobles in the midst of all their war and faction at that period.”

The following corruptions in the prologue were probably due to a fifteenth-century scribe:
Prologue line 28, *ra reith*; 87, *fororcnaít*; 38, *ro tinmit*; 47, *sonnad*; 50, *forthren*; 52, 330, *rig*; 54, *na sluaig*; 57, *rodan ort-sam*; 67, *arrochur*; 80, *membraid*; 91, *dorossa*; 143, *diafromam*; 186, *madaronaib*; 194, *mairit*; 201, *decais*; 231, *bithtrogaid*; 241, *dochingecht*; 247, *atuelat*; 262 *dilse*; 315, *nondlomaim*; 336, *fili*. The blunders *membraid* (Prologue 80) and *ma daronaib* (Prologue 186) seem to show that the scribe here copied from a manuscript in which the letters *b* and *d* were nearly identical in appearance.

Similarly, in the body of the poem and in the epilogue, we find Middle Irish <note>The stage of the Irish language used roughly between 900–1200 AD.</note> corruptions in *snadug* (January 21; Old Irish: *snádud*), *rofortad* (May 27; Old Irish: *dorortad*), *da primfeil* (May 31), *rosdail* (July 15), *arslaig* (September 29), *adorthair* (November 23), *rusfuc* (December 14), *biam* (Epilogue 165), and *ro herais* (Epilogue 474).

On the other hand, the scribe has preserved old and sound readings in the following instances: *andorogbus* (Prologue 18); *imrordus* (20); *biasta* (41); *ro uctha* (45); *morrig* (61); *dorogra* (112); *ro scáich* (121); *isliu* (153); *niptá* (185); *tathund* (217); *colléce* (239); and *fris'reith* (302). The same is true for *estecht* (January 19, 22), *damair* (February 16), *gene* (genitive singular, February 26), *forcennal* (February 28, April 30), *di* (read as *dí*, March 3), *ronn-ain* (April 22, October 29), *Trifonia* (October 18), *lasn-ort* (October 22), *geguin* (October 23), *troethsus* (November 16), *geisi* (read as *gessi*, December 2), *dosruimdemar* (Epilogue 6), *dodigset* (24), *conidnaicert* (105), *doragat* (115), *nogessed* (217), *adodpart* (269), and *atonididma* (494). Note, also, the preservation of the distinction between the non-relative infixed pronoun in *fo-m-gluaisi* and the relative pronoun in *fo-dom-gluaisi* (Epilogue 376, 377).

->*LB = Lebar Brecc*<-

The *Lebar Brecc*, or "Speckled Book," is a massive manuscript now held in the library of the Royal Irish Academy. It was compiled in the fourteenth century by the Mac Egan family of Dún Doighre (now Duniry, in County Galway). An account of its contents—though marred by mistakes in both Latin and Irish¹—is included in the introduction to the lithographic facsimile <note>An exact copy or reproduction of a manuscript.</note> published in 1876. A shorter but superior catalog can be found on pages 36–40 of Dr. Atkinson’s *Passions and Homilies* (Dublin, 1887). The copy of the Martyrology contained within it begins on page 75 of the facsimile and ends on page 106. There is also a photolithograph of the page containing the start of the prologue in the *National Manuscripts of Ireland*, Part III, Number 28. In this manuscript, long vowels are rarely marked, and the "infected" <note>lenited or softened consonants</note> *g*, *d*, and *b* are never specifically indicated. The Dominical letter <note>A letter used to determine the day of the week for any given date in the calendar year.</note> and the day of the month (using Roman notation) are written in the margin next to the first line of each quatrain <note>A four-line stanza of poetry.</note> (see Prologue 305, 335).

¹ See *Celtic Review* <note>original: *Revue Celtique*</note>, volume III, page 274.

# DESCRIPTION OF THE MANUSCRIPTS.

And in the upper margin of page 105 is the following note regarding the number of quatrains <note>original: "quatrains" — four-line stanzas</note> in the *Martyrology of Oengus*:

<note>original Irish: "A coic .lx. ar .ccc.aib hi curp in fhelire feisin ocus a se 7 oenfiche dec ina da brolaig, conid a hoen dec 7 cethri fichit 7 .u. cét insin uile .7rl."</note>
"Three hundred and sixty-five in the body of the Martyrology itself, and six and eleven score (226) in the two prologues, so that the total is eleven and fourscore and five hundred (365 + 226 = 591)."

The *Leabhar Breac* (LB) is enriched with copious glosses <note>interlinear or marginal explanations</note> and scholia <note>ancient grammatical or explanatory notes</note>, which are printed in the first edition of this Martyrology. However, although it is the oldest in date of all the manuscripts, it deviates the most from the archetype <note>the original source text from which others are copied</note>. Thus, in the prologue we find:

line 5, *romberthar* for *fordomberthar*; 28, *ritroich* for *ro rãith*; 57, *afirthuillem* for *ar firthuillem*; 60, *cenes marsium* for *cen aes muirsium*; 61, *Morrigu nangennli* for *Mórrig inna ngente*; 90, *gerait* for *gérat*; 99, 109, *noemainim*; *Næmainim* for *nóebainm*; 130, *andún* for *a dún*; 135, *nocon* for *nicon*; 146, *dianit* for *dia mbí* (or *dianid*?); 156, *na betha* for *na mbethae*; 157, 161, *hi táimne* for *hi táam*; 164, *ro pritcha* for *ro phraidchi*; 176, *ni trebthair* for *ni trebtar*; 188, *ni bet* for *ni beth*; 201, *déchaid* for *décaid*; 206, *imaroraid* for *immaroerad*; 210, *co ndessib is tririb* for *déssib ocus tririb*; 217, *Tathum* for *Táthunn*; 228, *icthar* for *icthair* or *iccthair*; 230, 232, *thrétha, gértha* for *thréta, gréta*; 240, *slebti* for *slébe*; 243, *combair* for *cobair*; 251, *Muire* for *Máiri*; 271, *robeosa* for *ro bithbeo*; 282, *cení clúinter* for *ce ro-clúnter*; 285, *rimther* for *rimter*; 297, *for crindither* for *for crinniur*; 300, *sluinnfet* for *sloindfith*; 302, *frisraith* for *fris’reith*.

[May, p. 87.]
The sixth month among the Greeks is *Arthemisios* <note>original: Ἄρτεμίσιος</note>.
May admires the horns of the Bull of Agenor <note>original: *Maius Agenorei miratur cornua Tauri*. This refers to the zodiac sign Taurus; in mythology, Jupiter took the form of a bull to carry away Europa, the daughter of Agenor.</note>.

[June, p. 89.]
The seventh month according to the Greeks is *Deseos* <note>original: Δαίσιος</note>.
The Sun has 30 days, the Moon 29.
June sees the Spartan twins <note>original: *Laconas*. This refers to the constellation Gemini, the twins Castor and Pollux, who were from Laconia/Sparta.</note> rise in the sky.
The third month of the Hebrews is Sivan.

[July, p. 91.]
The eighth month among the Greeks is *Panemos* <note>original: Πάνημος</note>.
The Sun has 31 days, the Moon 30.
July brings the star of the burning Crab <note>original: *Cancri*. The zodiac sign Cancer.</note> at the solstice.
The fourth month of the Hebrews is Tammuz.

[August, p. 93.]
The ninth month according to the Greeks is *Los* <note>original: Λῶος</note>.
The Sun has 31 days, the Moon 29.
The Lion, glowing with fire, scorches the month of August <note>original: *Leo*. The zodiac sign Leo.</note>.
The fifth month of the Hebrews is Thamni <note>original: *sic*. Likely a scribal error for the month of Av.</note>.

[September, p. 95.]
The tenth month among the Greeks is *Gorpiaios* <note>original: Γορπιαῖος; transcribed in the manuscript as Sgorpeos</note>.
There are no Kalends, no Nones, and no Ides among the Greeks and the Egyptians <note>original: *Cen kalne cen nona cen idu ic Grecaib 7 ic Egeptacdaib*. This is an Old Irish translation of the Latin note below.</note>.
The Sun has 30 days, the Moon 30.
September enriches the wine-harvest <note>original: *Bacchum*. Bacchus was the god of wine.</note> under your sign, O Virgin <note>original: *Virgo*. The zodiac sign Virgo.</note>.
The sixth month of the Hebrews is Elul.

[October, p. 97.]
The eleventh month among the Greeks is *Hyperberetaios* <note>original: Ὑπερβερεταῖος</note>.
October also balances the Scales <note>original: *Libram*. The zodiac sign Libra.</note> at the time of sowing.
The seventh month of the Hebrews is Tishrei.
The Sun has 31 days, the Moon 29.

[November, p. 99.]
The twelfth month among the Greeks is *Dios* <note>original: Διός</note>. November.
The Sun has 30 days, the Moon 30.
The Scorpion <note>original: *Scorpius*. The zodiac sign Scorpio.</note> commands wintry November to go headlong.
The eighth month of the Hebrews is Marheshvan.

# PREFACE.

[December, p. 101.]

This is the first month of the year among the Greeks, named Apilios <note>original Latin: *Hic est primus mensis anni apud Graecos nomine Apilios*</note> ['Απελλαῖος], who calculate their months according to the course of the sun.
The ninth month of the Hebrews is Kislev <note>original Latin: *Nonus mensis Ebreorum Casleu*</note>.
The Archer <note>original Latin: *Arcitinens*; referring to the zodiac sign Sagittarius</note> ends his signs in the middle of December <note>original Latin: *Terminat Arcitinens medio sua signa Decimbri*</note>.

->P = 23<-
->P. 3<-

This is a small folio parchment manuscript in the library of the Royal Irish Academy, now containing eleven leaves. The epilogue is written in double columns. In the rest of the poem, each quatrain <term>quatrain</term> <note>a stanza of four lines</note> runs, as a rule, in a single line across the page. The Martyrology is followed by a copy of the legend telling how Becán son of Cúla, St. Patrick's first convert, rescued Bresal's soul from hell (*Lismore Lives, xxvii–xxviii*). Then comes the colophon <term>colophon</term> <note>a statement at the end of a manuscript giving details about its production</note>:

> This is the age of the Lord: one thousand, four hundred, sixty and seven years. G is the Sunday letter and eight is the golden number. William, son of the physician, who wrote this, [prays that] he will die a good death. <note>original Irish/Latin: *ISsed is ais don Tigerna i. secht mbliadna 7 tri .xx. G an liter domhnaigh 7 a hocht in nuimir óir. Uilliam mac an legha qui scribsit [ut] bona morte peribit.*</note>

From this, it appears that the manuscript was written by William mac an legha <note>meaning "son of the physician" or "son of the leech"</note> in the year 1467, the Dominical letter <note>a method for calculating the day of the week for any given date</note> being G, and the golden number <note>used to determine the date of Easter</note> being eight. The prose preface and prologue are missing in this manuscript, as are the quatrains for the months of May, September, and December. The glosses <term>glosses</term> <note>brief explanatory notes</note> are written between the lines; the scholia <term>scholia</term> <note>longer explanatory comments or ancient commentary</note> are for the most part in the lower margins. Long vowels are often marked with accents.

A characteristic of manuscript *P* is the scribe's tendency to write *ld* instead of *ll*—as in *holdmuir* (Feb. 17), *Teilde* (June 25), *nold* (Aug. 8), and *celd* (Oct. 12 note)—and to use *nd* or *nn* for *n*—as in *ind-air* (Feb. 13), *Seirnd* (March 15), *ind amsir* (Epistle 116), *cond-aile* (Feb. 18), *cond huaige* (June 18), *Conningin* (March 8), and *ind n-airnecht* (Aug. 3). He sometimes uses *oi* instead of *ai*, as in *coin* (March 13, Oct. 10) and *moinich* (Oct. 27), which equals *cáin* in manuscript *L*. He writes *d* for *t* in names like *Padraicc* (Patrick) and *Pedair* (Peter), and in the word *adfed*. He uses *d* for *g* in *blod*, and *th* for *h* in *ingina thuage* (June 5). The spelling *Custatin* (for *Constantin*) on March 11 is noteworthy. Other notable spellings include *Faleran* (Aug. 11), *in* for *an* ("their") on July 17, *ir-rúamson* (for *ar-rúamsom*) on Oct. 28, and *landlech* (for *landrech*) on July 28.

Accurate readings found in manuscript *P* include *tar* (Feb. 13), *dobeir* (March 31), *nad* (April 9), *Ronnain* (April 22, Aug. 28), and *cimbith* (April 26, Aug. 14).

->R¹ = Rawlinson B. 505.<-

**R¹.** This is a parchment manuscript in folio <note>a large book format made by folding sheets of paper or parchment once</note> from the beginning of the
fifteenth century, preserved in the Bodleian Library and marked
Rawlinson B. 505. It contains 220 leaves. Its chief contents
are an incomplete copy of Jocelin's *Life of Saint Patrick* and the
Latin lives of thirty-eight other saints—one Welsh (Saint David,
folio 196) and the rest Irish.¹ The main body of the Martyrology begins
at folio 211 and ends at folio 220. There is a poor facsimile of
part of the four-line stanza <note>original: "quatrain"</note> for January 1 in O'Conor's *Irish Scriptural Writers* <note>original: "Rer. Hib. Scriptores"</note>,
volume 1, prologue, part 2, page 144, table 6, number 4. Although the
prose preface, prologue, and epilogue are missing, this copy is, so
far as it goes, by far the best that has survived.
For instance, the names of foreign saints are generally given with
exceptional correctness. For example:

A less admirable characteristic of R¹ is the scribe's fondness for "irrational" vowels <note>vowels added between consonants that were not originally there</note>. Thus we find *adabal* (June 26), *aidbile* (March 26), *Aperil* (March 27), *carann* (March 10), and *Librén* (March 11), respectively for the standard forms *adbul, aidble, April, crann,* and *Librén*. He rarely marks long vowels and never denotes "infected" <term>lenited</term> *g, d,* or *b*. He writes *l* instead of *r* in *damail* (Feb. 16) and *coclait* (Dec. 24), and *r* instead of *l* in *creir* (Aug. 16) and *tempuir* (Dec. 15).

Each quatrain <note>a four-line stanza</note> in R¹ is, as a rule, contained in a single line extending across the page. The <gloss>glosses</gloss> <note>brief explanatory notes</note> are, as usual, written between the lines. The <gloss>scholia</gloss> <note>longer explanatory comments or historical notes</note> are for the most part grouped together at the end of each month. They are rarely found in the margins or above the lines.

Folios 5–30 contain the older copy of the *Tripartite Life of St. Patrick*. The other contents of this <term>codex</term> <note>an ancient manuscript in book form</note> are catalogued in the introduction to the Rolls edition of that *Life*, pages xiv–xlv. at folio 59a <note>original: fo. 59ª</note>. The poem commences at folio 53b, but breaks off at line 60 of the prologue. At folio 54a begins the epilogue, and it ends at folio 56b. The seven succeeding folios from 57a to 64a are filled with notes on the body of the Martyrology, which unfortunately is missing in this manuscript.

The scribe's name was Dubthach O'Duibgennan, as appears from the following notes, which are in the same handwriting:

Folio 64b. . . . "Here for Gerald 'the Fane' <note>original: an Fáni</note>, son of George, for whom I have written this preface to the Martyrology <note>original: Feliri</note>. And may all the saints that Oengus has enumerated here be helping us both! I and Gerald, the vesper-time of the festival of Mary of the Salutation <note>Lady Day in spring, March 25</note> overtaking us. And may Mary and the saints of this book leave us their portion of delight, for we have not found [our] reward [yesterday] in Athboy <note>original: Baile Atha Buidi</note>. And let everyone who shall read this book bestow a blessing on the soul of the scribe. In the year 1500 of the Lord's age."

Folio 73a: "I am Dubthach O'Duibgennan who has copied the verse <note>original: rann</note> for Conchobar O'Maelchonairi, for his cousin, out of Gerald 'the Fane's' book; and we are waiting to ask a favor of Mac B. . .nan's daughter, the wife of O'Conor Roe. And may God grant that she gives that to us!"

The manuscript shows a tendency to use *ea* for *e*: *seacht* <note>seven</note> Prologue 2, *sealgatar* <note>they struck</note> Prologue 29, *do sealba* <note>of possessions</note> Epilogue 4, *ceacha* <note>each</note> Epilogue 5, *ronseart* <note>has strengthened us</note> Epilogue 11, *rofeas* <note>it was known</note> Epilogue 17, *beannacht* <note>blessing</note> Epilogue 66, *leathna* <note>broad</note> Epilogue 82, *teacht* <note>coming</note> Prologue 31. It uses *a* for *u*: *surna* (for Old Irish *surnu*, <note>furnaces</note>) Prologue 44, *ingra dindgna* (for *ingru dindgnu*, <note>wretched hills</note>) Epilogue 119, *echta* (for *lechtu*, <note>graves</note>) Epilogue 146, *noeba* (for *noebu*, <note>saints</note>) Epilogue 470. It uses *a* for *i*: *am* (for *im*, <note>about</note>) Epilogue 126, and *an* for *in* <note>the</note> Epilogue 130. It uses *d* for *t*: *coméd* <note>keeping</note> Prologue 6, *fodaimdis* <note>they used to suffer</note> Prologue 51, *ada-n* Epilogue 34. *Pedar* <note>Peter</note> 535. Long vowels are rarely marked; the "infected" or aspirated *d* appears only once.

Corruptions like *diultadach* <note>denying</note> Epilogue 371, *frisioirg* <note>he offends</note> Epilogue 444, and *doragsat* <note>they will come</note> Epilogue 115 are found in this copy. However, old forms are occasionally preserved—for example, *(a)slaige* <note>temptation</note> Epilogue 198, *no molur* <note>I praise</note> Prologue 13, and *r(o)raith* <note>he ran</note> Prologue 28—where other manuscripts have the corrupt forms *aslaigi, romolur, ra reith*. Similarly, in *laigne* <note>spears</note> Epilogue 324, *geinech* <note>genealogical</note> Epilogue 538, and *frisailiur* <note>I expect</note> Epilogue 560, the R² manuscript comes closer than the others to the <term>archetype</term> <note>the original manuscript from which others were copied</note>, which must have originally contained *laignea, genech, frisáiliur*.

## II. THE AUTHOR OF THE MARTYROLOGY.

Little that can fairly be called historical is known about the author of our Martyrology. The sources of the traditions concerning him are the Irish prefaces (two of which are printed and translated below, pages 2–14); the *Book of Leinster*, page 370ᶜ, where he is mentioned as one of the fraternity of Maelruain of Tallaght; the *Martyrology of Tallaght*, at March 11, where he is called a bishop and the grandson of Oiblén; and the following poem in the *Lebar Brecc* <note>The Speckled Book</note>, page 106ᵇ, which appears immediately after the epilogue to the *Martyrology of Oengus*:

1. Delightful is the seat here indeed, by the side of the cold-pure Nore;
Though it was full of troops, it was not a path of plunder, in victorious Dísert Bethech.
2. Dísert Bethech, where the man stayed to whom hosts of angels used to come;
A religious city with a circuit of crosses, where Oengus, son of Oiblén, used to be.
3. Oengus from the assembly of heaven, here is his tomb and his grave;
It is from here he went to death, on Friday to holy heaven.
4. It was in Cluain Eidnech he was reared; in Cluain Eidnech he was buried;
In Cluain Eidnech of many crosses, he read his psalms at first.
5. Oengus in a prison of restraint, by the will of the Son of God in Tallaght;
The vigorous life was not his, in the kiln while drying grain.
6. A hard measure of grain he had, while grinding seed, before anyone in the land had risen;
Three fifty psalms—a bright fulfillment—and three hundred prostrations every night.

### Modernized Translation.

1. It is delightful to sit here like this, by the side of the cold, pure River Nore: though it was once filled with troops, there was no path for violent raids in the gifted *Disert Bethech* ("The Birchen Hermitage").
2. *Disert Bethech* was the dwelling of the man whom hosts of angels used to visit; it was a pious cloister protected by a circle of crosses, where Oengus, son of Oibléen, used to reside.
3. Oengus of the assembly of heaven—here are his tomb and his bed: and from here he went through death on a Friday unto holy heaven.
4. It was in *Cluain Eidnech* <note>Clonenagh, Co. Laois</note> that he was reared; in *Cluain Eidnech* he was buried; and in *Cluain Eidnech* of the many crosses he first studied his psalms.
5. Oengus lived in a prison of bondage by the will of God’s Son in Tallaght: that was no life of ease, drying corn in the kiln.
6. Before anyone else arose in the country, he carried a heavy sack for grinding seeds; he recited the one hundred and fifty psalms—a clear fulfillment of his vows—and performed three hundred genuflections <note>term: ritual kneeling or bowing</note> every night.
7. Greenish corn-blades grew through the hair of his head, and a covering of hair grew over his body: for seven years he endured this godly fasting, without music and without rest.
8. He drank no ale from a cup, Oengus—who was God's "chosen wheat" <note>original: *tuirnd*; the author notes this refers to a saint</note>: often his face changed color, exposed to the wind and the dust of winnowing chaff.
9. He went one day to cut wood, Oengus the flame of Bregia: while lopping the wood—a tale of beauty—he accidentally struck off his "Gospel-hand" <note>original: *láim soscela*; his right hand. The author suggests Oengus may have been left-handed as he struck his right hand while working</note>.

10. Then the noble birds wailed sorrowfully: around the noble one, around the abbot, they cried a cry greater than any cry.

Hence, the kernel of fact in the traditional biography of Oengus may be shortly stated as follows: He was the son of Oengoba and a grandson of Oibléan. He was a contemporary of Aed Ordnigthe, the High King of Ireland from the year 793 to 817; of Fothuth of the Canon (who flourished around 804); and of Connmach, the bishop of Armagh (who died in 806). 

He became a monk in the monastery of Clonenagh on the banks of the River Nore in Queen's County <note>modern County Laois</note>. He afterwards joined the community of Tallaght near Dublin, which was then presided over by Saint Maelruain, who died in 787 and whom Oengus commemorates on August 11. Out of humility, he concealed his name, his holy orders, and his scholarly attainments; for some time, he was employed in kiln-drying, grinding corn, and cutting wood. 

He began his *Martyrology* <term>a catalog or list of Christian martyrs and saints arranged by their feast days</term> at Clonenagh, finished it in Tallaght, and showed it to Fothuth in 804. He afterwards became an abbot and a bishop, though likely a missionary bishop without a specific diocese. He died on a Friday and was buried at Clonenagh. His feast day <note>original: obitual day</note> is March 11, but the year of his death is unknown. It may have been 819, 824, or 830, as the eleventh of March fell on a Friday in each of those years.

Whether Oengus, son of Oengoba, was a <term>culdee</term> <note>original: "céle Dé"; a member of an ascetic spiritual order in the early Irish and Scottish churches</note> is a little doubtful. He certainly speaks of himself as *bochtán* ‘a pauper’ (Epistle 392), and as *pauperán trílagsa* ‘this wretched mendicant’ (Epistle 408), which points to membership in a society bound by obligations of poverty. Moreover, “the title,” says Dr. Reeves, “by which he is invariably designated is that of *Céle Dé*.” But he is not so styled in the Irish prefaces to the Martyrologies of Oengus and Gorman. In the Book of Leinster 354ᶜ 22 and the Lebar Brecc 23ᵃ 34 (where two lines of the Martyrology of Oengus are cited), the author is simply called Oengus hua Oibleain, or Aengus hua Oibleni. So in the manuscript Rawlinson B. 512, folio 94ᵃ, he is called merely Oengus mac Oiblen. This is also the case in the title to the Brussels copy of the Martyrology of Tallaght: “Here begins the Martyrology of Oengus, son of Oiblen, and Maelruain” <note>original: "Incipit Martira Oenghuis maic Oiblein 7 Maelruain (h)íc"</note>. In the body of that martyrology, he is called a bishop.

In fact, down to the seventeenth century, when the Martyrology of Donegal was compiled, our Oengus is never described as a *Céle Dé*. The “Oengus Celi-dé” to whom the *Saltair na Rann*—a poem from the end of the tenth century—is attributed in a twelfth-century manuscript, cannot possibly have been our Oengus, the grandson of Oiblen. Since the seventeenth century, he has, no doubt, been called by Colgan,¹ Lanigan,² and others, a *céle Dé* or <term>culdee</term>. This perhaps is all that Dr. Reeves meant to say, and, in accordance with current practice, Oengus is so styled on the title page of the present work.

What, then, is a <term>culdee</term>? The earliest instances of the use of the term *céle Dé*,³ literally “servant of God” <note>original: "servus Dei"</note>,⁴ are in the *Life of Saint Findan* <note>original: "Vita S. Findani"</note> and in the Milan gloss 30ᶜ 3, where it has no specific ecclesiastical significance. In Middle-Irish manuscripts, it is applied to foreign monks,⁵ to religious Irishmen practicing poverty,⁶ and even to the ascetic Indian Brahmans.⁷ Ultimately, the plural *céli Dé* denoted a kind of secular canons, who occupied—

### III. THE LANGUAGE OF THE MARTYROLOGY.

We have now to consider the characteristics of the language of the Martyrology, especially as bearing on the date of its composition. In the first edition, the following forms were cited as proving that the language was Early Middle-Irish, and that the Martyrology could not have been composed “much before the end of the tenth century.”

<term>nair</term> (January 8) was taken to be the Old Irish adverb <term>anair</term> with a Middle-Irish aphaeresis <note>the loss of a sound at the beginning of a word</note> of *a*. But it is actually for <term>náir</term>, the genitive singular masculine of the adjective <term>nár</term> ‘high,’ ‘noble.’

<term>na mbuidnib</term> (Epilogue 295) was taken to be for Old Irish <term>inna m-buidnib</term> ‘in their bands.’ But the true reading, preserved by manuscript P, is <term>hi mbuidnib</term> ‘in bands.’

<term>in gáir</term> (October 20) and <term>in togu</term> (Prologue 123) were supposed to be instances of the Middle-Irish disuse of the neuter article. But the true readings are <term>a ngáir</term> and <term>a togu</term>, the substitution of which leaves the poetic metre intact.

<term>inna</term> and <term>na</term> for the nominative plural masculine of the article were regarded as exclusively Middle-Irish. But they occur in the Old-Irish manuscripts Ml. 38c 9, 38c 8, 10, and Wb. 29a 16a: see below p. 338, under the word <term>ind</term>.

<term>hua</term> (June 21) is monosyllabic in the line <term>hua Liathain in ligach</term>. But the line should be corrected to <term>haue Liatháin ligach</term>, where <term>haue</term> is, as in Old-Irish, disyllabic <note>pronounced as two syllables</note>.

<term>cethri chét</term> and <term>ceithri deich</term> (September 1, October 16, 24) are probably mere corruptions of the Old-Irish <term>cethir chét</term> and <term>cethir deich</term>. Similarly, the accusative plural used for the nominative plural in <term>na rét(g)lanna</term> (July 29) and <term>tengtha</term> (Epilogue 125) might have been quoted as Middle-Irishisms; but the corrections <term>inna rétglann</term> and <term>tengaid</term> are obvious.

The proleptic <note>anticipatory</note> use of the possessive pronoun at July 17 (<term>a n-itge</term>)...

which I supposed to be only Middle Irish <note>The stage of the Irish language from roughly 900–1200 AD.</note>, is found in the Würzburg Glosses 8ᵈ 22 (*his shortness*) and 18ᶜ 6 (*his speed*).

The occurrence of the following verbal forms was also regarded as pointing to the tenth or eleventh century:
* *bebaís* "he died," Prologue 95, Feb. 18, April 23, was taken to be a Middle Irish formation from the Old Irish reduplicated preterite <note>A past tense form created by repeating a syllable.</note> *bebe*. But it is a regular s-preterite from a reduplicated verb corresponding with the Greek *bibdo* <note>original: βίβδω</note>, *bibemi* <note>original: βίβημι</note> and Sanskrit *jigāti*, and is used here euphemistically.
* *dorimemar*, Epilogue 6, was taken to be a Middle Irish 1st person plural preterite of the verb *dorímiu* (I reckon), which, in Old Irish, would be *dorúirmisem*. But the true reading is preserved in the manuscripts *L* and *P*, namely *do-ruimdemar*, a regular formation from the deponent verb <note>A verb with passive forms but active meaning.</note> *do-mídiur* (we have estimated).
* *conicsid*, Epilogue 393, is obviously a scribal corruption of the Old Irish *conissid* (you can).
* *berthair*, *trebthair*, Prologue 175, 176, used for the Old Irish plurals *bertair*, *-trebtar*. The correction is easy, and in Prologue 176, manuscripts *B* and *F* have the correct *bertair*.
* *asa* "whose is," Prologue 50, 98 etc., and *ata* "whose are," March 14 etc., were supposed to be only Middle Irish formations. But *as a* occurs in the Milan Glosses 2ᶜ 3, *issa* in Milan 90ᶜ 3, and *ata-n* in Würzburg 12ᵃ 11, Milan 12ᵇ, and many other Old Irish documents.

In syntax, the use of the dative case after the preposition *itir* (between), March 11, Nov. 23, and the accusative case after the preposition *iar* (after) in the phrase *iarsin mbaigse* (after that battle), Epilogue 315, are clearly Middle Irish corruptions which may be removed without injuring the meter. At March 11, the line containing *iter* (or *eter*) is found only in three manuscripts (*LB, P*, and *C*) and is apparently a comparatively recent substitute for *isind flaith uas flaithib* (in the kingdom above kingdoms), which is the reading of manuscripts *R¹*, *L*, and *F*. In Nov. 23, though all the manuscripts have *tonnaib* (waves) in line 2 of the quatrain, this seems a scribal error due to the presence of *thonnaib* in line 4. In Epilogue 315, manuscripts *C* and *B* have preserved the true reading, namely *iarsin baigse*.

The linguistic arguments against the antiquity of the Martyrology having thus been disposed of, let us now consider some archaic forms which point to the Old Irish period, that is, the seventh, eighth, and ninth centuries.

### Disyllabism <note>The quality of having two syllables.</note>
The following words, which are monosyllables in Middle Irish, are still disyllabic in our Martyrology: *aue* (grandson) Feb. 8, April 11, June 21,¹ genitive *haui* May 16, Oct. 27; *-bía* (will be), Jan. 13, Epilogue 168; *-gliad* (of a fight), *críad* (of clay) April 19; *déac*² (ten) July 15, Sept. 22; *deud* (end), Prologue 220; *dlis* (you deserve) Sept. 13; *dia* (day) July 16, Epilogue 166; *lia* or *lie* (stone) April 15; *luam* (pilot) Dec. 3; *Noís* Prologue 84; *óac* (young) Sept.

22, *siur* <note>sister</note>, July 6, Dec. 14; *triur* <note>three persons</note> Jan. 24, Dec. 14; *coair* <note>just/proper</note> Oct. 26, Epilogue 432, 433; *doaib* <note>to them</note> Prologue 17; *triut* <note>through you</note> Epilogue 438.
In the *Leabhar Breac* <note>The "Speckled Book," a medieval Irish manuscript</note> and the *Franciscan Manuscript*, disyllabism <note>the quality of having two syllables</note> is sometimes marked by doubling a vowel, for example: *cooir, Noois, siuur, triuur*.

### Declension

As a rule, the Old Irish paradigms <note>patterns of word endings</note> are followed. However, Oengus <note>the 8th-century author of the Martyrology</note> tends to make oblique cases <note>cases other than the subject, such as possessive or object forms</note> resemble the nominative singular. Thus, the masculine o-stems *Findach* and *Nárach* have their genitive singulars as *Findach* (May 22) and *Nárach* (March 8). The same occurs with *bordgal* <note>assembly</note> (Prologue 275), *baslic* <note>basilica/church</note> (Nov. 19), and possibly *trethan* <note>sea</note> (June 5). At Feb. 12, *crochthae* <note>crucified</note> is the dative singular feminine, and in Epilogue 458, the vocative singular masculine of *rathmar* <note>gracious</note> is identical to the nominative singular of that adjective. The genitive plural of *dér* <note>tear</note> (equivalent to the Greek *dakry* <note>original: δάκρυ</note>) is *dér* (Epilogue 400). The n-stems *brú* <note>womb</note>, *Hériu* <note>Ireland</note>, *íriu* <note>land</note>, and *díle* <note>flood</note> make their dative singulars *brú* (Epilogue 464), *Hériu* (July 31), *íre* (Epilogue 25, 450), and *díle* (Epilogue 452). The dative singular of the t-stem is *bethu* <note>life</note> (Epilogue 201). The accusative singular *feli* <note>feast</note> (Oct. 2, Dec. 30) seems to come from a feminine i-stem. Stems in *u* make their genitive singular in *-o*: *locho* <note>of a lake</note> (Feb. 7, Rawlinson manuscript), *geno* <note>of a mouth</note> (Oct. 3, Rawlinson B 512); or in *-a*: *gena* (April 13, Sept. 16); *betha* <note>of life</note> (Prologue 140, 195). June 29 uses *catha* <note>of battle</note> and *datha* <note>of color</note>.

Traces of a locative singular <note>a case indicating location</note> are: *grian már des-maig Midi* <note>"a great sun on the southern plain of Meath"</note> (Prologue 226); *Senóc Mugnai tuathmaig lethain* <note>"Senóc of Mugna on the broad northern plain"</note> (Dec. 11); *ni mair in drong úabair ráith Bécce* <note>"the proud host of Bécc's fort remains not"</note> (Prologue 197-8); *ráid a paiss cinn blíadnae* <note>"say his passion at a year's end"</note> (Sept. 17); *dogné init chorgaiss* <note>"you should do it at the beginning of Lent"</note> (Nov. 13).

The adjectival i-stems make their genitive plural in *-e*, even when not used as nouns. Thus *áille* <note>of beautiful things</note> (Epilogue 83) and *mathe* <note>of good things</note> (July 23).
The nominative of the feminine numeral *teoir* ("three") occurs in Sept. 1, where it is two syllables, like *teuír* (derived from the reconstructed form *tisores*), found in *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* Vol II, p. 291.

### Comparison

The superlative form ending in *-m* survives: *amram* <note>most wonderful</note> (Sept. 24); *ardam* <note>highest</note> (March 23, Dec. 27, Epilogue 207); *deodam* <note>most divine</note> (Epilogue 498); *nóibem* <note>holiest</note> (July 14). However, the Middle Irish habit of using the comparative form for the superlative is already beginning: *amru* <note>more wonderful</note> (Aug. 20); *cádu* <note>holier/more venerable</note> (March 20); *dánu* <note>bolder</note>, *daingniu* <note>firmer</note> (May 23); *dílsíu* <note>dearer/more certain</note> (Prologue 262); *díxu* <note>higher</note> (Jan. 18); *ferdu* <note>more manly</note> (Aug. 20); *glainiu* <note>purer</note> (Prologue 246); *ísiu* <note>lower</note> (Prologue 153); *nóebu* <note>holier</note> (Jan. 20, May 27); *úagu* <note>more perfect/virginal</note> (Nov. 30); *úaisliu* <note>nobler</note> (Prologue 263, Jan. 18).

### Infixed Pronouns

The infixed pronouns <note>pronouns placed inside a verb word</note> in the Martyrology are as follows:

| Non-relative forms | Dental forms <note>Forms containing a 'd' sound</note> |
|:--------------------|:--------------|
| Singular 1st person: *m*; before a vowel *mm* | ... -*dom*- |
| Singular 2nd person: *t* | ... -*dat*- |
| Singular 3rd person masculine: *an*; after *do* and *ní*, *n* | ... -*dn*-, -*d*-, -*idn*-, -*id* |
| Singular 3rd person feminine: *a*, *s(n)* | ... -*da*- |

The dental forms <note>Pronouns containing "d" or "t" sounds</note> are regularly relative <note>Used in "who/which" clauses</note>: see for instance *ar-don-sela*, "what escapes us," June 23, and Epilogue 376, 377, where *fo-m-glúassi* means "disquiets me," but *fo-dom-glúassi* means "**what** disquiets me." However, dental forms are also used after the prefix *ad*- and some other prepositions. Thus in *atateoch-sa* (derived from *ad-dat-t*), "I entreat you" Epilogue 304, there is no relative meaning.

It is unnecessary to quote examples of the first and second persons, which are easily recognizable. The various forms of pronouns for the third person are as follows:

**Singular 3 masculine:** *an*: *n-an-ále* February 7, *ó donánic* April 14 (which should perhaps be *ó d-an-ánic*), *imm-a-curtis* April 27, *f-a-rith* Epilogue 407.

### Verbal Particles.

The verbal particles are *ad-*, *com-*, *no*, *ro* and *ror*, of which *ad*, *com* and *ro* are used as perfective prefixes <note>prefixes that indicate a completed action</note>:
*ad-*: *conatuil* (*com-ad-t-*) ‘he has slept’ August 7, *con-idn-aicert* (*com-idn-ad-cert*) ‘has corrected it.’
*com-*: *as-chom-art* ‘who has been slain,’ October 19, *do-coemnagtar* (*\*to-com-nenigtar*) ‘they have washed,’ January 4.
*no* is here used (**a**) with the imperfect indicative of simple verbs, (**b**) to infix a personal pronoun or relative *n*, and (**c**) to express relativity.¹ Examples of (**c**) are *no molur* <note>whom I praise</note> Prologue 13; *no ráidiu* <note>that I speak</note>, Epilogue 358: *no guidiu* <note>whom I pray</note> Epilogue 387, *no charim* <note>whom I love</note> Epilogue 50: *no rádi* <note>which you say</note> February 18.
*ro*: Most of the occurrences of this common particle are collected in the glossarial index. In compound verbs it stands only after a preposition: *do-ro-dbad* <note>has been destroyed</note> Prologue 96; *imma-roerad* <note>has been carried out</note> Prologue 206: *fris-rocaib* <note>has ascended</note> October 24, *fris-rocabsat* <note>they have ascended</note> January 16: *con-ruala* <note>he has gone</note> July 12, *as-r-indaid* <note>he has told</note> January 12: *do-rósat* <note>he has created</note> Prologue 91, *do-r-indnacht* <note>he has bestowed</note> November 12, *do-s-rui-mdemar* <note>we have estimated them</note> Epilogue 6. When the compound contains only one preposition: *do-rignius* <note>I have made</note> *im-ro-rdus* <note>I have meditated</note> Prologue 20; *do-rui-rmius* <note>I have recounted</note> Epilogue 40, *ad-r-annad* <note>has been kindled</note> April 5, *ad-r-eth* <note>he has attained</note> Prologue 120, *do-r-ortad* <note>has been poured out</note> May 27, *ad-roe-thach* <note>I have besought</note> Epilogue 300. It is omitted in *atbath* <note>he died</note> Epilogue 318, *tinscann* <note>he begins</note> May 1, *fo-s-dail* <note>he distributed them</note> July 15, *fo-raith* <note>he helped</note> January 15, *fo-truicset* <note>they washed</note> May 8, *fris-indled* <note>it was prepared</note> May 23, and *nad chumscaigset* <note>who did not move</note> February 6. It is prefixed to an originally compound verb in *ro-s-tuirius* <note>I have searched them</note> January 26 (compare *ru tuirset* <note>they have searched</note> Milan Glosses 44, 23).
*ror*: *fo-ror-bairt* <note>it has increased</note> Prologue 172: *fo-ror-cennta* <note>they have been ended</note> Prologue 87: *dom-ror-bae* <note>it has profited me</note> Prologue 25; and, with the assimilation of *r* to the *l* of the root, *rol-eb-laing* <note>he has leaped</note> March 5.

### Conjugation.

In the verb, the Old Irish distinction between the absolute and the conjunct forms is invariably preserved. <note>Absolute forms are used when the verb stands alone; conjunct forms are used when the verb is preceded by a particle or preposition.</note> Thus in the 3rd person singular present indicative active we find the following absolute forms:
*maraid* <note>remains</note> Prologue 168, 204, 244, 252, *bith-maraid* <note>always remains</note> 232, 255. *moraith* <note>magnifies</note> 116, *bith-trágaith* <note>always ebbs</note> 231; and with affixed pronouns, *berth-i* <note>he takes it</note> Epilogue 196, *mórth-us* <note>he magnifies them</note> Prologue 132,
and the following conjunct forms:
I. *o-verbs*: *ní mair* <note>does not remain</note> Prologue 199, 203; *ní dlig* <note>does not deserve</note> January 6, *na dlig* <note>who does not deserve</note> March 7,

## THE LANGUAGE OF THE MARTYROLOGY.

<note>This section lists specific Old Irish verb forms found in the text, categorized by their grammatical class. The dates and abbreviations (e.g., Prol. for Prologue, Ep. for Epilogue) refer to where these words appear in the Martyrology.</note>

**I. Class 1 Verbs:**
April 25, *ar-dlig* <note>deserves</note>; June 1, August 5, *ní beir* <note>does not carry</note>; Prologue 223, *do-beir* <note>gives/brings</note>; March 31, November 30, *con-gaib* <note>contains/holds</note>; April 1, Epilogue 76, 279, *tuar-gaib* <note>raises up</note>; March 15, *ar-fich* <note>fights/vanquishes</note>; Epilogue 195, 206, *do-for-maig* <note>increases</note>; October 18, *do-n-for-maig* <note>increases us</note>; July 9, *mos-t-ic* <note>soon comes</note>; May 25, *to-t-ic* <note>comes to you</note>; July 19, *t-ar-ic*¹ <note>comes/arrives</note>; Prologue 302, *fris-reith* <note>runs against</note>; Epilogue 444, *fris-oirg* <note>offends/strikes</note>; April 16, *do-reith* <note>runs/hastens</note>.

**II. ā-verbs:**
February 23, *ad-idn-gialla* <note>who serves him</note>; June 23, *ar-don-sela* <note>who saves us</note>; July 31, *for-tn-iada* <note>which closes it</note>; November 15, *fo-t-botha* <note>which terrifies you</note>; Epilogue 178, *ar-id-léga* <note>who reads it</note>; Epilogue 102, *fo-d-fúasna* <note>which disturbs it</note>; Epilogue 282, *for-cenna* <note>ends/terminates</note>; June 21, November 29, *bruchta* <note>belches/bursts forth</note>.

**III. i-verbs:**
Prologue 110, *at-sluindi* <note>names/proclaims</note>; January 26, *do-don-farci* <note>who looks down upon us</note>; May 12, October 25, *don-ascnai* <note>who visits us</note>; June 29, *ni-s-tarcai* <note>does not surpass them</note>; July 9, *nond-áli* <note>who entreats him</note>; Epilogue 374, *ar-dom-túassi* <note>who listens to me</note>; Epilogue 376, *fo-dom-glúassi* <note>who moves me</note>; Epilogue 377, *fo-m-glúaisi* <note>who moves me</note>; April 9, *-dibdai* <note>extinguishes</note>; December 29, *donn-ecrai* <note>who covers us</note>.

The <term>conjunct form</term> <note>a verb form used after certain particles or in compound verbs</note> of the 1st person singular of the same tense is exemplified by:
Epilogue 320 etc., *ad-sluindiu* <note>I proclaim</note>; Epilogue 103, *at-biur* <note>I say</note>; Epilogue 304, *atateoch-sa* (*ad-dat-teoch*) <note>I beseech you</note>; Prologue 265, Epilogue 37, 312, 313, *no-t-guidiu* <note>I pray to you</note>; January 20, *con-úagu* <note>I stitch together</note>; January 23, *con-sádu* <note>I set together</note>; Epilogue 311, *no-t-caru* <note>I love you</note>; Epilogue 360, *ara mbáigiu* <note>for which I fight</note>; Epilogue 317, *do-rímu* <note>I enumerate</note>; Epilogue 559, *no-n-áilíu* <note>I entreat</note>.

**Relative forms:**
Singular 1st person: November 30, *no bágu* <note>I fight</note>; Epilogue 337, *no guidiu* <note>I pray</note>; Epilogue 358, *no ráidiu* <note>I speak</note>; Epilogue 50, *no charim* <note>I love</note>.
Singular 3rd person: *beres* <note>who carries</note>, *linas* <note>who fills</note>, *crothas* <note>who shakes</note>, *guires* <note>who heats</note>, *file* <note>who is</note>.
Plural 1st person: August 5, *dílme* <note>we release</note>; Epilogue 242, *canmae* <note>we sing</note>; Epilogue 243, *guidme* <note>we pray</note>; August 31, *molmae* <note>we praise</note>.
Plural 3rd person: December 28, *cantae* <note>they sing</note>; Prologue 194, *mairte* <note>they remain</note>.

Relativity is expressed by <term>aspiration</term> <note>a softening of the initial consonant sound</note> in Prologue 150, *ad-chissiu* <note>I see</note>, and October 19, *as-chomart* <note>who has struck</note>.

### Reduplicated Future.
<note>A future tense formed by repeating part of the verb root.</note>
Singular 2nd person: Prologue 309, 311, *lile-su* (so read) <note>you will follow</note>; Epilogue 494, *atom-didmae* <note>you will admit me</note>.

### É-Future.
<note>A future tense characterized by an 'é' vowel in the stem.</note>
Singular 3rd person absolute: December 12, *gébaid* <note>he will take</note>; Prologue 174, *méraid* <note>it will remain</note>.
Singular 3rd person conjunct: Epilogue 116, *at-béla* <note>he will die</note>; Epilogue 114, 166, *no-t-géba* <note>he will take you</note>.
Plural 1st person: Epilogue 86, *-célam* <note>we shall hide</note>.
Plural 3rd person: Prologue 247, *at-bélat* <note>they will die</note>.

### Reduplicated S-Future.
Singular 2nd person: December 16, *at-róiriss* <note>you will remain</note>.
Singular 3rd person: September 29, *ar-sil* <note>he will strike</note> (*sil* from *sisl*..., from *sligim* <note>to strike</note>); Prologue 326, *-fóir* (= *fo-rir*) from *fo-rigim* <note>to delay/detain</note>.

### Ā-Subjunctive.
Singular 1st person: Prologue 268, 269, *dorónsa* <note>I may do</note>.
Singular 2nd person: *tuicce* <note>you may understand</note>, *fortn-édae* <note>you may cover it</note>, *dogné* <note>you may do</note>.
Singular 3rd person: *dorogra* <note>he may call</note>, *ron-sbera* <note>he may carry us</note>, *ron-glea* <note>he may settle us</note>.
Plural 2nd person: Prologue 186, *darónaid* <note>you may do</note>.
Plural 3rd person: *don-r-emat* <note>they may protect us</note>, *cotom-róchat* <note>they may reach me</note>.

### S-Subjunctive
<note>The "s-subjunctive" is a specific category of the Old Irish verb system where an 's' is added to the root to indicate a wish, possibility, or future intent.</note>

**Absolute forms:** Singular 3rd person, <term>ainsium</term> (from *ainis-um) <note>may he protect me</note> January 31; Plural 1st person, <term>resme</term> (perhaps <term>resmi</term>?) <note>may we reach</note> Prologue 257.

Singular 3rd person, <term>-tecma</term> <note>it may happen</note> January 10, <term>ronn-ain</term> <note>may he protect us</note> December 22, <term>ro gé</term> <note>that he may pray</note> Epilogue 364. Plural 1st person, <term>risam</term> <note>that we may reach</note> December 17. Plural 2nd person, <term>con-íssid</term> <note>that you may be able</note> Epilogue 393. Plural 3rd person, <term>dodigset</term> <note>that they may come</note> Epilogue 24, <term>domm-ísat</term> <note>may they come to me</note> Epilogue 36, <term>-tísat</term> <note>that they may come</note> Epilogue 295, <term>do-airset</term> <note>that they may help</note> September 20, <term>-tairset</term> <note>that they may help</note> December 13.

**Secondary forms:** <note>Used for past intentions or conditional "would/should" statements.</note> Singular 3rd person: <term>tésed</term> <note>he should go</note> April 27, <term>no-gessed</term> <note>he used to pray</note> Epilogue 217, <term>nachat-rísed</term> <note>that it might not reach you</note> Prologue 284. Plural 3rd person relative: <term>tiastae</term> <note>who should go</note> Epilogue 470, <term>a ngestae</term> <note>what they used to pray</note> Epilogue 432, 433.

### S-Preterite
<note>The "s-preterite" is the standard past tense for many Old Irish verbs.</note>

Singular 2nd person: <term>sóerais</term> <note>you delivered</note> Epilogue 486; relative form, "as <term>sóersai</term>" <note>as you delivered</note> Epilogue 441, 445, etc.

Singular 3rd person absolute: <term>bebais</term> <note>he died</note> Prologue 95, February 18, April 23; <term>breuis</term> <note>he crushed</note> April 4; <term>carais</term> <note>he loved</note> January 15; <term>céssais</term> <note>he suffered</note> January 17; <term>crochais</term> <note>he crucified</note> March 8; <term>dálais</term> <note>he assigned</note> April 12; <term>gabais</term> <note>he took</note> July 6; <term>mórais</term> <note>he magnified</note> August 18; <term>sóerais</term> <note>he delivered</note> September 25. With an attached pronoun: <term>tróeths-us</term> <note>he overwhelmed them</note> November 16; <term>mórs-us</term> <note>he magnified them</note> January 30, June 5. In June 15 and July 9, <term>carais</term> seems to be a 3rd person singular relative form, like <term>caris</term> in the *Cambray Homily* (Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II. 247, line 4). The same applies to <term>sóerais</term> on September 25. However, in March 24, we find the form <term>car</term>.

Plural 3rd person conjunct: <term>-crochsat</term> <note>they crucified</note> Prologue 73; <term>-carsat</term> <note>they loved</note> May 8. Absolute: <term>carsait</term> <note>they loved</note> March 15, May 7; <term>lécsit</term> <note>they left</note> October 8.

### T-Preterite and Perfect
<note>A past tense category where a 't' is added to the verb stem.</note>

This tense occurs in the *Martyrology* only in the 3rd person singular and 3rd person plural.
Singular 3rd person: <term>ro-da-ort</term> <note>he slew them</note> Prologue 57; <term>as-ort</term> <note>he slew</note> April 23; <term>as-r-éracht</term> <note>he has arisen</note> Prologue 92, March 27; <term>dorósat</term> (from *to-ro-fo-ess-sem-t) <note>he created</note> Prologue 91; <term>birt</term> <note>she bore</note> January 27, June 2; <term>do-bert</term> <note>he gave</note> April 14, October 18, November 2; <term>adropart</term> <note>he offered</note> Epilogue 269.
Plural 3rd person: <term>ro stachtatar</term> <note>they spread out</note> Prologue 70.

### Reduplicated Preterite and Perfect
<note>An ancient past tense formed by repeating the first part of the verb root.</note>

The reduplicated preterite and perfect are still in constant use. For example:
Singular 1st person: <term>adróithach</term> <note>I have besought</note> Epilogue 300, 301 (from *ad-ro-tethach); <term>-cúala</term> <note>I heard</note> June 13.
Singular 3rd person: <term>cachain</term> <note>he sang</note> April 26, December 8 (should this be read as <term>cechain</term>?); <term>cechaing</term> <note>he stepped/went</note> January 25, May 22; <term>geguin</term> <note>he wounded/slew</note> October 23; <term>ro selaig</term> (from *seslaig) <note>he hewed</note> Prologue 101; <term>senaig</term> (from *sesnaig) <note>it dripped</note> May 15; <term>ar-ro-chiuir</term> (from *-ceciri) <note>it has perished</note>; <term>ro ír</term> <note>he granted</note> July 5; <term>ro tetha</term> <note>it has vanished</note> Prologue 193 (present indicative <term>tinim</term>); <term>t-ánic</term> <note>he came</note> January 11, April 14; <term>r-ánic</term> <note>he reached</note> May 2, Epilogue 17; <term>immeránic</term> <note>it happened</note> May 2; <term>do-da-farnaic</term> <note>it came to them</note> June 10.
Plural 3rd person: <term>-gegnetar</term> <note>they slew</note> May 19; <term>docoémnachtar</term> (from *to-com-ne-nigtar) <note>they were able</note> January 4; <term>ro selgatar</term> <note>they hewed</note> Prologue 29; <term>táncatar</term> <note>they came</note> Epilogue 88; <term>ráncatar</term> <note>they reached</note> Prologue 78.

<header>THE LANGUAGE OF THE MARTYROLOGY.</header>

### Unreduplicated Preterites and Perfects.
<note>In Old Irish, "unreduplicated" refers to past tense verbs that do not repeat the initial consonant of the root to indicate tense.</note>

Of these, besides the *s*- and *t*- preterites <note>past tense forms ending in -s or -t</note>, there are two classes:
(a) those with a long vowel before a single consonant;
(b) those with a short vowel:

(a) Singular 1st person: *ro gád-sa* <note>I prayed</note> Epilogue 412, *ro-n-gádsa* <note>I prayed to him/it</note>, 421.
Singular 3rd person: *ráith* <note>he ran</note> Jan. 6, Sep. 19; *fo-ráith* <note>he helped</note> Jan. 5; *ro scáich* <note>it has passed away</note> Nov. 22, Prologue 121; *ro fir-scáich* <note>it has truly passed away</note> Prologue 84; (with an attached pronoun *ro scáich-i* <note>it has passed away from him</note> Prologue 177); *docuaid* <note>he went</note> Epilogue 267 (from the root *\*to-co-fáith*). Plural 3rd person: *ráthatar* <note>they ran</note> Sep. 28; relative form *dochúatar* <note>who went</note> Prologue 279.

(b) Singular 3rd person: *rol-eb-laing* <note>he leaped</note> March 5 (from *lingim* <note>I leap</note>); *dr-eb-raing* <note>he climbed/leaped</note> April 2, 17; *do-ro-chair*, *-to-r-chair* <note>he fell</note> March 26, Epilogue 361 (which serves as the perfect tense to *dotuit* "falls"); *-sceith* <note>he vomited/poured out</note> Feb. 16; *frisnaig* <note>he washed</note> March 24; *luid* <note>he went</note> Prologue 128, Jan. 1 etc.; *mad tuluid* <note>if he came</note> July 12. Plural 3rd person: *lotar* <note>they went</note> May 5.

In *ro éra* <note>he refused</note> Epilogue 474, *ro phraidchi* <note>he preached</note> Prologue 164 (equivalent to *ropritchai* in the *Tripartite Life of St. Patrick*, 40. 1. 4), and *ro chruidi* <note>he milked/gathered</note> Epilogue 136, we seem to have present tense forms made into Preterites by the prefix *ro-*. See *Kuhn's Beiträge* (KSB) vii. 4; Strachan, *Verbal System of the Saltair na Rann*, p. 32, and compare the passive form *ro gabthar* "it was sung," *Milan Glosses* (Ml.) 24ᵈ 14.

### Deponents.
<note>Deponent verbs are those that have passive-style endings but an active meaning.</note>

The deponential forms in the Martyrology are:
**Present indicative** singular 1st person: *frisáiliur* <note>I expect</note> Epilogue 560; *no molur* <note>I praise</note> Prologue 13; and perhaps *conruidiur* <note>I intend/settle</note>, Prologue 277. Singular 2nd person: *armuinter* <note>you are called to mind</note> Oct. 2; *memraigther* <note>you remember</note>, March 2; *ro clunter* <note>you hear</note> Prologue 282. Plural 1st person: *no-s-molamar* <note>we praise them</note> Jan. 17 R¹.

**Imperative** singular 2nd person: *clúinte* <note>hear!</note> Epilogue 314, 365, 425; *molthae* <note>praise!</note> Sep. 2 (where the manuscripts have *molatha, molotha*).

**Subjunctive** singular 2nd person: *foraimmentar* <note>that you may remember</note> Sep. 8; *ro fésser* <note>that you may know</note> Feb. 4; *dian fésser* <note>if you should know</note> Oct. 24.

**Preterite** singular 3rd person: *génair* <note>he was born</note>, Dec. 25; *mad-génair* <note>blessed is he who was born</note> Prologue 251; *dámair* <note>he suffered/endured</note> Feb. 9, 16. **Perfect** singular 3rd person: *ro génair* <note>he has been born</note> Sep. 24. Plural 1st person: *do-s-ruimdemar* <note>we have thought of them</note> Epilogue 6. Plural 3rd person: *ro damnatar* <note>they have suffered</note> Prologue 53.

The transition from deponential to active forms is shown, I think, only in one verb, namely *molmae* <note>we praise</note> Aug. 31, the relative form of the present indicative plural 1st person of *molur*. That such a transition had commenced in the Old Irish period is proved by the *b*-future form *molfait* <note>they will praise</note> *Milan Glosses* (Ml.) 69ᵇ 1. The use of deponential inflection seems to prove that our Martyrology is, at the latest, not later than the ninth century.¹
<margin>¹ Strachan, *The Deponent Verb in Irish*, pp. 110, 111.</margin>

In the passive voice, the present indicative 3rd person singular and 3rd person plural still observe the difference between the absolute and the relative (identical with the conjunct) forms. Thus *bertar* Prologue 175, "who are carried"...

In the third-person singular preterite <note>the past tense</note>, the absolute forms end in *-tae*, *-thae*, and the conjunct forms in *-t*, *-th*: absolute <term>brethae</term> January 25, June 11, <term>carthae</term> May 9, <term>crochthae</term> February 12, <term>ortae</term> January 26, March 6, September 7; <term>séntae</term> Prologue 100: <term>slechtae</term> February 12: conjunct: *-airecht* August 3, *-ort* October 22, <term>as-ort</term> October 7, <term>as-chom-art* October 9, <term>do-rindnacht</term> November 12, *-sreith* February 20, June 16, <term>ro sreth</term> August 25, *-frith* March 10, June 16, July 30, (likewise <term>as-breth</term>, <term>do-breth</term>).
