In <term>-fess</term> Prologue 135, the *ss* comes from *d-t*.

In *a*-verbs, the third-person singular perfect ends in *-a-d*: <term>ro crochad</term> Prologue 89, <term>doro-dbad</term> 96: <term>ro mórad</term>, <term>ro rígad</term> 103, 104, <term>ro múchad</term> 169, <term>roérad</term> 206, <term>ro lénad</term> 253. In *i*-verbs it ends in *-ed*, such as <term>ro milled</term> Prologue 213.

In the third-person plural, the manuscripts of our Martyrology point to *-ta*, *-tha* for *o*- and *ā*-verbs, and to *-tea*, *-thea* for *ī*-verbs. This is the rule in the Old Irish glosses: see *Grammatica Celtica*, 2nd edition, page 478.

Reduplicated future third-person plural: <term>do-génatar</term>, Epilogue 176 (where *gén-* comes from *gign*-).

Participle of necessity <note>a verbal form indicating that something must be done</note>: <term>ráti</term> April 9, <term>gessi</term> December 2, September 28, <term>clithi</term> December 9, Epilogue 306, <term>fissi</term> Epilogue 335, <term>dénti</term> Epilogue 392.

### The Substantive Verb and the Copula.

The forms which in the Martyrology make up the substantive verb and the copula <note>the various forms of the verb "to be"</note> are collected in the glossarial index under the entries: *am*, *atá*, *bíuu*, *dianda*, *dochuissin*, *feil*, *ním-tha*, and *táu*. Of these, the unstressed *am* is from *em*, related to the Gothic *im*, Greek *eimí* <note>original: εἰμί</note>, Lithuanian *esmì*, and Sanskrit *asmi*: *táu*, *atá* (*ad-tā*), *dian-da*, and *ním-tha* are cognate with the Latin *stō* <note>I stand</note>: *bíuu* with the Latin *vīvo* <note>I live</note>; and *feil* (originally meaning "here is" <note>original: voici</note>) is related to the Irish *fili* 'poet' (originally 'seer'), the Welsh <term>gweled</term> 'to see,' and the Old Norse *völvu* 'seeress.' *Nímtha* 'not so is' comes from *ní-ímtha*, and *ím-tha* ('so is') is a compound of *tá* (equivalent to the Latin *stat* <note>he/she/it stands</note>) and *im*, which is cognate with the Latin *imitor* <note>I imitate</note>, *imago* <note>image</note>, and *aemulor* <note>I rival</note>.

### Syntax.

So much for the ancient grammatical forms of the Martyrology. Its syntax is also highly archaic. For example, the dative plural is often used as an "instrumental" case <note>indicating the means by which an action is performed</note>, without a governing preposition: for instance:

*iarna foebraib fennad* 'after flaying them with sword-edges,' Prologue 48.
*ind locáin ro gabtha déissib ocus trírib* 'the little places that have been taken by pairs and by trios,' Prologue 209.
*Agnetis deich n-úagaib* 'Agnes with ten virgins,' January 27.

<margin>¹ *Sarauw*, *Revue Celtique* volume 17, page 278: compare the Algerian Arabic *rā-h* 'he is,' literally 'here he is' <note>original: le voici</note>.</margin>

Ibid, page 348, line 5. For a similar construction in Old Welsh poetry, see *Rhŷs’s Lectures*, 2nd edition, page 153 (*Kenetyl noted* ‘the nation’s refuge,’ *Kimerev trin* ‘Cymmerau’s conflict,’ *riein gared* ‘delight of women’). To these we may perhaps add the Ogham inscription *Trennaccat lo* ‘Tringad’s grave,’ and part of the Gaulish bilingual inscription of Todi: *Ategnati Drutikni karnidu logan Koisis Drutiknos* ‘Coisis, son of Drutos, heaped up the tomb of Ategnātos, son of Drutos.’

A third archaism <term>archaism: an old-fashioned word or grammatical form</term> in our Martyrology <term>Martyrology: a list or calendar of Christian martyrs and saints</term> is the frequent placement of the adjective before the noun with which it agrees. For example: *cráibdig i féil Fursa* (pious on Fursa’s feast), January 16; *ard áige* (high pillar), Prologue 119, 243; *ard imbel* (high border), 131; *étrocht áge* (bright pillar), February 10; *cáin cathar* (fair city), August 15.

A fourth archaism is the occasional placement of the accusative <note>the direct object of a sentence</note> before the governing verb. For example:

> ‘For Christ’s sake he vanquished every lust,’ April 4.
> ‘Before high Christmas you should make great prayer,’ November 13.
> ‘The folk to whom I make welcome,’ Epilogue 49.
> ‘I have searched out martyrologies,’ Epilogue 109.
> ‘O Jesus, who has wrought great miracles,’ Epilogue 506.

The result is that, with one exception, the grammar and syntax of our Martyrology may be regarded as strict Old Irish. The exception is the occasional use of the comparative form for the superlative <note>using "better" instead of "best"</note>. It now seems to me that it is easier to believe that this Middle Irish trait existed as early as 800 A.D. than to cast aside the traditional evidence that Oengus wrote about that date. 

This belief is confirmed by several facts: 
1. The author mentions only one vigil (August 15).
2. He includes only five festivals of the Blessed Virgin Mary (whereas there are fourteen ‘of universal obligation’ in the later Roman calendar).
3. No saint or other person who certainly died in the ninth century is mentioned in his Martyrology. 

Paulus Diaconus (April 13), who died before 800 A.D., and Aireran of the Wisdom (August 11), who succeeded Maelruain in 792 A.D., are the most modern saints commemorated here. It is even possible that the commentator <note>original: scholiast</note> was mistaken, and that Oengus actually intended this Aireran to be Aileran the Wise <note>original: *Aileran ind ecni*</note>, who died in the year 604. That our Martyrology was not written before the ninth century is proved by the mention of Saint Joseph on March 19.¹

<page-num>xxxix</page-num>
<header>THE METRE OF THE MARTYROLOGY.</header>

### IV. THE METRE OF THE MARTYROLOGY.

Only five metrical martyrologies are known to me, namely: Bede’s *Poetic Martyrology*¹ (which at March 17 contains the line "Patrick, the servant of the Lord, ascends to the heavenly court" <note>original Latin: *Patricius Dominī servus transcendit ad aulam*</note>), the *Martyrology of Wandalbert*,³ the *Anglo-Saxon Poetic Menologium*,⁴ the *Martyrology of Gorman*,⁵ and the *Martyrology of Oengus*. The first two are written in Latin hexameters. The *Martyrology of Gorman* is in the Irish metre called <term>rinnard mór</term> ("great rinnard"), in which the stanzas may consist of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, or even 14 lines. The *Martyrology of Oengus* consists of 591 quatrains <note>four-line stanzas</note>, each of which is independent in sense. The elaborate metre (*rinnard*) in which they are written is described, though not quite completely, in the prose prefaces. Its chief characteristics are as follows:

1. Each line of the quatrain contains six syllables. The solitary exception is *Epilogue* 459, where *Lóth* should perhaps be corrected to *Lóthus*.
2. Each line must end (like the *Ovidian pentameter*) in a two-syllable word. To this rule there are exceptions in the case of the words *alaile* and *araile* <note>meaning "another" or "certain"</note> and of foreign proper names.⁶ Also, Irish verbs compounded with prepositional prefixes are, for metrical purposes, regarded as being in <term>tmesi</term> <note>a linguistic term where a word is divided into parts by intervening words</note>. Thus, the "proclitics"—the article, possessive pronouns, verbal prefixes, the copula <note>the verb "to be"</note>, prepositions, and negative particles—are not regarded as part of the words with which they are written in the manuscripts. On the other hand, the pronominal suffixes *-ni, -sa, -se, -si, -sin, -su, -som* are considered (for metrical purposes) to convert the one-syllable words to which they are attached into two-syllable words.
3. Each end-word must be accented on the second-to-last syllable <note>the penult</note>. Take, for example, the quatrains for January 1 and January 10:

Before the seed of the numerous people <note>original: *Ré síl dálach dóine*</note>
may the King who remains forever guide us, <note>original: *tóided in rí remain*</note>
Christ went under the high noble law <note>original: *luid fo recht ard erail*</note>
on the calends of January. <note>original: *Críst i callaind enair*</note>

Let us beseech them in prayer <note>original: *Álmini a n-itge*</note>
that no evil fate may befall us, <note>original: *náchan tecma drochrann*</note>
Holy Milit, a fair helmet <note>of protection</note>, <note>original: *Mílit cáid cain cathbarr*</note>
and Diarmait of Inis Clothrann. <note>original: *Diarmait Inse Clothrann*</note>

4. The end-words of the second and fourth lines must <term>assonate</term><note>Create a vowel rhyme or a specific type of consonant correspondence.</note>, meaning the vowels must be the same and the consonants must be of the same class.

The consonantal classes are as follows:
(1) *c, t, p*, and uninfected *g, d, b*.
(2) *ch*<note>The sound *cht* may rhyme with *t* (Epilogue 72).</note>, *th, ph, ff*<note>Thus *fethis*, *cathlaic*, and *clithi* respectively rhyme with *Effis*, *Affraic*, and *Liffi*. This is proof, if such were wanted, that in Old Irish *th* was pronounced somewhat like the English dental <term>spirant</term> (friction sound) in "thing." See *Celtic Review* III. 186, and *Journal of Celtic Philology* (*Celt. Zeits.*) I. 454.</note>.
(3) *gh, dh, bh, mh, n, r, l*.
(4) *mm, nn*<note>*nn* rhymes with *nnt* at July 30, and with *nt* at November 21.</note>, *ng, rr, ll*.
(5) *s*<note>See Prologue 17–19; 57–60; 62–64; 74–76; 150–152; 182, 184, etc. Exceptions to the rules as to classes—in other words, faulty consonantal rhymes—will be found in the Prologue 170, 172, and at February 15 (*bágaig, námaí*), September 19 (*taithlech, aithmeí*), and Epilogue 394, 396 (*tíchtu, íssu*).</note>.

5. Final *-e* in the first and third lines may assonate with final *-ae* in the second and fourth lines, and final *-i* in the first and third lines may assonate with final *-ai* in the second and fourth lines. Thus *ae* in *togae* (January 6) assonates with *nglaine* and *Maire*, and *ai* in *Tiamdai* (August 22) assonates with *náni* and *Emiliani*: see further Strachan, *Celtic Review* volume xx, pages 191, 295.

6. The end-word of the third line may assonate with a disyllable (a two-syllable word) in the interior of the fourth line. But where such assonance is absent, the final syllable of the third line must assonate with the final syllables of the second and fourth lines: see Prologue 25–28, where *-sa* in the third line assonates with *-sa* in the second and fourth<note>Thurneysen, *Celtic Review* VII. 88.</note>, or the final syllable of the third line must assonate with the final syllable of a word in the interior of

When the final syllables of lines 1, 2, 3, and 4 assonate, the metre is called <term>rinnard of four high points</term> <note>original: "rinnard cethir n-ard"</note>—that is, ‘<term>rinnard</term> of four rhyming final syllables.’ For example, at March 17 and June 17:

->Flame of a splendid sun,<-
->apostle of virgin Ireland,<-
->Patrick with a multitude of thousands,<-
->may he be the protection against our misery.<-
<note>original: "Lassar gréne áne / apstal Hérenn hóge / Pátraic co méit míle / rop dítiu ar tróge"</note>

->The bush of gold over borders,<-
->the splendid sun above tribes,<-
->champion of the King, a strong brother,<-
->a holy soldier, Moling of Luachair.<-
<note>original: "In doss óir ós chrícháib, / in grían án úas túathaib, / congreit ríg, balc bráthair, / cáid míl, Moling Lúachair."</note>

When the final syllables of lines 2, 3, and 4 assonate, the metre is called <term>rinnard of three high points</term> <note>original: "rinnard trí n-ard"</note>—‘<term>rinnard</term> of three rhyming final syllables.’ For example, at January 4 and June 14:

->The holy death of Aquilinus<-
->with a troop that was stronger;<-
->in the blood of Christ through their bodies<-
->they have washed their garments.<-
<note>original: "Bás caid Aquilíni / co mbuídin ba balcu / hi fuil Chríst trea curpu / docoemnachtar tlachtu"</note>

->They meet from both sides<-
->on one festival of a hostful sea,<-
->Nem, son of Birn the vigorous,<-
->with victorious Benedict.<-
<note>original: "Conrecat dib línib / for óenlíth ler slúagach, / Nem maccu Birn brígach, / la Benedicht mbúadach."</note>

and so in the quatrain for January 1, where -<term>ain</term>, -<term>ail</term>, -<term>air</term> are the three assonating <term>high points</term> <note>original: "ards"</note>, and in that for January 27, where lines 2, 3, and 4 end in -<term>aib</term>.

When the final syllables of only lines 2 and 4 assonate, the metre is called <term>rinnard of two high points</term> <note>original: "rinnard dá n-ard"</note>—‘<term>rinnard</term> of two rhyming final syllables.’ Thus at January 24 and June 22:

->To my soul, to my little body,<-
->may he be a great help against every wandering grief,<-
->Babylas, a mass of abundant gold,<-
->with his three little children.<-
<note>original: "Domm anmain, domm chorpán / rop mór ar cech merblén, / Babill, bruth óir forlan / cona thriur dedblén."</note>

->With James son of Alphaeus,<-
->two hundred and eight, a bright company,<-
->the feast of a man who loved not bodily pain,<-

<note>original: "La Hlacób nAlphaei / dá nócht cét, clíar ngeldae, / féil fir nád char corplén / Cronán fortrén Fernae."</note>

In the Irish prefaces, the quatrain for March 1 is given as an example of <term>rinnard of two high points</term>. If this is not a mistake, <term>Moysi</term> in line 3 should be <term>Moyse</term>, and then the two <term>high points</term> are the final syllables of <term>praying</term> <note>original: "ngudí"</note> and <term>Muni</term>.

7. In each quatrain there must be alliteration (<gloss>concord</gloss> <note>original: "úaim"</note>), that is to say, two, three or more accented syllables must begin with the same letter—all the vowels being, for this purpose, deemed identical, and *h*, infected *f* <note>a silent 'f' in Old Irish</note> and transported nasals being disregarded. For example, in the quatrain for January 7, <term>splendid</term> <note>original: "áni"</note>, <term>nobler</term> <note>original: "úaisliu"</note> and <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: "Íssu"</note> alliterate, and in the quatrain for January 4, <term>troop</term> <note>original: "mbuídin"</note> and <term>stronger</term> <note>original: "balcu"</note> are regarded as beginning with the same letter. It is unnecessary to quote other examples of consonantal alliteration.

<page-num>xlii</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

8. The last characteristic of *rinnard* <note>A specific meter in Irish poetry characterized by six-syllable lines ending in a disyllable.</note> is what the Irish preface in R² (see above, p. 14) calls "an harmonious juncture between the beginnings of the quatrains and the ends of the other (that is, the last preceding) quatrains" <note>original: *fidrad cubaid etir tosaichib na rann ocus deridib na rann ele*</note>, and what modern Irish scholars call *conachlann* <note>1</note>. This agreement is not obligatory. It may be either complete—as in the case of the third quatrain of the invocation prefixed to the prologue, where the first line is identical with the last line of the second quatrain—or partial, as when the first accented word in the second quatrain—*gelgrian* ("bright sun")—alliterates with *gile* ("brightness"), the final word of the first. Similarly, *rigraid* ("royal host"), the first accented word in the fourth quatrain, alliterates with *rigraid*. So in the quatrains for the first seven days of February, the pairs *Érenn* and *Airitiu*, and *airi* and *Andreas* each begin with a vowel; likewise, each of the pairs *Simfróni* and *Fronius*, *crésen* and *crochthae*, and *míli* and *Mellán* begin with the same consonant. The object of this device is, of course, to aid the memory. There is, I believe, in Welsh verse a similar device called *adgymmeriad* ("repetition" or "anadiplosis"), and there is something like it in a French poem quoted in Isaac Disraeli's *Curiosities of Literature* (London, 1838, p. 108), where the last word of every line is identical with the first word of the following line.

I have dwelt at some length on the characteristics of this meter, partly because nothing is more important for correcting the corrupt text of a poem (and every copy of the Martyrology is full of scribal errors) than a right understanding of the rules by which the author was guided. It is also because observing the technical skill of the poem's creator is almost the only source of pleasure to be found in his work. Finally, Ezzardi's suggestion <note>2</note> that the meter of the *Martyrology of Oengus* appears to have been the model for the Skaldic *dróttkvætt* <note>A complex Old Norse courtly meter.</note>, especially the *hattlausa* <note>A variation of the dróttkvætt meter without internal rhyme.</note>, makes the Irish *rinnard* a matter of interest for Germanic as well as for Celtic scholars.

### V. THE CONTENTS OF THE POEM. <note>3</note>

After an invocation of Christ, who is called "Lord of the seven heavens" and "King of the bright sun," and a reference to the saints—

After mentioning those recorded in the Martyrology <note>A list or calendar of martyrs and saints.</note>, the poet begins his prologue (lines 21–340). He describes (lines 29–48) the various modes of martyrdom which the warriors of Jesus (<term>mílid Ísu</term> <note>Old Irish: "soldiers of Jesus"</note>) suffered with cheerful heroism. They now, unlike the great pagan kings, enjoy their eternal reward with Mary’s Son, while their relics are enshrined in sparkling gold (lines 49–84). Herod and Pilate are then contrasted with Christ, Nebuchadnezzar with Paul the Monk, Herod and his queen with John the Baptist, Nero with Peter and Paul, and Pilate’s queen with Mary the Virgin.

Then come some reflections on the nothingness of earthly power and mundane potentates as compared with the love of Mary’s Son and with the lowly soldiers (<term>amsáin</term> <note>Old Irish: "mercenaries" or "soldiers," here used for the followers of Christ</note>) of Jesus. In Ireland, for example, Tara, the seat of the heathen high-kings, has perished, <margin>It was abandoned A.D. 561.</margin> while Armagh remains with her crowd of Christian champions. King Lóiguire’s glory has departed, but St. Patrick’s name lives on. Various ruined strongholds of the pagan Irish—Rathcroghan, Allen, Emain, and others—are then contrasted with the monasteries—Clonmacnois, Kildare, Glendalough, Ferns—which flourished in the ninth century. The forgotten renown of pagan chieftains, like Donnchad, Bran, and Domnall, is contrasted with the abiding glory of Christ and the Irish saints, Mael-rúain, Ciarán, and Cronán. The poet then breaks out into a praise of Jesus, prays for success in the work at hand, and concludes his prologue by describing the nature of the Martyrology.

Then comes the Martyrology itself, which consists of 365 quatrains <note>Four-line stanzas.</note> (or 366, if we include the one for the leap-year day <note>original: "bisextus"</note> in the note on February 23). Unlike the Martyrology of Tallaght and the Anglo-Saxon Menologium <note>A calendar of the months, often containing poems about saints' days.</note>, which begin with December 25, Oengus commences with the feast of the Circumcision <note>January 1</note>, and ends with that of St. Sylvester <note>December 31</note>. The Crucifixion and Conception of Christ are commemorated on the same day (March 25). As in the Hieronymian Martyrology and the Martyrology of Tours, <margin>See the abridgment in Gregory of Tours’ *History of the Franks* <note>original: "Historia Francorum"</note>, edited by Arndt, part I, page 445.</margin> the Resurrection of our Lord is fixed at March 27. His first Ascension is at May 5 (as seen in the manuscripts Galba A. xviii. folio 7a, and Harleian 863, folio 3a); the mission of the Apostles is at July 15; the birth <note>original: "nativity"</note> of Mary Magdalen is at July 22. In associating (January 6) the Epiphany with Christ’s Baptism, and not with the visit of the Magi <note>The Three Wise Men.</note>, Oengus follows the tradition of the Eastern, rather than that of the Western Church. <margin>See Plummer’s edition of Bede <note>original: "Baeda"</note>, volume II, page 237.</margin> Similarly, he follows the Greek, not the Roman, church in celebrating St. Euphemia on July 11. Probably there are other similar instances obvious to anyone more familiar with the subject.

than I am with Christian hagiology <note>The study of the lives of saints.</note>. St. John the Baptist's nativity is placed at June 24; his conception at September 24. Gallican <note>French/Gaulish</note> influence appears in the commemoration of the Circumcision (not the octave of the Nativity) on January 1; of the Assumption of the Virgin and the *Cathedra S. Petri* <note>The Chair of St. Peter</note> on January 18; of the Passion on March 25; of the Resurrection on March 27; and of St. John and St. James on December 27.¹

Oengus mentions (p. 270) as his foreign sources the "vast tome" (*pairt*) of Ambrose, the *Sensus* of Hilary, the *Antigraph* of Jerome, and the Martyrology of Eusebius.² What work of Ambrose (or Ambrosiaster) is meant, I cannot imagine. Hilary's *Sensus* is equally obscure, whether the Hilary referred to was Hilary of Poitou or Hilary of Arles.³ Jerome's *Antigraph* (from the Greek *antigraphon*, meaning "copy") is doubtless the Pseudo-Jerome, the so-called *Martyrologium Hieronymianum*, so carefully edited by De Rossi and Duchesne, and so often cited in this book as *Mart. Hier.* The manuscript used by Oengus resembled the Epternach copy, which is said to represent a British form of the Martyrology.³ The "Martyrology of Eusebius" may be the lost work of Eusebius on which the *Martyrologium Hieronymianum* is said to be based. Or it may be the "Ancient Collection of Martyrs" <note>original: *archaiōn martyriōn synagōgē*</note>, of which according to Herzfeld, one part, entitled *On the Martyrs of Palestine* <note>original: *De Martyribus Palaestinae*</note>, has been preserved.

Bishop Forbes has remarked that nearly all the Irish saints commemorated by Oengus are the same as those in the [twelfth century?] calendar contained in the Drummond Missal, but that the selection of non-Irish saints is very different.⁴

How little the Irish Church of the early Middle Ages knew of foreign saints is evidenced by the facts that Oengus, at May 28, mistakes Germanus of Paris (who died A.D. 576) for Germanus of Auxerre (died A.D. 448), the tutor of St. Patrick. At August 16, he puts Adrio for Orion, an Alexandrian martyr; at June 4, he puts Apollinaris for the Egyptian Apollonius. At July 21, he treats the Roman virgin Praxides as if she were a male saint; and at February 3 and 4, he has made imaginary saints, "Simfronius," out of the latter part of a place-name, *Forum Semproni* (now Fossombrone, in Umbria). The medieval glossators <note>Scholars who wrote explanatory notes in the margins of manuscripts.</note> are equally ignorant. Thus Siric, on November 26, said to be an Irish bishop of Mag Bolg, is certainly the Pope Siricius, who died on November 26, A.D. 398. St. Oswald, August 5, is confounded with Aldfrid (Flann Fína); Constantine, the—

### THE CONTENTS OF THE POEM.

The successor of Mochutu, abbot of Rathen (p. 92), is confused with Constantine, son of Fergus; Isidore of Antioch with Isidore of Seville; Lupus the martyr with Lupus, bishop of Troyes; Publius, an African martyr, with an unknown Paulus at February 19; and Apollinaris the Christian writer with Apollinaris of Ravenna, the martyr.

As is the case with the oldest martyrologies <note>A martyrology is a list or calendar of Christian martyrs and saints, usually arranged by their feast days.</note>, the entries in our *Félire* <note>original: "Félire"; an Old Irish term for a calendar or martyrology.</note> are generally of the most meager description. Here they consist of the name of the Irish or foreign saint commemorated, with some stock epithet or standing phrase tacked on so as to comply with the requirements of meter, rhyme, and alliteration. But sometimes brief reference is made to a tradition, a tale, or a legend. 

Thus in Prologue 2, and in Epilogue 120 and 401, Oengus speaks of the *seven heavens*, a number which seems ultimately derived from the Babylonian *seven layers* <note>original: "tubukāti"</note>,¹ from which came the seven heavens of Judaism, of Islam, and of the apocryphal Revelation of Peter,² chapter 27. At January 27, the poet mentions the wild story of Lí-bán or Muirgein, the mermaid, told in the *Book of the Dun Cow* <note>original: "Lebor na huidre"; one of the oldest surviving Irish manuscripts.</note>, pp. 40, 41.³ At February 6, he mentions the legend of Lucia, who could not be dragged to martyrdom; at February 16, the tradition of the introduction of bees into Ireland; at February 16, the legend of Juliana and the Devil;⁴ at March 9, the legend of the forty Cappadocian soldiers to whom the sun shone at the bottom of a lake; at April 9, the belief that the blood of the martyr Quadratus still remains. 

This belief is paralleled, and perhaps explained, by one still held in Ireland. In the southwest corner of Tech Molaisse on Inismurray is a dark red appearance caused by the growth of a small fungus. The natives say that it is caused by the blood of the martyred saint, and that however often it is scraped away, it will always come again.⁵ Then at April 5, we have the kindling (that is, the commencement) of baptism by Saint Patrick; at April 14, the tradition (mentioned also in Fíacc's hymn) that Bishop Tassach gave the Eucharist <note>original: "houseled"; to administer the Holy Communion to someone, especially the dying.</note> to the dying apostle of the Irish; at April 17, the pathetic tale of the martyrdom of Donnán of Eig; and at August 16, the story of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus.⁶

***

<header>PREFACE.</header>

On August 24, there is the mention of Patrick senior as the fosterer of St. Patrick¹; on August 25, the tradition of St. Bartholomew’s death; on September 4, the legend of the orphans playing around Ultan, who had saved them from dying of hunger; on September 23, the story of Adamnán’s liberation of Irishwomen from military service; on September 29, the legend of St. Michael the Archangel and the Antichrist; on October 23, the wounding of Christ by Longinus <note>The name traditionally given to the Roman soldier who pierced Jesus' side with a spear.</note>; on November 23, the legend of Clement and the sea; on December 8, that of Egbert and his skinless coracle <note>A small, lightweight boat; "skinless" implies it lacked the usual leather covering.</note>; and on December 21, the traditional death of St. Thomas in India. Here we see traces of that tendency to give a fuller form to the primitive martyrologies <note>Lists of martyrs and saints arranged by their feast days.</note>, which was first displayed by Bede (died 735), and then developed by Florus (about 830), Rabanus Maurus (about 840), Usuard (about 875), and Notker (about 912).

The body of our Martyrology is followed by the Epilogue, or, as the Irish oddly call it, the final Prologue. After referring generally to the Martyrology and acknowledging Christ’s help in composing it, Oengus prays for eternal life along with the saints whom he has commemorated. He declares that they have blessed whosoever shall sing it, and that they will come to attend him when he dies. The poet then enumerates his sources: the four works already mentioned, and "Ireland’s host of books, the martyrologies of the men of the Gaels." He again refers to the blessings bestowed on the reciter of his poem, the last mentioned (lines 221–224) being:

> “His soul without conflict
> in heaven with brightness,
> after him when he has attained it,
> the dew of his grave will heal.”²

The poet then classifies the persons commemorated—the nine ranks of angels, prophets, apostles, martyrs, bishops, saints, priests, monks, and virgins of Ireland, who will all, he says, befriend him. After praying the saints to beseech Christ on his behalf, he adjures Jesus by the sufferings of saints and penitents, by the offerings of His Body and Blood, by His Manhood and His Godhead, to grant him what he is contending for. The rest of the Epilogue resembles the *recommendation of the soul when the sick person is at the point of death* <note>original: "commendatio animae quando infirmus est in extremis"</note>,³ and is occupied with longings to pass—

<header>THE NOTES.</header>

## THE NOTES.

...from the afflictions of the world, and prayers to be saved like Elijah and Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Lot, Jonah, Isaac, Jacob, the Children of Israel, Job, Samson, David, Susannah, the three children <note>The three youths in the fiery furnace: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.</note>, Tobit, the people of Nineveh, Daniel, Moses, Paul and Peter, John "from the vat of fire," Martin "from the priest of the idol," Patrick "from the poisonous drink at Tara," Coemgin <note>Also known as St. Kevin of Glendalough.</note> "from the falling of the mountain."

The poem concludes with another prayer to be saved, and an entreaty that the saints commemorated in the Martyrology <term>Martyrology</term><note>A list or calendar of martyrs and saints, usually arranged by their feast days.</note> may convey us to our solace.

It must be confessed that in all this long composition there is not a trace of imaginative power or of observation of nature and human life as they really are. Here, as in the Martyrology of Gorman, the language is—as Wordsworth said of the English verse of the eighteenth century—the language of men composing without their eye on the object. Here, as in most of the Irish verse that has come down to us, substance is ruthlessly sacrificed to form, and the observance of the rigorous rules of metre seems regarded as an end in itself. Touches characteristic of the poet's time and country are here almost wholly absent. The four-line stanza <note>original: "quatrain"</note> for May 17, in which Oengus treats three saints as if they were three Irish chieftains making a raid into heaven in their war-chariots, is about the only passage that can be quoted as "racy of the soil."¹ It is perhaps an adaptation of a formula inherited from earlier bardic poetry. The frequent metaphorical use in the Martyrology of words meaning sun, moon, star, diadem, flame, gold, house-post, pillar, town, rampart, bush, and mountain may also be due to secular song. Compare, for instance, the poem in praise of King Crimthan, attributed to Dubthach ua Lugair (Book of Leinster, 45ª), where, in the course of the first five verses, that monarch is called *house-ridge of gold* <note>original: "drumne d'ór"</note>, *the warlike flame* <note>original: "in bréo bágach"</note>, *the mountain of red gold* <note>original: "in sliab dergbír"</note>, and lastly, *the bush that protects the troops of Meath* <note>original: "in doss dílnes dronga Domnann"</note>.

---

## VI. THE NOTES.

Every copy of the Martyrology contains, besides interlinear or marginal glosses <term>glosses</term><note>Brief explanations or translations of difficult words written between lines or in margins.</note>, bodies of notes in Irish, or medieval Latin, or a mixture of both, written between the lines, or on the...

margins, or after the quatrain or month referred to. Of the sources of these notes nothing certain is known. But from the statement in the manuscript Laud 610 at June 15 (see below, p. 140), we may fairly infer that a commentary (<term>trachtad</term> <note>original: "trachtad" — an Old Irish term for a treatise or commentary</note>) on the Martyrology existed in Armagh, if not "from the time of the saints," at least from an early period; and that some, at all events, of the entries in the notes were derived from this commentary.

For the entries relating to the constitution and discipline of the Irish church, to Irish architecture, metal-work, calligraphy, embroidery, music and verse, to the food, homes, morals, laws and amusements of the Gaels, reference may be made to the first edition of our Martyrology, pp. 24, 25, and to the Index of Things in the present volume. Here I shall only notice the scholia <note>scholarly notes or annotations</note> that throw some light on early Irish religious practices, superstitions, folklore, and legal antiquities.

### (a) Religious Practices.

Of these the most frequently mentioned is fasting (<term>troscud</term>), a practice belonging in ancient Ireland to the sphere of law¹ as well as to that of religion. Here it is used for the fall of a tree worshipped by the heathen (p. 118), for the cure of dumbness (p. 166), for the restoration of an eye (p. 244), and to procure the death of a hated saint (p. 204). It sometimes lasted for three days, and was then called <term>tredan</term> (pp. 36, 69, 235), a loanword from the Latin *triduana* <note>original: "triduana" — lasting three days</note>. The Lenten fasts of Moses and Jesus, each lasting for forty nights, are mentioned on pages 32, 42, and 234. For the benefits of fasting coupled with prayer, see *Adamnán’s Second Vision*, *Celtic Review* <note>original: "Revue Celtique"</note> xii. 432–438.

Prayer: for this there are no less than six native Irish words: *attach, aurgaiss, dubart, ernaigthe, guide, itge*, and one loanword, *diprecóit*. Prayer is addressed to God (p. 271), to Christ (pp. 279, 282, 283), and to the saints (pp. 17, 35, 80), and is made on our behalf by them and the martyrs (pp. 163, 274). The prayer of a hundred believers is said to be equivalent to a recitation of the Martyrology (p. 273). The Irish used at least three postures in their worship: namely, kneeling on both knees, kneeling with the arms stretched out in a cross <note>a posture known as cross-vigil</note>, and prostration. Erc Nascai (p. 130) prayed (standing upright?) in water² with a tie round his neck. Prayers, as well as curses, were most effective when the right hand was employed. See p. xxiv above, and p. 200 below. Genuflexion <note>the act of bending the knee</note> is twice mentioned (pp. 12, 154), and in the poem printed above on p. xxiv, Oengus is said to have made three hundred every night.

# THE NOTES.

**Austerities.**—It is difficult to determine whether Irish saints or Indian yogis <note>original: yogís</note> practiced the cruelest forms of self-denial. Many of these are described in *Lives of Saints from the Book of Lismore*, page 108, and in Cuimmín's poem in the *Journal for Celtic Philology* <note>original: Zeitschr. für celtische Philologie</note>, volume 1, pages 62–66. In the present work, the strangest acts are attributed to Findchu, who used to spend the first night lying with every corpse brought to his church for burial, and at other times sat suspended by a sickle placed in each of his armpits (page 246). Ciarán of Saiger used a stone for a pillow <note>original: bolster</note> (page 88). Columb Cille's broth was made of nettles (page 146). Flagellation <note>term: ritual whipping for spiritual discipline</note> is mentioned on page 280 as being practiced by Oengus himself. Íte kept a stag-beetle to pierce her side (page 42), and Fursa transferred to his own stomach the devouring reptile that Maignenn had hosted in his belly (page 44). The story of Scothíne sleeping with two young women (page 40) suggests the existence in Ireland of an ascetic practice favored by an early Christian sect and by Robert d'Arbrissel, the founder of the Abbey of Fontevrault.¹

**Pilgrimage.**—The Irish passion for pilgrimage lasted from the sixth to at least the ninth century. The subject is well-addressed in the Gaelic *Life of St. Columba*, *Lismore Lives*, lines 698–720, and in Plummer's edition of Bede, volume 2, page 170. In the present work, we read not only of pilgrimages to Glastonbury and Rome, but also to places within Ireland, such as Ferns and Rathen. A pilgrimage to Maelruain's grave is suggested on page 26. However, the great religious migration from Ireland to the European Continent, which was prevalent in the eighth and following centuries, was viewed with disapproval by Maelruain and the elders <note>original: sruithi; sages or senior monks</note> whom he consulted.²

**Collection and Veneration of Relics.**—Relics were not only worn on the person but were essential for the consecration of churches. The practice of gathering them is illustrated here by the story of Onchu and Maedóc (page 70), the tale of Patrick's leper, Comlach (page 204), and the account of Adamnán's collection (page 210). They were sometimes kept in gold shrines (page 20). Special notice is given to the relics of Saints Peter and Paul (pages 46, 220), Thomas (page 166), Martin (page 144), Patrick (page 204), Columb Cille (page 156), and the author of the Martyrology (page 274). A special feast of holy relics is set for October 1st; however, it is not clear from the commentary <note>term: scholium; a marginal note or explanatory comment</note> on page 220 where this feast was celebrated. The relics "consecrated to Michael" (page 12) may have been the contents of a reliquary in the monastery of Tallaght.

**Veneration of Crosses.**—This seems implied in the story about Hua Suanaig's cross (page 466), and in the poem cited above on page 24, sections 2 and 4. Regarding the "cloister behind the circle of crosses"—

## (b) *Superstitions and Folklore*.

Idolatry <note>original: *idoladrad*</note> is referred to on p. 74, in the case of the Roman virgin Juliana; and the Gaulish idol from whose priest Saint Martin was saved is mentioned on p. 288. But these are foreign instances. The oldest evidence that the Irish worshipped idols <note>original: *idula*</note> is contained in Saint Patrick’s *Confession*, Book of Armagh, folio 24b. In the curious passage cited from *F* <note>likely referring to a specific manuscript or "Félire" source</note>, below on p. 186, an Irish idol, Cermand Cestach, worshipped at Clogher, is described as being a gilded stone. Compare the accounts of Cenn (or Crom) Crúaich, in the *Tripartite Life*, p. 90, and the *Dindsenchas* <note>a collection of lore regarding the origins of place-names</note>, nos. 85, 149. His twelve sub-gods were probably fetish-stones, and the persistence of stone-worship in Ireland is proved by the expression "rock of adoration" <note>original: *ail adrada*</note> in the Brehon Laws, iv. 146, l. 16.^1 Other superstitions, which obviously originated in the times of savage heathenism, are exemplified by the three stories of miraculous impregnation—the birth of Ciarán of Saiger from a star (p. 86); that of Fínán Camm from a golden salmon^2 (p. 112); and that of Báithín from a sprig of cress, "covered with male seed" <note>original Latin: *semine virili cooperta*</note> (p. 134). As to the origin of such stories from an early theory of conception, see Dr. J. G. Frazer, in the *Fortnightly Review* for September, 1905, pp. 455–457. 

Here, too, may be mentioned the cure of leprosy by the blood of innocent children (p. 46): the tale of Fuinche the Rough and her miraculous dive under Lough Erne (p. 50) when she emerged, like Glaucus, covered with shells and seaweed.^3 The story of Lí-bán (or Muirgein) the mermaid (p. 52) caught in a fisherman’s net: the legends about Saint Brigit^4 (pp. 64, 66), especially the incident of the column of fire flaming from her head: the legend of Sillán of the deadly Hair (p. 206): the prevention of decay by healing (that is, magical) herbs (p. 246): and the exchange of diseases (p. 4).

^2 The Norsemen also had tales of men born of fishes; see S. Bugge, *The Home of the Eddic Poems*, p. 113, note 1. The exchange of names as a token of brotherly union (p. 224) is a practice which Captain Cook found in Tahiti, and which was also common among North American Indians. There is also the belief in shape-shifting evidenced by the tale of Ríóc and Drusticc (p. 238, note 1). Such superstitions may well have existed in a society where infants were exposed <note>abandoned or left outdoors to die</note> (p. 180), children were sacrificed (note 2), and women were driven to battle (note 3) (p. 210). The strange thing is that these have been recorded in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries by scribes who presumably believed what they wrote down. The raids of the Vikings, the Anglo-Norman invasion, and the constant inter-tribal wars account for some, but not all, of the deterioration of the medieval Gaels. "Christians in name, but pagans in reality" <note>original: *Christiani nomine, re pagani*</note>, as Saint Bernard says—without much exaggeration—of the contemporary Irish in his life of Malachi O’Morgair.

Six or seven other bits of folklore may now be briefly mentioned:
*   The weekdays on which the earth, sun, moon, and man were respectively created (p. 2), derived, of course, from Genesis 1.
*   The introduction of wheat, rye, and bees into Ireland (p. 112).
*   The church and tree which could not be found, even though the tree was seen and the bell was heard from the plain (p. 130).
*   The wondrous yew tree of Mughna (p. 258).
*   The bird bewailing one saint and singing to another for a hundred and fifty years (pp. 56, 158).
*   The "unboilable" ducks of St. Colmán’s church (p. 228).
*   The effect of an undeserved curse (p. 157).
*   The Devil’s knees "backwards" <note>original: *à rebours*</note> (p. 154).
*   The road-demon (p. 222).
*   The nurse of the Fians <note>The Fianna; legendary bands of warriors in Irish mythology</note> (p. 112).
*   The practice of giving names to a child based on words that were uttered or events which occurred on or about its birthday (Féchín, p. 48; Mo-ling, p. 150; Gillán, p. 220; Molua mac ocháe, p. 180; Cuimmín, p. 242). 

Examples in the *Mabinogion* <note>A collection of medieval Welsh legends</note> of names given in this way are Pryderi, Math son of Mathonwy, Dylan Eilton, Llew law gyffes, and Taliesin. Every scholar will also remember the origin ascribed to the name <term>Odysseus</term> <note>original: *Ὀδυσσεύς*</note>, meaning "man of wrath," in the *Odyssey*, book 19, lines 406–409 (note 4).

### (c) Legal Antiquities.

**The symbolical sod.**—Sods of earth, like branches, are used as symbols in the transfer of land (note 5). On page 13, the archangel Michael casts a sod from heaven to Maelruain as a sign that he might acquire land.

property at Tallaght. Compare the sea-god Triton’s gift to the Argonaut Euphêmos of a clod of Libyan earth.

*The four chief laws (cána) of Ireland*: said (p. 210) to be: not to kill clerics, not to kill women, not to steal cattle <note>original: "kine"</note>, and not to work on Sunday. The penalties <note>original: "sanctions"</note> are not mentioned.

*The honour-price of a provincial king, p. 88.* The Irish word *enecland*, rendered by "honour-price," literally means "face-plate." It is a compound of *enech* ("face" or "honour") and *cland*, borrowed from the Low-Latin *planta* ("a flat board or plank" <note>original: "tabula plana, asser"</note>, according to the scholar Ducange). That a gold plate the size of the face was anciently given as compensation for an insult to a king has been proved by Zimmer in Kuhn’s *Zeitschrift* <note>A German academic journal</note> xxxvi. 426.

*The punishment of expulsion from the tribe* is inflicted (p. 466) for murdering persons under a saint’s protection. A man so expelled was called *écland* ("clanless"), from the negative prefix *an-* and *cland*, borrowed (like the Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *plant*) from the Latin *planta* <note>meaning a sprout or offshoot</note>.<insert>1</insert>

*The punishment of death by a hill-fire.*—This, according to the legend on page 98, was inflicted upon a perjured harlot. Her unchastity, rather than her perjury, was the crime. Thus in the *Battle of Cnucha* (from the manuscript *Lebor na hUidre* 41b), when Murní’s father found her pregnant, he "told his people to burn her" <note>original: "asbert fria muntir a breoad"</note>. Similarly, in the tale of Corc mac Lugdach (from the *Book of Leinster* 287b 7), it is said of the Gaels of Scotland <note>original: "Alba"</note>: "it was their custom at first that any damsel who indulged in lust contrary to her compact should be burnt."<insert>2</insert>

Having thus described the manuscripts on which the present edition of the *Martyrology* is founded; noticed its author; considered the characteristics of the language as they relate to the date of its composition; explained the meter in which it is written; given some account of its contents; and indicated the passages in the Irish prefaces and scholarly notes <note>original: "scholia"</note> which throw light on medieval religious practices, superstitions, folklore, and legal antiquities, I have now to express my thanks to the Council of the Henry Bradshaw Society for printing so costly and troublesome a book. In doing so, they help the young School of Irish Learning in its effort to promote the study of the ancient Irish language and literature. Lastly, my heartiest thanks are due to Professor Strachan and the Rev. Charles Plummer for reading proofs and making corrections and valuable suggestions.

# THE PREFACE.

### I.

## THE SPECKLED BOOK <note>original: *Lebar Brecc*; a famous 15th-century Irish manuscript containing religious and hagiographical texts.</note>.

Page 75a. Four things are required for every work of art <note>original: *elathain*; can refer to a craft, science, or literary composition</note>: namely, place, time, person, and the cause of invention.

It is worth knowing why "place" should be asked for first, "time" in the second place, "person" in the third place, and the "cause of invention" at the end.

The reason "place" comes first is because places—that is, the primary locations—are measured in relation to cities and churches, and honor is due to them.

Times, however, are measured in relation to kings and territories. Therefore, "time" is the second place.

"Person" is in the third place because the author of every work of art comes from either the church or the laity.

The "cause" follows, because the poets found a reason for precedence <unclear>meretrix</unclear>. <note>The original text here is obscure. It may be a distorted reference to Boethius’ *Consolation of Philosophy*, where Philosophy calls the Muses "theatrical courtesans" (Latin: *scenicas meretriculas*).</note>

Or, alternatively, the sequence of the philosophers is followed here: "place" first, because place is corporeal. "Time" in the second place, because it is incorporeal. "Person" in the third place, because a person consists of both body and non-body <note>i.e., soul</note>. Then the "cause of invention" follows, as he said <note>original: *sicut dixit*</note>.

Or, it is the order of the creation of the elements that is followed: "place" first, because the earth was made on Tuesday. "Time" in the second place, because the sun and moon were made on Wednesday, and it is by them that times are measured. "Person" in the third place, because man was made on Friday. The "cause," however, is placed last because on Saturday God blessed the creatures and revealed the reason for their creation.

Now, the "time" in which Oengus <note>Oengus the Culdee, the 8th-century saint and author of this Martyrology.</note> composed the Calendar <note>original: *Félire*</note> was the time of Aed Ordníge, son of Niall Frossach, for it was he who held the sovereignty of Ireland...

<margin>Oengus, moreover, was the son of Oengoband, son of Oiblein, son of Fidrui, son of Diarmuit, son of Ainmire, son of Cellar, son of Oengus, son of Natsluaig, son of Coelbad, son of Cruindbadrai, son of Echu Cobai.</margin>

# TWO IRISH PREFACES.
## I.
### THE SPECKLED BOOK.

Four things are required for every work of art: namely, a Place and a Time, an Author and a Cause of invention.

It is worth knowing why Place should be required at the beginning, Time in the second place, Author in the third place, and Cause of invention *at the end* <note>original: "in fine"</note>.

This is why Place is foremost: because it is by cities and churches that places (that is, chief places) are estimated, and reverence is shown to them.

Times are then estimated by kings and peoples. The second place is given to these.

Author, however, is in the third place, for the inventor of every work of art belongs either to the Church or to the laity.

Cause follows afterward, for the cause of precedence has been established by the poets...

Alternatively, it follows the logic of the philosophers: namely, Place is foremost because Place is corporeal <note>physical or having a body</note>. Time is in the second place because it is incorporeal <note>having no physical body</note>. Author is in the third place because he consists of both body and non-body <note>soul</note>. Cause of invention follows then, *as he said* <note>original: "sicut dixit"</note>.

Or, it follows the order of the creation of the elements. Place is foremost, for it was on a Tuesday that the earth was made. Time is in the second place, for it was on a Wednesday that the sun and moon were made, and by them times are measured. Author is in the third place, for it was on a Friday that man was made. Cause, however, is at the end, for it was on a Saturday that God blessed the elements and revealed the cause of their invention.

Now, this is the time at which Oengus¹ composed the Martyrology: namely, the time of Aed the Dignified, son of Niall.

¹ Oengus, then, son of Oengoba, son of Oiblén, son of Fidrue, son of Diarmait, son of Ainmire, son of Cellar, son of Oengus, son of Natsluaig, son of Crundbadrai, son of Eochaid Coba. <note>This lineage traces Oengus back through several generations of Irish ancestry.</note>

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS: PROLOGUE

...after Donnchad son of Domnall, because Oengus comes into the first prologue of the *Martyrology* <note>original: *Félire*</note> following the death of Donnchad.

However, Oengus first revealed the *Martyrology* to Fothad of the Canon when Aed went [on] an expedition to Dun Cuair on the border of Meath <note>original: *Mide*</note> and Leinster <note>original: *Laigen*</note>, and when the clergy of Ireland went with him, led by Connmach, the successor of Patrick. It was on that expedition that the clergy of Ireland were exempted from military service and hosting, for it was Fothad of the Canon who delivered the judgment by which the churches of Ireland were freed, as he said:

The Church of the living God, leave to her what is hers,
Let her right be apart, as it was best observed,
Every true monk who is faithful to his conscience,
To the church to which he is bound, let him serve like any slave.
Every person free from vows after that, who is without law or obedience,
Is permitted to go to the battle of noble Aed, son of Niall.
This is the proper rule, neither too much nor too little,
Let everyone serve God's servant <note>meaning the Church or the clergy</note> without blemish and without death.
->The Church of the living God.<-

Aed Oirdnide <note>Aed "the Dignified," High King of Ireland 797–819</note> then exempted the churches of Ireland and their clergy from expeditions from that time forward. Then Fothad showed the "Song of the Canon" and the "Song of Complaint" to Oengus, and they made their union there. Each of them blessed the other's art, and they left many graces upon whoever would frequently recite the *Martyrology*. These indeed are the graces of the *Martyrology*, as they are found in the final prologue of the *Martyrology* itself.

It is now to be known what meter the *Martyrology* was composed in. It is not difficult: it is *Rindard* of six syllables. What is the recognition of *Rindard*? It is not difficult: six syllables in every quarter-verse, and twelve in the half-stanza; twenty-four, however, in the full stanza. And if it be more or less, it is an error (it is a pity). *Recomarc* <note>a technical term for a specific rhyme or ending</note> moreover, is disyllabic in its endings; it is in this that Oengus composed the *Martyrology*. It is of three types: namely, "smooth" *Rindard* (that is, *Rindard* of two "heights" or stresses), *Rindard* of three stresses, and *Rindard* of four stresses.

# MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. PREFACE I.

...the Showery—for it is he who obtained the kingship of Ireland after Donnchad, son of Domnall—since Oengus begins the first prologue of the Martyrology at the time of Donnchad's death.

Now, Oengus first showed the Martyrology to Fothuth of the Canon <note>Fothadh na Canoine, a famous 9th-century churchman and advisor</note> when Aed <note>Aed Oirdnide, High King of Ireland</note> had gone on the military expedition of Dún Cuair on the border of Meath and Leinster. The clergy of Ireland had gone with him, including Conmach, the successor of St. Patrick <note>The Abbot of Armagh</note>. It was during that expedition that the clergy of Ireland were freed from military service and hosting; for it was Fothuth of the Canon who delivered the legal judgment by which Ireland's churches were exempted, as he said:

> "The Church of the living God, leave to her what is hers; let her rights be set apart as they have always best been.
> "Every true monk that exists, let it be on his pure conscience; for the Church to which he is bound, let him work like any servant.
> "Every freeman then, who is not under a monastic rule or under obedience, is permitted to go to the battle of noble Aed, son of Niall.
> "This is the right regulation, neither too much nor too little: let every servant of God<gloss>1</gloss> serve without fault and without sin."<gloss>2</gloss>

So Aed the Dignified freed the Churches of Ireland and her clergy from military hosting from that time forward. Fothuth then showed to Oengus the *Song of the Canon* and the *Song of the Complaint*; and they formed a spiritual union there. Each of them blessed the other's work of art, and they promised many graces upon anyone who should recite the Martyrology often. These truly are the graces of the Martyrology, as set forth in the final prologue (the epilogue) of the Martyrology itself.<gloss>3</gloss>

It is worth knowing, then, in what poetic metre the Martyrology was composed. The answer is *easy*: it is *Rindard* <note>A specific form of Old Irish versification</note>. What is the characteristic of *Rindard*? The answer is *easy*: there are six syllables in every quarter-line, twelve in the half-stanza, and twenty-four in the complete stanza; if there are more or less, it is considered an error. It also uses *Recomarc*, which means it has two-syllable endings at the end of the lines. It is in this metre that Oengus composed the Martyrology, using three variations: namely, "smooth" *Rindard* (which has two end-rhymes), *Rindard* with three end-rhymes, and *Rindard* with four end-rhymes.

# MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. PREFACE I.

*Rinnard* <note>A specific Irish poetic meter characterized by short lines and specific rhyme schemes.</note> with two end-rhymes, in the first place, is this, as Beccan son of Cula said—or perhaps it is Erurach of Inis Móir:
> “Good Diarmait son of Cairell: sing of a chief without slackness; no robber would turn aside <gloss>¹</gloss> his slaughter or his quickness.”

And Oengus also said:
> “On the first of March, they are not haughty when we pray to them—Senán, Moinenn, Moses, and David of Cell Muine <note>St. David of Wales.</note>.”

Now *Rinnard* of three end-rhymes is this:
> “Fland the fiery of Tara, stern king of the land of Fotla <note>An ancient name for Ireland.</note>, henceforth I believe his is the clan I would choose.”

And as Oengus also said:
> “Before the many races of men, let the preeminent King lead: Christ on the first of January underwent the Law—a high requirement!”

*Rinnard* of four end-rhymes is this, as Fothuth of the Canon said:
> “Aed the Dignified of Obach, over the monster-filled realm of Banba <note>Another poetic name for Ireland.</note>, who is better in a quarrel than the Hector of Ailech?”

And as Oengus said:
> “Flame of a splendid sun, apostle of virginal Ireland, may Patrick, with many thousands, be a shelter to our wretchedness!”

The **Place** where this work of art was created is Cúil Bennchuir in Mag Rechet, in the territory of Húi Failgi <note>Modern Offaly.</note>, regarding its beginning. However, the greater part of it was written in Cluain Eidnech <note>Clonenagh.</note>, and the completion of it all was in Tamlachtu Librén <note>Tallaght.</note>, as some say.

Its **Author** was Oengus, son of Oengoba, son of Oiblén, of the community of Cluain Eidnech.

It was composed in the **Time** of Cobthach Coelbreg <note>This likely refers to a historical era or a specific king's reign.</note>.

This is the **Cause** <note>The "Occasion" or inspiration for the work.</note>. Once Oengus went to Cúil Bennchor in Mag Rechet. He saw a grave there, and the entire space between heaven and the ground over the grave was full of angels. So he asked the priest of the church: “Who has been buried in that grave?” 

“A wretched old man who lived in this place,” said the priest. 

“What good did he used to do?” asked Oengus. 

“I never saw any special good done by him,” said the priest.

"What exactly was he doing?" asked Oengus.

## II.
### LAUD 610.

<margin>folio 60a, column 1</margin> Four things are sought for every work of art: namely, place, person, time, and the cause of writing. These are also to be sought for this work of art.

As for the place, it was Cuil Bendchair in Mag Rechet in the territory of Offaly, and also the kiln in Tallaght where part of it was made. Its beginning, *however*, was in Cluain Éidnech; its continuation in Cuil Bendchair; and its completion in the kiln at Tallaght.

The cause, *moreover*, was this: One time Oengus happened to travel [from Dysert Enos] in Munster to Cuil Bendchair while on his way to accept Maelruain of Tallaght as his spiritual director <note>original: anmcharait; literally 'soul-friend'</note>. *He saw a grave in the church, and it was full of angels above it reaching up to heaven.* Oengus then asked the priest of the church who had been buried there.

## II.

### LAUD 610 <note>Refers to the specific medieval manuscript, Laud Misc. 610, held in the Bodleian Library.</note>

Four things are required for every work of art: namely, a Place, an Author, a Time, and a Cause for writing. These, then, should be identified for this work of art.

As for the Place: first, Cúil Bennchoir in Mag Rechet in the district of Húi Failgi; also, some of it was composed in the kiln at Tamlachtu. Its beginning was in Clúain Eidnech and Cúil Bennchoir, and its completion was in the kiln at Tamlachtu.

Now the Author is named Oengus, son of Oengoba, son of Oeblén, son of Fidrue, son of Diarmait, son of Ainmire, son of Cellar, son of Oengus, son of Natsluaig, son of Coelbad, son of Crund-badrai, son of Eochaid Coba, son of Lugaid, son of Ross, son of Imchath, son of Feidlimid, son of Cass, son of Fiachra Araide, from whom <note>original: "à quo"</note> the Dál n-Araide <note>A dynastic group in ancient Ulaid (Ulster).</note> descend.

This, then, is the Time at which it was composed: the time of Aed the Dignified, for it was he who took the kingdom of Ireland after Donnchad; Oengus begins the first prologue of the *Martyrology* after Donnchad's death.

Now this is the Cause. Once upon a time, Oengus traveled from Disert Oengusa in Munster to Cúil Bennchuir, intending to ask Maelruain of Tamlachtu to be his soul-friend <note>original: "soulfriend"; a spiritual director or confessor.</note>. He saw a grave in the church, and the space all over it was filled with angels reaching up to heaven. So Oengus asked the priest of the church, "Who has been buried there?"

"There was a certain wretched old lay-monk <note>original: *athlaech*; literally an 'ex-layman' or someone who took up religious life late in life</note> in the place," said the priest.

"What good did he do?" asked Oengus.

"We did not truly see him do any good," the priest replied, "except for reciting the names of the saints of the world when lying down and when rising, as is the custom of such old lay-monks."

"O God of Heaven!" said Oengus, "Whoever would compose a poetic tribute of praise to the saints, great would be his reward."

And so, he began the *Félire* <note>The Martyrology</note> right there at that moment; however, it was finished in Tallaght <note>original: *Tamlachtain*</note>.

There are twenty-four syllables in every stanza; if there be more or less, it is an error.

Oengus first revealed the *Félire* to Fothad of the Canon when he went on the hosting <note>a military expedition</note> of Dún Cuair. The clergy of Ireland were there with him, along with Connmach, the successor of Patrick. It was during that expedition that the clergy were exempted from military service, for it was Fothad who delivered the judgment by which the churches of Ireland were freed, as he himself said:

<margin>folio 60a, 2</margin>
> The Church of the living God: leave to her what is hers;
> Let her right be set apart, as it was best observed.
> Every true monk who exists, according to his clear conscience,
> To the church to which he belongs, let him serve as any laborer.
> Every person free from vows after that, who is under no rule or obedience,
> It is permitted that they go to the battle of noble Aed [son of Niall].
> [This is the right rule: neither too much] nor too little;
> Let every servant of God serve without blemish and without death.
>
> The Church.

Then Fothad showed the *Song of the Canon* and the *Song of the Complaint* to Oengus, and they made their union <note>a formal spiritual alliance</note> there. Each of them blessed the other's work, and they left many graces upon anyone who would recite it frequently. Indeed, there are many graces attached to the *Martyrology* itself, as is recounted in the final prologue.

That Oengus, moreover, was a humble and lowly servant to God. This is how he used to sing his psalms while he was at Dysert Enos <note>original: *Disiurt Oengusa*</note>: fifty psalms in the river with a withe <note>a flexible branch or rope</note> around his neck tied to a tree; fifty more under the tree itself; and fifty in his oratory.

4. God.

7. For "whoever would recite it."

"A certain wretched former layman <note>original: "ex-layman"; referring to a person who has left secular life to live as a penitent or monk</note> who lived in this place," said the priest.

"What good has he done?" asked Oengus.

"Truly, we did not see him do any good," the priest replied, "except that upon lying down and rising up, he would recite the names of the saints of the world, as is the custom of former laymen."

"O God of heaven," said Oengus, "whoever should compose a song of praise for the saints, great would be his reward!"

So then he began the *Martyrology* <note>A calendar of martyrs and saints arranged by their feast days</note> at once. However, it was completed in Tamlachtu <note>Modern Tallaght, near Dublin</note>.

There are twenty-four syllables in every quatrain <note>A four-line stanza</note>, and if there are more or less, it is an error.

Oengus first showed the *Martyrology* to Fothuth of the Canon when Fothuth went on the military expedition <note>original: "hosting"</note> of Dún Cuair with the clergy of Ireland. They were accompanied by Connmach, a successor of Saint Patrick. It was during that expedition that the clergy were freed from the obligation of military service, for it was Fothuth who passed the judgment by which the churches of Ireland were exempted, as he himself said:

> "The Church of the living God, leave to her what is hers: let her rights be set apart as they have best been established.
> 
> "Every true monk that exists, let it be on his pure conscience; let him work like any servant for the church to which he is bound.
> 
> "Every freeman then, who is without monastic rule and without obedience, is permitted to go to the battle of noble Aed, son of Niall.
> 
> "This is the right regulation, neither too great nor too small: let every servant of God serve without fault and without sin."

Then Fothuth showed Oengus the *Song of the Canon* and the *Song of the Complaint*, and they formed a bond there. Each of them blessed the other's work of art, and they promised many graces to anyone who should recite the *Martyrology* often.

Indeed, many are the graces of the *Martyrology*, as is recounted in the final prologue (the epilogue).

That Oengus, then, was a humble, lowly servant to God. It was his custom to chant his psalms in this way while he was at Disert Oengusso <note>Oengus's Hermitage</note>: fifty psalms in the river with a willow-withe <note>A flexible branch used as a rope</note> around his neck and tied to a tree; fifty under the tree; and fifty in his cell.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. PREFACE.

Afterward, he <note>Oengus</note> approached Maelruain so that he might be accepted as his spiritual advisor <note>original: anmcharait; literally "soul-friend"</note>.

Now, it was this same Maelruain who had determined that he would not accept any land in Tallaght <note>original: Tamlachtain</note> until Michael <note>the Archangel</note>, with whom he shared a special friendship, should accept it. <insert>And it is because of that friendship</insert> that there are relics consecrated to Michael in Tallaght. It happened once after that resolution that an epistle and a sod of earth were sent together from Heaven to Maelruain, instructing that the land should be taken; and it was then that Tallaght was established.

Afterward, Oengus came to him in the guise of a laborer <note>original: moghad; a servant or slave</note>, and Maelruain assigned him the task of tending the kiln. He took that work upon himself, and it is told that the corn-stalks grew through his hair because of the intensity of his service.

It happened then that a young boy was studying his psalms with Maelruain. One time, when the cleric went to the church, he commanded the boy to memorize his lesson so that it would be ready to recite upon his return. However, the boy ran away because he did not think he could do it, and he happened to go to the kiln where Oengus was. Oengus asked him what was the matter. The boy told him. "Come here," said Oengus, "and lay your head on my knee and sleep." It was done accordingly. The boy woke up afterward. Then Oengus said, "Recite your lesson, my son." The boy then recited even more than the assigned lesson. "What is this, my son?" asked Oengus. "I have all the learning now," said the boy. "Go now," said Oengus, "and do not admit who visited you."

The boy then went and recited the lesson for Maelruain. Maelruain noticed that he knew much more than required and asked him, "Who visited you, my son?" "I do not know," said the boy. "That is a lie," said the cleric, "tell me quickly." "I do not know," said the boy, "except that I happened upon the kiln and I slept with my head on the knee of the man at the kiln." "That is true," said Maelruain. "That man is Oengus, the Prophesied One."

Maelruain then rushed out suddenly, wearing only one of his sandals, and reached the kiln. "Well, Oengus," he said, "it was not right for you to deceive us, for it would be more fitting for us to serve you than for you to serve us."

Maelruain then took him away with great honor, and Oengus knelt to him, and they made their union—a union in Heaven and on earth. And that is how Oengus was revealed to Maelruain.

# MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. PREFACE II.

Afterward, he traveled to Maelruain so that he might have him as a <term>soul-friend</term> <note>Old Irish: *anmchara*; a spiritual director or confessor</note>.

Now, it was this Maelruain who had decided that he would not take possession of the land in <term>Tamlachtu</term> <note>Modern Tallaght, near Dublin</note> until Michael the Archangel, with whom he shared a friendship, should claim it first. Because of that agreement, there are relics consecrated to Michael in Tamlachtu. Once, after that decision was made, it happened that a letter, along with a piece of turf, was cast down from heaven to Maelruain as a sign that he should take the land; and that is how Tamlachtu was acquired.

Afterward, Oengus came to him in the guise of a slave, and Maelruain entrusted Oengus with the care of the corn-drying kiln. He took up that work, and it is told that the blades of corn actually grew through his hair because of the great intensity of his service.¹

It happened there that a little boy was studying his psalms with Maelruain. On one occasion, the cleric went to the church and ordered the boy to learn his lesson by heart, so that he would be ready to recite it before him. The boy, however, ran away because he did not think he could do it, and he came to the kiln to find Oengus. Oengus asked him, "What is the matter?" The boy told him. "Come here," said Oengus, "and put your head on my knee and sleep." It was done as he said. Afterward, the boy woke up. Then Oengus said: "Recite your lesson, my son." The boy then recited even more than the assigned lesson. "What is this, my son?" asked Oengus. "I have learned the whole reading," said the boy. "Go now," said Oengus, "and do not reveal whom you have visited."

So the boy went and recited the lesson to Maelruain. Maelruain perceived that he knew more than expected and asked him: "Whom did you visit, my son?" "I do not know," said the boy. "That is a lie indeed," said the cleric, "tell me quickly." "I do not know," said the boy, "except that I went to the kiln, and I fell asleep with my head on the knee of the kiln-man." "That is true," said Maelruain: "that man is Oengus, the prophesied one!"

Then Maelruain rushed out so suddenly that he had only one shoe on, and he sought out the kiln. "Well, O Oengus," he said, "it was not right for you to deceive us, for it would be more fitting for us to be serving you than for you to serve us."

Then Maelruain brought Oengus with him with great honor, and Oengus knelt to him, and they made their union—a bond recognized in heaven and on earth. So it was then that Oengus was revealed to Maelruain.

¹ The same is said of Niall: <term>the wood grew through his head</term> <note>original: *ind fídbað roás triana chend*</note> *Book of Leinster* 33b, 38.

<meta>This page continues the introductory preface (Remfócul) to the Félire Oengusso (The Martyrology of Oengus), focusing on the technical poetic structure of the work.</meta>

<page-num>14</page-num>
<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. PREFACE.</header>

It is to be known, then, what specific type of meter was used to compose the *Félire* <note>original: "Feilire"; a calendar of saints' feast days</note>. It is not difficult to answer: it is *Rindard* <note>a specific Irish syllabic meter</note>. It is also to be known what the recognition of *Rindard* itself is. It is not difficult: there are six syllables in its quarters <note>lines</note>, twelve in its half-stanzas, and twenty-four in its complete stanzas; and if there be more or less, it is a fault.

Furthermore, there is a "final rhyme" <note>original: "recomarc"</note> in its stanzas; *re chomraic* means "of two syllables" <note>referring to the two-syllable ending of each line</note>. It was upon a particular variety of this meter called *réidrindard* <note>"smooth rindard"</note>—specifically *rindard* of two "heights" <note>referring to the number of rhyming line-endings</note>—that Oengus composed the *Félire*. There are three types of this meter:

First, *réidrindard* of two heights, as Becán said, or as the Over-king of Inis Mór said:

> Diarmait the good, son of Cerball,
> Without a leader, without weakness;
> May no outlaw hear
> Of his slaying or his defeat.

*And as Oengus said:*

> On the *calends* <note>the first day</note> of the month of March,
> They are not too proud for us to pray to them:
> Senán, Moinend, Moses,
> And David of Cill Muine <note>St. David of Wales</note>.

*And there is réidrindard of three heights, as Mael Mura of Fahan sang:*

> Fiery Flann of Tara,
> Strong king of the land of Ireland;
> From of old I believe
> It is his clan I would choose.

*And as Oengus said:*

> Before the numerous race of men, etc.

There is also *Rindard* of four heights, as Fothad of the Canon said:

> Aed the Dignified of Obaig,
> Over the kingdom of famous Ireland;
> Who is better in a grudge
> Than Hector of Ailech?

The preface in the second manuscript <note>R²</note> ends thus:

*As Oengus said:*

> Flame of a splendid sun,
> Apostle of virgin Ireland:
> Patrick with a multitude of thousands,
> May he be a protection for our misery.

There is alliteration <note>original: "fidrad cubaid"</note> between the beginnings of the stanzas and the ends of the preceding stanzas.

> Let him come before us on a laborious path,
> With the noble ones of the fierce race of the Gaels,
> To the delightful, ship-filled house
> Which the family of high Eochaid occupied.

<meta>This page continues the technical preface to the Martyrology of Oengus, focusing on the poetic structure and metrical rules used in the work.</meta>

# MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. PREFACE II.

It is worth knowing what kind of <term>metre</term><note>The rhythmic structure of the poetry.</note> the <term>Martyrology</term><note>A catalog or list of saints and martyrs arranged by their feast days.</note> was composed in. The answer is simple: *Rinnard*. It is also worth knowing how to recognize the *rinnard* style itself. Simply put: there are six syllables in each of its quarters (lines), twelve syllables in each of its half-stanzas, and twenty-four syllables in its complete four-line stanzas. If there are more or fewer syllables than this, it is considered an error.

There is also a requirement for the <term>rhyme-structure</term><note>original: "Recomarc"</note> at the ends of its lines; specifically, they must be disyllabic <note>Words of two syllables</note>. <term>Oengus</term> composed the <term>Martyrology</term> in a specific variation of this metre called "smooth *rinnard*." There are three species of this metre:

First, "smooth *rinnard*" with only two end-rhymes, as <term>Becan</term>—or perhaps <term>Erurech</term> of <term>Inis Mór</term>—said:

> "Good <term>Diarmait</term>, son of <term>Cerball</term>, sing of the leader without laziness: no robber could withstand his slaughter or his quickness."

And as <term>Oengus</term> wrote:

> "On the first of March, they are not haughty when we pray to them: <term>Senán</term>, <term>Moinenn</term>, <term>Moses</term>, and <term>David</term> of <term>St. Davids</term> <note>original: "Cell Muine," the Irish name for St Davids in Wales</note>."

Second, there is smooth *rinnard* with three end-rhymes, as <term>Mael-Maire</term> of <term>Fathain</term> sang:

> "<term>Flann</term> the fiery of <term>Tara</term>, stern king of the land of <term>Ireland</term> <note>original: "Fotla," a poetic name for Ireland</note>; from now on, I believe his is the clan I would choose."

And as <term>Oengus</term> wrote:

> "Before the many races of men," etc.

Third, there is *rinnard* with four end-rhymes, as <term>Fothuth</term> of the <term>Canon</term> said:

> "<term>Aed</term> the Dignified of <term>Obach</term>, over the realm of monster-filled <term>Ireland</term> <note>original: "Banba," another poetic name for Ireland</note>: who is better in a fight than this <term>Hector</term> of <term>Ailech</term>?"

As <term>Oengus</term> wrote:

-> Flame of a splendid sun, apostle of virginal <term>Ireland</term>, <-
-> <term>Patrick</term> with many thousands, be a shelter to our wretchedness! <-

There is also a harmonious connection <note>A poetic device where the first word of a stanza echoes the last word of the previous one</note> between the beginnings of the stanzas and the ends of the preceding stanzas:

> "Let him lead us on the difficult way, along with the nobles of the fierce <term>Irish</term> <note>original: "Goedel"</note> race, to the good, delightful, heavenly mansion which the tribe of high <term>Eochaid</term> has claimed."

21. I have commemorated <note>original: *Imrordus*</note> the royal host <note>original: *rígraíd*</note>
around the King above the clouds,
some upon beautiful feast days,
others under vehement tears.

25. May it profit me for my comfort,
for I am a wretched, weary one,
the course which this host has run
according to the commandments of this King!

29. They have hewn out roads
which fools do not consider easy;
before going to the Kingdom,
they have suffered tribulations.

33. They have been impaled before hosts,
and they with their virtues;
they have been crushed in assemblies,
they have been slain before kings.

37. They have been torn with spear-points;
they have been racked in pieces;
they have been burnt over fires,
on white-hot gridirons.

41. They have been cast to wild beasts
by merciless ruffians;
they were scourged—a hard course—
through the fiery furnaces.

45. They have been brought out of dungeons and afterwards put on crosses; the pagan hosts reviled them after flaying them with the edges of swords.

49. They were joyful at every violent death, even those of excessive horror; they used to endure many tortures with splendid valor <note>original: "án croan"</note> before this.

53. They all have suffered—this lamentable thing—a great deed of valor, to earn a true reward from Jesus, the Son of Mary.

57. Woe to everyone who has killed them, who has dared to slay them! After their short period of labor <note>original: "sáethur gairsom"</note>, they are now ageless, just like Him <note>referring to Christ</note>.

61. The great kings of the pagans wail forever in the burning fires; but the hosts of Jesus, never to fall again, are joyful after their triumph.

***
