# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS: PROLOGUE

<note>The following verses are presented in the original Old Irish with a modernized English translation. The poet uses a rhythmic, four-line stanza structure typical of early Irish verse.</note>

65. The champions <note>original: *chóraíd*; here referring to the pagan persecutors</note> by whom the saints were slain, along with the abundance of their cruelty—their splendor has perished, and their strongholds are now desolate.

69. These are they who, after their afflictions <note>original: *sáethaib*; trials or labors</note>, have reached the Kingdom. Their graveyards are unconcealed <note>original: *cen táde*; without secrecy, meaning they are famous pilgrimage sites</note>; they are the assembly-places <note>original: *bordgala*; a difficult term likely meaning a place of great gathering or fame</note> of thousands.

73. The soldiers who crucified them, though they were strong in battle, their pains are now great, and their graves are unknown.

77. Not so are Jesus's soldiers: they have reached a radiant homestead. After them, their devout bodies rest in shrines of sparkling gold.

81. They are magnificent before the multitudes—Christ’s royal folk who suffered after their wounds. As for the kings of the world who followed their own desires, power has truly passed away from them.

85. Herod and Pilate, under whom our Lord <note>original: *Fíada*; an archaic Irish term for God or Lord</note> suffered: their powers have been ended, and their pains abide forever.

***

### Critical Notes on the Text
<note>These notes refer to the variant readings found in the original manuscripts (labeled L, LB, B, F, etc.) provided in the footer of the page.</note>

<margin>65. *chóraíd*: Variants include *coraith* and *choraid*. This refers to the "champions" of paganism.</margin>
<margin>69. *sáethaib*: One manuscript (B) reads *iarnar-rethib*, meaning "after their courses/runs."</margin>
<margin>73. *mílid*: The soldiers or executioners. The text notes that despite their earthly strength (*bailce bressa*), they are now forgotten.</margin>
<margin>77. *memraib*: Shrines or reliquaries. Derived from the Latin *memoria*.</margin>
<margin>81. *rígrad*: Literally "king-folk" or "royal line," referring to the martyrs as the nobility of Heaven.</margin>
<margin>85. *Fíada*: An Old Irish name for the Deity, often translated as "The Lord" or "The Witness."</margin>

### MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS: PROLOGUE

89. Jesus, though He was crucified, is our Lord and our champion <note>original: *ngérat*</note>. Over every element that He created, He has arisen as a perfect king.

93. Though Nebuchadnezzar "the Red," the very valiant, was once king of the world, since he departed this life with his household, his sovereignty has been destroyed.

97. Not so is Old-Paul <note>Saint Paul the Hermit, traditionally considered the first Christian hermit</note> the monk, whose hermitage is gloomy; yet by his holy name, endowed with great grace, every happy host is blessed <note>original: *séntae*, meaning sained or hallowed</note>.

101. Though a sword cut down the mighty John the Baptist, he has been magnified here in this world, and in God’s kingdom, he has been crowned as a king.

105. Herod and his queen, by whom John was slain amidst many shouts of triumph <note>original: *ilach*, meaning paeans or cries of exultation</note>—neither the earth nor the delightful heavens have received him. It is a hard path he has taken!

109. The holy name of the Apostle Peter is invoked by every synod <note>an assembly of clergy</note>. To a believer, it seems unworthy even to utter the name of Nero <note>The Roman Emperor who persecuted early Christians</note>.

<margin>113. Nero, not known is his grave: 'tis just, he was not godly: the world with a multitude of people magnifies Peter's little tomb.</margin>

<margin>117. (There is) a chief seat for Nero in the forefront of pain: Paul the Apostle—lofty pillar—attains the plains of heaven.</margin>

<margin>121. Nero's sovereignty has vanished: it is very far from this: Paul's name—lasting the choice—this is a-flowing (like a tide).</margin>

<margin>125. Though haughty was Pilate's queen out of abundance of down, her splendor has vanished since she went into a place of mold.</margin>

<margin>129. Not so is Mary the Virgin, beloved is her strong fortress: Adam's race, a lofty ambit, magnifies her, with a host of angels.</margin>

<margin>133. Though fair and many were the sons of wrathful Decius whom we love not, neither known nor very great is the name of any of them on earth.</margin>

177. Rathcroghan <note>The ancient royal seat of the kings of Connacht</note> has vanished along with Ailill, that offspring of victory: fair is the sovereignty over princes that now exists in the monastery-city of Clonmacnois.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS: PROLOGUE

<page-num>26</page-num>

205. The old cities of the pagans, where ownership was once established by long-standing custom <note>original: *rudrad* — a legal term in Irish law referring to the acquisition of property through long-term undisturbed possession</note>, are now desolate and without worship, like the ruins of Lugaid's House-site.

209. The small cells <note>original: *locáin* — small monastic settlements or hermitages</note> that were first occupied only by pairs and trios of monks, have now become "Romes" <note>original: *rúama* — great monastic centers or sanctuaries, named after the prestige of Rome</note> with great gatherings, with hundreds and with thousands of people.

213. Heathendom has been destroyed, though it was once beautiful and widespread; the kingdom of God the Father has filled heaven, earth, and the sea.

217. We have something even closer before our eyes—a holy psalm of God's power, a vigorous speech—here today at the end of the world.

221. Donnchad <note>Donnchad mac Domnaill, High King of Ireland (died 797)</note> the wrathful, the ruddy, the chosen; or victorious Bran of the Barrow <note>Bran Ardchenn, King of Leinster (died 795)</note>; visiting their tombs does not take away the weariness of my weakness.

225. But Mael Ruáin <note>Saint Mael Ruáin of Tallaght (died 792), founder of the Culdee movement and mentor to the author</note> after his pious service—the great sun over the southern plain of Meath—at his pure grave, the sigh of every heart is healed.

***

**A. The Calends of January <note>January 1st</note>**
Before the multitudinous race of men,

The great martyrdom of Rhodon
with his retinue, a fair moon;

**D. The Day before the Nones <note>January 4th</note>**
The holy death of Aquilinus
with a troop that was most strong;
in Christ’s blood, by means of their martyred bodies,
they washed their robes. <note>A reference to Revelation 7:14, where saints wash their robes white in the blood of the Lamb.</note>

**January 5: The Nones**
The calling of Simeon <note>original: *Semeoin*</note> the sage <note>original: *srotha*</note>
unto Christ—a form that may purify us;
she was a fair sun, a fresh champion:
Ciar, daughter of Dub-re.

**January 6: 8 days before the Ides**
He ran to his King—a right noble choice!
Julian, a rock of purity;
it deserves no outrage, but perfect gladness:
the great baptism of Mary’s Son. <note>The Feast of the Epiphany, commemorating the Baptism of Christ.</note>

**January 7: 7 days before the Ides**
The martyrdom of Lucianus
with a great host that was most exalted;

the beginning of Jesus’s Lent. <note>Refers to the tradition of Christ's forty-day fast beginning after his baptism.</note>

**January 8: 6 days before the Ides**
The departure <note>original: *Estecht*; literally "death" or "falling asleep"</note> of Egemonius,
a bishop of high penance;

and noble Nechtan from Alba. <note>Alba is the Gaelic name for Scotland.</note>

**January 9: 5 days before the Ides**
Beautiful hostages <note>term: *hostages*; here used metaphorically for saints who have surrendered themselves to God</note> with purity
before the King whom you have mentioned:
Faelan the godly and excellent,
Felix the fair, and Vitalis.

### A. 15th day before the Kalends of February (January 18)

### E. 19th day before the Kalends of February (January 14)
The departure <note>death</note> of **Marius** and **Martha**, a married couple <note>original Latin: "conjugum"</note> whom you invoke, along with the noble feast of **Old Paul**, fair and splendid.

### *Friday, 13th day before the Kalends of February [January 20]*
<note>original: F. xiii. cal. Febr.</note>
Splendid are the four with virgins <note>original: conúagu</note> whom I join together on one festival that is holiest: my Laca, my Ecu, Sebastian, and Óenu.

<note>original: A. xi. cal. Febr.</note>
The death <note>original: Estecht; literally "departure" or "hearing"</note> of Comgall's daughters; Colmán, descendant of Béógna; Valerius without reproach; and Felix, who found a melodious visit.

The suffering <note>original: Césad; martyrdom</note> of Severianus and of Clement, whom I place together: may they protect us to the Kingdom with their bold army!

<note>original: C. ix. cal. Febr.</note>
To my soul and to my poor body, may Babylas—an abundant mass of gold—with his three little ones <note>original: dedblén; literally "weaklings," referring to his three young companions in martyrdom</note>, be a great defense against every spiritual wandering.

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [JANUARY.]</header>

### D. *January 25 (8th day before the Kalends of February)*
Not puny <note>original: "dedbul"</note> is the day—a festival whereon shouts of joy are sent forth: a swarm of followers went unto Christ, and Paul was brought into baptism <note>This refers to the Conversion of St. Paul.</note>.

### E. *January 26 (7th day before the Kalends of February)*
Mighty seems their brilliance to the King who encompasses us: the host that was slain after famine, at the suffering <note>original: "pais" (passion)</note> of Polycarp.

### F. *January 27 (6th day before the Kalends of February)*
My Lord loved Muirgein <note>Muirgein is an Irish name meaning "sea-born"; she is often identified with the mermaid Liban who was baptized.</note>, a wondrous birth with victories! Agnes <note>original: "Agnetis"</note> with ten virgins won a pure victory before kings.

### G. *January 28 (5th day before the Kalends of February)*
With Accobrán <note>An Irish saint from Kilrush.</note> from among us, the suffering of eight splendid virgins: the great host of Messorianus gained a victory with righteousness.

### A. *January 29 (4th day before the Kalends of February)*
Splendid are the bishops I have mentioned; may they protect us to our own inheritance <note>original: "ndílius"</note>: Hippolytus, Paulus, Gildas, and Constantinus.

<page-num>40</page-num>
<header>THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS. [JANUARY.]</header>

### NOTES.
1. **Resil** <note>original: *Resil*</note>—that is, before all who follow. **Law** <note>original: *recht*</note>—that is, of the circumcision.

2. **Esodir** <note>original: *Essodir*</note>. From the city of Seville <note>original: *Aspala*</note> in Spain, where he held the bishopric.
**Manchine of Airce** <note>original: *Manchine Airce*</note>—that is, Airce is a river in Laigis in western Leinster; and from it he is named because his church is situated near it—that is, the Hermitage of the Son of Ciluírn <note>original: *Disert meicc Ciluírn*</note> is its name.
**Scoithine** of House-Scoithine <note>original: *Tigh Scoithine*</note> in Slieve Mairge. It is worth knowing why he was called "Scoithine." It is not difficult: because of the "skipping" <note>original: *scothad*—a pun on his name and speed</note> of travel he used to do—that is, going to Rome in one day and coming back from it on another single day. <margin>Or he was called Scoithine for this reason: Once he happened to meet Saint Barre, and he [Scoithine] was walking on the sea while Barre was in a ship. "What causes you to walk upon the sea?" asked Barre. "It is not the sea at all, but a flowery plain," said Scoithine; and he reached down his hand and plucked a flower <note>original: *scoth*</note>, and threw it to Barre in the ship. He then asked what caused a ship to swim upon a plain? At that word, Barre stretched his hand into the sea, took a salmon out of it, and tossed it to Scoithine. So it is from that flower (*scoth*) that Scoithine is named.</margin>
Furthermore, two firm-breasted maidens used to lie beside him every night so that his battle against the Demon might be the greater, and he was rumored to be defiled because of this. So Saint Brendan came to test him, and Scoithine said: "Let the cleric lie in my bed tonight." When it reached the hour of rest, the girls came into the house where Brendan was, carrying glowing embers in their laps, and the fire did not burn them; they poured the embers out before Brendan and got into the bed with him. "What is this?" asked Brendan. "This is how we do every night," said the girls. They lay down with Brendan, but he could not sleep at all because of his lust <note>original: *élscoth*</note>. "That is imperfect, O cleric," said the girls; "he who is usually here every night feels nothing at all. Why do you not get into the tub of water, cleric, if it would make it easier for you?" Often the cleric—that is, Scoithine—would undergo this penance. "Well," said Brendan, "it is right for us to have this test; this man is better than we are." They made their unity and their covenant after that, and they parted happily <note>original: *feliciter*</note>.

3. **Findlug**—that is, Lugaid the Fair. He was a disciple and brother of Fintan, and therefore he is named with him; and he went on a pilgrimage into the north. So he is the saint in Tamlachta Findloghain in Ciannacht of Glen Geimin.
**Dun-bléisci**—that is, Flesc is the name of the river which is near the town, and it is named from it. <margin>Blesc was the name of the swineherd of the King of Húa Cuanach; it was he who was in that fort (*dun*) at first, from which it is named.</margin>

4. **They cleansed** <note>original: *docoemnagtar*</note>—that is, they washed their garments beautifully—that is, their clothes—that is, their bodies <note>original: *corpora sua*</note>.

5. **Simeon**—that is, a priest. The priest who received Christ into his arms in the Temple, and who prophesied concerning Him; who is buried in the Valley of Jehoshaphat in a basilica with Joseph, the husband of Mary. **The calling of Simeon**—that is, the monk; he rested in peace in Antioch.
**Ciar**—she is from Muscraide Thíre, and of the race of Conaire—that is, she is in Mag Escat.

6. **Julian**—that is, a virgin.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly notes on the Martyrology of Oengus for the dates January 2nd through January 5th, focusing on the hagiographies and etymologies of Irish saints.</meta>

<page-num>41</page-num>
<header>JANUARY 1-6. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

### NOTES.

2. **Mainchine of *Airca***, that is, a river in Leix in the west of Leinster; and *Airca* is a river <note>original: "et ab eo nominatur"</note> and it is named from him, because his church, named *Dísert meicc Cuilinn*, was situated near it.
***Scothíne***. Scothíne of *Tech Scothíni* in *Sliab Mairge*. It is worth knowing why he was called Scothíne. It is easy to say: it was for the shortening <note>original: "scothad"</note> of the journey which he used to make—namely, to go to Rome in one day and to return from it the next. <note>original: "Vel ideo Scothíne dictus est"</note> Or he was called Scothíne for this reason: Once he met Saint Barre (of Cork) while he was walking on the sea and Barre was in a ship. “What is the cause of your walking on the sea?” says Barre. “It is not sea at all, but a plain full of clover-blossom,” says Scothín; and his hand touches a flower <note>original: "scoth"</note>, and he throws it to Barre in the ship, and said: “What is the cause of a vessel swimming on the plain?” At that word Barre stretches his hand into the sea, takes a salmon out of it, and flings it to Scothín. So it is from that flower <term>scoth</term> that he is named Scothín.

Now two maidens with pointed breasts used to lie with him every night so that the battle with the Devil might be the greater for him.¹ And it was proposed to accuse him on that account. So Brénainn <note>Saint Brendan</note> came to test him, and Scothín said: “Let the cleric lie in my bed tonight.” So when he reached the hour of resting, the girls came into the house where Brénainn was, with their lapfuls of glowing embers in their <term>chasubles</term> <note>liturgical vestments</note>; and the fire did not burn them, and they spill the embers in front of Brénainn and go into the bed with him. “What is this?” asks Brénainn. “This is what we do every night,” say the girls. They lie down with Brénainn, and in no way could he sleep because of longing. “That is imperfect, O cleric,” say the girls: “he who is here every night feels nothing at all. Why do you not go, O cleric, into the tub of cold water if it would be easier for you? It is often that the cleric, even Scothín, visits it.” “Well,” says Brénainn, “it is wrong for us to make this test, for he is better than we are.” Thereafter they make a union and their covenant, and they part <note>original: "feliciter"</note> happily.

3. ***Findlug***, that is, Lugaid the Fair, a disciple and brother of Finntan, <note>original: "and ideo etc."</note> and for that reason, etc., so that he is a saint in *Tamlachta Findlogan* in *Ciannachta* of *Glenn Gemin*.
**Of *Dún-bléisce***, that is, <note>original: "Flesc nomen amnis etc."</note> Flesc is the name of the river, etc. Blesc was the name of the swineherd of the king of *Húi Cuanach*. It is he who dwelt in that fort at first, <note>original: "unde nominatur"</note> from which it is named.

4. ***They have washed***, that is, they washed beautifully their <term>tlachtu</term> <note>original: "i.e. corpora sua"</note>, that is, their garments—meaning their bodies.

5. ***Simeon, a priest etc.*** The calling of Simeon, etc. ***Ciar***, that is, she is in *Muscraige Tíre*, and she is of the race of Conaire²; that is, she is in *Mag Escat*.

---

¹ Robert d’Arbrissel, founder of the monastery of Fontevrault, and the early Christian sect of the Apostolici (or Apotactici) had a similar practice <note>The practice of "syneisaktism" or spiritual marriage, where men and women lived together chastely to prove their self-control</note>. See also *The Knight de la Tour Landry*, chapter 134; Dr. Todd’s *Life of Saint Patrick*, page 91; an article in the *Saturday Review* for July 13, 1867, page 65; and Yule’s *Marco Polo*, first edition, volume 2, pages 353-357.
² The hero of the *Bruden Dá Derga* <note>The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel</note>, *Revue Celtique*, volume 22.

<keywords>Saint Scothín, Saint Barre, Saint Brendan (Brénainn), asceticism, Irish hagiography, etymology, Dísert meicc Cuilinn, Sliab Mairge, syneisaktism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the calendar of saints (Félire Oengusso) for the month of January, providing hagiographical notes and genealogical details for saints celebrated between the 7th and 15th of the month.</meta>

<page-num>42</page-num>
<header>THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS. [JANUARY.]</header>

**7.** **Lucian** <note>original: Luciani</note>, a priest of Antioch, suffered martyrdom under the Emperor Maximian.
Another Lent in the winter, keeping away from every feast is proper then; the great Lent of Jesus in the spring, and the Lent of Moses in the summer yonder. <note>This verse refers to the three "Lents" or periods of fasting observed in the early Irish church.</note>

**8.** **Ercnat** from Dún dá én <note>Fort of the two birds</note> in the Wood <note>original: Fidbaid</note> in Dál Araide. Or Ercnat was a young nun who was a cook and a robe-maker for **Colum Cille** <note>St. Columba</note>; and her church is Cell Chuaca (that is, Coca) in Cairbre Ua Ciardha. However, Ercnat is her true name, meaning "embroideress." For *ercad* in Old Irish used to mean "engraving," but now it means "embroidery," for that virgin was a skilled embroideress for the making and sewing of clothes for Colum Cille and his disciples.
**Nechtan**: his kindred is from Scotland <note>original: Albain</note>; that is, from Dún Geimin in Ciannachta Glinne Geimin. Or Nechtan is in Scotland.

**9.** **Faelan** of Cluain Moescna in Fera Tulach; Calue in Uí Tortain is his church.
**Felix** the fair and **Vitalis**: two saints.

**10.** **Evil portion** <note>original: drochrann</note>: a bad part among those in the lower world <note>original: mala pars apud inferos</note>.
**Milid**: Miltiades, an Abbot of Rome. Or Melito, Bishop of Laodicea in Asia Minor. Or Milid, as Oengus says, and it may be that Diarmait was so called from this. Diarmait was the priest of Ciaran.

**11.** **From Egypt**: Christ was in Egypt for four or five years, where, as they say, on the day of his arrival into the city, all the idols there were shattered, falling so quickly to the earth. **Afrodius** was the name of the prince of that city who kindly received Christ and his parents. Why is it a festival, the coming of Christ out of Egypt, and not a festival his going into it? It is not difficult to answer: because Egypt is the same as "darkness," and it is more proper to rejoice for someone's coming out of darkness than for their going into it.

**12.** **Laidgenn**: Laidgenn son of Baeth. *Bannach* <note>the energetic</note> and *Buadach* <note>the victorious</note> are his father's names. Laidgenn was from Cluain Ferta Molua, and his grave is there.

**13.** **Sulpicius**: who wrote the books of Martin <note>St. Martin of Tours</note>.
Here is **Mochonna** of Inis Patrick.

**14.** **Glycerius**: Glycerius was a disciple and deacon of Felix the martyr, who wrote the book of Felix.
**Nola**: the city of Felix the martyr in Italy. Or the river Nola; that is, from the estuary of the Noile on the boundary of Tirconnell and Tyrone, and a river therein which settled on the bank of the stream, namely the Noili.
**Flann the Fair**: in Cuillenn near Cork.

**15.** **Maurus**: a monk and disciple of Benedict the Abbot.
**Ite** of Cell Ite in Uí Conaill Gabra in Munster, which was previously called *Deserum* <note>The Desert</note>.

7. *Of Lucianus, a priest, etc.*

*Of Jesus’s Lent.*
There is another Lent in the winter; it is proper to set a hand to every food then.
Jesus’s Lent is in the vast springtime, and Moses’s Lent is there in the summer.

<insert>² There is a similar note in the Cheltenham Manuscript, page 25, translated by O’Curry.</insert>
What is the reason that Christ’s coming out of Egypt is a festival, but His going into it is not a festival? It is easy to say: because *Egypt* <note>original Latin: Egyptus</note> is the same as *darkness* <note>original Latin: tenebrae</note>, and it is more fitting to be happy at one’s coming out of darkness than at going into it.

12. *Laidgenn*, that is, Laidgen, son of Baith. Baith Bannach Buadach ("the Victorious") is his father’s name. Laidgenn was of Cluain Ferta Molua <note>modern: Kyle, Co. Laois</note>, and his grave is there.

13. *Sulpicius*, who wrote the books about Saint Martin.
Here Mochonna of Inis Patraic <note>modern: Patrick's Island, Skerries</note> is commemorated.

Or the sage of Nola, that is, of Indber Noile on the border of Tyrconnell and Tyrone; he was a sage who lived on the bank of the river Noile.
*Flann the Fair*: in Cullenn near Cork.

...it consumed her entire side, yet no one knew of it. One day she went out, and the beetle crawled out of its hiding place behind her. The nuns saw it and killed it. ->**The Poem of Little Jesus**<-

Little Jesus <note>original: *Isucán*</note> is nursed by me in my little hermitage;
Though a cleric might have many treasures, all is a lie except Little Jesus.

The fosterling nursed by me in my house is no fosterling of a lowly churl;
Jesus is with the men of heaven against my heart every single night.

Young Little Jesus, my eternal good, to pay attention to Him is <note>original: *is*</note> no small thing;
The King who rules over all—without praying to Him, one will be sorrowful.

Noble, angelic Jesus, not some common cleric,
Is nursed by me in my little hermitage—Jesus, the son of the Hebrew woman.

Sons of lords, sons of kings, though they should come into my land,
It is not from them I expect profit; I prefer Little Jesus.

Sing a chorus, O maidens, to Him who rightfully claims your tribute;
He is in His high mansion above, though Little Jesus is in my lap.

Míde <note>Saint Ita</note>, daughter of Cenn-faelad, son of Cormac, son of Concorp, son of Conchobar, son of Conall, son of Oengus, son of Art-chorp, son of Coirpre Rigfota, son of Fiachu Suigthe, son of Fedlimid the Lawgiver. <note>This is the genealogy of Saint Ita.</note>

However, Peter and Paul came in the night after the boys were collected, to protect the beautiful, melodious children and to cure the very comely king.

> “Submit yourself to baptism,” Peter said to the king, “do not be afraid, because your healing from sin shall come from the white, lasting, pure baptism. Go to Sylvester, the abbot <note>meaning the Pope or head of the Roman church</note> of the city, and submit to his hand, for he is full of grace. To believe in the threefold Trinity is a divine deed through which you will reach heaven.”

The apostles departed after leaving these swift words. The king fulfilled everything they had declared. He recognized the form of Peter of the judgments and of Paul distinctly; when day came, he identified their countenances by pointing them out. It is from that event that the magnifying of Peter the chief apostle began in the East. Rome has belonged to him and to Paul from that time forward, free from leprosy.

**Moecca**, however, is Fechin of Fore. He was called "Fechin" for this reason: It happened that he was gnawing on a bone as a child in his mother's presence, and his mother said, "That is my little raven <term>Irish: fiachán</term>." From that, he was called Fechin. He was called **Moecca**, however, because of his "bending" <term>Irish: feacaidecht</term>, for this bending happened to him as an example. Once, when Fechin was serving as an attendant to Ciaran of Clonmacnoise, it happened that his portion was left on the edge. Fechin was angered by this and went out afterward, leaving the church and going eastward. This was told to Ciaran. "Go after him," said Ciaran, "and if he does not come voluntarily, let him be brought by force." They went after him. Fechin then said he would not come while facing forward; so he came with his back turned toward them. "That man is bending <term>Irish: forfeccaid</term> now," said Ciaran. From that, he received the name Mo-Fecca.

**Fechine**, son of Caelcarna, son of Grilline, son of Cael, son of Aedh, son of Saine, son of Art Cirp, son of Coirpre Niadfer, son of Cormac.

**Sebastian:** "Sebaist" is the correct form, for Sebastianus is the Roman name. He was a man of Milan <note>original: "Vir Medolensis"</note> who suffered under the consuls Diocletian and Maximian in Rome.

**Oennu:** Aennu of Laigse, whose name was Oengus. He was of the Laigis of Leinster. He and two servants went on a journey to enter military service under a king...

The sage, the bishop, the king, Ninnid, great-grandson of Lóiguire, goes to heaven with his monks to join the good Eochaid, son of Aed. We have not heard the verse well; O Christ, O head of our dear clans, no true monk is free from prohibition unless he is truly pious toward the Church.

*Moéca, now—that is, Féichín of Fore. He was called Féichín for this reason:* When he was a child, he happened to be gnawing a bone in front of his mother, and his mother said: "There is my little wee raven!" <note>original: *Féichín* is a diminutive of *fiach*, meaning raven</note>. <note>original: *Inde Féichín ‘little raven’ dictus est*</note> Therefore he was called Féichín, "little raven." 

However, he was called Mo-éca <note>original: *Mo-éca autem dictus est*</note> because of his "backsliding." When Féichín was herding oxen for Ciarán of Clonmacnois, his portion of food happened to be left for him on a ledge. Féichín became angry at this; he departed and left the church, traveling eastward. This was told to Ciarán. 

"Go after him," said Ciarán; "and if he will not come willingly, let him be brought by force." They went after him. Then Féichín said that he would not return with his face forward, so he came back walking backward. "That man is a backslider," said Ciarán. <note>original: *Inde etc.*</note> That is how he got the name.

Féichín was the son of Caelcarna, son of Grillíne, son of Cael, son of Aed, son of Saine, son of Artcorp, son of Cairbre Nia, son of Cormac.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS
## [MONTH OF JANUARY]

<margin>January 20</margin>
...of Connacht, until he came to the port of Inis Clothrann <note>Inishcloghran, an island in Lough Ree</note> while attempting to cross westward over Lough Ree. It happened that Ciarán was on that island then, and he said, "Bring the young man in, for he shall be a man with the grace of God, and it is he who shall take my succession <term>comhorbus: the office of a successor or heir to a saintly founder</term> after me." Oengus was brought in. "How far does your journey take you?" asked Ciarán. "To the King of *Connacht*," said the lad. "Would you not prefer to make your contract with the King of heaven and earth?" asked Ciarán. "If it is right to do so," said the lad, "it is better." "It is indeed," said Ciarán. His hair was cut there <note>the tonsure of a monk</note> and he was reared for the church. He took the succession of Ciarán, as Ciarán had prophesied.

Oenu, son of the descendant of Laigse, successor of Ciarán of *Cluain* <note>Clonmacnoise</note>. Oengus was his name.

21. **"They were one,"** etc. This refers to Fainche, daughter of Cairell in the north—that is, from Ross Airthir at Lough Erne—and Fainche of fair Cluain in Eoganacht Cashel. Or it is Fuinche the Rough from Lough Erne, in Tuath Ratha in Iveagh of Ulster. Or Féme, who is at *the Oratory* in Mag Itha; she is Féme, daughter of Cairell and sister to Daig, son of Cairell. *Or* Fuinche and Féme are *two old women* <note>original Latin: et duae anus</note>.

This is why she was called "Rough": because a marriage was being arranged for her to a man, and when she heard that, she leaped into Lough Erne. She traveled under the water, through both fresh water and the sea, until she raised her head at Inis Clothrann and met Diarmait. He asked her what journey she was on. She told him her story, and she was covered in shells and marine debris <note>original: turscair</note> clinging to her. Because of that roughness, she is called Fuinche the Rough. Diarmait said to her: "You are rough, O Fainche."

Féme, daughter of Cairell, son of Laisre, son of Dallán, son of Eogan, [son] of Niall *of the Nine Hostages*.

Agnes, a virgin in Rome, was an adopted daughter of Jesus. She was thirteen years old when she suffered under Sempronius, the prefect of the city of Rome. By his vicar, named Aspasius, she was sent through many torments. She returned from these alive and healthy, but afterward a naked sword was driven into her mouth and reached her vitals, and thus she ended her life.
Agnes, Thecla, and Mary the mother of the Lord are the three most excellent virgins among the virgins of the Scripture.

Fland, Bishop of Finglas, on this day.

22. The daughters of Comgall are three sisters: Laissi, Boga, and Colman. At Letter in Dál Araide are the daughters of Comgall, as his female disciples say. Or Comgall is the name of their father, near Cluain Mór Maedóc. Or they are in Camus Comgaill, as others say.
Colman, that is, in Lismore.

23. Mo-Chellóc from Tulach na n-ann and Lucán of Tamhnach on this day.

24. Babylas, a martyr and bishop in Antioch; he was the fifteenth bishop of Antioch after Peter. When King Numerian came to the temple to sacrifice to his gods (that is, idols), Babylas strove to enter the temple of the Lord, and standing in the doorway of the temple, he resisted...

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [JANUARY.]

<margin>Numerianus said: "You shall not enter here, because a wolf ought not to enter among the sheep of the Lord." Then Numerianus ordered him to be tortured with three small disciples <note>original: *cum tribus discipulis paruis*</note>, that is, with his three little ones <note>original: *cona triur deidblen*</note>. The first boy was twelve years old, the second eight, and the third seven; and they suffered by the sword under King Numerianus.</margin>

With his three little ones, namely: Urbanus, Prilidanus, and Epalonus.

Or Babylas <note>original: *Babill*</note>, that is, Manchán of Liath in the district of Delbna Bethra, with three "dog-heads" <note>original: *cenofalis* (cynocephali)</note>, as some think; but this is false.

26. **Of Polycarp** <note>original: *Policarpi*</note>, a bishop in Asia Minor who was a disciple of the Apostles and was ordained by them to the bishopric of the church of Smyrna. He suffered in the time of the Emperors Marcus and Aurelius.

Bishop and martyr: he was the bishop of the city of Smyrna and a pupil of John the Apostle. He was ordained as a bishop by John himself. He was a prince over all of Asia Minor. Afterward, under Marcus Antonius and Lucius Aurelius <note>The text likely refers to Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus</note>, because the people of that city rose up against him, he was burned in fire and martyred along with twelve men in the same city.

27. **"He loved,"** etc. **Muirgein**, that is, "birth of the sea" <note>original: *gein in mara*</note>. This was the abbot of Glenn Uisen, as Oengus says. Or it was Muirgein, daughter of Aedán in Belach Gabráin, who used to nourish martyrs for the sake of God, and God loved him for this.

Or **Muirgein**, that is, "birth of the sea," namely **Líban**, daughter of Eochaid son of Muired, from whom Lough Neagh <note>original: *Loch n-Echach*</note> is named. She remained for three hundred years in Lough Neagh until Beoán the fisherman of Comgall caught her in his net. Comgall baptized her afterward, and she told her adventures to Comgall and went to heaven; and she narrated to him all the things that had happened to her in the waters.

As the poet said of her:
> Muirgein is a birth of many virtues, the daughter of proud Eochaid;
> She went beyond boundaries rightfully, though Jesus placed her in an unusual state.
> She loved the estuary more than a dwelling—Líban, the daughter of that man;
> She was appointed to be under the heavy flood until she gave her voice to Comgall.
> By the luck of his net and his gear, Beoán, the fisherman of Comgall,
> Brought her after her journeying in the east and baptized her in his dwelling.
> Strange was the shape in which the creature was—God performed a manifest miracle:
> Her upper part was a fair woman, though she was confined, but her half was a powerful salmon.
> When Oengus, the beautiful grandson of Oiblén, said "he loved Moeda,"
> "Moeda" means "my own God," and the "birth of the sea" was Muirgein.
> "Though I was a human, though I was a sea-monster, the seals of Mag Breg loved me;
> It was no nickname, 'brightness of color'—I loved the bright angel of the King."

# JANUARY 26, 27. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

With his trio of *weaklings*, that is, Urbanus, Grilidianus, and Epalonus. Or Babylas, that is, Manchan of Liath in Delbna Bethra <note>A territory in ancient Ireland, now in County Offaly</note> with three "dog-heads" <note>original: *cenofali* (cynocephali); mythical creatures with human bodies and dog heads</note>, as others think, *but this is false* <note>original: *sed falsum est*</note>.

26. Of *Polycarp*, that is, of a bishop, etc. Of a bishop and martyr, specifically the bishop of the city of Smyrna. He was a pupil of John the Apostle, and he was ordained as bishop by John himself. He was a leader in all of Asia Minor. Later, Marcus Aurelius <note>original: *Marcus Antonius* (corrected by editor)</note> and Lucius Verus <note>original: *Lucius Aurelius* (corrected by editor)</note> incited the people of that city against him. He was burned in a fire, and twelve men were martyred along with him in the same city.

27. My Lord loved Muirgein, whose name means "the birth of the sea." This refers to the abbot of Glen Uissen, as Oengus says. Or perhaps Muirgein, daughter of Aedán, in Belach Gabráin, *who etc.* <note>original: *qui etc.*</note>. Or Muirgein, "the birth of the sea," also known as Lí-bán, daughter of Eochaid, son of Muirid, after whom Loch n-Echach (*Lough Neagh*) is named. It is she who lived for three hundred years in Lough Neagh, until Beóan, St. Comgall's fisherman, caught her in his net. Comgall afterwards baptized her, and she told her story to Comgall and went to heaven, *and she narrated etc.* <note>original: *et narravit etc.*</note>.

As the poet said of her:
> Muirgein, hers is a birth of triumphs, daughter of the very haughty Eochaid,
> she passed rightly beyond the reach of taxes <note>original: "tributes"; likely meaning she was exempt from earthly obligations</note>, though Jesus put her in a pitiful state.
> She loved the estuary more than a house—Lí-bán, daughter of that man—
> her existence beneath the heavy current was trusted until she spoke
> to Comgall.
> By means of his net and his boat <note>original: "tree"</note>, Beóán, Comgall's fisherman,
> brought her in after her journey in the east, so that he baptized her
> in his dwelling.
> Strange was the shape from which power came; God had wrought a
> manifest miracle:
> her face was very white though she was a captive <note>original: *cacht* (bondmaid/prisoner)</note>, her side was that of
> an ever-strong salmon.
> When Oengus, the comely grandson of Oibléin, said *Moeda carais* ("My Lord loved"),
> *Moeda* was "my Lord" <note>original: *mo Fiada*</note> himself, and *muirgein* was "the birth
> of the sea."
> "Though I am human, though I am an animal, the nobles of Mag
> Breg <note>The "Plain of Bregia" in East Ireland</note> used to love me:
> 'Whiteness' and 'Beauty' <note>A play on her name Lí-bán</note>—it was no nickname—I have loved the
> King of the bright angels."

¹ Dog-headed men?
² That is, she was exempt from tribute?
³ "Her face very white though she was a captive." (Variants from different manuscripts: LU, R²).
⁴ See the name Lí-bán above.

# THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS
## [MONTH OF JANUARY]

<page-num>54</page-num>

Eochaid, son of Muiredach the beautiful, lies beneath the gray-green wave;
The good prince around whom women used to lie—I was his daughter.
<note>This verse is attributed to Aire.</note>
I shall not remain in this life after him, and I shall die of shame,
Because the people over there are saying, "I am Aire, the wife of Curnnán."

<margin>From this comes Carn Curnain: that is, after the death of Curnnán there, Aire died of grief, etc.</margin>

**28.** **Accobran**, a proper name: that is, he was one of the saints of Ireland, and he is in **Kilrush** <note>original: Cill rois</note> in the sanctuary of **Scattery Island** <note>original: Inis Cathaig</note>.

**29.** **Dallan mac Forgaill** from Maighin, and **Cronan**, and **Moconna** (or Mo-cenna, a virgin), **Blath**, and **Baithin** are on this day.

**30.** **Fifty or 140** <note>The text offers two traditions for the number of martyrs.</note> died at the "door": that is, martyrdom. For martyrdom is the door to heaven or the place of heaven.
**Énan**, son of Gemman, in **Rossmore** <note>original: Rus mór</note> in Ui Dega in **Hy Kinsellagh** <note>original: Uib Ceinnselaig</note>; he is the same as **Mo-Menoc** of Glen Faidli in Ui Garrcon.

**31.** **Maedoc of Ferns**: that is, "my little Aed." He was of the **Fir Luirc** from **Lough Erne**.
Maedoc, son of Setna, son of Erc, son of Feradach, son of Fiachra, son of Amalgaid, son of Muiredach, son of Cairthinn... son of Eochaid Doimlén.

Fifty bishops came to **Maedoc of Ferns** from the Britons of **St. Davids** <note>original: Cilli Muine</note>; they came on a pilgrimage because Maedoc of Ferns had been a pupil of **David of St. Davids**. From the time of David, no meat was ever brought into the refectory of the church until the successor of Maedoc brought it. Because of this, David granted a seat and equal status to the successor who would bring it, and allowed him to stay in the refectory—that is, in the abbacy of St. Davids—and his feet should not touch the ground as long as he lived.

These bishops came on a pilgrimage to Maedoc. They were taken into the guest house during the spring Lent. There were given to them fifty loaves of bread, some herbs, and a vessel of whey-water for their meal. "Why was this brought?" asked the bishop. "For you to eat it," said the **steward** <note>term: ferthaigis; the official in charge of the household or monastery</note>. "Take it away again," said the bishop, "for nothing made from the carcasses of pigs or cattle shall be eaten here." The steward told this to Maedoc. "Permission granted," said Maedoc. It was brought to them. "It is well," he said, "let them eat the meat." They stayed there until the next morning. Maedoc blessed them.

"Well," said Maedoc, "it is not too much to reprimand us for eating meat during Lent and for refusing the bread." "You did not learn that from your reading, Maedoc," said the bishop. "Well," said Maedoc. "It is not difficult to explain," said the bishop: "The pig and the ox that were brought to us drank only their mothers' milk and ate nothing but the grass of the earth. But there were **three hundred and sixty-five work-efforts** <note>original: uroibri; referring to the manual labor of the peasants</note> involved in making that bread; that is why we did not eat it."

**Mael Anfaid**: that is, the Abbot of **Darinis**. Darinis is near **Lismore of Mochuta**, where the great river flows into the sea.

# JANUARY 28–31. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

Eochaid, son of handsome Muirid, he is under the ocean-blue wave; the good noble with whom <unclear>(?)</unclear> women used to lie, I was a daughter of his.
Said Aire:
I am not alive for this, and I will die of shame,
The men there saying it that I am Airiu Curnán’s wife.¹
*Therefore Carn Curnain* <note>original: Unde Carn Curnain</note>, that is, named after Curnan’s death there from grief for Aire, etc.

28. **Accobran**, a proper name; he was one of the saints of Ireland, and he is in Cell Rois in the sanctuary <term>original: termon; a piece of church land exempt from secular taxes</term> of Inis Cathaig.

29. **Dallán** ‘son of testimony,’ of Maigen, and **Cronan**, and **Moconna** (or **Mocenna**) a virgin, **Bláth** and **Baithin** on this day.

30. Fifty or forty and a hundred, the door of martyrdom magnified them; for martyrdom is the door of heaven or a door to heaven.
**Énán** son of Gemmán in Ross Mór in Húi Dega in Húi Cennselaig.
The same as my-**Ménóc** of Glenn Faidli in Húi Garrchon.

31. **Maedóc** of Ferns, that is, "my Aedóc"; he was of the Fir Luirc of Lough Erne.
Maedoc son of Sétna, son of Erc, son of Feradach, son of Fiachra, son of Amalgad, son of Muiredach, son of Cairthenn, son of (Colla Uais) son of Eochaid Doimlén.²

Fifty bishops of the Britons of Cell Muine <note>St. David's in Wales</note> came on their pilgrimage to Maedóc of Ferns. They came to him because Maedóc of Ferns was a pupil of David of Cell Muine. From David’s time, meat was not brought into the refectory of Cell Muine until Maedóc’s successor brought it. Hence <unclear>(?)</unclear> is David’s strife and stubbornness <unclear>(?)</unclear> toward the successor that brought it, remaining in the refectory—that is, in the abbacy of Cell Muine—with his feet not touching the ground so long as he was alive. 

So they came in pilgrimage to Maedóc. They were taken into the guest-house during the Spring Lent. There was brought to them for dinner fifty cakes, leeks, and whey-water. 
“Why has this been brought?” says the bishop. 
“For you to consume it,” says the house-steward. 
“Take it away,” says the bishop: “none of it shall be consumed until there is a pig and an ox there.” 

The house-steward relates this to Maedóc. 
“Permission is granted,” says Maedóc. 
It is brought to them. “It is well,” said the bishop; they eat the meat. They stay there until the next day. Maedóc salutes them. 
“Well,” says Maedóc: “it is not too much to reprove you for eating meat in Lent and refusing the bread.” 
“You have not delivered that judgment from careful study, O Maedóc,” says the bishop. 
“How so?” says Maedóc. 
“It is easy to say,” said the bishop, “the pig drank only its mother’s milk, and the ox which was brought to us ate nothing except the grass of the earth. But in the cake there were three hundred and sixty-five weevils <unclear>(?)</unclear>; therefore we did not consume it.”³

**Mael-anfaid**, that is, abbot of Dairinis; Dairinis is at Mochutu’s Lismore, where a great river *flows out into the sea* <note>original: in mare exit</note>.

¹ See the story of Liban told in prose, *Leabhar na hUidhre* <note>original: LU</note>, pp. 40, 41.
² See the pedigree in *Book of Leinster* <note>original: LL</note>, 347ᵃ.
³ See another version of this story in the *Book of Leinster* <note>original: LL</note>, 285ᵇ.

<header>JANUARY 31.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

Mael-anfaid son of Anfadach, son of Garbán, son of Crunnmal, son of . . . Iachtar, son of Dungal, son of Murgal, son of Bran, son of Mael . . . chine, son of Senach, son of Nathi, son of Trichem, son of Erc . . . . . . of Erc the Victorious. <note>This is a genealogy tracing the lineage of the saint back through several generations of Irish nobility.</note>

That is the Mael-anfaid who beheld a certain little bird wailing and lamenting. "O my God," says he, "what has happened over there? I will not eat any food until it is revealed to me." Now while he was there, he saw an angel coming towards him. "That is well, O cleric," says the angel: "do not let this cause you any more grief. Molua mac Ocha <note>Also known as Saint Lugaid, founder of the monastery of Clonfertmulloe.</note> has died, and therefore all living creatures bewail him; for he never killed any animal, small or large. Therefore, human beings do not mourn him any more than the other animals do, including the little bird which you see."¹

Bríg, that is, a virgin *with them* <note>original: "cum eis"</note> in the territory of the Déisi of Munster: Bríg is located near Mochutu's Lismore, or in Carbury O'Kiery <note>original: "Carbre úa Ciardai"</note> in the north of Meath; or at Wexford <note>original: "Loch Carman"</note>; or beside Kildare . . . . that is, a prioress.

Bríg at Tech Bríge <note>The House of Bríg</note>: it was by her power that the cows were milked three times in the same day for the bishops, and it was by her that there was reaping on the harvest-day when a rainstorm was falling throughout the rest of the country.²

Barr-find, that is, he is the "fair top" <note>A play on his name: "Barr" meaning top/head and "find" meaning fair/white.</note> and completion to the host of January.

---

¹ A similar tale is told of Iuchna Echbél in the *Book of Leinster* <note>original: "LL"</note> 160ᵇ.
² In Broccán's hymn (lines 29-32) these miracles are attributed to Saint Brigid. See *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* <note>original: "Thes. pal. hib."</note> ii. 334, 335.

It highlights the Irish hagiographical tradition of saints having a supernatural kinship with nature and performing agricultural miracles.</summary>

<keywords>Mael-anfaid, Molua mac Ocha, Saint Bríg, Irish hagiography, animal mourning, agricultural miracles, Déisi, Lismore, genealogy</keywords>

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF FEBRUARY.]</header>

### THE MONTH OF FEBRUARY.
### FEBRUARY.

**D. February 1 (The Calends of February).**
They magnify the Calends <note>The first day of the month</note> of February,
A shower of great, pure-colored martyrs;
Brigit the fair, strong and praiseworthy,
The chaste head of Ireland's nuns.

**E. February 2 (The 4th day before the Nones).**
The reception of Mary’s Son
In the Temple—certain and inestimable;
A great host of gentle martyrs,
With Findech of Dorn, the excellent.

**F. February 3 (The 3rd day before the Nones).**
May they protect us fully
Always against every misery:
The fair, modest host
Of Felix and Symphronius!

**G. February 4 (The day before the Nones).**
Sempronius and Magnus,
And Gelasius, whom you should know;
German, a noble martyr,
And Cúanna, the pious and holy.

**A. February 5 (The Nones of February).**
Crucified was the body of Agatha,
The pure champion;
With bright Jesus,
She has much good because of it.

### G. 3rd Ides of February [February 11]
My Gopnat <note>Saint Gobnait of Ballyvourney, patron saint of bees</note> with pure goodness, who was wealthy in the love of God: beloved Bishop Ethchen <note>Bishop of Clonard, said to have ordained St. Columba</note> likes to be called upon continually.

### A. The day before the Ides of February [February 12]
Around Bishop Simplex was slain a prime, proven host. Damianus, a soldier and a crown of martyrdom, was crucified along with fair children.

### B. The Ides of February [February 13]
In a little boat <note>original: curchán; a coracle</note> from the east, over the pure-colored sea, my Domnóc <note>Saint Modomnoc</note> brought—a vigorous cry!—the gifted race of Ireland’s bees. <note>Tradition holds that Modomnoc first introduced honeybees to Ireland from Wales.</note>

### C. 16th Kalends of March [February 14]
In Valentine’s field, Marcellus has been tortured: in Christ’s kingdom, eighty fair champions have been planted.

### D. 15th Kalends of March [February 15]
Sing a Sunday’s celebration on the feast of warlike Berach, along with the suffering of a vigorous host: the victory of the Son of God over His enemy.

<page-num>64</page-num>
<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF FEBRUARY.</header>

## NOTES.

**1. Brigid.** Brigid, daughter of Dubthach, son of Demre, son of Bresal, son of Connla, son of Art Cerp, son of Cairbre Nia, son of... Aengus Mind, son of Eochaid Find Fuathairt, son of Fedlimid Rechtmar. <note>This is Brigid’s genealogy tracing her lineage back to high kings of Ireland.</note>

The three "eights" of Brigid: her birth was on the eighth day of the lunar month <note>original: "uathaid" — the first period of the moon's cycle</note>, her veiling <note>original: "caille" — taking her religious vows</note> was on the eighteenth, and her death was on the twenty-eighth.

The fair one from the Liffey of the slopes, daughter of Dubthach from Druim Derg; tomorrow *she goes quickly*, so that hers is the last testament of Patrick. <note>This verse emphasizes her connection to the Liffey region and her spiritual inheritance from St. Patrick.</note>

Bishops came to Brigid from Ui Briuin Cualann <note>A territory south of Dublin</note>—that is, from the Hill of the Bishops to Kildare—to New-Milk Lake <note>original: "Loch Lemnacht"</note> beside Kildare to the north. Brigid asked her cook, Blathnait, if she had food for the bishops. She said no. Brigid felt shame. An angel told her to milk the cows again. The cows were milked until they filled the vats, and they would have filled all the vessels of Leinster, for the milk went over the vessels until it made a lake of it; hence it is called New-Milk Lake.

A robber came to Dubthach, and Dubthach gave him a piece of meat from the cauldron. The robber made five portions of it. He entrusted Brigid to guard it, but a miserable dog came to her, and she gave the five portions from the cauldron to it. Yet, the five portions were found in the cauldron afterward. <insert>This was told to Dubthach</insert>, and Dubthach gave the land to her <insert>and to God</insert> after that—namely, the space of an oratory in Tuath Da Maige.

A young cleric of the community of Ferns the Great, a foster-son of Brigid, used to come to her with offerings. He was in the refectory with her to eat food. Once, after coming from communion, he struck the clapper <note>original: "bascrann" — a wooden knocker used to signal mealtimes or gatherings</note>. "Well now, young cleric," said Brigid, "do you have a soul-friend?" <note>term: "anmchara" — a spiritual director or confessor</note> "I do," said the young cleric. "Let us chant his dirge," said Brigid, "for he has died. I saw when you had finished half your portion, it was into a neck that you were putting your food <insert>and you were without a head at all</insert>, because your soul-friend has died; for a body without a head is a person without a soul-friend. Eat no more until you take a [new] soul-friend."

The Marvel of Plea, etc. This is a city belonging to Brigid on the shore of the Ictian Sea <note>The English Channel</note> or the Tyrrhenian Sea, and it is its Rule that the community of Brigid follows. And so it was done: Brigid sent seven men from her to learn the Rule of Peter and Paul, for God did not permit her to go there herself. They did not bring back the Rule, so she sent a third time eastward, and her blind youth went with them, for everything he heard he remembered. When they reached the Ictian Sea, a storm fell upon them. They cast their anchor down, and it caught on the pinnacle of the oratory [beneath the waves]. They cast lots among themselves as to who should go down, and it fell to the blind youth to go. He loosened the anchor and stayed there until the end of a year learning the Rule, until the other party came back from Rome to him. A storm happened to them again in the same place, and they let [down the anchor]...

<summary>This page provides hagiographical legends and genealogical details regarding Saint Brigid of Kildare, including the miraculous origin of "New-Milk Lake" and the importance of having a spiritual director (soul-friend).</summary>
<keywords>Saint Brigid, Kildare, Dubthach, Loch Lemnacht, soul-friend, anmchara, Rule of Peter and Paul, Irish hagiography</keywords>

<page-num>65</page-num>
<header>FEBRUARY 1.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

## NOTES.

1. *Brigit*. Brigit, daughter of Dubthach, son of Demre, son of Bresal, son of Connla, son of Art Corp, son of Cairbre Nia, son of Cormac, son of Oengus the Dumb, son of Eochaid Find Fuathnairt, son of Feidlimid Rechtmad. <note>This traces Brigit's lineage through the royal and noble lines of ancient Ireland.</note>

Brigit’s three eighths: namely, her birth on the eighth (of the month), her receiving the veil on the eighteenth, and her death on the twenty-eighth. <note>These dates likely refer to the lunar calendar or specific local traditions regarding her life milestones.</note>

The white one from the Liffey of the slopes, daughter of Dubthach of Druim Derg: tomorrow she goes quickly, so that from her hand comes Patrick’s bequest.

Eight bishops came to Brigit out of Húi Briuin Cualann—that is, from Telach na n-epscop <note>The Hill of the Bishops</note> to Loch Lemnachta <note>New-milk Lake</note> beside Kildare on the north. Brigit asked her cook, Bláthnait, whether she had food for the bishops. *She said no* <note>original Latin: "Dixit illa non"</note>. Brigit was ashamed, so the angel told her to milk the cows again. The cows were milked and they filled the tubs; they would have filled all the vessels in Leinster, so that the milk overflowed the vessels and made a lake of it, *wherefore* it is called Loch Lemnachta, or "New-milk Lake" <note>original Latin: "unde... dicitur"</note>.

A robber came to Dubthach, who took a joint of meat out of the cauldron for him. He made five pieces of it and gave them to Brigit to keep. But a wretched hound came to her, and she gave it the five pieces out of the cauldron; yet the five pieces were then found in the cauldron again. That was told to Dubthach, and then he gave to her and to God the land—namely, the site of an oratory in Tuath dá Maige.

A young cleric of the community of Ferns, a foster-son of Brigit’s, used to come to her with his requests. He was with her in the refectory to partake of food. Once, after coming to communion, she strikes a clapper.

“Well, young cleric there,” says Brigit, “do you have a <term>soulfriend</term>?” <note>original: "anmchara"; a spiritual director or confessor.</note>

“I have,” replied the young cleric. 

“Let us sing his requiem,” says Brigit, “for he has died. I saw when half your portion had gone, that your quota was put into your trunk, and you were without any head on you; for your <term>soulfriend</term> died, and anyone without a <term>soulfriend</term> is a body without a head. Eat no more until you get a <term>soulfriend</term>.”

*The Wonder of Plea* <note>original: "Amra Plea"</note> etc., a convent of Brigit’s which is on the brink of the Sea of Wight, or the Tyrrhene Sea, and its Rule is that of Brigit’s community. *And so it was done* <note>original Latin: "Et sic factum est"</note>. Brigit dispatched seven persons to learn the Rule of Peter and Paul, for God did not determine that she herself should go. And they did not bring back the Rule. So she sent eastward a third time, together with her blind boy, for everything he used to hear, he remembered. When they reached the Sea of Wight a storm fell upon them, so they let down their anchor, which stuck on the peak of the oratory <note>This suggests a miraculous underwater church or a mystical geography</note>. They cast lots *among themselves* <note>original Latin: "inter se"</note> as to who should go down, and it fell to the blind boy. He loosed the anchor, *and stayed* <note>original Latin: "et stetit"</note> there until the end of a year, learning the Rule, until the rest of the party came back to him from Rome. A storm fell upon them again in the same place, so they let down their anchor...

<margin>2 That is, a <term>spiritual director</term>.</margin>

...unpious <note>original: *ingoir*</note>, that is, downwards, until the blind boy came up with them with the Order of Plea and with a shining bell; and it is the Order of Plea that remains today.

Brigit desired to have the orders of penitence <note>likely referring to the taking of the veil</note> conferred upon her. She traveled to Bri Eli with seven nuns accompanying her when she heard that Bishop Mel was there. When they arrived, Bishop Mel was not there, but had gone into the territory of the Ui Neill. She followed the next day with Mac Caille acting as her guide to Monagh Faithnigh. Brigid turned the marsh into a smooth, flowery plain for them. When they came near the place where Bishop Mel was, Brigid told Mac Caille to place a veil over her head so that she would not go to the clerics without a veil; and it is that veil which is commemorated here. After she reached the clerics, a pillar of fire blazed from her head to the roof of the church. Mac Caille said, "This is the famous nun from Leinster, namely Brigid." "Welcome to her," said Bishop Mel; "It was I," he said, "who prophesied her while she was in her mother's womb, and it is I who shall confer orders upon her."

Once, Bishop Mel came to the house of Dubthach <note>Brigit's father</note> and saw Dubthach’s wife in sorrow. The bishop asked, "What ails the woman?" "I have cause for sorrow," she said, "for Dubthach prefers the handmaid who is washing your feet over me." "It is right for you to feel so," said Bishop Mel, "for your offspring shall serve the offspring of the handmaid."

"Why have the nuns come?" asked Bishop Mel. "To have the orders of penitence conferred on Brigid," said Mac Caille. Thereafter, the orders were read over Brigid. However, it was the orders of a Bishop that Bishop Mel conferred upon her, and it was then that Mac Caille held a veil over her head. Because of this, the successor of Brigid <note>the Abbess of Kildare</note> is entitled to have episcopal honors conferred upon her.

While he was reading the orders, Brigid stood with her hand on the leg of the altar. Seven churches were later burned, yet that altar leg was not burned; *but it was preserved by the grace of Brigid* <note>original Latin: *sed servata est per gratiam Brigitae*</note>. Others say that church was in Fera Tulach, as Bishop Mel related.

> Beloved little month of dear February, which contains those feasts for us:
> The feast of Brigid of the glowing passion... the feast of Fintan whom I have chosen.
>
> Except for Great Mary of good fame, the mother of the Lord Jesus,
> There was never found a child under heaven more wonderful than bright white Brigid.

...down an anchor, and the blind boy came up from below with the <term>Rule of Plea</term> <note>original: "Cáin Phádraig" or Law of Patrick; "Plea" refers to a legal petition or rule</note> and with a beautiful bell, and it is the <term>Rule of Plea</term> that remains to this day.¹

Now Brigit was eager to have the orders of penitence conferred upon her; so she went to <term>Bri Eile</term> <note>modern Croghan Hill, County Offaly</note>, accompanied by seven nuns, since she had heard that Bishop Mel was there. When they arrived, Bishop Mel was not there, but had gone into the district of the <term>Húi Néill</term> <note>The territory of the descendants of Niall of the Nine Hostages</note>. So she set out the next morning with <term>Mac Caille</term> before her as a guide to <term>Móin Faithnig</term> <note>Faughalstown bog</note>. Brigit worked a miracle so that the bog became a smooth, flowery plain for them. When they drew near the place where Bishop Mel was staying, Brigit told Mac Caille that she would wear a veil on her head so that she might not appear unveiled before the clerics; and that may be the veil that is commemorated here. Now, after reaching the clerics, a fiery column flamed from her head to the ridge of the church. Mac Caille said: “This is the famous nun of Leinster, even Brigit.” “She is welcome,” said Bishop Mel: “It is I,” he said, “who prophesied her while she was in her mother’s womb, and it is I who will confer the orders upon her.”¹

Once upon a time, Bishop Mel came to Dubthach’s house and saw Dubthach’s wife in grief. So the bishop asked, “What is the matter with the woman?” “I have cause for grief,” she said, “for the bondmaid who is washing you is dearer to Dubthach than I am.” “You have good reason,” said Bishop Mel, “for your descendants will serve the descendants of the bondmaid.”¹

“Why have the nuns come?” asked Bishop Mel. “To have the orders of penitence conferred on Brigit,” said Mac Caille. Thereafter the orders were read out over Brigit, and Bishop Mel bestowed episcopal <note>the rank of a Bishop</note> orders upon her, and it is then that Mac Caille set a veil on her head. Hence, Brigit’s successor is entitled to have episcopal orders conferred upon her.¹

As long as he was reading out the orders, Brigit stood with the foot of the altar in her hand; and seven churches were burnt with that foot <note>referring to a wooden altar-post</note> in one of them; yet it was not burnt, *but etc.* <note>original: "sed etc."</note>¹ *Others say* <note>original: "Dicunt alii"</note> that the church was in <term>Fir Tulach</term> <note>Fartullagh, County Westmeath</note>, as Bishop Mel declared:

Beloved and short is the month of dear February, which contains these festivals for us,
Brigit’s festival . . . Finntain’s festival which I have chosen.
Except for Great Mary, of good fame, Mother of the Lord Jesus,
no woman under heaven has been found more wondrous than bright-white Brigit.²

**3.** Blaise, *bishop* and *martyr*, and Caelfinn, *virgin*, and Cuanan of Glenn Magne Bile, and Colman son of Duach, and Laurentin, *martyr*, on this day.

Lucia, whom a thousand could not move. Many thousands failed to move her.
<note>The following is translated from the original Latin</note>
For Lucia was in Sicily, in the city of the Syracusans, and she was betrothed to a man. It happened, before they came together, that she went with her mother Euticia to the city of the Catanians to visit Saint Agatha, to pray to her for her mother, who for seven years had been exhausted by a flow of blood. Her mother was freed from the aforementioned plague, and Agatha appeared to Lucia in a dream, and Lucia herself rejected the marriage bed of her betrothed. Then the betrothed went to Paschasius the proconsul, who was in the city of Syracuse, and told him everything. The proconsul said: "Take her by force." But he alone could not move her; he brought others with him to move her, and the number of those pulling was increased to a hundred, but they did not move her. Then to a thousand, and afterward to many thousands, and many pairs of oxen were brought, and they could not move her from her place; but there she was struck with a sword.

**7.** Meallan from Inis Maic hua-Chuind on Lough Corrib in the west of Connacht.
Lomman, that is, Lomman is from the Great Island of Lough Ennell. That is, from Tech Lomain at Lough Ennell. That is, of the Great Island of Lough Ennell in Meath.
Lomman of Lough Ennell in Meath, and Lomman of Lough Gill, son of Dallan, son of Bresal, son of Maine, son of Domnall, son of Eochaid, son of Fiachra, son of Cairbre Lifechar.

**8.** The splendid descendant of the poet, that is, Onchu, or Ternoc, strong his profit. He is to the west of the River Barrow. That is, in Congbail Glinne Suaide—the name of a river.

Sliab Mairge Finnech Duirn is, <note>original: *ut alii putant*</note> as others think. Or Dorn *Dinaisc* was her father's name, that is, whatever was bound upon him he used to fulfill. Finnig, daughter of Dorn, is in Ossory.

**The grandson of the poet** etc. <note>original: "Ua ind ecis"</note>—that is, Onchu was his name. He is in the oratory of the Cemetery of the Angels in Cluain Mór Máedóc. He was a good silver-poet <note>original: "aircetlaid," likely meaning a skilled poet or reciter</note> and a wise man. He turned his attention to one thing: collecting the relics of the saints of Ireland. He would not stay in any church without some relics being given to him, so that he had a great shrine of the relics of the saints after collecting them. 

Then he went to Cluain Mór Máedóc—that is, Máedóc son of Dunlaing of the Leinstermen, and not Máedóc of *Ferns*. It happened that Máedóc was alive when he arrived. # FEBRUARY 8, 9. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

<page-num>71</page-num>

**February 8.** "Splendid descendant of the sage," etc. This refers to **Onchu** <note>original: Onchu</note>. He is buried in the oratory of *Relic na n-aingel* (**the Angels' Graveyard**) in **Cluain Mor Maedoc**. He was a talented poet, and he devoted himself to collecting the relics of Ireland's saints. He refused to stay in any church unless he was given some of that saint's relics. Consequently, he amassed a great shrine of the holy remains he had collected. 

Eventually, he went to **Cluain Mor Maedoc**—referring to **Maedoc hua Dunlaing** of Leinster, not **Maedoc of Ferns**. This Maedoc happened to be alive at the time. Onchu said to him, "Give me a portion of your own relics, O cleric, so that they may be kept with these other holy remains." 

"That is a hard request," the cleric replied. 

"It must be done, however," said the poet. 

So the cleric cut off his own little finger and gave it to the poet. The cleric suffered great pain from this, and he declared: "All that you have collected shall remain here, and your own relics shall remain here as well." And this prophecy has been fulfilled. <note>Compare the similar story of Cormac and Colum Cille later on page 157.</note>

"Splendid descendant of the sage": he is in **Cluain Mor Maedoc**, and he is originally from Connaught. It was he who collected the saints' relics in the oratory of the graveyard of **Cluain Mor Maedoc**.

**Fiachra**, abbot of **Iraird**: he is from **Iraird** in **Ui Drona**, Leinster. My **Colmoc** of **Cluain Iraird** is celebrated on this day <note>original: in hoc die dicitur</note> at **Ard na Sruithe** in **Ui Drona**.

**Fiachra** was the son of Colman, son of Eogan, son of Baetan, son of Ailill, son of Suibne, son of Mael-duin, son of Finan, son of Ailill, son of Muredach, son of Imchad, son of Colla Fochri, son of Eochaid Doimlen. <note>See the genealogy in the Book of Leinster, 347h.</note>

**February 9.** My **Cuaroc**: he is in the **Desi of Munster**, and also in **Leix** beside **Tech Mochua**. This is why he is called "**Mo-Chuaroc of the None**," because he was the first to divide the celebration of the office of None <note>The prayer service traditionally held at the ninth hour, or 3:00 PM</note>, because etc. <note>original: quia etc.</note>

He is in the **Desi of Munster**, and is also called **Cronan mac Nethsemon**.

**Cairech Dergain** of **Cluain Bairenn** in **Ui Maine**, located on the banks of the **Shannon**. She was a sister of **Enda of Aran**.

**Cairech Dergain**, **Nes Ernaigthe**, **Caurcan**, and **Duthrach** were the four daughters of Cormac, son of Enda, son of Cormac, son of Fergus, son of Crimthann. <note>The Book of Leinster (348f) lists them as the four daughters of Enda.</note>

Alternatively, **Cairech Dergain** was the daughter of **Conall the Red**, son of **Damine Daim-argait**, and she was a sister of **Enda of Aran**. It was that Conall who separated **Lough Erne** from Connaught, and **Dubthar** from Leinster, and hunted the **Ulaid** eastwards over **Glenn Rige**. Those are Conall's three "manly deeds." This Conall's daughter was **Cairech Dergain**, and her full brother was **Enda of Aran**, who was one of the three <term>athlaechs</term> <note>original: athlaechs; laymen who became monks in their old age</note> of Ireland.

She was called **Cairech Dergain** because she was once searching—

That is, **Enne**. It happened then that a reproach was cast upon her brother. When this was told to her, she blushed with shame; and from that fault <note>original: *cair*</note> and that blushing <note>original: *imdergad*</note> she is called **Cairech Dergain** <note>The Red-Blushed Cairech</note>.

**Bishop Ronan**, that is, from **Lismore Mochuta**. **Ronan the Fair**, son of Saran, son of Colgan, son of Tuathal, son of Fedlimid, son of Feichine, son of Fiachra, son of Colla Fochri.

### 10. Cronan
**Cronan**, son of Mellan from **Glas More** in the **Decies of Munster**; or from **Glas More**, a church that was beside **Swords** on the southern side, until the foreigners <note>Vikings</note> of **Inver Domnand** came to it and killed all its community in a single night. Or, **Cronan** is in **Cluain Cian** in **Bretaig of Ulster**, near **Morglais**, and he is a brother to **Molaise of Devenish**.
**Glas More**, that is, a vacant church near **Swords** to the south, in the **Decies of Munster**.

### 11. Mogobnat
**Mogobnat** of **Muskerry Mitaine**, that is, a "sharp-beaked" nun <note>original: *caillech gobger*</note>; **Ernaide** is the name of the place where she is. Or **Gobnat** of **Bairnech** in **Moin More** in the south of Ireland, and she is of the race of **Conaire**. A virgin of the race of **Conaire**.

**Etchen**, that is, in **Cluain Fota Baetan** in **Farbill**.
**Bishop Etchen** from **Cluain Fota Baetan**; he was an abbot in **Farbill** which is in southern **Meath**, and he was of the **Dal Mescorp of Leinster**. It was to visit him that **Colum Cille** <note>Saint Columba</note> went, in order to have the rank of bishop conferred upon him. **Colum Cille** sat under a tree <note>original: *baiscni*</note> to the west of the church and asked where the cleric was. "There," said a man, "he is down on the field at the plow." "I think," said **Colum Cille**, "it is not right for us to ask a plowman to confer holy orders upon us. Nevertheless, let him be tested by us, since we have come to him."

First, they asked him for the plowshare. He gave it to them immediately, and the oxen did not plow any less for it. "The cleric is a good man," they said. "Test him further," said **Colum Cille**. They asked him for the outer ox. He gave it to them immediately, and **Bishop Etchen** commanded a wild stag that was in the forest to perform that labor, and it did so at once.

**Colum Cille** then went to the cleric after testing him and told him why he had come. "It shall be done," said the cleric. However, the rank of priest was conferred upon **Colum Cille**, though it was the rank of bishop he had wished to have conferred upon him. The cleric prayed until the following morning. "That is a pity, O cleric," said **Colum Cille**, "the rank you have given me; however, I shall never change it as long as I live. In exchange for that, moreover, no one shall ever come to this church to have orders conferred upon them until Doomsday"—and that is still fulfilled today.

**Bishop Etchen**, son of Maine the Poet, son of Fergus, son of Corp, son of Fergus, son of Fothad; and **Bishop Aidan**, son of Maine; and **Kevin**, son of Coemlog, son of Coimed, son of Corp.

### 12. Around Bishop Simplex, etc.
That is, **Modiuuit**, a bishop from **Kill Modiuuit** in **Hy Many** in **Sogan**.

# FEBRUARY 10–12. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

That is told to her, and she blushes at the news; because of the blame and the blushing <note>original: *imdergad*</note> she is called *Cairech Dergain* <note>The name implies "Cairech of the Reddening" or blushing.</note>.

Bishop *Rónán*, that is, of *Lismore* <note>original: *Les mór Mochutu*</note>.
*Rónán Find*, son of *Saran*, son of *Colgan*, son of *Tuathal*, son of *Feidlimid*, son of *Féichíne*, son of *Fiachra*, son of *Colla Fochri*.

10. *Cronan*. *Cronan*, son of *Mellán*, of *Glas mór* in the *Decies* <note>original: *Dési*</note> of *Munster*, or of *Glas mór*, a church that was beside *Swords* on the south. Foreigners from *Malahide* <note>original: *Inber Domnann*</note> came to it and killed the whole of its community in **one night** <note>original: *una nocte*</note>. Or *Cronán* is in *Cluain cáin* in *Bretach Ulad* near *Mor-glas*, and he is a brother of *Molaisse* of *Devenish*.
Of *Glas már*, that is, a desolate church to the south of *Swords*.

11. *My Gobnat* <note>The prefix "My" (Mo) was a common Irish devotional addition to a saint's name.</note> from *Muskerry* <note>original: *Muscraige Mitaine*</note>, that is, a sharp-beaked nun; *Ernaide* is the name of the place where she is. Or *Gobnat* of *Bairnech* in the Great Bog <note>original: *Móin Mór*</note> in the south of Ireland, and she is of the race of *Conaire*: a virgin of *Conaire*'s race.

*Etchen*, that is, in *Clonfad* <note>original: *Clúain fota Baetáin*</note> in *Farbill* <note>original: *Fir bile*</note>.
Bishop *Etchen* from *Clonfad* in *Farbill* is in the south of *Meath*, and he is of the *Dál Mescorp* of *Leinster*. It was *Colum Cille* <note>Saint Columba</note> who went to him to have the orders of a bishop conferred upon him.¹ Then *Colum Cille* sat under the tree to the west of the church and asked where the cleric was. "There he is," said a man there, "in the plowing-field below." "It seems to me," said *Colum Cille*, "that it is not proper for us that a plowman should confer orders upon us. However, since we have come for this purpose, let us test him." So first, he asked *Etchen* for the plowshare. He gave it to them at once, and the oxen continued to plow no less effectively. "The cleric is a good man!" they said. "Test him even further," said *Colum Cille*. He asked him for the outer ox. *Etchen* immediately gave it to them; then Bishop *Etchen* ordered a stag that was in the forest to do that work, and it did so immediately.

Then *Colum Cille*, having tested the cleric, went to him and told him why he had come. "It shall be done," said the cleric. Then the orders of a priest <note>sacerdotal orders</note> were conferred on *Colum Cille*, even though it was the orders of a bishop that he wished to have. The cleric prayed until the morning. "That is a mistake, O cleric," said *Colum Cille*, "the order that you have conferred upon me; and yet I will never change it as long as I am alive. In exchange for that mistake, now, no one shall ever come to this church to have orders conferred upon him." And this is still fulfilled.

Bishop *Erc*, son of *Maine* the poet, son of *Fergus*, son of *Corp*, son of *Fergus*, son of *Fothad*; and Bishop *Aedán* son of *Maine*; and *Coemgein*, son of *Coemlug*, son of *Coimedais*, son of *Corp*.

12. Concerning Bishop *Simplex*, that is, *Modiuít*, a bishop from *Cell Modiuít* in *Hy Many* <note>original: *Húi Maini*</note> in *Sogain*.
