# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [THE MONTH OF FEBRUARY.]

**Damán** <note>February 12th</note>: namely, from Tech Damáin in Ui Crimthannáin. Damán, Lithgen, Miada, Abban, Senchan, Dubán, and Toimdenach were seven brothers. Mell was their mother, and she was the sister of Saint Kevin <note>original: Coemgen</note>. Damán was the son of Laignech, son of Cainnech, son of Labraid, son of Imchad, son of Cú Corb.

**13. Mo-Domnóc**: namely, the feast of the death <note>original: étscehta</note> of Mo-Domnóc. He is from Tiprait Fachtna in Ossory <note>original: Osraigi</note>.
*The seed of the bees of Ireland.* <note>Mo-Domnóc is traditionally credited with bringing the first honeybees to Ireland from Wales.</note>

**14. In the field of Valentinus, etc.**: namely, the field of land where Valentinus was crucified; it was there that Marcellus was torn into pieces and fragments.

**15. Without celebration, etc.**: namely, it is not excessive to have a Sunday celebration on this feast always, for there is always a Sunday celebration on every chief festival in the year.
*With the feast of Berach, etc.*: namely, Berach son of Nemnán, son of Nemnangen, son of Fintan, son of Mál, son of Dobtha, son of Oengus, son of Erc Derg, son of Brian, son of Eochaid Mugmedón. His feast is fifteen days into spring, and his hermitage is in Cinél Dobtha in Connacht, namely at Cluain Coirpthi. An angel spoke this verse, and whoever recites it at the hour of death shall not be a person of hell:

> Berach and Mo-Choem, *delightful was their company,*
> *whoever prays to them at the lips of death,*
> *shall not go to death—that is, to hell.*

**16. To the virgin Juliana.** Juliana was in prison where she was being urged to worship idols. The Demon came to her in the night in the shape of an angel to persuade her toward that worship, until... a *good angel* <note>original: bonus angelus</note> came to her and said to her: "Do you know who is talking to you?" "I do not know," she said. "A demon," said he, "and do not let him go; hold him fast if you wish that he himself should tell you his stories." So she held him, and after that he revealed to her his deceits since the beginning of the world. "I," said he, "am Iafer the Black <note>original: Iafer niger</note>. It is I who persuaded Adam and Eve to the sin, and Cain to kill Abel; indeed, every evil that is done in the world, it is I who shapes them all," etc.

**To the virgin Juliana**: namely, a Roman virgin who bound the demon with a single hair of her head. Now, the name of this demon was Iafer the Black, and he is the same as Lucifer. Afterward she put him under a dunghill, and he confessed there that it was he who tempted Adam and Eve, and Cain, and Christ, and Judas, and others, and Juliana. **Juliana the Virgin**: namely, Iafer the Black is the name of the demon who tempted Eve and Adam and Cain and Christ and likewise Juliana. **Indel**: namely, she endured his snares. Or **Indel**: namely, his binding, because Juliana bound him with physical chains, and being bound, he told all his crimes to the virgin. She suffered <note>martyrdom</note> under the Emperor Maximian and Eleusius the prefect, her suitor, in the province of Nicomedia.

**17. The feast of Cormac, etc.**
*Cormac, bishop of Ath Truim <note>Trim</note> in Brega, or he was a successor of Patrick.* Namely, a bishop from Ath Truim in Loegaire in Meath.
*The feast of Fintan.* Fintan son of Gaibréne, son of Corcrán, son of Eochaid, son of Bresal, son of Dén, son of Connla, son of Art Cerp, son of Coirpre Nia, son of Cormac, son of Oengus.

# FEBRUARY 13-17.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

Daman, that is, of Tech Damáin <note>Damán's House</note> in Húi Cremthennáin. Damán, Lithgen, Miada, Abban, Senchan, Duban, and Toimdenach are seven brothers <note>original Latin: *septem germani sunt*</note>. Mell, who was the sister of Saint Coemgen <note>Kevin of Glendalough</note>, was their mother. Daman was the son of Laignech, son of Cainnech, son of Labraid, son of Cú-corp.

13. **My-Domnóc**, that is, the festival of Modomnóc's death. He is from Tipra Fachtnai <note>Fachtna's Well</note> in the west of Ossory.¹
*The race of Ireland's bees.* <note>Modomnóc is traditionally credited with bringing the first honeybees to Ireland from Wales.</note>

14. **In Valentine's field** etc., that is, the field of land in which Valentine was crucified.² It is there that shreds and pieces were made of Marcellus <note>original Latin: *de Marcello*</note>.

15. **Sing a Sunday's celebration**, that is, the Sunday's celebration on this feast is not superfluous, for there is always a Sunday's celebration on each chief festival in the year.
*With Berach's feast*, that is, Berach son of Nemnann, son of Nemangen, son of Findtan, son of Máil, son of Dobaid (?), son of Oengus, son of Erc the Red, son of Brian, son of Eochaid Muigmedón. His festival is a fortnight before spring, and he is in the desert <note>hermitage</note> of Cenél Dobtha in Connaught, that is, in Clúain Coirpthi. An angel said this verse, and whoever recites it at the hour of death will not be a dweller in hell:
> Berach and Mo-chóem, pleasant was their society:
> Whoever entreats them at death's lips will not go to death, that is, hell.

16. **To the virgin Juliana.**³ Juliana was in a dungeon, as the pagans were ordering her to worship idols. At night the Devil came to her in the shape of an angel to tempt her to that worship. But a good angel came to her and said: “Do you know who is conversing with you?” “I do not know,” she answered. “The Devil,” said he; “and he has not deceived you. Fasten him to you if you wish him to tell you his news.” So she bound him, and he declared to her his deceits from the beginning of the world. “I,” said he, “am *Iafer Niger* <note>Iafer the Black</note>: it is I who tempted Adam and Eve to sin, and Cain to kill Abel. Indeed, every evil that is done in the world, it is I who frame them all.”
*Juliana*, a Roman virgin who bound a devil with one of the hairs of her head. Iafer the Black was that devil's name, and he is the same as Lucifer.⁴ Afterwards she put him under a dunghill, and there he confessed that it was he who had tempted Adam, Eve, Cain, Christ, Judas, and others, including Juliana herself.
*Juliana the virgin*, that is, *Iafer the Black*, etc. <note>original Latin: *Iuliana uirgo, i.e. Iofer niger*</note>.

17. **Feast of Cormac**⁵ etc. Cormac, bishop of Áth Truim <note>Trim</note> in Bregia. Or he is a successor of Patrick, that is, a bishop from Áth Truim Húi Loeguiri in Meath.
*Feast of Finntan.* Finntan son of Gabrín, son of Corcran, son of Eochaid, son of Bresal, son of Dian (?), son of Condlae, son of Art cirp, son of Coirbre Nia, son of Cormac, son of Oengus.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF FEBRUARY.

On the feast of **Finntan** the prayerful. He lived for 115 years, and for seven score years <note>140 years</note> Finntan’s life was spent singing psalms over the brink of a well.
**Finntan** the generous—he never consumed during his whole life
Anything but withered barley bread and clay-colored water.

*I found a coldness*—this host was not protected, etc.

**Comgall** sang this verse for **Finntan** when he saw 170 saints along with him.
**Berchan** sang concerning the stone on which **Finntan** was baptized:
"Wonderful is this victorious anvil that happened upon the path;
Whoever walks around it three times will surely return again."
**Finntan** of **Clonenagh**; that is, he is in the territory of **Leix** in **Leinster**.

18. *He died*, etc. This refers to **Colman** of **Ardboe** in **Cinel Eogain**, or in **Scotland** north of the Mounth. <margin>Or **Colman** of **Ardboe** on the shore of **Lough Neagh**.</margin> <margin>Or **Colman Ciarda** from **Cluain-rois** on the northern shore of **Lough Derg**.</margin>

**Colman**, son of Aed, son of Guarc, son of Amalgad, son of Muiredach, son of Cairthenn, son of Erc, son of Echaid, son of Colla Uais.

**Molipa** in **Iveagh** of **Ulster**, or in **Ui Garrchon** in the **Fortuatha** of **Leinster**. <margin>**Molipa** from **Enach** in **Ulster**.</margin>
**Moliba**, son of Lainnedon, son of Finntan, son of Lugaid, son of Enna Boguine, son of Conall Gulban, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages.

19. **Baethine**, son of Cuanu, son of Cam, son of Enna; he is from **Tech-Baithine** in western **Meath**. There are three "Houses of Baithine": **Tech-Baithine** in **Meath**, **Tech-Baithine** in **Tirconnell**, and **Tech-Baithine** in **Airtech** to the west of **Rathcroghan** in **Connacht**. As it was said:
"Four namesakes have been counted—**Baethine**, strong and victorious:
The son of Finnach, the son of mighty Brenann, the son of Alla, and the son of Cuanu."

**Baithin**, son of Finnach, son of Echaid, son of Barr, son of Cairthenn, son of Columb, son of Lugna, son of Eogan, son of Guarc, son of Erc, son of Lugaid, son of Conall, son of Amergin.

20. **Gaius**, the Pope. He suffered <note>martyrdom</note> under Carullus or Carus.

21. *A calling*, etc. **Finntan Corach** <note>Finntan "of the Pledges" or "the Changeable"</note>. He went on a pilgrimage to **Connacht**, and they took sureties <note>guarantees</note> from him, whether he were alive or dead, that he would return again. **Finntan Corach** is in **Lemchaill** in the land of **Ui Duach** and **Leix**, or in **Clonenagh** in **Leix**, or in **Clonfert-Mulloe**; a choir is maintained at his grave, and nothing is more beautiful. He is called *Corach* <note>of the Pledges</note> because of the pledge <term>cor</term> regarding his returning again, alive or dead (or because of the contracts that were taken from him) when he went toward heaven. <margin>Or he threw the shrine in which his relics were kept into a whirlpool <term>cuire</term>.</margin> <margin>Or it is he who made a "choir" <term>cora</term> in a new-fashioned order, as in:</margin>

"May the merits of Saint **Columba**, and the most worthy **Baithin**,
and all the deeds of **Adamnan**, help us from the highest heavens."
<note>original Latin: "sancti Columbae merita / Bathinique dignisima, / ac Adamnani omnia, / adiuuent nos celsisima."</note>

# FEBRUARY 18-21. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

At the feast of *Finntan the prayerful*¹ <note>original: "Finntan chráibdig"</note>. One hundred and thirty-five years <note>original: "Fifteen years and six score"</note> was the age of Finntan while he was chanting psalms over the brink of a well. Generous Finntan never consumed anything during his life except bread made of woody barley and the muddy water of the earth.
"I have found something to protect this host," etc.

Comgall recited this verse to Fintan when he saw a thousand saints gathered together with him.

Berchan sang to the stone on which Fintan had been baptized:
"Wondrous is this anvil of victory which has appeared in my time!
Whoever shall turn it three times will surely return again."
*Fintan of Clúain ednech* <note>modern: Clonenagh</note>, which is in the territory of Leix in Leinster.

**18.** *He went etc.* This refers to Colmán from Ard bó in Cenél Eogain <note>modern: Ardboe, County Tyrone</note>, or perhaps in Scotland to the west of the Mounth <note>original: "Monad"</note>. Or it may be Colmán of Ard bó on the shore of Lough Neagh. Or Colmán Ciarda from Clúain rois on the northern shore of Lough Derg.

Colmán was the son of Aed, son of Gúaire, son of Amalgaid, son of Muredach, son of Cairthenn, son of Erc, son of Eochaid, son of Colla Úais.

*Others say* <note>original: "Alii dicunt"</note> that he is Colmán son of Aed, who is in Ardbó on the shore of Lough Neagh, *or this is because* <note>original: "Vel hoc quod"</note> etc.

Moliba is in Húi Echach (Iveagh) of Ulster; or in Húi Garrchon in the Fortuatha of Leinster.

Moliba was the son of Lainnedon, son of Finntan, son of Lugaid, son of Enda Bóguine, son of Conall Gulban, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages.

**19.** *Boethíne*, that is, the son of Cuana (?)² son of Caem (?), son of Énna; he is of Tech Baithíni <note>modern: Taughboyne</note> in the west of Meath. There are three "Houses of Baithíne": Tech Baithín in Meath, Tech Baithín in Tyrconnell, and Tech Baithín in Airtech to the west of Cruachan in Connaught, as it is said:
"Four names were counted: Boethíne the strong and victorious,
son of Findach; Boethíne the vigorous son of Brenan; Boethíne son of Alla; and Boethíne son of Cuana."

Baithín was the son of Findach, son of Eochaid, son of Barr, son of Cairthenn, son of Colum, son of Lugna, son of Eogan, son of Gúaire, son of Erc, son of Lugaid, son of Conall, son of Amergen.

**20.** *Gaius*, that is, a pope, *and so on* <note>original: "et etc."</note>.

**21.** *Finntan Corach*: on his pilgrimage he went into Connaught, and the people took pledges from him that he would return again, whether alive or dead. Finntan Corach is associated with Lemchoill in Tír úa nDuach and Laigis; or he is in Clúain Aitchen in Laigis, or in Brendan’s Clonfert. It is said that *choruses* <note>original: "Cóir"</note> are sung at his grave, rather than just praise. He is called "Corach" <note>meaning "of the pledges"</note> because of the pledge to return alive or dead. Or perhaps the shrine containing his relics turns on its own (?). Or it was he who made adjustments (*cora*) to the order of the new rite, *as the Saints* <note>original: "ut Sancti"</note> etc.

Or what is more true: the four Finntans are in Clonenagh <note>original: Cluain ednech</note>.
Finntan the Melodious, Senach the Rough, and Colman son of Comgall the Affectionate;
A trio of them with a shout of valor, one after another in the abbacy.

**22.** **In Antioch** <note>original: IN Antuaig</note>—that is, the ordination of Peter in Antioch. It was in Antioch that Peter’s hair was cut <note>referring to the clerical tonsure</note>, and it was there he gave his first sermon, and there these names were first found: "Christian" and "Church" <note>original: Christianus et ecclesiae</note>.

**Lawrence** <note>original: Laurint</note>—that is, a deacon of Rome; he was a wise man who answered the gentiles.

**23.** **Matthias** <note>original: Madian</note> the apostle, or the apostle Matthias.
That is, Ernin of Leighlin <note>original: Lethglinde</note> is on this day along with Matthias.

**24.** **Or the Passion of Peter’s successor**—Noble John <note>original: Eoin</note> the seeker;
The day on which the leap year <note>original: bisex</note> falls every fourth year.
<note>This refers to the angel’s judgment given to the saints regarding the arrangement of the leap year.</note>
Toward the leap year it happens, every fourth year;
So that the feast for this host should not disturb the rule.

**24.** **Lucian**—that is, a priest.
**Cummine**—that is, Cummine son of Dinertach; it is he who brought the relics of Paul and Peter with him to Disert Cumin in the sanctuary of Roscrea, until they escaped from him to Roscrea.

**25.** **He found** <note>original: Fofraith</note> etc.—that is, forty years after his passion. Petronilla, the daughter of Peter the apostle, found the head of Paul the apostle forty years after he was beheaded by Nero.

**27.** **The feast of Comgan**: Comgan of Glen Uissen. Comgan with his siblings: Comgan, Mernoc, Moelchu, Mirili, Moeldub, Teldub Tebard, and Aidne; the seven sons of Uthenn, daughter of Fedlimid.
A mighty tower, three loving gridirons <note>possibly a reference to martyrdom or asceticism</note>;
The sister of just Colum Cille, of the famous family of Conall the Great—she was his mother.
Comgan, son of Diarmait, son of Dega, son of Fer-corp, son of Mug-corp, son of Cormac, son of Ailill Olum.

**The finding of the head of John**: That is, the first finding of the head of John the Baptist <note>original: Iohannis Baptiste</note> is remembered here, 260 years after he was beheaded by Herod. However, the head of Paul the apostle was found forty years after his beheading, having been killed by Nero.
Two hundred and sixty years—a long, good period—are counted through the rules,
Since the treachery was committed against the man, and the head of John the Baptist was hidden.

**28.** **Sillan**—that is, the abbot of Bangor <note>original: Bennchoir</note>. A priest. Sillan the priest and successor of Comgall of Bangor.

# FEBRUARY 22-28.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

*Or what is more true*, in Cluain Eidnech <note>modern: Clonenagh</note> are the four Finntans.
Finntan Corach, Senach the rough, and friendly Colmán son of Comgall;
a trio of them with valorous warfare, one after the other in the office of abbot.

22. *In Antioch*, etc., that is, the installation of Peter in Antioch,¹ <note>original: "Antiochiae, Cathedra Sancti Petri Apostoli"</note> meaning that in Antioch Peter's hair was clipped <note>a reference to the clerical tonsure</note>, and there he gave his first sermon, and there these names, *Christian* and *church* <note>original: "Christianus" and "ecclesia"</note>, were invented.
*of Laurence*, that is, a deacon in Rome: he was a wise man who replied to the heathens.
23. *Matthias the apostle*, or the apostle Madian.
Erníne of Leighlin is commemorated on this day with Madian.
24. Or: The Passion of Peter's successor, seek the noble John:
on the day on which the *leap day* <note>original: "bisextus"</note> occurs every fourth year.
This is the angel's sentence to the saints concerning the intercalary day:
The *leap day* is to be inserted every fourth year
. . . a festival to this host so that it does not disturb your rule.

Cummine, that is, Cuimine son of Dínertach: it is he who brought the relics of Paul and Peter to Dísert Cumin in the precinct of Roscrea, and they fled from him to Roscrea.
25. *Has been found*, that is, *after* <note>original: "post"</note> etc. Petronilla, etc.
27. *Feast of Comgan*. Comgan of Glenn Uissen. *Comgan with his brothers* <note>original: "Comgan cum germanis"</note>, that is, Comgan, Mernóc, Moelchú, Mírili, Moeldub, Teldub, and Tebard Aidne—the six sons of Uthenne, daughter of Fedlimid.
A populous (?) tower, through . . .
The sister of Colum of the eminent clan of great Conall was his mother.
Comgan son of Diarmait, son of Dega, son of Fir corp, son of Mog cuirp, son of Cormac, son of Ailill Ólommm.²
*finding of John's head*:
Two hundred and sixty years, lasting and good, are reckoned by the rules,
after the treachery which the men used to practice (?), John the Baptist's head was hidden.
28. *Of Sillán*, that is, an abbot of Bangor <note>original: "Bennchor"</note>, who was a priest. Sillán, a priest and a successor of Comgall of Bangor.³

---
¹ *At Antioch, the Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle; who, having been freed from chains, after he had restored to life the dead son of Theophilus the governor, presided over the Church of Antioch for seven years, after Simon the sorcerer had been driven out.* See the *Martyrology* <note>original: "Martyrologium"</note> at Feb. 22.
² See Comgan's pedigree in the *Book of Leinster* <note>original: "LL"</note> 351ᶜ, where *Son of Themne* <note>original: "Maic Themne"</note> comes between *Son of Dega* and *Son of Fir chorb*.
³ The *Sinlanus* (likely to be read as *Silnanus*) of the Antiphonary of Bangor, *Treasury of Old Irish* <note>original: "Thes. pal. hib."</note> II. 282.

# THE MONTH OF MARCH

<center>### MARCH ###</center>

**D. March 1 (The Calends of March)**
On the first day <note>original: "calends"</note> of the month of March—they are not haughty when one prays to them—are **Senán**, **Moinenn**, **Moses**, and **David** of Cell Muini <note>St. David of Wales, patron saint of Wales; Cell Muini is the Irish name for St. Davids</note>.

**E. March 2 (6 days before the Nones of March)**
If you remember the feasts on the suffering <note>original: "passion"</note> of **Lucilia**, there is also the birth of **Old Paul**—a sound rampart—and the fair feast of **Fergna** of Iona <note>Fergna Brit, the fourth abbot of Iona</note>.

**F. March 3 (5 days before the Nones of March)**
At the suffering of **Florianus**, there are two preeminent stars: **Céle Críst**—a fair injunction!—and my **Macru**, son of Senan.

**G. March 4 (4 days before the Nones of March)**
Proclaim the bishop’s royal, brilliant suffering in Rome with a vast angelic host: **Lucius**, a shining light <note>Pope Lucius I</note>.

**A. March 5 (3 days before the Nones of March)**
Not silently has their renown leaped over the eastern sea: **Carthach** the royal and city-founding, and **Ciarán** of Saigir <note>St. Ciarán of Saighir, one of the Twelve Apostles of Ireland</note>, leader of hosts.

# MARCH 6–11. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.

<page-num>81</page-num>

**B. March 6** <note>original: *Pridie nonas Martii* — the day before the Nones of March</note>
May they protect us <note>original: *Ron-snádat*</note> through their piety straightway to God’s kingdom: the splendid host that was slain on the feast of Victorinus.

**C. March 7** <note>original: *Nonis Martii* — the Nones of March</note>
Dear is the godly pair that deserves no reproach from our song: the hallowed Felicitas and the excellent Perpetua. <note>Felicitas and Perpetua were famous early Christian martyrs in Carthage, North Africa.</note>

**D. March 8** <note>original: *viii. idus Martii* — eight days before the Ides of March</note>
Senan of Inis Cathaig <note>modern: Scattery Island</note> gibbeted <note>original: *crochais* — literally "crucified" or "hung," here meaning he overcame or subdued</note> the enemy of Nárach. Conandil, a victorious pillar, and Bishop Beó-áed the warlike.

**E. March 9** <note>original: *vii. idus Martii* — seven days before the Ides of March</note>
The death of forty soldiers with a great host that was brighter, to whom the sun arose with paeans <note>original: *hilchu* — songs of joy or shouts of victory</note> in a black, dark place. <note>This refers to the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste, who were left to freeze in a lake.</note>

**F. March 10** <note>original: *vi. idus Martii* — six days before the Ides of March</note>
To the angels has been summoned Constantine the fair and luminous, by whom was found the angelic shaft: the tree of the Lord’s Cross. <note>This refers to the legend of the Discovery of the True Cross, often associated with the Emperor Constantine or his mother Helena.</note>

**G. March 11** <note>original: *v. idus Martii* — five days before the Ides of March</note>
They are attendants <note>original: *coimti*</note> of our Lord <note>original: *Fíadat*</note> in the Kingdom above kingdoms: Librén, perennial Senan, and Constantine, King of Rathen. <note>modern: Rahin, near Tullamore.</note>

***

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>
<header>[THE MONTH OF MARCH.]</header>

**A. March 12 (4th Ides of March)**
Before reaching his territory <note>original: *ferainn*; referring to the heavenly kingdom</note>, the organ of a hundred victories, the very vehement Gregory of Rome <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note>, crucified his body for the sake of Christ.

**B. March 13 (3rd Ides of March)**
May my Coemóc <note>Saint Mo-Choemóc</note> convoy us to the eternal protection that is to come; and Cuangus the chaste, a man of wisdom <note>original: *soas*; science or spiritual knowledge</note>, from Liath Mór <note>Leighmore, County Tipperary</note>—they are a goodly pair!

**C. March 14 (Day before the Ides of March)**
Dionysius the bishop, whose companies <note>original: *cléri*; clergy or trains of followers</note> are lovely: may Christ’s namesake <note>original: *comainm*; likely referring to the name "Christian"</note> convoy us! May the Savior <note>original: *Saluator*</note> save us!

**D. March 15 (The Ides of March)**
Proclaim the sovereignty of James; Luke is over the hair of the sea <note>original: *lir úas trilis*; a poetic metaphor for the waves or the shore</note>: the sons of Nessán from the island <note>Ireland's Eye, near Howth</note> loved whispered prayer to Christ.

**E. March 16 (17th day before the Kalends of April)**
Eugenia was beloved on earth by all except the Devil. Also Abbán, an angelic bush of gold, and the radiant Fínán the Leper <note>Saint Fínán Lobur</note>.

**F. March 17 (16th day before the Kalends of April)**
The flame of a splendid sun, the apostle of virginal Ireland: may Patrick, with his many thousands, be the shelter for our wretchedness!

<header>MARCH 18–23.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>
<page-num>83</page-num>

### G. 15th day before the Kalends of April <note>original: xv. cal. Apr. (March 18)</note>
With the great troop of martyrs whose faults were not many, beside Timothy was reckoned a score of glorified soldiers.

### A. 14th day before the Kalends of April <note>original: xiu. cal. Apr. (March 19)</note>
My Lachtóc with Gregory, the lovable champion who is highest; Joseph, a name that is nobler—Jesus's pleasant fosterer <note>foster-father</note>.

### B. 13th day before the Kalends of April <note>original: xiii. cal. Apr. (March 20)</note>
The departure <note>death/passing</note> of Polycronius, a holy bishop who is most noble; he stepped a step that is straighter, with a great host that was bolder.

### C. 12th day before the Kalends of April <note>original: xii. cal. Apr. (March 21)</note>
To the world he was many victories, Benedict the stout pillar; on the same festival—a sea full of hosts—is the conspicuous Éndae of Aran <note>Saint Enda of the Aran Islands</note>.

### D. 11th day before the Kalends of April <note>original: xi. cal. Apr. (March 22)</note>
The high suffering <note>martyrdom</note> of Secundus, fair in words of might; a strong light over the sea's rampart is Failbe, the hero of Iona.

### E. 10th day before the Kalends of April <note>original: x. cal. Apr. (March 23)</note>
The daughter, with a vast host, of Feradach who is highest; from Christ he sets forth nobility, my Maedóc, the diadem of Alba <note>Scotland</note>.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF MARCH]

<page-num>84</page-num>

*   **F. 9th of the Calends of April [March 24]**
    Splendid the lustrous couple
    whom plenteous penitence washed:
    Fair Scíre <note>A female saint of Killiskey</note> who loved fasting for three days,
    and Mochtae <note>Saint Mochta of Louth</note>, pious and devout.

*   **24.** Splendid the lustrous couple which plenteous penitence washed: fair Scíre who loved fasting for three days, Mochtae pious, devout.

*   **G. 8th of the Calends of April [March 25]**
    The Crucifixion and Conception
    of Jesus Christ are fittingly
    on one pious festival,
    along with the passion of James.

*   **25.** It is fitting that the Crucifixion and Conception of Jesus Christ occur on one pious festival with the passion of James.

*   **A. 7th of the Calends of April [March 26]**
    In Letha <note>original: Letha; likely referring to Brittany or Rome in this context</note> has fallen
    my Cellóc after many days;
    the feast of the eternal Sinchell
    of vast Cell Achid <note>Killeigh, County Offaly</note>.

*   **26.** In Letha has fallen my Cellóc after many days: the feast of the perennial Sinchell of vast Cell Achid.

*   **B. 6th of the Calends of April [March 27]**
    On the sixth of the calends of April,
    after releasing the souls,
    Jesus—a mighty tale—
    has arisen out of the womb of the earth.

*   **27.** On the sixth of the calends of April, after releasing the souls, Jesus—a mighty tale—has arisen out of the womb of the earth.

*   **C. 5th of the Calends of April [March 28]**
    May she call us, may she save us
    from pains, may she bless <term>sain</term> <note>original: ron-séna; to bless or protect with a sign</note> us;
    may Mary magnify us,
    the great Magdalene!

*   **28.** May she call us, may she save us from pains, may she bless us, may Mary magnify us, the great Magdalene!

*   **D. 4th of the Calends of April [March 29]**
    With the festival of the daughters of Baite,
    the passion of a great host with hospitality;
    on the feast of the man of virginity,
    Gregory of Nazianzus.

## E. 3rd Calends of April [March 30]
Announce my Cua of Balla, <note>original: Slúind mo Chúae Ballae</note>

## F. The day before the Calends of April [March 31]
The fork-shaped cross <note>original: Croch nínach; referring to a gallows or a specific shape of crucifix</note> of Anissus,
with a fair company that was swifter;
it puts a crown forever
upon the swarm of the hosts of March.

30. Announce my Cua of Balla,
a vessel with abundant sovereignty:
Colman from beautiful Lann, at
the feast of devout Tola.

31. The fork-shaped cross of
Anissus, with a white train that
was swifter, forever puts a

of March. <margin>See below, November 30.</margin>

## NOTES.

1. **Senan**—that is, the abbot of Scattery Island <note>original: Indsi Cathaig</note>, son of Gerrcend, son of Dubthach, son of Deice, son of Imchad, son of Corb. <margin>R²</margin>. Senan of Scattery Island died on this day. <margin>R¹</margin>.
**Moinenn**—that is, a "psalm-singer," bishop Moinenn and successor <note>term: comarba; the heir or successor to a founding saint's office</note> of Brendan of Clonfert. <margin>R²</margin>.
**Moisi** or **Maisi**—a monk from Egypt. Or Maisi, son of Amram. <margin>R²</margin>. That is, the son of Amram <note>The biblical Moses</note>. <margin>R¹</margin>.
**David**—that is, of the Southern Britons; David, the Archbishop of the island of Britain. <margin>R²</margin>. David—that is, David of Menevia <note>St. David's in Wales</note> of the Southern Britons. <margin>L</margin>.

2. **Old Paul**—that is, Paul the Hermit. <margin>R¹</margin>.
**Fergna**—that is, Fergna the Briton, Abbot of Iona <note>original: Iæ Coluim cille</note>. Fergna, son of the poet, son of Finntan, son of the son of Cuinnedda, son of Daithim, son of Cas, son of Fraech, son of Cumscrach. <margin>R²</margin>.

3. **Cele Crist**—that is, from the Church of Cele Crist in the territory of Ui Dunchada in Leinster.¹ <margin>R²</margin>.
**Mo-achru**—that is, abbot of Clonenagh in Leix, or from House of Tachru near Tallaght. <margin>R¹</margin>.

4. **Suffering** <note>original: cesad</note>—that is, he was beheaded in Rome under the Emperors Gallienus and Valerian. <margin>F</margin>.
**Lucius**—that is, Pope and martyr. <margin>F</margin>.

5. **Cartach**: Cartach, son of Finan, son of Noah, son of Cellan, son of Saiglenn, son of Cerb, son of Ambrie, son of Imchad. That is, Cartach was the foster-son of Ciaran of Saighir and he was the son of the King of the Eoganachta of Cashel,² and his place is in Carbury of the O'Kearys—namely, Druim Fertáin—and he also possesses Inis Uachtair on Lough Sheelin.³ He was also the foster-father of Saint Mochuta, as Saint Ita said:

> Cartach shall come to you, a man with a vessel of faith,
> A son shall be born to Cartach <gloss>(namely, Molua son of Ocha)</gloss> who shall not die at all.

It was this Cartach, the foster-son of Ciaran, who was sent to Rome by Ciaran on a pilgrimage because he had met a woman⁴ from whom Molua son of Ocha was born. <margin>R²</margin>.

**Ciaran.** Ciaran of Saighir, "bishop of bishops." He was of the Dal Birn, and "Uar" is the name of his well, as Saint Patrick said:

> Seek Uar, build a city on its bank;
> After thirty long, active years, I and you shall meet there.

> Pious Ciaran, noble successor, senior of the saints, heaven is under his rank;
> Wonderful was the birth of the King's champion, whose peaceful dwelling is Great Saighir.

> Son of Lugna, a sea of vast wisdom, if he occupies the earth—a shore that is no lie—
> On the day when Judgment spreads, happy <gloss>(literally: well-born)</gloss> is everyone who shall be his follower.

> Liadaine <gloss>(Ciaran's mother)</gloss> was asleep on her bed—a saying that is not false—
> When she turned her face toward heaven, a star fell into her mouth.

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF MARCH]</header>

From this was born a wonderful child—let **Ciaran of Saighir** be named by you; and of him it was said—a saying without pride—that **Luaigne** said, "He shall be my son." <note>original: "nim-ba mac" - literally "he shall be my son" or "he is my son."</note>

**Liadaine**, daughter of **Maine Chirr**, son of **Aengus**, of the family of **Lugaid son of Ith**, was the mother of **Ciaran of Saighir**. He was born in **Finntracht Glére** <note>Clear Strand, likely Sherkin Island, Cork</note>. It was there he was born, and the angels of the Lord attended his birth, and the ranks of heaven baptized him. It was in **Corca Luigde** <note>A kingdom in South-West Cork</note> that the Cross was first believed in in Ireland; for Ciaran of Saighir took up his station thirty years before **Patrick**, as it is said: "Seek [Saig] etc."

->The boy born in **Tulach Tinn** shall be pure in his union with us;<-
->many monks and a slow-moving community shall **Conall** find after him.<-

It was then that Ciaran prophesied concerning **Conall** and **Fachtna of Rosscarbery**. It was Ciaran who left to the descendants of **Etersceoil** the kingship and leadership forever. He also left to the King of Corca Luigde the honor-price <term>eneclann: a legal value based on social status</term> of a provincial king, because they first believed in the Cross through him, and because they maintained Ciaran’s church. This Ciaran is also the senior of the saints of Ireland.

Ciaran, son of Luaigne... son of **Duach**, son of **Conall**, son of **Cairbre**, son of **Buan**, son of **Imbuan**... of **Leithtriun**, son of **Amalgad**, son of **Loegaire Birn**, son of **Aengus of Ossory**.

Truly, this holy Ciaran of Saighir was wonderful. He possessed much livestock, for there were ten gates upon the fold of his cows, and ten pens for every gate... and there were ten calves in every pen, and ten cows for every calf. Yet Ciaran never ate any portion, small or great, of the condiment <term>anlann: a side-dish or relish eaten with bread</term> or the produce of those animals while he lived; instead, he distributed it all to the poor and the needy of the Lord. Furthermore, Ciaran had fifty broken horses for plowing and tilling the earth, but it is likely that although they plowed, he never ate a single loaf of the harvest while he lived. His dinner every night was a small morsel of barley bread and a drink of pure spring water, with two roots of sea-fern <note>original: "murrathaig"</note> as a condiment. Moreover, the skins of wild animals were the clothes he wore, with a wet cloak over them outside. A stone pillow was under his head when he slept, as Ciaran said:

Ten gates on the enclosure of my cattle, ten pens for every bright-faced gate,
Ten calves in every pen without distress, ten foolish cows around every calf.

I confess to the **Son of Mary**, though it may seem strange to you all,
Nothing the size of a mite <note>original: "friged" - a tiny insect or atom</note> of that condiment ever passed my teeth.

Fifty colts in my fair church at Saighir tilling the earth,
By my confession, O pleading Christ, I never ate one loaf from them.

A little cake of barley and pure water, that was my dinner at all times;
The condiment I was accustomed to was two roots of sea-fern.

<summary>This page details the hagiography of Saint Ciaran of Saighir, asserting his status as a "senior" saint who preceded Saint Patrick. It emphasizes his extreme asceticism, noting that despite his vast herds and agricultural wealth, he lived on barley bread, water, and wild roots.</summary>

# MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

MARCH 5.]

From that union was born the wondrous child, Ciarán of Saiger—let him be mentioned by you—and because of this (it is a saying without pride) Luaigne declared that Ciarán was not his biological son. <note>This refers to the tradition of Ciarán’s miraculous or divine associations at birth.</note>

Liadaine, daughter of Maine Cerr, son of Oengus, of the race of Lugaid son of Ith, was the mother of Ciarán of Saiger. He was born in Findtracht Glére <note>Modern: Clear Island, County Cork</note>, and after his birth, the angels of the Lord tended to him, and the ranks of heaven baptized him. It was among the people of Corcu Luigdech that the Cross was first believed in within Ireland, for it was thirty years before Patrick arrived that Ciarán established Saiger, as the saying goes: *Seek, etc.*

"A son who is born in Tulach Tenn, pure shall be his union with us; many a monk and gentle nun will follow after him under Conall's care."

It was then that Ciarán foretold the coming of Conall and Fachtna of Ross Ailithir; and it was Ciarán who granted to the Etersceoil family kingship and leadership forever. He also granted to the king of the Corcu Luigde the honor-price <note>term: a legal payment reflecting a person's social status</note> of a provincial king, because they were the first to believe in the Cross, and because they defended the rights of Cell Ciaráin. Ciarán is also considered the senior (eldest) of the Saints of Ireland.

Ciarán was the son of Luaigne... son of Dua, son of Conall, son of Cairbre, son of Buan, son of Imbuan... Lethtrén, son of Amalgad, son of Loeguire, Birn... son of Oengus of Ossory.

Wondrous, indeed, was the holy Ciarán of Saiger. He possessed many cattle, for there were ten doors to his cowshed and ten stalls for every door... and there were ten calves in every stall, and ten cows with every calf. As long as he lived, Ciarán never consumed any portion of their meat or side-dishes <note>original: *obsonium* — a Latin term for food eaten with bread</note>, nor any of their great produce; instead, he distributed it all to the poor and the needy of the Lord. Furthermore, Ciarán had fifty horses broken-in for ploughing and tilling the earth, but it appears that he never ate a single cake made from the grain they tilled as long as he lived. This was his dinner every night: a small piece of barley-bread and spring water to drink, with two roots of sea-fern (?) as a side-dish. He wore the skins of fawns as his clothing, with a wet quilt over them on the outside. A stone bolster was at his head when he slept.

As Ciarán said:
> Ten doors on the cattle-fold <note>original: *booley* — a traditional Irish mountain hut or enclosure for cattle</note> of my kine, ten stalls for every red-faced door, ten calves for every stall, without suffering, ten simple cows with every little calf.
>
> By my confession to Mary’s Son, though all this seems strange to you, never did so much as a flesh-worm pass under my tooth.
>
> Fifty young horses <margin>literally: foals</margin> in my fair church in Saiger which till the ground; on my conscience, O pleading Christ, I never ate one cake produced by them! <margin>meaning: from the grain they helped to till</margin>
>
> A small loaf <note>original: *manchet* — a fine white bread, though here specified as barley</note> of barley and pure water was my dinner every time; this is the side-dish I was accustomed to: two roots of sea-fern (?).

<summary>This page details the genealogy, miraculous birth, and extreme asceticism of Saint Ciarán of Saiger, emphasizing his role as a precursor to Saint Patrick in Ireland. It highlights his vast herds and resources, all of which he gave to the poor while living on a meager diet of barley bread and water.</summary>

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS [MONTH OF MARCH]

<page-num>90</page-num>

Two calfskins, end to end; a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> under my side; a stone under my head.
A wet quilt around me always, every single day and every single night.

This is my Saigir <note>Seir Kieran</note> at all times; whoever reaches it will be pure.
It shall be a communion for each one individually, until the end of fifteen days.

Cairnech the Bald, however, was the scribe of Ciarán of Saigir. It was he who wrote that wonderful manuscript, namely the *Wandering of Ciarán*, with its many beautiful and various decorations; and this book still remains in Saigir. And let everyone who reads it offer a blessing for the soul of Cairnech the Bald and for my own soul as well.

**6.** Coirpre Crom, Mael Ruain, Maeldubh, Muadan, Odhran, and Julian from the Church of the Pious Daughters of Leinin in the district of Ui Briuin Cualann <note>modern south Dublin/north Wicklow</note> on this day.

**7.** Felicitas and Perpetua were given to the wild beasts at Carthage in Africa. <note>original: "apud Cartaginem in Affrica bestiis datae sunt"</note> Mochelloch and Mettan of Tuaim Atha, a virgin, and Cairitan of Druim Lara on this day.

**8.** **Senán of Inis Cathaig** <note>Scattery Island</note>. **He crucified**—that is, he suspended or bound—the beast named Cathach, from whom Inis Cathaig is named. The reason he bound it was because it had killed the blacksmith named Nárach. Senán resurrected the blacksmith—that is, he brought him out from the belly of the beast. The beast was an enemy to the blacksmith, and Senán was a "crucifier" <note>punisher/subduer</note> to the beast.

There was a certain beast <note>original: "Quaedam bestia"</note> that lived on this island before Senán, and the island is named after it, for the beast used to fight against the crowds there and killed many in the regions around the island. Therefore it is named Inis Cathaig <note>Island of the Battler</note>. But Senán bound it with an iron chain according to the history, or by the power of God he restrained it. Hence it is said, "he crucified an enemy in a bond"—that is, the enmity that was ready for battle, he "crucified" it in a bond (in a fetter), so that it might do no evil to anyone.

Or, Senán "crucified" the enemy of Nárach. There was a certain blacksmith <note>original: "quidam faber"</note> in that region named Nárach, whom the beast called Cathach killed. Senán therefore "crucified" the one who was an enemy to Nárach the blacksmith. This day is recorded as the day of his burial.
Senán, son of Gerrchenn, etc.

Nárach the smith, generous and brave,
Went in a boat upon the sea;
Across the hair of the ocean <note>original: "trilis lir" - a poetic term for waves</note> he surely goes,
Over to Inis Cathaig.

When he reached the middle of the water,
The beast of persecution caught him;
Senán was told of this,
While he was there at prayer.

The cleric goes with fierce speed
To the edge of the grey sea;
He bound the beast away from him,
So it would no longer be an enemy to Nárach.

Nárach arrives—a goodly fight—
He was sound, he was completely alive;
The track of the beast was made clear,
And the miracle of Senán is magnified.

**Connadil**—that is, at the Waterfall of the Son of Erc in Connacht. "Conna" is the name, and his mother, out of affection, added the syllable "dil"—meaning "dear to me" or "dear to God." Conna means a "prop" or "pillar." Conna was the name, and his mother added a syllable to it out of fondness: "dil lim é" (he is dear to me), hence Connadil. Or **Conainne**—that is, from the Church of Conainne in Ui Maine of Connacht (in Sogan); she was a maternal sister to Senán of Inis Cathaig.

Two fawn-hides, head to head, a grave at my side, a stone under my head, a wet quilt over me always, every single day and every single night. There is my Saiger <note>Saighir, the monastery founded by St. Ciaran</note> every time! Whoever shall reach it will be pure: to everyone apart there will be communion, to the end of fifteen days.

Now Cairnech the Bald was the scribe of Ciaran of Saiger. It is he who wrote the wonderful manuscript, namely *Ciaran's Journey*, with its many various illuminations, and this book still remains in Saiger. And let everyone who shall study it give a blessing on the soul of Cairnech the Bald, and on my own soul.

**6.** Cairbre the Bowed, and Maelruain and Maeldub and Muadan and Odran and Julian [and Lenin's daughters] of the Church of the daughters of Lenin in Húi Briuin Cualann <note>A territory in modern County Dublin/Wicklow</note> on this day.

**7.** Felicitas and Perpetua, etc. Mochellóc and Mettan of Tuaim átha, a virgin, and Cairitan of Druim lara on this day.

**8.** Senan of Inis Cathaig <note>Scattery Island</note>, *hanged*, that is, Senán "hanged" or fettered the monster named Cathach, from which Inis Cathaig is named. He fettered it because it killed the smith whose name was Nárach, and Senán brought the smith back to life—that is, he brought him out of the monster's belly. The monster was a foe to the smith, and Senán was a "hangman" to the monster.¹

> A certain beast, etc. <note>original: *Quaedam bestia etc.*</note> for the monster used to battle against a multitude out of the water, and it killed many, etc. <note>original: *multos occidebat etc.*</note> from which it is said “he hanged the foe in a fetter,” meaning the enmity that it showed in battle, he hung that in an *árach*, which is a fetter, so that it could not [harm anyone], etc. <note>original: *ut nec etc.*</note> Or Senán hung the foe of Nárach, a certain smith who was [there], etc. <note>original: *qui fuit etc.*</note> So Senán hung that which was an enemy to Nárach the smith. Here [is the story], etc. <note>original: *Hic etc.*</note>
> Senán son of Gerrchenn, etc.

Nárach the smith, a man of hospitality and valor, went in a boat upon the sea: over the "hair of the ocean" <note>a poetic term for waves</note> he surely went away into Inis Cathaig.

When he had crossed half the water, the persecuting monster took him: this was reported to Senan while he was praying.

The cleric goes with fierceness to the edge of the green sea; he bound the monster away from him, for it was a foe of Nárach's.

He comes to Nárach—a good fight—who was safe and quite alive; the track of the monster was white <note>perhaps referring to foam or a miraculous trail</note>, and the miracle is magnified by Senán.

*Connadil*, that is, at Ess mac nEirc in Connaught. *Conna* is the name, and his mother, out of piety, added the syllable *dil* <note>original: *per pietatem additamentum syllabae dil*</note>, meaning "dear," either to me or to God. *Conna* means a pillar or house-post. *Conna* was the name, and his mother gave it the addition of a syllable from affection, saying *dil* (“dear”) is he to me: *Conna-dil*. Or Conainne, of the Church of Connainne in Húi Maini of Connaught (in the district of Sogan), a daughter of the mother of Senán of Inis Cathaig.

**Bishop Beoid**, that is, "living fire" <note>original: *béo aed*</note>, from Ardcarne in Moylurg, in the territory of Connacht.
**Bishop Beoid**, son of Olcan, son of Cuman, son of Maidne, son of Triun, son of Liun, son of Lugaid Mac Con.

**9. The death of the forty soldiers.** <note>The Forty Martyrs of Sebaste</note> Forty soldiers were cast into a cold lake by Lucinus, son of Lucine and nephew of Constantine. Guards were placed all around the lake so they could not escape and would drown. It was then that the sun shone upon them from the bottom of the lake. When the persecutors could not prevail against them, they were taken out of the lake, their legs were broken, and they were afterwards burned.
<note>original Latin: *Forty soldiers under Lucinus, nephew of the Emperor Constantine; they were first condemned to the water and afterwards, with broken legs, were consumed by fire.*</note>

> Forty soldiers, alas!
> were cast into a cold lake in the East;
> the sun shone for them with great heat

**11. *They are the companions of our Lord, etc.*** Or:
**A prayer on the feast of the son of Oiblen—Oengus among princes.**
That is, Oengus son of Oengobann, son of Oiblen, of the community of Clonenagh; it is he who composed the *Martyrology* <note>original: *Félire*</note> in Tallaght. Oengus sang:
> I have prayed to my merciful, mighty King,
> excellent is his heart-story,

**Constantine**, that is, the son of Fergus, successor of Mochuta of Rahen, in Delvin Ethra in Meath. He was a King of the Britons who left his kingdom and came on pilgrimage to Rahen in the time of Mochuta. He was also a King of Scotland <note>original: *Alban*</note>, and he traded the wealth of the earth for pilgrimage to seek heaven. He gave himself to service like any servant-monk to God. It was he who marked out the church, namely Rahen, and he dug its dyke and cultivated the field known as "Constantine’s Field" to the south of Rahen. His appetite was great—a "strong meal" <note>original: *proinn clít*</note> was what sustained him—until the leftovers of Mochuta were given to him. Mochuta blessed his mouth, and thereafter he ate only as much as any other monk; yet his strength did not fail, even though his appetite was diminished.

His humility was of great profit to the monks, for he had the strength of a hundred men. He then asked Mochuta for permission to go to Scotland to get news of his children and his kin. Mochuta gave him leave, and he returned again. His portion of food had been kept for him while he was away in the East; it was placed on a hide before him in a mixture—clerical porridge, milk, and corn—and some of it had turned sour. # MARCH 9-11. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

Bishop Beoid, that is, *béo-aed*, which means "living fire": of Aed Carna in Mag Luirg in Connaught. <note>Aed Carna and Mag Luirg are historical locations in County Roscommon, Ireland.</note>
Bishop Beo[á]id was the son of Olcán, son of Cuman, son of Maidne, son of Trén, son of Lén, son of Lugaid Mac-con. <note>This is a traditional Gaelic genealogy tracing the bishop's lineage.</note>

9. **Death of forty soldiers, etc.** This refers to forty soldiers who were cast into a cold lake by Licinius, the son of [the text is missing a name here], who was the son of Constantine's sister. Every one of them was placed around the lake so that they could not escape until they drowned. It was then that the sun shone upon them from the bottom of the lake. <note>original Latin: *sol ob signum supernae claritatis et consolationis emicuit* — "the sun shone forth as a sign of heavenly brightness and consolation."</note> Since the heathens could do nothing more to harm them, they were taken out of the lake, their legs were broken, and then they were burned. *Forty soldiers, etc.* <note>original Latin: *Quadraginta milites*</note>

> Forty soldiers, alas! in the east were cast into a cold lake:
> the sun shines for them, with much glowing heat, in the bottom of the great lake.

10. **Constantin**, that is, Constantine, the son of Helena, by whom Christ's cross was found. Constantine, son of Helena, *concerning whom*, etc. <note>original Latin: *de quo*</note>

11. ***They are comrades of our God.*** Or "a prayer on the feast of Oiblén's grandson, Oengus among princes" (this is another reading).
That is, Oengus son of Oingoba, son of Oiblén, of the community of Clúain Eidnech <note>modern Clonenagh, County Laois</note>; it was he who composed the Martyrology in Tallaght. Oengus sang:

> I have asked of my king, merciful and mighty—excellent is his heart-story—
> that Christ may be very indulgent to me so long as I am in the flesh.

**Constantine**, that is, the son of Fergus, successor of Mochutu of Rathen in Delbna Ethra in Meath. He was a king of Britain who left his realm and came on a pilgrimage to Rathen during the time of Mochutu. He was also king of Scotland, and he traded the wealth of the earth for a pilgrimage in order to gain heaven. So he gave himself to manual labor like any monk serving God; it was he who marked out the church at Rathen, dug its ditch, and improved *Cepach Cusantín* or "Constantine's Plot," to the south of Rathen. 

At that time, his appetite was enormous; specifically, the dinner of a hundred men was what it took to satisfy him. Therefore, the leftovers of Mochutu were given to him. Mochutu blessed <term>sained</term><note>original: "sained" — to sign with the cross or bless</note> his mouth, and after that, he would consume only the same amount as any other monk. And though his meal was reduced, his strength was not diminished. <note>The text compares this to a miracle performed by Saint Brigit.</note>

Indeed, the monks profited greatly from his humility, for he possessed the strength of a hundred men. Eventually, he asked Mochutu for permission to go to Scotland to visit his children and his kindred. Mochutu gave him permission, and he went and returned again. His share of dinner had been set aside for him while he was in the east; it was placed on a hide before him, all mixed together—the clerics' porridge, milk, and corn—and some of it had turned to worms. Nevertheless, he tightened his girdle around him and [pulled] the share toward him with both hands until it was clear that he had consumed it all.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF MARCH.]

The clerics <note>original: clérig</note> then ground the grain steadily and beautifully, for the steward was watching them to ensure that nothing remained of the meal without being consumed. "Go into the oak wood now," [said Mochuta,] "until tomorrow, and vent your anger there. Why did you force me to go to my chores at the beginning of last night as I did?" <note>original: dochúad</note> "Never before has such weakness come upon me that I could compare to this. Every weakness that ever overtook me, I cast off through my power. Every good thing I had, I made permanent." He went into the oak wood after that and cleared it.

On another occasion, while he was in the trench doing his work, the clerics ate their meal and he was forgotten. He became angry at this, so that he threw a shovel-full of earth from the trench onto the skylight of the dining hall, so that his portion reached his dish and the dish of every monk in the house.

Mochuta went to seek him out [afterward]. It was then that streams of sweat were pouring over him from the intensity of the labor. Mochuta put his palm to his forehead, and then put it to his own forehead. "Well, cleric," said Constantine, "the sweat of one's own brow heals everyone." "You have spoiled it," said Mochuta, "for had you not said that, even the dew of your burial place would heal everyone."

In the week before Constantine's death, while they were celebrating service in their church, Mochuta saw Satan standing over Constantine. "What brought you there?" asked Mochuta. "This man is a monk of mine," he said, "for the world is still on his conscience." "It is likely a small matter," said Mochuta. "It is a sin even if it is small," he replied. "Well, cleric, make your confession," said Mochuta. "I confess indeed, Lord," said Constantine, "that there is nothing of the world on my conscience, except I only think that I would like the flagstone upon which you say your prayers <note>original: patz (pater noster)</note> to be the one placed over my face." "It shall be so indeed," said Mochuta. "As for you, Satan, go into the standing stone that is south of the church, and do no harm there except to those who come against the church."

It was this aforementioned Constantine who obtained a respite of three years from Blathmec and Diarmait (the two sons of Aed Sláine), and from the communities of Finnian, Ciaran, and Colum Cille, so that Mochuta would not be expelled from Rahan <note>original: Raithin</note>. It was to this same Constantine that the clerics of Leth Cuinn <note>The northern half of Ireland</note> and the family of Aed Sláine gave a harsh refusal when he went to ask for a second year's respite from Mochuta's expulsion from Rahan. "He is the same old churl," everyone said, "and he shall have no welcome this time." "It is a harsh refusal, young men," said Constantine, "for we were once in the same prosperity that you are in now, until we sold it for the Lord <note>original: Coimdid</note>. I had seven forts <note>original: duine</note> on my conscience, and a queen for every fort, and gold and silver and herds of horses and white cows for every fort. I left all that so that I might be in servitude here for the love of the Lord. If you would grant a respite to me and to the one who sent me, it would be a great reward." A lot was cast between the communities of Finnian, Ciaran, and Colum Cille to see which bishop among them would go with Diarmait to seize Mochuta by the hand—for Diarmait was sent first to seize Mochuta's hand, but he failed...

# MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.
### MARCH 11-13.

Mochutu blessed Diarmait. Then came the turn of the community of Clonmacnois. They went to their cells. Then came the turn of the community of Cluain Cuangusa at the end of Ardgal. “I will go,” says their <term>erenagh</term><note>original: "erenagh"; a hereditary warden or administrator of church lands</note>, “to expel him.” Then the erenagh of Cluain Congussa goes to expel Mochutu. “Will you expel me?” says Mochutu. “You shall not sit in the abbot’s seat,” says the cleric. “You shall have neither heaven nor earth,” says Mochutu; “and may your erenagh always be a servant of straw-wisps and a laughingstock in assemblies and meetings!” 

“Woe to him who takes you and by whom you are taken!” says the prior of Cell Ached. “A blessing,” says Mochutu; “and with you will be the dignity of your church.” 

“Take him away,” says the sub-erenagh of Clonmacnois: “let not the fellow delay, a wordy log in the church.” “May neither heaven nor earth be yours,” says Mochutu, “and may cold and hunger always carry off your successor!” 

“It is a great pity what you do,” says the prior of Durrow. “It is you,” says Mochutu, “who will be prior and erenagh always in your place.” 

“Drag him down!” says the erenagh of Durrow. “May the hatred of your congregation be upon you,” says Mochutu, “and on your successor always! And may a finger always be needed to point the way to you in meetings, and to teach your successor.”

Then he turned to the community of Clonard, and cursed a part of them and blessed another part. Blathmec himself went up to him, along with Cronan the Red, the successor of Ciaran. “Why have you come?” says Mochutu. “To expel you,” says Blathmec. “You shall not,” says Mochutu. “You shall not hold the abbot’s seat against him,” he said. “Then I will expel you from the seat in which you are, and I will rob you of heaven and earth, so that neither king nor crown-prince shall descend from you.”

**12.** Gregory of Rome: that is, he was of the Children of Dega, and abbot of Rome. And it is he who bequeathed his body in a casket upon the river Tiber, with an ounce of gold on its breast—that is, the ounce of virginity—and God sent it to Aran. From this, the strand on which it arrived is named, and his relics are there, as Fercertne the poet of Cú-rói prophesied, saying, “Judgment will be born,” etc.

> Descendant of Dega, son of Sen, 
> Gregory of Ardmáil, abbot of Rome of full Latium <note>original: "Latium"; the region of Italy including Rome</note>, 
> goes into Ireland, for it is in his portion.

> wherein keen Gregory will be chief 
> of the pure, fair Gaels <note>original: "Góedil"</note>, 
> the race of bright Gaedel that branches out; 
> though it be a severe saying, I will say it.¹

**13.** <note>original: "nouissimus dies"</note> The last day, on which Shrovetide falls.
My Coemóc: that is, of Liath Mochoemóc in Eli.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF MARCH.

**Cuangus** <note>original: Cuangus</note>: he was a blind son. *L.* Cuangus, son of Ailell. *LL. 357*. From **Liathmor** <note>original: Liath mór; "Great Liath"</note> in southern Éile <note>a medieval kingdom in Munster</note>; they are from Liath together. *L.* From Liath **Mochoemoc** in Éile. *R¹*. From Liathmor in Éile of Munster. *R¹*.

### 14.
**Dionis** <note>Dionysius</note> the bishop: perhaps this is the Dionysius of this cycle. *R¹*. That is, of the cycles, as others think. A cycle does not come to an end until five hundred and thirty-five years have passed, according to the correct full count. *R²*.

### 15.
**James** <note>original: Iacop</note>: the brother of the Lord. *R²*. The ordination of James, the brother of the Lord, in Jerusalem. **Luke** the Evangelist, "a sea over tresses" <note>original: ler uas trilis</note>: that is, his city is on the brink of the sea. *R¹*.

**The sons of Nessan** from the island to the south of Reachrainn <note>Lambay Island</note>. *R¹*. That is, three brothers from the Island of the sons of Nessan <note>Ireland's Eye</note> in Fingal or in Brega: namely, **Monisiu**, **Neslogha**, and **Dichuil the Red**. *L.* Three brothers: Monisiu, Neslago, and Dichuil the Red. From the Island of the sons of Nessan in western Brega. *R¹*.

### 16.
"Beloved by all but the Demon," etc.
**Eugenia**, daughter of Philip. Philip went to take the kingship of Alexandria and Egypt by the command of the Emperor—namely, Commodus <note>original: Cemmonti</note>—and he took with him his wife, **Claudia**, and his two sons, **Sergius** and **Habitus**, and his daughter Eugenia, and her two eunuchs, **Protus** and **Hyacinthus** <note>original: Protinus 7 Nacinti</note>, along with her. 

It happened one day that she and her eunuchs passed by a monastery. At that hour, they were singing therein: "All the gods of the Gentiles are demons, but the Lord made the heavens" <note>original: Dii gentium demonia, at uero Dominus celos fecit</note>. "It is a pity for us indeed," she said, "if those we adore are demons. I will go," she said, "and offer myself to the God whom these people adore." 

She went then and took a male form upon her, for there were no women in the monastery. She was baptized by the name of **Elinus**, the name of the bishop who instructed and baptized her in Egypt <note>original: qui cataciazuit et bautizauit eam in Egipto</note>. (Steren, truly, is the name of the magus who subverted Ethiopia). 

She lived in such excellence that she was entrusted with the leadership of the monastery upon the death of the head monk. Then a harlot made an attempt upon her to have union with her. When she did not obtain it from her, the harlot said that the monk had raped her. Then the king of the land came to take vengeance upon her, and he was her own father, Philip. 

Then she called him aside to her and said to him: "Did you have a daughter?" she asked. "I did indeed," he said, "but I do not know her fate." She then revealed herself to him, and in that way, she and the monastery were cleared of the charge. Afterward, a hill-fire <note>a bonfire or execution by burning</note> was made of the harlot. She is the same Eugenia who suffered under the Emperor Commodus in Nicomedia, and her passion <note>martyrdom</note> is on the day of the Nativity of the Lord. **Melantia** is likewise the name of the woman after whom Eugenia suffered. *R²*.

**Abbán**, son of the descendant of **Cormac**, from Mag Arnaide in Hy Kinsella and from Kill Abbán in Hy Muiredaig. *R¹*.

**Finan the Leper** from Swords of Colum Cille, or from Clonmore Maedoc in Leinster, or from Innisfallen on Lough Leane in Munster. *R¹*.

### 17.
**Flame of the Sun** <note>original: Lasair gréne</note>. **Patrick**, that is, "father of the citizens" <note>original: pater ciuium</note>. *R¹*. That is, **Sinell son of Finnchad** is the first person whom Patrick baptized in Ireland; and **Nessan of Cork** was with Patrick on this day. Or **Lasair** is the name of the seventh daughter of **Brainin**.

# MARCH 14-17. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

Cuangus, that is, he was a blind son. <note>From the *Leabhar Breac*</note>, of Cuangus son of Ailill.
From Liathmor, that is, in southern Éli; they are from Liath at the same time, that is, from Liathmor in Éli of Munster.

14. *Dionysius the bishop*; this may be Dionysius of the cycle, that is, *of the cycle, as others think* <note>original Latin: *cicli, ut alii putant*</note>. The cycle does not come until the end of 535 years after a proper <term>ogtach</term> <note>likely a technical term for a calendrical beginning or golden number</note>.

15. *James etc. Luke the evangelist* over a sea's hair, that is, his city is on the sea-brink.
Sons of Nessán from the island to the south of Rechru <note>modern Lambay Island</note>, that is, *three brothers* <note>original Latin: *tres fratres*</note>, from the Island of the Sons of Nessán <note>Ireland's Eye</note> in Fingal, or in Bregia; namely, Monesi with Nesloga and Dicolla the Red.¹

16. Dear save to the Devil etc.
*Eugenia*. Eugenia, daughter of Philip. By command of the emperor Commodus, Philip went to take the governorship <note>original: "kingship"</note> of Alexandria and Egypt, and brought with him his wife, Claudia, his two sons, Sergius and Habitus, and his daughter Eugenia, and her two <term>eunuchs</term> <note>castrated male attendants</note>, Protas and Hyacinthus, along with her. It happened one day that she and her attendants were passing by the monastery of Edeb (?), and this is what the monks were then chanting: “The gods of the heathen are demons, but the Lord has made the heavens.” She said: “It is sad for us if it is demons whom we worship. Truly I will go and offer myself to the God whom these adore.” So she goes and assumes a man's form, for the name of the bishop who catechized and baptized her in Egypt.
*But Steren* <note>original Latin: *Steren vero*</note>, etc. Such was her excellence that after the death of the head of the monks, she was appointed to the leadership of the monastery. And a harlot tempted Eugenia to lie with her. But when nothing was gained from her, the harlot said that Eugenia had outraged her. So then came the king of the country to take revenge upon her, and he was her father, Philip. Whereupon she called him aside privately, and she said to him: “Had you a daughter?” “I had,” he answered, “and I know not her fate.” Then the king recognizes her, and thus she and the monastery were saved. Thereafter a hill-fire was made for the harlot. *She is the one* <note>original Latin: *Ipsa est*</note>, etc.²

Abbán <term>maccu Cormaic</term> <note>of the kindred of Cormac</note>, from Mag Arnaide in Húi Cennselaig and from Cell Abbáin in Húi Muiredaig.

Finán the leper, from Colum-cille's Swords <note>Skerries/Swords, Dublin</note>, or from Clúain mór Maedóic in Leinster, or from Inisfallen on Loch Léin in Munster.³

17. *Flame of a splendid sun* etc. Sinell son of Finnchad is the first person whom Patrick baptized in Ireland, and Nessán of Cork (is commemorated) *with Patrick on this day* <note>original Latin: *cum Patricio in hoc die*</note>.⁴

Or Lassair is the name of Brainín's seventh daughter, and in Cell...

<margin>² In four stanzas at the foot of the *Book of Leinster* 357, ‘Sergius’ is ‘Severus,’ ‘Protas’ is ‘Prothius,’ the two attendants are called Eugenia’s foster-children (*dalta*), and Elinus is stated to be the abbot of Heliopolis. # THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS [MONTH OF MARCH]

And at the Church of the Daughters of Brainin in Leix <note>original: Laigis</note>; and Clidna was the name of another daughter, from whom comes Clidna’s Wave <note>original: Tonn Clidna; a famous landmark in Glandore Harbour</note>.

**18.** Timothy <note>original: Tiamda</note>, perhaps he was the disciple of Paul the Apostle.
Mochta, that is, the Bishop of Louth <note>original: Lugmaid</note>. On this day, Domangart son of Eochaid from Slieve Donard <note>original: Sliab Slánga</note>. And Bishop Mac Cairthainn of Clogher is on this day.

**19.** Molachtóc, that is, Lachtain of Freshford <note>original: Achad úir</note> in Ossory.
Gregory, that is, the Abbot of Rome, the Pope. Gregory the Pontiff.
Joseph, that is, the spouse of Mary: it is more noble to call him the foster-father of Jesus than just Joseph. The spouse of Mary the Virgin.

**20.** Polychronius, who suffered <note>original: passus; i.e., was martyred</note> in the city of Babylon under the Emperor Decius.

**21.** Benedict, the supreme abbot of the monks of Europe. The head of the monks of Europe. And Enda of the Cremthanna of Brea.
Enda, that is, the son of Conall the Red, son of Daimin. And the daughter of Ainmire, King of the Men of Arda, was his mother.

**22.** Failbe, the Abbot. Failbe, Abbot of Iona <note>original: Ia</note>.

**23.** My Maedoc, that is, the son of Midna, son of Mete, son of Ninnid, son of Naxar, son of Crimthann, son of Cathair the Great.

**24.** Scire, at the Church of Scire <note>original: Cill Scire</note> in Meath.
Mochta, the Bishop of Louth.
Domangart, son of Eochaid.

**25.** The Crucifixion and the Conception, etc. It is clear to everyone that they are on the same festival. Or Corait and Caimin of Inis Cealtra on the same day.
In Nazareth of Galilee, the Annunciation of the Lord by Gabriel the Archangel to Mary the Virgin, when the angel said to her: "Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Jesus"; and on the same day He suffered under Pontius Pilate.
Our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified, and conceived, and the world was made <note>referring to the medieval belief that the Creation, Incarnation, and Crucifixion all occurred on March 25th</note>.
James of the Knees <note>original: Iacop Gluinech; James the Just</note>, the son of Alphaeus, suffered. Or the son of Cleophas, or the son of Joseph the brother of the Lord, and the first prince after Christ in Jerusalem for thirty years. He ruled the church in Jerusalem.
James, that is, James son of Alphaeus, the brother of the Lord and Bishop of Jerusalem, who was struck in the head with a fuller’s club and cast down from the pinnacle of the Temple and died. He was of the tribe of Judah. And on this day was the conception of Saint Mary in her mother’s womb.

**26.** In Letha, that is, the day on which he died. Or "in Letha" is the name of a spring or a wood where he died. Or perhaps it was in Rome of Letha <note>Letha often refers to Letavia/Brittany or Latium/Rome</note> that Mochelloc of the Church of Dachelloc in Hy-Corpri of Munster died; but it is more true that Cillin son of Tulodran of the Fortress of the son of Conchaid—which is not now in Letha—is mentioned here. Letha is the name of a great wood in the Decies of Munster, and that city was once located within it.
Sinchell of the Church of Achad <note>original: Cill Achith</note> in Offaly <note>original: Huib Failge</note>.
Sinchell, that is, the Elder Sinchell in Offaly in Leinster.
> Three hundred years—a pleasant satisfaction—
> That was the lifespan of Sinchell;
> With thirteen years clearly added,
> Without sin, without idleness.

# MARCH 18–26. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

The daughter of Brainín is in Leix (where her relics are kept), and *Clídna* is the name of another daughter of his, after whom is named *Tonn Clídna* "Clidna’s Wave." <note>original: *Tonn Clídna*. Clídna was a figure in Irish mythology; her "wave" refers to a famous surge in Glandore Harbour, County Cork.</note>¹

**18.** Timothy: he may be the pupil of Paul the apostle.
*Mochta*: that is, the bishop of Louth. On this day <note>original: *in hoc die*</note> are also remembered Domangart, son of Eochaid of Sliab Slanga, and bishop Mac Cairthind of Clogher.

**19.** *My-Lachtóc*: that is, Lachtain of Achad Úr in Ossory.²
Gregory: that is, the abbot of Rome, the pope. Gregory the Pontiff.
Joseph: that is, Mary’s spouse. It is considered nobler to call him "Jesus’s foster-father" than simply "Joseph."

**20.** Of *Polycronius*, etc.

**21.** Benedict: that is, the highest <note>original: *summus*</note> etc.,³ and Énna of Cremthainn Brea.
*Énna*: that is, the son of Conall the Red, son of Daimín; his mother was the daughter of Ainmire, king of Fir Arda.⁴

**22.** *Failbe*: that is, the abbot of Iona <note>original: *Colum cille’s Hí*</note>.

**23.** *My Maedóc*: that is, the son of Midgna, son of Meite (<unclear>?</unclear>), son of Naindid,⁵ son of N . . . son of Crimthan, son of Catháir Mór.

**24.** *Scíre*: that is, in Cell Scíre in Meath.
*Mochta*:⁶ that is, the bishop of Louth.
Domangart, son of Eochaid.

**25.** The Crucifixion and the Conception, etc.: it is clear to everyone that these events are observed on the same festival. Or, "in a yoke" <note>original: *corait*</note> is the correct reading; and Caimín of Inis Celtra is remembered on the same day <note>original: *in eodem die*</note>.
In Nazareth of Galilee, the Annunciation, etc.

Our Lord <note>original: *Dominus noster*</note> etc.
*James of the Knees*: that is, the son <note>original: *filius*</note> etc.
Of *James*: that is, James the son of Alphaeus, etc.

**26.** In *Letha* he has fallen, etc.: that is, the day on which he died. Or, *Letha* is the name of a spring or a wood <note>original: *nomen fontis uel silue*</note>, and he died there <note>original: *ibi obiit*</note>. Or it may be that in Rome of Latium <note>original: *Letha* was often used in Irish to mean Latium or Rome</note> *Mochellóc* died, who was from Cell Mochellóc in Húi Coirbri Muman. However, it is more likely <note>original: *sed uerius est*</note> that Cillín, son of Tulodran from Cathir meic Conchaid (which is not now called Letha), is the one mentioned here. *Letha* is the name of a great wood in the Déisi of Munster, and that city was formerly located within it <note>original: *et in ea ciuitas illa olim fuit*</note>.⁷
Sinchell of Cell Achid in Offaly.
Of Sinchell: that is, of Sinchell the Elder <note>original: *Sinchell senior*</note>, in Offaly in Leinster.
Three hundred years—a fine satisfaction—that was Sinchell’s age; with thirty years lived brightly, without sin and without ease.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF APRIL.

### THE MONTH OF APRIL.
**G. April 1 (The Calends of April).**
The calends <note>The first day of the month</note> of April ennoble
Ambrose, with great purity;
he possesses what is the greatest happiness,
one of the feasts of Mary. <note>This refers to the Annunciation, often celebrated near this time, or a specific local commemoration.</note>

**A. April 2 (Four days before the Nones).**
The great host of Amphianus,
because of whom the Devil was sorrowful,
passed, after a hard battle,
into the noble, happy peace.

**B. April 3 (Three days before the Nones).**
The host of noble Evagrius
has escaped by ways of tribulation;
forty kings
along with two fair hundreds.

**C. April 4 (The day before the Nones).**
Sing of pious Tigernach; for
Christ’s sake he vanquished <note>original: *breuis*</note>
every lust—
out of whom burst a stream of knowledge,
Tigernach of beautiful Clones <note>original: *Clúain Euis*</note>.

**D. April 5 (The Nones of April).**
On the great feast of Béccán, son of Cula,
with the victory of piety;
the excellent baptism of Patrick
has been kindled in Ireland.

***

<margin>
1. Ambrose ennobles the start of April.
2. Amphianus's victory over the Devil.
3. Evagrius and his companions escape suffering.
4. Tigernach of Clones, a fountain of wisdom.
5. Béccán mac Cula and the spreading of Patrick's baptism.
</margin>

<note>The footnotes provided in the original text (1 through 24) represent various manuscript readings from sources such as the Leabhar Breac (LB), the Laud MS (L), and the Rawlinson MS (R¹). These variants show minor differences in spelling and word choice, such as "sorait" vs "særait" (ennoble) or "cethracha" (forty) vs "sechtmoga" (seventy).</note>

¹⁹ Ross in R¹. LB. Ros in F. Rus in B. L.

²¹ happy in R¹. B. L. happy in F.
²² Cuana in F. L. Cuanda in R¹. Cuanna in LB.

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF APRIL.]</header>

### C. *April 11 (3rd day before the Ides)*
May the precious Maedóc <note>original: Maedóc máinech; also known as Saint Aidan</note> protect us, for he is a valiant kinsman; a grandson—except that he has been made holy—of Dunlang <note>Dunlang was a King of Leinster</note>, the firm and many-descended.

### D. *April 12 (The day before the Ides)*
Christ—a difficult task—allotted to the relic of the Cross <note>original: Cruiche cretair</note>: Bishop Julius <note>Pope Julius I</note>, leader of the people, the noble pillar of Peter’s seat.

### E. *April 13 (The Ides of April)*
With his happy, chief host, guarding against the <unclear>gabéoil</unclear> <note>The original term "gabeóil" is of uncertain meaning, possibly referring to the "snares" or "takings" of the mouth/speech</note> of every mouth; Christ’s champion went well—may Paul the deacon shelter us!

### F. *April 14 (18th day before the Calends of May)*
The royal bishop, your Assach <note>Saint Tassach of Raholp</note>, gave—when he came to him—the Body of Christ, the truly strong King, as Holy Communion unto Patrick <note>This refers to Tassach administering the last rites to Saint Patrick</note>.

### G. *April 15 (17th day before the Calends of May)*
An excellent flame that does not ebb, who conquers urgent desires; he was a fair and precious stone: Ródan, the lamp of Lorrha <note>Saint Ruadhán, founder of the monastery of Lorrha</note>.

***

<margin>11. May my precious Aedóc protect us, for he is a warlike kinsman,—a grandson—save that he has been hallowed—of Dunlang the firm, multitudinous.</margin>

<margin>12. Christ—a difficult work—allotted to the relic of the Cross: bishop Julius, abbot of the people, noble chief of Peter's see.</margin>

<margin>13. With his chief host happy because of the . . . of every mouth, Christ's champion went well, may Paul the deacon shelter us!</margin>

<margin>14. The royal bishop, thy Assach, gave when he came to him, the Body of Christ, the truly strong King, at the communion, unto Patrick.</margin>

<margin>15. An excellent flame that is unebbing, that vanquishes urgent desires, fair was the precious stone, Ródan, the lamp of Lorrha.</margin>
