<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS</header>
<meta>Running header: APRIL 16–21.]</meta>

**April 16 (16th day before the Calends of May)**
With royal Carissima, whose burial place is Roman, the feast of the deacon Felix <note>original: deochoín</note> runs to you swiftly.

**April 17 (15th day before the Calends of May)**
At the feast of Peter the deacon, who advanced to victorious martyrdom, along with his followers—a fair assembly—is Donnán of chilly Eig <note>Eig (modern Eigg) is an island in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland where Donnán and his community were martyred.</note>.

**April 18 (14th day before the Calends of May)**
On the feast of Septimus, declare that noble deacons were comforted. Also Laisrén, a victorious flame and the gentle abbot of Leighlin <note>Laisrén, also known as Molua, was a prominent Irish saint and founder of the monastery at Old Leighlin, County Carlow.</note>.

**April 19 (13th day before the Calends of May)**
Famous Hermogenes went to Jesus—a splendid transformation!—after finishing his struggle, leaving behind the coldness of his poor earthly body.

**April 20 (12th day before the Calends of May)**
With the suffering of Herodius, a priest <note>original: cruimthir (presbyter)</note> who crucified his worldly desires; and the feast in Rome—that most noble place!—of the saints of all Europe.

**April 21 (11th day before the Calends of May)**
In Scotland <note>original: Albain</note> with purity, after renouncing every earthly joy, our brother Mael-rubai <note>Mael-rubai was an Irish saint who founded the monastery of Applecross in Scotland.</note> departed from us along with his mother.

***

### Critical Notes on the Text
1. **Carissima:** Various spellings in manuscripts: *Carissa, Carissem, Carisim, Carisæ*.
2. **Runs:** *Doreith* (B. R¹. F.), *doreth* (LB).
3. **Deacon:** *Deochaín* (H. F. LB).
4. **Advanced:** *Drebraing* (or *trebraing* in F).
5. **Eig:** *Eca* (LB), *Ega* (R¹. L. H. F.), glossed as *fons* (well/spring) in B.
6. **Declare:** *Arfét* (R¹. LB), *Atfed* (B. L.), *Atfet* (F).
7. **Flame:** *Lassar* (F), *lasair* (B), *iassar* (R¹. L. LB).
8. **Famous:** *Airdirc* (R¹. F), *urdraicc* (L), *erdairc* (LB).
9. **Herodius:** *Herodi* (LB), *eradi* (R¹), *heradi* or *hirodi* (F).
10. **Place:** *Baile* (R¹), *bodi* (B).
11. **Europe:** *Eorapa* (B), *neorpa* (F), *na orpa* (R¹).
12. **Scotland:** *Albain* (R¹. L), *n-alpain* (LB).
13. **Leaving:** *Lécud* (L. LB), *lecu* (R¹).

<header>THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF APRIL.]</header>

### G. 10th of the Calends of May (April 22)
May Philip the Apostle protect us,
he who is vaster than any sea;
whose name, from the Father’s mystery,
is the wide mouth of a lamp. <note>original: "gin lócharne lethan." This is an etymological play on the name Philip, common in medieval texts.</note>

### A. 9th of the Calends of May (April 23)
The light of Bishop Ibar,
who struck down the head of every heresy;
a splendid flame over a sparkling wave,
he passed away in Little Ireland. <note>original: "in Hérinn Bicc" (Beggerin Island, Wexford).</note>

### B. 8th of the Calends of May (April 24)
The triumph of the three innocent children
in the furnace—a famous generation;
the passion of George, a sun of victories,
with thirty great thousands. <note>Refers to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and the martyrdom of St. George.</note>

### C. 7th of the Calends of May (April 25)
Noble Mark in Egypt,
who deserves no word of neglect;
a rod of gold, a vast ingot,
and the great bishop, Mac-caille.

### D. 6th of the Calends of May (April 26)
Cyril, a fair captive,
suffered the spear-points of battle;
unto Christ he sang a song of praise
with a vast host around him.

### E. 5th of the Calends of May (April 27)
Angels used to carry him,
though he might go out of dungeons:
noble Alexander, the Abbot of Rome,
the pious one. <note>Alexander I, early Pope and martyr.</note>

<page-num>110</page-num>
<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>
<header>[MONTH OF APRIL.]</header>

### NOTES.

1. **Ambrose**: that is, he who composed hymns, and was the bishop of the city of Milan <note>original: *Mediolani*</note> in Italy.
    **Mary**: that is, perhaps it was on this day that she sang the chant, the *Magnificat*, after the conception of Christ in the house of Elizabeth. For on the eighth day before the Kalends of April <note>March 25th, the Feast of the Annunciation</note> Christ was conceived, and afterwards, three months having passed or a little more, she came to Elizabeth, as Luke also testifies; and she remained there for about three months until the birth of John. Some think it is the Nativity of Mary, but it is more truly felt by others that on this day she performed the *Magnificat* in the house of Elizabeth.
    **Aedhan of Cill Aedhan** in the side of Ulster; and **Tuan son of Cairell** from Tamlachta in Bairche; and **Ceallach**, successor of Patrick, on this day.

2. **Bronach**, a virgin from Glenn Sechis; and **Conall son of Aedh** on this day.

3. **The host of Evagrius**: that is, 240 in the city of Chomis; here he suffered with his companions.
    **Coman son of Domhuingin** on this day.

4. **Where Tigernach [is sung]**, etc.: that is, Tigernach son of Cairpre, son of Cathair of the Leinstermen; or his father was of the Laigis, or of the Ui Bairrche. **Darfraich**, however, daughter of Eochaid son of Crimthann, King of Oirgialla, from Rigraith above Clogher, was his mother. Now, Cairpre took him under his cloak to Kildare. He went into the guest-house. **Brigit** saw a watch of angels above the house. She asked who was there. "One young warrior is there," said the attendant. "Look yet again," said Brigit. He looked. "There is," said he, "a small infant there in the warrior's lap." "The infant is good," said Brigit. Brigit came into the guest-house and the child was baptized, and Brigit held him at baptism, etc.

    **Tigernach**: that is, of the Ui Failgi or the [Ui] Bairrche; and what is more true is that he is in Clones <note>original: *Cluain Euis*</note>. He was of the Ui Bairrche from the west of Leinster.
    **Clones**: the name of a swineherd of Conchobar who used to be there.

    Tigernach sang:
    > A little morsel of barley bread—it was my portion on the table;
    > A sprig of watercress and warm water—it was my portion every night.

    "What brought you, O Cuachan, over the back of Muadan <gloss>from below</gloss>?"
    That is, an angel said:
    "Your piety and your diligence, and the generosity <gloss>hospitality</gloss> of Guaire."

    Darfraich was the mother of Tigernach; it was to her that Cechtamair of Druim Dubain said this, after the wood failed to split for her while she was building her oratory:

    > O Darfraich! O mother of holy Tigernach!
    > Let your help not be slow; split the log where the craftsman is!

<page-num>III</page-num>
<header>APRIL 1-4. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

### NOTES.

1. *Ambrose, that is, the one who composed hymns, etc.* <note>Saint Ambrose of Milan (c. 340–397), a doctor of the Church known for his influential Latin hymns.</note>
*Mary, that is, it may be on that day she would sing the canticle—the Magnificat—after the Conception of Christ in Elizabeth's house; for on March 25th Christ was conceived, and afterward, etc.*
*The birth of Mary is, etc.* <note>original: "Mariae natiuitas est etc."</note>

Aedán of Cell Aedáin Léith in Ulster, and Tuan son of Cairell, from Tamlachta in Bairche, and Cellach, a successor of Patrick, *on this day.* <note>original: "in hoc die."</note>

2. *Brónach the virgin, from Glenn Sechis, and Conall son of Aed on this day.*

3. *The host of Evagrius, that is, 240 people, in the city, etc.* <note>original: "in ciuitate etc."</note>
Comman son of Domangen *on this day.*

4. *Sing of Tigernach: that is, Tigernach son of Cairbre, son of Catháir, of Leinster; or his father was of Leix, or of Húi Bairche. Darfraich, daughter of Eochaid son of Crimthann, king of Airgéill, from Rigraith over Clochar, was his mother. Now Cairbre brought him under cover to Kildare. He goes into the guest-house. Saint Brigit sees a watch of angels above the house. She asked who was there. “One young warrior is there,” says the attendant. “Look again,” said Brigit. He looks. “There is,” he says, “a little infant in the young warrior’s bosom.” “The infant is good,” says Brigit. Brigit goes into the guest-house, and the child is baptized, and Brigit holds him at the baptism, etc.*

Tigernach, that is, of Offaly or Ui Barrchi, and, *which is more true,* <note>original: "quod uerius est"</note> he is in Cluain Euis of Húi Barrchi; he is from the west of Leinster.
Of Cluain Eois: that is, Eoas is the name of King Conor’s swineherd <insert>1</insert> who used to be there.

Tigernach sang:
A small bit of a cake of bright barley, this is my portion on the table; a sprig of watercress and warm water, this is my share every night.
What has brought you, O Cuachán, over Muadán’s hair (that is, from below)?

(An angel said:)
“Your piety and your devotion and Guaire’s generosity.”

Tigernach’s mother was Darfraich. It is to her that Cechtamair of Druim Dubain said, after being unable to split the tree while building her oratory:
> O Darfraich! O mother of holy Tigernach!
> Let your help come, which was not slow; split the tree near the craftsman.

<margin>1 In the *Book of Leinster* (folio 358, right margin), Oois is said to be the name of a swineherd of the king of Airgéill <note>original: "ainm muccida rig Airgiall"</note> who was in that place before Tigernach.</margin>

<page-num>112</page-num>
# THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS [MONTH OF APRIL]

**Tigernach**, son of Cairpre, son of Fergus, son of Enna, son of Laban, son of Briun, son of Eochaid, son of Daire Barrach, son of Cathair the Great.

**5. Cula** <note>original: Cula</note>, that is, the mother of Cula herself; and **Beccan** is in Imliuch Fia in Fera Cula Breg. *Fia* is the name of a fountain <note>original: nomen fontis</note> near the city. *Cula* was his mother's name, and he was of the lineage of Cremthann.

Beccan was of the Dal Cais, and it was he who raised Bresal Brec from the dead.
The three former-laymen <term>original: athlaich; refers to warriors or laymen who turned to the religious life in old age</term> of Ireland were: Beccan son of Cula, MoCua son of Lonan, and Enna of Aran.

**The Baptism of Patrick**, etc. That is, **Sinell** son of Finnchad of the Ui Garrcon; he was the first person whom Patrick baptized in Ireland.

**6. Bishop Cathub** and **Cronbecan** on this day.

**7. Cennetig** <note>modern: Kinnitty</note>, that is, "Etęch," the foster-mother of the Fianna, was killed there. Or, *Cell Eti* <note>Church of the Wing</note> from the wing of the bird that Brendan sent before him from the north, from Clonfert-Brendan.

**Bladma** <note>Slieve Bloom</note>, that is, named from Blad son of Conmac Cas Clothach, grandson of Tachal, son of Cermait, son of the Dagda. Or, Blad son of Breogan, from whom Slieve Bloom is named.

**Finan Cam of Kinnitty**, that is, he was of the Ui Luchta, of the Corca Duibne; and he was of the Ciarraigi Luachra on his mother's side. There was a squint in his eyes <note>original: In oculis eius ista obliquitas fuit</note>; that is, he looked askew at his tutor when he was asking for something for guests. "It is permitted for you to be always like that," said the tutor, namely Brendan son of Finnlog.

**Finan the Crooked**, he was of the Corca Duibne and is in Kinnitty. That is, his eye was squinted. Kinnitty is in Slieve Bloom. He was of the Corca Duibne.

> A salmon of red gold appeared to him in the west after sunset,
> Within the womb of fair Becnat <gloss>that is, the mother of Finan</gloss>, so that he was her companion,
> While she was bathing in Loch Lein, as it is said:

> "Therefore, you have no earthly father; the Holy Spirit <note>original: Spirut Noem</note> has saved you and reared you."

Regarding this, another said:

> Becnat, daughter of Idgna, passes away—the precious stone that was not scarce;
> In the likeness of the Son of the Virgin, Finan the Crooked was born from her.

> In Becnat's womb he remained for a time, from when he was conceived through the word of God:
> "You have no earthly father; the Holy Spirit has saved you and reared you."

Finan the Crooked brought wheat into Ireland—that is, he brought his shoe full. Declan brought the rye—that is, his shoe full. Modomnoc brought bees—that is, his bell full; and they were all brought in one ship.

> Finan is entitled to a true visitation, a measure of wheat from every household;
> The full of his bronze shoe, a tax that no holy saint took before him.

<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>
APRIL 5-7.]

5. Tigernach son of Cairbre, son of Fergus, son of Énda, son of Laban, son of Briun, son of Eochaid, son of Daire Barrach, son of Catháir Mór.<note>original: "His pedigree in LL. 351d." LL refers to the Book of Leinster, a medieval Irish manuscript.</note>
    5. *Cula's* son, that is, Cula was his mother; and Béccán is in Imiliuch *Fia* in Fir Cúla Breg. *Fia* is the name of a well, *Cula* the name of his mother, and he is of the race of Cremthann. Béccán was of the Dál Cais, and it is he who raised Bresal Brecc from death.<note>original: "See the story in LL. 358, and Lives of Saints from the Book of Lismore, p. xxvii."</note>
    The three *former laymen*<note>original: "athlaechs" — literally "ex-warriors" or laymen who became monks in their old age.</note> of Ireland: Béccán, Cula's son; Mochua, Lonán's son; and Énda of Arann.
    *Patrick's baptism* etc., that is, Sinell son of Findchad, of the Húi Garrchon; he is the first person whom Patrick baptized in Ireland.
    6. Bishop Cathub and Cronbecán *on this day*<note>original: "in hoc die"</note>.
    7. Of Cenn-etig, that is, Etech, the nurse of the Fians <note>The Fianna were legendary bands of warriors in Irish mythology.</note>, was slain there. Or *Cell eti* (is the right reading) from the flying of the (pet) scallcrow that Brénainn sent out of the north from Clúain ferta Brénainn.
    *Bladma*, that is, from Blad son of Conmac Cas Clothach, grandson of Tachall son of Cermait, son of the Dagda, *from whom it is named*<note>original: "a quo nominatur"</note>. Or Blad son of Breogan, *from whom comes Slíab Bladma*<note>original: "a quo Slíab Bladma" — Slieve Bloom Mountains.</note>.
    *Finán the Crooked of Cenn Etig*. He was of the Húi Luchta, that is, of Corcu Duibne, and his mother was of Ciarraige Luachra. That crookedness was in his eyes, that is, he looked crookedly at his foster-father when he was asking something for his guests.
> “You have leave to be thus *always*<note>original: "semper"</note>,” says the foster-father, even Brénainn son of Findlug.
    *Finán Camm*, that is, crooked was his eye, of Cennetig in Slíab Bladma. He was of the Corcu-duibne.<note>original: "His pedigree LL. 350 g."</note>
    A salmon of red gold came: it went in the west after sunset, against the womb of white Beccnat (Finán's mother), so that it became her husband,
    (that is) when she was bathing in Loch Lein: *as it is said*<note>original: "ut dicitur"</note>:
> Now you have no earthly father: the Holy Ghost has saved you, has fostered you.
> *Hence another said*<note>original: "Inde alius dixit"</note>:
> Beccnat, daughter of vast Idgna, the precious stone that was not scanty: like the Son of the Virgin, Finán Camm was born of her.
> In Beccnat's womb you were for a while, for you were conceived through God's word: an earthly father you have not, the Holy Ghost has saved you, has fostered you.
    Finán Camm brought wheat into Ireland, that is, he brought the full of his shoe. Declán brought the rye, that is, the full of his shoe. Modomnóc brought bees, that is, the full of his bell<note>original: "See above, p. 75."</note>: and they were brought in one ship.
    Finán is entitled to true circuits <note>A "circuit" refers to a formal journey to collect ecclesiastical dues or tributes.</note>, a measure of wheat for every household, the full of his brazen shoe: a tribute that no great saint had taken.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS
## [THE MONTH OF APRIL]

**Fínán the Crooked** <note>original: *Fínán Cam*</note> with power brought wheat from the land of **Letha** <note>likely Brittany or Rome</note>; a bronze sandal full of it he brought to sow the corn of Ireland.

**8.** **Cenn Fáelad**, abbot of **Bangor** <note>original: *Bennchoir*</note>.

**9.** **Seven holy virgins**. That is: in the city of **Sirmium**, these seven virgins suffered. Seven virgins who deserved to be crowned together.
*Whose blood does not vanish*: That is, their blood still remains in the place where they suffered. <note>original: *acht maraid adhuc sanguis earum in loco ubi passe sunt*</note>.

**10.** **Apollinaris the Priest** <note>original: *crumthir*</note>: That is, a priest [or] a bishop.
**Cuanna**: That is, from **Rush** <note>original: *Rus eo*</note> in **Mag Lacha** in western **Bregia**. **Cuanna**, that is, Cuanna son of Midorn, son of Dubrath, son of Enna, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages <note>original: *Nóigiallaig*</note>; a virgin noble in body and spirit.
**Erednat** and **Berchán of Eigg** <note>original: *Aego*</note> and **Midgus** on this day.

**11.** **Ronán** and **Maedóc the wealthy** <note>original: *mainech*</note> etc. That is, from **Cluain Mór**. Maedóc son of Midna, son of Meta, son of Ninded, son of Naxar, son of Crimthann.
For he is a "warlike brother": That is, they are both of the **Leinster** people <note>original: *Laignib*</note>.
**Archbishop of Ireland**: That is, the Senior, son of Máel Dalua, who rested in peace on the third day before the Ides of April <note>April 11th</note>, as a certain person said:

->The son of Máel Dalua of the diligent study,<-
->his death is a cause of dread for Ireland;<-
->in reward for his righteous deeds from long ago,<-
->he found heaven on the third day before the Ides of April.<-

**12.** **Pope Julius**, and he was a bishop. That is, the Pope of the people in **Rome**.
**Gregory** says this: that Pope Julius was a confessor; that is, **Gregory** says this in the *Roman Martyrology*.

**13.** **Mocammóc of Inis Caín** and **Riachaill** son of **Buachalla** and the **Sons of Morchar** (or the sons of Terchor) from **Loch mac Néill** on this day.

**14.** **The royal bishop Tassach**, etc. That is, the artisan and bishop of **Patrick**, from **Raholp** <note>original: *Raith Cholpthai*</note> in **Lecale** <note>original: *Leith Chathail*</note> in **Ulster**.

**15.** **Ruadán**: That is, he was of the **Eoganacht of Cashel**; that is, the abbot of **Lorrha** <note>original: *Lothra*</note>.

**16.** **Carissima**: That is, the feast of the virgin Carissima; she was noble both in flesh and spirit.
**Felix**: That is, in the territory of **Ui Diarmata** is the hermitage of the deacon Felix.

**17.** **Peter the Deacon**: That is, he suffered in **Antioch**.
**Stephen**, **Lawrence**, **George**, the **Holy Innocents in Bethlehem**, **Peter the Deacon**, and **Donnán of Eigg** with all the martyrs of the world are commemorated on this day.
**Eigg** <note>original: *Ego*</note>: That is, the name of a fountain in **Caithness** <note>original: *Cattaib*</note> in the north of Scotland <note>original: *Alban*</note>, and there Donnán underwent martyrdom with his followers. That is to say, a certain wealthy woman was envious of him, because before Donnán lived there, the cattle of that same woman used to graze there. Because of this <note>original: *propter hoc*</note>, she persuaded certain robbers to kill Donnán and his people. But when the same robbers arrived there, they found them in the oratory singing psalms, and there they were not able [to kill them yet]...

# APRIL 8–17. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

7. **Finán Camm** with power brought wheat out of the country of **Letha** <note>original: *Letha*; likely referring to Armorica/Brittany or Rome</note>: the full of his brazen shoe of our seed went into Ireland.

Of deacon **Peter**, that is, he suffered in **Antioch**. **Stephen** and **Laurence** and **George**, and the infants in **Bethlehem**, and Peter the deacon, and **Donnán of Eig**, with all the masters of the world, are commemorated on this day. ***Ego***, that is, the name of a well in **Caithness** in the north of Scotland, *and there Donnán was with his companions, etc.* <note>original: *et ibi Donnán cum suis etc.*</note>

<note>original: "eosdem interficere..."</note> They intended to kill them. Donnán then said to his disciples: "Let us go into the refectory <note>original: "pransatorium"</note> so that they may kill us where we used to live according to the flesh; for as long as we are in the place where we have strived to please God, we cannot die. # APRIL 18, 19. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

Thus, then, they were slain in the refectory <note>a room used for communal meals in a monastery</note>, fifty-four in total; this is the number that went to martyrdom together with Donnán.

Donnán of Eig—that is, Egha is the name of a river in Scotland. Or it is an island, and it is there that Donnán is located; or in Caithness in the north of Scotland. There, holy Donnán died with his community, namely fifty-five (though the text should likely read 52). It was this Donnán who went to Colum Cille <note>Saint Columba</note> to ask him to be his soul-friend <note>term: soul-friend; original: *anam-chara*; a spiritual counselor or confessor</note>. Colum Cille said to him, "I will not be your soul-friend, for you and your entire community with you will face red martyrdom <note>death for the faith, as opposed to 'white martyrdom' or asceticism</note>." And this was fulfilled. 

Then Donnán went with his community into Galloway and took up residence where the queen of the country's sheep used to graze. This was reported to the queen. "Let them all be killed," she said. "That is not a pious act," everyone replied. Nevertheless, men came to them to slay them. The cleric was then at Mass. "Grant us a respite until the Mass ends," said Donnán. "It will be granted," they said. The entire group was then slain at once.

Ega is the proper name of a place. It is there that Donnán suffered: the name of a spring in Old Saxony <note>original: *All-Saxain*</note>, or in Caithness, and there Donnán, with his community <note>original: *cum sua familia*</note>, fifty-four in number, suffered his passion <note>original: *passus est*; refers to his martyrdom</note>.

**18.** On the feast of Septimus, declare: Seven noble deacons died then. [Or] Septimius is a proper name. Lugna, son of Maenach, son of Fiachna, son of Ros, son of Erc, son of Trén, son of Dua, son of Mac Niad, son of Mac Con, son of Lugaid. These are his seven brothers <note>original: *Hi sunt .vii. germaini eius*</note>: namely Bishop Brannaib, Causan, Factna, Lugna, Lochan in Hui Echach, Cailcin, and Mainchine of Cúlcaís.

Molaisse, a flame of fire, in partnership with the choirs, abbot of Ráthchell, king of the synod, son of Maithgemm of Monad. <note>Maithgemm was Molaisse’s mother; she is elsewhere called the daughter of Aedán mac Gabráin, King of Scotland.</note>

This refers to Molaisse of Lethglenn, to console seven deacons who died there. He was the son of Cairell, son of Ardgal, son of Muredach Redneck, and Domangort, son of Eochaid, son of Cairell, in Lethglenn, and Ernéne, son of Finán, son of Cairell.

**19.** Hermogenes, a proper name; that is, the wizard who engaged in a great dispute against James, son of Zebedee, and afterwards believed <note>original: *et postea credidit*</note>. In Armenia, etc. <note>The legend states: Hermogenes was first a magician, and through James the son of Zebedee, he believed in God. He sent his disciple Philetus to James, and Philetus himself believed in God. Then Hermogenes sent demons to James to bind him, but an angel bound the demons with fiery ropes. James then sent the demons back to Hermogenes with his hands tied behind his back, and so after many torments, he believed in God and James.</note>

The passion of Heradius (likely Heraclius or Herodion).

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS [MONTH OF APRIL]

**20.** The feast of the saints of Europe. <note>original: néb Eorapa</note> This refers to a great tree that was in Rome <note>original: ir-Roim</note> which the pagans used to worship. The Christians fasted against the saints of Europe so that the tree would fall, and it fell immediately. <note>original: et statim cecidit</note>

**21.** **Mael Rubai.** This is the feast of the death <note>original: eitsechta</note> of Mael Rubai. He was of the Kinel Owen <note>original: Ceinel Eogain</note> people, but his church is in Scotland <note>original: ind Albain</note>, and this is the feast of his passing. Subthan, daughter of Comgall (or daughter of Setna), was his mother. His church is at Applecross <note>original: Apur crosen</note>.

**22.** **Philip.** He was buried in Phrygia. <note>original: in Frigia sepultus</note> When Philip was eighty-seven years old, he was stoned in Hierapolis, a city of the Gauls in Phrygia. <note>original: Cum esset Pilipus .lxxxvii. annorum in Erapoli Gallorum ciuitate Frigia[e] lapitatus est</note>
Philip remained in the mystery of the Father <note>original: hir-ruin Athar</note>, that is, in the mystical canon. Without a lantern <note>original: gin locharna</note>, which is interpreted as "the mouth of a lamp." Twenty years after the Passion of the Lord, Philip preached the Gospel to the Scythians and other nations. At last, when he was eighty-seven years old, he was crucified and stoned in Hierapolis, a city of Phrygia. He was of the same tribe and city as Peter and Andrew.
The birth <note>meaning his "birthday" into heaven/death</note> of Philip the Apostle.

**23.** **Bishop Ibar**, who died in Beggerin <note>original: Bec-erind; literally "Little Ireland"</note>. This is an island in the sea off the coast of Wexford <note>original: Huib Censelaigh</note>. He was Ibar, son of Lugna, son of the descendant of Corc, son of Corp, son of Coirpre, son of Niall, son of Eochaid... <note>The text continues a long genealogy tracing him back to Aengus Tuirbech</note>.
It was this Bishop Ibar who had a conflict with **Saint Patrick**. It was he who left the roads full and the storehouses empty at Armagh <note>original: Ard Macha</note>. Patrick was then angry with him and said, "You shall not be in Ireland <note>original: Éri</note>." "Ireland shall be the name of the place where I am," said Bishop Ibar. From this, "Little Ireland" <note>original: Bec-éri</note> is named; it is an island out in the sea in Wexford.
The feast of Saint Ibar, Bishop.

**24.** The victory of the **three innocent youths**. Their names among the Chaldeans were Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego <note>original: Sedrac, Misac, Abdinagó</note>. Their names among the Hebrews were Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael <note>original: Annamsas, Acarias, Misael</note>. These three were cast by Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: Nabgodan</note> into a blazing furnace of fire, and God saved them so that the fire did them no harm. This occurred in the plain of Shinar <note>original: Sennan</note> at Babylon under King Nebuchadnezzar.

**25.** **Mark** the Evangelist. He suffered <note>was martyred</note> in Alexandria.
**Mac Caille**, Bishop of Cruachan Brí Éle in Offaly <note>original: Huib Fáilge</note>. His church is located there.

**26.** **Cyril**, Bishop in Jerusalem.

**28.** **Christopher.** A "dog-head" <note>original: conchend; a reference to the medieval legend that St. Christopher belonged to a race of dog-headed humans</note>. He was a believer and suffered under the Emperor Decius. Christopher was a pure cleric; he was the pious Christian who, before his calling, was a traveler across the sea without dishonor. His proper name was Christopher.
He was a "dog-head" who suffered under Decius the persecutor. His name before he found faith was Reprobus.
The feast of Christopher and his companions, numbering 10,504. Everyone who fasts on his feast day shall find rest with the Lord.
**Cronan**, son of Aele. He was of the descendants of Oela and was previously called **Mochua**.

# APRIL 20–28. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

20. *The feast of the saints of Europe: that is, there was a great tree in Rome¹ and the heathens worshipped it, until the Christians fasted in honor of the saints of Europe so that the tree might fall, and it fell immediately <note>original Latin: et statim cecidit</note>.*

21. *Mael-rubai*,² *that is, the feast of Mael-rubai's death <term>obit: the anniversary of a person's death</term>. He was of the kindred of Eogan, but his church is in Scotland, and this is the feast of his death. His mother was Subthan, daughter of Comgall, and his church is in Applecross <note>original: Apurcrosen</note>.*

22. *Philip: that is, he was buried in Phrygia, etc.*
    *May Philip protect us: in the mystery of the Father, that is, in the mystical canon: "mouth of a lamp," that is, his name is interpreted as "the mouth of a lamp"³ <note>original Latin: os lampadis interpretatur</note> etc.*
    *The birth <term>nativity</term> of Philip the apostle.*

23. *Of bishop Ibar: that is, Ibar son of Lugna, son of Maccu Cuirc, son of Corp, son of Cairbre, son of Niall, son of Eochaid (from whom the Hui Echach of Ulster are named), son of Sen, son of Rosen, son of Tren, son of Rogen, son of Airnel, son of Maine the Great, son of Fidach Forga, son of Feradach, son of Ailill Erann, son of Fiacha, son of Oengus Turbech T.*
    *This is the bishop Ibar who had a conflict with Saint Patrick. It was he who left the roads full and the store-rooms empty in Armagh. Because of this, Patrick was angered with him and said: "You shall not be in Ireland <note>original: Ériu</note>," says Patrick. "Ireland shall be the name of the place where I usually stay," says bishop Ibar. From this, "Little Ireland" <note>original: Becc-Ériu</note> is named; it is an island in the territory of the Hui Cennselaig out in the sea.*

24. *The triumph of the three innocent children: that is, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego <note>original: Sedrac, Misac, Abdinago</note> are their names among the Chaldeans; Ananias, Azarias, and Misael are their names among the Hebrews. And 30,729.⁴ The three of them were put by Nebuchadnezzar into a blazing fiery furnace, but God preserved them so that the fire did them no harm.*

25. *Mark the evangelist: he suffered martyrdom in Alexandria.*
    *Mac Caille: that is, a bishop. His church is in Cruachan Bri Ele in Offaly.*

26. *Cyrillus: that is, a bishop in Jerusalem.*

28. *Christopher: that is, a "dog-head."⁵ He was pious and suffered under the Emperor Decius.*
    *He was a cleric of purity; he was a devout Christian. Before he was called, he was without reproach across the sea; his proper name was Christopher, that is, a "dog-head." He suffered under the persecutor Decius. His name was Reprobus before he found the faith <note>original Latin: ante fidem</note>.*
    *Of Christopher with his followers <note>original Latin: cum suis</note>, 10,404. Whoever fasts on his feast day will find rest with the Lord.*
    *Cronan: that is, Cronan son of Aele <unclear>[?]</unclear> was he, the great-grandson of Oela <unclear>(?)</unclear> who was first called Mochua.*

***

¹ *So in the Book of Leinster <note>LL.</note> 359, left margin: "A great tree was in Rome, and the heathens used to worship it, until the Christians of Rome fasted to all the saints of Europe for its destruction, and specifically to Saint Martin, and it fell immediately."*
² *See Reeves, Columba, p. 376. Mael-rubai, abbot of Bangor, Book of Leinster 359b. Pedigree of Mael-rubai son of Elganach, Book of Leinster 347c.*
³ *Regarding the title "mouth of a lamp," see Isidore's Etymologies <note>Origg.</note> vii. 9, and Herzfeld’s note, Old English Martyrology, p. 230.*
⁴ *This is a <gloss>gloss on "with thirty great thousands"</gloss>.*
⁵ *“The man was of the race of the dog-heads, from the land of the man-eaters,” from the Acts of Saint Christopher and Saint Marina, cited by Herzfeld, Old English Martyrology, p. 229.*

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.
# [THE MONTH OF MAY.

## THE MONTH OF MAY.

**B. The Calends <note>The first day</note> of May.**
On the Calends of May is the feast of Neth-Cóeme; and the birth of Philip, who is most exalted. Then began that which is noblest: the delightful preaching of Jesus.

**C. The 6th day before the Nones <note>May 2nd</note> of May.**
The departure of Saturninus <note>original: Saturnín</note>, who has gone to meet Christ, along with the death—after a long sigh—of Nechtán, the foster-son of Saint Patrick.

**D. The 5th day before the Nones <note>May 3rd</note> of May.**
The first finding of the wood of Christ’s Cross <note>The feast of the Invention of the Holy Cross</note> with its many virtues; the death of Conlaed, a fair pillar of the church; and the great feast of the Virgin Mary.

**E. The 4th day before the Nones <note>May 4th</note> of May.**
During the suffering of Anatherius, my fair Cua went to heaven—he was the son of the famous Cummíne—on the feast of Silvanus the deacon.

**F. The 3rd day before the Nones <note>May 5th</note> of May.**
The deacons Euthymius and Hilary <note>original: Helair</note> have passed beyond their pains; they departed on the festival day upon which our Lord <note>original: Fíada</note> ascended.

->**G. May 6 (The day before the Nones of May)**<-

A man who has written without stint <note>original: "cen tercai" — without scarcity or sparing</note> fair stories of Christ crucified; the great birth of Matthew the magnified is venerated by princes.

Victor and Maxim, they have offered themselves for Christ; for the love of the King whom they adored, they bathed themselves in their own blood <note>A reference to their martyrdom</note>.

The great manifestation of Michael to the world—it was a proven story; the passion of fair Cyril who was loved; and the famous Bishop Sanctáin.

->**D. May 10 (6 days before the Ides of May)**<-

Into the peaceful kingdom of the other world, where the sound of every temple dwells, may the leader of hosts protect us: the victorious Comgall of Bangor <note>original: "Bennchuir"</note>.

->**E. May 11 (5 days before the Ides of May)**<-

The triumph of Job without oblivion; he was renowned to the King of Clouds. Also my-Critóc, a fair servant of God, and the priest <note>term: "cruimther" — an archaic Old Irish word for a priest or presbyter</note> Cormac.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS [MONTH OF MAY]

### May 24 (9th day before the Kalends of June)
Augustine the bishop,
Hermes, <note>original: Hermes abb mór míle</note> a great leader of thousands,
Colmán, a beloved pillar,
and Aidbe of the northern territory <note>original: Tír dá glas (Terryglass)</note>.

### May 25 (8th day before the Kalends of June)
To you comes the feast of John,
a lovable pillar of purity,
Dionysius the steadfast and bold,
and Dunchad of chilly Iona.

### May 26 (7th day before the Kalends of June)
The proper reception of Colmán Stellán,
declare it clearly <note>original: cen ladnae; literally "without dumbness" or "without stammering"</note>:
Béccán who loved night-vigils;
in Clonard was his dwelling.

### May 27 (6th day before the Kalends of June)
Aculius the priest <note>original: cruimther; an archaic Irish word for a priest, derived from the Latin 'presbyter'</note>,
with his company who are most holy;
his blood, in the sight of every nation,
has been poured out upon the paths.

### May 28 (5th day before the Kalends of June)
May he protect us unto the angels—
that lovable, prosperous company—
Germanus, the sun of our elders,
and the tutor of Patrick of Armagh.

### May 29 (4th day before the Kalends of June)
May Pollio’s great host
protect us to the starry heaven,
along with Cummain of pure goodness,
the beloved daughter of Allén.

***

->**Modernized Translation of the Stanzas**<-

**24.** Augustine the bishop; Hermes, a great lord of thousands; Colmán, a beloved pillar; Aidbe the northern of Tír dá glas.

**25.** To you comes the feast of Johannes <note>John</note>, a lovable pillar of virginity; Dionysius the sure and bold; Dunchad of chilly Iona.

**26.** Declare the fitting reception of Colmán Stellán without silence; Béccán who loved vigils; in Clonard was his abode.

**27.** Aculius the priest, with his train that is holiest; his blood before every tribe has been spilled on the roads.

**28.** May he convoy us to the angels, that lovable prosperous swarm: Germanus, sun of our elders, tutor of Patrick of Armagh!

**29.** May Pollio's great host convoy us to the starry heaven, with Cummain the pure and good, daughter of lovable Allén!

<lang>Irish</lang>
<page-num>128</page-num>
<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF MAY]</header>

### NOTES.

1. **Nethchoemi** (Mochoemi) <note>original: Mochoemi</note>. That is, he was the brother of Kevin of Glendalough <note>original: Cóemgein Glinde da lacha</note>, and abbot of Terryglass <note>original: Thim da glas</note>.
**James** <note>original: Iacobus</note>, the brother of the Lord, and **Matthew** <note>original: Matha</note> the apostle are commemorated here.
**Philip**. That is, Philip the apostle. It is not the birth of Philip according to the flesh that is mentioned here, but his falling asleep <note>term: dormitatio; a common ecclesiastical term for the death of a saint</note> that is remembered here, as is read in the *Passions of the Apostles*.

2. **Nechtain**. Nechtain was a foster-son of Patrick, from Killunchi in Conaille. Moreover, he was the son of Lemna; that is, Liamain, daughter of Calpurnius <note>original: Charplaind/Chalpuirn</note>, was his mother. This foster-son of Patrick is at Finnabair Abha on the bank of the Boyne in Brega. When he was near death and Patrick was at his departure, he asked for a drink, because Patrick saw his reward and his glory in heaven before he died. Liamain, daughter of Calpurnius and sister of Patrick, was the mother of Nechtain.

3. **The First Finding of the Wood of the Cross** <note>original: Primairec crainn Cruiche</note>. That is, the honorable finding of the cross of Christ in the time of Constantine, son of Helena, 220 years later. That is, the discovery of the holy cross of Christ when it was found in the time of Constantine, son of Helena. The cross was found because when the Romans with Titus and Vespasian burned Jerusalem, the cross was hidden in the 40th year after the Passion of the Lord.
**The death of Conlaed**. That is, the bishop of Kildare. Wild dogs <note>original: coin allta</note> devoured him at Scetha Conlaed beside Liamain in the Plain of Leinster <note>original: Maig Laigin</note>. He was the bishop and the craftsman <note>term: cerd; a skilled artisan or goldsmith</note> of Brigid, and wolves devoured him at Scetha Conlaig in the Plain of Leinster. Conlaed, bishop of Kildare: his name was *Cundail-Aed*, meaning "Prudent Aed," and wild dogs devoured him at Lemain in eastern Leinster.
**Conlaed**, bishop of Kildare. Conlaed, that is, "half to the dogs" <note>original: leth do chonaib</note>, because dogs ate him after he attempted to go to Rome in defiance of Brigid's wishes. He was Brigid's chief craftsman, and "Conlaed's Half" in Kildare is named after him. His name was previously Roncenn. **Mochonna of Derry** is commemorated with Conlaed.
**The great feast of Mary the Virgin.**

4. **Anateri** or **Anterini**. That is, pope and martyr. He was pope and suffered under Maximian.
**The son of Cummini**. **Mochua**, that is, the son of Cummini from Slieve Eibhlinne in Munster.
**Siluain**. That is, Silvanus, bishop of the city of Gaza. Siluain the deacon.

5. **The deacon Justinus**. That is, the deacon Jus who is in Connacht at Fuerty <note>original: Fidarta</note> in Mag Ai. It is he who baptized Ciaran of Clonmacnoise, and he was of the Franks. As some think, Saint Eustinus the deacon suffered at Alexandria; and in Gaul, the feast of Saint Hilary, bishop and martyrs. Eutimus, and not Justinus, as some manuscripts have it.

6. **The departure of Noah from the ark.**
Here occurs the miraculous escape of Saint **John**, apostle and evangelist, who by the command of the Emperor Domitian was cast into a vat of boiling oil before the Latin Gate at Rome. This is where the escape of John the apostle from the vat of boiling oil is recorded; he was put into it in Rome "before the Latin Gate" <note>original: ante portam latinam</note> by the command of Domitian.

***

¹ Daughter of Calpurnius. ² Honorable findings. ³ At. ⁴ Devoured him. ⁵ Pope Antherus and 40 others. ⁶ Who is in Connacht. ⁷ Eutimus.

<header>MAY 1-6. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

### NOTES.

1. **Neth-choéme (My-Cóeme)**: That is, he was a brother of Cóemgein <note>St. Kevin</note> of Glendalough and abbot of Tir-dá-glas.
James, the Lord's brother, and Matthew the apostle are commemorated here.
Philip, that is, *Philippus*, etc.

2. **Nechtán**: Nechtain, St. Patrick's foster-son, of Cell Umhe in Conailli. He was a son of Liamain—meaning Liamain, daughter of Carplann <note>original: "Carplann," a corruption of Calpurnius</note>, was his mother. He is associated with Findabair Aba on the banks of the Boyne in Bregia as Patrick's foster-son. When he was dying and Patrick was present at his passing, he asked for a drink; Patrick beheld his reward and his glory in heaven before he died.
Liamain, daughter of Calpurn and Patrick's sister, was Nechtan's mother.

3. **The first finding of the wood of the Cross**: That is, the authentic discovery of Christ's Cross in the time of Constantine, son of Helena. <note>original Latin: "inuentio sanctae Crucis"</note>
**The death of Conlaed**: He was a bishop of Kildare, and wolves devoured him in Sceich Condlaid beside Liamain in Mag Laigen.
Conlaed, bishop of Kildare. Con-laed—that is, "half" (*leth*) to "wolves" (*coin*)—because wolves devoured him when he was traveling to Rome in defiance of St. Brigit. He was Brigit's chief artisan, and Leth Conláid in Kildare is named after him. His name was previously Roncenn. <note>original Latin: "Roncenn nomen eius prius"</note>
Mochonna of Daire is mentioned along with Conlaed.
The great feast of the Virgin Mary. <note>This refers to the Conception of the Virgin Mary; see footnote 3.</note>

4. **Of Anatherius**, etc.
**Son of Cummen**: Mochua, son of Cumnene, from Slíab Oeblinne (Eiblinne) in Munster.
**Of Silvanus**, etc.

5. **The deacon Justinus**: That is, deacon Ius who is in Connaught at Fidarta in Mag Ái. It was he who baptized Ciarán of Clonmacnoise. He was from France, as some believe. <note>original Latin: "ut quidam putant"</note> He is also called Saint Eustinus, etc. Eutimus, not Justinus, as some manuscripts have it.

6. **The Departure of Noah from the Ark** <note>original Latin: "Egressio Noe"</note>, etc. **Here falls** <note>original Latin: "Hic cadit"</note>, etc. Here occurs the escape of the apostle John from the vat of boiling oil into which he was cast in Rome before the Latin Gate <note>original Latin: "Porta Latina"</note> by the order of Emperor Domitian.

***

¹ A corruption of Calpurnius <note>St. Patrick's father</note>.
² See *Treasury of Old Irish* <note>original: "Thesaurus pal. hib."</note> II. 347: his pedigree in the *Book of Leinster* (*LL*) 351e differs from the pedigree in the *Speckled Book* (*LB*).
³ The Conception of the Virgin Mary. <note>original Latin: "Mariae Virginis conceptio"</note> The *Book of Leinster* 360ª notes: "This was her beginning, as others think—but it took place in the month of February or March, because she was born seven months later, as is told—or any other of her feast days." See Rev. H. Thurston, S.J., in *The Month*, May, 1904.

OENGUS.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF MAY.]

**7.** The entry of Noah into the ark. <note>original: *ingressio Noe in arcam*</note> My-Cuaróc of Breccán. Breccán, also known as of Horse-Ridge <note>original: *Ech-droma*</note>, is the same as Ciaran and My-Cuaróc.
<margin>Breccán, that is, from Druim Breccáin which is on the border of Dál Araide and Dál Riata; or from the Oak-grove of Horse-Ridge <note>original: *Daire Ech-droma*</note> in Hy Kinsellagh.</margin>
In the Oak-grove of Horse-Ridge, that is, in the north of Dál Araide. Or it is in Mag Muccraime in western Connacht that the Oak-grove of Horse-Ridge is located. It is said that the sacred tree of the church is visible from the plain, but when one goes to search for that church in the oak-grove, it cannot be found; yet the voice of the bell and the chanting of psalms are heard there, though the church itself is not discovered.

**8.** Victor, that is, the beheading of Victor under the Emperor Maximian in the city named Milan <note>original: *Mediolanum*</note>.

**9.** The Revelation <note>original: *Faillsiged*</note>, that is, on Mount Gargano. Michael, a man's proper name. This is the story of Garganus remembered here: when a certain man sought his bull and shot an arrow at the bull, his own arrow returned upon himself; by this sign, Michael was revealed to the West. <note>original: *quando quaesiuit [aliquis] suum taurum...*</note> The revelation of Michael the Archangel. The passion of Quirillus. Santán "Large-head" of the Church of the Two Forts <note>original: *Cill da les*</note>.
<margin>Bishop Santán: he is from the Church of the Two Forts, as Oengus says, from the Church of Bishop Santán in Hy Kelly in eastern Leinster.</margin>

**10.** Comgall, son of Sétna, son of Eochaid, [son of Brón], son of Forgo, son of Ernán, son of Crimthann, son of Eochaid, son of Lugaid, son of Ros, son of Imchad, son of Fedlimid, [son of Cas], son of Fiachra Araide.
Bangor <note>original: *Bennchuir*</note>; it is called *Bennchur* (Horn-casting) because Conall Cernach, son of Amergin, went on a raid among the Picts <note>original: *Cruthnechaib*</note> and brought many cows with him. It was there he heard that Cú Chulainn had been killed, and he cast the horns <note>original: *benna*</note> of the cows into the earth; hence it is called *Bennchur*.
Mael-geimridh said:
> Lovely, pure Bangor, a place for the forgiveness of sins:
> A time will come when, by the power of the abbots, it will be a dwelling for sharp-nosed dogs <note>term: "sharp-nosed dogs" likely refers to wolves or hunting dogs, implying future desolation</note>.

**11.** The victory of Job, that is, his deliverance from his martyrdom, or his death; that is, when he won the battle against the Demon and was freed from his suffering. This refers to the deliverance of Job from his martyrdom, who suffered for thirty years, but was tested in the seventy-ninth year of his age and lived for 140 years afterward.
My-Critóc, that is, on the bank of the Dodder in Hy Dunchada in eastern Leinster. My-Critóc is Critán, son of Illadon.
Priest <note>original: *Cruimther*</note> Cormac, that is, Cormac the priest in Achad Sinche or Achad Finnniche. He is also in Aran. It was he who asked the Devil how he might reach heaven, to whom the Devil said: "If you would be a cleric, etc."

**12.** Cyriacus, who is the same as Judas. Cyriacus, who found the Cross of Christ. His name was Judas previously.
The Pilgrim <note>original: *Ailithir*</note>, a proper name; he is in Muicinis on Lough Derg. Erc, from Magheralin <note>original: *Tilaig lis*</note> in Upper Iveagh <note>original: *Uaib Echach Ulad*</note>.
Nascai, so called from the ring <note>original: *nasc*</note> that used to be around his neck while he was in the water praying. That is, a ring was under his neck while he was in the river bathing <note>note: a common ascetic practice of praying while immersed in cold water</note>.

# MAY 7-12. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

7. *The entry of Noah into the Ark, etc.* <note>original: Ingressio Noe etc.</note> of Breccan, that is, of (Daire) Echdroma and of Quiaran, the same as Mochuaróc.
Breccán, that is, of Druim Breccain, which is on the border of Dalaradia and Dalriada, or of Daire Echdroma in Huí Censelaig.
*In Daire Echdroma*, that is, in the north of Dalaradia. Or in Mag Mucrame in the west of Connaught is Daire Echdroma; and the tree of the church is seen from the plain, but when one goes seeking it in the oakwood it is not found; and the voice of the bell and the singing of psalms are heard, but the church itself is not found.

8. *Victor*, that is, the beheading of Victor under the Emperor Maximian in the city called Milan <note>original: Mediolanum</note>.

9. *Manifestation*, that is, on Mount Garganus, of *Michael*, which is the proper name of a man. This may be the story of Garganus which is commemorated here: *when, etc.* <note>original: quando etc.</note>
*The Revelation of Michael, etc.* <note>original: Revelatio Michaelis etc.</note> Santan "Great-head" in Cell, that is, (Cell) dá les.
*Bishop Sanctáin*, that is, he is of Cell da leis, as Oengus says, [or] of Cell espúic Sanctáin in Huí Cellaig in the east of Leinster.

10. Comgall son of Sétna, son of Eochaid, son of Broen, son of Forgo, son of Ernan, son of Crimthan, son of Eochaid, son of Lugaid, son of Ross, son of Imchad, son of Feidlimid, son of Cass, son of Fiachra Araide.
*Of Bennchor*: Bennchor <note>modern Bangor</note> is so called because Conall Cernach, son of Amargen, went on a raid into Pictland <note>Scotland</note> and carried off many cows. It was then he heard that Cúchulainn was killed; so he put (<gloss>placed</gloss>) the horns (<gloss>horns/peaks</gloss>) of the cows into the earth. *From this it is called Benn-chor <note>Horn-casting</note>.*
Mael-geimrid said:
Bangor delightful, pure, place of forgiveness of crimes:
A time will come for the power of the abbots: it will be a dwelling of sharp-nosed dogs.

11. *The triumph of Job*, that is, his liberation from his martyrdom: or his death, that is, when he routed the Devil, *and was delivered, etc.* <note>original: et liberatus etc.</note>
My-Critóc, that is, on the brink of the Dodder in Huí Dunchada in the east of Leinster.
*The priest Cormac* <note>original: presbyter Cormac</note>, that is, Cormac the priest in Ached Sinche, that is, in Ached Findniche. And he is in Aran. It is he who asked the Devil how he should reach heaven: to whom the Devil said: "If I were a cleric," etc.

12. *Cyriacus, that is, the same as Judas. Cyriacus who, etc.* <note>original: Cyriacus, i.e. idem et Iudas. Cyriacus qui etc.</note>
Ailither, which is a proper name: he is in Mucc-inis in Lough Derg.
*Erc*, that is, of Telach lis in Huí Echach of Ulster.
<term>nascai</term> <note>the tied one</note>, that is, a tie (<gloss>binding/collar</gloss>) used to be around his neck as long as he was in the water praying; that is, a tie that used to be under his neck while he was in the river washing.

# THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS
-> [MAY] <-

**14.** **Corona**, that is, the wife of a certain soldier <note>original: *uxor alicuius militis*</note>; specifically, a soldier of the Roman King. *F.*
**Corona** and **Victor** suffered their passion <note>martyrdom</note> in Alexandria under the Emperor Antoninus <insert>and under Salucius. *F.*</insert> *R¹.*
**Carthach**, also known as **Mochuta of Lismore**; or **Findall** was the name of his brother. *F.*

**15.** **Grace of the Sevenfold Spirit** <note>original: *Rath in Spirta secta*</note>: that is, the grace of the sevenfold Spirit poured out upon the Apostles and their followers on this day during the first Pentecost. *L.*
**Timothy** <note>original: *Tiamda*</note>, not the disciple of Paul, but another. *R¹.*
**Sarán**, that is, Sarán son of Airachur from Inis Mór in Uí Mac Caille in Munster *R¹.* or in Uí Liatháin. *F.*
**Duiblitrech**. **Dublittir**, that is, the abbot of Finglas Cainnig *R¹.* beside Dublin. *F.*

**16.** **Brendan**, that is, the son of Findlug, grandson of Alta, of the Ciarraige Luachra; [he is] from Uí Mac Caille or from Clonfert. *L.*
**Brendan**, son of Findlug, son of Olchu, son of Alta, son of Ogaman, son of Fidchuire, son of Delbra, son of Enna, son of Uasasal, son of Asdoman, son of Modta, son of Ciar, son of Fergus. *L.*
**Brendan**, son of Findlug, son of Elchu, son of Alta, of the Ciarraige Luachra, from Alltraige Caille. He was born at the same time as Oengus son of Nadfraech, King of Munster. It was his mother who saw a vision: it seemed to her that a bar of gold <note>original: *tinne de ór*</note> fell into her lap, and her two breasts blazed upon her chest. Findlug told this vision to his soul-friend <note>confessor</note>, namely Bishop Erc son of Ogaman, son of Fidach; and he said that a wonderful child would be born of the woman who saw the vision. *Bishop Erc also saw a vision:* it seemed to him that there was a brilliance of fire over the territory of Alltraige, and it was full of angels from heaven to earth. *Bishop Erc went* to Findlug’s house the next day and took the boy into his lap, and offered him his protection and union. That was the night that Bec Mac Dé the prophet happened to be in the house of the son of Arda, son of Fidach, King of Ciarraige Luachra. The King asked him: "What do you see for us tonight, Bec?" "I see that your king is born to the west of you and the sea." "We do not know indeed," said the son of Arda, "of any noble seed between us and the sea who would take the kingship over us." *Bec said:* "The son born tonight to Findlug shall be your king forever." Moreover, a swift drop <note>original: *bróen dian*</note> came from the fountain of Jordan and fell upon him during his baptism. *From this he was called 'Brendinus,' that is, 'swift drop' from above.* Or [it happened] during his baptism. *LL. 371 a, b.*
**Cairnech**, that is, from Tuilen. Cairnech was of the Britons of Cornwall. *L.*
**Cairnech** from Tuilen near Kells of the Kings. *R¹.*

**The descendants of Suanach** <note>original: *húi Suanaig*</note>, that is, from Rahan. <margin>In the margin:</margin> **The descendants of Suanach**, that is, **Fidmuine** was his name and **Fidairle** was his brother's name; and the feast of **Buite** of Monasterboice is with these, because on this day he raised Mael Caich from the dead, crossing the river with dry feet. *L.*

The union of **Cainnech** and **Barra** and **Brendan**, both of them:
Whoever outrages any of them, the miracles of the three shall avenge it. *F.*

# MAY 14-16. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

**14.** **Corona**, that is, *the wife of a certain soldier* <note>original: uxor alicujus militis</note>, specifically a soldier of the Roman king. Corona and Victor: *under etc.*
Of **Carthach**, that is, **Mochutu of Lismore**, or **Findall** is his brother's name (which is the correct reading).

**15.** **The grace etc.** that is, the grace of the sevenfold Spirit showered at the first Pentecost upon the apostles and their household on this day.
**Timothy**, not the disciple of Paul but another of the same name.
**Sarán**, that is, Sarán son of Airachor (?), of **Inis Mór** in **Húi Mac Caille** in Munster. Or in **Húi Liathain**.
Of **Duiblitir**, that is, the abbot of **Finglas** <note>original: Findglas Cainnig</note> near Dublin.

**16.** Of **Brendan** <note>original: Brénann</note>, that is, the son of Findlug, grandson of Alta of **Ciarraige Luachra**; he is associated with **Húi Mac Caille** and **Clonfert**. Brendan was the son of Findlug, son of Olchu, son of Alta, son of Ogaman, son of Fidchuire, son of Delbra, son of Eunne, son of Uasalec (?), son of Ard oman, son of Modta, son of Ciar, son of Fergus.

Brendan, son of Findlug, son of Elchu, son of Aelta, of the Ciarraige Luachra of Alltraige Caille. He was born at the same time as **Oengus son of Natfráich**, the King of Munster. It was his mother who saw the vision: it seemed to her that an ingot of gold fell into her lap, and her two breasts glowed with flame. Findlug described that vision to his spiritual advisor <note>original: "soul-friend" (anam-chara)</note>, **Bishop Erc** son of Ogaman, son of Fidach. Erc said that a marvelous child would be born to the woman who saw the vision. Then Bishop Erc saw this: it seemed to him that a fiery glow hung over the district of Alltraige, and that the space from heaven to the ground was full of angels. Bishop Erc went the next morning to Findlug's house, took the boy into his arms, and placed him under his protection and spiritual union. 

That is the night when **Becc mac Dé** the prophet happened to be in the house of Mac Ardae, son of Fidach, King of Ciarraige Luachra. The king asked him:
> “What do you see for us tonight, O Becc?”
> “I see,” said Becc, “that your king is born between you in the west and the sea.”
> “Truly,” said Mac Ardae, “we know of no noble family between us and the sea that would have a right to rule over us.”
Becc replied:
> “The son born to Findlug tonight—he will be your king forever.”

Now a swift rain came from the source of the Jordan and dropped on Brendan at the time of his baptism. For this reason he was called *Brendinus*, which is interpreted as a rain (*broen*) swift (*dian*) from above (*di-anuas*); or perhaps named for the time (*denus*) of his baptism.¹
<note>¹ The Irish text of this legend was first printed, with a French translation, by Henri Gaidoz, in the *Collection of Foreign Texts* (Recueil des textes étrangers), Paris, 1888. See also *Lives of Saints from the Book of Lismore*, pp. 100, 349–350.</note>

Of **Cairnech**, that is, from **Tuilén**: he was one of the Cornish Britons.
Of Cairnech from Tuilén near **Kells of the Kings**.
Of **Suanach's descendant**, that is, of **Rahan** <note>original: Rathen Húi Suanaig</note>. **Fidmuine** is his name, and **Fidairle** is his brother's name. And the feast of **Buite** from Monasterboice <note>original: Manister</note> is *with these because etc.*²
<note>² However, Buite's feast day is December 7th according to the Martyrology. The legend of Maelcáich is unclear to me.</note>

The spiritual union of **Cainnech**, **Barre**, and both the Brendans: whoever offends any one of them, the miracles of the trio will punish him.

**18.** **Mark**, that is, the Pope. <note>original: pappa</note> **L.** <note>L. refers to the Laud Manuscript</note> That is, the Evangelist. **R¹.** <note>R¹. refers to the Rawlinson Manuscript</note> He was enthroned, meaning the honor of an Apostle was given to him by the nations after he separated from Peter. **R¹.**
**My-Maedoc**, that is, of Fiddown <note>original: Feda duin</note> in the south of Ossory. **L.**
**My-Domnoc**, that is, from Tibberaghny <note>original: Tiprait Fachtna</note> in Ossory. **L.**
**Clane** <note>original: Claenad</note>, that is, a church which is in Uí Faeláin in Leinster. **L.**

**19.** **Urban**, that is, Urban, Bishop of Rome; he suffered <term>martyrdom</term> under Aurelius Alexander. **L.**

**20.** **Marcellossa**, virgin and martyr. **R¹.**
**Colman** of Daire Mór, and **Daniel** of Tulach, and **Mac Laithbe** of Donaghmore, and **Crom the Hermit** from Inis Crainn are commemorated on this day. **F.** <note>F. refers to the Franciscan Manuscript</note>

**21.** **Timothy** <note>original: Tiamda</note>, not the disciple of Paul, but another. **F.**
**Of the wheat**, that is, of the wheat of God, because the saints are the wheat of God <note>original: quia sancti triticum Dei sunt</note>; or "I enumerate" <note>original: tuirmim</note>, as a certain person said:

> O mill, you have ground much wheat;
> It was not a grinding upon a bitter pool, but what you ground for the descendants of Cerball.
>
> The grain the mill grinds is not oats but red wheat;
> It is from the fruit of the great tree, the foundation of the mill of Maelodrain.

This refers to the two sons of Blathmac, son of Aed Sláine, namely **Dunchad** and **Cathal**, who were slaughtered by Marcan of Leinster in a certain bakehouse <note>original: in quodam pistrino</note>; it is to those two sons of Blathmac that the "red wheat" refers. **F.**
**Colman the Leper**, that is, Colman from Mayo in Dal Chais. **L.** From Magh n-Éna in Dal Chais. **R¹.**
**Barrind.** Barrind of Druim Cuilinn in Fircall <note>original: Feraib cell</note> in the south of Meath. **R¹.** That is, Barrind son of Muiredach, son of Fiacha, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. **L.**
**Of Druim Cuilinn**, that is, in Fircall. **L.** That is, it is in Leinster. **R¹.**

**22.** **Ronan**, that is, from Magheralin <note>original: Laind Ronain Find</note> in Uí Echach Ulad. **L.**
That is, Ronan the Fair, son of Saran, son of Colcu, son of Tuathal, son of Crummael (from whom the Uí Cruind Beoil descend), son of Fedlimid, son of Fiachra, son of Colla Fochríth. **L.**
**Baithine**, that is, Baithin from Inis Baithin in eastern Leinster in Dál Messin Corb; and **Trea**, daughter of Ronan, King of Leinster, was the mother of Baithin, son of Finnach. **L.**
And this is how Baithin was born: Finnach the outlaw happened to be in the top of a whitethorn tree above a well, intending to commit robbery and theft upon the church one day. Then **Creda** came to the well to wash her hands, and when Finnach saw her, he desired her. His seed fell from him onto a sprig of watercress that was in front of him. The maiden then ate the sprig of watercress upon which the seed had fallen, and from that, the "ever-living" Baithin was born. However, it was a miracle of God that caused that, as was said:

> Creda, she was a good woman, the daughter of Ronan, King of Leinster;
> With her usual pure reliquary, she was the mother of Baithin, son of Finnach.
>
> Finnach the outlaw was stealing, in the whitethorn above the well,
> When something of his bodily desire reached the soft-topped watercress sprig.
>
> When the keen outlaw gazed upon the very gentle daughter of Ronan,
> When she went to wash her hands—Creda, the strong-pointed daughter of Ronan.

<header>MAY 18–22.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

**18.** *Of Mark, that is, a pope; or, the evangelist. He has been crowned, meaning he received the dignity of an apostle from the nations after separating from Peter.*
**My-Máedóc**, <note>original: Mo-Máedóc; the prefix "My" is a common Old Irish devotional hypocoristic, expressing affection for a saint.</note> that is, of Fid Duin in the south of Ossory.
**My-Domnóc**, that is, of Tipra Fachtnai in Ossory.
**Clóenad**, that is, a church which is in Húi Faeláin in Leinster.
*Of Urbanus, that is, Urban, Bishop of Rome, etc.*

**20.** *Marcellosa, a virgin and martyr.*
**Colman** of Daire Mór, and **Daniel** of Tulach, and **Mac Laithbe** of Domnach Mór, and **Crom Dithraib** of Inis Crainn *on this day.* <note>original: in hoc die</note>

**21.** *Of wheat, because the saints are God’s wheat; or "detoirim," meaning "tuirmim" (I reckon), as a certain person said: "I reckon" (is the right reading):*
> O mill, that has ground much wheat (*tuirind*).
> It was not a grinding on a *serblenn* <note>The meaning of "serblenn" is uncertain; it may refer to a specific type of millstone or a poor quality of grain.</note>; you ground on Cerball’s grandsons.
> The grain which the mill grinds is not oats, but red wheat:
> The feed of Maelodráin’s mill is from the fruit of the great tree.

That is, the two sons of Blathmec, son of Aed Sláine—namely, **Dunchad** and **Cathal**—who were slain by Marcán of Leinster in a certain mill.
"It is those two sons of Blathmec who are called 'the red wheat'."¹

**Colmán the Leper**, that is, Colmán of Mag Eo <note>likely Mag n-Éne</note> in Dál Cais.
**Barrind**, that is, in Fir Cell, which is in the south of Meath; he was Barrind, son of Muredach, son of Fiacha, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages (see *Book of Leinster* 347d).
*Of Druim Cuilinn, that is, in Fir Cell, which is in Leinster.*

**22.** *Of Rónán, that is, of Land Rónáin Find in Húi Echach of Ulster,* that is, Rónán the Fair, son of Sarán, son of Colchu, son of Tuathal, son of Cruindbél (from whom the Húi Cruindbeoil descend), son of Fedilmid, son of Fiachra, son of Colla Fochri.

**Báithíne**, that is, Báithín of Inis Báithín in the east of Leinster in Dál Mesincorp. And Trea, daughter of Rónán, King of Leinster, was the mother of Báithín, son of Findach.

And this is how Báithín was born: Findach, a robber, happened to be one day in the top of a thorn tree over a well, intending to rob and plunder the church. Cred came to the well to wash her hands, and when Finnach saw her, he longed for her, *and his male seed fell upon a sprig of watercress in front of her. Then the virgin ate the sprig upon which the seed had fallen, and from that was born Báithín the ever-living.* <note>original: et cecidit semen eius virile super nasturtii surculum coram eam. Tunc edit virgo surculum super quem fuit semen.</note>

However, it was God’s miracle that caused it, *as it was said*:
> Creda was a good woman, daughter of Rónán, King of Leinster;
> With her dear church—constant and pure—she was the mother of Báithín, son of Findach.
> Findach the robber was stealing in the thorn tree over the well,
> When *some of his male seed* <note>original: aliquid seminis eius virilis</note> went onto the soft-topped sprig of cress.
> Since the keen robber looked upon the daughter of Rónán at the very moment
> When she went to wash her hands—Cred, the star-strong daughter of Rónán.

***

¹ See the story in Rawlinson B. 502, folio 73b 2; and Rawlinson B. 512, folio 115b, edited by Kuno Meyer in *Hibernica Minora*, page 71.

The girl ate the stalk on which was the equal-growth conception, and from that—fair was the fight—ever-living Baithin was born.

### May 24
**Augustine**—that is, he was of the community of Gregory of Rome and the bishop of the Saxons. <note>original: migrauit ad Dominum Agustinus</note> Augustine departed to the Lord in the seventieth year of his age, and in the fortieth year of his episcopate.
**Hermes**—that is, a Pope of Rome.
**Colman**—so that he is the third Great Colman of Meath; that is, Colman of the Reliquary <note>original: comraisi; likely comraire</note>, and Colman son of Luachan from Lann Luachain, and Colman from Lann Ela. Colman—that is, from Tir da Glas. And Augustine, Bishop of Laodicea, is on the same day as Colman; it was he who led all the English people to Christ, having been sent by Gregory with forty disciples to preach the Word of God to the island of Britain.
**Aidbe**—Aidben is the name of the saint, and his church is located there, to the south of Emly, high in the breast of Sliabh Crot. It was there that Conaing, grandson of Dath, lived in piety for seven years. *Or Aidbe*—that is, a saint who is in a portion of land in Connacht. That is, the abbot of Tir da Glas. His church is there to the south of Emly, *or* in Brechmag in Carra in western Connacht. *Or Aidben* is the name of the saint. *Or Aidhben*—that is, "Living Aed," <note>original: eo quod uiuus est in mirabilibus</note> because he is alive in miracles. He is in Tuatha Fertir in Connacht. Brechmag is the name of the city.

### May 25
John the Evangelist, but not his falling asleep <note>death</note>.
**Dionis**—that is, the Bishop of Milan. *Or Lannan*, a proper name—that is, from Cluain Aird na Liatan in Ciarraige Ai. It was called "Litana" because they used to sing litanies there—that is, hymns and psalms.
**Dunchad**—that is, the abbot of Iona of Colum Cille. That is, Dunchad son of Cennfaelad, son of Mael Coba, son of Aed, son of Ainmire. He was the abbot of Iona; it was under him that the community of Iona adopted the lawful Easter <note>referring to the resolution of the dating of Easter controversy</note>.

### May 26
**Colman**.
**Stellan**—that is, from Tir da Glas.
**Becan**—that is, in Cluain Aird Mo-Beccoc in Muscraige Breogain in Munster, and Cluain Aird is his dwelling. *Or here* at the House of the O'Connells in Ui Briuin Cualann.

### May 27
Bishop **Cillin** from Tech Talain, and **Echfritan** son of Osu, and Bishop **Eithirn** of Domnach Mor are here.

### May 28
**Germanus**—that is, the master of Patrick. **Furudran** in Lann Turu, and **Faelan**, and seven bishops from Tech na Comairce are here.

### May 29
**Cumain**—that is, a female saint, and she is in Ard Ulad. Cumman the virgin in Dal Buinni in Ulster.
**The Daughter of Allin**, from Ard Ulad. That is, she is at Daire Ingen Aillein at Ard Ulad.

### May 30
**Eutychius**—that is, a Pope.
**Gobban** the abbot and **Saergus** of Druim are here.

### May 31
**Petronilla**—that is, the daughter of Peter the Apostle. According to the testimony of Gregory, she rested in peace without the cutting of iron <note>meaning she died naturally rather than by the sword of martyrdom</note>.

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. THE MONTH OF JUNE.</header>

## THE MONTH OF JUNE.

### June 1st (The Calends of June)
Give heed <note>original: "Oid menmain"</note> to the feast of **Thecla**,
which has a right to be sung by us,
with a vast, noble host
at the beginning <note>literally: "on the forehead"</note> of the calends of June.

### June 2nd (The 4th day before the Nones of June)
**Erasmus** the bishop,
a splendid flame with vigorous strength,
brought to Christ a triumphant company,
three hundred praiseworthy thousands.

### June 3rd (The 3rd day before the Nones of June)
A soldier of Christ in the land of Ireland,
a high name <note>original: "ard n-ainm"</note> across the sea's waves:
**Kevin** <note>original: "Cóemgen"</note>, the chaste, fair warrior,
in the Glen of the two broad lakes <note>Glendalough</note>.

### June 4th (The day before the Nones of June)
**Apollinaris** went
to the kingdom of God directly,
with his virginal company,
at the translation <note>The moving of a saint's relics</note> of **Martin**.

### June 5th (The Nones of June)
The martyrdom of **Marcianus**
was magnified by many triumphs;
one of a great man—a goodly generation—
another of a virginal maiden.

---

L, LB, F follow this, but compare *oid menmain* (glossed as "behold" or "gaze upon") in the Milan Glosses 24c 13, 101b 5. ² *dun* in LB. ³ *dim* in B; *din* in R1, B, L; *dind* in F. ⁴ *cétal* in B; *chetal* in R1, L; *ceatal* in F; *cetul* in LB. ⁴ *Heresmus* in L; *Erasmus* in R1, LB; *Hirasmus* in F. ⁵ *bríge* in R1, LB; *mbrígi* in L; *bríghe* in F. ⁶ *mbúada* in R1; *mbuada* in L, LB; *buadha* in F. ⁷ *ardainm* in E; *ardd ainm* in F. ⁸ *dar* in LB; *tar* in E, R1, L; *uas* in F. ⁹ *cathar* in R1; *caithéir* in L; *caithfer* in LB; *cathfer* in F. ¹⁰ *o glind* in R1; *inglind* in L, F; *anglind* in LB. ¹¹ *appollináris* in R1, L; *apollonaris* in LB; *appollinaris* in F. ¹² *co morslúag* (with a great host) in B, L; *co mor cleir* in LB; *co morcleir* in F. ¹³ *co n-áni* (with splendor) in B, L; *co nuagi* in F, R1; *conuaige* in LB. ¹⁴ *tarmrith* in R1, L, F; *tairmrith* in E; *tarmbreith* in LB. ¹⁵ Thus in R1, L, LB; *marcionis* in F. ¹⁶ *feir* in R1; *fir* in L, LB, F. ¹⁷ *ingena huaga* in R1; *ingeine huaga* in L; *ingena huaga* in LB; *ingena huagha* in F.

<page-num>139</page-num>
<header>JUNE 6-10.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

### June 8th (The 8th day before the Ides of June)
The perfect suffering <note>original: *Ógcéssad*</note> of **Amantius**; it is a great deed if you conceal it. **Mael-aithgin**, with pure goodness, went under the shelter of the earth <note>original: *túbai*; referring to burial</note>.

### June 7th (The 7th day before the Ides of June)
The calling of **Paul** the martyr, after a great deed with strength. The feast of **Colomb** without pride <note>original: *šotlai*</note>, the great descendant of **Artae**.

### June 8th (The 6th day before the Ides of June)
The reception of the holy **Job**, after triumph and a "white battle" <note>original: *bánchath*; a spiritual struggle or martyrdom without the shedding of blood</note>. The feast of **Medrán**, a great solace; the feast of **Murchú** with great grace.

### June 9th (The 5th day before the Ides of June)
May they convoy us to the eternal kingdom, where there is always a shining light: **Baethíne**, high and angelic, and **Columba** <note>original: *Colomb Cille*</note>, the lustrous!

### June 10th (The 4th day before the Ides of June)
They meet on the same path—happy is he who has found them: the chief feast of **Mark**, a famous diadem <note>original: *mind*; a term for a holy relic or crown</note>, along with the triumphant feast of **Barnabas**.

---

<margin>
**Notes on the text:**
1. *Perfect suffering*: The original *Ógcéssad* implies a complete or virginal martyrdom.
2. *Mael-aithgin*: An early Irish saint; the text notes his burial ("under ground").
3. *Colomb*: Not to be confused with Columba of Iona (who follows on June 9th), this refers to a different holy man of the Artae lineage.
4. *White battle*: A common Celtic Christian concept of "white martyrdom" (*bán-mhartra*), meaning a life of asceticism or exile rather than death by the sword.
5. *Columba*: This is the famous St. Columba (Colum Cille), the apostle of Scotland and founder of Iona.
</margin>

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF JUNE]</header>

### A. *June 11th (The third day before the Ides of June).*
Victorious Basilla,
who was carried from us into joy;
the feast of the hallowed Mac Táil <note>original: Macc tháil; likely St. Mac Táil of Kilcullen</note>,
along with the passion of Fortunatus.

### B. *June 12th (The day before the Ides of June).*
The feast of the pious Coemán,
to whom "Sanct-lethan" <note>original: sanctlethan; meaning "Holy-Broad"</note> is a title;
and Torannán, lasting and full of deeds,
who came over the wide, ship-filled sea.

### C. *June 13th (The Ides of June).*
With the active Bartholomew—
you are dull <note>original: meirb; meaning weak or sluggish</note> if you have not heard of him—
the chaste Mac Nissi of Clúana <note>original: Clúain mic Nois or Connor</note>
journeyed from us to the Kings <note>original: cor-ríga; referring to the Kingdom of Heaven</note>.

### D. *June 14th (The 18th day before the Kalends of July).*
Both of them meet
on the same festival—a host-filled sea!—
the vigorous Nem, descendant of Bern,
along with the victorious Benedict.

### E. *June 15th (The 17th day before the Kalends of July).*
A blessing on the champion
who loved Christ with true prosperity;
with whom went a host of great valor:
Vitus, the marvelous child.

### F. *June 16th (The 16th day before the Kalends of July).*
My champion is Quiricus <note>original: Giric</note>,
around whom a holy host was slain;
no equal or likeness to him
has been found among the sons of the world.

against whom bursts the monster-filled sea;<gloss>17</gloss>

the beautiful grandson of Liathán.<gloss>19</gloss>

**E. 10th day before the Kalends of July (June 22).**
With James son of Alphaeus,
twice eight hundred—a brilliant following;<gloss>20</gloss>
the feast of a man<gloss>21</gloss> who loved not<gloss>22</gloss> bodily ease,<gloss>23</gloss>
mighty<gloss>24</gloss> Cronán of Ferns.

<page-num>142</page-num>
<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF JUNE.]</header>

### *Friday, the 9th day before the Kalends of July.* <note>June 23rd</note>
The commemoration of my Coe <note>original: *mo Choe*; likely St. Mochua</note>,
there is nothing that escapes us;
may the famous, happy champion
from Nendrum <note>original: *Oendruimm*; a monastery on Mahee Island, Strangford Lough</note> protect us!

### *Saturday, the 8th day before the Kalends of July.* <note>June 24th</note>
The royal birth of John the Baptist,
if you have attended to it diligently,
along with the translation <note>original: *tathchor*; the "removal" or transfer of relics</note> without disgrace
of John the son of Zebedee to Ephesus.

### *Sunday, the 7th day before the Kalends of July.* <note>June 25th</note>
The feast of Sinchell, the feast of Telle <note>Saints of Killeigh and Tehel</note>,
they were the heights of Ireland;
along with my pure, brilliant Luóc <note>St. Moluag of Lismore</note>,
the sun of Lismore of Scotland <note>original: *Liss móir de Albae*</note>.

### *Monday, the 6th day before the Kalends of July.* <note>June 26th</note>
Vast is their suffering,
their passion, for I have searched into it:
Gallicanus, the fair sun,
and Johannes and Paulus <note>John and Paul, Roman martyrs</note>.

### *Tuesday, the 5th day before the Kalends of July.* <note>June 27th</note>
They have been proven through martyrdom,
whose storms <note>original: *trethain*; literally "seas" or "tempests"</note> are great and heavy:
seven brothers, warriors,
in Rome of broad Latium <note>original: *Lethai*</note>.

<header>JUNE 28–30.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

->**June 28**<-
<note>original: D. iv. cal. Iulii.</note>
In great Leccan <note>modern Leckin</note> of Meath
is Crummíne with splendor;
on the same festival, observed with piety,
is the holy <note>original: "white"</note> passion of Fabianus.

->**June 29**<-
<note>original: E. iii. cal. Iulii.</note>
The feast of Paul and Peter,
with the vastness of the cries of prayer unto them;
the noise of battle upon the world's breast
does not surpass the fame of this day.

->**June 30**<-
<note>original: F. Pridie cal. Iulii.</note>
The triumph of Saul and Timothy,
and the death in bed <note>term: "bed-death" refers to a natural death rather than martyrdom</note> of wealthy Job;
these draw a fair, concluding bolt
upon the host of dear June.
