<page-num>170</page-num>

# FÉLIRE OENGUSSO. [JULY.]

18. **Of the queen, that is, Christina.** It is from her that Lake Christina near Rome <note>original: *prope Romam*</note> is named, at a distance of a three-stage journey <note>original: *spaitio iteineris trium oistentorum*</note>. Or **Christina**: It was his [a king's] desire for her, so that by her was made one causeway from Rome to this history of the Romans <note>original: *senchus Romanorum*</note>, and by her was made one causeway from Rome to Mount Gargano <note>original: *Sliab nGarggan*</note>. It happened in this way: a certain man, a king, gave great love to her, but she said she would not unite with him for any reason unless he helped in the construction of that great causeway <note>original: *morumaloidei*</note>. It was done accordingly, and he offered the causeway through the king's help. The grace of God came upon the king himself through that deed, and he served the Lord <note>original: *Choimde*</note>, and he never had relations with Christina.

19. **Sisinnius,** that is, Sisinnius, a famous leader <note>original: *dux clarus*</note> of the family of Emperor Nerva, but he was baptized by Pope Clement with all his family. There were 333 nobles, and those three were friends of Nero. Through Sisinnius they believed in God, but he himself believed first through his wife Theodora; his passion <note>term: the suffering and death of a martyr</note> is not narrated here.

20. **Romula,** that is, she lived in Rome.
**Curphine,** that is, in Ui Fidgenti <note>a tribal kingdom in modern County Limerick</note>. **Curuphin,** that is, he is in the middle of Munster in Ui Fidgenti. In Munster is Curufin or Curbin.

21. **Praxides,** that is, a virgin and martyr.

22. **Magdalene.** "Magdalene" is so called after the village of Magdala in which she was born or raised, and she was the sister of Lazarus. There were eighteen women in the company of Christ, and four of them were called by the name Mary. The first was the mother of the Lord. The second was the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who was the sister of the Lord’s mother. The third was the mother of the sons of Alphaeus, and she too was a sister of the Lord’s mother. The fourth was Mary Magdalene. It was she who sat at the feet of Christ and poured oil over his head and feet, and washed them with her tears and cleaned them with her hair. He gave her forgiveness for her sins, and the Pharisee was angry with him for allowing a harlot to be near him.
**Apollinaris,** that is, Apollinaris, bishop of Ravenna, who suffered under Emperor <unclear>Vespasian</unclear>.
**Mobí of Inis Cuscraid,** that is, beside Downpatrick <note>original: *Duin da leathglas*</note>.

24. **Declan,** that is, from Ardmore in the Deisi of Munster. That is, Declan of Ardmore, son of Erc, son of Niad, son of Brian, son of Eogan, son of Bric, son of Artcorb, son of Fiacha Suidhe.

25. **My Colmoc,** that is, Colman, grandson of Liathan and a pupil of Moling; he is in Tech Moling and in Lismore of Mochuta.
**Mosiloc,** that is, a pupil of Moling Luachair, and he is in Tech Moling, or he is in Lismore of Mochuta.
**Nessan,** that is, Deacon Nessan. Nessan in Munster; Nessan was his name, and he was a deacon, and he is in Mungret <note>original: *Mungarit*</note>.
**Brother of John, James.** That is, James the son of Zebedee, brother of John, who suffered at the hands of Herod Agrippa in Jerusalem. He was the first of the apostles to suffer martyrdom, but along with James the son of Zebedee, the memory of the martyr Christopher is celebrated among the Romans. ### JULY 18–25. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS: NOTES.

18. **Of the queen**, that is, **Christina**: From her is named Lake Christina <note>original: *Lacus Christinae*</note>, near Rome, at a distance of a journey of three ostents <margin>According to the scholar Rhabanus, an "ostent" was one-sixtieth of an hour. It seems synonymous with an *unga* (from the Latin *uncia*), the twelfth part of a moment.</margin>. Or **Christina**: This is a story of the Romans, saying that she built a causeway from Rome to Mount Garganus <note>Mount Gargano in Italy, a famous site of the sanctuary of Monte Sant'Angelo</note>. This is how it happened: a certain man—a king—loved her deeply, but she said that she would not unite with him for any reason unless he would help in performing that great deed of humility <note>original: lowliness</note>. Thus it was done, and through the king's help, she offered the causeway to God. Through that deed, divine grace came upon the king himself; he served the Lord, and he and Christina did not unite <margin>For a completely different legend of St. Christina, see the *Martyrology of Gorman*, p. 121.</margin>.

19. **Of Sisinnus**, etc.

20. **Romula**, that is, she was in Rome.
**Curphine**, that is, in Huí Fidgente in Munster is Curufin or Curbin <note>Huí Fidgente was a tribal kingdom in what is now County Limerick</note>.

21. **Of Praxides**, that is, a virgin and martyr.

22. **Magdalena**, so called from Magdalum <note>the town of Magdala</note>, etc. 
That is, it is she who sat at Christ’s feet and poured oil over His head and over His feet, and washed them with her tears and cleansed them with her hair; and He gave her forgiveness for her sins, even though the Pharisee rebuked Him for letting a harlot near Him.
**Apolnair**, that is, Apollinaris, bishop of Ravenna, who [suffered under Emperor Vespasian] <note>original: *qui etc.*</note>.
**Mobí** of Inis Cuscraid <note>Inch, County Down</note>, that is, beside Dún dá lethglas <note>Downpatrick</note>.

24. **Declan**, that is, from Ardmore in the Déssi of Munster <note>the Déisi Muman, a powerful group in early medieval Ireland</note>. That is, Declan of Ardmore, son of Erc, son of Nia, son of Brian, son of Eogan Brecc, son of Artcirb, son of Fiacha Suigde <margin>See two different pedigrees in the *Book of Leinster* (LL) 348e.</margin>.

25. **My Colmóc**, that is, Colmán grandson of Liathain, a fosterling <note>term: *dalta*, a student or spiritual ward</note> of Moling; and he is in Tech Moling <note>St. Mullins</note> and in Lismore <note>original: *Les mór Mochutu*</note>.
**Mo-Síloc**, that is, a fosterling of Moling of Luachair, and he is in Tech Moling, or in Lismore.
**Nessán**, that is, deacon Nessán in Munster; that is, Nessán was his name, and he was a deacon <note>original: *et diaconus fuit*</note>, and he is in Mungret <note>original: *Mungarit*</note>.
**Brother of John**, etc. **James** son of Zebedee, etc.

...stored in their final borders <note>original: *ultimis fimbrilis*</note>, they are honored with the most famous veneration of those peoples. *F.*

26. That is, **Mount Tabor** <note>original: *sleib Taboir*</note>, in the tribe of Naphtali <note>original: *tribu Neptolim*</note>. *L.* In the mountain of Galilee. *F.*

**Toman of Mungret** and **Furudhran** are commemorated here. *F.*

27. **Simeon the Monk** <note>original: *Semeoin manaig*</note>: he suffered <note>original: *pasus est*; referring to martyrdom</note> in Antioch. *L. F.*

28. That is, **Theophilus** and **Pantaleon** are martyrs. *L.* **Theophilus** was the bishop of Antioch. **Pantaleon** was a martyr and he suffered in Nicomedia. *F.*

29. That is, **Lupus**, **Simplex**, and **Prossus** are three bishops. *L.* **Lupus** and **Simplex** were bishops who suffered under the Emperor Diocletian. *R¹.*

30. **Abdon** and **Sennes** <note>original: *Sendis*</note>: those who suffered in Rome under the Emperor Decius. *R¹.* That is, two martyrs who suffered by the sword in Rome. *F.*

31. **Colman, son of Dairine**: that is, he was Dairine's sister's son and also her foster-son <note>original: *dalta*</note>. Or, **Dairine** was his mother’s name. This son of Dairine is at the Plain of the Great Oak-Wood <note>original: *Clar Daire moir*</note> in Mag Airb <note>a plain in modern County Tipperary and Kilkenny</note>. **Natail** of Kilnamanagh <note>original: *Chill Manach*</note> in western Ossory is commemorated on the same day as him. *L.* He is from the Great Oak-Wood of the son of Dairine in Mag Airb, and **Rathail** of Kilnamanagh in western Ossory is on the same day. *R¹.* From the Great Oak-Wood of the son of Dairine, between Ossory and Ele Muman <note>the kingdom of Ely in Munster</note>. *R¹.*

**Colman, son of Dairine**, then: Dairine was the sister of Colman's mother, and he was her foster-son. **Sanct**, however, the sister of Dairine, was Colman’s mother. Dairine was barren <note>original: *aimrit*</note>, while her sister Sanct had many children <note>original: *clannmar*</note>. Dairine asked for Colman to foster him immediately after his birth <note>original: *fochétóir*</note>. Sanct gave him to her, and so it was Dairine who raised him. Because of this, he is called "Colman son of Dairine." He is at the Great Oak-Wood in Mag Airb, between Ossory and Ele. **Natail** <insert>reading: Natail</insert> of Kilnamanagh in western Ossory, and **Bishop German** <note>St. Germain of Auxerre</note>, the tutor <note>original: *aiti*; foster-father or teacher</note> of Saint Patrick, and **Iarnóc the Sick** <note>original: *uithir*</note>, and **Fallamhon** are commemorated here. *F.*

<header>JULY 26–31.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

26. He is on **Mount Tabor**, that is, in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali <note>original: *Nephthalim*</note>, on a mountain in Galilee. This marks the **Transfiguration of Christ**, and so on.

31. **Colmán, son of Dairine**.⁴ That is, his mother’s sister was Dairine, and he was her foster-child <note>original: *fosterling*</note>. Or Dairine was his mother's name <note>original: *nomen matris eius*</note>. That is, Dairine’s son is at the Plain of the Great Oak-wood <note>original: *Clár Dairi móir*</note> in Mag Airb <note>a plain in modern County Tipperary/Kilkenny</note>. **Natail** of Kilnamanagh <note>original: *Cell manach*</note> in western Ossory is also commemorated on the same day as him. That is, he is from the Great Oak-wood of the sons of Dairine <note>original: *Daire móir meic Darane*</note> in Mag Airb, and Rathail (corrected to Natail) is from Kilnamanagh in western Ossory on the same day <note>original: *in uno die*</note>. This Great Oak-wood is located between Ossory and Ely <note>original: *Éle*</note> of Munster.

Regarding Colmán, son of Dairine: Dairine was the sister of Colmán’s mother, and he was her foster-child. **Sanct**, Dairine’s sister, was Colmán’s actual mother. Dairine was barren, but Sanct was prolific. Therefore, Dairine asked for Colmán immediately after his birth. Sanct gave him to her so that Dairine could foster him, and for this reason, he is called "Colmán, son of Dairine." He is associated with the Great Oak-wood <note>original: *Daire móir*</note> in Mag Airb, between Ossory and Ely.⁵

Also commemorated here are **Natail** <note>original: *Mac tail*, corrected to *Natail*</note> of Kilnamanagh in western Ossory; **Bishop Germanus**, who was Saint Patrick’s tutor; **Iarnóc the Sickly**; and **Fallamon**.

⁵ The same legend is told in the *Book of Leinster*, pages 350c and 372b, where **Sanct** is called "daughter of Gése" <note>original: *ingen Gési*</note>.

### THE MONTH OF AUGUST.

*August 1. On the Calends <note>original: Calendis Augusti; the first day of the month</note> of August.*
1. On the first day of August,
the feast of the sons of the Maccabees <note>seven brothers martyred in the 2nd century BCE</note>
brought great strength,
along with eighty thousand martyrs.

*August 2. The 4th day before the Nones <note>original: iv. nonas Augusti</note> of August.*
2. Alongside that great mother,
the steadfast <note>original: "durable one"</note> Theodota,
those three good children
went to their triumph <note>referring to their martyrdom</note>.

*August 3. The 3rd day before the Nones <note>original: iii. nonas Augusti</note> of August.*
3. In Jerusalem <note>original: "John's metropolis"</note>, a beloved and
splendid feast, where
the noble body of Saint Stephen <note>the first Christian martyr</note>
was found in holiness.

*August 4. The day before the Nones <note>original: Pridie nonas Augusti</note> of August.*
4. He will be joyful upon
arriving in heaven;
I have great confidence in him,
the noble royal champion,
Molua son of Ocha <note>an Irish saint and founder of the monastery of Clonfertmulloe</note>.

*August 5. On the Nones <note>original: Nonis Augusti</note> of August.*
5. The glorious martyrdom of Herentius
deserves a loving commemoration,
along with Saint Oswald, whom we pray to,
the noble high king of the Saxons <note>Oswald of Northumbria, d. 642</note>.

<header>AUGUST 6–11. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

### A. *August 6. The 8th day before the Ides of August.*
Bishop Sixtus of Rome <note>original: "Sistán epscop rúamach"</note> carried a buoyant troop upward, along with my Cua <note>Saint Mochua</note>, a victorious pillar from the populous Clondalkin.

### B. *August 7. The 7th day before the Ides of August.*
Proclaim the five and three fifties of years <note>155 years</note>—a strength you have watched over—seven great men without reproach slept in Ephesus <note>referring to the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus</note>.

### C. *August 8. The 6th day before the Ides of August.*
The feast of Beóán, son of great Nessán—it is no prayer of the insignificant <note>original: "ni hattach mbille"</note>—and Colmán, a praiseworthy bishop from the Island of the White Cow <note>Inishbofin</note>.

### D. *August 9. The 5th day before the Ides of August.*
Observe the passion <note>martyrdom</note> of Antony and the very strong family of Firmus; in fair Achonry <note>original: "Achud cháin"</note> is buried the faithful priest Nathí.

### E. *August 10. The 4th day before the Ides of August.*
The heavy cross of Lawrence the deacon <note>Saint Lawrence, martyred on a gridiron</note> was hard upon his poor body; along with a healthy, noble, and fair company is beautiful Bláán of Kingarth <note>original: "Cinn Garad" in Scotland</note>.

### F. *August 11. The 3rd day before the Ides of August.*
Pray to Airerán the Wise <note>original: "Airerán necnaí"</note> whose fame is not hidden, along with the pure Valerian and the strong, wise Tiburtius.

### 6. Sixtus, a Roman bishop,
carried a buoyant troop upward, along with my Cua <note>Saint Mochua</note>, a triumphant pillar from the populous Clondalkin.

### 7. Announce the five and
three fifties of years—a strength which you have observed—seven people without disgrace have slept in Ephesus.

### 8. The feast of Beóán, son of
great Nessán—this is no prayer of the weak; also Colmán, a praiseworthy bishop from the Island of the White Cow (*Inishbofin*).

### 9. Consider the passion
of Antony and of Firmus, a mighty family; in fair Achonry is buried Nathí, the pious priest <note>original: "presbyter"</note>.

### 10. The heavy cross of Lawrence
the deacon was hard upon his poor body; with a healthy, noble, and distinguished host comes fair Bláán of Kingarth.

### 11. Beseech Airerán of the
wisdom, whose fame is not hidden; along with the pure Valerian and the strong, prudent Tiburtius.

12. The calling of Lassrén <note>Saint Laisrén of Inishmurray</note> of the Isle of Muredach, who is great and magnified; he comes with a holy company that does not fade <note>original: "nád athbi" — literally "does not ebb"</note>; and the feast of the famous Segéne <note>Abbot of Iona</note>.

13. The martyr Hippolytus <note>a Roman saint reportedly dragged to death by horses</note>—his shining company was marvelous; along with a vast and noble host is my Máedóc <note>Saint Máedóc of Ferns</note>, the crown <note>original: "mind" — literally a diadem or a precious relic</note> of the Gaels.

14. With the calling of Fortunatus across a sea crowded with ships <note>original: "lir longaig"</note>, we celebrate the feast of Fachtna, son of Mongach; he was the son of the craftsman <note>original: "macc in tsáir"</note> and a fair captive.

15. On the great feast of her commemoration—the true Mother of our Father <note>The Assumption of the Virgin Mary</note>—with a host of kings in a truly splendid assembly; also Fer dá chrích <note>Saint of Derryloran</note>, a fair champion.

16. At the cross of Adrio, with a company that did not love lawlessness <note>original: "díchmairc" — referring to doing things without permission or through theft</note>, we celebrate the nativity of Mary <note>original: "gein Maire"</note>, a virginal and strong crown, the holy Mother of my high King.

<header>AUGUST 17–22.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

### *E. August 17. The 16th day before the Kalends of September.*
Ro céss¹ Mammes martir
mórphéin² i croich calaid,
la³ cléir cáin cen⁴ chinaid,⁵
taimthiu Temnén manaig.

17. Mammes the martyr suffered great agony on a harsh cross, along with a fair, innocent company. It is also the day of the natural death <note>original: "taimthiu" — refers to a peaceful death in bed rather than martyrdom</note> of Temnén the monk.

### *F. August 18. The 15th day before the Kalends of September.*
Macc Cresséni m'Ernóc
mórais⁶ Fiadat⁷ fairinn:
ba fer raith diar turinn
Daig mór maith macc Cairill.

18. Ernóc, the son of Cresséne, brought glory to the Lord’s <note>original: "Fiadat"</note> company. Daig the Good, the great son of Cairell, was a man of grace among our "wheat" <note>original: "turinn" — a metaphor for the chosen people or the community of the faithful</note>.

### *G. August 19. The 14th day before the Kalends of September.*
Croch in martir Magni⁸
co cléir co mbúaid⁹ bláthe,
Mochtae mór maith síthbe,
Enán Dromma Ráthe.¹⁰

19. The martyrdom <note>original: "croch" — literally "cross"</note> of the martyr Magnus, with a triumphant and flourishing company. Also Mochta the Great, a fine leader <note>original: "síthbe" — literally a general or chieftain</note>, and Enán of Druimm Ráthe.

### *A. August 20. The 13th day before the Kalends of September.*
Ro céss¹¹ Dioscorus,¹²
ar Chríst, cing as¹³ ferdu,¹⁴
Pampil, breó as amru,
co mórslúagad geldu.¹⁵

20. Dioscorus, a most courageous champion, suffered for Christ. Also Pamphilus, a most wonderful flame <note>original: "breó" — often used metaphorically for a saintly person</note>, with a vast and shining host.

### *B. August 21. The 12th day before the Kalends of September.*
Guid i féil Uincení
do chongnam¹⁶ frit anmain
epscop Senach sulbair¹⁷
Clúana hIraird adbail.

21. On the feast of Vincentius <note>Saint Vincent</note>, pray for help for your soul from the eloquent Bishop Senach of great Clonard <note>Clúain Iraird was one of the most famous monastic schools in early medieval Ireland</note>.

### *C. August 22. The 11th day before the Kalends of September.*
Attaig itge Tiamdai¹⁸
daltai Pól co náni,¹⁹
guid maccraid²⁰ co nóibi
ind nóib²¹ Emiliáni.²²

22. Seek the prayers of Timothy, the splendid pupil of Paul; entreat the holy youths <note>original: "maccraid" — a collective term for young men or disciples</note> of the holy Emilianus.

<header>THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS <note>original: "FELIRE OENGUSSO"</note>. [THE MONTH OF AUGUST.]</header>

### D. August 23. The 10th day before the Kalends of September.
At the martyrdom <note>original: "paiss," from the Latin *passio*</note> of **Fortunatus**¹
with whom went a great host of warriors,²
on the same festival—the talk of the world!—
is the feast of **Eogan** of Ardstraw <note>original: "Aird sratha"; Eogan was a 6th-century bishop in County Tyrone</note>.⁴

### E. August 24. The 9th day before the Kalends of September.
With the ranks of the host⁵ of **Zenobius**⁶,
whose story⁷ has been heard,
is **Old Patrick** <note>original: "sen-Phátric"; likely referring to Patrick of Auvergne or a contemporary of the apostle Patrick</note>, a champion of battle,
the beloved foster-teacher of our sage.

### F. August 25. The 8th day before the Kalends of September.
The story of his suffering has been spread
to every⁸ side, even to the streaming sea;
after the great cross, he was crowned—
the triumphant **Bartholomew**⁹.

### G. August 26. The 7th day before the Kalends of September.
The victory of **Abundius**¹⁰ the martyr—
arise to celebrate¹¹ it!
To heaven with a very devoted¹³ host¹²
he has climbed¹⁴ after his journey through hardship.

### A. August 27. The 6th day before the Kalends of September.
The troop of the pure¹⁵ martyr
**Rufinus**¹⁶, the fair and melodic¹⁷,
to the holy rampart of the King¹⁸ of Clouds¹⁹
passed through the field²⁰ of spears.

<meta>This page contains the "Notationes" or explanatory notes for the start of the month of August in the Martyrology of Oengus. These notes provide hagiographical details and etymological legends for the saints mentioned in the calendar, specifically the Maccabees, St. Stephen, and St. Molua.</meta>

<lang>Irish</lang>
<page-num>180</page-num>
<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF AUGUST.]</header>

### NOTES.

1. **The Maccabees** <note>original: "Mochabae"</note>: that is, seven sons with their mother (namely, Machaba) suffered <note>original: "passi sunt"</note> in Antioch under Antiochus, who is called Epiphanes, in the city of Dalpia in Armenia.

2. **Theodota** <note>original: "Teothota"</note>: she suffered with her three sons in Bithynia under the Emperor Diocletian.
On this day is the passion of the three virgin sisters in Rome: namely, **Faith, Hope, and Charity** <note>original: "Fides, Spes, Caritas"</note>, the daughters of **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientia/Sophia"</note>.

3. **The metropolis of John** <note>original: "Metropoil ind Eoin"</note>: the name of the place or city where John lived; John was in Antioch.
<gloss>The noble body of Stephen</gloss> <note>original: "corpán sóer Stefani"</note>: Here the body of Stephen, the first martyr of the New Testament, was found. And it was found in this way: Lucian, a priest of the church in the village of **Caphargamala** <note>original: "Capargan"</note>, revealed the body of the martyr Stephen to the Christians. This village is not far from Jerusalem. But **Gamaliel**, a scribe of the Law who was in the same tomb as Stephen, revealed this through a vision to Lucian, saying: "I, Gamaliel, and **Nicodemus** my nephew, and **Abibus** <note>original: "Abilus"</note> my most beloved son, are in one tomb with Stephen; make this known to the Christians so that his bones may be revealed."

4. "He shall be joyful," etc. **Molua, son of Ocha** (that is, *ochsal*, "armpit") of **Clonfertmulloe** <note>original: "Chluain ferta Molua"</note>, and of **Slieve Bloom** <note>original: "Sleib Bladmai"</note>, and of **Druim Snechtai** in Farney, and in other places. Molua, son of Ocha, was named in this way: Once, it happened <note>original: "dorala"</note> that **Comgall of Bangor** <note>original: "Comgall Bennchuir"</note> was traveling on his way with his followers; suddenly <note>original: "Ecmaine"</note> they heard the cries of an infant in a **clump of rushes** <note>original: "tuirpill luachrai"</note>. Or, as another version says, Comgall was walking one day with his companions and, lifting his eyes to heaven, he saw angels ascending from the earth to the sky not far from the road. He sent one of his companions to see the vision, but after he arrived, he found nothing remarkable. The monk gave a **kick** <note>original: "lua"</note> to the clump of rushes and saw an infant in the middle of it, and he carried the child back in his **armpit** <note>original: "ochsaill"</note>. Comgall asked him, "What did you find?" He said, "I found an infant." Comgall asked, "What did you do to it?" The monk replied, "I gave my kick (*lua*) to it, and brought it with me in my armpit." Comgall said, "His name shall be **Molua son of Ocha**," because he was found in the rushes, or because of the kick (*lua*) the monk gave to the clump of rushes where he was. "Son of Ocha" means "son of the armpit," because among the ancients, *ocha* meant *ochsal* (armpit). He was thereafter raised by Comgall.

"Son of Ocha" means "son of the armpit," for the history is this: when Comgall of Bangor was traveling his way, <unclear>he saw</unclear> a service of angels over a bank of rushes a short distance from the road. Comgall said to a man of his community, "Go and see for yourself what is in that rush-bank over there." The man went and gave his kick (*lua*) to the bank, and saw an infant in the middle of it, and brought him back in his armpit. Afterward, Comgall asked him, "What did you find?" The man said, "I found a little infant." Comgall said, "What did you do to him?" And he said, "I gave my kick (*lua*) to him and brought him with me under my armpit." Then Comgall said, "His name shall be Molua son of Ocha," because *ocha* is used today where *ochsal* was used before.

Suddenly, when Molua was a student <note>original: "scoloc"</note>, Comgall went with him and the others to the church. It was revealed to Comgall that the entire group of them were walking **without heads upon them** <note>A common hagiographical motif suggesting spiritual blindness or that the monks were "dead to the world"</note>. Comgall then blessed their eyes, and they saw the same thing. They wondered greatly. "This is the reason for this," said Comgall, "that he is my **soul-friend** <note>original: "anmchara," a spiritual director or mentor</note>..."

<summary>This page provides background stories and etymologies for saints commemorated in early August, including the discovery of St. Stephen's relics and the legendary origin of St. Molua's name, involving a miraculous find in a rush-bank.</summary>
<keywords>Maccabees, St. Stephen, St. Molua, Comgall of Bangor, hagiography, etymology, Irish saints, martyrdom</keywords>

<lang>English, Latin, Irish</lang>
<page-num>181</page-num>
<header>AUGUST 14.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

### NOTES.

1. **The Maccabees**, that is, the seven sons with <note>original: *cum*</note> [their mother], etc.<sup>1</sup>
2. **Theodota**, that is, with her three sons, etc.<sup>2</sup>
   On this day <note>original: *In hoc die*</note>, etc.
3. **The metropolis of John**, that is, a name <note>original: *nomen*</note>, etc.
   **Stephen's noble body**, that is, here was discovered<sup>3</sup> the body of **Stephen**<sup>4</sup>, the first martyr of the New Testament, and so <note>original: *et sic*</note> [it was found], etc.

"**Blithe will he be**" <note>This refers to a specific line in the poetic calendar for the day</note>, etc. **Molua**, son of <term>Ocha</term> <note>original: *ochae*</note>, which means "armpit." He is from **Clonfertmulloe** <note>original: *Clúairferta Molua*</note>, from **Slieve Bloom** <note>original: *Slíab Bladma*</note>, and from **Druim Snechta** in **Farney** <note>original: *Fernmag*</note>, and in other places <note>original: *et in aliis locis*</note>. As for the name "Molua, son of Ocha," this is how he received it: **Comgall of Bangor** <note>original: *Bennchor*</note> once happened to be traveling with his household. It happened that they heard the cries of an infant in a clump of rushes. Or, Comgall, while walking <note>original: *Vel Comgall ambulans*</note>, etc. One of Comgall's monks gave a kick to the thicket of rushes and saw a baby in the middle of it; he then carried it back in his armpit. Comgall asked him, "What have you found?" He answered, "I have found a baby." "What did you do with it?" asked Comgall. "I gave it a kick," said the monk, "and I have brought it here in my armpit." "This shall be his name," said Comgall: "**My-kick** <note>The name Molua is treated here as a pun on the Irish *mo* (my) and *lua* (kick)</note>, son of **Armpit**," because he was found in the rushes, or because of the kick the monk gave to the thicket where he was. (**Mac Ochae** means "son of armpit," for among the ancients <note>original: *apud ueteres*</note> the armpit is called <term>ocha</term>.) Afterward, the child was fostered by Comgall.

"**Son of Ocha**," that is, "son of armpit." For this is the story: when Comgall of Bangor was traveling, he saw a group of angels descending toward a bank of rushes a short distance from the road. He said to one of his community, "Go and see what is in that bank of rushes." The man went and kicked the bank, saw a baby in the middle of it, and carried it back in his armpit. Then Comgall asked him, "What did you find?" The man said, "I found a little baby." Comgall asked, "What have you done to it?" He replied, "I gave it a kick, and I have brought it under my armpit," etc.

Now it happened that when Molua was a student, he and Comgall came with the others <note>original: *cum caeteris*</note> to the church. It was revealed to Comgall that everyone inside appeared to have no head. So Comgall blessed <note>original: *sained*</note> their eyes, and they saw similarly <note>original: *similiter*</note>. They marveled greatly. "This is why this is happening," said Comgall: "my soul-friend <note>original: *anam-chara*; a spiritual director or confessor</note> has died, and I am [without a head]..."

<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF AUGUST.]</header>

"...he died, and now I am without a head, and you are here also without a head; for a person without a <term>soul-friend</term> <note>original: *anmcharait*</note> is like a body without a head. What is your advice further?" "**Molua** said to him: 'Bring the Gospel of **Christ** to you and let someone hold it before you, and bow down to it until you find a soul-friend through it.' 'Go toward it yourself,' said **Comgall**, 'for you are the youngest'; and he went then and brought it. **Comgall** looked at him and said: 'Since it fell into your hand, it is you who shall be my soul-friend.' Thus it was that his own pupil became his soul-friend. And **Comgall’s** 'head' <note>his spiritual authority</note> was seen upon every person in the house, and it was seen similarly by others."

It was he (that is, **Molua**) who was the soul-friend to **David of St. Davids** <note>original: *Dabíd Cille Muine*</note>, to **Caemóg**, to **Maedhóc**, and to **Comgall**, as a certain person said:

> Molua was a soul-friend to **David**, across the slow-moving sea,
> and also to **Caemóg**, to **Maedhóc**, and to **Comgall**.

Moreover, it was this **Molua** who never killed a bird or any other animal. **Maelanfaidh** saw a bird mourning for him; and it was concerning him that **Míthiden**, the angel of **Saint Míte**, gave this testimony <note>original: *test*</note> when **Míte** was rebuking the angel for forgetting her food for three days (for her portion used to be brought to her from heaven every evening). The angel said:

> Men of heaven, men of earth—a mighty possession—
> it seemed to them that **Lughaidh’s** <note>Molua’s</note> death was like the Day of Judgment.
> No other saint has reached, or will reach, or shall ever come
> to have a greater honor with God.

<margin>Or:
No other saint has reached or will reach a path of such valor;
no other man of heaven will find a more joyful welcome.</margin>

5. **Oswald**, that is, **Flann Fína**, son of **Oswiu** <note>original: *Ossa*; Flann Fína was the Irish name for King Aldfrith of Northumbria</note>.

6. **Sixtus** <note>original: *Sistan*</note>, the Roman bishop, from Rome. **Sixtus** <note>original: *Xisdus*</note>, the bishop of Rome, suffered martyrdom in Rome under **Decius** at the Temple of Mars. A part of the temple fell and was shattered when **Sixtus**, along with two deacons, was beheaded by the sword. He was born in **Athens** and was well-educated—that is, Sixtus was first a philosopher and afterward a disciple of Christ, and he was Pope in Rome. Three hundred and ten others were martyred with him.
**Mochua**, that is, the son of **Lugadh**, who was previously called **Cronán**.

7. **The seven sleepers** <note>original: *morfeser*, literally 'the big seven'</note> in **Ephesus**, that is, in a cave near Ephesus. These were the seven brothers sleeping in Ephesus, and these are their names: **Maximianus**, **Malchus**, **Dionysius**, **Manianus**, **Johannes**, **Serapio**, and **Constantinus**. However, they also have other names: **Achelius**, **Diomedius**, **Eugenius**, **Stephanus**, **Probatus**, **Sambatus**, and **Cyricius**.
But the Emperor **Decius** ordered them to be tonsured—that is, to have a slave's tonsure <note>original: *berrad moghadh*</note> put on them—because of the lowliness of that appearance, so that they might suffer under that mark. He ordered them to go before him to **Ephesus** and remain there until he himself arrived after them, so that he might punish them there in the sight of their friends. <header>AUGUST 5-7.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

"...headless, and you, too, are headless, for a man without a <term>soul-friend</term> <note>original: anmcharait; a spiritual director or confessor</note> is like a body without a head.” 

“And what is your advice besides?” 

“Here is mine for you,” says **Molua**: “take **Christ’s** Gospel to you, and let someone hold it up before you, and kneel to it until you find a soul-friend through it.” 

“You go for it,” says **Comgall**, “for you are the youngest.” 

So he goes and fetches a Gospel. **Comgall** looked at him and said: “Since it happens to be in your hand, it is you who shall be my soul-friend.” 

Thus it was his own pupil <note>original: fosterling</note> who became his soul-friend; and **Comgall** saw a head <note>meaning a spiritual authority</note> on everyone inside, and they saw <note>original: similiter</note> similarly.

Now it is **Molua** who was the soul-friend to **David of St Davids** <note>original: Cell Muine</note>, and to **Cóemóc**, and to **Máedóc**, and to **Comgall**, as <note>original: ut quidam dixit</note> someone said:

> **Molua** was soul-friend to **David** over the slow . . . sea,
> and to **Cóemóc** and to **Máedóc** and to **Comgall**.

Now this is the same **Molua** who never killed a bird or any other living thing, and **Máel-anfaid** saw the bird mourning for him. Of him too, **Mithiden**, the angel of **Saint Ita** <note>original: my-Íta</note>, gave testimony when **Ita** was reproaching the angel for his forgetfulness for three days in not bringing her food; for her portion used to be brought to her from heaven every day at noon. So the angel said:

> The men of heaven, the men of earth—mighty is the gloom—
> it seemed to them that **Lugaid’s** <note>Molua’s formal name</note> death was Doomsday.
> Never came, never will come, never will reach heaven
> another saint whose honor is greater with **God**.

Or:

> Never came, never will come—a course of valor—
> another saint to whom the welcome of the men of heaven will be greater.

5. **Oswald** <note>original: Osuall</note>, that is, **Flann Fina** son of **Oswiu** <note>original: mac Ossa</note>.¹

6. **Sixtus**, a Roman bishop, that is, at Rome. **Sixtus**, etc.²
**Mochua**, that is, the son of **Lugaid**, who was first called **Cronán**.
"With my **Cua**," that is, **Mochua** son of **Lugaid**, abbot of **Clondalkin**, who was first called **Cronán**.³

7. Seven men in **Ephesus**, that is, in a cave near **Ephesus**, that is, the <note>original: septem fratres</note> seven brothers, etc.⁴

...the cave of Mount Caelion <note>original: spelonca montis Cellei</note>. Now **Decius** <note>the Roman Emperor</note> closed the cave, placing stones at its mouth. After a long time, a certain man living on the mountain named **Diabus** opened the mouth of the cave, wanting to use those stones for a wall around his cattle. Then one of those men <note>the sleepers</note> went out through the door of the cave to buy food for them, after they had risen from their sleep—as it seemed to them—and he then offered his money in the city. 

“Away, O man!” they said. “You have old money; it will not be accepted here.” 

“What is this?” he said. “Why do you call it old money?” 

“It was made in the time of **Decius**,” they said, “and that was one hundred and fifty-five years ago. Now there is a Christian king, **Constantine** son of **Helena**.” 

Then he realized what had happened to him, and he gave thanks to God and told his whole story. His companions were brought out of the cave by the <term>bishop</term> <note>original: espoc</note> of **Ephesus** at that time, who was called **Marinus**, and they told their whole story to the king, **Constantine**. Or, they came out in the time of **Theodosius** son of **Arcadius**. Thus the name of God was magnified through that miracle, and the resurrection <note>of the dead</note> was confirmed.

And after they had risen from their sleep—as it seemed to them—one of them went out through the door of the cave to buy food, and thereafter he produced his money in the city <note>original: *ciuitate*</note>. “Go away, man,” they said. “What you have is ancient money; it will not be accepted here.” “What is that?” he said. “What makes it ancient money?” “It was coined in the time of **Decius**,” they answered, “and that was one hundred and fifty-five years ago. <header>CALENDAR OF OENGUS</header>
<header>MONTH OF AUGUST</header>

**Fachtna** <note>His pedigree is in the Book of Leinster 351a.</note>, that is, from **Rosscarbery** <note>original: *Rus ailithiri*</note>. He was the abbot of the monastery of **Máel Anfaid**.

**of the hairy son** <note>original: *maic mongaig*</note>, that is, he had a great mane <note>original: *mong*</note> of hair on him when he was born. It is for that reason that everyone used to call him "the hairy son."

15. **the noble king of Clogher**, that is, the bishop of **Drumclogher**.
**Clogher** <note>original: *clochar*</note>, that is, a congregation; or "Clogher," that is, "stone of gold" <note>original: *cloch óir*</note>. This was a stone covered in gold that the pagans used to worship, and a demon used to speak out of it whose name was **Cerman Cestach**. That was the primary idol of the north. It is that short stone on your right hand as you enter the church of **Clogher**, and the marks of the gold and silver joints still remain in it, as we ourselves have seen <note>original: *ut uidimus ipsi*</note>.

**Man of two districts** <note>original: *Fer dá crích*</note>, that is, the abbot of **Dairinis**, or Bishop **Mac Cairthinn**.

->Aed was the man’s true name <note>the footnote says: "his deeds were good"</note>, the grandson of **Aithmet** of many deeds <note>the footnote says: "it was sweet"</note>,<-
->his name in the church of **Clogher** <note>perhaps "church" should be plural here</note> was Bishop **Mac Cairthinn**.<-
->**"Man of Two Districts"** was his name at first—I shall tell you his history—<-
->a true brother of victory and fame to **Máel Ruain**, his teacher.<-

He was the maternal uncle of **Máel Ruain**, the foster-father of **Oengus**. It is from him that **Máel Ruain** took the bell of **"Man of Two Districts"** which is now in **Tallaght**.

16. **the birth of Mary**; the falling asleep <note>original: *dormitatio*</note> of Mary. And **Máel Coisne** from **Kilmeelchon** <note>original: *Cill Maili coisne*</note> in **Uí Maine** in **Connacht** is on the same feast day as Mary, the mother of Jesus.

17. **Mammes**: At **Caesarea** in **Cappadocia**, under the Emperor **Aurelian**, **Mammes** suffered <note>original: *passus est*</note>. He suffered under **Alexander**, the governor for Emperor **Aurelian**. He used to tame wild beasts along with his shepherds and preach the word of God to them, and they would listen to him. He milked the wild beasts, and the Gospel was given to him. He suffered under Emperor **Aurelian** in the city of **Caesarea** in the province of **Cappadocia**. He was a boy of fifteen years when he suffered. Or **Mammes** was a saint in **Langres** <note>original: *Longanaib*</note> in **France**, and he was a noble martyr and confessor, as the inhabitants of that place affirm.

**He suffered** <note>original: *Ro cess*</note>, that is, he is a saint who is in **Langres** in **France**, and he was a martyr.

**Temnén**, that is, from **Linn Uachaille** on the bank of the **Cassán Linne** in the **Ards**.

**natural death** <note>original: *taimthiu*</note>, that is, a peaceful death without the violence of a persecutor <note>original: *sine uiolentia persecutoris*</note>.

18. **M'Ernóc**, that is, the son of **Creisine** from **Rathnew** in **Uí Garrchon** in the **Fortuatha** of **Leinster**, and from **Killidrinagh** in **Uí Drona**.

**to our wheat-harvest** <note>original: *diar tuirind*</note>, that is, to our wheat, because the saints are the wheat of God <note>original: *quia sancti triticum Dei sunt*</note>.

**Daig**, that is, **Daig** son of **Cairell**. This **Daig** was a smith, a craftsman, and a scribe. It was he who made three hundred bells, three hundred crosiers, and three hundred Gospel-books. He was the chief craftsman for **Ciarán** of **Seir** <note>original: *Ciaran Saigre*</note>. He was **Daig** son of **Cairell**, son of **Laisre**, son of **Dallán**, son of **Eogan**, son of **Niall of the Nine Hostages**. **Daig** son of **Cairell** from **Inishkeen** <note>original: *Inis cain Dega*</note> in **Muirthemne**.

The three chief craftsmen of Ireland were **Tassach** with **Patrick**, **Conláed** with **Brigid**, and **Daig** with **Ciarán**; and those three were bishops.

19. **Mochta**, bishop of **Louth**. **Leader** <note>original: *sithbe*</note>, that is, a long ridge of land. Likewise, **Mochta's** fame is always long-lasting.

**Fachtna**, that is, from **Rosscarbery** <note>original: *Ross Ailithiri*</note>, the abbot of **Máel Anfaid’s** monastery. 

**of the hairy son**, that is, he had a great mane of hair on him when he was born; because of this, everyone used to call him the "hairy son."

15. **famous king of Clogher**, that is, the bishop of **Drumclogher**.
**Clogher** <note>original: *Clochar*</note>, that is, an assembly; or **Clogher**, that is, **stone of gold** <note>original: *cloch óir*</note>, referring to a stone covered in gold which the pagans possessed and worshipped. A demon used to speak out of it whose name was **Cermand Cestach**, and it was the primary idol of the north. That is the short stone on your right hand as you enter the church of **Clogher**; the marks where the gold and silver joints were attached still remain in it, as we ourselves have seen <note>original: *ut uidimus ipsi*</note>.

**man of two districts**, that is, the abbot of **Dairinis**, or Bishop **Mac Cairthinn**.

->**Aed** is truly the man's name, grandson of **Aithmet**, with many deeds:<-
->his name at **Clogher** of the churches was afterwards Bishop **Mac Cairthinn**.<-
->**"Man of two districts"** was his name at first; I will tell you his history,<-
->a true brother in victory and fame to **Máel Ruain**, his teacher.<-

He was the maternal uncle of **Máel Ruain**, the tutor of **Oengus**, and it was from him that **Máel Ruain** brought the bell of **Fer dá chrích**, which is now in **Tallaght**.

16. **The nativity of Mary**:¹ her falling asleep <note>original: *dormitatio Marie*</note>. Also **Máel-coisne** of **Cell Máele-coisne** in **Húi Maini** in **Connaught** is celebrated on the same feast day as Mary, the Mother of Jesus.

17. **Mammes**, that is, at **Caesarea** <note>original: *apud Caesaream*</note> etc. Or **Mammes**, a saint who is in **Langres** in the land of the Franks <note>original: *Frankland*</note>, and noble <note>original: *et nobilis*</note> etc.

**he suffered**, that is, that saint is in **Langres** in the land of the Franks, and he was a martyr.

**of Temnén**, that is, from **Land Fuachail** on the bank of the **Cassan Line** in **Ard**; that is, from **Land Uachaille** on the bank of the **Cassan Linne**.

**natural death** <note>original: *taimthiu*</note>, that is, death came upon him without the violence of a persecutor <note>original: *sine violentia persecutoris*</note>.

18. **my Ernóc**, that is, the son of **Creisíne** from **Ráith Noe** in **Húi Garrchon** in the **Fortúatha** of **Leinster**, or from **Cell draignech** in **Húi Drona**; that is, from **Rath Noe** etc.

**to our wheat** <note>original: *to our tuirenn*</note>, that is, to our wheat, because the saints are considered God's wheat.²

**Daig**, that is, **Daig** son of **Cairell**. He was a smith, a skilled artisan, and a scribe. It was he who made 300 bells, 300 croziers, and 300 Gospel books; he was the chief artisan for **Ciarán of Saiger**. He was **Daig** son of **Cairell**, son of **Laisre**, son of **Dallán**, son of **Eogan**, son of **Niall of the Nine Hostages**. This **Daig** was from **Inis cáin Dega** in **Conaille Muirthemne**. There were three chief artisans of Ireland: **Tassach** with **Patrick**, **Conlaed** with **Brigit**, and **Daig** with **Ciarán**; and all three were bishops.

19. **Mochtae**, that is, the bishop of **Louth**. **A ridge** <note>original: *sithbe*</note>, that is, a long ridge of earth; just so is **Mochtae**, for his renown is always long-lasting.

Mochta's tooth—it is no empty fame—for three hundred years, a lasting duty <note>original: *buan a chís*</note>, no stray word passed over it upward, and no morsel of fat passed over it downward.
<margin>From the upper margin of the Book of Leinster, page 357.</margin>

### Regarding Mochta:

It was not a narrow life for Mochta of the fort of Louth <note>original: *Lughbaid liss*</note>:
three hundred priests and two hundred bishops were along with him.

Eighty psalm-singing noble clans were his household—vast journeys!—
without plowing, without reaping, without kiln-drying, without any labor except for study.
Though he was clever at handling cold stones, though he was skilled at wielding the ax,
though his chant was sweet with songs, I have heard it said that he who does not read is a boor.

Enán of Drumrat <note>original: *Dromma Raithi*</note> in western Meath. That is, Enán son of Ernín, son of Cáel, son of Áed, son of Art corp, son of Nia-corb. Drumrat is located in western Meath. 

20. **Dioscorus**, that is, he was a priest in the Thebaid <note>a region in ancient Egypt</note> who had a hundred monks.

**Pamphilus**, that is, a martyr and bishop, and many others with him. That is, a martyr and priest of Eusebius, the bishop of Caesarea; he suffered under the Emperor Diocletian. Dioscorus... and Bishop Pamphilus with his clergy.

21. **Vincent**, that is, a bishop, namely Unnic the Thatch-clad <note>original: *Tuignech*</note> of the Uí Dortain. Or perhaps it is Uncenti, that is, it might be Unnic in Tuighniath or Uncan of Tuighneáth.

**Senach**, that is, the abbot after Finnian. He was the foster-father of Failbe and the successor of Finnian. Bishop Senach was at Cluainíne in Feraítha, or at Cluain Fota Libráin. He was from Cluain Fota mac Fine in western Fertullagh; he was the first abbot after Finnian. Bishop Senach was from Cluain Fota mac Fine in Fertullagh, and he was the abbot of Clonard <note>original: *Cluana hRaird*</note>.

22. **Timothy** <note>original: *Tiamdai*</note>: Gregory says that this Timothy is a martyr who suffered in the time of the kings, and he is not the disciple of Paul the apostle.
**Emilianus**, that is, Emilianus suffered along with eight sons.

23. **Fortunatus**, that is, in Antioch.

**Eoghan of Ardstraw**, that is, Eoghan, son of Bishop Erc of Slane, son of Deg, son of Brancon, son of Armor, son of Caither, son of Imchad, son of Dubthach, son of Ross, and so forth. He was the son of Bishop Erc of Slane, as the experts say. Eoghan, bishop of Ardstraw.

24. **Old Patrick** <note>original: *Senpatraic*</note>, that is, Old Patrick is at Rossdela in Mag Lacha. Or, Old Patrick is in Glastonbury of the Gaels <note>original: *nGlostimber na nGoedel*</note>; that is a city in the south of England <note>original: *Saxan*</note> where the Irish <note>original: *Scoti*</note> used to live. That is, he is from Rossdela in Meath—specifically in Mag Lacha. Or, what is more true: his city is in the southwest of England, and the Irish lived there in pilgrimage. Old Patrick of Rossdela in Mag Lacha; but it is more likely that Old Patrick is in Glastonbury of the Gaels in the south of England. For the Irish formerly lived there in pilgrimage. Patrick, abbot and bishop of Rossdela. Patrick, the doorkeeper and abbot of Armagh.

25. **Bartholomew**. Bartholomew went into India and suffered there under Astriges, their king. He was beheaded with a sword, or buried alive, after his skin was stripped from his entire body beforehand; and so he ended his life.

Mochta's tooth—his fame is no empty thing—his tribute lasted three hundred years; not a word of error ever passed up over it, and not a single bit of savory food <note>original: "relish"</note> ever passed down over it.
It was not a life of stinginess for Mochta of the monastic enclosure <note>original: "garth"</note> of Louth: three hundred priests and two hundred bishops were with him.
Eighty psalm-singing nobles were his household—an immense procession—living without plowing, or reaping, or kiln-drying, and without any work except for study. 
Though he may be clever at carving cold stones, and though he may be skilled at wielding an axe, and though his chanting of songs is sweet, I have heard it said that he who does not study is a fool <note>original: "dull"</note>.

Enán of **Drumrat** <note>original: *Druim ráthe*</note>, in the west of Meath; that is, Enán the son of Ernín, son of Cáel, son of Aed, son of Art Corp, son of Nia Corb. Drumrat is in the west of Meath.

20. **Dioscorus**, that is, a priest in the Thebaid <note>a region in Egypt</note>, etc. 
**Pamphilus**, that is, a martyr and bishop, along with many others: he was a martyr and a priest of Eusebius, the bishop of Caesarea, and he suffered under the Emperor Diocletian.

21. Regarding **Vincent**, that is, a bishop, namely Unnic the Thatch-clad <note>original: *Tuignech*</note> in the territory of the Uí Dortain, who was a bishop. Or perhaps **Uncenti** is the correct reading, so that he may be Unnic in Tugniath, or Uncan Tuigneth.
**Senach**, that is, the abbot after Finnian; he was the foster-father of Failbe and a successor of Finnian. Bishop Senach is in Cluain Fine in the territory of the Fir Itha; or he is from Clonfad of Librán <note>original: *Clúain fota Libran*</note>, that is, from Clonfad of the sons of Fine <note>original: *Clúain fota macc Fin[e]*</note> in the west of Fir Tulach. He was the first abbot after Finnian and was also the abbot of Clonard.

22. Regarding **Timothy**. Gregory <note>likely Pope Gregory the Great</note> says that this Timothy was a martyr who suffered in the time of the Kings, and he was not the disciple of Paul the Apostle.
Regarding **Emilianus**, etc.

23. Regarding **Fortunatus**, that is, in Antioch.
Regarding **Eogan of Ardstraw** <note>original: *Ard sratha*</note>, that is, Eogan the son of Bishop Erc of Slane, son of Dega, son of Brancu, son of Armuir, son of Caither, son of Imchad, son of Dubtaige, son of Ross, etc.

24. **Patrick Senior** <note>also known as Old Patrick or Sen-Phátraic</note>, that is, Patrick Senior is at Rossdalla in Magheragal <note>original: *Ross dela in Mag locha*</note>. Or, Patrick Senior is in Glastonbury of the Gaels, which is a monastery in the south of England where the Irish <note>original: *Scotti*</note> used to live. Or, what is more likely true <note>original: *Vel quod uerius est*</note>, his convent and the Irish <note>original: *et Scotti*</note> are in the southwest of England. 
Regarding Patricius, the abbot and bishop of Rossdalla; and regarding Patricius, the doorkeeper and abbot of Armagh.

25. **Bartholomew** traveled into India, etc.; that is, he was beheaded with a sword, or he was buried alive, etc.

26. He was buried alive <note>original Latin: *uiuus sepultus est*</note> [in the city called Hebron <note>original: *Cariatharbe*</note>] after his whole skin was scraped from his entire body.

27. **Rufus**, that is, he suffered in the city of Capua.

28. **Cyriacus**, that is, a martyr, with his clergy, numbering 904.
The illustrious one from Africa, that is, **Augustine**. It may be that this is Augustine, the wisest author of books <note>original: *sapientissimus librorum*</note>. That is, Augustine, the wisest man of the Africans.

29. Relate the suffering of **John the Baptist**.
He is called this because he first performed baptism, or because he baptized Christ. His actual beheading was not on this day, but rather this is the second discovery of his body. He suffered in the spring before Easter... and he was buried in the city of Sebaste... and in the following Easter after the passion of Christ.

The beheading of beloved John, that is, in great Machaerus <note>a fortress near the Dead Sea</note>. Sebaste is where it is written his grave was—the name of the town where he was buried.
Whether he was struck, or slain, or axed—mighty is the reason—his equal, that pleasant stone <note>referring to a precious person</note>, shall not be on the brink of Ireland <note>original: *Banba*</note> until the Judgement.
The women of the world, except for a few of them, in the blazing fire of Judgment, it is not proper to speak with them after the murder of John.

It is in vengeance for the killing of John the Baptist, moreover, that the **Broom from Fanad** <note>original: *scuab a Fanait*, a legendary plague or "scourge" prophesied to cleanse Ireland</note> comes to thoroughly clean Ireland toward the end of the world, as Ailerán the Wise and Colum Cille prophesied. That is, specifically on the third day the Broom from Fanad shall come, as Colum Cille said: "Like the madness of two horses in a carriage, such will be the diligence with which it shall cleanse Ireland."

Ailerán said of the Broom: "There shall be two ale-houses in a single court, side by side; the man who goes from one house into the other will find no one alive before him in the house he enters, and he shall not find anyone alive afterward in the house he left." Such will be the swiftness with which the Broom from Fanad shall travel.

Riagail said: "For a year and three days and three nights this plague shall be in Ireland. When a boat is visible on Loch Rugraide from the door of the refectory, it is then that the Broom from Fanad comes."

The Tuesday of spring after Easter, moreover, is the day of the week on which the Broom shall come in vengeance for the suffering of John, as Moling said:
"On the feast of John the scourge <note>original: *in tres*</note> shall come, which shall search Ireland from the southwest; a fierce dragon that will burn everyone it can reach, without communion, without the sacrifice <note>the Eucharist</note>, etc."

30. **Agatha**, that is, a virgin. **Agappa**, that is, a virgin who suffered in Sicily. She endured many torments under the Emperor Decius or the consul Quintilianus, specifically in the city of Catania.
The Passion of **Agapé**, **Chionia**, and **Irene** <note>original: *Agapae et Chionae et h-Erennae*</note>.

31. **Aidan** of Kilmore <note>original: *Cill mór*</note> in Mennut Tire in Airgialla. Or in the northeast of the Saxons is **Lindisfarne** <note>original: *Inis Medcoit*</note>, and Aidan is there.
Aidan, Bishop of Lindisfarne. That is, at Scattery Island <note>original: *Inis Cathaig*</note> or in the northwest of the Little Saxons is Lindisfarne, and Aidan is there.

**Paulinus**, that is, the bishop of the city of Nola in Italy.
"Of the widows," that is, because a widow delivered him up in place of her son into the service of Geiseric, King of the Vandals <note>a Germanic tribe in Africa</note>.

AUGUST 28–31.

26. At Rome... of the holy martyrs, Irenaeus and Abundius, who under the Emperor Decius... earned the crown [of martyrdom], *Roman Martyrology* <note>original Latin: *Romae...sanctorum martyrum, Irenaei et Abundii, qui Decio imperatore...coronam promeruerunt, Mart. Rom.*</note>.

27. **Of Rufus**, that is, he suffered in the city of Capua.¹

28. **Cyriacus**, that is, a martyr; **with his train**, that is, 903 followers.
    The famous one out of **Africa**, that is, **Augustine**. This may be Augustine, the *wisest author of books* <note>original Latin: *sapientissimus librorum*</note>,² meaning the wisest of the Africans.

29. **Declare the passion of John the Baptist**.
    *It is said for this reason* <note>original Latin: *ideo dicitur*</note>, etc.
    The beheading of beloved John took place in great Machaerus <note>original: *Macerunda*, a fortress near the Dead Sea</note>,³
    Sebaste—where the account is written—is the name of the village where he was buried.
    Whether he was struck, or slain, or axed—the cause was mighty—his equal, that pleasant jewel, will never again be on Ireland's <note>original: *Banba's*</note> shore.
    The women of the world, except for a few of them, shall burn in the fires of Judgment <note>original: *Doom*</note>; it is not fitting to speak with them after the murder of John.
    In vengeance for the killing of John, the **Broom from Fanad** <note>original: *Besom out of Fanait*</note>⁴ comes to purge Ireland at the end of the world, as Aileran the Wise foretold, and Colum Cille. That is, at exactly the third hour <note>original: *terce*</note> will come the Broom from Fanad, *as Colum Cille said* <note>original Latin: *ut dixit Colum cille*</note>: "Like the grazing of two horses in a single yoke will be the diligence with which it will cleanse Ireland <note>original: *Erin*</note>."
    Of the Broom, Aileran said: "Two alehouses shall be side by side in one yard. He who goes out of one house into the other will find no one alive before him in the house he enters, and no one alive in the house from which he came. Such will be the swiftness with which the Broom shall go out of Fanad."
    Riagail said: "This plague will be in Ireland for a year, three days, and three nights. When a boat on Dundrum Bay <note>original: *Loch Rudraigi*</note> can be clearly seen from the door of the monastery dining hall <note>original: *refectory*</note>, then comes the Broom from Fanad."
    A Tuesday in spring is the day of the week on which the Broom will come in vengeance for John's suffering <note>original: *passion*</note>, as Moling said:
    On John's festival the onslaught will come, which will search Ireland from the southeast,
    a fierce dragon that will burn everyone it can, without communion, without sacrifice, etc.⁵

30. **Agatha**, that is, a virgin. **Agapa**, that is, a virgin, etc.

31. **Aedán**, from the Great Church <note>original: *Cell Mór*</note> in the district of Mennat Tíre in Oriel <note>original: *Airgéill*</note>. Or in the northeast of England is Lindisfarne <note>original: *Inis Medcóit*</note>, and Aedán was there; or he is of Scattery Island <note>original: *Inis Cathaig*</note>; or in the northwest of "Little England" <note>likely referring to a different geographic tradition</note> is Lindisfarne, and Aedán was there.
    **Paulinus**, that is, the bishop of Nola, a town in Italy.
    **Of the widow**, that is, *because* <note>original Latin: *quia*</note>, etc.

### THE MONTH OF SEPTEMBER.

**F. September 1 (The Calends of September)**
On the calends <note>The first day of the month</note> of September,
Caecilia with righteousness—
four hundred virgins,
and twenty-three thousand martyrs.

**G. September 2 (The 4th Nones of September)**
Praise Theodota
along with Senán; they are noble.
With fair Christ is their reward;
with their following, they are beloved.

**A. September 3 (The 3rd Nones of September)**
Colmán of Druimm Ferta,
Longarad, a delightful sun,
and Mac Nisse with thousands,
from great Connor <note>original: *Conderi*, modern: Connor, County Antrim</note>.

**B. September 4 (The day before the Nones of September)**
In the great, sinless Kingdom,
where little ones are blooming,
children play joyfully
around Ultan of Ardbraccan <note>original: *Ard Breccáin*, County Meath. Saint Ultan was famous for his care of orphans, feeding them with cow's milk using primitive bottles</note>.

**C. September 5 (The Nones of September)**
With Breccbúaid, who has been
called out of Ireland <note>original: *Hére*</note>,
you shall count holy Eolang of Aghaboe <note>original: *Ached Bó*, County Laois</note>,
a beautiful pillar, a triumph of piety.

---

### SEPTEMBER.

1. On the calends of September, Caecilia with righteousness, four virginal hundreds, and twenty-three thousands.

2. Praise Theodota along with Senán; they are noble. With fair Christ is their reward; with their train, they are dear.

3. Colmán of Druimm Ferta, Longarad, a delightful sun, and Mac Nisse with thousands, from great Connor.

4. In the great, sinless Kingdom, where little ones are blooming, children play greatly around Ultan of Ardbraccan.

5. With Breccbúaid, who has been called out of Ireland, you shall reckon holy Eolang of Aghaboe, a beauteous pillar, a triumph of piety.

---

<header>SEPTEMBER 6–11. | MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS</header>

**D. September 6 (The 8th Ides of September)**
With Mac Cuilinn <note>original: *Macc cuilinn*</note> of Lusk <note>original: *Luscae*</note>,
you share <note>original: *adrannai*; possibly "apportion"</note> a fair couple:
here we have the feast of Scíath,
and that of Columb of bright Ros Glandae.

**E. September 7 (The 7th Ides of September)**
The pure suffering of Sinotus,
whose tracks <note>original: *slechtae*</note> are shining;
the host of Anastasius who were slain,
along with the multitude of their miracles.

**F. September 8 (The 6th Ides of September)**
You shall commemorate Mary—
you are not dulled <note>original: *marbdae*, literally "deadened"</note> by a meager meal <note>original: *tercphit*</note>—
along with Timothy after the world’s ways,
and three hundred martyrs.

**G. September 9 (The 5th Ides of September)**
Great is the festival that fills countries,
that shakes swift ships:
the festival of the Carpenter’s son <note>original: *Maicc in tsáir*; Saint Ciarán, whose father was a chariot-maker</note>, greater than kings,
the beautiful feast of Ciarán of Clonmacnoise <note>original: *Clúain*</note>.

**A. September 10 (The 4th Ides of September)**
A pillar <note>original: *Clí*; literally a house-post or king-post, used figuratively for a support or leader</note> of pure red gold;
he came over the swelling sea with the Law—
a sage for whom Ireland is weary <note>original: *inmalli*</note>—
Finnian <note>original: *Findbarr*</note> of Movilla <note>original: *Mag Bili*</note>.

**B. September 11 (The 3rd Ides of September)**
The passion of Protus and Hyacinthus;
it was with great <note>original: *imbud*; abundance</note> sorrow.
Sillán, the "psalm of every sick man,"
is sung in fair Imlech Cassáin <note>original: *Imbliuch*</note>.

***

6. With Mac Cuilinn of Lusk, you share a fair couple: here we have the feast of Scíath, and that of Columb of bright Ros Glandae.

7. The pure suffering of Sinotus, whose tracks are shining; the host of Anastasius who were slain, with the multitude of their miracles.

8. You shall commemorate Mary; you are not deadened on a scanty meal; with Timothy after the world’s ways, and three hundred martyrs.

9. Great is the festival that fills countries and shakes swift ships: the festival of the Carpenter’s son, surpassing kings, the fair feast of Ciarán of Clonmacnoise.

10. A pillar of pure red gold who came over the swelling sea with the Law; a sage for whom Ireland is weary: Finnian of Movilla.

11. The passion of Protus and Hyacinthus; it was with an abundance of sorrow. Sillán, the "psalm of every sick man," is sung in fair Imlech Cassáin.

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS — SEPTEMBER</header>

**C. September 12 (The day before the Ides of September)**
Celebrate the feast of Ailbe <note>original: *Ailbi*; Saint Ailbe of Emly, a major early Irish saint</note>
along with the radiant and buoyant Fled <note>original: *Fleid*</note>;
it is also the feast of the beautiful Laissrén <note>original: *Laissrén*</note>
from the crowded island of Devenish <note>original: *Daminis*</note>.

**D. September 13 (The Ides of September)**
Declare twenty-two
martyrs of great holiness,
together with the champion of battle,
Dagán <note>original: *Dagán*</note> of Inis Deimle <note>original: *Indber Dóile*</note>.

**E. September 14 (The 18th day before the Kalends of October)**
The feast of Coemán the Speckled <note>original: *Chóemáin Bricc*</note> springs toward you,
along with a pair of noble scholars <note>original: *mbolmair*; possibly meaning "learned" or "prolific"</note>;
the holy passion of the great Cyprian <note>original: *Cipriáin*</note>,
with the fair suffering of Cornelius <note>original: *Cornail*</note>.

**F. September 15 (The 17th day before the Kalends of October)**
At the dedication of the church <note>original: *baslicc*; from the Latin *basilica*</note>
of Mary—a sturdy fortress—
Cyrinus <note>original: *Cirinus*</note>, without vanity,
joined a great host in martyrdom.

**G. September 16 (The 16th day before the Kalends of October)**
A great trio that is not humble <note>original: *nád donae*</note>:
my Ninn <note>original: *mo Ninn*</note>, the praise of every voice;
on Iona <note>original: *Hí*</note>, the happy Laissrén <note>original: *Laissrén*</note>,
along with the great Laissrén of Men <note>original: *Mena*</note>.

**A. September 17 (The 15th day before the Kalends of October)**
Euphemia <note>original: *Eufemia*</note> without blemish—
recall her passion at the end of a year;
you should count Broccán of Ross Tuirc <note>original: *Broccán Roiss Tuirc*</note>
at the excellent feast of Ríaguil <note>original: *Ríaglae*</note>.

<header>SEPTEMBER 18–22.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

### B. September 18 <note>original: *xiv. cal. Octobris*; the 14th day before the Kalends of October</note>
They sped into heaven <note>original: *ir-riched*</note>,
seven hundred blooming soldiers,
at the fair, faultless birth <note>original: *cen dígnae*; literally "without reproach"</note>,
of Énán of Druimm Ráthe <note>original: *Énán Dromma Ráthe*; Saint Énán of Drumraney, County Westmeath</note>.

### C. September 19 <note>original: *xiii. cal. Octobris*; the 13th day before the Kalends of October</note>
He sped with a famous multitude
to Christ, a lovable reconciliation <note>original: *cóemdae taithlech*; "taithlech" can mean satisfaction, peace, or reconciliation</note>—
with the host of preeminent kings <note>original: *ríġ remain*</note>,
Januarius, a dear commemoration! <note>original: *Énair, inmain aithmet*; Saint Januarius, Bishop of Benevento, martyred in 305 AD</note>

### D. September 20 <note>original: *xii. cal. Octobris*; the 12th day before the Kalends of October</note>
Let us beseech the virgins <note>original: *Attecham na hóga*</note>,
may they visit our assemblies! <note>original: *doairset ar ndála*</note>
May the queen Daroma <note>original: *rígain Daroma*</note>
with her host protect us!

### E. September 21 <note>original: *xi. cal. Octobris*; the 11th day before the Kalends of October</note>
May the champion of many hosts protect us <note>original: *Snaidsiunn in sab slúagach*</note>
into the high, sparkling station <note>original: *i sossad nárð nóiblech*</note>,
the bright sun with beauty:
Matthew, the strong, shining rampart! <note>original: *Mathae múr trén tóidlech*; St. Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist</note>

### F. September 22 <note>original: *x. cal. Octobris*; the 10th day before the Kalends of October</note>
Pantaleo <note>St. Pantaleon</note> and Mauricius <note>original: *Muric*; St. Maurice, leader of the Theban Legion</note>—
their great hosts, what are they?
Six hundred—a fair army of warriors—
and twelve thousand <note>referring to the traditional number of martyrs in the Theban Legion</note>.

***

18. **They sped into heaven:** <note>original: *Rathatar ir-riched*</note> Variants: *Rothatur* (B), *rethatar* (E), *Rathutar* (LB). Heaven: *ir-richeg* (LB), *hi rigtigh* (E).
**Seven hundred:** <note>original: *secht cét*</note> Variants: *secet* (R¹), *uii. cet* (L, F, B).
**Soldiers:** <note>original: *míled*</note> Variant: *mile* (L).
**Druimm Ráthe:** <note>original: *Dromma Ráthe*</note> Variants: *Raithe* (R¹, B), *Rathne* (F), *Raithne* (LB).

19. **Reconciliation:** <note>original: *taithlech*</note> Gloss: "making peace" (F).
**Preeminent kings:** <note>original: *ríġ remain*</note> Variants: *rig ran remain* (R¹, F, L, H).
**Januarius:** <note>original: *Énair*</note> Variant: *Enain* (L).

20. **Let us beseech:** <note>original: *Attecham*</note> Variants: *Atneochain* (R¹), *Ateocham* (L, LB).
**Virgins:** <note>original: *hóga*</note> Variants: *hogha* (F, L), *huaga* (R¹, LB).

21. **May he protect us:** <note>original: *Snaidsiunn*</note> Variants: *Snaidsiund* (L), *Snaidsium* (LB, F).

**Beauty:** <note>original: *lígdath*</note> Variants: *ligdaid* (R¹), *ligach* (F).
**Shining:** <note>original: *tóidlech*</note> Variant: *taidlech* (R¹).

22. **What are they?:** <note>original: *cat-éat*</note> Variants: *cateot* (R¹), *cadéat* (F, L).
**Six hundred:** <note>original: *sé cét*</note> Variants: *ocht cet* [800] (L, F), *uii. cet* [700] (B), *.c.viii.* [108] (LB).
**Warriors:** <note>original: *óac*</note> Variants: *ooc* (R¹, LB), *oacc* (F).
**Twelve:** <note>original: *díb ... déac*</note> Variant: *for* (LB, F).

<meta>This page continues the calendar of saints for late September from the Martyrology of Oengus. It moves from September 23 to September 27, featuring prominent figures such as Adamnán of Iona and Saint Finbarr of Cork.</meta>

<page-num>196</page-num>
<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF SEPTEMBER.]</header>

### G. September 23 <note>original: *ix. cal. Octobris*; the 9th day before the Kalends of October</note>
To Adamnán of Iona <note>original: *Adamnán Íae*; the 7th-century Abbot of Iona and biographer of St. Columba</note>,
whose following is radiant;
noble Jesus has granted
the lasting liberation of the women of the Gaels <note>original: *sóerad mbúan mbannGóidel*; this refers to the *Cáin Adomnáin* (Law of Adamnán) of 697 AD, which protected women, children, and clerics from violence and military service.</note>.

### A. September 24 <note>original: *viii. cal. Octobris*; the 8th day before the Kalends of October</note>
The conception of noble John the Baptist,
whose story is greater than can be told:
except for Jesus, he is the most wondrous 
of all men ever born.

### B. September 25 <note>original: *vii. cal. Octobris*; the 7th day before the Kalends of October</note>
With the followers of Eusebius <note>original: *cléir Eusebi*; likely referring to Pope Eusebius</note>,
who freed everyone from excessive banquets;
along with the festival of that lovable man,
the feast of Barre of Cork <note>original: *Barri ó Chorcaig*; Saint Finbarr, the patron saint and founder of the city of Cork.</note>.

### C. September 26 <note>original: *vi. cal. Octobris*; the 6th day before the Kalends of October</note>
Colmán of Lynally <note>original: *Colmán ó Laind Elo*; Saint Colmán Elo, who founded the monastery at Lynally, County Offaly</note>,
with his perfection in high studies,
so that he is—hear the splendid cry!—
the great "John" among the sons of Ireland <note>original: *Iohain már macc nÉrenn*; Colmán was so highly regarded for his holiness and scholarship that he was compared to John the Baptist.</note>.

### D. September 27 <note>original: *v. cal. Octobris*; the 5th day before the Kalends of October</note>
Our two heart-champions <note>original: *ndí géraít chridi*</note>,
whose cross was not distasteful to them;
may Cosmas and Damianus <note>original: *Cosmas, Damíanus*; twin brothers and physicians martyred under Diocletian</note>
guide us to our eternal home! <note>original: *diar ndúilius*; literally "to our element" or "to our property," referring to the heavenly inheritance.</note>

***

### Textual Variants and Manuscript Notes
<note>These notes record variations in spelling and phrasing across different medieval manuscripts, such as those labeled R1, L, LB, and F.</note>

1. **Adamnán of Iona:** Spelled *adomnan ia* in manuscript R1; *adamnan iae* in L; *adomnan iae* in LB; *adamhnan ia* in F.
2. **Has granted:** *ro fhír* in L; *ro hír* in LB and F; *roir* in R1.
3. **Gaels:** *goidel* in R1; *goeidel* in L; *ngoidhel* in F; *ngoedel* in LB.
4. **Baptist:** As spelled in F, R1, and L; *baubtaist* in B; *bauptaist* in LB.
5. **Except:** *ach* in L; *acht* in F, R1, and LB.
6. **Of men:** *do dáinib* in L; *do doinib* in B; *do dhoinib* in F; *de doinib* in R1.
7. **Is:** *as* in R1, L, and F; *is* in LB.
8. **Wondrous:** As spelled in R1; *amra* in L; *amru* in LB and F.
9. **Born:** *ni* in R1; *ro* in F, L, and LB.
10. **Eusebius:** *iosebi* in R1; *eusebii* in L and LB; *iosebii* in F.
11. **Freed:** *særas* in LB; *soerais* in B, R1, and F; *særais* in L.
12. **Every:** *gach* in F; *cach* in L; *cech* in R1 and LB.
13. **Festival:** "To Christ" (*do crist*) in R1 and F; "with the festival" (*la líth*) in L and LB.
14. **The:** *in* in LB; *ind* in R1, F, and L.
15. **Barre:** *barre* in R1; *barri* in L; *bairri* in B; *bairre* in LB and F.
16. **Laind Elo:** *alo* in R1; *ela* in L and LB; *hela* in F.
17. **Perfection:** *huaigi* in R1 and LB; *hoghe* in L; *hoághe* in F.
18. **So that he is:** *comba* in R1; *comad* in L; *conid* in LB; *conidhe* in F.
19. **Cry:** *hualland* in F; *húalann* in LB; *núallan* in R1 and L.
20. **John:** As spelled in R1; *eoin* in B and L; *ioin* in LB; *eohain* in F.
21. **Heart-champions:** *Ardiargeraít* (with a flat stroke over "iar") in L; *Arndigeraít* in B, F, and R1; *Ard igeraít* in LB.
22. **Heart:** *craide* in L; *craidhe* in F, R1, and LB; *cride* in B.
23. **Was not:** *nibu* in L; *nirbo* in LB; *nirbu* in B and F.
24. **Distasteful:** *airlius* in R1, F, L, and LB; *ceannais* in E.

<meta>This page concludes the month of September in the Martyrology of Oengus, focusing on the final three days of the month (September 28–30). It follows the previous entries for late September saints such as Adamnán and Finbarr.</meta>

<lang>Irish</lang>
<page-num>197</page-num>
<header>SEPTEMBER 28–30. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

### E. September 28 <note>original: *iv. cal. Octobris*; the 4th day before the Kalends of October</note>
The two bright Finnians <note>original: *Dá Findio geldaí*; likely referring to St. Finnian of Movilla and St. Finnian of Clonard</note>
are to be invoked for every aid;
the great company <note>original: *clíar*; a clergy or train of followers</note> of humble Marcellus;
with the festival of infirm Junillus.

### F. September 29 <note>original: *iii. cal. Octobris*; the 3rd day before the Kalends of October</note>
At the battle against the many-encountered dragon <note>original: *draic ndálach*; the "multitudinous" or "fateful" dragon</note>
by Michael the strong and victorious,
the white-sided, host-leading soldier
will strike down the wrathful Antichrist. <note>This refers to the feast of Michaelmas and the traditional role of the Archangel Michael in defeating the dragon/Satan and his prophesied role in the end times.</note>

### G. September 30 <note>original: *Pridie cal. Octobris*; the day before the Kalends of October</note>
After the swarms of September <note>original: *Septimbir iar saithib*; referring to the many saints' festivals throughout the month</note>
comes the sound, eloquent sage,
fair Jerome of Bethlehem <note>original: *Ciríne bán Bethil*; St. Jerome, the translator of the Bible (the Vulgate)</note>,
whom our sisters used to visit. <note>original: *atsaigtis ar sethir*; Jerome was famous for his spiritual guidance and correspondence with a circle of noble Christian women in Rome and later in Bethlehem.</note>
