<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>
<header>THE MONTH OF SEPTEMBER.</header>

### NOTES.

1. **Cecilia**, that is, a virgin and martyr. <note>original: *R¹*</note>. Also, four thousand, four hundred and twenty [others]. And **Jesus son of Nun** <note>original: *ihs. mac aue nó Iesu mac Nuin*; the biblical Joshua, successor to Moses</note>. <note>original: *F*</note>.

2. With **Senan**, that is, from Lathrach Bríuin <note>modern Laraghbryan, County Kildare</note> in the territory of the **Uí Faeláin**. <note>original: *R¹, L*</note>.

3. **Colman of Druim Ferta**, that is, Colman from Cluain Ferta Mongáin in the territory of the **Uí Faeláin**, and Mongán in the territory of the **Uí Failge**. **Druim Ferta** <note>literally "Ridge of Miracles"</note> is a hill near the church where many miracles used to be performed. <margin>Druim Ferta: a hill near the city; there Saint Colman performed many wonders. <note>original: *L*</note></margin> **Colman**, that is, from Cluain [Ferta] Mongáin in Uí Failge. Druim Ferta is a hill near the city, and Colman performed miracles there. <note>original: *R¹*</note>. The rest of Colman with all the fathers. He made wine three times from spring water: the first time for **Colum Cille** <note>St. Columba</note>; the second time for **Fechín of Fore** <note>St. Fechín of Fabar</note> when he gave him his eyes; and the third time for **Ruadán of Lorrha**. That well is in the darkness behind Ruadán’s stone to the east in his cemetery, and every person into whom the water of that cemetery enters, their soul is not punished. <note>original: *LL*</note>.

**Longarad of the White Foot** <note>original: *Longarad Coisfind*</note> and so on. In Mag Tuathat in the north of **Ossory**, specifically in the territory of the **Uí Forchelláin**; that is, in Mag Garad, specifically in Dísert Garad and in Cell Gapra on Slieve Margy in the fortress of Longarad. <note>original: *R²*</note>.
**White-foot**, that is, very great white hair grew through his feet, or his feet were very white. He was a master of learning, of legal judgment, of history, and of poetry. **Colum Cille** once visited him, and Longarad hid his books from him. Colum Cille left a curse upon his books, saying: "May that which you are being ungenerous with be of no use to anyone after you." And that was fulfilled, for the books still exist, but no man can read them. <note>original: *R²*</note>.
When **Lon** <note>Longarad</note> died, the book-satchels that were in the cell where **Colum Cille** was staying all fell down. Everyone was silenced by the noise of the falling books. Then Colum Cille said: "Longarad," said he, "the master of every art in Ossory, has just died." "It will be a long time before that is proven," said Baithíne. "You are doubting my successor," said Colum Cille. Then Colum Cille composed this verse:
> Lon of Cell Garad is dead; great is the misfortune.
> It is the loss of learning and schools to Ireland across her borders. <note>original: *R²*</note>.

**Mac Nissi**, that is, **Cnes** of the Dál Cethirn was his mother (the daughter of Conchaid), and from her he was named Mac Nissi, meaning "Son of Cnes." Or **Mac Cneissi**, that is, "Son of [Patrick's] skin," because he was Patrick’s skin <note>original: *cnis Patraic hé*; likely meaning he was Patrick's foster-child or intimate companion</note>. <note>original: *R¹*</note>. **Mac Cniss** of Patrick, because he used to sleep with him. <note>original: *R¹*</note>. For he was fostered by Patrick and slept with him. His true name was **Caemán Brec** <note>Caemán the Speckled</note>. <note>original: *F*</note>. **Fobrec** was his mother's name. His own first name was **Oengus**. <note>original: *L*</note>.
**Condeire** <note>modern Connor, County Antrim</note>, that is, "Oak-wood of the hounds/wolves," for it was a wood where packs [of wolves] used to be; that is, there was an oak-wood there previously, and wolves lived in it. <note>original: *F*</note>.

4. **Ultan**, as if *altan* <note>meaning "razor"</note>, because of his sharpness and his keenness in wonders and miracles.

<header>SEPTEMBER 1-4.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

### NOTES.

1. **Caecilia** and others; and **Joshua son of Naue**, also known as **Joshua son of Nun** <note>Naue is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Nun</note>.

2. *With Senán*,¹ that is, from Lathrach Briuin in the territory of the **Uí Faeláin** <note>modern Laraghbryan, County Kildare</note>; specifically, with Senán in Lathrach Briuin in the territory of the Uí Faeláin.

3. **Colmán of Druim Ferta**, that is, Colmán from Clúain Ferta Mongáin in the territory of the **Uí Failge** <note>modern Offaly</note>. Mongán was in Uí Failge, and **Druim Ferta** <note>literally "Ridge of Miracles"</note> is a hill near the church—a place where many miracles used to be performed by Colmán. "Of Druim Ferta" means "of the hill" <note>original: *collis*</note>, and so on. Colmán, etc.
**The rest of Colmán with all the fathers** <note>original: *Quies Colmáin cum omnibus patribus*</note>, who three times turned well-water into wine: the first time for **Colum Cille** <note>St. Columba</note>; the second time for **Féchín of Fore**, when Colmán gave his own eyes to him; and the third time for **Rúadán of Lorrha**. That well is in the darkness behind Rúadán's flagstone to the east in his graveyard. It is said that anyone who is touched by the water in that graveyard will not have their soul punished.
**Lon-garad "Whiteleg"** and others. He was in Mag Túathait in the northern part of **Ossory**, specifically in the territory of the **Uí Forcelláin** at Mag Garad—precisely in Díserd Garad—and in Cell Gabra in Slíab Mairgi <note>Slievemargy</note> at Les Longarad.
*Whiteleg*, meaning he had great bright hair covering his legs, or perhaps his legs were simply brilliant white. He was a master of academic study, law, history, and poetry. **Colum Cille** once came to visit him as a guest, but Lon-garad hid his books from him. In response, Colum Cille left a curse on the books, saying: "May that which you show such inhospitality toward be of no profit to anyone after you!" This has been fulfilled, for the books still exist today, yet no one is able to study or understand them.
When Lon-garad died, the book-satchels hanging in the cell where Colum Cille was staying suddenly fell down. Everyone fell silent at the noisy shaking of the books.³ Then Colum Cille said: "Lon-garad, the master of every art in Ossory, has just now died." "May it be a long time before that proves true!" said **Báithíne**. "May disbelief be the mark of your successor!" replied Colum Cille. Then he composed this verse:
> Dead is Lon of Cell Garad—a great tragedy!
> For Ireland, throughout all her borders, it is the ruin of study and scholarship.

**Son of Cnes**, that is, **Cnes** of the Dál Cethirn was his mother (the daughter of Conchaide), **and he was named after her as Mac Nissi** <note>original: *et ab ea nominatus est Mac nissi*</note>, meaning "Son of Cnes." Or perhaps *Mac cneise*, meaning "Son of the Skin," because he was fostered by **Saint Patrick** and used to sleep with him <note>a sign of close spiritual kinship</note>. **Cáemán Brecc** was his real name. Fobrec was his mother's name. Oengus was his own first name.
**Condeire** <note>modern Connor, County Antrim</note>, meaning "wolf-oakwood"—that is, an oakwood where wolves used to live, or simply a place where there was once an oakwood, **and** <note>original: *et*</note> so on.

4. For the allusion to children in Paradise, see Matthew 19:14.

---
¹ His genealogy is found in the *Book of Leinster* (LL), page 352d.
² See Colgan, *Acta Sanctorum*, page 136b, section 30 of the second life.
³ According to the *Leinster* version: when he died, all the book-satchels fell, for there were books of every science in the room where Colum Cille was; and Colum Cille and everyone in the house were amazed. According to the *Book of Leinster* (LL) 371c: It is said that on the night of Lon-garad's death, all of Ireland's book-satchels, gospels, and teaching books fell from their shelves, as if they understood that no one like Lon-garad would ever come again.

--- Page 256 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary and legends surrounding the saints of September, specifically focusing on Saint Ulltan (Ultan) of Ardbraccan and his miraculous care for orphans during the plague.</meta>

<page-num>200</page-num>
<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF SEPTEMBER.</header>

He was called the "Cleric of the Infants," because every child in Ireland who was left without care—specifically after the **Yellow Plague** <note>original: *Buide Connaill*; a devastating plague in the mid-7th century</note>—was brought to Ulltan. He frequently had fifty or even a hundred and fifty of them at one time, and he would feed them himself. <margin>Another version says:</margin> These were the children of the women whom the Yellow Plague had killed. This is what Ulltan used to do: he would cut the teats of cows and pour milk into them, and the infants would play around him.

It is also said that he used to walk with his Gospel book on his back without any strap at all to hold it.

**Diarmait son of Cerbaill** was the King of Ireland at that time. It happened then that a vast sea-fleet arrived, filling the greater part of the harbors of Ireland. A great fear came upon Diarmait, and he said: "That cleric of the infants who walks with his Gospel on his back without a strap—let someone go from us to seek his protection, so that this plague of invaders may be removed from us." 

Messengers were then sent from them to find Ulltan. Ulltan was feeding the infants when the messengers arrived, and they delivered their message to him. "That is a pity," said Ulltan, "that you did not leave me alone so that my right hand might be free. Since only my left hand is free, I will raise it against these ships." It was done accordingly; the ships were scattered and vanished into nothing. "If it had been my right hand, however," said Ulltan, "no foreigner <note>original: *gall*; at this time referring to any foreign invader</note> would ever come into Ireland for all time." From that event comes the saying, "Ulltan’s left hand against evil," from then until now.

Ulltan was feeding another infant and had a spoonful of porridge in the child's mouth, with some of it still on his finger, when the king’s servant arrived. Ulltan did not speak to the servant but simply raised his left hand. The servant returned to the king and told him, and the king understood that the cleric had raised his left hand to drive away the fleet. From that comes the phrase "Ulltan’s left hand against every evil" from then on, as it is said:

> Feeding his foster-children, Ultan—
> Whose living battle-host perished—
> He destroyed and ruined upon the shore
> Three times fifty ships with his left hand.

> Had it been the right he turned against them—
> Noble Ulltan from our side here—
> No foreigner would have come, here or there,
> Until Doomsday to the borders of Ireland.

### Moninde sang:

> It is not to mock anyone’s face,
> For all the clerics are ruddy-faced;
> It is a small thing that makes the face pale
> Of Ulltan, son of Conchobar’s descendant.

> It is a great effort to maintain the heights while in the valley;
> contending for glory with the Son of God—
> that is what makes the cheeks pale.

Ulltan was chosen for the abbacy of **Mochta** in **Louth** <note>original: *Lugbaid*</note>, and **Fursa** was sent out from there before him.

--- Page 257 ---
<meta>This page continues the legends of Saint Ultan of Ardbraccan, focusing on his miraculous care for orphans after the Yellow Plague and his supernatural defense of Ireland against foreign invaders.</meta>

<page-num>201</page-num>
<header>SEPTEMBER 4.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

Ultan is like *altan* <note>original: *altan*; an Old Irish word for razor</note>, meaning 'razor,' because of his keenness and sharpness in performing miracles and marvels. He used to be called "the cleric of the children" because after the plague known as the **Yellow Plague** <note>original: *Buide Connaill*; a 7th-century pandemic</note>, every babe left without support was brought to Ultan. Often fifty, or even a hundred and fifty of them, were with him at the same time, and he himself used to feed them—specifically the children of the women whom the Yellow Plague had killed. This is what Ultan used to do: he would cut off cows' teats... and pour milk into them, and the infants would play around him.

This is how he used to travel: with his Gospel book on his back, hanging there without any strap to hold it!

At that time, **Diarmait son of Cerball** was the King of Ireland. It happened that a vast seafleet of foreigners arrived, filling most of Ireland's <note>original: *Erin's*</note> estuaries. Great fear affected Diarmait, and he said: "That cleric of the children who travels with his Gospel on his back and no strap to it—let us put our trust in him so that this plague of invaders may be taken from us." 

So envoys were sent from Diarmait to Ultan. Ultan was feeding the children when the messengers arrived, and they told him their mission. "It is a shame," said Ultan, "that you did not leave me alone until my right hand was free. Since my left hand is the only one free, I will raise it against these ships. But if it were my right hand, no foreigner would ever invade Ireland again." Because of this, the proverb arose: "Ultan's left hand against the evil!"

<margin>Another version says:</margin> Then Ultan was feeding certain children, with a bit of porridge on his lips and some of it on his finger, when the king's servant <term>gillie</term> arrived. Ultan did not speak to the servant but simply raised his left hand. Then the servant returned to the king and told him this, and the king understood that the cleric had raised his left hand in order to expel the fleet. Therefore, from that time to this, the proverb is: "Ultan's left hand against every evil."

Through the feeding of his foster-children, Ultan... wrecked, destroyed, and stranded one hundred and fifty ships three times over with his left hand.

Had it been the right hand that the noble Ultan raised against them, from that moment on, no foreigner would have ever come here or there into the land of Ireland.

**Moninne** <note>likely Saint Moninne of Killeavy</note> sang:

> Not from a blow to anyone's face are all the clerics red: it is a small thing that turns the face of Ultan, the great-grandson of **Conchobar**, white.
>
> It is a great labor to strive for the heights while staying in the valley; to strive for perfection with the **Son of God**—that is what makes the cheeks grow pale.

Ultan was elected to the abbacy of **Mochta** in **Louth**, and before him **Fursa** <note>Saint Fursey, a famous Irish visionary and missionary</note> had been removed from that position.

<meta>This page continues the notes on the saints of the Martyrology of Oengus for the month of September, providing genealogical details for Saint Ultan and beginning the entries for early September, including Saint Mac Cuilinn of Lusk and the famous Saint Ciarán of Clonmacnoise.</meta>

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [THE MONTH OF SEPTEMBER.</header>

Ultan, son of Ernan, son of Gabran, son of Senach, son of Muiredach, son of Talglunn, son of Brocan, son of Cormac, son of Tadg, son of Tadg, son of Cian, son of Ailill Olum. <note>original: R² refers to a specific manuscript recension.</note>

**5. With Breccbuaid** etc. That is, Breccin of Tuaim Drecon <note>now Tomregan on the border of Cavan and Fermanagh</note> in the district of Breifne in Connacht. <note>original: R¹</note>. That is, Bricin of Tuaim Drecon in Breifne. **Or "victory"** <note>original: *buaid*</note>, meaning men and women brought "victory" to him—that is, they went to martyrdom along with him—for that is a victory for him, since he was the one who preached the word of God to them. <note>original: *L* refers to the Leabhar Breac manuscript</note>.
**The learned one** <note>original: *Eolach*</note>, he is at Achad Bó Caindig <note>now Aghaboe, County Laois</note>. <note>original: *L*</note>. At Achad Bó Cainnig. <note>original: R²</note>.

**6. Lusk** <note>original: *Lusca*</note> in Fingal. <note>original: *L*</note>. It is a "house that was first made of herbs" <note>original: *lusrad*</note>, and from that it is named Lusk, as if it were "herb-house," because what is called a "house" <note>original: *tech*</note> today was formerly called *ca*. <note>original: R¹</note>. **Mac Cuilinn**, that is, Luachan son of Cuillenn, as others think <note>original: *ut alii putant*</note>. Cuinnid was his name formerly <note>original: *prius*</note>. Cathmog was his father's name <note>original: *nomen patris eius*</note>. <note>original: R²</note>. Of Mac Cuilinn, bishop of Lusk. <note>original: *LL* 362c refers to the Book of Leinster</note>.
**Sceithe**, from Firt Sceithe in Munster. <note>original: *L*</note>. From Firt Sceithe in Muscraige Tri Maige in Munster. <note>original: R¹</note>. The arrival of the relics <note>original: *aduentus reliquiarum*</note> of Sceithe, daughter of Mechi, to Tallaght. <note>original: *LL* 362c (at Sept. 3)</note>.
**Colum Cruaire**, a scribe at Rus Giallain in Ui Liathain in Munster. <note>original: R²</note>. That is, Colum of Domnach Imclair in Ui Liathain. <note>original: *L*</note>. Or Colum of Great Domnach of Mag Imclair. <note>original: R¹</note>. **Of Colum**, that is, a cross-bearer from Ross. He is the same as Colum of Midísel. <note>original: *LL* 362c</note>.

**7. Senoti.**

**8. It is commemorated** <note>original: *Foraithmentar*</note>, that is, the birth of Mary according to the Romans <note>original: *natiuitas Maire secundum Romanos*</note>. <note>Note: The Greek calendar also records the birth of the Mother of God, *Tò γενέθλιον τῆς Θεοτόκου*</note>. The birth of Mary is commemorated here. <note>original: *F*</note>. **Upon a small meal** <note>original: *for tercfit*</note>, meaning on a meager portion of food, for *fit* means "food," as if he had said "do not fast on the feast day of Mary" <note>original: *quassi dixisset ne ieiunes in feria Marie*</note>. <note>original: R¹</note>.

**9. The great feast of Ciarán of Cluain.** Beoán, a carpenter of the Lathrannaib Molt of Dal Airide, was his father. Darerca, however, was his mother, as Ciarán himself said <note>original: *ut dixit ipse Ciarán*</note>:
> Darerca was my mother, she was no bad woman;
> Beoán the carpenter was my father, of the Lathrannaib Molt.
In the house of the son of the carpenter <note>Ciarán is often called "the Son of the Carpenter"</note> he was brought up. <note>original: R²</note>.

When Ciarán reached the age for training, he asked his father for something to bring with him so that he might pursue his learning, for he intended to go to Clonard to Saint Finnian, the tutor of the saints of Ireland, to study. Beoán said: "Go through the cattle," said he, "and whatever follows you, take it with you." A dun cow followed him, and that was the **Dun Cow of Ciarán** <note>original: *Odor Ciarain*; famous for the hide upon which the 'Book of the Dun Cow' was later written</note>. Twelve measures of milk were given from her at one time—that is, a measure for each of the twelve apostles of Ireland. <note>original: R²</note>.

Then, when Ciarán was beginning to translate the Gospel <note>or study the Gospel</note> with Finnian, or to do his reading with Finnian: "I find it hard for you to make a Gospel," said Finnian to him, "for everyone is doing it." Ciarán had only one book of his own. "It is dutiful," said **Colum Cille**, "and I will go to visit Ciarán." He went then. Ciarán was there interpreting his Gospel lesson, and this was the specific thing he spoke: **"In everything, do to others what you would have them do to you."** <note>original: *Omnia quaecunque uultis ut faciunt uobis homines sic facite illis*; Matthew 7:12</note>. Colum Cille went into the hut. "Will you give me a share of the book?" asked Colum. "It is not easy for me not to give it," said Ciarán, "if we do not practice what we just spoke against ourselves. Let the book be yours, then, with a blessing." "Half of Ireland to you!" said Colum Cille. <note>original: R²</note>.

<meta>This page continues the genealogical notes for Saint Ultan and provides historical and legendary commentary for the saints commemorated from September 5th to September 9th, including the famous Saint Ciarán of Clonmacnoise.</meta>

<page-num>203</page-num>
<header>SEPTEMBER 5-9.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

Ultan son of Ernan, son of Gabrán, son of Senach, son of Muiredach, son of Talglonn, son of Broccán, son of Cormac, son of Tadg, son of Cian, son of Ailill Ólomn.

5. **With Brecc-buaid**, etc. That is, Breccín of Tuaimm Drecon <note>now Tomregan</note> in Breifne of Connaught. Or *búaid* meaning "victory"—that is, men and women going to martyrdom together with him—for that is a victory for him, because it was he who had preached the word of God to them.

**The Learned One** <note>original: *Eolach*</note>, he is in Achad Bó Cainnig <note>now Aghaboe</note>.

6. **Lusk**, in Fingal. A house that was built of weeds <note>original: *lusrad*</note> was there formerly, and for that reason the place is named *Lusca*, as if it were "herb-house" <note>original: *lusrad-thech*</note>, because what is now called a "house" <note>original: *tech*</note> was formerly called *cae*. **Mac Cuilinn**, that is, Luachán Mac Cuilinn <note>son of Cuilleann</note>,¹ as others think <note>original: *ut alii putant*</note>. Cuinnid was his name at first. Cathmog was his father's name.

**Scéithe**, from Fert Scéithe in Muscraige Tri Maige <note>the "Muskerry of the Three Plains"</note> in Munster.

**Colum the cross-bearer** <note>original: *croxaire*</note>. He is a scribe at Ross Giallâin in Uí Liatháin in Munster; that is, Colum of Domnach Imchláir in Uí Liatháin. Or Colum of Domnach Mór Maige Imchláir. Colum, the "cross-bearer" <note>original: *crossaire*</note> of Ross, is the same as Colum Midísil.

7. **Of Senotus.**²

8. **Is commemorated**, that is, the Nativity <note>original: *natiuitas*</note>, etc. Mary's Nativity is commemorated here. **"On a scanty meal,"** for *pít* means a meal; as if he had said <note>original: *quasi dixisset*</note> you should not fast on Mary's feast day.

9. **The great festival of Ciarán of Clonmacnoise.** <note>original: *Clúain*</note> Beóán the Wright, of Lathranna Molt in Dál Araidi, was his father. Now Darerca was his mother, as Ciarán himself said:

> Darerca my mother, she was an excellent woman,³
> Beóán the Wright my father, of Latharna Molt.

He was raised in the house of the "son of the wright."

Then, when the proper time came, he asked his father to give him something to support his education, for he planned to go to Clonard to study under Finnén, the teacher of Ireland's saints.

Beóán said, "Go through the herds and take whatever follows you." A dun cow followed him, and that cow became known as "Ciarán's Dun." It used to yield twelve measures of milk at once—one measure for each of the twelve apostles of Ireland.⁴

Now, when Ciarán was beginning to copy a Gospel book with Finnén, Colum Cille came to Finnén to study. "Do you think it is a pious act to copy a Gospel?" Finnén asked him, "for everyone is doing it. Ciarán alone has the text of it." "It is pious," said Colum Cille, "and I will go to Ciarán." He went accordingly. Ciarán was then preparing his Gospel lesson, and he specifically spoke these words: "Whatever you wish men to do to you, do also to them." <note>Matthew 7:12</note> Colum Cille entered the hut. "Will you share the book with me?" asked Colum Cille.

"It is not easy for me to refuse," said Ciarán, "since the words we just spoke would condemn us unless we shared it. So, let the book—and my blessing—be yours."

"Half of Ireland to you!" said Colum Cille.

¹ Mac Cuilinn's pedigree is found in the *Book of Leinster* (LL) 352g.
² *Old English Martyrology* p. 164.
³ That is, according to the Irish idiom, she was an excellent woman.
⁴ See their names, mentioned previously on p. 168.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS [SEPTEMBER

When Ciarán’s period of service <note>original: *gres*</note> was finished, he asked Finnian what should be done. "Let her stay with the one she follows," said Finnian. She followed Ciarán after that, and it is her hide that is the precious relic called the **Hide of Ciarán’s Dun Cow** <note>original: *Sechi na hUidri Ciaráin*; this refers to the famous "Book of the Dun Cow," one of Ireland's oldest manuscripts, said to be written on this vellum</note>. R²

Ciarán was thirty-three years old when he died. The saints of Ireland fasted against him concerning his death, for all of Ireland would have been his had that not been done. Odhrán of Latteragh and Mac Cuilinn of Lusk went to tell him why they had fasted. "You have permission to go and bless the air before us," said Ciarán, "and you shall be given what you seek." And it was then he composed this:

->Wait for me, O King of the noble Heavens, etc.<- R²

The shortening of Ciarán’s life, the sending of Colum Cille across the sea, and the expulsion of Mochuta from Rathan: these are the "three false whispers" <note>or "bad counsels"</note> of the saints of Ireland. R²

There were three counsels, then, that were the worst ever made through the advice of the saints: the shortening of Ciarán’s life, the exile of Colum Cille, and the driving of Mochuta out of Rathan. F.

Patrick prophesied Ciarán’s birth sixty years before it happened. Comlach, Patrick’s leper, went across the sea to collect holy relics, and he brought the relics to the place where Bothcaind <note>now unknown</note> stands today. There was a large elm tree there at that time with a hollow in it. They placed the book-satchel in the hollow, along with the bag containing the relics. They rose the next morning to depart. Though they searched diligently, they saw neither the hollow nor the bag. They began looking at the tree and could do nothing to it, for every chip they chopped off it would grow back on again. Comlach then went into Connacht and told Patrick. "It is true," said Patrick, "those relics were not intended for the one who has come there; for sixty years from today a son shall be born whose fame will fill Ireland and Scotland <note>original: *Eri 7 Alba*</note>. His church will be in that place, and only one out of every hundred from it shall go into hell. Your own relics will be there as well," said Patrick. "They shall not be there," said Comlach, "unless your own relics are there too." "By my God’s doom" <note>original: *Mo debroth* - Saint Patrick's characteristic oath</note>, said Patrick, "it is my wish, if it be God’s wish." And so it is in the "sun-gathering" <note>original: *griandáil*</note> at Clonmacnoise that Patrick’s relics are kept, as others think <note>original: *ut ali putant*</note>. R²

**The Genealogy of Ciarán:**
Ciarán, son of Beoán, son of Olcán, son of Corc, son of Cuinenn, son of Cuineda, son of Fiacc, son of Mál, son of Carrthach, son of Laisre, son of Lasrend, son of Altrai, son of Gluinech, son of Cairpre, son of Lugh, son of Meadh, son of Dubh, son of Lughna, son of Feidlimid, son of Eochaid, son of Bressal Bán, son of Deg, son of Reosoirche. R²

10. **The Law** <note>original: *recht*</note>, that is, of Moses. This verse relates that it was Finnian of Magh Moisi who first <note>original: *artús*</note> brought the Law of Moses to Ireland, if it be true <note>original: *si uerum*</note>. Or the name "Law" <note>original: *nomen legis*</note> is applied here to the Gospel, for he was the first to bring the whole Gospel <note>original: *totum euangelium*</note> in one volume to Ireland, as they say, if this same thing be true <note>original: *ut ferunt, si uerum est hoc idem*</note>. F.

**Finnbarr**, that is, from Movilla <note>original: *Maig bile*</note> in Ulster. R¹

**Finnbarr**, that is, Finnian. This verse says that it was Finnian of Movilla who first <note>original: *prius*</note> brought Moses’ Law into Ireland. Or they give the name "Law" here to the Gospel, for it was Finnian who first brought the whole Gospel to Ireland. For it was Finnian of Movilla who first brought the Gospel of Colman to Ireland. R¹

<header>SEPTEMBER 9, 10. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

Now when Ciarán finished his work, he asked Finnian, “What shall be done?” “Let it be with whatever follows you,” says Finnian. Thereafter, she (the dun cow) follows Ciarán, so that her hide became the goodly relic which is called ‘the Hide of Ciarán’s Dun Cow.’ <note>The "Book of the Dun Cow" (Lebor na hUidre), one of the most important medieval Irish manuscripts, was traditionally said to have been written on vellum made from this cow's hide.</note>

Ciarán was thirty-three years old when he died. Ireland’s saints had fasted against him <note>In ancient Irish tradition, "fasting against" someone was a legal and spiritual method to compel them to do something or, in this case, to accept a divine decree</note> to bring about his death, for the whole of Ireland would have belonged to him and his monastery had that not been done. Odhrán of Latteragh <note>original: Letracha Odráin</note> and Mac Cuilinn of Lusk went to tell him why they had fasted. “You have permission... to go and bless <note>original: *sain*; to protect or consecrate with a sign</note> the air before us,” says Ciarán, “and what you seek will be given to you.” So then he composed the verses beginning:

->Wait for me, O King of splendid heaven.¹<-

The shortening of Ciarán’s life, the sending of Colum Cille across the sea, and the expulsion of Mochuta from Rathan—those are the three "bad stories" <note>or "false whispers"</note> of the saints of Ireland. The three worst decisions that were made through the counsel of the saints were: shortening Ciarán’s life, banishing Colum Cille, and putting Mochuta out of Rathan.²

Now Patrick had prophesied Ciarán’s birth sixty years before it happened. Comlach, Patrick’s leper <note>leper: In this context, a humble servant or ascetic companion who may have suffered from a skin condition</note>,³ went overseas to collect saints’ relics, and he brought the relics to the place where Bothcrainn⁴ is today. A great elm tree was there then with a hollow in it. The book-satchel was put into the hollow along with the satchel containing the relics. On the following morning, they arose. Though they were quick, they could see neither the hollow nor the satchel. They began cutting the tree, but they could do nothing to it, for every chip they struck from it would return to its place. Thereafter, Comlach goes into Connaught and tells this to Patrick. “It is true,” says Patrick: “those relics are not unnecessary for the one who shall come there; for, at the end of sixty years from today, a son will be born of whom all Ireland <note>original: Erin</note> and Scotland <note>original: Alba</note> will be full. His church will be *there*, and only one in a hundred out of it will ever go to hell, and *there* your own relics will be,” says Patrick. “They will *not* be,” says Comlach, “unless your relics are there also.” “By my God’s judgment,” <note>original: *debroth*; a characteristic oath used by Saint Patrick</note> says Patrick, “I am willing, if God is willing.” Accordingly, Patrick’s relics are in the *griandál* <note>a gravelly or sunny assembly plot</note> of Clonmacnoise, as others believe <note>original: *ut alii putant*</note>.

Ciarán was the son of Beoán, son of Olcán, son of Corc, son of Cuiniu, son of Cuinnid, son of Fiac, son of Mál, son of Carthach, son of Laisre, son of Lasriu, son of Altra, son of Glúinech, son of Coirpre, son of Lug, son of Mid, son of Dub, son of Lugna, son of Feidlimid, son of Eochaid, son of Bresal Bán, son of Dega, son of Reo-soirche.

10. **Findbarr**, that is, of Movilla <note>original: Mag bile</note> in Ulster. Findbarr is the same as Finnian. What this verse says is that it was Finnian of Movilla who first brought the Law of Moses <note>Referring to the Old Testament or a specific set of penitential canons</note> into Ireland.⁵ Or, the name ‘law’ was given to the Gospel here <note>original: *hic*</note>, for it is Finnian who first brought the complete Gospel to Ireland. For it is Finnian of Movilla who brought Colmán’s Gospel to Ireland.

¹ The poem is found in the *Book of Leinster* (LL) 374c; see also Cormac’s Glossary. ² See the notes for March 11. ³ Mentioned also in *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 339 and in the *Tripartite Life of Patrick*, 546. ⁴ Meaning 'a wooden booth' or hut. ⁵ A less favorable story is told about this saint in the preface to the hymn of Saint Mugint (see page 238).

<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF SEPTEMBER]</header>

Finnian of Movilla <note>original: Maige bile</note>, son of Cairpre, son of Ailill, son of Trithem, son of Fiacc, son of Imchad, son of Bresal, son of Sirchad, son of Fiacha Find.

**September 11.** The Passion of Protus and Hyacinth <note>original: Pais Prothi, Iacinthi</note>: they were two eunuchs who came to the faith along with the virgin Eugenia. They were two men of Eugenia's household. Protus was martyred in Rome.

Sillán, from Imliuch Cassáin in Cooley <note>original: Cuailngi</note>. "Psalm" <note>original: Salm</note> here refers to a prayer <note>original: oratio</note> for every sick person—that is, every person who was suffering from a heavy disease. For it was the common desire of all that they might look upon the hair <note>original: finna; this refers to a legendary poisonous hair in the saint's eyebrow</note> of Sillán’s son so they might die quickly. It was the nature of that hair that anyone who saw it in the morning would die immediately. 

It happened then that Sillán came to Leighlin <note>original: Lethglind</note>, and Saint Molaise came around the cemetery early that morning. He met Sillán of the "hair" face-to-face. "This hair shall no longer be killing everyone," said Molaise, and he pulled it out by force. Molaise himself died immediately after seeing the hair, and from this event, the saint was called Sillán <note>The name is traditionally linked to "sil," a look or eye</note>.

**September 12.** Ailbe, from Emly <note>original: Imliuch Ibair</note>.

Ailbe, son of Olcán, son of Arra, son of Dala, son of Laidír, son of Imros, son of Firtlachta, son of Celtchar.

Fleid: the name of a virgin in the border-territories of Leinster <note>original: Fortuathaib Laigin</note>. She was the daughter of the King of Leinster, from the House of Fleid <note>original: Tig Fleighi</note> in the territory of the Uí Garrchon.

Laisrén, also known as Molaise of Devenish <note>original: Daminse</note> from Lough Erne. He was Molaise, son of Nad-fraech, from Devenish; he belonged to the Eoghanacht of Cashel and was one of the twelve apostles of Ireland.

Molaise, son of Nad-fraech, son of Barrán, son of Conbran, son of Tuailsen, son of Deg, son of Crunn, son of Echu, son of Lugaid, son of Mros, son of Imchad, son of Cas, son of Fedlimid, son of Cas, son of Fiacha Araide.

Molaise of Devenish, the son of Nad-fraech, is located on Lough Erne. Molaise sang these verses:

> We have found a land we sought,
> a wide lake upon a mountain field;
> a common sanctuary <note>original: ruaim</note> for the Gaels,
> the beloved home <note>original: domhnus</note> of God the Father.

Devenish <note>original: Daiminis, "Ox Island"</note>: it was so named because the oxen <note>original: daim</note> of Conall Derg, son of Daimíne, used to stay there.

**September 13.** Dagán the priest, son of Colmada, of Inis Doile. "Doile" comes from Dael, the name of a river <note>original: amnis</note> on the border of the territories of Uí Fénechlais and Dál Mescorp in the border-lands of eastern Leinster.

**September 14.** Caemán Brecc <note>original: "the Speckled"</note> from Russagh <note>original: Rus ech</note> in Caille Follamain in Meath. He is located in Russagh, and Mac Rustaing is there with him; they were both children of the same mother. Some say Caemán Brecc is in Ros Liag.

Regarding the burial place of Mac Rustaing in Russagh: no woman has the power to look at it without breaking wind <note>original: maidhm a delma</note> or without afterwards falling into a fit of foolish, loud laughter, as the poet said:

<header>SEPTEMBER 10–14.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

Finnián of Movilla <note>original: Mag bile</note>, son of Cairbre, son of Ailill, son of Trichem, son of Fiacc, son of Imchad, son of Bresal, son of Sirchad, son of Fiacha the Fair.

**September 11.** The passion of Protus and Hyacinthus, two eunuchs, etc. <note>See the legend of Eugenia, on page 98.</note>

Sillán—that is, from Imbliuch Cassain in Cooley <note>original: Cualnge</note>. "Psalm" <note>original: salm</note> here means a prayer <note>original: oratio</note> for every feeble person—that is, everyone who used to be in sore sickness. For it was the common wish of them all to see the hair of Sillán’s eyebrow so that they might die quickly; for this was the strange power of that hair: everyone who saw it in the morning died at once. Now Sillán happened to come to Leighlin <note>original: Lethglenn</note>, and Saint Molaisse came early in the morning to walk around the graveyard. Sillán "of the Hair" happened to meet him. “This hair,” said Molaisse, “shall not go on killing everyone,” and he plucked it out by force. Then Molaisse, after seeing the hair, died at once, and hence **he was called Sillán** <note>original: Sillán dictus est</note> (Sillán of the Hair).

**September 12.** Of Ailbe—that is, from Emly <note>original: Imlech Ibair</note>. <note>See his metrical Rule in the Brussels MS. 5100-4, p. 24.</note>

Ailbe, son of Olcán, son of Arra, son of Dala, son of Láiter, son of Imros, son of Fer-tlachta, son of Celtchar. <note>See the pedigree in the Book of Leinster (LL) 349c.</note>

Fled—that is, the name of a virgin in the border-territories <note>original: Fortuatha</note> of Leinster, daughter of a king of Leinster, of Tech Fleide in Húi Garrchon.

Lassrén—that is, Molaisse of Devenish <note>original: Daminis</note>, from Lough Erne. He was Molaisse, son of Natfraich, of Devenish; he belonged to the Eoganacht of Cashel and was one of the twelve bishops of Ireland <note>original: Erin</note>.

Molaisse, son of Natfraich, son of Barrán, son of Conbran, son of Tuailsiu, son of Dega, son of Cronn, son of Eochaid, son of Lugaid, son of Mros, son of Imchad, son of Cass, son of Feidlimid, son of Cass, son of Fiacha Araide.

Molaisse of Devenish—that is, the son of Natfraich; he is located on Lough Erne.

Molaisse sang:
> The land we found has been found; a broad lake is our mountain-pasture, a common cemetery for the Irish <note>original: Gaels</note>, God the Father’s own domain.

Devenish <note>original: Dam-inis</note>—that is, the "Island of Oxen"—because the oxen <note>original: daim</note> of Conall the Red, son of Daimine, used to be kept there. That is how it was named.

**September 13.** Of Dagán, a priest, son of Colmaid, of Inber Dóile <note>modern Ennereilly</note>. "Of Dáel"—that is, Dáel is the name of a river on the common frontier of Húi Fenechlais and Dál Mescorp in the border-territories of Leinster in the east. <note>See his pedigree in LL. 351f.</note>

**September 14.** Of Cáemán the Speckled <note>original: Cáemán Brecc</note>. He is from Russagh <note>original: Ross ech</note> in Caille Fallamain in Meath, and Mac Rustaing is there along with him; the pair of them were children of the same mother. Or, Cáemán the Speckled is in Ross liac. <note>See his pedigree in LL. 351f.</note>

Now the grave of Mac Rustaing is in Russagh. No woman can see it **without breaking wind** <note>original: sine crepitu ventris eius</note>, or without a loud, foolish laugh afterward, **as the poet said** <note>original: ut dixit (poeta)</note>:

<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [SEPTEMBER.</header>

> Cridan was the name of noble Mac Rustaing,
> Garb Daire was the name of Mac Samhain,
> Aindiar was the name for Mac Conglinne,
> who composed many poems.
> The grave of Mac Rustaing is said to be
> in Russagh <note>original: Ros ech</note> without shame;

**September 14 (continued).** Cornelius, Pope of Rome. <note>original: Cornil papa Rome</note> Cornelius, and so forth. He was the Bishop of the city of Rome and ruled the church under the emperors Gallienus and Valerian for fifteen years. After he was crowned with martyrdom for Christ, Lucius succeeded him.

Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage in Africa. Cyprian the African first taught rhetoric gloriously. Then, having become a Christian at the persuasion of Caecilius, he gave away all his wealth to the poor, and afterward was appointed Bishop of Carthage. It is unnecessary to describe his genius here, as his works are clearer than the sun. He suffered under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus during the eighth persecution, on the same day that Cornelius suffered at Rome, but not in the same year.

**September 15.** The Dedication of the Basilica of Mary. <note>original: Dedicatio basilicae Mariae</note>
*Basilica*—that is, of a church; *basilica*—that is, "royal." <note>The word derives from the Greek for "royal hall."</note> Boniface IV, Bishop in Rome, requested from the Emperor Phocas <note>original: Focate</note> that the building <note>the Pantheon</note> be given to the church.
Cirinus—that is, a bishop and martyr.

**September 16.** A trio—that is, three people, or "three great heads": Moinenn of Cloncurry <note>original: Clúana Conaire</note>, Toman in northern Uí Faeláin, Laisrén, abbot of Iona <note>original: Ia Coluim chille</note>, and Laisrén the Great (that is, Laisrén of Mena), the son of the descendant of Laeguire.

*Laisrén of Mena*—that is, Molaisse of Mena Droichit. *Men* is the name of a river, and there is a bridge (*droichet*) across it; it is located in Leix <note>original: Laigis</note>. Or it is called *Mena Droichit*—that is, "smooth bridge" <note>original: min drochet</note>. This is because a certain gathering of many saints once came to that city for some reason, and a certain thief among the inhabitants of the city said, "It is smoothly <note>or "entirely"</note> they reach <note>original: is min doroichet</note> us, all these men, in this night." One of the arriving saints said, "Let that be the name of this place forever: *Min Doroichet*."

*Molaisse, descendant of Lugair.* His church is in Uí Fairchelláin.

*Laisrén, abbot of Iona.* He is mentioned alongside Laisrén of Mena—that is, Molaisse of Mena Droichit. *Men* is the name of a river with a great confluence across it, located in Leix.

*Laisrén*—that is, the abbot of Iona and Molaisse of Mena Droichit. *Mena* is the name of a river with a bridge over it, and the church is named after it. Molaisse, son of the descendant of Lugair, has his church in Uí Fairchelláin. Alternatively, *Min* is a great river between Dál Araidi and Cenél nEógain, and Molaisse lives on its bank.

**September 17.** Euphemia—that is, a virgin and martyr. That is, Feme, daughter of Cairell, a virgin and martyr; Euphemia "of the prayer" in Mag Itha.

*Ross Tuirc*—that is, in Mag Raigni in Ossory and in Cluain Imarchuir. Flannán, son of Tairrdelbach, once came to the place so that he was being carried <note>original: imorcor</note> in the meadow <note>clúain</note>; and from that it is called *Cluain Imarchuir* ("Meadow of the Carrying").

*Riagla*—that is, Riaguil of Muckinish <note>original: Muccinis</note> on Lough Derg.

SEPTEMBER 15-17.]

1. Critan was the name of the noble Mac Rustaing, Garbdaire was the name of Mac Samain, and Aindiar was the name for Mac Conglinne—he composed many poems. <note>original: "lays"</note>
2. You say Mac Rustaing's grave is in Russagh <note>original: Ross ech</note> without shame; if a woman sees it, she talks, she farts <note>original Latin: *pedit*</note>, and she laughs aloud.
   *Cornelius, Pope of Rome, and others. Cornelius, and so forth.*
   *Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage in Africa, and others. Cyprian the African, and so forth.*

### 15. The Dedication of the Basilica of Mary.
Of the basilica—that is, a church. *Basilica* <note>original Greek: βασιλική (*basilikē*)</note> means a "royal house."
Boniface IV, the fourth bishop in Rome after Gregory, and others.
Cyrinus, a bishop and martyr.

### 16. A Trio
That is, three great chiefs: namely, Moenenn of Clúain Conairi Toman <note>modern: Cloncurry</note> in the north of Húi Faeláin <note>an ancient territory in modern County Kildare</note>; Laissrenn, the abbot of Iona <note>original: Hí</note>; and Laissrén Mór, also known as Laissrén of Men, who was the great-grandson of Lóeguire.

Laissrén of the Men—that is, Molaisse of Men-drochat. *Men* is the name of a river <note>original: *Men nomen amnis*</note> with a bridge (*drochat*) across it, located in Leix <note>modern: Laois</note>. Alternatively, is it named Men-drochet from *mín-drochet*, meaning "smooth-bridge"? It is said that a large congregation of many saints was once at that town for some reason, and a certain robber among the inhabitants said: "Smoothly <note>original: *mín*</note> do all those come to us tonight," as if to say they come industriously. One of the visitors then replied: "This shall be the name of the place until doomsday: Mindroíchet."

Molaisse, the great-grandson of Lugar. His church is in Húi Fairchellain <note>modern: Offerlane, County Laois</note>.

Laissrén, abbot of Iona, the monastery of Saint Columba <note>original: Colum cille's Hí</note>. He is commemorated with Laissrén of Men—that is, Molaisse of Men-drochait. *Men* is the name of a river <note>original: *Men nomen amnis*</note> and there is a great confluence <note>the original text has a question mark regarding this translation</note> across it in Leix.

Laissrén, the abbot of Iona. Molaisse of Mena drochit. *Mena* is the name of a river <note>original: *Mena nomen amnis*</note> with a bridge across it, and the church is named after it. Molaisse, the great-grandson of Lugar, has his church in Húi Fairchellain. Alternatively, Min is a great river located between Dalaradia and Tyrone, and Molaisse is situated on its bank.

### 17. Euphemia, a virgin and martyr. 
Feme, the daughter of Cairell, a virgin and martyr—that is, Feme of the prayer <note>the editor notes this interpretation is uncertain</note> in Mag Itha.

Of Ross tuirc—that is, in Mag Raígni in Ossory and in Clúain Imarchuir. Flannán, the son of Toirdelbach, <note>Saint Flannán of Killaloe, a 7th-century bishop</note> came sometimes to the place and was carried into the meadow; because of this, it is called Clúain Imorchuir, which means the "meadow of carrying."

Of Riaguil—that is, Riaguil from Mucc-inis on Loch Derg.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF SEPTEMBER.

### 18. Enan.
That is, Enan of Drumraney <note>original: *Dromma ráthi*</note> in western Meath.

### 19. Januarius <note>original: *Enair*</note>.
That is, a martyr and priest under Bishop Felix of the city of Tapstua <note>The location "Tapstua" is likely a transcription error in the original manuscript</note>.

### 20. Doroma.
That is, a virgin, with her five companions.

### 21. Matthew.
That is, the Apostle.
<margin>Matthew, apostle and evangelist of the Lord, was beheaded in the church next to the altar in the city called Danam, which is in Ethiopia, under King Hyrtacus <note>original: *Nirtgo*</note>. He suffered in Ethiopia.</margin>

### 22. Pantaleon.
That is, a legate <note>original: *legait*</note> to the Romans. He was the son of a certain senator named Extargius in the city of Nicomedia; he suffered under Emperor Maximian, the persecutor of Christians.
Maurice <note>original: *Muric*</note> in the city of Sion <note>original: *Sedunum*</note> in Gaul. Maurice suffered with his companions under Caesar Maximian. He is named Maurice <note>original: *Mauricius*</note> because a crowd of the faithful followed him—that is, 6,600 men—and they suffered with Maurice at the place called Agaunum near the Alps under Maximian. Pantaleon, however, suffered with four men in the city of Nicomedia under Emperor Maximian.

### 23. Adomnan, Abbot of Iona <note>original: *Iae*</note>.
Adomnan—that is, a diminutive form of the name Adam. Adomnan was the son of Ronan, son of Tinne, and Ronnat was his mother's name.
Adomnan <note>his full genealogy follows</note>, son of Ronan, son of Tinne, son of Aed, son of Colum, son of Setna, son of Fergus, son of Conall, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages.
It happened once that Adomnan was traveling through the Plain of Brega <note>original: *Maig Breg*</note> with his mother on his back, when they saw two battle lines clashing against each other. It happened then that Ronnat saw a woman with an iron sickle <note>original: *corran*</note> in her hand, dragging another woman from the opposing army by her breast—for in those times, men and women alike used to go into battle.
Then Ronnat said: "I will not let you take me from this place until women are freed forever from this condition—namely, from expeditions and hosting armies." Adomnan then promised her this. Later, a great assembly took place in Ireland, and Adomnan went there with the best of the Irish clergy and subsequently freed the women.
These, then, are the four Laws of Ireland:
1. The Law of Patrick: not to kill the clergy.
2. The Law of the Sabbath <note>original: *Cain Domnaig*</note>: not to work on Sunday.
3. The Law of Daire: not to kill <note>or steal</note> cattle.
4. The Law of Adomnan <note>The text repeats *Cain Domnaig* in error</note>: not to kill women.

That Adomnan was wonderful. He had great love for God and for his neighbor. It was he who gathered the great relics of the saints into a single shrine; and it was that shrine that Cilline Droichtech <note>literally "Cilline of the Bridge"</note>, son of Dichlocha, brought to Ireland to establish peace and a covenant <note>original: *cotaig*</note> between the Cenél Conaill and Cenél Eogain. This is the number of the relics, as Adomnan sang: [The poem follows].

### 24. The Conception of John the Baptist.
Faelchu of Finglas, and Lith daughter of Cainnech from Mag Locha, and Ceallachan of Clones <note>original: *Clúana tiprat*</note> in Ulster, and Caelchu of Lusk <note>original: *Lui erthir*</note> on this day.

### 25. Eusebius.
Experts say that no feast is harmful if the cross of God and of Eusebius is placed over it, even if there is an excess of food. Eusebius, a bishop.

Bairre <note>Saint Finbarr of Cork</note>. He was of the descendants of Brian, son of Eochaid Mugmedon...

### 18. Enan.
That is, in Meath; in the west of Meath is Enan of Drumraney <note>original: *Druimm raithe*</note>.

### 19. Januarius.
That is, a martyr, etc.

### 20. Doroma.
That is, a virgin with her five companions.

### 21. Matthew.¹
That is, an apostle, etc.

### 22. Pantaleon.
That is, a legate of the Romans, a son <note>original: *filius*</note>, etc.
*Maurice <note>original: *Mauric/Mauricius*</note>*² in Sion <note>original: *Sedunum/Sion/Sitten*</note>, a city of Gaul, etc.
*Maurice*, that is, from the name *Mauricius*, etc.

### 23. Adamnan, Abbot of Iona.
*Of Adamnan*, that is, a diminutive of the name *Adam*. Adamnan was the son of Ronan, son of Tinne; and Ronnat was the name of his mother. That is, Adamnan, son of Ronan, son of Tinne, son of Aed, son of Colum, son of Setna, son of Fergus, son of Conall, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. 

It happened that Adamnan was once traveling in Mag Breg with his mother on his back, and they saw two armies <note>original: *battalions*</note> striking each other. It happened, moreover, that Ronait saw a woman with an iron sickle in her hand dragging another woman out of the opposing army, and the sickle was in her breast <note>original: *pap*</note>. For at that time, women as well as men used to take part in battle. Then Ronait said:
> “You shall not carry me out of this place until women are freed forever from things of that kind,” —that is, from fighting and military service <note>original: *hosting*</note>.

Then Adamnan promised that thing. There happened to be a great convention in Ireland. So Adamnan, with the best <note>original: *pick*</note> of Ireland’s clergy, went there and freed the women. Now these are the four laws of Ireland <note>original: *Erin*</note>: Patrick’s law, not to kill the clergy; Adamnan’s law, not to kill women; Daire’s law, not to kill cattle <note>original: *kine*</note>; and the law of Sunday, not to transgress at all on that day.

*Admirable was Adamnan*. Great was his love of God and his neighbor. It is by him that the great holy relics were collected in one shrine; that is the shrine that Cilline the Bishop <note>original: *Pontifex*</note>, son of Dichloch, brought to Ireland to make peace and a treaty <note>original: *compact*</note> between Tyrconnell and Tyrone. This is the number of the relics, as Adamnan sang.³

### 24. Conception of John the Baptist.⁴
Faelchu of Finglas <note>original: *Findglas*</note>, and Lith⁵ daughter of Cainnech from Mag locha, and Cellachan of Cluain tiprat in Ulster, and Caelchu from Lui erthir on this day <note>original: *in hoc die*</note>.

### 25. Eusebius.
Experts declare that no banquet causes harm if the cross of God and of Eusebius be placed over it, even if it be an overindulgence <note>original: *surfeit*</note>. Eusebius was a bishop.
*Bairre*, that is, of the descendants <note>original: *children*</note> of Brian, son of Eochaid Muigmedon.

### 26. Colman.

Ela was the name of a woman <note>original: *nomen mulieris*</note> who lived in that place before Colman, and from her the city is named <note>original: *nominatur ciuitas*</note>, that is, Lynally <note>original: *Lann Ela*</note>. ### 27. Cosmas and Damian.

### 28. Findia.
Of Findia, of Finio and Gillae; these two saints are in Aran. Or "Findia the lad" <note>original: *gillda*</note>, that is, Finnian of Clonard <note>original: *Finden Clúana hIraird*</note> is remembered here. Or Gillae is the name of a saint, or of Findia. Others say that it is he who was in these verses <note>original: *isna Rannaib si*</note>, which is the truth. Of Finnio: a lad <note>original: *gilla*</note>, that is, Finnian of Clonard, and he was a lad when he performed the miracle for which he is remembered here. Or perhaps it should be "to the two Findias" there—that is, two Findias who are in Aran and the feast of both of them is on this day of the solar month. Or perhaps it should be "of India the bright" <note>original: *de India gelia*</note>, as Gregory testifies, that is, Marcellus with his companions was from India.

**Marcill:** That is, Marcialis.

**Iunaill:** That is, Junallus; he is from the east, or in Corcu Baiscinn in Munster <note>original: *Mumain*</note>.

*Iunilli:* That is, the infirm <note>original: *infirmi*</note>.

### 29. Michael.
The soldier <note>original: *in míl*</note>, that is, the warrior. Michael, which is interpreted as "Who is like God" <note>original: *qui sicut Deus*</note>: on Mount Gargano <note>original: *in Monte Gargain*</note>.

On this day was the dedication of the basilica of Michael <note>original: *dedicatio basilicae Michaelis*</note>, with the order of the Lord's Day, white vestments upon the altar, and without servile labor <note>original: *sine labore seruili*</note>, the communion of the body and blood of Christ, the giving of alms to the poor, and the preaching of Michael to the crowds.

Against the Antichrist <note>original: *arsil Ancrist*</note>.

### 30. Jerome.
**Our sisters:** That is, our sisters <note>original: *ar sethir*</note> Paula and Eustochium and others, at whose request Jerome <note>original: *Hironimus*</note> translated the Old Testament. That is, those who came to Jerome: the widow Paula and her daughter Eustochium, companions of Cyrene.

**Bethlehem:** That is, from Bethlehem of Judah.

> With Patrick, with Giric, with Laisren with sharpness,
> with Beoc without decay, they are the ridge-pole of every quarter.

> the feast of Ciaran, the feast of Molaisse,

> remember them together

> and the first of September <note>the Calends</note>,
> the feast of Bartholomew (a struggle with strength), 
> the birth of Mary, and the feast of Michael;
> it is fitting to count them in every house 
> as falling on that same day.

**Two Findias and Gillas**, that is, these two saints are in Aran. Or *Findia the golden* <note>original: *Findia gillda*</note>, meaning Finnian of Clonard is commemorated here. Or Gilla is the name of a saint. Or two Findias. Some say that he is the one who used to be in Whithorn <note>original: *Whitern*</note> in the Rhins <note>original: *Renna*</note>, if it is true <note>original: *si uerum est*</note>. To Finnian, a boy—that is, Finnian of Clonard—and he was just a lad when he performed the miracle for which he is commemorated here. ### 29. The Soldier
**The soldier** (whose name, **Michael**) is interpreted as "who is like God" <note>original: *qui sicut Deus*</note>, on Mount Garganus.
On this day <note>original: *Hoc die*</note>, etc.³
He will slay the Antichrist.⁴

### 30. Our Sisters
**Our sisters**, that is, Paula and Eustochium, etc. They used to come to Saint Jerome; Paula was a widow and Eustochium was her daughter, and they were companions <note>original: *sociae*</note> of Jerome.
**Bethlehem**, that is, from Bethlehem of Judea <note>original: *Bethlehem Iudaeae*</note>.

Saint Patrick’s day (March 17), Saint Cyriacus’s day (June 16), the day of Laisrén with keenness (September 16), and the day of Beóc without decay (December 16)—these four mark the start <note>literally "the roof"</note> of every quarter of the year.

New Year's Day <note>original: "Little Christmas"</note> (January 1), Saint Patrick’s feast (March 17), Saint Adamnán’s feast (September 23), Saint Martin’s feast (November 11), Saint Ciarán’s feast (September 9), and Saint Molaisse’s feast (August 12)—I tell you without haste, let them be remembered by you together as falling on the same day of the week.⁵

Saint Columba’s feast (June 9), the feast of bright Cyriacus (June 16), the first of September (September 1), and Saint Bartholomew’s feast (August 25)⁶—say it vigorously—the Nativity of Mary (September 8), and Saint Michael’s feast (September 29); it is fitting to count these feasts in every house as falling on the same day of the week.⁷

¹ His pedigree is in the *Book of Leinster* (LL) 352f. ² See their legend in the *Old English Martyrology* (O.E. Mart.) page 180. ³ For the consecration of St. Michael’s church see *O.E. Mart.* 182. ⁴ See Daniel 12:1 and Revelation 12:6. Some of the signs of Antichrist’s birth are mentioned in the *Colloquy of the Two Sages*: monsters born, streams flowing backwards, water tasting like wine, etc. (Rawlinson manuscript B 502, folio 62b). ⁵ Thus in the year 1904, these days all fall on a Friday. ⁶ In the *Martyrology of Donegal* (Mart. Don.) and in the current calendar, Bartholomew’s day is August 24. But in the *Martyrology of Oengus* (Fél. Oeng.) it is August 25. ⁷ In the year 1904, all these days fall on a Thursday.

### THE MONTH OF OCTOBER.
#### A. *The Calends of October* <note>original: Calendis Octobris; October 1st</note>
The triumph of Priscus,¹ the passion of Luke,²
the festival of Germanus, a sun of songs,
the feast of the holy noble relics³ ⁴
at the start of October.⁵

#### B. *The 6th of the Nones of October* <note>October 2nd</note>
Eleutherius⁶ the martyr,
you celebrate⁷ his⁸ feast,
at the same time⁹ on the same day
with the passion of Eusebius.¹⁰

#### C. *The 5th of the Nones of October* <note>October 3rd</note>
The noble birth of Mark in Egypt,¹¹
the declaration of every¹² mouth!¹³
Candida, the happy sun;
the fair birth of Colmán of Lynally.¹⁴ <note>original: Colmán Ela</note>

#### D. *The 4th of the Nones of October* <note>October 4th</note>
Pray to Bishop Marcellus,¹⁵
with his vast power,¹⁶
at the suffering of the virgin¹⁷
the fair-skinned Balbina.¹⁸

#### E. *The 3rd of the Nones of October* <note>October 5th</note>
A fragment of the¹⁹ precious stone,
with a crowd²⁰ of wonderful martyrs,
Sínech, daughter of Fergna,²¹
of the Mound²² of the River Plain.²³ <note>original: Crúachan Maige Abnae</note>

### OCTOBER.
1. The triumph of Priscus, the passion of Luke: the festival of Germanus, a sun of songs: the feast of the holy noble relics at the start of October.

2. Eleutherius the martyr, you celebrate his feast, at the same time on the same day as the passion of Eusebius.

3. Mark's noble birth in Egypt, the declaration of every mouth! Candida, the happy sun; the fair birth of Colmán of Lynally.

4. Pray to Marcellus the bishop, with his vast power, at the suffering of the virgin, the fair-skinned Balbina.

5. A fragment of the precious stone, with a crowd of wonderful martyrs, Sínech, daughter of Fergna, of the Mound of the River Plain.

---

6. Lucell, the abbot of Cluain, <note>Likely Cluain Eidnech or Cluain Mic Nois</note> along with the vigorous Baithine (also known as Aed). There is also Fer Da Chrich <note>meaning "Man of Two Countries"</note>, a triumphant pillar of the church, and the beautiful Bishop Lugdach.

7. Along with Matthew and Bishop Marcus, a great host was slain in hardship. We also celebrate the feast of the eager Cellach, accompanied by a fair and melodious choir.

8. They surrendered earthly power and splendor for the eternal inheritance of the Kingdom—a flock of virginal maidens who died during the pure martyrdom <note>original: passion</note> of Faustinus.

9. On the feast of Eusebius, a vast host of kings—three hundred and fifty in number—ascended the paths to heaven.

10. Three hundred and thirty others joined a man who was fair and honest: Fintan the Fair, the "root of the vine" and the pillar of Druimm Ingaird.

11. Of the trio whom we commemorate, their followers are magnificent: Fortchern, Lomman "of the scales," <note>original: lainnech; this may refer to a skin condition or wearing a coat of mail</note> and Cainnech, a descendant of Dala. <note>This is St. Canice, the patron of Kilkenny</note>

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS</header>
<header>THE MONTH OF OCTOBER</header>

#### E. *The 4th day before the Ides of October* <note>original: iv. idus Octobris; October 12th</note>

Announce Fiacc and Fiachra at the same time—great is that treasure! Also celebrate my Bí <note>Mo Bí, also known as Berchan of Glasnevin</note>, whose triumph is strong; he is that fair, flat-faced one <note>original: clárainech; a nickname for Mobi, suggesting a facial deformity or a "board-faced" appearance</note>.

#### F. *The 3rd day before the Ides of October* <note>original: iii. idus Octobris; October 13th</note>

Comgan and Marcill, with the great breadth of their wisdom <note>original: al-linde</note>; and the feast of fair Findsech, the purified princess.

#### G. *The day before the Ides of October* <note>original: Pridie idus Octobris; October 14th</note>

The feast of Bishop Calixtus <note>Pope Calixtus I</note>, announce him on the same line with the martyrdom of the virginal Bishop Paulinus.

#### A. *The Ides of October* <note>original: Idibus Octobris; October 15th</note>

The foremost martyrdom of the Mauri <note>original: Maurorum; referring to the Moorish martyrs of the Theban Legion</note> has been heard of throughout the crowded world; they endured many afflictions after being held in bitter, shackled dungeons.

#### B. *The 17th day before the Kalends of November* <note>original: xvii. cal. Novembris; October 16th</note>

Ciar, along with three hundred and forty fair followers, went to that triumph; Riaguil ran that course, and Colman from Cell Ruaid <note>modern: Kilroot, County Antrim</note>.

***

<header>OCTOBER 17-21.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

### C. The 16th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: xvi. cal. Nouembris; October 17th</note>

The heavenly martyr¹ Nicodemus² suffered³ much,
along with his followers—a beautiful assembly—
the powerful expeller of demons⁴.

### D. The 15th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: xv. cal. Nouembris; October 18th</note>

Truly⁶ with the passion of Philip⁷,
a leading martyr who strengthens us;
to the fasting¹⁰ Tryphonia⁸,
fair Christ gave⁹ beautiful aid¹¹.

### E. The 14th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: xiv. cal. Nouembris; October 19th</note>

May Eusterius¹² be a help to us,
who was slain¹³ through¹⁴ tortures;
may the host of Sosius¹⁷ protect¹⁵ and save¹⁶ us
from¹⁷ pain!

### F. The 13th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: xiii. cal. Nouembris; October 20th</note>

The martyrdom of Eutychius along with Fintan¹⁸
Maeldub—great is that fame!¹⁹—
a beautiful sun at that mountain²⁰,
from those splendid²² descendants of Eogan²¹ <note>original: Eoganacht; a powerful ruling dynasty in Munster</note>.

### G. The 12th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: xii. cal. Nouembris; October 21st</note>

A brilliant flame with the fervor of the Fathers²³,
Fintan¹⁸, true gold put to the test!
The son of Telchán²⁴, brave and fasting,
a faithful, spiritual soldier, crucified²⁵ <note>meaning: one who has crucified their worldly desires</note>.

### A. The 11th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: xi. cal. Nouembris; October 22nd</note>

The cross of Bishop Philip¹
with whom a pious multitude² was slain³;
Matthew, the crown of every kingdom⁴,
along with the suffering of Eusebius.

### B. The 10th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: x. cal. Nouembris; October 23rd</note>

The departure⁵ of Longinus⁶ <note>Longinus is the name given in tradition to the Roman soldier who pierced Jesus' side with a spear</note>
to the highest royal kingdom⁷:
he pierced⁸—a most noble⁹ deed!—
the bright,¹⁰ beautiful side of Jesus.

### C. The 9th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: ix. cal. Nouembris; October 24th</note>

The noble proclamation of Severus,
it is better for you¹¹ if you know it¹²:
he has ascended to high heaven
with forty¹³ holy people <term>original: chréssen; pious ones or religious devotees</term>.

### D. The 8th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: viii. cal. Nouembris; October 25th</note>

Four tens and two fifties¹⁴ <note>Totaling 140 companions</note>
with Maximus, who comes to us¹⁵;
at the feast of Christ’s chosen man,
Lassrén the Great, son of Nascae.

### E. The 7th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: vii. cal. Nouembris; October 26th</note>

Nassad,¹⁶ Beóán,¹⁷ and Mellán¹⁸—
in every way I weave them together¹⁹:
the feast of the daughters of Mac Íair²¹—
dear is that righteous group of four²⁰ <term>original: coair; a just tetrad or group of four</term>.

***

<header>OCTOBER 27-31. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

### F. The 6th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: vi. cal. Nouembris; October 27th</note>

Erc of wealthy¹ Domnach Mór <note>original: Domnaig Móir; "The Great Church"</note>; Abbán, a fair² and seafaring <term>original: clárach; literally "of the boards," implying a boat-user or ship-builder</term> abbot; Odrán, a strong,³ noble, and buoyant <term>original: snámach; a good swimmer</term> figure; and Colmán, the grandson⁴ of Fiachra.⁵

### G. The 5th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: v. cal. Nouembris; October 28th</note>

Vast⁶ is their assembly: Babylon⁷ is their burial ground; Thaddaeus⁸ and Simon—their host is immense.

### A. The 4th day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: iv. cal. Nouembris; October 29th</note>

May the host of Quintus⁹ with great fervor¹⁰ protect us¹¹ against every¹² danger!¹³ They gained¹⁴ victory through forgiveness with the soothing¹⁵ of Táimthene.

### B. The 3rd day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: iii. cal. Nouembris; October 30th</note>

Two hundred and sixty¹⁶ in full on the same festival—a sea of great triumphs!¹⁷ Ernach¹⁸ a virgin,¹⁹ a lofty pillar, and Colmán of the Gúale people.²⁰

### C. The day before the Kalends of November
<note>original: Pridie cal. Nouembris; October 31st</note>

Fair Quintinus, who was crucified;²¹ Faelán with many bands of workers;²² together with a host of fathers,²³ they declare the noble end²⁴ of October.

<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF OCTOBER.]</header>

### NOTES.

1. **Priscus**, a martyr <note>original: Prisci .i. mairtir</note>. **Luke** the Evangelist <note>original: Lúcae euangeliza</note>. **Germanus**, a bishop and the teacher of **Patrick** <note>original: German .i. espoc 7 maígisdir Patricii</note>. <note>Latin original: Germani episcopi Autisidori ciuitatis; "Of Germanus, Bishop of the city of Auxerre."</note>

**The festival of the saints' cemetery** <note>original: Feil noeb reilge</note>: This refers to when the relics of **Peter** and **Paul**, along with the hair of **Mary** and the remains of the great martyrs in Rome, were brought to **Armagh** by **Sechnall**. Or, it was then that the cemetery of **Máel Ruáin** in **Tallaght** was consecrated. Or perhaps those relics were brought to the community of Tallaght and are kept there, as some say. Others say those relics—the shrine of Peter and Paul—are in Armagh, and it was Sechnall who brought them from abroad. <note>Latin/Irish original: aduentus reliquiarum Marie Virginis...; "The arrival of the relics of the Virgin Mary, the apostles, martyrs, and other saints to Tallaght of Máel Ruáin or to Armagh."</note> It is said the relics of Paul and Peter were in a shrine, and it may have been Sechnall who brought them to Ireland <note>original: ad Hiberniam</note>.

2. **Onme** means "at the same time" <note>original: simul</note>. Or Onme was the son of the King of **Leinster** <note>original: Lagén</note>, and he was given as a hostage <note>original: i ngiallacht</note> to the King of the Northern Half of Ireland <note>original: Leithe Cuinn</note>. That king placed him in the care of **Brigid** <note>original: Brigte</note> to satisfy the demands of his father. One day, Brigid’s disciples said to her: "This little hostage <note>original: gillán</note> is beautiful today." Brigid replied, "Let his name be **Gillán**." His name was Onme before that, and he is the one associated with **Cell Gillán** in Leinster.
**Eusebius**, bishop and martyr. <note>Latin original: quem Grigor[i]us confessorem esse refert...; "whom Gregory reports to be a confessor and not a martyr."</note>

3. **Mark** <note>original: Maire</note> the Evangelist: on this day he reached the angels <note>original: ad angelos peruenit; he died</note>. **Candida**, a virgin.
**Colmán Elo** <note>original: Colmain Ela</note>: from **Lann Ela** in the territory of the **Fir Cell** <note>original: Tír cheall; "Land of the Churches"</note>.

4. **Balbina** <note>original: Baluina</note>: she is in the East; or she is **Bicsech** from **Cell Bicsige** in the territory of the **Ui Macc Uais** of Meath <note>original: Huaib macc Cuais Midhe</note>. <margin>Balbina, virgin and martyr.</margin> Or it could be that Balbina is Bicsech of Cell Bicsige in Meath, but that is not certain.

5. **A fragment of the stone** <note>original: Blogh don lig</note>, etc.: This refers to **Sinech**, daughter of Fergna. Or she is Sinech the Wise, located at **Cruachain Maige Abna** in **Éoganacht Caisil**. Fergna was the name of her father. "Wise" <note>original: ergna</note> here means "good."

6. **The Abbot of Clonmacnoise**, **Lucell**: the successor of **Ciarán** of **Clonmacnoise** <note>original: Cluana mic Nóis</note>. He is also at **Rus Fothairbe** on the shore of **Lough Mask** <note>original: Locha Mesca</note> in western Connacht. <margin>Lucell, successor of Ciarán of Clonmacnoise.</margin>
**Boithéne**: I do not know where he is from, unless he is **Baithene** son of Alla.
**Fer dá Chrích**: from **Daire Éidnech**, also known as **Daire na Flann**, in **Éoganacht Caisil**.

7. **Lugaid**: from **Cell Aithgén** in the territory of **Leix** <note>original: Laichis</note> or from **Cell Chuair** in **Offaly** <note>original: Uaib Failgi</note>. Or Bishop Lugaid in **Cúil Bennchoir** in **Lúrc** on the shore of **Lough Erne**, or at **Daire Mochua** in **Kerry** <note>original: Ciarraige Luachra</note>.
**Matthew** the Evangelist. **Mark**, bishop and evangelist. According to Gregory, he was a Pope of Rome and a confessor.
**Cellach**: **Cellach the Deacon** is in **Ui Máil**, at **Disert Cellaig** to the southwest of **Glendalough** <note>original: Glenn da lacha</note>. Also **Cellach the Saxon** of Glendalough.

<header>OCTOBER 1-7.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

### NOTES.

1.  *of Priscus, that is, a martyr.*
    *of Luke, the evangelist.*
    *of Germanus, that is, a bishop and Patrick's tutor.* Of Germanus, bishop of the city of Auxerre.
    *The feast of the holy relics:* This refers to when the relics of Peter and Paul, along with Mary's hair and other remains from the great shrine in Rome, came with Sechnall <note>St. Sechnall (Secundinus) was a 5th-century bishop and nephew of St. Patrick.</note> to Armagh. Alternatively, it is the day that Maelruain's reliquary <note>A container for holy relics.</note> was completed. Or, it is to the community of Tallaght that these relics <note>original: istae reliquiae</note> were brought, and they remain with them, as others say <note>original: ut dicunt alii</note>. Some say that these relics <note>original: istae reliquiae</note>—namely the shrine of Peter and Paul—are in Armagh, and it was Sechnall who brought them there.¹

2.  *onme, that is, at the same time <note>original: simul</note>.* Or *Onme*, who was the son of a king of Leinster. He was given as a hostage to a king of "Conn's Half" (the northern half of Ireland), and the king placed him in Saint Brigit’s care to ensure his father’s obedience to her. One day, Brigit's disciples (the nuns) said to her: "Delightful is this little hostage" (*gillán*). "That shall be his name," said Brigit, "Gillán." His name was Onme at first, but he is known as a saint in Cell Gilláin in Leinster.²
    *of Eusebius, bishop and martyr, that is, a pope of Rome, etc.*
    *of Mark the evangelist, etc. Candida, that is, a virgin.*
    *of Colman Ela, that is, of Land Ela in Tír chell <note>Modern Lynally, County Offaly.</note>.*

3.  *of Mark the evangelist, etc. Candida, that is, a virgin.*
    *of Colman Ela, that is, of Land Ela in Tír chell.*

4.  *Balbine:* She is in the East. Or it refers to Bicsech of Cell Bicsige in the territory of the Huí macc Uais in Meath. <margin>In the margin:</margin> Baluina, virgin and martyr. Or perhaps Baluina is Bicsech of Cell Bicseche in the territory of the Huí Macc-uais of Meath; but this is not true <note>original: sed non est uerum</note>.

5.  *A fragment of the precious stone, that is, Sinech daughter of Fergnae.* Or she is called "excellent" (*ergna*), from Cruachan Maige Abna in the territory of the Eoganacht of Cashel. *Sinech: Fergna is her father's name.* Or she is called *ergna* (good/wise) from Cruachan Maige Abna, etc.

6.  *Lucell, abbot of Clúain, that is, abbot of Clonmacnois.* He is a successor of Ciarán of Clúain, and he is located at Ross Fothairbe on the shore of Lough Mask in the west of Connaught.
    *Boithéne:* I do not know where he is from, unless he is Baithéne mac Alla.
    *Fer dá chrích, that is, from Daire eidnech,* which is Daire na flann in the Eoganacht of Cashel.
    *of Lugaid, that is, from Cell Aitgin in Leix,* or from Cell Chúair in the territory of the Huí Failge. *Lugach, that is, bishop Lugaid* in Cúil Aithgén in Leix, or in Cúil Bennchoir in Offaly. Or he is bishop Lugach in Cúil Bennchoir in Lurc on the shore of Lough Erne. Or in Daire Mochua in Ciarraige Luachra.

7.  *Matthew, that is, the evangelist. Mark, that is, a bishop and evangelist.³*
    *According to Gregory, a pope, etc.*
    *of Cellach, that is, in the territory of the Huí Máil* is deacon Cellach; he is in Dísert Cellaig to the south-east of Glendalough. He is known as Cellach the Saxon from Glendalough.

¹ The arrival of the relics of Jesus Christ and Mary and the apostles and martyrs and prophets and virgins <note>Latin original: Aduentus reliquiarum Iesu Christi et Mariae et apostolorum et martyrum et profetarum et uirginum</note> *LL*. 363c. ² The same story is found in the *Book of Leinster* (*LL*), page 363, in the upper margin. ³ Regarding Pope Marcus, see the *Old English Martyrology* (*O.E. **Cainnech**, he was a son of Aed the Handsome <note>original: *Aed alaind*</note>, and Aghaboe is his primary church, and he has a monastery <note>original: *reicles*</note> in St. Andrews <note>original: *Cill Rigmonaig*</note> in Scotland <note>original: *Albain*</note>. Cainnech of Aghaboe.
**Loman of the scales** <note>original: *lainnech*</note>, that is, there were scales of leprosy <note>original: *lanna claime*</note> upon him.
**Cainnech, descendant of Dalann**, he was the son of Aed the Handsome, and Aghaboe is his primary church. Once, Cainnech went to Finnian to ask for a place to stay. "I do not see any space here now," said Finnian, "for everyone has taken a spot before you." "What is that empty, waste space over there?" asked Cainnech. "A demon occupies that assembly-place² <note>original: *ceti*</note>," said Finnian, "to test the monks <note>original: *mac n-ecailsi*, literally 'sons of the church'</note>." "Send me to drive him out," said Cainnech. "May it be easy for you," said Finnian. When the demon saw him coming, he said: "O you little shaven cowl³ <note>original: *cuilchi máil mbic*</note>, this shall not be your path!" "Leave the place where you are immediately!" said Cainnech. At that, the demon rose and left, and Cainnech inhabited the place after that⁴. "In the presence of God, dear brothers," said Cainnech to the people who were with him, "there is no organ of sensation in me⁵; neither my right nor left hand has ever touched it [the demon/the temptation] etc."

Fiacc, bishop of Sletty, and Fiachra his son. Fiacc, bishop of Sletty in the territory of the Ui Bairche, and Fiachra his son, and he is with him.
**Omne**, that is, a small church. The **name of a place in the wood** <note>original: *nomen loci in silua*</note> between Aghowle <note>original: *Achad Aball*</note> and Clonmore of Maedoc <note>original: *Cluain Moir Maedóc*</note>, and Fiacc and Fiachra are there. **Or Omin**, meaning **together** <note>original: *simul*</note>. **Or Little Omin** <note>original: *Omin becc*</note> is the name of a place in the wood which is between Clonmore of Maedoc and Aghowle, and it is there that Fiacc is, **as the experts say** <note>original: *ut periti ferunt*</note>. Omin, that is, a small plain between Clonmore of Maedoc and Aghowle, and it is there that Fiacc is, as the experts say.
**Mobí**, that is, from Glasnevin <note>original: *Glaissi nóiden*</note> on the north bank of the River Liffey. Mobí, son of Beoan, of the Corco Tri of the Luighne of Connacht. Huaine, daughter of Finnbarr, was **his mother** <note>original: *mater eius*</note>. He was conceived and born in the Church of the Son of Tadg <note>original: *Cill maic Taidg*</note>, and he was born from a dead woman⁸. He was "Flat-faced" <note>original: *clár-enech*</note>, because the earth pressed down on him⁹ until his face was one flat surface. Mobí the Flat-faced of Glasnevin in the territory of the foreigners <note>original: *hi nGallaib*, likely referring to the Norse area of Dublin</note>.
