10. **Fintan**¹ of Druim Ing in the territory of the Ui Segain. "Of Fintan an abbot," etc.

11. **Fortchern, Lomman**, that is, Fortchern, son of Loeguire, son of Niall, and he is in Trim <note>original: *Áth truim*</note>. Or Fortchern, that is, in the Church of Fortchern <note>original: *Cell Fortcheirn*</note> in the territory of the Ui Trea are Fortchern and Lomman. Both of them are of Trim in Brega <note>original: *Bregia*</note>; that is, Fortchern son of Loeguire of Trim in the territory of Loeguire in the east of Meath, and Lomman is also there, in Trim. Or Fortchern of the Church of Fortchern in the territory of the Ui Drona. Cainnech of Aghaboe <note>original: *Achad bó*</note> is celebrated **on the same day** <note>original: *in eodem die*</note>.

Cainnech, that is, he is the son of Aed Alaind, and Aghaboe is his principal church, and he has an abbey-church in Kilrymont <note>original: *Cell Rigmonaid*</note> (St. Andrews) in Scotland. Cainnech of Aghaboe of Cainnech.

Lomman the **scaly**, that is, because he had scales of leprosy on him.

Cainnech **of the Dálann clan** <note>original: *maccu Dálan*</note>, that is, he was the son of Aed Alaind, and Aghaboe is his principal church. Cainnech once went to Finnian <note>original: *Findén*</note> to ask for a place in which he might live. "I see no place there," says Finnian, "for everyone has taken one before you." "What is that empty place over there?" asks Cainnech. "The demon of that road is there," says Finnian, "testing the churchmen." "Let me go to him to drive him out," says Cainnech.² "May it be easy for you!" says Finnian. When the demon saw him coming towards him, he said this: "O little bald-head in a cloak!" <note>original: *clérechán*</note> says he, "this is not your path."⁴ "Leave the place where you are at once," says Cainnech. At that, the demon arose and left it, and thereafter Cainnech inhabited the place. "Before God, my dear brothers," says Cainnech to the people who were with him, "there was no limb of knowledge (?) there; neither my right hand nor my left came in contact with him," etc.³

12. **Declare Fiacc and Fiachra**, that is, **tell of** <note>original: *narra*</note> Fiacc of Sletty <note>original: *Slébte*</note>; that is, Fiacc, bishop of Sletty, and Fiachra his son. Fiacc of Sletty in the territory of the Ui Bairche, etc.

**Omne**, that is, a small church; the name of a place in a wood between Aghowle <note>original: *Achad Aball*</note> and Clonmore of Maedoc <note>original: *Cluain mór Maedóic*</note>, **and there are** <note>original: *et ibi sunt*</note> Fiacc and Fiachra. Omin, that is, **at the same time** <note>original: *simul*</note>. Or Omin the Small, etc. Omin, that is, a small plain between Clonmore of Maedoc and Aghowle, and Fiacc is there, as experts say.

**Mobi**, that is, of Glasnevin on the bank of the river Liffey on the north side. Mobi⁴ son of Beóán, of the Corco Tri of the Luigni of Connaught. Uaine, Finnbarr’s daughter, was his mother. He was conceived and brought forth in the Church of the son of Tadg <note>original: *Cell maic Taidg*</note>, and he was begotten of a dead woman.⁵ He was "table-faced," for the earth pressed him down, so that

¹ His genealogy is in the *Book of Leinster* <note>original: *LL*</note>, page 350g.
² The *Franciscan Manuscript* <note>original: *F.*</note> has: “The place shall be left,” says Cainnech. He fades away at once, and Cainnech inhabited the place.
³ The *Franciscan Manuscript* <note>original: *F.*</note> has: “the limb by which my disgrace was caused you have never seen.”
⁴ See his genealogy in the *Book of Leinster* <note>original: *LL*</note>, page 352g.
⁵ This horrible sin <note>referring to the circumstances of his birth</note> was the first of the four for which there was no penance in Ireland: that is, **intercourse with a dead person** <note>original: *coiblige mairb*</note>, **incest with a relative** <note>original: *díall fri coibdelaig*</note>, **falling from high holy orders** <note>original: *toitim fo uasalgrad*</note>, and **malicious informing** <note>original: *forneis*</note>.

<header>THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS.</header>

<header>[THE MONTH OF OCTOBER.</header>

**Berchan** is the name of **Mobi**. **Beóáith** son of **Senach** was his father's name <note>original: *nomen patris eius*</note>, and **Huanir the Fair**, daughter of **Finnbarr**, was his mother's name <note>original: *nomen matris eius*</note>.
**Mobi**, that is, from **Glasnevin** <note>original: *Glais Noeden*</note> on the bank of the river **Liffey** <note>original: *Lifi*</note> for the festival from the north. Mobi son of Beoid of the Corcu Fir of the **Luigne of Connacht**. **Hunide** daughter of **Finnbarr** was his mother. He is also associated with **Cill Maic Taidg**. <gloss>¹ Roeden</gloss>

13. **Marcill**, that is, a bishop. **Marcellus** suffered martyrdom in **Scotland** <note>original: *in Caledonia passus est*</note>.

**Findsige**, that is, from **Irnaide** in the territory of the **Ui Airennain** in **Tyrone** <note>original: *Ceinel Eogain*</note>, or perhaps she was at **Slieve Guaire** in **Gailenga**. **Finsech** the virgin <note>original: *uirgo*</note>, and **Irnaide** is the name of her foundation <note>original: *nomen ciuitatis eius*</note> in Slieve Guaire in Gailenga.

14. **Calesti**, that is, **Pope Callixtus** suffered under **Alexander** <note>original: *Calistus papa sub Alaxandro passus est*</note>. **Colum** the priest from **Lough Melvin** <note>original: *Loch Melge*</note> is celebrated here.

15. **Maurorum**, that is, a great race of people <note>original: *cined mor do dáinib*</note>. The **Moors** suffered in **Gaul** <note>original: *Mauri in Gallia passi sunt*</note>.

16. **Ciar**, that is, in **Africa** <note>original: *in Affrica*</note>.

17. **Riagail**, that is, the saint of **Mucinnis** <note>original: *sanctus Mucinnssi*</note> <gloss>² Muiccinsi</gloss> on **Lough Derg** <note>original: *Loch Deirgdeirc*</note>.
**Colman**, that is, the bishop of **Killruadh** in **Dal Araide**. **Colmán of Killruadh** on the bank of **Belfast Lough** <note>original: *Locha lóig*</note> in **Ulster**, and he was a bishop.

18. **Trifonia**, that is, the wife of **Decius**, King of the Romans <note>original: *uxor Deci regis Romanorum*</note>. **Drofime**, that is, the wife of Decius, Emperor of the Romans <note>original: *uxor Deci imperatoris Romanorum*</note>.

19. **Beronic** and **Maignenn**, abbot of **Kilmainham** <note>original: *Cille Maighnenn*</note>, and **Crinan** of **Cuil Connlaigh**, and **Cronan** of **Tomgraney** <note>original: *Tuama Gréné*</note>, and **Faelan** are here.

20. **Eutychius** the martyr <note>original: *Eutaicc martir*</note>. He suffered martyrdom in **Nicomedia** <note>original: *in Necomedia passus est*</note>.

21. **Fintan Maeldub** of **Durrow** <note>original: *Dermaig*</note> <gloss>³ dirmaich</gloss> in the territory of the **Ui Duach** in **Ossory**. **Maeldub** <note>meaning: "Black-tonsured one"</note> was his proper name, but he made a union with **Fintan of Clonenagh** <note>original: *Cluana ednech*</note> in **Laois** <note>original: *Laichis*</note>, so that each was given the name of the other; and "Fintan" is said of him in commemoration of their fellowship <note>original: *in commemorationem societatis eius*</note>. As a sign of the union.

Concerning **Maeldub**, however, they say he might have belonged to the **Eoganacht of Cashel**, or he is of the seed of **Brian** son of **Eochaid Mugmedon**: that is, Maeldub son of **Amalgaid**, son of **Fothad**, son of **Conall Gulban**, son of Brian, son of Eochaid Mugmedon.

It is this **Maeldub** who took **Feichin of Fore** <note>original: *Feichín Fobair*</note> as his student and sent him to study. Feichin’s good deeds and piety grew so much that Maeldub made Feichin the cellarer <note>steward of the monastery</note> over the community, and the **People of Maeldub** <note>original: *Muinter Mail duib*</note> are descended from him. And it was after Maeldub's death that Feichin said:

Maeldub was an enemy to the dark, enslaving demons; <gloss>⁴ so in L. dark-black R².</gloss>
except for his cowl and his linen shroud, he possessed nothing of the world.

Michael the Archangel gave testimony of Maeldub—good is he for whom it was given;
since he entered into noble piety, he never laid his ear upon a pillow.

Michael’s testimony for Maeldub—great is that testimony for a son of man;
except for the King of the stars, the Son of Mary, there is no one better to pray to.

Though he might say, "My back is sore," it was not from carrying a heavy burden;
the bent body would not be weary if he had done any evil or error.

### MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

<margin>OCTOBER 13–20.</margin>

...he was like a single flat board. **Mobí the Table-faced** <note>This refers to the nickname *Clárenech*, meaning "flat-faced" or "board-faced," often associated with a miraculous physical condition or an ascetic practice.</note> of **Glasnevin** in the territory occupied by the Danes. **Berchán** was Mobí's original name. **Beóáith** son of **Senach** was his father's name, and **Huanir the Fair**, daughter of **Finnbarr**, was his mother's name. Mobí, etc.

13. **Findsech**, that is, from the **Irnaide** <note>modern: Urney</note> in the territory of the **Uí Airennáin** in **Tyrone** <note>original: *Cenél Eogain*</note>; or it may be that Irnaide should be located in **Slieve Guaire** in **Gailenga**. **Findsech** was a virgin, and Irnaide is the name of her convent in Slieve Guaire in Gailenga.

14. Of **Calixtus**, that is, a pope of **Rome** who suffered martyrdom under **Alexander**.¹ **Colum** the priest <note>original: *presbyter*</note> of **Lough Melvin** <note>original: *Loch Melge*</note> is commemorated here.

15. Of the **Mauri**, that is, a great race of men <note>The Moors</note>.

16. **Riagail**, that is, a saint of **Muckinish** <note>original: *Mucc-inis*</note> in **Lough Derg**.
**Colmán**, that is, the bishop of **Cell Rúaid** in **Dalaradia**. Colmán of Cell Rúaid is on the shore of **Lough Larne** <note>original: *Loch Lóig*</note> in **Ulster**, and he was a bishop.

18. Of **Tryphonia, wife of Decius** <note>original: *Trifoniae uxoris Decii*</note>, *Book of Leinster* <note>original: *LL*</note> 364a.²

19. **Beronicus** and **Maignenn**, abbot of **Kilmainham**, and **Crinán** of **Cúil Connlaigh**, and **Cronán** of **Tuamgraney** <note>original: *Tuaim gréne*</note>, and **Faelán** are celebrated here.

20. **Fintan Maeldub** of **Durrow** <note>original: *Daermag*</note> of the **Uí Duach** in **Ossory**. Now, **Maeldub** was his proper name; but he and **Fintan** of **Clonenagh** <note>original: *Clúain Eidnech*</note> in **Laois** <note>original: *Leix*</note> made a spiritual union, and each of them gave his name to the other **in commemoration of their friendship** <note>original: *in commemorationem societatis eius*</note>.

**Maeldub**: However, some say that Maeldub was of the **Eoganacht of Cashel**; or he is of the race of **Brian** son of **Eochaid Muidmedón**, namely Maeldub son of **Amalgad**, son of **Fothad**, son of **Conall Glúne**, son of Brian, son of Eochaid Muidmedón.

It is that Maeldub whom **Féchin of Fore** took with him as a foster-child and set to his studies. His good work and his devotion increased so much that Féchin made him the steward <note>original: *cellarer*</note> for the community; and from his family comes the **Muintir Maelduib**. After his death, Féchin said:

> Maeldub, foe of the base, dark devils,
> Except for his cloak and his linen sheet, he owned nothing of this world.
> The testimony which **Michael** bore for Maeldub—
> Good was he for whom the angel gave it:
> Since he entered the noble religious life, he never rested his ear upon a pillow.
> Michael’s testimony of Maeldub—great witness for a son of man;
> Except for the King of the stars, Mary's Son, there is no one better to pray to.
> Though I should say "my back is sore," it would not be from carrying a heavy burden:
> Even a small midge would not grow weary from the weight of the evil or error that Maeldub committed.

...confession <note>original: *choibsen*</note>, *Yellow Book of Lecan* <note>original: *Lebar Brecc*</note> 10ᵇ. See Liebrecht, *On Folklore* <note>original: *Zur Volkskunde*</note>, p. 54 (The Dead of Lustnau), and especially the extracts from Mapes in the same work, p. 58. See also *The Book of John Mandeville* and the Gaelic version § 36, *Celtic Journal* <note>original: *Celt. Zeitsch.*</note> ii. 26.

I will give a testimony for **Maeldub**,
It is not the testimony of a man in peril,
That a fly could not escape from his grasp,
[In spite of] all that Maeldub of the back of the head <note>original: *do chul Moel dub*</note> did of sin.

21. **Fintan**, that is, **Munnu**. He is Fintan, that is, **Munna**, son of **Telchán** the druid. For this reason he is called Fintan here: he made a union <note>original: *aenta*</note> with **Fintan of Clonenagh** in **Leix**, so that each of them gave his name to the other in commemoration of their fellowship <note>original: *in commemoratione societatis*</note>. He is Munna son of Techlán from **Taghmon** <note>original: *Tig Munnu*</note> in **Hy Kinsellagh** and in **Meath**.

<insert>[son of Telchán]</insert> **Munna** and **Digde** were the children of **Telchán**, son of **Deg**, son of **Trén**, son of **Dubthach**, son of **Bán**, son of **Fiacha Araide**, son of **Feidlimid Rechtada**, son of **Carthach** <unclear>(?)</unclear>, son of **Daigre**, son of **Erc**, son of **Imchad**, son of **Lám-feola**, son of **Cliathaire**, son of **Focha**, son of **Dubthach Donn**.

<insert>[Colum Cille said:]</insert>
O little servant of powerful God,
O son of Telchán, O staff-bearer,
A beloved son has been born to my people;
The mother who bore you, O **Fintan** (that is, **Munna**).

"Crucified" <note>original: *crochtha*</note>, that is, he had leprosy <note>original: *claime*</note>. And **Mochua** son of **Lonán** healed him of the leprosy.
**Munna** son of **Telchán** said this below:

A victory of craft and a victory of a house
From me to the grandson of **Lonán of Meath**,
A victory of a son for whom Ireland shall be full,
As a reward for his rising to the grandson of **Tulchán**.

He fell by fair **Fintan**,
Before every tooth that was in his head,
And he shall fall by him shortly before the Judgment,
The king to whom beautiful **Tara** is a hereditary right.

22. **Philip**: At **Adrianople** in **Thrace**, **Philip** and **Eusebius** suffered martyrdom <note>original: *passi sunt*</note>.

23. *The departure <note>original: *Escomlud*</note> of Longinus*. **Longinus** and **Egitianus** are the names of the soldiers who stood near the cross of Christ <note>original: *iuxta crucem Christi*</note>. Longinus pierced the side of Christ <note>original: *taeb Crist*</note> and preached after his tongue was cut out <note>original: *precisam lingam*</note>. **Egitianus** gave him wine mixed with vinegar <note>original: *uinum acetum*</note>. Longinus, seeing the signs that occurred on that day—namely, the sun darkened, the rocks split, and the earth shaken—believed in the Lord Jesus. He lived in the city of **Caesarea** in **Cappadocia** and in the region of the province which is in **Asia Minor**, leading the quiet life of a monk <note>original: *monócorum*</note>. He lived for twenty-eight years and suffered martyrdom under the governor <note>original: *praeside*</note> **Octavian**.

24. **Erc**, daughter of **Sinill**, from **Imlech**; **Finngán**, son of **Airchinnech**, from **Diamar**; **Daliba**, from **Cúil maic Lurchaire**; **Lonán** of **Cluain Tibrinne**; and two named **Colmán** are commemorated here.

25. **Laisrén**, that is, from **Ard maic Nasca** <note>original: *Ard míc Naxair*</note> in **Ulster**. **Laisrén** from **Ard maic Nasca** on the shore of **Lough Larne** <note>original: *Loch Laig*</note> in **Ulster**.

26. **Nassán**, **Beóán**, **Mellán**, that is, from **Tamlaght** <note>original: *Tamlachtu*</note> near **Lough Brickland** <note>original: *Locha Bricrenn*</note>. These are three British saints in one church in **Iveagh** <note>original: *Huaib Echach*</note> of **Ulster**, near the Tamlaght of the son of **Ua Caill** in **Lough Brickland**.

### OCTOBER 21–26.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

I will bear witness regarding **Maeldub**—and it is not the witness of a reckless man—that a midge could carry in its claw every sin that **Maeldub** ever committed. <note>Compare this to the Quran, Chapter 99: "And whoever shall have wrought an atom's weight of good shall behold it; and whoever shall have wrought an atom's weight of evil shall behold it."</note>

21. **Fintan**, also known as **Munnu**. He is **Fintan**, also called **Munnu**,<sup>1</sup> son of **Telchán** the druid <note>original: "wizard"</note>. He was called Fintan because of the spiritual union that he and **Fintan of Clonenagh** in **Leix** formed; they exchanged names in commemoration of their fellowship <note>original: *in commemoratione societatis*</note>. This is **Munnu** son of **Techlán**, of **Taghmon** <note>original: *Tech Munnu*</note> in **Wexford** <note>original: *Húi Cennselaig*</note> and in **Meath**.
**Munnu** and **Digde**<sup>2</sup> were the children of **Telchán**, son of **Dega**, son of **Tren**, son of **Dubthach**, son of **Ban**, son of **Fiacha Araide**, son of **Feidlimid Rechtaid**, son of **Carthach**, son of **Daigre**, son of **Erc**, son of **Imchad**, son of **Lám feola**, son of **Clíathaire**, son of **Focha**, son of **Dubthach Donn**.

**Colum Cille** said:
> O little servant of mighty God, O son of **Telchán**, O fellow,
> The mother who bore you, O **Fintan** (that is, **Munnu**), 
> Bore a hardy son for my company!

*Crucified*: This means he suffered from leprosy, and **Mochua** son of **Lonán** healed him of the disease.
**Munnu** son of **Tulchán** said the following:
> A gift of knowledge and a gift of a house from me to the grandson of **Lonán of Meath**,
> A gift of a son of whom Ireland will be full, a reward for his rising to **Tulchán’s** grandson.
> There fell by **Fintan the Fair** a king for every tooth in his head,
> And shortly before the Judgment <note>original: "Doom"</note>, there will fall by him a king to whom flower-swarded **Tara** is due.

**Philip**: At **Edirne** <note>original: "Adrianople"</note> in **Thrace**, **Philip** and **Eusebius** suffered martyrdom.

23. **The departure of Longinus**: **Longinus** and **Egítianus**, etc. This refers to **Longinus**<sup>3</sup> who wounded Christ’s side and preached the Gospel even after his tongue had been cut out. **Egítianus**, etc.

24. **Erc**, daughter of **Sinell**, of **Imlíuch**; and **Finngan** son of **Airchinnech**, of **Diamair**; and **Daliba** from **Cúíl mic Lurchairi**; and **Lonán** of **Clúain Tibrinne**; and two **Colmáns** are commemorated here.

25. **Laisrén**: From **Ard macc Nascai** (?) in **Ulster**; that is, from **Art maic Nasca** on the shore of **Belfast Lough** <note>original: *Loch Laig*</note> in **Ulster**.

26. **Nassan, Beoan, Mellan**: In **Tamlachta** near **Loch Bricrenn**. These are three saints of **Britain** in the same church in **Iveagh** <note>original: *Húi Echach*</note> of **Ulster**, near **Tamlachta Maccu-cuill** on **Loch Bricrenn**.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [THE MONTH OF OCTOBER.]

**Násad**, **Beoan**, and **Mellán**: these are three saints from **Britain** who are together in one church—namely, in **Tamlachta Menann** by **Lough Brickland**.
**Násad**, **Beoan**, and **Mellán**: three from **Britain** in one church—namely, in **Tamlachta Menann** in **Iveagh**, **Ulster**.

<margin>1 Or "they are eaten" <note>This may be a wordplay or a reference to a variant reading "íthfíadar"</note>, namely four sons.</margin>
The four—namely, the four daughters of **Hier**: **Dairblinn**, **Dairmill**, **Coel**, and **Comgall** from **Kill-na-ningean** <note>original: "Cill na n-ingen," meaning "Church of the Maidens"</note> south of **Tallaght** <note>original: "Tamlachta"</note> in **South Dublin** <note>original: "Uí Dunchada"</note>; or they are from the **House of the Britons** in the sanctuary of **Kells**, as some say. They are from **Kill-na-ningean** beside **Tallaght** of **Maelruain**.

27. **Erc of Donaghmore**, etc.: from **Maynooth** near **Laraghbryan** in **North Kildare** <note>original: "Uí Faeláin"</note>. From **Maynooth** in the northern part of **North Kildare**.

**Abban**, descendant of **Cormac**: from **Killabban** in **Leix/Carlow** <note>original: "Uí Muiredaig"</note> and from **Moyarney** <note>original: "Mag Ernaidi"</note> in **Wexford** <note>original: "Uí Ceinnselaig"</note> (specifically in **Uí Buide**). He is himself the grandson of **Cormac**, and his birthday is celebrated here.

**Abban**, son of **Laignech**, son of **Cainnech**, son of **Imchad**, son of **Cormac**, son of **Cú Corb**.

> Seventeen bright years—an addition to the count of three hundred—
> Was the lifespan of the beautiful, noble **Abban**, while he was in the body.
<note>This suggests Abban lived to the legendary age of 317 years.</note>

**Abban** in **Uí Muiredaig**; the grandson of **Cormac** in **Moyarney** in **Wexford** and in **Killabban** in **Uí Muiredaig**.

**Odran**: a priest from **Tyfarnham** in **Meath**, or from **Latteragh** <note>original: "Lettracha Odran"</note> in **Munster**, or from the cemetery of **Odran** in **Iona**.
**Odran**: namely, **Odran** from **Latteragh** in **Munster**, and from **Tyfarnham** in **Meath**, or from **Iona**; or he is in **Gair meic Moga**—that is, a desert island in **Corca Dhuibhne**, and it was by swimming that he went into it.

**Colman**, grandson of **Fiachra**: in **Templeshanbo** <note>original: "Senbothaib fola"</note> in **Wexford**. In his church are the "ducks," and no one dares to harm them. For even if they are cast by mistake at night into water over a fire—even if the wood of the entire world were burned under the cauldron—the water does not get hot until they are put back into the same pond.

If you have food on Sunday, give it for God’s sake;
If you do not have it, buy it; if you cannot buy it, lament. <note>original: "Ma rotfia caith i ndomnach ar Día..." This is a pious maxim about charity and observing the Sabbath.</note>

<margin>2 This note appears in the lower margin of the Leabhar Breac MS: "If you have food on Sunday for God... if you have it not, buy it... if you buy it not, weep."</margin>
A priest performing Communion or baptizing—small is the profit <note>original: "tarba"</note> of it; no baptism comes from him after he has visited his mistress <note>original: "cailligi"</note>. <note>A stern warning regarding clerical celibacy and the validity of sacraments performed by "unworthy" priests.</note>

28. **Jude and Simon**: namely **Judas** by another name, and **Simon the Zealot** <note>original: "Simon Cannaneus"</note>.
**Thaddeus**, who is called **Judas**, but not the betrayer of **Christ**. **Simon the Zealot**, who is said to be the brother of **Jude** the apostle.

<margin>3 "His baptizing is of little profit," from Brussels MS 5100.</margin>
29. **Quintus**: a martyr, and many others with him. **Taimthene**: a virgin.
A proper name of a virgin.

<header>THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS.</header>

# NOVEMBER.

**November 1.** *The Calends <note>The first day</note> of November.*
Lonán, Colmán, and Cronán, with their bright, radiant following; the vast and certain hosts of Hilarius <note>original: *Helair*</note> surely honor the stormy festival of All Saints <note>original: *samain síanaig*</note>.

**November 2.** *The 4th day before the Nones of November.*
The senior apostle of our land, Patrick—a primary pillar—granted a blessing of victory to Bishop Erc of Slane.

**November 3.** *The 3rd day before the Nones of November.*
Announce Hilarius from across the great sea; Murdebar, the crown <note>original: *mind*; literally "diadem" or "relic"</note> of a synod; and the fair festival of Corcu-nutan, held on the feast day of Cóemán of Enach.

**November 4.** *The day before the Nones of November.*
Beloved as the sun that never fails, with a great and fearless following, is Perpetua, who is without reproach and the excellent wife of Peter <note>original Latin: *coniunx Petri*. Tradition identifies her as the wife of the Apostle Peter</note>.

**November 5.** *The Nones of November.*
The passion <note>The suffering or martyrdom</note> of the famous Domninus, around whom young boys were slain. Colmán of Glenn Delmaicc was also filled to the brim with the grace of God.

<lang>Irish</lang>
<page-num>233</page-num>
<header>NOVEMBER 6–10.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

### November 6. <note>original Latin: *B. viii. idus Novembris*</note>
Although people destroyed them by a splendid martyrdom, the host of Adrianus <note>Saint Adrian and his companions</note> has reached the mysterious Kingdom of Heaven.

### November 7. <note>original Latin: *C. vii. idus Novembris*</note>
The vast company of Eusebius—though their slaughter was painful—has found a mighty prize: a great land on the plain of heaven.

### November 8. <note>original Latin: *D. vi. idus Novembris*</note>
In heaven rises the shout of Claudinus; a beautiful procession went without any insults <note>original: *áera*; referring to satires or poetic curses, suggesting they died in peace or with dignity</note> to the festival that fills the lands of Barrfind, the great son of Aed.

### November 9. <note>original Latin: *E. v. idus Novembris*</note>
Donatus and Damian were not shameless mockers <note>original: *ecnaig anblí*; literally "shameless revilers"</note>; celebrated at the same joyful festival is the feast of the wealthy <note>meaning spiritually rich or well-provided</note> Sínech.

### November 10. <note>original Latin: *F. iv. idus Novembris*</note>
Aed, son of Brecc, of the royal line; he was almost greater than death itself. He stands high in the great Kingdom, the champion of the descendants of Conn of the Hundred Battles <note>Conn Cétchathach, a legendary High King of Ireland and ancestor of the Uí Néill dynasty</note>.

***

<vocab>Martyrology of Oengus: A 9th-century Irish calendar of saints; Adrianus: A martyr likely associated with the group of Nicomedian martyrs; Eusebius: Likely the Bishop of Vercelli or one of several martyrs by this name; Barrfind: An Irish saint associated with Druim Cuilinn; Aed mac Bricc: A 6th-century bishop and saint from Meath, famous for his miracles; Conn of the Hundred Battles: A legendary ancestor of many Irish dynasties; Old Irish: The language of the original poem (c. 800 AD); Middle Irish: The language of the later manuscript copies.</vocab>

The text emphasizes the spiritual triumph of these figures over physical death and their high status in the "Kingdom of Heaven."</summary>

<lang>Irish</lang>
<page-num>234</page-num>
<header>THE CALENDAR OF OENGUS</header>
<header>THE MONTH OF NOVEMBER</header>

### November 11 <note>original Latin: *G. iii. idus Novembris*</note>
Carbre of Coleraine <note>original: *Cúlae Rathin*</note>—
royal grace across the great sea!
Saint Martin <note>Saint Martin of Tours, a highly influential monk and bishop in Western Christianity</note>—a noble comparison—
the mountain of gold of the western world.

### November 12 <note>original Latin: *A. Pridie idus Novembris*</note>
There has been given,
along with wisdom, knowledge <note>original: *soas*; refers to specialized or spiritual learning</note>, and much prudence,
to my Cumman of beautiful spiritual warfare <note>original: *mílti*; often refers to the "soldiery of Christ" or monastic discipline</note>,
the fair, tall son of Fiachna.

### November 13 <note>original Latin: *B. Idibus Novembris*</note>
On the Ides of November was the death <note>original: *estecht*; literally "hearing" or "departure"</note> of Eutychius,
a martyr, if you have commemorated him;
before high Christmas, you should offer
great prayer at the beginning of the Lent of Moses <note>Advent, the forty-day period of fasting before Christmas, which in the early Irish church was sometimes called the "Lent of Moses" or "St. Martin's Lent"</note>.

### November 14 <note>original Latin: *C. xviii. cal. Decembris*</note>
Celebrate the feasts
of Clement and Colmán;
in preparation for the birth of the Virgin-born Christ,
begin your diligent lessons <note>original: *lechsa*; likely referring to spiritual readings, chants, or monastic rules</note>.

### November 15 <note>original Latin: *D. xvii. cal. Decembris*</note>
At the suffering of Secundinus <note>Saint Sechnall, a 5th-century bishop and contemporary of St. Patrick</note>,
with a host of every color <note>possibly referring to various ranks of martyrs or monks</note>,
if the coming Lent <note>Advent</note> alarms you,
begin a portion of your spiritual battle.

***

¹ **Carbre:** Variants include *Corpbri* or *Cairpre*.
² **Grace:** "Without a synonymous name, without speech | east and west / With a synonymous name, with speech, or Carbre of Cúil Rathin." Another version: "Fair the name, fair the speech | east and west, even across the great sea."
³ **Western:** Various spellings for "western."
⁴ **Has been given:** Various manuscript spellings of the verb.
⁵ **Wisdom:** Variants include *saithi* or *suidhe*.
⁶ **Knowledge:** Or *sofis* (literally "good knowledge").
⁷ **Prudence:** Variants include *tiachraid*, *ciachra*, or *tiachrae*.
⁸ **To:** Or *do*.
⁹ **Cumman:** Variants include *Cumma* or *Chumíne*.
¹⁰ **Spiritual warfare:** Variants include *milte*, *milti*, or *milnecht*.
¹¹ **Fiachna:** Some manuscripts list the name as *Fiachrai*.
¹² **On the Ides:** "Forrith" or "For íd."
¹³ **Death:** Variants of *etsecht* (departure/death).
¹⁴ **If you have commemorated:** *ma imrordaiss*; glossed as "if I have recounted/mentioned."
¹⁵ **Christmas:** Various spellings of *Notlaic*.

<header>NOVEMBER 16–20.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

### November 16 <note>original Latin: *E. xvi. cal. Decembris*—16 days before the Calends of December</note>
The company <note>original: *clíar*</note> of Bishop Augustine, who loved a three-day fast <note>original: *tredan*</note> above all else; a great and sharp grief overcame them—forty beautiful and faithful souls.

### November 17 <note>original Latin: *F. xv. cal. Decembris*—15 days before the Calends of December</note>
Celebrate the feast of Thecla; it was after her victory that she passed away <note>literally: "she has fallen"</note>. Buaidbeo <note>likely a place name or personified city</note> is a lasting, strong city, along with the beautiful Duilech of Clochar.

### November 18 <note>original Latin: *G. xiv. cal. Decembris*—14 days before the Calends of December</note>
Sing of the consecration of the churches <note>original: *neclas*</note> of Peter and of excellent Paul; it is the bright feast of royal Ronan, the virginal son of Berach.

### November 19 <note>original Latin: *A. xiii. cal. Decembris*—13 days before the Calends of December</note>
Tell of the consecration of the basilica of John, a son without reproach; forty sinless ones went with Maximus, among many champions.

### November 20 <note>original Latin: *B. xii. cal. Decembris*—12 days before the Calends of December</note>
Beseech Escon along with Froechan in front of strong Slieve Bloom <note>original: *Bledma*</note>, together with the mysterious sufferings of the hosts of Bassus beneath the clouds.

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS [MONTH OF NOVEMBER]

### November 21 <note>original Latin: *C. xi. cal. Decembris*—11 days before the Calends of December</note>
A holy pair <note>original Old Irish: *Nóebdecheng*</note> has departed to Christ on the feast of Clement's birth: Colmán, son of Commán, from the island of Aran, and Aedán, son of Congrad, from Ireland.

### November 22 <note>original Latin: *D. x. cal. Decembris*—10 days before the Calends of December</note>
After suffering martyrdom—O Mary, what a shining light!—the beautiful and radiant Cecilia <note>St. Cecilia, the patroness of music</note> ran to the angelic Prince <note>original: *rígmacc nainglech*, literally "angelic King-son," referring to Christ</note>.

### November 23 <note>original Latin: *E. ix. cal. Decembris*—9 days before the Calends of December</note>
The fair suffering of Clement occurred among the waves of the sea; his city is now honored <note>original: *adorthar*</note> beneath the waves of the wide ocean <note>original: *lir lethain*. This refers to the legend that the sea receded every year to reveal a divinely built temple containing the tomb of St. Clement, who was martyred by being drowned with an anchor.</note>.

### November 24 <note>original Latin: *F. viii. cal. Decembris*—8 days before the Calends of December</note>
Along with Cianan of Duleek <note>original: *Doimlíacc*, meaning "House of Stones," referring to one of the first stone churches in Ireland</note>, who is like a fine ear of our wheat <note>a metaphor for a choice soul</note>; also Colmán, the energetic son of Lenéne, together with Colmán Duib of Cuilenn.

### November 25 <note>original Latin: *G. vii. cal. Decembris*—7 days before the Calends of December</note>
With John Cassian, whose clerical tonsure <note>original: *corann*, "crown" or tonsure</note> is most beautiful; and from the fair territory of Croch went Findchú of Brigown <note>original: *Bríg gobann*, meaning "Hill of the Smiths"</note>.

# NOVEMBER 26–30: THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS

### November 26 <note>original Latin: *A. vi. cal. Decembris*—6 days before the Calends of December</note>
Beseech a steadfast, numerous pair,
along with a holy <note>original Old Irish: *bán*, literally "white" or "fair"</note>, triumphant people:
Banbán, a sparkling spark of gold,
and Bishop Syricus <note>likely Pope Siricius</note>, the prolific.

### November 27 <note>original Latin: *B. v. cal. Decembris*—5 days before the Calends of December</note>
A stream of wisdom with splendor:
Sechnall <note>also known as St. Secundinus, traditionally a nephew of St. Patrick</note>, the crown of our lords,
who sang a melody—a noble benefit!—
in praise of Patrick of Armagh <note>this refers to the *Audite Omnes Amantes*, the first Latin hymn written in Ireland</note>.

### November 28 <note>original Latin: *C. iv. cal. Decembris*—4 days before the Calends of December</note>
A chief trio that is not fleeting,
along with Trophimus the persistent;
the three sons of Bochra—a perpetual triumph!—
from the smooth field of Achad Rathin.

### November 29 <note>original Latin: *D. iii. cal. Decembris*—3 days before the Calends of December</note>
The royal feast of Brendan of Birr <note>one of the "Twelve Apostles of Ireland"</note>,
against whom the surface of the sea bursts forth;
he was a fair crown, a great cry <note>original: *már ńualann*</note>,
the holy leader of Ireland’s prophets.

### November 30 <note>original Latin: *E. Pridie cal. Decembris*—the day before the Calends of December</note>
Andrew <note>St. Andrew the Apostle</note>, who is the boldest,
facing the cross—a step most perfect—
crowns the hosts of November, 
as I declare.

***

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [NOVEMBER.]</header>

### NOTES

**1. Lonán, Colmán, Cronán.**
That is <note>original: *.i.*, an abbreviation for the Latin *id est*</note>, Lonán son of Talmag from Treoit in Brega <note>a region in north County Dublin and Meath</note>. Or perhaps Lonán son of Telchán from Cluain Fota in Laighis <note>modern County Laois</note>.
Lonán was the son of Talmag, and his mother was Dustricc, daughter of the King of the Britons. It was she who gave her love to Rioc of Inis Bó Finne <note>the Island of the White Cow</note>. Talmag went to her in Rioc’s shape, and she became pregnant by him. It was because of this that Mugint was killed later, as it was said:

->Talmag, a disciple without reproach, was together with Finnian;<-
->his son was Lonán, a festival without fault, and Dustric was his mother.<-

->Dustric, daughter of the King of the Britons, though she was active, she was not afraid;<-
->she was young, her hand <note>original: *dót*</note> was perfect, until she gave her love to Rioc.<-

Colmán son of Dimma from Tig macc nDimma in Uí Cellaig Cualann <note>a territory south of Dublin</note>. And from Daire Dimma near Cluain Eidnech. Or Colmán son of Findchad, son of [ ], from Cluain Bruiches beside the river Flesc, and he was in Dun Fleisci before that.
Cronán, that is, Cronán son of Ua Cuinn from Tuaim Gréne <note>modern Tomgraney</note> in Munster.

**2. He gave a blessing.**
That is, at Ferta Fer Feic on the western side of Síd Truim, Patrick gave a blessing to Erc of Slane during the first Easter of his arrival in Ireland. Bishop Erc of Slane's son was the bishop of Arda Sretha <note>modern Ardstraw</note>.
Slane, that is, in Brega.

**3. Hilary.**
That is, the Pope of Rome <note>referring to Pope Hilarus</note>. Or Hilary, the bishop and abbot of Poitiers, who composed the hymn *Ymnum Dicat* <note>original Latin: *Ymnum dicat fecit/cecinit* — "He made/sang the hymn 'Let us say a hymn'"</note>.

<margin>¹ As recorded in the Book of Leinster, page 373: Trust, the king of the noble harbor by the shore, possessed an only daughter, completely sound; Dustric, distinguished for every happiness, was the mother of Lonán son of Talmag.
² *Engach* is interpreted as "pure from sin."
³ Possibly meaning "labor" or "hardship."
⁴ The story is told in the preface to the hymn of Saint Mugint (*Parce Domine*, "Spare, O Lord"): Finnian of Moville went to study with Mugint, along with Rioc, Talmag, and others. Drust was then King of the Britons and had a daughter named Drusticc. He gave her to Mugint to be taught. She fell in love with Rioc and said to Finnian: "I will give you all the books Mugint has for you to copy if you give Rioc to me in marriage." That night, Finnian sent Talmag to her in the form of Rioc. He slept with her, and thus Lonán of Treoit was conceived and born. However, Drusticc believed that Rioc had slept with her and claimed Rioc was the father. But this was false, for Rioc was a virgin. Mugint was then enraged and sent a certain boy into the church, saying to him: "If anyone enters the church tonight before you, strike him with an axe." He said this because Finnian usually went to the church first. Yet that night, by the Lord's prompting, Mugint himself arrived at the church first, and the boy struck him. As the prophet said: "His sorrow shall be turned upon himself and his iniquity shall descend upon his own head." Then Mugint said, *Parce* ("Spare me"). The scene of this tragedy was Futerna, now Whithorn in Galloway.</margin>

<header>NOVEMBER 1-3.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

## NOTES.

1. **Lonán, Colmán, Cronán.**
**i.** Lonán son of Talmach, from Treoit in Brega <note>an ancient territory in modern-day Meath and Dublin</note>. Or perhaps Lonán son of Telchan, from Cluain Fota in Leix <note>modern County Laois</note>.
Lonán was the son of Talmach, and Drustic, daughter of the king of Britain, was his mother. It was she who fell in love with Ríóc of Inis Bó Finne <note>the Island of the White Cow</note>. Talmach, taking Ríóc’s shape, went to her, and she became pregnant by him. Because of this, Mugint was later killed, as it was said <note>original: *ut dixit*</note>:
->Talmach, a disciple without disgrace, was with Finnian,<-
->Lonán—a festival without shame—was his son, and Drustic was his mother.<-
->Drustic, daughter of the king of Britain, though she was innocent, she was not timid;<-
->she was a virgin, her hardship was great, so that she gave her love to Ríóc.<- <note>See the margin for the full story of this deception.</note>
**Colmán** son of Dimma, of Tech mac nDimmai in Uí Cellaig Cualann <note>a territory south of Dublin</note>, and of Daire Dimma near Clonenagh. Or Colmán son of Findchad son of . . . , from Cluain Bruiches beside the river Flesc; he was originally based in Dún Fleisce.
**Cronán**, that is <note>original: *.i.*</note>, Cronán the great-grandson of Conn, from Tomgraney in Thomond <note>modern County Clare</note>.

2. **He bestowed a blessing**, that is, in Ferta Fer Féic <note>the Grave of the Men of Fiacc</note>, on the western side of Síd Truim. There, Patrick gave a blessing to Erc of Slane during the first Easter <note>original: *prima pascha*</note>, and so on. Bishop Erc of Slane, then—it was a son of his who was bishop of Ardstraw. Slane is located in Brega.

3. **Hilary**, that is, a pope of Rome; or perhaps the bishop and abbot of Poitiers, who composed the hymn beginning “Let a hymn be said” <note>original: *Hymnum dicat*</note>.

<margin>¹ The story of Ríóc and Drustic is translated as follows by Dr. Todd (*Book of Hymns*, p. 97): “Finnian of Moville went to Mugint for instruction, and Ríóc, Talmach, and several others went with him. Drust was King of Britain and had a daughter named Drustic. He gave her to Mugint to be taught how to read; however, she fell in love with Ríóc. She said to Finnian: ‘I will give you all the books which Mugint owns so that you may copy <note>original: *transcribe*</note> them, if you will give me Ríóc in marriage.’ Finnian sent Talmach to her that night in the form of Ríóc, and he slept with her; from that encounter, Lonán of Treoit was conceived and born. But Drustic believed that Ríóc had been with her, and she claimed that Ríóc was the father of her son. This was false, because Ríóc was a virgin <note>in this context, meaning he was celibate</note>. Then Mugint was angry <note>original: *wroth*</note> and sent a certain youth into the temple, saying to him: ‘Whoever comes first to you tonight in the temple, strike <note>original: *smite*</note> him with an axe.’ He said this because Finnian was usually the first to go to the temple; however, on that night, by the providence of the Lord, Mugint himself went first to the church, and the youth struck him, just as the prophet says: ‘For his labor shall come [upon his own head], and his wickedness shall fall on his own crown’ [Psalm 7:16]. Then Mugint said, ‘Spare’ <note>original: *Parce*</note>, etc. ² See his genealogy in the *Book of Leinster* <note>original: *LL.*</note> 349b. ³ See Todd, *Book of Hymns*, 148 and following, and the *Antiphonary of Bangor*.</margin>

"Across the great sea," that is <note>original: *.i. (id est)*</note>, across the great sea for him, that is, across the Red Sea from the south, that is, from Egypt.

**Murdebur**, that is, a wise man <note>original: *sapiens*</note> from Disert Muirdebuir in Uí Conaill Gabra <note>a territory in modern County Limerick</note>.

<margin>In Darbais, in the southeast of Scotland; that is, in the land of Martin near Buchan, and Oenglais is the name of its place now <note>original: *nomen loci eius nunc*</note>.</margin>

**The fair festival of Corcu-nutain**, that is, from ivy-clad Darine. From Daire na Flann in Eoganacht Chassil <note>the territory around Cashel, Tipperary</note>. That is, from Daire na Flann in Munster.

**Coemán**. Caemán of Enach Truim in Leix <note>modern County Laois</note> in western Leinster, and he was the brother of Coemgen <note>original: *frater Coemgini; Coemgen is St. Kevin of Glendalough*</note>. Brother of Coemgen of Glendalough. Three brothers: Coemgen, Mocoeme (abbot of Terryglass), and Coemán of Enach Truim. Coemlog was the name of their father <note>original: *nomen patris eorum*</note> and Coemgel was the name of their mother <note>original: *nomen matris eorum*</note>.

4. **Without hesitation**, that is, regarding the committing of sin or the denial of God. **Without fear**, that is, regarding suffering for Christ's sake.

**The wife... of Peter**, that is, before his apostleship <note>original: *ante apostulatum*</note>.

**Tigernach** of Daire Melle is here <note>original: *hic*</note>.

5. **Of the Lord**, that is, Domangin or the bishop of Alexandria.

**Colmán**: from Glenn Delmuic in Mag Raigni in Ossory <note>an ancient kingdom in modern Kilkenny and Laois</note>.

6. **Fedbair the virgin** <note>original: *uirgo*</note> from Botha Ech Uaicnich in Tir Ratha; and **Aedán son of Colcu** from Lann Abhaich in Ulster is here.

7. **Fintan** and **Colmán** of Inis Mocholmóc, and **Sodhalach the anchorite** <note>original: *ancorita*</note> are here.

**Barrfind**. Barrind son of Aed from Achad Caillden in Uí Dróna <note>modern County Carlow</note>. 
That is, in Achad Caillden in Uí Dróna, to the west of the Barrow River; that is, in Uí Reithe, south of Leighlin. However, they call him Barrfind of Inis Doimle.

12. **To Cumman**, that is, Cuimmini son of Fiachna, successor <term>original: comarba; the heir or successor to a founding saint's monastery</term> of Brendan of Clonfert; he was of the Eoganacht of Loch Léin. <note>The Eoganacht were a powerful group of dynasties in Munster.</note>

The Cuimine mentioned here was a king of West Munster and a sage. Fiachrai committed incest with his own daughter while in a state of drunkenness <note>original: per ebrietatem</note>. He asked his daughter, "Who is the father of the child you carry?" and she said, "Yours." Fiachnai said, "He must die." "Let it be so," said the daughter. But when he was born, he was taken to the church of St. Ita and left there on the arm of a cross in a little basket <note>original: cuimin bic; this provides a folk etymology for his name</term>. From this, he was named Cuimin. He was raised and educated there, and for a long time, no one knew where he came from. His mother came to visit him at the house of St. Ita's successor one day. The successor was not there to meet her. Cuimin asked for a drink, and his mother gave him the drink out of the abbess’s vessel, and he drank from it. The abbess rebuked her for giving him the vessel, and then he said: "Do not notice," etc., and the verses following it.

**Cumain Fota** <note>meaning "Cumain the Tall"</note> son of Fiachna, son of Fiachrach Gairine, son of Duach, son of Maine, son of Coirpre, son of Corc, son of Lugaid.

13. **Eutychius**. Eutychius suffered <note>original: passus est; martyred</note> in Thrace.
<gloss>Clementinus died in Thrace. Not the Pope, but another.</gloss>

14. **Clement**, that is, he may have been the Abbot of Rome. (Note: Not the Pope, but another).
<gloss>Colmán, from Inis mo Cholmóc in Uí Enechlais in Leinster.</gloss>
<gloss>In eastern Leinster. And he was a leper <note>original: lobar</note>.</gloss>

15. **Secundus**, that is, in Africa.

16. **Augustine**, that is, not the author of books <note>referring to St. Augustine of Hippo</note> but the other Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Canterbury</note> who was sent with forty others by Gregory to preach to the British, and he ordained him as Archbishop of the island of Britain. He came, therefore, with forty disciples, as Bede says in his history.

17. **Thecla**, that is, a virgin and martyr.
<gloss>Buaid Beó, that is, Buaid Beó son of Lugaid, son of Liathchú, son of Araide, from whom the Dál n-Araidi are named; from Cill Mhór in the east of the territory <note>original: fíne</note>, which is at the head of Magh Elta.</gloss>
<gloss>Duilech from Clochar Dúilich in Fingal <note>original: Fine Gall; a region north of Dublin</note>. South of Faeldrum in Fingal.</gloss>

18. **Rónán**. Rónán son of Berach from Druim Inisclainn in Conailli Muirtheimne <note>modern-day Dromiskin, County Louth</note>. He was Rónán son of Berach, son of Crimthann, son of Erc Loga, son of Ernaide, son of Murene, son of Sechnusach, son of Colum Cuile, son of Muredach, son of Laegaire, son of Niall; he is at Druim Inisclainn in Conailli Muirtheimne.

20. **Escon with Froechan**. Escon and Froechan from Bóchluain in Leix <note>modern County Laois</note> in western Leinster are celebrated together. Or it should be Froechan there, as others say.

# NOVEMBER 12-20. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.

12. **To my Cummain**, that is, Cummíne,¹ son of Fiachna, a successor <term>original: comarba; the administrative and spiritual heir of a founding saint</term> of Brendan of Clonfert. He was of the Eoganacht of Cashel. <note>The Eoganacht were the ruling dynasties of Munster.</note>

The Cummíne² mentioned here was a king of West Munster and a sage. Fiachna fathered him through drunkenness <note>original: per ebrietatem</note> upon his own daughter. When Fiachna questioned his daughter, "By whom did you have him?" she replied, "By you." Fiachna said, "He must die." "So be it," said the girl. However, when he was born, he was brought to the church of St. Ita <note>Cell Íte</note> and left there in a little basket <note>original: *cuimín*, which provides a folk etymology for his name</note> on the arm of a cross. Thus he was named Cummíne. He was nursed and educated there, and no one knew his origin until his mother came to visit the house of Ita's successor one day. Ita's successor was not present when she arrived. Cummíne asked for a drink, and his mother gave him the Abbess's bowl to drink from, and he drank it. The abbess rebuked the mother for giving him the vessel, and then the mother said, "Do not notice," and so on, followed by the verses:³

**Cummáin the Tall**, son of Fiachna, son of Fiachra Gairine, son of Duach, son of Maine, son of Cairbre, son of Corc, son of Lugaid.

14. **Clement**, that is, he may be the abbot of Rome, but not the Pope <note>original: non papa</note>, etc.
**Colman**, that is, of Inis Mocholmóc in the territory of Huí Fenechlais in eastern Leinster; he was a leper.

15. **Of Secundus**, that is, in Africa.

16. **Augustine**, not the famous author, but the other Augustine who was sent, etc. <note>likely referring to Augustine of Canterbury</note>.

17. **Thecla**, virgin and martyr.
**Búaid beó**, that is, Búaid-beó son of Lugaid, son of Liathchú, son of Araide, from whom the Dál Araidi tribe is named <note>original: a quo Dál Araidi</note>. He is from the Great Church of the Eastern Tribe <note>Cell mór Airthir fine</note>, which is at the end of the Plain of the Birds <note>Mag n-elta</note> in Gaill <note>the Plain of Clontarf</note>.
**Duilech**, that is, from Duilech’s Stone Church <note>Clochar Duilig</note> to the south of Faeldruim in Fingal.

18. **Of Rónán**, that is, Rónán⁴ son of Berach, from Druimm Inesclainn in Conailli Muirthemni. Specifically, Rónán son of Berach, son of Crimthann, son of Erc loga, son of Ernaide, son of Murene, son of Sechnasach, son of Colum cuile, son of Muredach, son of Lóiguire, son of Niall. He is at Druim Inesclainn in Conailli Muirthemni.

20. **Escon with Froechán**, that is, Bó-chluain in Leix in western Leinster. Alternatively, "Bishop Froechán" would be appropriate there, as others think <note>original: ut alii putant</note>.

¹ His pedigree is found in the *Leabhar Breac* (LL) 351c.

Fiachna fathered him through drunkenness upon his own daughter, for the girl used to sleep with her mother. Her father forced her to confess to find out who the son's father was, and she admitted it was he. The child was wrapped in purple clothing—was this to mark the child's royal descent, or to appease the gods? <note>original Latin: *purpura dis advocatur placandis*, "purple is summoned for the appeasing of the gods," Pliny, Natural History ix. 60</note>. <header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF NOVEMBER.]</header>

...from Clonenagh slightly to the east. He is called "Esconn" <note>Esconn means "impure" or "unclean" in Old Irish</note> because he spent thirty years without baptism. <note>original: Ideo Esconn dicitur quia .xxx. anni sine babtismo</note>

21. **Noibdecheng**, that is, two strong saints <note>original: duo sancti fortes</note>. That is, "two heads." <note>original: duo capita</note>

<margin>**Mac Comain of Aran**, that is, his name is Colman, from eastern Aran. Or, **Aru and Eire** are the two hills side by side. **Mac Congraid of Ireland**, etc., that is, his name is Aedan son of Conchraidh, and Aedan the pilgrim, son of Concraidh, is in Clonenagh; or Aedan son of Jacob, as others say. That is, Aedan son of Congnaid from Clonenagh or from Enoch thruim. And **Longinus the martyr** is commemorated today, but not the one who pierced Christ's side <note>original: non iugulator Christi</note>.</margin>

22. **Cecilia the virgin**, in Rome.

23. **Clement**, that is, Clemens, a bishop in Rome. There is a remarkable city for Clement under the sea where he was drowned, and the sea recedes every year on the feast of Clement, so that the city is visible among the waves—that is, among the voices of the waves of the sea. People go there to fast, and it once happened that a certain woman left her son there by mistake, and he was found alive and well at the end of a year. Again, this was through the grace of God and Clement. He was the third Pope after Peter, and was drowned by the Emperor Trajan in the Tyrrhenian Sea near the city of Cherson <note>original: a Traiano imperatore dimersus est in mari Terreno iuxta Cersonam ciuitatem</note>.

24. **Cianán**, that is, from Duleek <term>original: Dom liacc; literally "House of Stones," one of the first stone churches in Ireland</term> of Cianán in Brega.

It is said that the body of Cianán remains without decaying or dissolving in the tomb <term>original: membra; a shrine or tomb-structure</term> to the east of the stone church. The reason for this is as follows: Cairnech of Tuilen once came to Duleek to visit Cianán. A bath was prepared for him, but no bottom could be found for the vat. "That is a pity," said Cianán. "Why?" asked Cairnech. "Because there is no bottom in the vat," said Cianán. "Put the water into it," said Cairnech, "and let the washing be done." The water was poured in and not a drop leaked out. "Get into the vat, Cairnech," said Cianán. "Let us go in together," said Cairnech. They did so. "The body is beautiful, O cleric," said Cairnech. "As it is indeed," said Cianán. "I pray to God then," said Cairnech, "that as it is now, so may it remain forever without decaying or dissolving until Christ comes to the great assembly of Judgment." *And that is indeed what has been fulfilled.*

Furthermore, a high bishop used to trim his hair and nails every Maundy Thursday <term>original: dardain caplaiti; the Thursday before Easter</term> each year until the time of Adamnan <note>A famous 7th-century abbot of Iona and hagiographer</note>. Adamnan then went into the tomb to see and touch the body. His sight was immediately taken from him. He fasted because of this, and his sight was restored to him. Since then, no one has dared to enter the tomb.

It was Patrick who wrote Cianán's "Canon" <note>likely a copy of the Gospels or a rule</note>, and Cianán who wrote Patrick's "Canon," for they made an exchange. Patrick requested this because Cianán's handwriting was better. *And this is how the alliance between Columba and Cianán was made: Columba's hand was reached through the southern side of the tomb-wall and Cianán's hand reached out through the other side, and they made their alliance in that way.*

After a long time, following the killing of **Niall of the Nine Hostages** by Eochaid son of Enna Ceinnselaig, and after Niall had taken the kingship as far as the English Channel <note>original: Muir n-Icht</note>, there came...

<header>NOVEMBER 21–24.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

...a little east of Clonenagh <note>original: Clúain eidnech</note>. *He is called Esconn* <note>original: Ideo dicitur Esconn</note> ("impure") because he was unbaptized for thirty years.

21. A holy couple, that is, two mighty saints, or two chiefs.
**Clement**, who was a pope and bishop of Rome.
**The son of Coman of Aran**—his name was Colman, from eastern Aran. Or, Aru and Eire are the names of two hills side by side.
**The son of Congrad of Ireland**—his name is Aedan son of Congrad. In Clonenagh, there is Aedan the pilgrim, son of Concrad. Or Aedan son of Jacob, as others say <note>original: ut alii dicunt</note>. He is Aedan, son of Congnad, from Clonenagh or Annatrim <note>modern: Enach truim</note>.

22. **Cecilia**, a virgin in Rome. <note>See her legend in the Old English Martyrology, p. 208.</note>

23. **Regarding Clement**—he was the bishop and abbot of Rome. There is a magnificent monastery <note>original: convent</note> dedicated to Clement beneath the sea where he was drowned. Every year, on Clement’s feast day, the tide recedes so that the monastery stands clear among the waves—that is, amidst the sound of the ocean waves. People go there to fast. It is said that a certain woman once accidentally left her child there, and the child was found completely whole at the end of a year. He came to meet her again through the grace of God and St. Clement, and so on. <note>See Old English Martyrology, pp. 211, 239. Bede, ed. Giles, iv. 166–7; Jameson, Sacred and Legendary Art, 627.</note>

24. **Cianan from Duleek** <note>modern: Daimliac</note> **in Bregia**. <note>His pedigree is found in the Book of Leinster (LL) 350d.</note> Cianan's body remains in the tomb to the east of the stone church <note>term: damliac; a stone church, as opposed to a wooden one</note> without decaying or dissolving. <note>See the Irish Nennius, 221n. The reason generally given for incorruption after death is that it was a sign of chastity during life (Plummer, Bede II, 151, 240, 271).</note> The reason for this is as follows: Cairnech of Dulane <note>modern: Tuilén</note> once visited Cianan at Duleek, and they prepared to give him a bath. No bottom <note>original: domain</note> could be found for the tub. 
"That is a shame," said Cianan. 
"What is?" asked Cairnech. 
"That the tub has no bottom," replied Cianan. 
"Pour the water into it anyway," said Cairnech, "and let the washing be done." 
Water was poured in, and not a single drop leaked out. 
"Get into the tub, Cairnech," said Cianan. 
"Let us go in together," replied Cairnech. 
They both entered. 
"Your body is beautiful, O cleric," said Cairnech. 
"Indeed it is, as it is now," replied Cianan. 
"I pray to God," said Cairnech then, "that it may remain exactly as it is forever, without decaying or dissolving, until Christ comes at the Great Judgment <note>original: assembly of Doom</note>." 
And so it was fulfilled.

A high bishop used to cut Cianan’s hair and nails every Maundy Thursday each year until the time of Adamnan. Adamnan once entered the tomb to see and touch the body. Immediately, his eye was struck out. He fasted in penance for this, and his eye was then restored to him. From that time on, no one has dared to enter the tomb.

Now Patrick once copied Cianan’s transcript of the Canon <note>term: the canonical Scriptures; compare Fiacc’s hymn, verse 12: "He read the Canon with Germanus" (original: légais canóin la German)</note>, and Cianan copied Patrick’s. They did this as an exchange, and Patrick requested it because Cianan’s handwriting was superior.

The spiritual alliance <note>original: union</note> between Colum Cille and Cianan was made in this way: Colum Cille reached his hand halfway into the southern side of the tomb, and Cianan reached his hand out halfway to meet him. In this way, they formed their bond.

At the end of a long time after the killing of Niall of the Nine [Hostages]...

<meta>This page continues the commentary for the month of November in the Martyrology of Oengus, specifically providing additional legendary details for the saints of late November, including St. Cairnech, King Niall of the Nine Hostages, St. Colmán, and St. Finnchú.</meta>

<page-num>246</page-num>
<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [NOVEMBER.]</header>

Cairnech, along with his monks, arrived in Ireland and came to Tulach Maine <note>modern: The Hill of Maine</note>. Maine and his descendants knelt before him and offered the hill to him and the clerics, so that it is called Tulach Maine today. Maine also gave his own service and the service of his descendants after him to that church. Furthermore, the body of Niall <note>Niall of the Nine Hostages, a legendary High King of Ireland</note> was afterwards taken from the ground by Cairnech; and it seemed as if he had only just died at that hour, so that there was no loss of form or beauty upon him, for he had been placed in a vat filled with healing herbs. A Mass was then performed by the clerics over Niall’s body, and the herbs were washed away from him with holy water. The King's body was then buried again in Tulen by Cairnech, and so Niall was the first person to be buried at Tulen. **F.** <note>The Feast of</note> the son of Lénéne—that is, Colmán was his name, from Cloyne <note>original: Cluáin húama</note> in Ui Liatháin in Munster.

**Colmán of Dubh Chuilinn.** <note>original: Colmán Duib Chuilinn</note>. Colmán "the Black" from Cuilenn—that is, a mountain at Belach Conglais in Leinster. Colmán of Dubh Chuilinn in the Rinn—that is, from Dun Reichet and from Belach Conghais in Leinster and from other places <note>original: ab aliis locis</note>. Comgall of Bangor went to the house of the father of Colmán of Dubh Chuilinn. His wife was barren. The cleric then requested "black writing" <note>ink</note> for the barren woman. It was given to her. From this, Colmán was conceived <note>The text suggests she swallowed the ink or it was part of a miracle</note>, and for this reason he is called "Colmán of the Black Ink" <note>original: Colman duibh cuilind; a pun on 'Cuilenn' (holly) and 'Scribinn' (writing)</note>. His mother was barren at first, but she tasted the black ink of Comgall of Bangor and conceived immediately, which is why he is called Colmán of Dubh Chuilinn.

---

25. **John Cassian**—that is, the bishop of Constantinople.

**Croich**—that is, Croich is the name of a river in Mugdorna where it is located; and Cluain Crucha in Carbury is the name of the church from which he came.

**Finnchú of Brigown** <note>original: Brí gobann</note>—that is, in Fermoy <note>original: Feraib maige</note> in Munster.

It was the custom of Finnchú that every dead person brought to the church for burial would be slept beside by him on the first night. The reward he requested for this was that every person who prayed to him at the time of their death would not be overcome by demons and would not go to hell.

And this is the "prison" <note>term: carcar; an ascetic's cell or posture of penance</note> in which he stayed: a stone slab was over his head and an iron sickle was under each of his two armpits, so that his head did not strike the stone above nor did his feet touch the floor. Eventually, Comgall of Bangor came to him and said, "Come down from there." Then Finnchú said:

> This is the prayer I ask, upon my release from this trap:
> That no one who prays to me at death shall be a person of hell.

Comgall said: "You shall have that from God."

---

<note>² Read: "Conception."</note>

<meta>This page continues the notes for late November in the Martyrology of Oengus, concluding the story of St. Cairnech and the preservation of King Niall's body, and detailing the lives and legends of St. Colmán and St. Findchú.</meta>

<page-num>247</page-num>
<header>NOVEMBER 25.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

[Niall was taken as one of the] hostages by Eochaid, son of Éndae Cennselach <note>A king of Leinster; original: Éndae Cennselach</note>. After Niall had expanded his kingdom as far as the sea by the Isle of Wight <note>original: sea of Wight</note>, Cairnech came with his monks to Ireland and reached Tulach Maini <note>The Hill of Maine</note>. Maine and his children knelt before him and offered the hill to him and to the clerics; for this reason, it is now called Tulach Maini. Maine also gave to that church his own personal labor <note>original: manual service</note> and the service of his children after him. 

However, Niall’s body was later taken out of the ground by Cairnech. You would have thought that he had died that very hour, for there was no loss of his physical shape or form; this was because he had been placed in a tub filled with healing herbs within his grave. A mass was then said by the clerics over Niall’s body, and when holy water was sprinkled, the herbs fell away from him <note>original: the herbs part from him</note>. The King’s body was then re-buried in Tuilén <note>modern: Dulane, County Meath</note> by Cairnech, so that he was the first person ever buried at Tuilén.

<margin>The son of Lenéne—that is, from Cloyne in Ui Liatháin in Munster: his name was Colmán.</margin>

**Colmán of Dubh Chuilinn**, that is, "Black Colmán" from Cuilenn, which is a mountain at Belach Conglais in Leinster. He is also called Colmán of the "ink" (or blackness) of Cuilenn in the Rinn <note>original: Renna</note>—that is, from Dún Rechet and from Belach Conglais in Leinster, and from other places. 

Comgall of Bangor once visited the house of the father of Colmán of Dubh Chuilinn, whose wife was barren. The cleric asked the barren wife for some writing ink. It was given to her, and she tasted it. Because of this, Colmán was conceived. For this reason, he was called Colmán of the "ink" <note>original: duib, meaning black or ink</note> of Cuilenn.

25. **John Cassian**, that is, a bishop of Constantinople. <note>A noted Christian saint and theologian, though he was a monk rather than the Bishop of Constantinople.</note>

<margin>Into Croich—that is, Croich is the name of a river in Mugdoirn; Cluain Crocha in Cairbre is the name of the church from which he departed.</margin>

**Findchú of Brí Gobann**, that is, in Fir Maige in Munster <note>modern: Mitchelstown, County Cork</note>. 

Now, this was Findchú’s custom: for every corpse brought to the church, he would lie beside it for the first night. The reward <note>original: guerdon</note> he asked for this was that the Devil should not defeat any person who prayed to Findchú at the time of their death, and that such a person should not go to hell. 

And this is the "prison" in which he sat: he had a flagstone over his head and an iron sickle in each of his armpits from which he hung suspended, so that his head would not touch the stone above nor his feet touch the floor below. Comgall of Bangor happened to visit him and said, “Come down.” 

Then Findchú said:
> “This is the one prayer that I pray as I leave this device <note>original: engine, referring to his suspension apparatus</note> of torture: 
> that no one who prays to me at their death shall dwell in hell.” 

Comgall replied: “That you shall have from God.”

<note>original: So the Dagda put myrrh...</note> Similarly, the Dagda <note>a chief god of the pagan Irish</note> placed myrrh, frankincense, and herbs that prevent decay around the body of his son Cermait "Honeymouth."

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES. [MONTH OF NOVEMBER]</header>

**26.** The honoring of Michael in the East today <note>original: *honoir Michaelis in oriente hodie*</note>.
Banbán, that is, the bishop of Leighlin <note>original: *Lethglenn*; a historic diocese in County Carlow</note>.
Bishop Siric, that is, from Mag Bolg in Fir Chúl of Bregia <note>modern: Moybolgue, County Meath</note>, or perhaps another.

**27.** Sechnall <note>also known as St. Secundinus</note>, that is, from Dunshaughlin <note>original: *Domnach Sechnaill*; meaning "The Church of Sechnall"</note> in the south of Bregia <note>the ancient kingdom of Meath</note>.

> He paved a road, great was his choice,
> Sechnall, the diadem of our sages <note>original: *flathae*, "of our lords/sovereigns"</note>,
> Throughout Ireland’s host, beautiful and blessed,
> He sang the praise of Patrick of Armagh.

<note>This refers to the *Audite omnes amantes*, a famous Latin hymn composed by Sechnall in honor of St. Patrick; it is considered one of the earliest pieces of Latin poetry written in Ireland.</note>

That is, he was a son of Patrick’s sister and came from Dunshaughlin in Fir Breg. He was of the Lombards of Italy <note>original: *Longbardaib Letha*</note>. He was born in Lombardy, and there his name was Secundinus.

**28.** *Trophimus*.
A triad—that is, three chiefs.
The sons of Bochra, that is, three brothers from Achad Ráithin in the Decies <note>original: *Désí*</note> of Munster. Bochra was their mother's name. Their names were Laidgenn, Cainnech, and Aed Cobrán <note>original: *nomina ipsorum*</note>.

**29.** Brendan of Birr <note>modern: Birr, County Offaly</note>, located on the border of Fircell and Éile. That is, Birr is on the boundary of Éile and Fircell; it is near a great water—his church is on the bank of the water.

**30.** Andrew. Andrew, the brother of the apostle Peter, who was a disciple of John the Baptist first and of Christ afterward <note>original: *Andreas frater Petri apostoli, discipulus Iohannis babtiste prius et Christi postea*</note>.

---

1. *Honour.* 2. *Today.* 3. See Sechnall’s hymn, *Audite omnes amantes* (Hear, all you who love), in the *Liber Hymnorum*. 4. Their own names. 5. His pedigree is found in the *Book of Leinster* (LL) 348h. 6. His legend is found in the *Old English Martyrology*.

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS — DECEMBER</header>

**D. 8th day before the Ides of December (December 6).**
The feast of Gobbán,
a shout of thousands!
With a great company of martyrs,
the angelic fortress and virginal abbot,
the radiant descendant <note>original: *maccu*; a term for a clan-name or descendant</note> of Lán.

**E. 7th day before the Ides of December (December 7).**
With the suffering <note>original: *paiss*; from the Latin *passio*, meaning martyrdom</note> of Polycarp
and his noble, flowing company:
the bright feast of the victorious Buite,
from wealthy Monasterboice <note>original: *Mainistir máinig*; literally "treasurous monastery"</note>.

**F. 6th day before the Ides of December (December 8).**
The triumph of humble Egbert <note>original: *Íchtbrichtáin*</note>,
who traveled across the great sea:
he sang a prayer to Christ
in a small boat made without animal skins <note>original: *curchán cen choduil*; a "hideless coracle." This likely refers to a wooden boat, suggesting a miraculous or ascetic sea-journey without the traditional leather covering of an Irish coracle.</note>.

**G. 5th day before the Ides of December (December 9).**
Beautiful are the two daughters
of Ailill, who should not be hidden:
fair is the host of their feast day—
the two suns of the eastern Liffey <note>original: *Liffi*; referring to the region of the River Liffey</note>.

**A. 4th day before the Ides of December (December 10).**
With two virginal fifties
and an exact thirty in full <note>A total of 130 people</note>,
the festival of Capitolinus,
and the feast of my brave Dimóc.

11. Damasus with my Senóc of (Belach) Mugnae, in the north, a broad plain; the feast of my Elteóc, a holy, true warrior <note>original: *cáid cathfír*</note>, with a valiant host across the sea.

12. A tower of gold over every sea-plain: he will take my soul by the hand <note>original: *gébaid coir*; literally "take a hand," meaning to help or guide</note>, Finnian the fair, a beloved root, of vast Clonard <note>original: *Clúana Iraird*</note>.

13. For the dear, crowded day <note>original: *dil ndálach*; referring to a day with many celebrations or a large assembly</note>, may they come with many thousands: the pious Báethán of Clúain, and Colomb the fasting <note>original: *trednach*; referring to Saint Columba of Terryglass</note> of Tír (dá glais).

14. May he summon us to the royal kingdom of the King whom our Sister <note>The Blessed Virgin Mary; in early Irish tradition, Mary was often referred to as "our sister"</note> brought forth—the holy champion, the subduer, the just Drusus with his three companions.

15. The calling of happy Faustinus, with the fair company of his temple, along with the feast of Flann the modest ruler <note>original: *impir*; literally "emperor," here used as a title of honor for an abbot</note>, the eternal successor <note>original: *comarbai*; the heir or administrative successor of a founding saint</note> at Bangor <note>original: *Bennchuir*</note>.

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF DECEMBER]</header>

### G. 17th day before the Calends of January <note>original: *xvii. cal. Ianuarii*; December 16</note>
The holy triumph <note>original: *Búaid find*; literally "white triumph," meaning pure or blessed</note> of Valentinus
with a beautiful clergy you will attain;
the feast of my excellent Beóóc,
from lustrous Ard Cáinroiss <note>This place name likely means "the high, shining promontory."</note>.

16. The pure triumph of Valentinus with a fair train of followers, you will join him: the feast of my excellent Beóóc, from lustrous Ard Cáinroiss.

May Victor’s host protect us
after the triumph of a deed of valor,

17. May Victor's host protect us after the triumph of a courageous deed, so that we may attain—in splendid bliss—Jesus, Mary's great Son.

### B. 15th day before the Calends of January <note>original: *xv. cal. Ianuarii*; December 18</note>

Magniu <note>Also known as Maignenn of Kilmainham.</note>—this crown is good;

18. The great sun of these clans, Magniu—a good diadem is he: Diucaill, and this swift group; may they be cheerful toward me!

### C. 14th day before the Calends of January <note>original: *xiv. cal. Ianuarii*; December 19</note>
May she be joyful toward my soul,
with the greatness of her host,
the fair, pure manna of the God of elements <note>original: *Dé dúilig*; a common Irish title for the Creator</note>,
Samthann of Clúain Brónaig!

19. May she be joyful to my soul, along with her vast host—the fair, pure manna of the Creator God, Samthann of Clúain Brónaig <note>Clonbroney, County Longford.</note>!

### D. 13th day before the Calends of January <note>original: *xiii. cal. Ianuarii*; December 20</note>

23. The passion of eight hundred fair martyrs, along with sixty noble ones who were slain: together with my Temnióc of the royal folk of truly good Clonfert-Mulloe.

<header>CALENDAR OF OENGUS [MONTH OF DECEMBER]</header>

### A. 9th day before the Calends of January <note>original: *ix. cal. Ianuarii*; December 24</note>
The attendance of Lucianus
with my Cua <note>Saint Mochua</note>, a fair couple;
Mac Lonáin, who happens to come to us
on the night before Christmas.

### B. 8th day before the Calends of January <note>original: *viii. cal. Ianuarii*; December 25</note>
On great, marvelous Christmas,
Christ was born of pure, white Mary,
bringing the destruction of darkness—
the luminous King of Adam’s race.

### C. 7th day before the Calends of January <note>original: *vii. cal. Ianuarii*; December 26</note>
Let us pray to him for our protection <note>original: *diar ñdigdi*</note>,
my Commóc in his splendor;
a beautiful sun that warms thousands,
and the luminous name of Stephen <note>Saint Stephen, the first Christian martyr</note>.

### D. 6th day before the Calends of January <note>original: *vi. cal. Ianuarii*; December 27</note>
The peaceful death <note>original: *Slánchotlud*, literally "sound sleep"</note> of John
in Ephesus—a magnificent assembly <note>original: *bordgal*; likely referring to a famous gathering or a place of pilgrimage</note>—
along with the dignity <note>original: *ordan*</note> of James,
his brother, who is most high.

---

### 24.
The attendance of Lucianus with my Cua, a fair couple; Mac Lonáin who happens to come to us on the night before Christmas <note>Christmas Eve</note>.

### 25.
At great, marvelous Christmas, Christ was born of pure, white Mary to the ruin of darkness—Christ, the luminous King of Adam's race.

### 26.
Let us pray to him to bless us, my Commóc in his splendor: a fair sun that warms thousands, and the luminous name of Stephen.

### 27.
The peaceful death of John in Ephesus—a splendid assembly—along with the dignity of his brother James, who is highest.

<header>DECEMBER 28–31.] MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS.</header>

### E. 5th day before the Calends of January <note>original: *v. cal. Ianuarii*; December 28</note>
Famous is the eternal cry,
beyond every lovely company <note>original: *methil*; a group of reapers or workers, here used for a band of martyrs</note>,
sung above to their Father
by the small children from Bethlehem <note>The Holy Innocents, the children murdered by King Herod</note>.

**28.** Famous is their eternal acclamation, beyond every lovable band, which the little children from Bethlehem sing above to their Father.

### F. 4th day before the Calends of January <note>original: *iv. cal. Ianuarii*; December 29</note>
Swift will be their help;
may it shelter us at every hour!
Victor and a famous host,
with Airerán the Wise <note>original: *necnae*; of wisdom. Likely refers to Ailerán the Wise of Clonard</note>.

**29.** Swift will be their aid: at every hour may it shelter us! Victor and a famous host, with Airerán the sage.

### G. 3rd day before the Calends of January <note>original: *iii. cal. Ianuarii*; December 30</note>
The hardship of a prison
crucified the great host of Mansuetus;
along with the pure Ailbe,
we shall reach his feast day.

**30.** A dungeon's compulsion crucified the great host of Mansuetus: with virginal Ailbe <note>Ailbe of Emly, though his main feast is September 12; this may refer to another saint of the same name</note>, we shall attain his feast.

### A. The day before the Calends of January <note>original: *Pridie cal. Ianuarii*; December 31</note>
Lochán and Éndae;
Silvester, a noble talent <note>original: *talland*; a gift or talent</note>!
From their feast—no feeble leap—
let us strive to step into the New Year <note>original: *caland*; the Calends of January</note>.

**31.** Lochán and Endae. Silvester <note>Pope Silvester I</note>, noble desire! From their feast—no very feeble leap—let us strive to step to the calends of January.
