<header>MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. [MONTH OF DECEMBER.</header>

### NOTES.

**1.** Candida, a holy virgin in Rome. Or Candida, who is a bishop, the son of Cainde from Ath da Ioarcc <note>original: *Áth dá loarcc*; Ford of the two forks</note> beside Kells, as they say. Pancratius, that is, he suffered <note>original: *passus est*; died as a martyr</note> under Diocletian. Nesan of Inis Ulad <note>original: *Inis Ulad*; Island of the Ulstermen</note>, that is, the Ulaid <note>the people of Ulster</note> live there. Inis Ulad and Inis Doimle are the same. Also Nessan of Cork on this day. And Bishop Brecan and Brendan of Druim Liac are here.

**2.** Parmenius the martyr <note>original: *Parmeni martiris*</note>.

**3.** Maelodran, that is, Maelodran from Tuaim Inbir in western Meath. That is, from Tuaim Inbir or Druim Inbir in western Meath. And from Inis Angin on Lough Ree <note>original: *Loch Ríb*</note>.
Macc Oige, that is, the abbot of Lismore of Mochuta. And he was called "the disturbed" or "the terrified" one. This is the reason why: when he was a small boy, the plow-teams of the world would flee in terror and great panic <note>original: *a scén 7 a mascén*</note> before him when they saw him, as would every other kind of livestock that served men. From this was understood the great service <note>original: *mórfognam*</note> that all would give to him afterwards.

**4.** Merobus and Cludicus, that is, in Laodicea where they both suffered martyrdom <note>original: *ambo passi sunt*</note>.
Fer Da Lethe <note>original: *Fer dá lethe*; Man of two halves</note>, that is, Berchan of Cluain Sosta in Offaly <note>original: *Huib Failge*</note>. Or Fer Da Lethe in Laid Treoit in Scotland <note>original: *Albain*</note>. He was a priest <note>original: *sacardos*</note>. He was called "Man of Two Halves" because half of his life was spent in the world and his other half in pilgrimage <note>original: *ailithre*</note>, as the experts <note>original: *periti*</note> say.

**5.** Amantius <note>original: *Amanti*</note>, that is, a bishop.

**6.** Gobban, that is, from Cill Lamraige in western Ossory. That is, from Cill Lamraide in Ui Caitrenn in western Ossory. A thousand monks were with him, as the experts say.
Angelic wall <note>original: *Mur ainglech*</note>, that is, angels built the wall of his monastery <note>original: *cathrach*</note> for him.
Laine, that is, an ancient tribe <note>original: *sentuath*</note> that was in the south of Ireland at one time, and Gobban belonged to them.

**7.** Polycarp, that is, the bishop of the Ephesians <note>original: *episcopus Efesorom*</note>. With his clergy and a martyr, they suffered <note>original: *passi sunt*</note> in Antioch.
Buite of Monasterboice <note>original: *Manistir*</note> in Mag Breg. Buite, that is, "living" <note>original: *beo*</note>. Or Buite, that is, "fire," as it is said in the proverb, "a cow throughout Brega," from which the place is called "buittelach" today, where there was once a great fire. Or Buite as if "beati" from the word "beatus" <note>original: *beatus*; blessed</note>. "Beatus" is said as if "well increased" <note>original: *bene auctus*</note>, for his increase was fair: a star revealing his conception just as a star revealed Christ. Or Buite as if "alive for God" <note>original: *beo Dé*</note>, for he was alive for God, just as it is written: "those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them" <note>original: *qui uiuunt iam non sibi uiuant...*; a quote from 2 Corinthians 5:15</note>, meaning not according to their own will in this world, but according to the will of him who suffered for them.
Buite son of Bronach, son of Balar, son of Cas, son of Nia, son of Airmedach, son of Fergus, son of Isinchain, son of Fiac.

**8.** Egbert <note>original: *Ichtbrichtain*</note>, that is, from Dun Gemin in Ciannacht Glinne Gemin, or in Mayo of the Saxons <note>original: *Maig eó na Sachsan*</note> in western Connacht. Or in Tallaght <note>original: *Talaig*</note> of the Saxons in Ui Conaill Gabra in Munster, and Beridcheirt is the name in that city. Or in Connacht, that is, in Mayo of the Saxons in Carra <note>original: *Cera*</note>.

<keywords>Candida, Pancratius, Maelodran, Macc Oige, Lismore, Fer Da Lethe, Gobban, Polycarp, Buite, Monasterboice, Egbert, Mayo of the Saxons</keywords>

<header>DECEMBER 1-8. MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS. NOTES.</header>

### NOTES.

**1.** *Candida*, a holy virgin in Rome; or *Candida*, that is, Bishop Mac Cainde of Ath da Loarc <note>original: *Áth dá loarc*; the Ford of the Two Forks</note> beside Kells, as they say <note>original: *ut ferunt*</note>.
*Pancratius*: he suffered under Diocletian.
*Nessan* of Inis Ulad <note>original: *Inis Ulad*; Island of the Ulstermen</note>, so named because the Ulaid <note>the people of Ulster</note> dwell there. Inis Ulad and Inis Doimli are the same place. Also *Nessan* of Cork is commemorated on this day, as well as *Breccan*, a bishop, and *Brendan* of Druim Liac.

**2.** *Parmenius, a martyr*.
*Maelodran*, that is, Maelodran of Tuaim Inbir or Druim Inbir in the west of Meath.

**3.** *Macc Oige*, that is, the abbot of Lismore of Mochuta <note>original: *Lessmór Mochutu*</note>. He was called "the Frightener" or "the Disturber," and this is the reason: when he was a little child, all the plow-teams of the world and every other kind of cattle that serve human beings would flee before him in panic and terror whenever they saw him. From this, it was understood that they would all eventually be in great service to him thereafter.

**4.** *Merobius* and *Claudicus*. Both of these suffered in Laodicea.
*Fer Da Lethe* <note>original: *Fer dá lethe*; the Man of Two Parts</note>, that is, Berchan of Cluain Sosta in Offaly. Or Fer Da Lethe in Laid Treoit in Scotland. He was a priest. Half of his life was spent in the secular world and the other half in pilgrimage, as the experts say <note>original: *ut ferunt periti*</note>.

**5.** *Amantius*, that is, a bishop.

**6.** *Gobban*,¹ that is, of Cell Lamraide in Hui Cathrenn in the west of Ossory; experts say it had a thousand monks.
*Angelic wall*, meaning that angels founded the wall of his church for him.
*Lane*, that is, an ancient tribe which was once in the south of Ireland, and Gobban was one of them.

**7.** *Polycarp*, that is, a bishop of the Ephesians and a martyr. He and his followers <note>original: *cum suis*</note> suffered in Antioch.
*Buite*, from Monasterboice <note>original: *Manistir*</note> in Mag Breg. *Buite*, meaning "living." Or *bute*, meaning "fire," as is said in the proverb "fire throughout Bregia" <note>original: *bot fo Bregaib*</note>, meaning a place where there has been a great fire.² Or *bute* as if it were *bete*, from "blessed" <note>original: *beatus*</note>. But "blessed" is so named as if "well-increased" <note>original: *Beatus autem dicitur quasi bene auctus*</note>, for his growth was beautiful, and a star manifested his conception, just as happened at the manifestation of Christ. Or *bute* as if "living unto God" <note>original: *béo Dé*</note>, for he was alive unto God <note>original: *Dia*</note>, as it has been written: "those who live shall not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto Him who died for them and rose again," <note>original: *2 Corinthians 5:15*</note> doing in this world not their own will, but His who suffered for them.

*Buite* was the son of Bronach, son of Balar, son of Cass, son of Nia, son of Airmedach, son of Fergus, son of Isinchan, son of Fiacc.³

**8.** *Ichtbrichtan* <note>the Irish name for St. Egbert</note>, that is, from Dun Geimin in the territory of the Ciannachta of Glenn Geimin, or in Mayo of the Saxons in the west of Connaught. Or in Connaught, specifically in Mayo of the Saxons in Cera. Or in another place, various <note>original: *Vel in alio loco diuersi*; the text breaks off here</note>

---
¹ There is a pedigree of Gobban Find, son of Lugaid, in the *Book of Leinster* (*LL*), page 351c. ² See O'Davoren's Glossary, No. 265. ³ See his pedigree in the *Book of Leinster* (*LL*), page 351b.
OENGUS.

Or, in another place, different writers have different opinions. Or he is from *Tulach Leis na Saxan* <note>original: *Tulaig leis na Saxan*; "The Hill of the Saxons"</note> in Munster,¹ and his name is Bercert. Or he is Ichtbricht <note>Egbert</note> who is in *Tech Saxan* <note>original: *Tig Saxan*; "The House of the Saxons"</note> in *Ui Eachach* of Munster. He was a brother to Benedict of *Tulach Leis na Saxan*, and Cuthbert was their brother; he remained there.

**9.** The two daughters: that is, Mugain² and Feidlimid in *Cill Ingen n-Ailella* <note>original: *Cill ingen n-Ailella*; "The Church of Ailill's Daughters"</note> in western Liffey;³ they are beside Liamain. 
Of Ailill: that is, Ailill son of Dunlang, King of Leinster, was their father. Mugain and Feidilin are their names. He was the son of Dunlang, King of Leinster.⁴ And in *Cill Aililla* in the west of the Plain of Liffey, Mugain and Feidelem are their names together. These women are in the Church of Ailill's daughters in the Plain of Leinster.

**10.** *Capitolinus*: a martyr. 
My *Dimoc*: in *Cluain Cain Arad* in Munster.

**11.** *Damasus*: Abbot <note>or Pope</note> of Rome. 
*Senoc*: My *Senoc* in *Belach Mughna* <note>Ballaghmoon</note> in western Leinster, on the bank of the River Barrow. 
My *Senoc* of *Mughna* then: Mughna was a great sacred tree <note>original: *darbile*; usually an oak</note>, and its canopy was as broad as the entire plain. It bore three crops of fruit every year. It had survived hidden since the time of the Great Flood until the night Conn of the Hundred Battles <note>a legendary High King of Ireland</note> was born, at which time it was revealed. That tree was thirty cubits <note>original: *edh*; a measure of length</note> in girth and three hundred cubits in height. However, Ninine the poet overthrew that tree, as he said:
> The Tree of Mughna, great was that tree,
> Thirty cubits was its girth;
> In secret for a long time it remained,
> Three hundred cubits was its height, etc.

Funech of *Cluain Bronaigh*, Senchan, and the virgin Dunsech from *Cill Dunsighe* in Ulster (she has three churches in Ulster), and Crunnmael the Foolish, and Colum son of Aed of the clan of *Cuile Briuin* are commemorated here.

The Lifting Up of Buite <note>original: *Tocbail Bute*</note>: that is, the bodily elevation of Bishop Boethius by angels and his return to earth <note>original: *elevacio Boeti episcopi in corpore ab angelis et reversio eius ad terram*</note>. However, this occurred at *Elaid* of the *Arad* in the Cemetery of Eogan <note>original: *Reilic Eogain*</note>. There, the fellowship of Colum Cille and Buite was established in the thirtieth year after Buite’s death and in the thirtieth year of Columba's age.

North of the broad plain <note>original: *tuath maig lethain*</note>: that is, on the broad plain to the north, a plain where there are many tribes, namely the Plain of Liffey <note>original: *Mag Life*</note>. Or, north of the Plain of Ailbe <note>original: *Mag n-Ailbe*</note. 
My *Elteoc*: Eiltene of Kinsale <note>original: *Cenn Sáile*</note> in the south of Ireland.

**12.** *Findén*: the grandson of Telldub,⁵ Abbot of Clonard <note>original: *Cluain Iraird*</note>. He was Finnian, son of Finntan, son of Concrad, son of Daircella, son of Senach, son of Diarmait, son of Aed, son of Fergus, son of Ailill Telldub, son of Celtchar, son of Uithechar.

**13.** *Baethan*: that is, Mobi of *Cluain Dadond Abair* <note>sic</note> in *Ui Muiredaig* in Leinster. Or Baethan of *Cluain Annabair* in *Ui Muiredaig*, also known as My Bi <note>Mobi</note>, the grandson of Alta, etc.

Opinions differ <note>original: *diuerse sentiunt*</note>. Or he is from Tulach Leis of the Saxons in Munster, and his name is Berchert. **9.** *The two maidens*: that is, Mugain and Feidlimid. They are in *Cell Ingen n-Ailella* ('The Church of Ailill's Daughters') in the west of Liffey, near Liamain.

*Of Ailill*: that is, the son of Dunlang, King of Leinster, was their father. In *Cell Ailella* in the east of the Plain of Liffey, Mugain and Liamain are there together <note>original: *sunt simul*</note>. They are in *Cell Ingen n-Ailella* in the Plain of Leinster.

**10.** *Of Capitolinus*: that is, a martyr.

My Dimóc: that is, in *Clúain Cáin Árad* in Munster.

There, the alliance of Columba <note>original: Columb Cille</note> and Buite took place in the thirtieth year after Buite's death and during the thirtieth year of Columba's age.

**13.** **Colum**: that is <note>original: *.i.*</note>, Colum son of Crimthann from Terryglass <note>original: *Thir da glas*</note> in Munster.

**Lucia**, virgin and martyr here. After emerging unharmed <note>original: *saer*</note> from a vat of boiling oil, she died by the sword under the Emperor Diocletian.

**14. Our sister**: that is, Mary.

**Thyrsus** <note>original: *Trursus*</note>: that is, a martyr, with his three companions. A martyr in Antioch, according to Gregory, along with his companions.

**15. Of Faustus**: that is, a priest. Faustinus suffered in Africa.

**Mugain**, virgin of *Cluain Bairenn* <note>Cloonyburren</note>, and **Fethain** from *Cuil Grainc*, and **Uidhrin**, a descendant of Bochaile, and **Cronan** are here.

**16. Of Valentine**: that is, a bishop in Ravenna.

**My Beóc**: that is, from Wexford <note>original: *Loch Garmain*</note>. Or My Beóc of Lough Derg in the north.

**17. Victor**: that is, in Africa; a martyr. And **Senchaidh** of the *Uí Aedha* in *Brega*. **Lazarus** and **Moliac** and **Crunnmael** of Iona <note>original: *Ia*</note> and **Maedhog** son of Mursan are here.

**18. Great Sun of these children** or **Flannan**, prince of gentleness.

**Magniu** or **Magnend** from Kilmainham <note>original: *Chill Maignenn*</note>, which is located beside Dublin <note>original: *Áth Cliath*</note>.

**Diucaill**: he is of the *Mugdorna* of Maigen. That is, My Diucla of Lilcach in the territory of the *Uí Faeláin*.

**19. Samthann of Clonbroney** <note>original: *Clúana Bronaig*</note>: that is, in the territory of Cairbre in Tethba. Samthann was the daughter of Diamran, son of Ferdomnach, son of Dichu, son of Fiac, son of Trichem, son of Imchad.

**20. Ignatius**: that is, a martyr and bishop. He held the office of bishop second after Peter, but suffered under the Emperor Trajan. His body was brought to Edessa; he had been given to the lions and other beasts.

**21. Of Thomas.** Thomas, the apostle, suffered in India, but his body was brought to the city of Edessa in Syria under the Emperor Alexander, King of the Romans... and there with honor he awaits the resurrection of the righteous.

**22. Roman of the silent prayer**: "Tua" <note>meaning silence</note>, that is, from Taghmon <note>original: *Tig Tuae*</note> in the territory of the *Uí Faeláin*. He is the same as Ultan of Taghmon. He is called "The Silent" <note>original: *Tua*</note> because a stone was placed in his lips throughout the entire time of Lent <note>original: *quadragesimae*</note> so that he could not speak. For this reason, he was called "The Silent."

**Itharnaisc**: that is, from Clane <note>original: *Chloenad*</note> in the territory of the *Uí Faeláin*, together with Bran.

**Emene**: that is, in *Ros Glaisse*. That is, from *Ros Glaisse* of the Munstermen on the bank of the River Barrow. Emianus (or Eminán) was born to his father Hiaman. Hiaman was his father's name, and Iamnat was his mother's name. He was of the *Corcu Solgoinn* of *Cruach-a-chend*, specifically of the *Uí Senaig*. It is he who went in place of Bran son of Conall to the martyrdom of fifty saints; he went in place of Bran, King of Leinster <note>original: *Lagen*</note>, and fifty kings, during the "Yellow Plague" <note>original: *mbudechair*; a 6th-century pandemic</note>.

**23. Temneoc**: that is, from *Cluain Ferta Molua* <note>Clonfert-Mulloe</note>. That is, the cook of Molua of Clonfert.

**13.** **Colum**, that is, Colum¹ son of Crimthann, of Terryglass <note>original: Tír dá glais</note> in Munster.

**Lucia**, a virgin and martyr here <note>original: hic</note>. After coming safe out of her tub of boiling oil, she died by the sword under the Emperor Diocletian.

**14.** ***Our sister, that is, Mary.***

**Thyrsus**, that is, a martyr, etc.

*15. of Faustus [read <note>original: leg.</note> Faustinus], a priest <note>original: presbyter</note>. Faustinus, etc.*

**15.** **Mugain**, a virgin of Cloonyburren <note>original: Clúain Bairenn</note>, and **Fethain** of *Cúil Grainc*, and **Uidrín**, great-grandson of *Bóchaill*, and **Cronán**, are here <note>original: hic</note>.

*16. of Valentine, that is, a bishop, etc.*

**My-Beóóc**, that is, of Wexford <note>original: Loch Garmán</note>. Or my Beóóc of Lough Derg <note>original: Loch Gerg</note> in the north.

**17.** **Victor**, that is, a martyr; and **Senchaid** of the *Uí Aedha* <note>original: Húi Aeda</note> in *Brega* <note>original: Bregia</note>, **Lazarus** and **Moliac**, and **Crunnmael** (abbot) of Iona, and **Maedóc** son of Marsan are here.

*18. "The great sun of these clans," or "Flannán, prince of gentleness" (is the correct reading).*

**Maigmenn**, that is, from Kilmainham <note>original: Cell Maigmenn</note> beside Dublin <note>original: Áth cliath</note>.

**Diucaill**, that is, he is of *Mugduirn Maigen*; that is, my Diucla (?) of Lilgach in the territory of the *Uí Faeláin* <note>original: Húi Faeláin</note>.

**19.** **Samthann** of Clonbroney <note>original: Clúain Brónaig</note>, that is, in the territory of *Cairbre* <note>original: Crích Cairbri</note> in *Tethba*. Samthann was the daughter of Diamrán, son of Ferdoman, son of Díchu, son of Fiacc, son of Trichem, son of F . . ., son of Imchad.²

**20.** **Ignatius**, that is, a martyr and bishop, etc.

*21. of Thomas, that is, Thomas,³ an apostle: he suffered in India, but <note>original: sed</note> etc.*

**22.** "May Tua’s prayer protect me," that is, **Tua** from *Tech Tuae* in the territory of the *Uí Faeláin* <note>original: Húi Faeláin</note>, the same person as **Ultan** of *Tech Tuae*. Therefore, he is called Tua, meaning "silent" <note>original: Ideo Tua ‘silent’ dicitur etc.</note>.

**Itharnaise**, that is, from Clane <note>original: Clóenad</note> in the territory of the *Uí Faeláin* <note>original: Húi Faeláin</note>, together with **Bran**.

**Emene**, that is, in *Ros Glas* <note>original: Ross glaisse</note>, that is, from *Ros Glas* of the Munstermen on the banks of the River Barrow.

**Emmeanus**, that is, **Eminán**, was born of a father named Iaman. Iamnan was the name of his father, and Iamnat was that of his mother. His kindred was of the *Corco Solgoinn Cruaich*, and of the *Uí Senaig* in particular. It is he who died <note>literally: went</note> to martyrdom from the Yellow Plague, following **Bran** son of Conall,⁴ with his fifty saints, and Bran, king of Leinster, with his fifty kings.

**23.** **Temneóc**,⁵ that is, from *Cluain Ferta Molua* <note>Kyle, County Laois</note>, that is, the cook of **Molua** of *Cluain Ferta*.

**24.** **Lucian**, that is, a martyr.

**My-Chua**, that is, from Timahoe <note>original: Tech Mo chua</note> in Laois <note>original: Laigis</note>. That is, My-Chua son of Lonan from Timahoe in Laois in Leinster, and from Derrymiss <note>original: Daire Mis</note> in Slieve Fuad <note>original: Sliab Fuait</note>.

My-Chua son of Lonan, son of Senach, son of Oengus, son of Lugna, son of Bregdulb, son of Art corp.

My-Chua (<gloss>that is, **Cronan**</gloss>) son of Lonan... abbot of Killeigh <note>original: Cill achid</note>.

**25.** ***The great miraculous Christmas***, that is, it is on the great Christmas that the birth of Christ took place <note>original: facta est natiuitas Christi</note>.

**26.** **My-Commóc**, that is, **Coman** son of Faelchu from Roscommon <note>original: Rus comain</note> in *Mag Ái*. That is, Coman from Roscommon in Connacht; and **Iarlaithe** of Tuam <note>original: Tuaim dá Gualann</note> on the same day as Coman.

**Stephen**, that is, the stoning of the first martyr, Stephen, in Jerusalem in the year of Christ's Ascension <note>original: desgabala Crist</note>.

**27.** ***A splendid assembly*** <note>original: án bordgal</note>, etc. That is, a "splendid assembly" means there was a splendid fervor in Ephesus, the fervor of **John**. It was a fervor that went out "over the border" <note>original: bord</note>, as if one said that Ephesus was full of his works <note>original: quasi dixit ro ba lán Efis de operibus eius</note>. Or, the fervor of John in Ephesus.

***His brother who is highest***, that is, his (or this man's) solemnity is greater. The ordination of **James** <note>original: Iacob</note> is recorded in another source on this day.

**28.** ***Famous is their lasting cry***, etc. That is, the cry of the children who were killed in Bethlehem by Herod <note>original: Iruath</note> for the sake of Christ <note>original: pro Christo</note> is famous and lasting.

***A lovely company*** <note>original: coemda methel</note>, that is, they are a lovely company because of their innocence <note>original: propter innocentiam</note>.

***Singing to God*** <insert>[their Father]</insert>, that is, they sing praises to God in heaven <note>original: canunt laudes Deo in caelo</note>; that is, the infants <insert>[who]</insert> were killed in Bethlehem. How many of them were there? Some say 2,220 were killed. Others say 2,240. The Prophet said:

->One hundred and forty—a bright fulfillment—<-
->of children, and two thousand,<-
->were slain in Bethlehem with victory<-
->by the Emperor Herod.<-

->Thirty fair, pleasant plains<-
->around Bethlehem roundabout;<-
->one hundred from every plain were killed there,<-
->of the pleasant children of noble families.<-

->One hundred and forty—sad the encounter—<-
->in Bethlehem alone.<-

**29.** **Victor**, that is, a martyr and Pope of Rome.

**Aireran**, that is, the scholar <term>fer leigind; lector</term> of Clonard <note>original: Cluain Iraird</note>.

**30.** **Ailbe**, that is, of Emly <note>original: Imlech Ibair</note>.

**31.** **Lochan** and **Enna**. That is, these two are in *Cell na Manach* in *Uí Dunchada*, and in *Cell meic Cathail* in *Uí Bairrchi*, which is in *Belach Gabráin*.

**Sylvester**, that is, Pope of Rome and confessor.

Every saint who was, who is, who shall be,
Until the victorious Day of Judgment throughout the world,
In the company of devout Christ,
May they be helping me.

May they be helping me
On heaven and on earth,
So that they might come in their ranks
To help my soul,
O beloved Little Jesus <note>original: Isucán</note>,
May it be fulfilled thus!

Every saint, every pure saint, every martyr
I have enumerated, every noble apostle,
I offer <note>original: atágur</note> their prayer with me to God,
To protect me from every harsh danger.

**24.** *Of **Lucian**, that is, a martyr.*

*With my **Cua**, that is, of Timahoe <note>original: Tech Mochua</note> in Laois <note>original: Leix</note> of Leinster and of Derrymiss <note>original: Daire Mis</note> in Slieve Fuad <note>original: Sliab Fuait</note>. **Mochua**¹ son of Lonán, son of Senach, son of Oengus, son of Lugna, son of Breg-dolb, son of Art Corp.*

**25.** *On **Christmas day**, a great marvel, that is, on the great Christmas <note>original: Natalicia</note> Christ’s Nativity took place.*

*My **Commóc**, that is, **Commán** son of Fáelchu, from Roscommon in Mag Aí; and **Jarlath** <note>original: Iarlathe</note> of Tuam <note>original: Túaim dá gúalann</note> on the same day as Commán.*

**26.** *Of **Stephen**, that is, the stoning of the first martyr <note>original: protomartyr</note> Stephen in Jerusalem in the year of Christ’s Ascension.*

**27.** *A splendid **assembly** <note>original: bordgal</note>, that is, John’s valor <note>original: gal</note> was in Ephesus a splendid valor; that is, a valor that went out over the border <note>original: bord</note>, as if one said <note>original: quasi dixisset</note> that Ephesus was full of his works <note>original: de operibus eius</note>.*

*His brother is highest, that is, the greater is the solemnity <note>original: sollemnitas</note>, etc.*

**28.** *Famous the lasting acclamation, that is, famous and lasting is the shout of the children who were killed in Bethlehem by Herod for Christ <note>original: pro Christo</note>.*

*A lovable band, that is, they are a dear band because of their innocence <note>original: propter innocentiam</note>.*

*Who sing above to their Father, that is, they sing praises <note>original: canunt laudes</note>, etc.*

*Two thousand, one hundred and forty children—a bright fulfillment—were slain in Bethlehem with victory by the ruler, Herod.*

*Thirty famous, pleasant plains were all around Bethlehem;*

*In every plain, a hundred of the pleasant children of the nobles were slain;*

*One hundred and forty—sad the doom!—in Bethlehem alone.*

**29.** ***Victor***, *that is, a martyr and pope of Rome.*

***Ailerán*** <note>original: Áireran</note>, *that is, the lector of Clonard <note>original: Cluain Iraird</note>.*

**30.** ***Ailbe***, *that is, of Emly <note>original: Imbliuch Ibair</note>.*

**31.** ***Lochán*** *and **Enda**: these two are in the Church of the Monks <note>original: Cell na manach</note> in Húi Dunchada, and in the Church of the son of Cathal <note>original: Cell maic Cathail</note> in Húi Bairrchi, that is, in the Gowran Pass <note>original: Belach Gabráin</note>.*

***Silvester***, *that is, a pope of Rome and confessor.*

> May every saint who has been, is, and will be until the Day of Doom—a victorious division—
> in Christ’s pious company, may they be helping me!
> May they be helping me in heaven and on earth,
> and come in their bands to work along with my soul.
> O dear little Jesus, may it thus be fulfilled!
> Every saint, every holy virgin, every martyr whom I have recounted,
> every high apostle,
> may their prayer for me to God, whom I fear, protect me from every fierce danger!

### EPILOGUE

1. From one start of the month <note>original: calends</note> to the next,
we have offered up our search;
O Jesus, with true joy,
You possess Your year!

5. The host <note>original: buiden</note> of every single day
we have measured out as described before;
we have cut off the excess <note>original: aurain</note>,
bringing our end <note>December 31st</note> to meet the start <note>original: head</note> of January. <note>January 1st</note>

9. Our strength was weak
in a poor body that is very lowly;
but the highest love of Jesus’s host <note>original: arbair; refers to the army of saints</note>
has strengthened us.

13. Though patriarchs and prophets
were companions <note>original: céli; often used for "servants" or "spouses" of God</note> of Christ,
to the multitude of people <note>original: la dóini il-láini</note>,
their feast days are unknown.

17. But it is known that,
except by observing one of these festivals,
not a soul from this enduring world
has reached the high heaven of this King.

<header>THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS: EPILOGUE</header>

21. The full crew <note>original: luchtlach</note> of each day,
in the vessel of the beautiful realm <note>original: il-lígflatha lestur; heaven is often depicted as a ship or vessel in early Irish poetry</note>,
after victory and triumph,
may they come to attend to us!

25. Those who have gone to heaven
every day from the earth <note>original: dind íre</note>,
it is no lie if you claim <note>original: báige</note>
that they are more than thousands of thousands.

29. From that great mass of thousands,
from that mighty, eternal sea,
we have cited from that number
only the "kings" <note>original: ríga; here referring to the most prominent or influential saints</note> of those hosts.

33. Each day’s fair host <note>original: slúaged</note>,
whose powers <note>original: bríga</note> are vast,
from every side across the nations,
may they come to me along with the kings!

37. O holy King, I beseech You;
it is after great fatigue that I have laid me down:
may I be forever in Your paradise <note>original: pardus</note>
with the host I have recounted!

41. The royal company <note>original: rígrad</note> I have recounted—
and it is only a "sip from the ocean" <note>original: loimm de romuir; a common medieval idiom for an incomplete summary</note>—
may each of them, with their pious following <note>original: cléir chredail</note>,
come to my aid!

45. May they all lift me up to my King, whose princes are numbered <note>original: *rímter*; meaning the saints are a vast but recorded multitude in heaven</note>! 65. May my mentor <note>original: *a m'aite*; referring to his spiritual teacher</note> bring me 
to Christ, beloved beyond all affection, 
through his pure blessing, 
and the true desire of his heart!

69. O Christ, let me be protected 
below and above from every shame; 
at my earnest prayer, with sinlessness, 
for the sake of Your champions <note>original: *gérat*; referring to the saints as warriors of the faith</note>!

73. The race <note>original: *grafand*; literally a "horse-race," used here as a metaphor for his poetic effort or the course of life</note> we have run 
is for the love of Christ's Kingdom; 
because we have searched through books, 
this work contains much that is profitable.

77. It is a benefit to the unlearned <note>original: *oscraib*; those without formal ecclesiastical training</note>, 
to whom it will be a breastplate <note>original: *lúrech*; a "lorica" or prayer of protection</note> of piety; 
every generation sings it 
to discover the feast days.

81. Though those who study it 
are sages whose wisdom is as vast as pools, 
there are many delightful harmonies within it 
that sharpen its melodies.

# MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS

85. The King of Heaven with His angels,
whose fame we shall not hide—
every martyr of whom we tell
came to help compose this work.

89. It was not human skill <note>original: *soas*; literally "good knowledge" or "artistic craft"</note> that created
this diligent, radiant little book,
but the help of the angelic King:
the fair and shining dear little Jesus <note>original: *Íssucán*; a diminutive of endearment for Jesus, often used in Early Irish devotion</note>.

93. A holy assembly <note>original: *Cáinsénad*; literally a "fair synod"</note> came to me
in the central hall <note>original: *midchuairt*; the "mid-court" or main hall of a residence</note> of my house,
to refine and correct this work before you
according to the rule of the King of Heaven.

97. It was not mere cleverness that brought it about;
it would be a sin for us to claim it.
Instead, every holy saint in their purity
has crafted their own chapter <note>original: *choiptel*; a loan-word from the Latin *capitulum*</note>.

101. As for the order of these chapters—
if there is anyone who would disturb it,
I declare before this great number:
it is a spiritual ruin <note>original: *díthár*; literally "destruction" or "slaughter"</note> to this host of saints.

### MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS: EPILOGUE

105. The heavenly host has corrected it <note>original Irish: *In slúag conidn-aicert*</note>,
this diligent little book;
through their holy passing <note>original Irish: *nestecht*; literally "departure," referring to their death or martyrdom</note> in perfection,
they have established the dates of their feasts.

109. I have searched through calendars of saints <note>original Irish: *Félire*; a martyrology or calendar of feast days</note>
both far and near;
with great devotion <note>original Irish: *la dúthracht*</note> I have labored,
and I have dedicated this work to the saints.

113. They have bestowed their blessing
on everyone who shall recite <note>original Irish: *nod-géba*; literally "who shall take" or "sing" it</note> it;
they will come to attend him
at the hour of his death.

117. His soul shall live
in the kingdom of the bright sun;
after being carried past all torments,
he shall reach the peaks of the seven heavens.

121. There was neither forgetfulness nor neglect
concerning anyone who was not specifically named <note>original Irish: *nád ro thuirmed*</note>;
rather, the speech was shortened <note>original Irish: *cuimbrigud indsce*</note>
using the art of poetry <note>original Irish: *fo sóas*; literally "under wisdom" or "by skill"</note> to maintain the rhyme and harmony.

***

145. I testify without blushing <note>original Irish: *cen rudiud*</note> that even if you were to travel to the very graves of the saints, you would not find among any people a martyrology that is more accurate.

149. It is a city of protection to sing this work without error; it is a strong rampart <note>original Irish: *múr trén*</note> providing swift defense against both men and devils.

153. Toward God, it is a fervent prayer; against the Devil, it is a vast strength. It is a psalm that proclaims great power; it is a truly accurate martyrology.

157. For everyone who makes this noble, everlasting song their music, this host of saints will escort them into the eternal kingdom <note>original Irish: *mbithflaith*</note> of this King.

161. Regarding the excellent host of this King, with whom I am allied in my struggle <note>original Irish: *bágsá*</note>—I stand as surety <note>original Irish: *ráthsa*; a legal term for a guarantor or bondsman</note> on their behalf that this cry of praise will serve as a successful combat against the enemy.

165. I am the guarantor <note>original Old Irish: *ráthsa*; a legal term for a person who goes bail or acts as a surety for another</note> for the grace of the one who shall sing this every day. I testify without any falsehood that he will dwell in the eternal kingdom.

It is a substitute for the "three fifties"—the one hundred and fifty Psalms—for the free person who shall sing it.

185. Is fírtahart coibsen,¹
is arrae trí² tredan,
do³ chách⁴ phurt í canar
ernaigthe⁵ céit⁶ chredal.

It is a true act of confession; it is a spiritual substitute <note>original Old Irish: *arrae*; a "commutation" or devotional credit in Irish penitential law</note> for three three-day fasts. In every place where it is sung, it counts as the prayers of a hundred believers.

189. Is cretar,⁷ is communn,⁸
is cantaic for salmaib,⁹
is dídnad do chredlaib,
is écnaire do marbaib.¹⁰

It is a holy relic; it is Holy Communion; it is a sacred song added to the Psalms. It is a comfort to the faithful and a funeral mass for the dead.

193. Is todiuscd¹¹ étlae
cid¹² dúrdae¹³ a chride,
doformaig a ánae,¹⁴
berthi¹⁵ hi flaith nime.

It awakens penitence, even if a person's heart has grown hard. It increases one's spiritual wealth and carries them into the kingdom of heaven.

197. Is lúrech im chrabud
fri¹⁶ aslaige demnae,
is díorad¹⁷ figle,
is íccid¹⁸ cech thedmae.¹⁹

It is a breastplate <note>original Old Irish: *lúrech*; a protective prayer, from the Latin *lorica*</note> surrounding one's devotion against the temptations of demons. It enhances the merit of a vigil and heals every disease.

201. Is écnaire²⁰ i mbethu²¹
fri homun cech báeguil,²²
is nóebad²³ do gnímaib,
is tinbúanad sáeguil.²⁴

It is a prayer for the dead <note>original: *écnaire*; usually a requiem, but here used as a protective litany during life</note> offered during life against the fear of every danger. It hallows one's deeds and lengthens one's lifespan.

205. Is foillsiugud fertae,
doformaig cech mbordgal,²⁵
dobeir grád as²⁶ ardam,
is cumgabáil ordan.²⁷

It is a manifestation of miracles. It increases the grace of every gathering <note>original: *bordgal*; possibly meaning a famous assembly or a place of pilgrimage</note>. It bestows the highest rank and uplifts one's dignity.

***

<note>These notes record variations in the original Irish spelling and phrasing across different medieval manuscripts, including the Leabhar Breac (LB), the Book of Leinster (L), and the Rawlinson manuscripts (R²).</note>

<summary>In this concluding section of the Epilogue, Oengus describes his Martyrology as a potent spiritual tool, acting as a "breastplate" against demons and a substitute for rigorous penance. He claims the text has the power to heal diseases, hallow the soul, and ensure the reciter's entry into the kingdom of heaven.</summary>

209. It is the holy awe <note>original: *auromun*; a profound, reverent fear</note> of the Lord;
it is a divine and steadfast love;
it is the driving out of demons;
it is the invitation of angels.

213. All the miracles which we declare are wondrous;
a blessing on every person
who shall recite them hereafter.

217. If this is what a person prays
to the Lord with beauty,
the worms of the earth <note>original: *míl úre*; literally "beasts of the soil," referring to the creatures that consume the body after death</note> will not test him,
and his physical remains <note>original: *thaissi*; often used to refer to the relics of saints</note> will not decay.

221. His soul, without struggle,
will enter into bright heaven;
after he has reached it,
the dew of his grave will heal the living.

225. At the commemoration of their feasts,
may the constant work of their prayer protect us;
it is no empty labor,
for we have recounted them all.

229. The royal assembly of saints <note>original: *rígrad*; literally "king-folk" or "royal line"</note> I have recounted
is close to us in friendship;
after reckoning their feast days,
I will now number their ranks <note>original: *ndrungu*; troops, companies, or divisions of the heavenly host</note>.

# MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS: EPILOGUE

233. The host of heaven's archangels,
led by noble, holy Michael,
along with the nine ranks <note>In medieval theology, the celestial hierarchy was organized into nine ranks, such as Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones.</note> of the gracious King
who dwell in the City of the mighty King.

237. The host of ancestors led by Noah
across the ranges of the great seas;
the servants of the bright-realmed King;
they were the rebirth of the world <note>original: *aithgin mbetha*; referring to Noah's family repopulating the earth after the Great Flood.</note>.

241. The host of prophets led by
Isaiah, that fair prophet <note>original: *propheta*</note> whom we sing;
and the patriarchs whom we beseech,
along with wondrous Abraham.

245. The host of apostles led by Peter,
with the disciples of Jesus;
Paul the excellent and fearless,
the leader of the highest wisdom!

249. The host of martyrs led by Stephen,
a golden branch <note>original: *doss órdæ*; literally "golden bush," a metaphor for a protector or a flourishing leader.</note> of purity!
The anchorites around Old-Paul <note>original: *sen-Phól*; this refers to St. Paul of Thebes, traditionally considered the first Christian hermit.</note>,
and the host of holy virgins around Mary.

253. The host of the holy bishops of Rome,
around Peter, the splendid *bordgal* <note>original: *án bordgal*; a term of uncertain meaning, possibly referring to a "gathering of nations" or a "metropolis," often used to describe Rome or great religious centers.</note>;
and the bishops of Jerusalem,
along with James of the high dignities.

257. The company of bishops in Antioch, led by Peter, that primal flame <note>original: *breo*; a metaphor for a shining spiritual leader.</note>; and the bishops of Alexandria with Mark—royal and fiery <note>original: *rúadgorm*; literally "red-blue," a term used in Old Irish poetry to describe something brilliant, intense, or shimmering like a flame or a gem.</note>.

261. The holy company of Honoratus <note>Saint Honoratus of Arles (c. 350–429), founder of the famous monastery of Lérins.</note>, a famous warrior leading a great host; and the company of wisdom, which has been crowned, along with victorious Benedict <note>Saint Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547), the father of Western monasticism.</note>.

265. The illustrious <note>original: *airdirc*</note> company of George <note>Saint George the Martyr.</note>—it is no small thing to contemplate—and every child who went to martyrdom under Herod in Bethlehem <note>The Holy Innocents, the young children of Bethlehem slain by Herod the Great.</note>.

269. The company of priests who have offered the Body of Christ, who suffered on the Cross, to help me every day; along with Aaron, that pillar <note>original: *sab*; literally a "staff" or "prop," used here as a metaphor for a strong leader or support of the faith.</note> of the elders.

273. The company of monks around Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great (c. 251–356), the desert father who pioneered Christian monasticism.</note>, whose spiritual paths are mystical; along with Martin <note>Saint Martin of Tours (c. 316–397), a soldier turned bishop.</note>, the soldier of battle, a company of the high saints of the world.

277. The troop of the noble saints of Ireland <note>original: *Erin*</note>, with Patrick who is highest; and Columba <note>original: *Columb Cille* (Dove of the Church), the apostle to the Picts.</note>, who resides <note>original: *congaib*; meaning to hold, establish, or dwell.</note> with the troops of the saints of Scotland <note>original: *Alba*</note>.

281. The final, vast troop, which completes a bright chain: Saint Brigit <note>One of Ireland's patron saints, often called the "Mary of the Gael."</note> after her triumphs, with the virgins of Ireland.

285. All these troops with noble high-kings <note>original: *ardrígaib*; supreme rulers, used here metaphorically for the highest saints.</note>—may they come to help me, a shining white following, a vast host of saints.

289. Every saint who has been, is, and shall be until the Last Judgment <note>original: *Doom*</note>—a mighty division!—in the company of holy Christ, may they be helping me!

293. May they be helping me in heaven and on earth; may they come in bands to assist my soul!

297. My soul and my wounded body, while they are at labor <note>While the soul and body continue to toil through the hardships of earthly life.</note>, may they be consoling me—the royal host <note>original: *rígrad*; literally "king-folk" or "royal company," describing the saints in God's kingdom.</note> whom I have entreated!

301. I have entreated the royal company <note>original: *rígraíd*; literally "king-folk," referring to the assembly of saints in heaven</note> for whom there has been a search: O Jesus, with true goodness, I entreat You afterwards.

305. After recounting these troops, O High King <note>original: *ardrí*</note> who cannot be hidden, O Christ, whose servant I am, **have mercy on me** <note>original Latin: *miserere mihi*</note>.

309. **Have mercy on me** <note>original Latin: *miserere mihi*</note>, O royal Prince in abundance <note>original: *for tuiliu*; literally "upon a flood"</note>, O Jesus, I love You, O great God, I beseech You!

313. O great God, I entreat You, hear my wretched sigh! May I be, after this battle <note>original: *báigse*; the struggle or "contest" of earthly life</note>, in the everlasting company of this host!

317. The great host which I count, who died in every nation <note>original: *béscnu*; can mean language, custom, or nation</note>—to You, O Christ, who are noblest, I appeal by their sufferings.

321. I appeal by their truly innocent blood shed on the roads: I appeal by their limbs, and their spears <note>original: *laigniu*; lances or spears</note> through their sides.

I appeal <note>original: *adsliundiu*; a legalistic term for making a formal claim or appeal</note> by their groans and their sharp sighs; to You, O Christ, in my misery, I appeal by their festival days.

Against the temptations <note>original: *tudrach*; incitement or provocation</note> of the world—for its power is great—I appeal by the longing of those who stand around You in white robes <note>original: *rínbántlacht*; literally "star-white clothing"</note>.

I appeal by their spirits in Your beautiful royal kingdom; to You—for they are renowned <note>original: *fissi*; literally "to be known" or "worthy of knowledge"</note>—I appeal by their holy relics.

Whatever prayer I offer to You, I appeal by the tears on their pale faces so that You will not refuse it.

I appeal by Your heavens and their constant wonders, with holy ranks of angels from the center to the edge.

I appeal by every offering <note>original: *audpairt*; specifically referring to the sacrifice of the Mass</note> through which Your Body has been offered amidst showers of tears, beneath the clouds upon holy altars.

349. I appeal <note>original: *Adsluindiu*; a formal legal term for making a claim or invoking a protection</note> by the shout of triumph that every devoted person <note>original: *macc lére*; literally "son of devotion," often referring to a monk or student</note> cries out, and by the rain of cold blood that poured through His own side.

353. I appeal by Your humanity <note>original: *dóenacht*</note> and Your divinity <note>original: *déacht*</note>, along with Your beautiful <note>original: *delbdae*; well-formed or beautiful</note> Holy Spirit. I appeal by Your union with the heavenly Father.

357. I appeal to You alongside Your saints, by everything I say—that I may possess in Your kingdom everything I strive for.

361. In every struggle where my proud, joyful mind has stumbled, and in the disciplining <note>original: *béim*; literally "smiting" or "striking"</note> of my conscious body, may Your heavenly household <note>the angels and saints</note> pray to You!

365. Hear me, O Jesus—Your weak exile! <note>original: *deórudán*; a diminutive of *deórad*, meaning a pilgrim, stranger, or exile</note> I would rather be separated from this world than remain here.

369. May my suffering <note>original: *barae*; can mean wrath, affliction, or a burden</note> be healed through the granting of my prayers; my Friend <note>Christ</note> does not refuse me: I appeal to You by all these things.

393. Ma choníssid¹ coicsed²
    ba mithig³ far tíchtu,⁴
    atá sund as huatiu⁵
    dedblén⁶ de⁷ thúaith Íssu.⁸

If you are able to feel compassion, your arrival would be timely: here is one who is loneliest, a weakling <note>original: *dedblén*; a diminutive form meaning a small, weak, or pitiful person</note> among Jesus’s people.

397. Cé ní⁹ eslind¹⁰ líbsi
    ar gnúis ind¹¹ rígnélsa,¹²
    ol am¹³ dedblén¹⁴ trúagsa
    cen chobair mo dérsa.

Though you face no danger <note>original: *eslind*; peril or vulnerability</note> before the face of this King of Clouds, yet *I* am a wretched weakling without help to dry my tears.

401. Á drong nóeb secht¹⁵ nime,
    ol is mór for¹⁶ ngaire,
    slánaigid mo chride
    ar écnaire Maicc Maire.¹⁷

O holy host of the seven heavens, since your tenderness <note>original: *gaire*; can mean piety, duty, or localized care/tenderness</note> is so great, heal my heart for the sake of Mary’s Son.

405. Ar écnaire ind¹⁸ rígsá
    frisn-agar an¹⁹ núallsa,
    farith²⁰ asin²¹ tsnimsa,²²

For the sake of this King, to whom this cry is made, help him out of this sadness—this wretched beggar <note>original: *pauperán*; a Latin-derived term for a poor person or mendicant</note>!

409. Cid trúag lasna bráithrea²³
    na guidise uili,
    duit,²⁴ á Chríst, in tráthsa²⁵
    ro gádsa²⁶ mo guidi.

Though all these prayers may seem wretched to the brothers, to You, O Christ, at this time, I have offered my prayer.

413. Guidiu itge²⁷ náile
    tarcenn fer in betha,

    á rí beres²⁸ bretha!

I pray another prayer on behalf of the men of the world, O Lord of the kingdom, O King who delivers judgment <note>original: *bretha*; dooms or legal decisions</note>!

417. Perhaps all this supplication
may not be pleasing to everyone;
so that no anger remains after us,
let the prayer be changed.

421. The prayer that I have prayed
is not intended to harm anyone;
I would rather be separated from unrighteousness
than remain in it.

425. Listen, O Jesus,
O Christ, whose servant I am,
may you grant the entire prayer
of every son of piety! <note>original: *maicc lére*; an Irish idiom for a devoted or pious person.</note>

429. The prayer of every son of piety,
O Lord, is not in vain; <note>original: *hespae*; meaning idle, useless, or without result.</note>
may you grant it to them,
if what they ask for is appropriate.

433. If what they ask for is appropriate,
O King who rules the earth,
may you save their bodies,
and may you sanctify their souls!

437. The soul of every "son of Life" <note>original: *maicc bethad*; a term for a person who is spiritually alive or among the saved.</note>
has been sanctified through you;
Adam’s race <note>original: *síll nÁdaim*; humanity.</note>, which is the highest of creations,
has been saved by Jesus.

441. May you save me, O Jesus,
my body and my soul,
from every evil that exists,
that causes harm on the earth. <note>original: *frisoirg*; meaning to strike against, offend, or injure.</note>

445. May you save me, O Jesus,
O Lord of fair gatherings,
just as you saved Elijah,
along with Enoch, from the world. <note>Elijah and Enoch are the two biblical figures said to have been taken up to heaven without dying.</note>

449. May you save me, O Jesus,
from every evil on earth,
just as you saved Noah,
son of Lamech, from the Flood.

453. May you save me, O Jesus,
O King of pure radiance,
just as you saved Abraham <note>original: *Abram*</note>
from the hands of the Chaldeans.

457. May you save me, O Jesus,
O mysterious and gracious King!
just as you saved Lot
from the sin of the cities. <note>Referring to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah.</note>

461. May you save me, O Jesus,
O noble and wondrous King!
just as you saved Jonah
from the belly of the great whale. <note>original: *ceti magni*; Latin for "of the great sea-monster" or whale.</note>

465. <note>original Irish: *Rom-śóerae, á Íssu, it riched ilrathach, amail soersai Ísac de lámaib a athar.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, into your heaven of many graces, just as you saved Isaac from the hands of his father. <note>Referring to the "Binding of Isaac" in Genesis 22, where Isaac was spared from sacrifice.</note>

469. <note>original Irish: *Rom-śóerae, á Íssu, lat nóebu tan tíastae, amail soersai Teclam de ginol na bíastae.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, with your saints when they come, just as you saved Thecla from the jaws of the monster. <note>Saint Thecla was a popular early Christian saint said to have been miraculously saved from wild beasts in the arena.</note>

473. <note>original Irish: *Rom-śóerae, á Íssu, ro éra do máthre, amail soersai Iacób de lámaib a bráthre.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus—whom your mother’s people rejected—just as you saved Jacob from the hands of his brothers. <note>This likely refers to Jacob’s flight from his brother Esau or his sons' survival in Egypt.</note>

477. <note>original Irish: *Rom-śóerae á Íssu, ar cech nolc nád rachrad, amail soersai Ióain de neim inna nathrach.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, from every evil that might not perish, just as you saved John from the poison of the serpent. <note>A reference to the legend of St. John the Apostle, who survived drinking from a poisoned chalice.</note>

481. <note>original Irish: *Rom-śóerae, á Íssu, ar iffern co tróigi, amail soersai Dauíd de gail claidib Góli.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, from hell and its misery, just as you saved David from the power of Goliath’s sword.

485. <note>original Irish: *Rom-śóerae, á Íssu, ro sóerais na huili, Susannam co nordun iarsind forgul fuirri.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus; you who have saved everyone, just as you saved the noble Susanna after the false testimony against her. <note>Susanna was a biblical figure vindicated by the prophet Daniel after being falsely accused of a crime.</note>

# THE MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS: EPILOGUE

489. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, ar écnaírc do báge, amail sóersai Nínuén i n-aimsir na pláge.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, for the sake of your struggle, as you saved Nineveh in the time of the plague. <note>Nineveh was spared from destruction after its people repented following the preaching of Jonah.</note>

493. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, glé lim atom-didmae, amail sóersai popul Israél de Gilbae.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus; I am certain that you will acknowledge me, just as you saved the people of Israel from Mount Gilboa. <note>Mount Gilboa was the site of a major battle where King Saul fell; the poet invokes God's protection of His people during such trials.</note>

497. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, a Choimmdiu as deodam, amail sóersai Daniél assin chuithi leoman.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, O Lord who is most divine, as you saved Daniel from the den of lions.

501. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, a rí sochlaí sóbis, amal sóersai Moisén de manu Fáronís.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, O famous and gentle King! As you saved Moses from the hand of Pharaoh. <note>original: *de manu Pharaonis*</note>

505. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, mórférta dorigñis, amail sóersai maccu de camíno ignis.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, you who have performed great miracles, as you saved the three children from the fiery furnace. <note>original: *de camino ignis*</note> <note>Referring to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the Book of Daniel.</note>

509. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, a rí cecha clainde, amail soersai Tóbe de thróge na daílle.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, O king of every tribe, as you saved Tobit from the misery of blindness. <note>In the Book of Tobit, the protagonist's sight is miraculously restored.</note>

513. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, ar écnaírc do martrae, Pól Petar fíad rígaib, de dígaíl na carcrae.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, for the sake of your martyrs—as you saved Paul and Peter before kings—from the punishment of the prison.

517. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, ar accais cech thedmae, amal sóersai Iób de fochidib demnae.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, from the cause of every disease, just as you saved Job from the tribulations of demons.

521. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae á Íssu, á Chríst, ní rop áilsed, amail sóersai Dauíd ar Sául dia tháinsem.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, O Christ—let there be no neglect—just as you saved David from Saul and from his accusation. <note>The poet asks for protection against being overlooked by God, citing how David was protected from King Saul’s jealous pursuit and slander.</note>

525. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, ar écnaire do máthre, amal sóersai Ióséph de lámaib a bráthre.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, for the sake of your Mother's kindred, just as you saved Joseph from the hands of his brothers. <note>Referring to Joseph, son of Jacob, who was sold into slavery by his brothers but eventually rose to power in Egypt.</note>

529. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, á rí benedicte, Israél co nóibi de dóiri Égipte.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, O blessed King, as you saved holy Israel from the bondage of Egypt.

533. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, ol is frit mo chairde, amail sóersai Petar de thonnaib na fairge.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, for my covenant is with you, just as you saved Peter from the waves of the sea. <note>Referring to Jesus reaching out to save Peter when he began to sink while walking on the water (Matthew 14:30-31).</note>

537. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, ar iffern ngér ngenech, amail sóersai Ióain assin dabaig thened.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, from sharp, gaping hell, just as you saved John from the vat of fire. <note>Referring to the tradition that Saint John the Apostle was thrown into a vat of boiling oil at the Latin Gate in Rome and emerged unharmed.</note>

541. <note>original Irish: *Rom-sóerae, á Íssu, á rí úas na flathib, amail sóersai Samsón térnae assin chathir.*</note>
May you save me, O Jesus, O King above all princes, just as you saved Samson, who escaped from the city. <note>Samson famously escaped the city of Gaza by ripping up its gates and carrying them away (Judges 16).</note>

# MARTYROLOGY OF OENGUS

545. May you save me, O Jesus, my soul from every punishment, just as you saved Martin from the priest of the idol. <note>original Irish: *Rom-śóerae, á Issu, m'anmain ar cech ńdígaíl, amail sóersai Mártain ar śacart ind ídail.* St. Martin of Tours was famous for his confrontations with paganism.</note>

549. May you save me, O Jesus, for the sake of your household <note>meaning the community of saints or the Church</note>, just as you saved Patrick from death by poison at Tara. <note>original Irish: *Rom-śóerae, á Issu, ar écnaire do theglaig, amal sóersai Pátric de thonnud hi Temraig.* This refers to a legend where St. Patrick survived a poisoned drink offered by a druid at the court of the High King.</note>

553. May you save me, O Jesus, for I am a servant of yours, just as you saved Kevin from the falling of the mountain. <note>original Irish: *Rom-śóerae, á Issu, ol is duit am céle, amal sóersai Cóemgein de chutaim in tslébe.* Cóemgein is Saint Kevin of Glendalough; this refers to a miracle involving protection from a landslide or collapse.</note>

557. May you save me, O Jesus—your miracles are everlasting! O Lord whom I entreat, I await your messengers. <note>original Irish: *Rom-śóerae, á Issu, it bithbúana t'ferta, á Chommdiu non-áiliu, frisáilur do thechta.*</note>

561. When that great blessing <term>original Irish: *irguis*</term> comes to me, whether at Easter or in Lent, may the royal host <note>the saints</note> I have commemorated convoy me into paradise! <note>original Irish: *Tan domm-techt irguis, cid i caisc nó chorgus, rom-śnádat i pardus ind rígrad imrordus.*</note>

565. I have commemorated the royal host around the King above the clouds, etc. <note>original Irish: *Imrordus in rígraíd immon ríġ úas nélaib, etc.*</note>

->IT ENDS. Amen.<-

***

<meta>This page begins the "Glossarial Index," providing a dictionary of Old Irish words used in the text, organized alphabetically. It starts with various grammatical uses of the word "a" and continues through "accais" (cause).</meta>

# I. GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

1. **a** *his, its*: *his* dignity <note>original: ordan</note>, February 6, 22, causing aspiration <note>a softening of the following consonant</note>; *his* of land <note>original: ferainn</note>, March 12; *his* blood <note>original: fuil</note>, May 27; to serve him <note>original: dia frestul</note>, Epilogue 115; *his* three <note>original: threta</note>, Prologue 230; with *his* household <note>original: lia theglach</note>, Prologue 95; with *his* trio <note>original: con-a thriur</note>, January 24; with *his* chief army <note>original: con-a phrímsluag</note>, April 13; *his* temple <note>original: thempuil</note>, December 15; *his* battle <note>original: chatha</note>, Prologue 139; *his* passion <note>original: chéssad</note>, February 20; with *his* clergy <note>original: con-a chléir</note>, January 3, 12, September 2.
2. **a** *her*: *her* fort <note>original: dún</note>, Prologue 190; *her* sovereignty <note>original: flathe</note>, Prologue 166; *her* stones <note>original: clocha</note>, Prologue 194; *her* singing <note>original: cétol</note>, June 1; with *her* sisters <note>original: con-a sethraib</note>, August 30. Before a vowel: *her* fasting <note>original: a h-áine</note>, Prologue 127; *her* commemoration <note>original: a haithmit</note>, August 15. Before the letter r: *her* redness or fame <note>original: a rrúan</note>, Prologue 192.
3. **a n-** *their*. Before a vowel: *their* fasting <note>original: a náine</note>, Prologue 67; *their* prayer <note>original: a nítge</note>, January 10, July 17; for *their* watch <note>original: a nfarair</note>, Prologue 290. Eclipsing <note>adding a nasal sound to the start of the next word</note>: *their* slaying <note>original: a nguin som</note>, Prologue 58; *their* shouts <note>original: a ngretha</note>, Prologue 154; *their* forts <note>original: a ndúine</note>, Prologue 66, 68, 150. Before b and m: *their* powers <note>original: a mbríga</note>, Prologue 87; with *their* powers <note>original: con-a mbrígaib</note>, Prologue 34; *their* blessing <note>original: a mbendacht</note>, January 13; *their* tomb <note>original: a mmemrae</note>, Prologue 224. Before r: *their* number <note>original: a rím som</note>, Prologue 268; *their* Rome <note>original: a rrúam</note>, Prologue 192, October 28. Before l: *their* grave <note>original: a llíge</note>, Prologue 76; *their* lightning <note>original: a llóchet</note>, January 26; *their* waters <note>original: a llinde</note>, October 13; *their* graves <note>original: a llechtu</note>, Epilogue 146, January 4. *Their* help <note>original: a cobair</note>, July 28. Before t: before *their* coming <note>original: rían-a techt</note>, Prologue 31. Before p: *their* passion <note>original: a paiss</note>, June 26. Before s: at *their* snare-making <note>original: occ-a sinnad</note>, Prologue 47; after *their* hardships <note>original: iarn-a sáethaib</note>, Prologue 69; with *their* host <note>original: lia sluag</note>, July 30.
4. **a**, for **(s)a(n)**, neuter article in the nominative and accusative singular: the choice <note>original: a togu</note>, Prologue 123; with the victory <note>original: lasa mbúaid</note>, August 2; this time <note>original: a n-ámm-sa</note>, December 18; the shout <note>original: an núall</note>, December 28, Epilogue 163; this diadem <note>original: a mmind-sa</note>, December 18; the sea <note>original: a mmuir</note>, Epilogue 30; the day <note>original: a llathe</note>, January 25.
5. **a**, for **(s)a(n)**, relative pronoun: who went up <note>original: a conrualae</note>, Epilogue 25; around whom prostrated <note>original: imm-a slecht</note>, February 20; around whom were prostrated <note>original: imm-a slechta</note>, November 5; to whom he raised up <note>original: dia túargaib</note>, March 9; with whom was found <note>original: lassa frith</note>, March 10; but when it was <note>original: dia mbo</note>, July 10; for *their* fight <note>original: ar a mbáigiu</note>, Epilogue 360.
6. **a**, a prefix used with numerals when they are not followed by a noun: ten <note>original: a deich</note>, October 9, Manuscript R¹; four <note>original: a cethair</note>, page 146.
7. **a**, out of, a preposition used with the dative case <note>original: cum dat.</note>: out of prisons <note>original: a carcraib</note>, Prologue 46; out of Ireland <note>original: a Hére</note>, July 31; out of Aran <note>original: a hÁraind</note>, November 21. From **as, ass**, the unstressed form of **ess**, equivalent to the Latin *ex*. Found before "cold" <note>original: úacht</note>, April 19, and before articles (Epilogue 407, 500, 540, 544) and pronouns.

**á**, interjection meaning *O* (Greek and Latin *ō*), Prologue 1, 8, 9, and throughout <note>original: et passim</note>. In the manuscripts, the mark showing a long vowel is usually omitted here, but in "O man" <note>original: á fir</note>, Wb. 10ᵃ 10; "O righteous ones" <note>original: á firianú</note>, Wb. 25ᵈ 11; and "O all you men" <note>original: á huili duini</note>, Wb. 1ᶜ 8, it is correctly written.

**abann**, feminine noun meaning *river*, page 40, Ascoli 52; dative case *abainn*, page 10, page 130, last line. On pages 224 and 226, *abann* is in the genitive singular <note>possessive form</note>, as if derived from a nominative form *abae* or Middle Irish *aba*.

**abb, ap**, masculine noun meaning *abbot*, January 2, 13, February 8, 24, April 8, 12, 18, 27, May 24, October 6, 27, December 6; *ap*, page 46, Ascoli 53; genitive case *apad*; accusative case *apid*, *abbaith*, Thesaurus volume II, page 242. From this comes **apdaíne**, meaning *abbacy*, pages 54, 78.

**abbán** (from *ad-bán*), meaning *very white*, page 52, Leabhar na hUidhre 40ᵇ 16.

**ac**, a preposition used in place of **oc** (at or with), see that entry. *ac-a*, Prologue 227 L; *acom*, Epilogue 44, 292, 293 in the Leabhar Breac.

**accais**, meaning *cause*, singular accusative case, Epilogue 518, Book of Leinster 92ª 36, 42; genitive case *aicsen*; borrowed from the Latin *occasio*, Ascoli 45.

aicsen: of a cause (genitive)
occasio: occasion/cause (Latin)
</vocab>

# I. GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**ached, achad**, *field*, Thesaurus II. 267, 278, Ascoli 43, genitive **achid, achaid**, March 26, dative September 5, **achud** August 9, November 28.
**-achrad**? *against every evil that should not...* <note>original: ar cech ulc nad r-achrad</note>, Epilogue 478, meaning obscure.
**acht**, *save, but, except*, except/outside <note>original: ἐκτός</note>, Prologue 194. Appendix 11, Epilogue 11, 17, 20, 32, 91, 131. Ascoli 43: with subjunctive *provided that*.
**1. acus**, *near*, Epilogue 110. *whether far off or nearby* <note>original: imb icéin fa in-accus</note> Würzburg Glosses 23ᵇ 41, Welsh <note>original: Cymr. agos</note>.
**2. acus**, *and*, see *ocus*.
**ad-**, *perfective particle* <note>a grammatical marker indicating a completed action</note>, Sarauw page 45: *he has slept* <note>original: conatuil</note> August 7, = *he has slept* <note>original: conatil</note> Würzburg Glosses 29ᵈ 15, from **com-ad-tuil*. See *contuil*.
**adaig**, feminine, *night, eve*, December 24, genitive **aidche**. Cognate with the Latin for dark-colored <note>original: aquilus</note>.
**adamrae, adamre**, *wondrous*, Ascoli 41, plural nominative feminine **adamrai**, Epilogue 213. Hence **adamraigim** ‘I admire’ <note>original: admiror</note>, *they marveled at* <note>original: ad-ru-amraigset</note> Milan Glosses 88ᵃ 18. See *amrae*.
**ad-andaim**, *I kindle, metaphorically I begin*. Ascoli 39, preterite <note>past tense</note> active singular 3rd person *he kindled* <note>original: ad-r-ann</note> Saltair na Rann 2919, preterite passive singular 3rd person *it was kindled* <note>original: ad-r-andad</note> Appendix 5: verbal noun **andud** *inflaming*, Milan Glosses 131ᵈ 14, *beginning*, Laws III. 318.
**adbae**, feminine, *a dwelling, a house*, May 26.
**adband**, masculine, *a strain of music*, genitive singular and plural nominative **adbaind**, page 158: compare with *bind* <note>meaning sweet or melodious</note>.
**adbul**, *vast, mighty*, genitive **adbail** February 17. Hence *aidbligim*.
**ad- (aith-)comaingim**, *I strike off*, preterite singular 3rd person *struck* <note>original: adcomaing, glossing the Latin pulsauit</note> Milan Glosses 19ᶜ 17, enclitic s-preterite plural 1st person *we have struck* <note>original: co n-ecmaingsem</note>, Epilogue 7.
**ad-cíu**, *I see*, present indicative singular 2nd person *you see* <note>original: ad-chíssiu</note> Prologue 150, where the aspiration <note>a softening of the consonant sound</note> expresses relativity <note>used in a relative clause</note>: likewise in the preterite passive *it was seen* <note>original: adchess</note> Würzburg Glosses 23ᶜ 11. Except in the plural 2nd person (*you saw* <note>original: adced</note> Würzburg Glosses 11ᵇ 22), the subjunctive is deponent <note>having a passive form but active meaning</note>: *that I may see* <note>original: adcear</note>, Thesaurus II. 293, line 6. For the perfect singular 3rd person, *he has seen* <note>original: adcondairc</note> is used.
**ad-cosnaim (ad-com-sním)**, *I strive after*: see *ascnam*.
**ad-cuaid (ad-co-faith)** *he narrated* <note>original: narravit</note> Milan Glosses 65ᵃ 1, a form of *adfét*: subjunctive singular 2nd person with an infixed pronoun *you may tell it* <note>original: atcois</note> from **adcofess*, Prologue 182.
**ad-damaim, atmaim**, *I confess, I acknowledge*, reduplicated future *you will acknowledge me* <note>original: atomdidmae</note>, Epilogue 494. The perfect is deponent: singular 1st person *I have acknowledged* <note>original: adrodamar</note>, Thesaurus II. 9: singular 3rd person *he has acknowledged* <note>original: adrodamair</note>. *he did not acknowledge* <note>original: ní ardamair</note>, Book of Leinster 287ᵇ 5, imperative singular 2nd person *do not acknowledge* <note>original: na hataim</note>, page 12.
**ad-ethaim**, *I go to, I attain*, present indicative singular 3rd person *he attains* <note>original: adetha</note> Milan Glosses 48ᵈ 2, s-preterite singular 3rd person, *he attained* <note>original: ad-r-eth</note> Prologue 120, July 7, August 30, November 6, Saltair na Rann 5877. plural 3rd person, *they attained* <note>original: adrethsat</note> Lebor na hUidre 66ᵃ 36: compare with Latin for *approach/go to* <note>original: adito</note>.
**ad-fíadaim**, *I narrate, set forth*, Ascoli 330, present indicative singular 3rd person *he relates* <note>original: adfét</note> March 23 (corruptly *arfét*) plural 1st person *we relate* <note>original: ad-fíadam</note>, Epilogue 214.
**ad-gabaim**, *I accept*, preterite singular 3rd person with infixed pronoun *he accepted it* <note>original: r’atgab (ad-d-g.)</note>, Prologue 107.
**ad-gíallaim**, *I give hostages, I serve*, *who serves him* <note>original: ad-id-gialla</note> February 23, plural 3rd person, *they serve* <note>original: adgíallat</note>, Epilogue 60. Laws IV. 346.
**ad-glíunn**, *I search out*, imperfect plural 3rd person, with infixed pronoun *they used to search them out* <note>original: atglentis</note> July 30.
**ad-légaim**, *I read out*, see *arlégaim*.
**admat**, *timber, material*, Prologue 294. Saltair na Rann 7266, genitive **admait** Book of Leinster 117ᵇ 9. The *-mat* is from **mazdo* = German for mast <note>original: mast</note>, Latin for mast <note>original: mālus</note> from **mādus*.
**ad-muiniur**, *I venerate*, October 2, Ascoli 380, see *armuniur*.
**ad-nacim**, *I bury*, *he was buried* <note>original: ro-adnacht</note>, page 8, *he has been buried* <note>original: ad-ra-nact</note>, Thesaurus II. 242, line 10, *until he was buried* <note>original: co ro adnacht</note> Lebor na hUidre 98ᵇ 34. **adnacul**, *a grave*, page 8, *near her grave* <note>original: gair a hadnacal</note>, page 46.

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**ad-oprim (ad-od-berim)**, *I offer up*, t-preterite <note>a specific type of past tense in Old Irish</note> 3rd person singular, *ad[r]opart*, Epilogue 269, Thesaurus II. 242; passive preterite 3rd person singular, *it was offered up* <note>original: adroipred</note>, Epilogue 346, *adropred* Würzburg Glosses 15ᵈ 20.

**ad-oraim**, *I adore*, passive present indicative 3rd person singular, *adorthar*, November 23; preterite active 3rd person singular with an infixed pronoun <note>a pronoun placed inside the verb</note> *atror* (ad-d-r-or) Milan Glosses 69ᵈ 3; b-future <note>a future tense marked with 'b'</note> 3rd person singular, *ad-n-orfa*, Milan Glosses 81ᵈ 6.

**adrad**, *worship*, genitive *adartha*, verbal noun of **adoraim**, Prologue 187, 207.

**ad-rannaim**, *I apportion, I divide*, present indicative 2nd person singular, *adrannai* September 6, 3rd person singular *adranna* Book of Leinster 28ᵇ 17. For *rannaim* see Ascoli 185.

**ad-rímiu**, *I recount, reckon*, Ascoli 210, 1st person plural, *adrímem* July 17, Epilogue 87; verbal noun **áram**, see that entry <note>original: q.v.</note>. Cognate with **do-rímiu** and **rím**, see those entries.

**ad-riug**, *I tie*, Ascoli 204, reduplicated future <note>a future tense formed by doubling a syllable</note> 2nd person singular, *atróiris*, December 16: compare Irish **con-riug, cuimrech** and Latin *cor-rigia* "shoetie."

**ad-saigim**, *I visit*, imperfect 3rd person plural, *atsaigtis* September 30.

**ad-sluindiu**, *I appeal*, Epilogue 320, 321, 323, 325, 328, 332, etc., present indicative 3rd person singular, *atsluindi* (ad-d-sl.) Prologue 110: see **slondim**.

**ad-sníaim**, *I weave together*: with infixed *da*: *ata-sníaim* October 26.

**ae** see **cechae**.

**áer**, feminine, *satire*, plural accusative *aéra* November 8.

**áeraim**, *I satirize, I reproach*, *r'áerad* April 8.

**áes**, neuter, *age, old age*, genitive *áis*, accusative singular *áes* Prologue 60.

**agaim**, *I drive* (Latin *ago* <note>original: ago</note>), present indicative 3rd person plural, *agait* September 4, *agar*, Epilogue 406, see **do agaim**.

**agaid i n-agaid**, page 6, note 5, *face to face*, *agid in-agid*, Book of Leinster 288ᵇ 35.

**áge, áge**, masculine, *a pillar*, Prologue 119, 243, 339, February 7, 10, March 21, May 3, 24, 25, July 6, 31, September 5, October 10, November 2; *aga* Book of Leinster 29ᵇ 3: *a chief*, accusative singular, page 6, line 3.

**agnomen**, masculine, page 166, borrowed from Latin <note>meaning an additional name or nickname</note>.

**ái**, *hers*, page 4, see Ascoli 17.

**aicbéil**, *corruptly aicméil, terrible*, page 120, Contributions 8.

**aiccept**, masculine, *a lesson* (also *aiccecht*), genitive *aiccepta*, page 21. Late Latin *accepturium*, that is, *a lesson/reading* <note>original: lectionem</note>, Bodleian 572, folio 47ᵃ.

**áil**, *pleasing*, July 24 R¹ F. (from *pagli*, Gothic *fagrs*, Strachan). In *aill* (*áill?*) *do dáinib*, Epilogue 417, the second 'l' may be due to the following 'd'; so in *mad aill duib*, Thesaurus I. 583, line 23.

**aile** (equivalent to Latin *alius* <note>original: alius</note>) *other*, accusative masculine and neuter, Epilogue 413, pretonic *ala*.

**-áliu**, *I beseech, I entreat*, Epilogue 559, Ascoli 20, *nodn-áli* July 9, *non-áilem* July 14, *áilmini* January 10, relative *áilme* August 5, imperative *áil* October 4.

**aill** .i. *aill, some . . . others*, Prologue 23, 24, June 5: compare Revue Celtique xiv. 412 (Book of Leinster 109ᵃ).

**1. aille**, feminine, *praise*, genitive *aille* July 3, August 8, dative *ailli* Thesaurus I. 609, line 26, accusative *ailli*, April 26, Thesaurus I. 495, line 1: borrowed from the Greek *Hallelujah* <note>original: 'Αλληλούια</note>.

**2. aille, aill-e**, *hear? let him hear?* Epilogue 373, compare *aill*, that is, *hear* <note>original: cluin</note> (O'Clery), and *hear* <note>original: cluinti</note> (O'Davoren no. 14).

**áilsed**, *neglect*, Epilogue 522. Laws i. 58, iv. 318.

**aimrit**, see **ambrit**.

**aimser**, feminine, *time*, page 2 (corruptly *aimsir*, page 8), Ascoli 41, singular dative *aimsir* Epilogue 116, 492, plural nominative *aimsera* page 1.

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**ain**, see *angim* <note>the verb "to protect" or "to save"</note>.

**áinbech**, *plenteous*, March 24 (rhyming with *cráibdech*, meaning "devout"); dative singular feminine *áinbich*, March 30 (rhyming with *chrábdig*, also meaning "devout").

**áinbil**, adjective, *shameless*? Accusative singular feminine *ánbil*, Saltair na Rann <note>a Middle Irish collection of biblical poems</note> 4718; nominative plural *ánbli*, November 9. Derived from *ánfial* (un-modest), just as *áinble* comes from *ánféle* (un-modesty).

**áine**, *craft* or *cunning*, Epilogue 97. In Manuscript C, this is explained as *forbas*, meaning a "snare" or "ambush" (O'Davoren's Glossary, no. 941).

1.  **áine**, *splendour*, Prologue 67, 127. Dative form *áni* appears on various calendar dates: Jan. 19, 28; Feb. 6; March 6; June 4; July 2, 13; Aug. 3, 22; Oct. 8; Nov. 6, 27; Dec. 5, 26.

2.  **áine**, a Middle Irish corruption of *óine*, meaning *fasting* <note>original Latin: ieiunium</note>. Genitive case: *dia haine* (Friday, literally "the day of fasting"), page 2.

**aineach (enech)**, *face*. Cognate with the Sanskrit word *anīka* (face/front). See also the entries for *airenach* and *clárainech*.

**aingel**, *angel* <note>original Latin: angelus</note>. Plural genitive: Prologue 132, Epilogue 344; dative *ainglib*, Epilogue 85; accusative *aingliu* or *angliu*, Prologue 7, 159; March 10; May 23, 28; July 12.

**ainglech**, adjective, *angelic*. Found on March 4, 10, 16; June 9; July 28; Nov. 22; Dec. 6; Epilogue 91.

**ainglide**, *angelic*, page 44.

**áinle** (perhaps should be read as *áinli*?), March 22, June 21. This appears to be a compound of *án* ("splendid") and *lí* ("beauty"), where the second vowel was shortened. In the manuscript H. 2. 17, page 137b, Paris is called "the candle, the hero, and the darling of all Asia" <note>original: caindel 7 ánle 7 dretel na huile hAsia</note>. *Ánle* can also mean *warrior* or *hero*.

**ainm**, neuter noun, *a name*. Prologue 171, Jan. 31, etc. See Ascoli’s *Glossarium Palaeo-Hibernicum*, page 37. Accusative singular *ainm*, Prologue 112; nominative plural *anmann*, May 19. Cognate with the Welsh *anu* or *enw* (plural *anuein*). Compound: *nóeb-ainm* (holy name), Prologue 99, 109.

**airchetlaid**, masculine noun, *poet*, page 70, line 2; also in the Book of Leinster 285b. This is a derivative of *airchetal*, meaning "a poem."

**aircthid**, *inventor* or *author*, page 2. A derivative of *airic* (the act of finding/inventing).

**airdirc**, *conspicuous* or *prominent* <note>original Greek: περιδεικής (perideikēs), meaning "very visible"</note>. March 21, April 19, June 10, Aug. 28, Nov. 5, Dec. 28, Epilogue 265. Related to Old Breton *erderth* <note>explaining the Latin: evidentis, "evident/visible"</note>.

**aire**, feminine noun, *care* or *heed*. Dative singular *airi*, Prologue 15.

**airec**, *the act of finding or inventing*, February 27. This is the verbal noun of the verb *ar-icim* (I find or invent). Past tense 3rd person singular: *ara-anic* ("he found") in the St. Gall Glosses 217a 4. See also *prím-airec* (the first finding).

**airem**, *ploughman*, page 71. Plural genitive *aireman*, Book of Leinster 46b 37.

**airenach**, *forefront*. Dative singular *airenuch*, Prologue 118.

**airi**, *for him*, Epilogue 176.

**airitiu**, feminine noun, *reception*, February 2, May 26, June 8. Dative and accusative forms: *airitin*.

**airle**, *counsel* or *will*, Prologue 261. The phrase *far n-arle* ("your counsel") is glossed as *for comarli* ("on counsel") in the manuscript *Lebor na hUidre* 19b 26.

**airther**, *the eastern part, the east*, or *the front part*. Genitive singular *airthir*, December 9; dative *airthiur*, *Lebor na hUidre* 90b 44.

**aisndéid**, August 29, October 14. *Announce*. See the verb *as-indfédim* (I declare or announce).

**aiste**, pages 4, 14. *A peculiar kind of verse or metre*.

**aite**, *foster-father* or *tutor*. March 19, May 28, Epilogue 65.

**áith**, feminine noun, page 8. *A drying-kiln*. Genitive *átha*; dative *áith*, pages 8, 12. Cognate with the Welsh *odyn* (kiln).

**aithbe (athbe)**, *an ebbing* or *ebb-tide*. Genitive singular *aithbi*, April 15, August 12; dative *in aithbiu* <note>explaining the Latin: remeat, "it flows back"</note>.

**aithgein (aithgin)**, neuter noun, *rebirth* or *renewal*, Epilogue 240. See also *gein* (birth).

**aithigid**, *the act of visiting*, Prologue 224. Dative: *co a athigid* ("to his visit"), Book of Leinster 153a 21; *ecluis d’athighidh* ("visiting a church"), Laws volume I, page 60. This is the verbal noun of the verb *aithigim* ("I frequent" or "I visit").
