<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**aithis**, *disgrace*. Singular accusative: June 24, Aug. 7.

**aithmet**, *commemoration*. Sept. 19. Genitive case: *aithmeit*, Aug. 15.

**aittreb**, *habitation* or *dwelling*. See also the entries for *bith-aittreb* and *treb*.

**álaib**, *beautiful* or *delightful*. Sept. 3. Cited in O'Davoren’s Glossary <note>an early Irish law glossary</note>, no. 76. Or it may be the dative plural of *ál*, meaning *clever*, O'Davoren’s Glossary, no. 181.

**ailaile**, *another*. Accusative singular feminine: *ailaili*, Prologue 325.

**álaind** (derived from *ad-laind*), *beautiful*, *pleasant*, or *delightful*. March 19, May 1, Aug. 30. Genitive singular masculine: *Cluána álne* <note>meaning "of beautiful Cluain"</note>, April 4. Singular accusative: Oct. 23 (where one would expect the phrasing *tóeb nán nálaind níssu* <note>a grammatical note on the expected syntax</note>). Nominative plural: *áilli*, Prologue 133; *áildi*, Jan. 9. Genitive case: *áille*, Epilogue 83.

**álges**, *importunity* <note>meaning persistent or urgent requests</note>. Singular accusative: *álgis*, Jan. 13, where it rhymes with *Pictavis* <note>original: "Poitiers," a city in France</note>. Hence the related word *álgesach*.

**all**, Neuter. *cliff* or *rock*. Jan. 6. This is a stem in *s* <note>a specific category of noun in linguistics</note>. Genitive singular: *for bru inn aille* <note>original: "on the edge of the cliff"</note>, Lives of the Saints from the Book of Lismore, 2164.

**alltar**, *altar* <note>from the Latin "altare"</note>. Ascoli’s Glossary, 22. Also means *another place* or *the other world*. Genitive singular: *altair*, May 10; Leabhar Breac 74a. Accusative: *alltar*, Prologue 283. The *-tar* ending seems to be a comparative suffix, as seen in *centar* <note>meaning "this world" or "the near side"</note>.

**1. alt**, *high*. Sept. 26. Defined as *noble* <note>original Irish: "uasal"</note> in O'Clery’s Glossary. Also means a *height*. Contributions to Irish Lexicography, 81. Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note>: *g-allt*.

**2. alt**, Masculine. *joint* or *limb*. Ascoli’s Glossary, 23. Accusative plural: *altu*, Epilogue 323. Genitive case: *alta*, Revue Celtique xiv. 485. This is a stem in *u*. Cornish <note>original: "Corn."</note>: *chef-als*, which is a gloss for the Latin *artus* <note>meaning "joints" or "limbs"</note>.

**altae**, Epilogue 134. In the phrase *co lúthigi altae* <note>meaning "with the vigor of limbs"</note>, this seems to be the genitive plural of **2. alt** ("limb"). Compare this meaning to the Greek *μέλος* <note>original: "melos"</note>, which can mean *limb*, *song*, or *strain*.

**altóir**, Feminine. (Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note>: *allor*, from the Latin *altāre*): Ascoli’s Glossary, 23. Genitive singular: *altoire*, page 66. Dative plural: *altórib*, Epilogue 348.

**am**, *I am*. Prologue 26, Epilogue 164, 165, 399, 554; Ascoli’s Glossary, 222. This is an unstressed form of *im*, derived from the ancient root *ésmi*.

**1. a-m**, a neuter form of the definite article used before a labial <note>a sound made with the lips, like b, p, or m</note>. Dec. 18, Epilogue 29, 30.

**2. a-m**, *their*. The third-person plural possessive pronoun used before a labial. Prologue 34, 87, Sept. 2, Epilogue 113.

**amail**, *like* or *as*. Prologue 208. Old Welsh <note>original: "O. Cymr."</note>: *amal*. Because the word is unstressed, the initial *s* sound was regularly lost.

**ambrit** (derived from *am-berit*), *barren*. Page 246; *aimrit*, page 172; *ambreit*, Saltair na Rann 5372.

**amlabar**, *mute* or *dumb*. June 20. Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note>: *aflafar*. See the entry for *labrae*.

**ámm**, Neuter. Equivalent to the Latin *agmen* <note>meaning "a troop" or "a multitude"</note>. Dec. 18. See Contributions to Irish Lexicography, page 86.

**ammus** (derived from *ad-mid-tu-*), *temptation* or *attempt*. Ascoli’s Glossary, 395. Genitive plural: *ammus*, Jan. 30 (perhaps a mistake for *aimse-n*?). Similarly, *dér* in Epilogue 400 stands for *dérae-n*.

**amrae**, adjective. *wondrous*. Feb. 8, July 4, Oct. 5; Epilogue 175, 244, 462; Ascoli’s Glossary, 41. Comparative form: *amru*, Aug. 20, where it is used as the superlative *amram*, Sept. 24. See also the entry for *adamrae*.

**amsán**, Masculine. A diminutive form of *amus* or *amos*, meaning *soldier*. Nominative plural: *amsáin*, Prologue 152.

**1. an-**, an adverbial prefix found in words like *an-air* ("from the east") and *an-all* ("from that side").

**2. an-**, a negative prefix found in *an-fót* ("carelessness"), July 30.

**3. an-**, an intensive prefix <note>used to add emphasis</note> found in *an-bal* ("excessive").

**-an-**, an infixed pronoun for the third-person singular masculine. See the entry for *darrala*.

**án**, adjective. *splendid* (derived from the root *agno-*). Prologue 13, Jan. 11, etc. Dative singular feminine: *áin*, Oct. 20. Accusative singular feminine: *áin*, May 16 (in manuscripts R¹ and L). Compound form: **án-breó** ("splendid flame"), April 23, June 2, Oct. 21.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical "Glossarial Index" of Old Irish terms, specifically focusing on nouns, verbs, and particles beginning with "an-" and "ap-".</meta>

<page-num>298</page-num>
<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

**anad**, *the act of resting, remaining, or staying*. Epilogue 367, 423. This is the verbal noun of the verb *anaim*. It is related to the Greek word *μένω* <note>original: "menō," meaning to stay or remain</note>. Ascoli’s Glossary, 33.

**ánae** (possibly *anae?*), *wealth*. Accusative singular: Epilogue 195. Plural dative: *anaib, anib, ánib*. Accusative: *anu*. Ascoli’s Glossary, 35.

**anall**, Adverb. *from that place* <note>original Latin: "illinc"</note>. Pages 6, 14; Ascoli’s Glossary, 22. *otha anall* means *from henceforward* or *from that point on*.

**anamcharae**, Middle Irish *anmchara*. *soul-friend* or *spiritual guide*. This is equivalent to the Sanskrit term *kalyāṇa-mitra* <note>meaning a "noble friend" who helps one on a spiritual path</note>. Dative singular: *anmcharait*, pages 8, 12. From this comes *anmchairdes*, meaning *spiritual friendship*. Genitive: *anmchair desa*, page 12, note 1.

**anas**, *what is*. Page 4, line 9. *anas dílsiu* means *what is more proper* or *more appropriate*. Prologue 262.

**an-bal**, **anbail**, *very great*. O’Clery’s Glossary defines it as *anbhal*, meaning *romhór* <note>original: "very great"</note>. Genitive singular masculine: *anbail*. Feb. 17, Leabhar Breac.

**ancharae**, Masculine. *anchorite* <note>a person who has retired to a solitary place for a life of religious seclusion; a hermit</note>. Book of Leinster 373d7. Nominative plural: *ancharait*, Epilogue 251.

**and**, **ann**, Adverb. *there* or *then*. Prologue 164, May 1. *ann-som* means *therein* or *in that very place*. Prologue 260.

**andach**, **annach**, *evil* or *iniquity*. Genitive singular: *andaig*, Prologue 237; *annaig, andaich*, Feb. 16.

**andgraib**, *a copy* or *example*. Derived from the Greek *ἀντίγραφον* <note>original: "antigraphon," meaning a copy or transcript</note>. Epilogue 139. Also appears as *angraib* in the Würzburg Glosses 26b18. Dative plural: *ona engraifib*, which glosses the Latin *exemplaribus* <note>original: "from the copies"</note>. Lebor na hUidre 12a.

**anfót**, *carelessness* or *heedlessness* <note>original Latin: "incautio"</note>. July 30. O'Clery’s Glossary defines *anfótt* as *ainbfios* <note>original: "ignorance"</note>. Genitive: *anfoit*. Laws, Volume 1, page 14.

**angim**, *I protect*. 3rd person singular subjunctive: *-ain*. Prologue 18, April 11, 22, Aug. 28, Oct. 29, Dec. 22, Epilogue 226. With an attached pronoun: *ainsium* <note>meaning "protect me"</note>, Jan. 30. Past subjunctive: *no-s-ainsed* <note>meaning "he should protect her/it"</note>, Saltair na Rann 5568. Perfect 3rd person singular: *ro anacht* <note>meaning "he protected"</note>.

**animm**, **anim**, Feminine. *soul*. May 22, Epilogue 19, 53, 221, 297, 437. Genitive singular: *anmae*, Epilogue 117, 169, 183. Dative: *anmain*, Jan. 24; *anim*, Epilogue 52. Accusative: *anmain*, Aug. 21, Dec. 12, Epilogue 296, 436, 442, 546. Genitive plural: *anman*, March 27.

**an-irdalta**, *uncertain*. Page 146. Compare with *erdalta*, meaning *certain*. Windisch’s Dictionary.

**anmech**, **ainmech**, *a rain-storm*. Page 56. Genitive: *anbige*. *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II, 335.

**ansae**, later *ansa*. *difficult*. April 12. Compare to the Welsh (*Cymric*) word *hawdd*, which means *easy*.

**apréil**, *April*. Derived from the Latin *aprēlis*. Genitive singular: March 27, Epilogue 1, 30. Welsh: *ebrill*.

**apstal**, *apostle*. Derived from the Latin *apostolus*. Ascoli’s Glossary 54. Genitive singular: *apstail*, Prologue 109, Jan. 18. Nominative dual: *dá apstal* <note>meaning "two apostles"</note>, July 15. Genitive plural: *apstal*, Nov. 2.

**1. ar**, Preposition. *for*. Prologue 12, 55, Aug. 20, Oct. 8, Epilogue 422. Also means *for the sake of*, March 12. Used with verbs meaning "to protect" or "to save," it means *against* or *from*: Jan. 24, 30, Feb. 3, Oct. 29, Epilogue 482, 538, 548. Used with numbers, it means *on* or *in addition to*: Sept. 22, Oct. 10. See the entry for *arbélaib*.

**2. ar**, Conjunction. *for, because,* or *since*. Prologue 263.

**ár**, *slaughter* or *carnage*. Derived from the reconstructed root *\*agros*. Compare to the Welsh *aer*, Old Breton *air* (which glosses the Latin *stragem* <note>meaning "slaughter"</note>), and the Greek *ἄγρα* <note>original: "agra," meaning a catching or hunting</note>. See also the entry for *díthár*.

**ar-ái**, *as regards* or *concerning*. Page 6, line 21. Contributions to Irish Lexicography 112.

**áram**, Feminine. Derived from the root *\*ad-rimā*. *a number* or the *act of numbering*. Ascoli’s Glossary 211. Accusative singular: *árim*, July 15. This is the verbal noun of *adrímiṁ*.

**arbar**, *a host, throng,* or *cohort*. Ascoli’s Glossary 30. Genitive singular: *arbair*, Epilogue 12. This is the same as *arbir*, which glosses the Latin *coortis* <note>original: "of a cohort"</note>, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* I, 498. Dative: *arbur*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* I, 177 (line 24) and 347 (line 25). Middle Irish: *cossind arba<insert>r</insert>* <note>meaning "with the host"</note>, Book of Leinster 289b46.

**ar-bélaib**, Nominal preposition. *before* or *opposite*. *ar Bledma bailc bélaib*, Nov. 20, which is equal to *arbélaib Bledma bailc* <note>meaning "before strong Slieve Bloom"</note>. See the entry for *bél* below.

**archaingel**, *archangel*. Genitive plural: Epilogue 233.

### GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**ar-crinim** (possibly *ara-crinim?*) *I perish, decay, or fail.* Perfect tense, singular 3rd person (with reduplication): *ar-ro-chíuir* (Prologue 67, 127). Plural 3rd person: *co n-arrceoratar* (Milan Glosses 26d 6, likely read as *-ar-ro-cheoratar?*), *arrochíuir* (Lebor na hUidre 23d 19). See *do-crinim*.

1. **ard** *Adjective. high.* Feb. 6, June 9, July 21, 31, Nov. 10, Dec. 3. Nominative singular neuter: *ard n-imbel* (Prologue 121), *ard n-ainm* (June 3). Genitive singular feminine: *airde* (July 27, Nov. 13). Plural nominative masculine: *aird* (Prologue 155). Comparative forms: *ardu, artu* (Ascoli, page 29). Superlative forms: *ardam* (March 23, Dec. 27, Epilogue 207, 278). Compounds found with: *áge* <note>pillar or period</note> (Prologue 119, 243, Feb. 7, Oct. 30); *céssad* <note>suffering or passion</note> (March 22); *erail* <note>exhortation</note> (Jan. 1); *ethre* <note>end or tail</note> (Oct. 31); *gaire* <note>shortness</note> (page 206); *ídal* <note>idol</note> (page 186); *les* <note>court or benefit</note> (page 48); *nóeb* <note>saint</note> (Epilogue 276); *rí* <note>king</note> (Aug. 5, Epilogue 60, 286, 306); *riched* <note>heaven</note> (Epilogue 18).

2. **ard** *Feminine noun. a height.* (Prologue 168). Genitive: *arde* (July 24). Plural nominative: *ardae* (June 25), equivalent to *artda* in the *Life of Adamnán* (Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus, volume 2, page 274). Elsewhere, *ard* is declined as a masculine o-stem: singular genitive *aird* (Aug. 23), dative *ard* (Dec. 16). Similar forms in the *Book of Armagh*: genitive *airdd*, dative *ardd*, accusative *ardd* (Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus, volume 2, pages 261, 262, 266, 267, 269, 271). Compare with Latin *arduus* <note>meaning high or steep</note>.

3. **ard** *Feminine noun. an assonance or end-rhyme.* Plural genitive: *ard* (pages 4, 5, 14, Epilogue 83). Dual genitive: (pages 6, 14). Compound: *rind-ard* (see that entry).

**ardáig ná**, *in order that not.* (Page 78). Compare *ardáigh co-n* in *Revue Celtique*, volume 10, page 186.

**ar-dlígim**, *I am entitled to* or *I deserve*. Present indicative, singular 3rd person: *ardlig* (June 1, Aug. 5). *arfét* (March 23, Leabhar Breac F.); see *ad-f-* <note>referring to the verb ad-fét, meaning "he tells"</note>.

**ar-fíuch**, *I overcome* or *I vanquish*. (Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus, volume 2, page 249, line 7). Present indicative, singular 3rd person: *arfich* (April 15). *arfiches gail* (Book of Leinster 188b 26).

**ar-gnúis**, *A nominal preposition followed by the genitive case: before.* (Jan. 9, Epilogue 398).

**ar-icim**, *I find* or *I invent*. Preterite <note>past tense</note> passive, singular 3rd person: *-airecht* (Aug. 3). *arrícht* (St. Gall Glosses). Middle Irish: *airnecht* (Saltair na Rann 860). Verbal noun: *airec* (see that entry).

**ar-légaim**, *I read out* or *I recite*. (Ascoli, page 159). *ar-id-léga* (Epilogue 178). Future tense: *ar-da-légfa* (Epilogue 216). Preterite singular 3rd person: *con da-arleg* (Milan Glosses 43b 14). Middle Irish preterite passive, plural 3rd person: *ro hírlégait* (page 66). Verbal noun: *airlegann* (page 66).

**árlius** (Sept. 27). *distasteful?* or *loathsome?* Compare *líus*, meaning *distaste* or *disgust* <note>original Latin: "fastidium"</note> (Milan Glosses 34b 6; St. Gall Glosses 106b 14). Genitive: *liussa* (Würzburg Glosses 13b 6).

**armad** for *ar-an-bad* (page 2).

**ar-muiniur**, *I venerate.* Present indicative, singular 2nd person: *armuinter* (Oct. 2). Singular 3rd person: *ar-as-muinethar* (Milan Glosses 36a 18, 124c 16). Passive present indicative, singular 3rd person: *armuinter* (May 6). Preterite: *ar-ru-muinset* (Milan Glosses 90a 1).

**ar-n**, *our.* Used before a vowel, or the letters *g* and *d* (Prologue 90, 293; Aug. 15; Sept. 20; Epilogue 2). The form **ar-m** appears before *b* (April 21). The form **ar** appears before other letters (Prologue 86, 141; May 28, 30; Aug. 24; Sept. 30; Nov. 2, 27; Dec. 14; Epilogue 9).

**arná** (derived from *aran-ná*) *that not*. *arná bé* (Prologue 297). *arná-p*, meaning *that it may not be* <note>original Latin: "ne sit"</note> (Prologue 323; Epilogue 419).

**arnách** (derived from *aran-nách*) found in *n-éra* (Epilogue 338). Here, *nách* is the dependent negative form used before an infixed pronoun.

**ar-petim**, *I make music* or *I delight*. Present indicative, singular 3rd person with an affixed pronoun: *arpet-i* (Epilogue 79). Verbal noun: *arfitiud* (Book of Leinster 207a 12).

**arrae** (Related to Late Latin *arreum* <note>a payment or substitute for penance</note>), *a penitential commutation* <note>the replacement of a long period of fasting or penance with a shorter, more intense religious act</note> (Epilogue 177, 179, 181, 186).

**ar-ricim**, *I attain*. Future tense <note>specifically a "b-future"</note>, plural 1st person: *arricfam* (Dec. 30).

**ar-selaim**, *I escape* or *I evade?* *ar-don-sela* (June 23).

**ar-sligim** (possibly related to *selgim*?), *I slay*. Present indicative, plural 3rd person: *arselgat* (Lebor na hUidre 21b 35). Future tense, singular 3rd person: *arsil* (Sept. 29); see *sligim*. Verbal noun: *airlech* (Meyer's *Contributions to Irish Lexicography*, page 61).

### GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**arthrach**: *increase*. Dative singular, page 86. See *Revue Celtique* volume 12, page 62, section 23: *arthraighis*, that is, *médaighis* <note>original: "arthraighis i. médaighis, O'Cl."; meaning he increased, referencing O'Clery's Glossary</note>.

**ar-túassim**: *I am silent, I listen*. Present indicative singular 3rd person: *ar-dom-thúassi* <note>meaning "he listens to me," with an infixed pronoun</note>, Epilogue 374. B-future singular 3rd person: *artúaisfi*, *Saltair na Rann* 8299. Verbal noun: *aurthuasacht*, *Lebor na hUidre* 88b 26.

1. **as**: *who (or what) is*. Prologue 185, January 7, March 20, August 30, September 24, October 23, Epilogue 10, 28, 55; *an as-n ái*, pages 4, 10.

2. **as**: Preposition (see entry 7 a). See **ass**, meaning "out of" <note>original: "Lat. ex"</note>.

**asa, assa**: *whose is*. Prologue 50, 98, 330, April 9, 16, August 11, September 23, November 25, Epilogue 86, 142. Compare *as a* in the Milan Glosses 2c 3, and *íssa* (glossed as "of whom" <note>original: "Lat. quorum"</note>) in Milan Glosses 90c 3.

**as-biur**: *I say, I declare*. With an infixed pronoun: *atbiur* (from *ad-d-b.*), Epilogue 103. See Strachan’s *Selections*, page 45.

**ascaid cinn**: Page 70. *Searching or examining a head (for lice)*. See Kuno Meyer, *Contributions to Irish Lexicography* under the word *aiscim*, and see *Lebor na hUidre* 68a 15 (*ac escaid a léine*, "searching his shirt") and the *Yellow Book of Lecan* 124d.

**-ascnam**: *let us strive after*. December 31. Imperative plural 1st person of the verb *ad-cosnaim* (I strive after). Otherwise, see Ascoli, page 288.

**asennath**: *afterwards, at last*. Prologue 46. Appears as *asennad* in the Milan Glosses 24b 19 and Ascoli, page 31.

**as-éirgim**: (from the roots *ess-ess-reg-*). *I arise*. See Ascoli 19b. T-preterite singular 3rd person: *asréiracht* <note>meaning "he arose"</note>, Prologue 92, March 27, Würzburg Glosses 4d 27, etc. Verbal noun: *eséirge* <note>resurrection</note>.

**as-ind(f)édim**: *I declare, I expound*. See Ascoli 331. Present indicative singular 3rd person: *feib asindfet* ("as he declares"), *Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie* volume 3, page 21. Perfect active singular 3rd person: *as-r-indaid* ("he has declared"), January 12 (same as *asrindid* in Milan Glosses 58a 8, 107a 12). Imperative singular 2nd person: *asneid* ("declare!"), November 13 (Rawlinson manuscript). Plural 2nd person: *aisndéid* (see that entry). Verbal noun: *aisndís* (feminine), genitive *aisndísen*.

**aslach**: *seduction* (from the root *ad-slig*, he entices). Plural accusative: *aslaige*, Epilogue 198. Genitive singular: *aslaig*. Dative singular: *aslug*. See Ascoli 279.

**as-luim**: *I escape*. See Ascoli 178. Preterite singular: *as-ru-luús* ("I have escaped"), Würzburg Glosses 17d 16. Singular 3rd person: *as-rola* ("he escaped"), April 3. Verbal noun: *élúd* <note>escaping or evading</note>. See Ascoli 179.

**as-midim**: *I am unable*. (Cognate with Welsh *meddu* [to be able or to possess], and Greek *medeōn*, *medontes* <note>original: "μεδέων, μέδοντες," meaning ruling or lords</note>). See the entries for *émsither* and *coimmidiu*.

**as-orgim**: *I smite*. T-preterite: *asort*, *as-r-ort*, April 23. Preterite passive: *asort*, *as-r-ort*, October 7. Plural 3rd person: *ho r-esarta* ("when they were smitten"), Milan Glosses 34b 13. With the perfective prefix *com*: *aschomart*, October 19, Milan Glosses 34a 18 (where the aspiration expresses a relative clause). Verbal noun: *esorgun* <note>smiting or slaughter</note>.

**ass**: Preposition. *out of*. April 19. This is the pretonic form of the prefix *ess-* (equivalent to Latin *ex* and Greek *ex* <note>original: "ἐξ," meaning out of</note>).

**asslondud**: *declaration*. July 9, October 3, 24. (See entry for *slondad*). This is the verbal noun of the verb *ad-sluindim* (I declare).

1. **at**: *you are*. July 19, Epilogue 510 (Leinster manuscript). See Ascoli 222.

2. **at**: *who are*. Prologue 246, May 7.

**ata**: *whose are*. Prologue 162, March 14, April 6, June 27, August 24, Epilogue 274, *Lebor na hUidre* 61a 17, 63a 44. In Epilogue 34, we find *ata-n* before a vowel, where the *n* seems to be a remnant of the relative particle.

**atá**: *is* (asserting existence). Prologue 172, Epilogue 395. Plural: *atát*, page 12. Singular 1st person: *ató* ("I am"), Würzburg Glosses 26d 17. See entries for *taú* and *táth*. For other forms of the substantive verb, see *bíuu* and *feil*.

**at-balim, -eplim**: *I die, I perish*. Future singular 3rd person: *atbéla*, Epilogue 116 (plural *-biblát*). Plural 3rd person: *atbélat*, Prologue 247. T-preterite: *atrubalt* ("he has died"), Milan Glosses 144d 3. Plural: *attrubaltar*, Milan Glosses 100a 1.

**at-bath**: *he died, he perished*. <note>original: "obiit, periit"</note>. Prologue 165, 190, Epilogue 318. Plural 3rd person: *atbathadar*, *Revue Celtique* volume 10, page 72. This seems to be a middle aorist from the root *bhā* (see Strachan, "The Particle *ro*," page 75, note).

**atbiur**: Epilogue 103. See entry for **asbiur**.

<term>aurgaiss</term>: *a great prayer*? November 13.

<term>auromun</term>: *dread*, Epilogue 209. Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note>: *arofn*. See *omun*.

<term>aurtach</term>: *festival*. Genitive: *aurtaig*, Epilogue 181. *ertaig* <note>original: "gl. reficiendi"</note>, meaning "of refreshing" or "restoring," Milan Glosses 108ᶜ 7. This is the verbal noun of *arutaing*.

<term>bad</term>: *let it be*, Prologue 261.

<term>báegul</term>: *danger*. Genitive: *báeguil*, Epilogue 203.

<term>báes</term> Masculine: *folly, lust*. *báos*, meaning *druis* <note>lust</note> according to O'Clery. Genitive: *baois*, *Uga Cormaic*. Accusative: *báis*, April 4.

<term>báeth</term>: *a fool*. Plural accusative: *báethu*, Prologue 30. Diminutive: *baethán*, *a calf*, page 88. From this comes *baethaim* or *baethaigim*, *I befool*.

<term>bág</term> Feminine: *a fight, battle*, Epilogue 162, 361.
*   Singular genitive: *báge*, July 24, September 13, Epilogue 490.
*   Accusative: *báig*, pages 4, 10, Epilogue 315.

<term>bágach</term>: *warlike, combative*, March 8, April 11. Singular accusative and masculine genitive: *bágáig*, February 15. Accusative: *bágách*, Prologue 190.

<term>bágaim</term>, **no bágu**: *I engage, declare, promise*, November 30. Subjunctive singular 2nd person: *ro báige* (or *no báge* in the Laud manuscript), Epilogue 27.

<term>bágim</term>, **-báigiu**: *I fight*, Epilogue 360.

<term>baid</term>: meaning *buan* <note>lasting</note>, O’Donovan’s Supplement, August 2 (where it rhymes with *maith*, "good"). Compare Gothic: *batiza* <note>meaning "better"</note>. The word *báid* (as in the compound *báid-athair*, "fond father," page 146, *Book of Leinster* 290ᵃ 37), with which this *baid* has been confused, seems related to the Greek words for "dear" or "beloved" <note>original: "φώτιον προσηφιλές, φῶ, Hesych."</note>.

<term>bail</term>: *goodness, excellence*. See *Contributions to Irish Lexicography*, page 166. See *fírbail* (true goodness), *glanbail* (pure goodness), and *mórbail* (great goodness).

<term>bailc</term>: *strong*, September 29. Plural nominative: *bailci*, Prologue 73. See *balc*.

<term>baile</term>: *a stead, an abode*, Prologue 146, April 20.

<term>baiscne</term> (perhaps *báiscne* <unclear>(?)</unclear>): *a large tree*, page 72, line 21.

<term>balb</term>: *stammering, silent*. Genitive singular feminine: *balbae*, December 22. From the Latin *balbus*.

<term>balbdae</term>: *silent*, March 5.

<term>balc</term>: *strong*, January 13, February 1, March 21, June 17, July 1.
*   Singular dative: September 29, November 17.
*   Comparative: *balcu*, January 4, where it is used as a superlative.
*   Related to the Welsh word *balch*, meaning "proud" <note>original: Cymr. balch</note>.

<term>ball fessa</term>: literally *limb of knowledge*, page 222; the meaning is obscure.

<term>ball-gel</term>: *bright-limbed*, October 4.

<term>ban-n</term>: January 15, September 23; the genitive plural of <term>ben</term> <note>meaning "woman"</note>.

<term>bán</term>: *white, fair*, January 15, February 1, September 30, December 7.
*   Dative singular masculine: *bán*, November 26.
*   Feminine: *báin*, March 31.
*   Plural accusative feminine: *bána*, Epilogue 339.
*   **Compounds:**
    *   *bán-chath*: *a white fight*, June 8, page 144.
    *   *bán-gel*: *white-bright*, dative singular feminine *bángil*, December 25.
    *   *bán-glan*: *white-pure*, dative singular feminine *banglain*, December 25.
    *   *bán-lucht*: *a white folk*, Epilogue 331.
    *   *bán-martra*: *a white martyrdom*, page 116.
    *   *bán-tlacht*: *a white garment*, Epilogue 331.

<term>báne</term>: *whiteness*, Prologue 307.

<term>ban-macc</term> Masculine: *female child, girl*.
*   Plural nominative: *banmaicc*, July 20.
*   Diminutive: *banmaccán*.

<term>ban-nóeb</term>: *female saint*, page 136.

<term>bann</term>: *a work, deed*. Defined as "deed" <note>original: i. gníomh</note> in O'Clery's glossary.
*   Plural dative: *bannaib*, December 21.

<term>bannach</term>: *deedful*, June 12.
*   Genitive singular masculine: *bannaig*, January 12.

<term>baptaist</term>, **bauptaist**, **babtaist**: from the Latin *baptista* <note>meaning "Baptist"</note>.
*   Genitive singular: June 24, August 29, September 24.
*   Accusative: Prologue 102.

1. <term>barae</term>: *grief, affliction*, Epilogue 369. Defined as "sorrow" <note>original: baire i. brón</note> by O'Davoren. Related to the Latin *gravis* <note>meaning "heavy" or "serious"</note> and the Greek *baphys* <note>meaning "heavy" or "deep"</note>, *baros* <note>meaning "weight"</note>, and Ionic *baphia* <note>originals: βαφύς, βάρος, βαφία</note>.

2. <term>barae</term>: *anger*, Epilogue 419. Also appearing as *barann*. Related to the Welsh word *bár*, meaning "indignation" or "anger" <note>original: Cymr. bár</note>.

<term>bárc</term> Feminine: *a barque* <note>a ship or boat</note>.
*   Plural accusative: *barca*.

<term>bar-n</term>: *your*, August 30, Epilogue 63, 375. See *far-n* and *for-n*.

<term>barr</term>: *top, end*.
*   Singular dative: *baurr*. Related to the Welsh word *bar* <note>meaning "top"</note>.
*   **Compounds:** *cath-barr* (helmet), *barr-bocc* (soft-topped), page 134.

<term>bás</term> Neuter: *death*, January 4, 18, March 9, April 8, May 3, July 1 (*the death of Aaron* <note>original: bás nAroin</note>), 25, September 14, December 22.
*   Hence the verb *básaim*, meaning *I kill*.

<term>bas-crann</term>: *a clapper* <note>a percussion instrument or wooden signal</note>, page 64.

<term>baslec</term> Masculine (formerly Neuter): from the Greek *basilikon* <note>original: βασιλικόν</note>, meaning a *palace*.
*   Genitive: *baslic*, September 15, November 19.
*   In Middle Irish, this word is feminine, derived from the Latin *basilica* or Greek *basilikē* <note>originals: basilica, βασιλική</note>, and refers to a *cemetery*.
*   This is the origin of the place names *Baslick* in County Roscommon and *Paisley* (Gaelic *Paislig*) in Scotland.

<term>bathes</term>, **baithes** Feminine: *baptism*, January 6, April 5.
*   Accusative: *bathis*, January 25.

<term>bebais</term>: *he went*, used in the sense that *he died* <note>originals: ivit, mortuus est</note>, Prologue 95, February 18, April 23.
*   Plural: *bebsait*.
*   This is the 3rd person singular s-preterite of a reduplicated verb related to the Greek *bibemi* and *bibao* and the Sanskrit *jigāti* <note>originals: βίβημι, βιβάω, jigāti</note>.

<term>becc</term>: *little*, November 10.
*   Genitive singular masculine: *bicc*, May 18.
*   Dative singular feminine: *biec*, April 23.
*   Related to the Welsh words *bach* and *bychan*.

<term>beccán</term>: *a very little child* <note>original Latin: parvulus</note>.
*   Plural nominative: *beccáin*, September 4.

<term>bech</term> Masculine: *a bee*.
*   Plural nominative: *beich*.
*   Genitive: *bech-n*, February 13.

<term>béim</term>: (derived from *beismen*), *a blow* or *a smiting*, Epilogue 363.
*   This is the verbal noun of the verb *benim* <note>meaning "I strike"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the "Glossarial Index" of Old Irish terms, focusing on words beginning with the letter 'b'. It includes etymological connections to Welsh, Latin, and Gothic, as well as grammatical forms and usage in the hagiographical text.</meta>

<page-num>303</page-num>
<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

**beith**: a corrupted form of *buith* (Welsh: *bod* <note>original: Cymr. bod</note>), meaning **to be**, Epilogue 172, 375.

**bél**: Masculine. **Lip** or **mouth**. (Derived from the root *gvetlo*, related to the Gothic *qipan*, meaning "to speak" <note>original: Goth. qipan</note>). Plural dative: *bélaib*. Used in the nominal preposition *arbélaib* (meaning "before" or "in front of"), November 20.

**ben**: Feminine. **Woman** or **wife**. Plural nominative: *mná*; genitive: *ban-n*, January 15, September 23. (Welsh: *benw*, *benyw* <note>original: Cymr. benw, benyw</note>).

**bendachim**: **I bless** (from the Latin *benedico* <note>original: benedico</note>). Preterite singular 3rd person: *ro-s-bennach*, page 4; *ro-bendach*, page 10.

**bendacht**: **A blessing** (from the Latin *benedictio* <note>original: benedictio</note>). Prologue 275, January 13, June 15, Epilogue 56, 215. Accusative: *bendacht-n*, November 2, Epilogue 113. Compound: *lán-bendacht* (a full blessing), Epilogue 61. (Welsh: *bendith* <note>original: Cymr. bendith</note>).

**benim**: **I strike** or **slay**. Present indicative active plural 3rd person: *benait*, January 31, June 30. Future relative: *bhias*, glossed as *gonfas* (meaning "who will wound") in O'Clery's Glossary <note>original: .i. gonfas O'Cl.</note>. Past participle: *bithe*. Verbal noun: <term>béim</term> (a blow or stroke). Root: *bhei*.

**béo**: Adjective. **Alive** or **living**. (Welsh: *byw*; Latin: *vivus* <note>original: Cymr. byw, Lat. vivus</note>). Genitive singular masculine: *bíí*, page 4 (where it is treated as a two-syllable word). From this comes *beóigur*, meaning "I bring to life" or "I quicken" <note>original: vivifico</note>.

**berg**: Feminine. **Brigand** or **ruffian**. O'Mulconry's Glossary 139. Plural accusative: *berga*, Prologue 42. Genitive: *ar dianbas, ar bedg, ar brataib na mberg, rom-ain Isu ard* (meaning "Against swift death, against a sudden start, against the robberies of the brigands, may high Jesus protect me"), found in manuscript 23 N. 10 (Royal Irish Academy), page 19.

**berim**: Root *-biur*, equivalent to the Latin *fero* (**I bear** or **carry**). Present indicative singular 3rd person: *-beir*, Prologue 223. With an affixed pronoun: *berth-i*, Epilogue 196. Relative form: *beres*, Epilogue 416. T-preterite singular 3rd person: *birt* (or *bert* in the P manuscript), January 27. Passive present indicative plural 3rd person relative: *bertar*, Prologue 175. Preterite singular 3rd person: *brethae*, January 25, June 11. Perfect plural 3rd person: *ro uctha*, Prologue 5. Compounds: <term>as-biur</term> (I say) and <term>do-biur</term> (I give).

**bescnae**: (derived from *béss-gnae*) **Nation**? Literally meaning **customary law**. Singular dative: *béscnu*, Epilogue 318. The form *bescnad* in Epilogue 157 (L manuscript) seems to be a misspelling. Similarly, *bélre* (language) is used to mean "nation" in the Würzburg Glosses 28^b^ 1.

**béss**: **Perhaps**, Epilogue 417.

**bethu**: Masculine. **Life**. Singular genitive: *bethad*, Epilogue 437; dative: *bethu*, Epilogue 201; accusative: *bethaid*, Epilogue 117, 169. From this comes *bethaigim*, "I quicken" or "I bring to life."

**bíae**: March 22. Genitive singular. Meaning **of might**? Compare with *bía*?

**bíast**: (Welsh: *bwyst* <note>original: Cymr. bwyst</note>). Derived from the Latin *bestia* (**beast**). Genitive: *bíastae*, Epilogue 472. Plural nominative: *béssti*, Würzburg Glosses 31^b^ 21; dative: *bíastaib*, Prologue 41. Later form: <term>péist</term>; genitive: *piasta*, page 44.

**bibdu**: Masculine. **A guilty person**. Plural nominative: *bidbaid* (used for *bibdaid*), Prologue 175; accusative: *bidbada*. Old Welsh: *bibid*, glossing the Latin *rei* (guilty ones) <note>original: O. Cymr. bibid (gl. rei)</note>, Book of Leinster 106^a^.

**bile**: Neuter. **A sacred tree**. Singular genitive: *bili*, September 10. Found in the phrase *in campo bili* (in the field of the tree) <note>original: in campo bili</note>, Book of Armagh 10^b^ 2. Dative: *biliu*, Saltair na Rann 1020. See <term>darbile</term>.

**bille**: **Paltry** or **mean**, July 3, August 8.

**bind**: **Melodious**. Plural nominative feminine: *bindi*, Prologue 181. Equative form: *binnidir* (meaning "as melodious as"), Book of Leinster 55^b^ 41. Old Breton: *bann*, glossing the Latin *canora* (melodious) <note>original: O. Br. bann (gl. canora)</note>. From this comes *bindigur*, meaning "I am in harmony" <note>original: concors sum</note>.

**binde**: Feminine. **Melodiousness**. Singular dative: *bindi*, August 27, October 7.

**bisex**: Genitive: *bisecsa*, page 78. From the Latin *bisextus*, meaning **an intercalary day** (a leap day).

**bith**: Masculine. **World**. Prologue 115, 157, August 29. Singular genitive: *betha*, Prologue 140, 195, June 29, Epilogue 240, 276, 414; dative: *bith*, March 21, May 9, Epilogue 19; accusative: *bith-n*, October 15. Plural genitive: *betha*, Prologue 156 (which, as the scholar Strachan notes, points toward an Old Irish form *bethae*); accusative: *bithu*, Prologue 156, March 31. (Welsh: *byd* <note>original: Cymr. byd</note>).

**bith-**: A prefix meaning **always**, **everlasting**, or **eternal**.
*   **bith-aittreb**: **eternal possession**.
*   **bith-balc**: **ever strong**, page 52, October 8.
*   **i mbith-bí**: **in which it always is** <note>original: in quo semper est</note>, June 9.
*   **ro bith-béo**: **may I live forever** <note>original: semper vivam</note>, Epilogue 39.
*   **bithbuuan**: **everlasting**; plural nominative feminine: *bithbuuna*, Epilogue 558.
*   **bith-choemnae**: **eternal protection**; dative: *bithchoémnu*, March 13.
*   **bith-flaith**: **eternal kingdom**, Prologue 272, May 16, June 9, December 14 (L manuscript), Epilogue 159, 168.
*   **bithgnás**: **lasting custom** <note>original: lasting gnás</note>, Epilogue 316.
*   **bithgolait**: **they always weep** <note>original: semper plorant</note>, Prologue 62.
*   **bithmaith**: **ever good**, page 44.
*   **bith-maraid**: **it always remains** <note>original: semper manet</note>, Prologue 255.
*   **bithmarait**: **they always remain** <note>original: semper manent</note>, Prologue 88.
*   **bithmáraíd**: **ever magnifies**, Prologue 232.
*   **bithtrágaith**: **ever diminishes** <note>original: ever minishes</note>, Prologue 231.
*   The Welsh word *byth* <note>original: Cymr. byth</note> seems to be borrowed from the Irish *bith-*.

**bíuu**, **I am**, or **I live** <note>original Latin: vivo</note>:
*   **Present indicative singular:** 1st person *-biu*, page 54; 2nd person *-bí-siu*, Prologue 274; 3rd person *-bí*, meaning **is wont to be** <note>habitual present</note>, Prologue 146, page 78, April 7. **3rd person singular imperative:** *bíd*, page 41, line 10.
*   **Preterite indicative (Past tense) singular:** 3rd person *ro bái*, page 4, line 10; *bói*, Epilogue 289. 
*   **Copula <term>copula</term> <note>a linking verb, like "is" or "was," that joins a subject to a description</note> without the prefix *ro*:**
    *   *ba*, Prologue 139, January 14, February 8, March 20, 31, April 7, May 11, June 21, July 6, August 10, November 5, December 20, Epilogue 9.
    *   *níbo* (it was not), Prologue 114; *nípu*, September 27.
    *   *dia mbu* (when it was), April 2; *ná bu*, November 10; *frisim-ba* (to which it was), Epilogue 392.
    *   **Plural:** 3rd person *batir*, June 19, Prologue 25; *cé-ptar* (although they were), Prologue 74; *cia-ptar*, Prologue 133, Epilogue 14; *naptar* (they were not), March 18; *ni-ptar*, November 9.
*   **Copula with the prefix *ro*:** *raba*, Epilogue 302; *cia r'bu* (although it was), Prologue 125; *cia r'bo*, Prologue line 214; *ce r'bo*, Prologue 93.
*   **Future indicative singular:** 1st person *bé*, Wb. 4ᶜ 18. Middle Irish forms: *bíam*, LU. 61ᵃ 9, Saltair na Rann 855. 3rd person *ro-n-bía*, January 13; *ro-m-bía*, Epilogue 168. **Relative form <note>used in "who will be" or "which will be" constructions</note>:** *bías*, March 13, Epilogue 289. **Plural:** 3rd person *biait*, Prologue 308; relative *bete*, Epilogue 298. 
*   **Future copula:** singular 3rd person *-ba*, Prologue 294, Epilogue 78. Plural 2nd person *-beth*, Prologue 138; 3rd person *bit*, Prologue 155.
*   **Present subjunctive singular:** 1st person *ro beó*, Epilogue 315; *ro bith beó*, Prologue 39; *beósa*, Prologue 271; *ro beósa*, Prologue 273. 3rd person *-roib*, Prologue 11, Epilogue 359.
*   **Subjunctive copula:** singular 3rd person *arná-p* (so that it may not be), Prologue 323; *rop*, January 24, March 17, December 19. Relative form *bas*, Epilogue 148. Plural 3rd person *ropat*, January 21; *robet*, Epilogue 44, 292, 293, 299.
*   **Past subjunctive singular:** 3rd person *-beth*, Prologue 241; *ma beth* (if it were), Epilogue 102. Plural 3rd person *betis*, Epilogue 125.
*   **Imperative:** 3rd person singular *bíd*, Prologue 141. **Copula:** 3rd person singular *bad*, Prologue 261.
*   **Verbal noun <term>verbal noun</term> <note>a noun derived from a verb, similar to the English "being"</note>:** *both* (feminine), Epilogue 172; accusative *buith*, Epilogue 375.
*   For other forms of the substantive verb, see *feil*, *atá*, and *tá*.

**blae** (also *bla*), **linen sheet** or perhaps a **linen shirt**, page 224; found in the lower margin of the Book of Leinster, page 348.

**bláthe**: Feminine. **Blossoms**. Genitive singular: August 19, September 4, 18. A collective noun derived from *bláth* (Welsh: *blawd* <note>original Cymr. blawd</note>). The genitive singular is also found in the *Laws* (Volume II, page 120) and the *Voyage of Bran* (Section 2).

**bleded**: **Monster-filled** or **haunted by stags**? Dative singular neuter: April 7; feminine *bledig*, page 6, line 15. Derived from *bled*, meaning **animal**, page 52. Plural *bleda*, glossed as "wild fawns" <note>original: .i. aige alta</note> in the B. gloss for April 7.

**blíadain**: Feminine. **Year**. (Welsh: *blwydyn* <note>original Cymr. blwydyn</note>). Singular genitive: *blíadnae*, September 17; dative: *blíadain*, Prologue 281, 292; accusative: *blíadain*, page 78 and perhaps Epilogue 4. Plural genitive: *blíadnae*, August 7.

**blog**: Feminine. **Fragment**, October 5. Accusative: *bloig*, Book of Leinster 125ᵃ 20. Nominative and accusative plural: *bloga*, page 641.

**bó**: Feminine. **Cow**. Singular genitive: *bó*, August 8. (Welsh: *bu* <note>original Cymr. bu</note>; Greek: *bous* <note>original: βoῦς</note>).

**bochtán**: Masculine. **A poor little person** <note>original Latin: pauperculus</note>, Epilogue 392. Genitive: *bochtáin*. A diminutive form of *bocht* (**poor**).

**bolg**: Masculine. **A bag**, March 30.

**bolmar**: **Learned** or **wise**. Singular accusative feminine: *bolmair*, September 24. Derived from *bol* (genitive *buil*), which means **poetry** or **a poet** <note>original: .i. eigsi no eicceas</note> according to O'Clery's Glossary and Cormac's Glossary (Translation page 27).

**bordgal**: Neuter. Meaning obscure, December 27, Epilogue 254. Singular genitive: *bordgal*, Prologue 275 (where it rhymes with *ordan*); accusative: *bordgal*, Epilogue 206. Plural nominative: *bordgala*, Prologue 72. Perhaps from the Low Latin *burdigalum*, meaning a **fish-pond**, used here metaphorically.

**borg**: Masculine. **A burgh** or **fortified town**. Singular nominative: Prologue 189, 193; genitive: *buirg*, Book of Leinster 259ᵃ 21. Plural accusative: *burgu*, Prologue 140.

**both**: Epilogue 172, 375. **To be**, sometimes written corruptly as *buith* or *beith*. (Welsh: *bod* <note>original Cymr. bod</note>). Genitive form: *buithe*.

**bótt** (also *bot*): **Fire**, page 256. Found in Cormac’s Glossary and other Irish texts.

**1. brass**: **Great**. Plural nominative feminine: *brassa*, Prologue 75. (Welsh: *bras* <note>original Cymr. bras</note>).

**2. brass**: **Quick**. Hence:
**brasse**: Feminine. **Boldness**? or **quickness**? Singular dative: *brassi*, June 19. Mentioned in O'Davoren's Glossary, number 263.

**bráth**: Masculine. **Doom** or **judgment**. Genitive: *brátha*, Prologue 174; accusative: *bráth*, Epilogue 127, 290. (Old Welsh: *braut*; modern Welsh: *brawd* <note>original O. Cymr. braut, now brawd</note>).

**bráthir**, **bráthair** Masculine. **brother**, April 11, 21, June 17, December 27; genitive **bráthar**, July 25, plural genitive **bráthre** July 10, 18, Epilogue 476, 528, accusative **bráithre** Epilogue 409. Welsh: *brawd*.

**bréc** Feminine. a **lie**, Prologue 145, page 12, Sanskrit: *bhrāṇça* meaning 'falling' or 'loss.' Hence **brécaím**, 'I deceive, beguile,' and the verbal noun **brécad**, page 12.

**brecc**, **speckled** (Welsh: *brych*), genitive singular masculine **bricc** September 14; from the root *mreknó-s*. Related to Lithuanian *márgas* <note>meaning variegated or party-colored</note>, if we assume sister-roots *m.r.k.* and *m.r.g.*

**breó**, **flame**, April 15, August 20, Epilogue 258. *Breó tulcha* <note>flame of the hill</note>, page 98, see **án-breó**.

**bress**, **great**, "Bress is everything that is great and big" <note>original Irish: bress is oll gach ní is mór</note>, Book of Leinster 395ª, plural nominative **bressa** Prologue 74.

**brestae** singular dative feminine **brestai** July 19, accusative **brestae** June 13, July 20. The meaning of this word is quite obscure: see the speculative guesses in Cormac's Glossary <note>Corm. Tr. 25</note>, O'Davoren's Glossary <note>nos. 262, 264</note>, and O'Mulconry's Glossary <note>142</note>.

**breth** Feminine. 1. **bearing, carrying**, verbal noun of *berim*, singular dative **breith**, Epilogue 119.
2. **breth** Feminine. **decision, doom**, genitive **brethe**, singular accusative **breith** page 4, plural accusative **bretha** Epilogue 416.

**bríathar** Feminine. **word**, genitive **bréthre**, accusative **bréthir**, plural dative **briáthraib**, March 22.

**bríg** Feminine. **vigour, might**, Prologue 145, 147, August 7, singular genitive **bríge**, February 7, June 2, August 1, October 4, plural nominative **bríga** Prologue 87, Epilogue 34. dative **brígaib** Prologue 34. Hence:
**brígach**, **vigorous, mighty**, January 26, February 13, December 20, Epilogue 30, genitive singular masculine **brígaig**, February 15, accusative **brígach** Prologue 102, June 14, October 6, Epilogue 290.

**brodlan**, **brodlaind**, page 154, a **trifle**? *Brod* or *broth* (glossing the Latin *arista* <note>the beard of grain</note>) means a straw, a **trifle** (compare Latin *frutex* <note>a shrub or stalk</note>); but what is *lan* or *laind*?

**bróen** Masculine. **rain, a shower**, plural dative **bróenaib** Epilogue 346.

**bróenán** Masculine. **a little rain, showerlet**, May 19, Epilogue 351.

**brolach** from Latin *prologus*. *brolach tóisech* <note>first prologue</note>, pages 4, 8, a **prologue**, *brolach dédenach* <note>final prologue</note>, page 4, an **epilogue**.

**brónach**, **mournful**, plural nominative masculine **brónaig** Prologue 188, derived from **brón, sorrow** (from *brugno*, Welsh *brwyn*).

**brú**, **brink, edge**, ablative <term>ablative</term> <note>a grammatical case indicating movement away from or location</note> singular December 22.

**brú**, genitive **bronn**, **womb, belly**, dative singular **brú**, March 27, Epilogue 464. Welsh: *bru*.

**bruchtaim**, I **burst**, present indicative singular 3rd person, **bruchta**, June 21, November 29, preterite (past tense) singular 3rd person, **-brucht** April 4.

**brúim**, I **forget**, b-future plural 1st person **-brúifem** Prologue 304. O'Davoren's Glossary no. 256.

**brúim** (possibly **breuim**?), I **break, crush**, active preterite singular 3rd person **breuis**, **brúais**, **brúis**, April 4. passive preterite plural 3rd person **ro brúithea** Prologue 35.

**bruinne** Masculine. **breast**, singular genitive **bruinni**, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 255, plural dative **bruinnib**, June 29. Welsh: *bronn, bron*.

**bruth** I. **fervor**, genitive **brotha**, singular dative June 2, October 21. Old Welsh *brut*, now *brwd*. Compound: **mór-bruth** <note>great fervor</note>, October 29. II. a **glowing mass of metal**: *bruth óir* <note>a mass of gold</note>, January 24, February 10, November 26. Hence **bruthnaigim**, "I glow" <note>original Latin: ferveo</note>.

**búadach**, **victorious**, Prologue 191, 222, February 13, 19, March 8, April 18, May 10, 18, August 6, 25, October 6, genitive singular masculine **búadaig** December 7, dative singular masculine **búadach**, September 29, November 26, feminine **búadaig** Prologue 272, accusative singular masculine **búadach**, June 14, Epilogue 264: feminine **búadaig**, May 16, June 10.

**búaid** Neuter. 1. **victory**. 2. **prize, booty, virtue**, Prologue 3, February 15, April 9, 24, May 11, September 2, October 1, 12, November 28, December 8, 16. Singular genitive **búada** Prologue 183, Epilogue 349, **búadae**, January 16, February 10, April 24, **búade** singular 171, June 2, November 2, dative **búaid** April 5, June 20, August 19, October 16, November 17, December 17, Epilogue 23, accusative **búaid**, January 28, July 6, August 2, October 29, plural genitive OENGUS. **buadae** March 12, 21, October 30, **búade** May 3, June 5, dative **búadaib**, January 27, August 30, Epilogue 283. Meaning "victories" or "triumphs." Welsh: *budd* ("profit"). Compound: *glan-búaid* ("pure victory"), January 27.

**búan** **lasting** (from the root *bhuvano-s*), Prologue 123, 302, June 12, November 17, Epilogue 30, 158; genitive singular masculine **búain**, December 15; dative **búan**, Epilogue 19; accusative **búan**, September 23; plural nominative feminine **búana**, Prologue 181. See compound **bith-búan** ("ever-lasting").

**búanaigim** **I make lasting, I perpetuate**, past tense singular 1st person: *ro búanagus*, page 94, line 6. Verbal noun: **búanugud** ("perpetuating").

**buide** Feminine. **thanks, reward**, plural genitive **buide**, Prologue 55.

**buiden** Feminine. **a band, a troop**, Epilogue 5; singular dative **buidin**, January 4; plural dative **buidnib**, Epilogue 295. Welsh: *byddin*; Old Breton: *bodin* <note>original Latin gloss: "manus," meaning a hand or a band of men</note>, plural *bodiniou* <note>original Latin gloss: "phalanges," meaning battalions or ranks</note>.

**buidnech** **troopful** (having many bands), accusative singular masculine, October 15.

**builid** **blooming, beautiful**, page 46.

**buith**, **beith**, see **both** <note>archaic forms of the verb "to be" or "being"</note>.

**buittelach** **a place (perhaps a hill) where there has been a great fire**, page 256. See **bot** <note>meaning "fire"</note>.

**cach** **every** (used with a noun), Prologue 11, page 78; the unstressed form of **cách**.

**cách** **every one** (Old Welsh: *paup*), page 4, line 16, Prologue 57, 248, February 17, July 9, December Epilogue 48; dative *cosin cách*, Epilogue 50; accusative *sech cách*, December 28.

**cád** **holy**, *Martyrology of Gorman* 260; comparative **cádu**, March 20, where it rhymes with *dánu*.

**cádlae** **beautiful**, plural nominative feminine **cádlaí**, December 9.

**cádus** **reverence, respect**, page 2; **cádas**, *Martyrology of Gorman*, March 25.

**caid** (perhaps **cáid**?), **pure, chaste, holy, or noble**, January 4, (written *caith* in manuscript R¹) February 1, 10, 18, March 13, May 16, June 3, 13, September 5, 14, December 14. Comparative **caidiu**, *Laws* volume 2, page 394. According to the glossators, there seem to be two words: **cáid** meaning "noble" <note>original Irish: "uasal," O'Davoren nos. 465, 530, 573</note>, and **cáid** (perhaps should be read as **cáid**?) meaning **holy** <note>the text notes: "it is not different from 'caid sanctum'" (caid is a holy thing)</note>, Cormac's Glossary. O'Clery defines *caidh* as **chaste** <note>original Irish: "geanmnaidh"</note>. Kuno Meyer in his *Contributions* (page 299) has **caid** as "chaste, pure" and **cáid** as "holy, revered." Perhaps *caid* is related to the Greek **καθαρός** <note>original Greek: "katharos," meaning pure</note> and *cáid* (alternative form *cáid*) is a loanword from the Hebrew **qādōsh** <note>original Hebrew: "holy"; mentioned as "Caddos sanctus" in the Latin Glossaries, meaning "Caddos is holy"</note>.

**caillech** **nun**, plural genitive **caillech-n**, February 1. A derivative of *caille* ("veil"), which was borrowed from the Latin **pallium** <note>meaning a cloak, cover, or specifically a nun's veil</note>.

**cáin** **clear, bright, fair**, Prologue 139, 192, 249, February 10, March 10, June 3, August 10, 14, November 22, December 19, 24, Epilogue 242; genitive singular masculine: January 19, April 13, May 4, August 27; dative singular feminine: January 12, February 12, 21, July 26; accusative singular masculine: May 22; dative dual and plural **cáinib**, April 3, October 16, Epilogue 62. Compound: **cáinšlúag** ("fair host"), September 22. In the following instances, **cáin** appears before the noun it describes:
*   *cáin áige* (fair leader), July 6, September 5
*   *cáin cathar* (fair city), August 15
*   *cáin cimbid* (fair captive), April 26, August 14
*   *cáin cinged* (fair champion), February 14
*   *cáin clerech* (fair cleric), June 21
*   *cáin cocrait* (fair confidants), December 24
*   *cáin decheng* (fair pair), September 6
*   *cáin días* (fair couple), November 24
*   *cáin ésce* (fair moon), January 3
*   *cáin grían* (fair sun), January 5, June 26, October 20, December 26
*   *cáin kalland* (fair kalends), Prologue 324
*   *cáin míl* (fair soldier/beast), June 17
*   *cáin ordan* (fair dignity), Prologue 179
*   *cáin popul* (fair people), Prologue 19
*   *cáin scéla* (fair tidings), May 6
*   *cáin uaitne* (fair pillar), April 29.
Old Welsh: *cein*, now *cain*.

**caindeltae** **luminous, flaming**, February 19. A derivative of *caindel* ("candle"), Welsh *cannuill* <note>original Latin gloss: "lichinum," meaning a lamp-wick</note>, now *canwyll*, from the Latin **candēla**.

**caindlech**, **coindlech** **lustrous, shining-white**, March 10, June 9, November 22, Epilogue 92; dative singular masculine: July 28, December 16; accusative singular masculine: March 4.

**caiptel**, **coiptel** Masculine noun (from the Latin **capitulum**, meaning "little head" or "chapter"). **a stanza**, Prologue 299, Epilogue 100; plural nominative **caiptil**, Prologue 327; genitive **caiptel**, Prologue 295, 332, 333, Epilogue 101.

**cairde** (perhaps **cairte**?) **compact, covenant**, Epilogue 534; *cairdde*, Book of Leinster 152ª; *cairte*, Lebor na hUidre 67ª.

**calad** **hard**, Prologue 43, 107, August 10, December 1; dative singular masculine **calad**, April 2; feminine **calaid**, August 17; plural nominative masculine **calaid**, January 17. Welsh: *caled*; Old Breton: *calat*.

<meta>This page continues the "Glossarial Index" of Old Irish terms, moving through words starting with "ca-." It covers terms related to the calendar, music, ecclesiastical concepts like "canon" and "Maundy Thursday," and several variations of the word for "battle" or "warrior."</meta>

<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

**calland** Feminine. **calends**, especially the calends of January. Singular genitive: *calne* (Prologue 306); dative: *callaind* (Prologue 325), January 1 (Epilogue 1); plural genitive: *dá sé cáin calland* (Prologue 324). Compare to the phrase "Cuchulainn’s slaughter of sixteen good heroes" (*Toscara Cuchulainn da sé ndéc ndaglaech*), from the manuscript *Lebor na hUidre* (LU. 67a 19). Welsh: *calan*. <note>The "calends" was the first day of the month in the Roman calendar.</note>

**camm** **crooked, squinting**, Appendix 7. Welsh: *cam*. Gaulish: *cambo-*; Greek: *σκαμβός* <note>original Greek: *skambos*, meaning "bow-legged" or "crooked"</note>.

**canim** **I sing** (from Latin *cano* <note>meaning "I sing"</note>). Present indicative singular 3rd person: *canaid* (Appendix 26, *Leabhar Breac*); plural 1st person relative: *canmae* (Epilogue 242); 3rd person relative: *cantae* (December 28). Imperative singular 2nd person: *cain*, *can* (February 15); plural 4th person: (November 11, *Leabhar Breac*). Imperfect singular 3rd person: *no chanad* (Prologue page 3, line 10); plural 3rd person: *no-cantais* (July 32). Perfect singular 3rd person: *cachain* <note>original Latin: *cecinit*, meaning "he sang"</note> (Appendix 26, December 8). Passive present indicative singular 3rd person: *-canar* (Epilogue 187), *canair* (September 11). Perfect: *ro cét*. Compare to Welsh: *cant* ("he sang").

**canóin** Feminine. **a canon**, singular genitive: *canoine*, *canone* (pages 4, 10). Welsh: *canon*. <note>Refers to church law or the accepted list of books in the Bible.</note>

**cantaic** **a canticle** (from Latin *canticum*), Epilogue 190. Welsh: *canig*.

**caplait** from Low Latin *capillatio* <note>literally "hair-removal" or "the plucking out of hair," from *capillorum evulsio*</note>, as cited by Ducange: *dardáin caplaite* (page 244), **Maundy Thursday**. Welsh: *dydd iau cablyd*. <note>Maundy Thursday is the Thursday before Easter; the name "caplait" likely refers to the ritual washing and grooming performed on that day.</note>

**carae** Masculine. **friend**, Epilogue 371; genitive: *carat*. Welsh: *cár*, plural *ceraint*. See also **anamcharae** <note>meaning "soul-friend" or spiritual advisor</note>.

**carim** **I love**. Present indicative: *no charu* (Epilogue 311), *no charim* (Epilogue 50); plural 1st person: *-caram* (Prologue 134). Imperfect plural 3rd person: *no chartais* (November 16). Imperative plural 1st person: *caram* (Prologue 364). S-present singular 3rd person: *carais* (January 15, 27, May 26, June 15, July 9). The form *car* (March 24), used for *ro car*, is abnormal. Plural 3rd person: *ro charsat* (May 8), *carsait* (March 15, May 7). Passive imperfect singular 3rd person: *carthae* (May 9). Welsh: *caru* ("to love").

**caratrad, caradrad** **friendship**, page 12.

**carcar** Feminine. **a dungeon** (from Latin *carcer*), July 10; singular genitive: *carcrae* (December 20, Epilogue 516); plural dative: *carcraib* (Prologue 45, Appendix 27). Welsh: *carchar*; Old Breton: *carcar*.

**casc** Feminine. **Pasch, Easter** (from Latin *pascha*), dative: *caisc* (Epilogue 562). Welsh: *pasc*.

**catamail** **authentic**, page 128, in *perso chatamail* <note>meaning "an authentic person," glossing the Latin *utentica persona*</note>, Chalcidius, *Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung* (KZ) xxix. 374.

**catéat** **what are they?** September 22 (rhyming with *déac*), *Würzburg Glosses* (Wb.) 31a 7, *Tripartite Life of St. Patrick* 54, 21. Perhaps for *coteet* or *cia-teat*?

**cath** Masculine. **battle**, Prologue 242; singular genitive: *catha* (Prologue 139, June 29, August 23, 24, November 15, Epilogue 275); dative: *cath* (Appendix 2). Welsh: *cad*. Compounds: **bán-chath** (June 8), **cathbarr**, **cathfer**, **cathmíl** (see below). Hence **cathaiguir**, meaning "I fight" <note>from Latin *pugno*</note>.

**cathair** **champion**, June 3, August 15 (rhyming with *athar*). This is a phonetic spelling of **cathfer**, see below.

**cathardu** **cathedrals?** Accusative plural, page 2. Perhaps for **cathadru*, borrowed from Latin *cathedra* <note>meaning "a bishop’s throne"</note>. Compare to Welsh *cadeiriol* or *cadeir-dy* ("chapter-house").

**cathbarr** **battle-top, helmet**, January 10.

**cathfer** **battle-man, champion** (Welsh: *cadwr*), June 3 (F). Singular genitive: *cathfīr* (December 11); plural nominative: *cathir*, *cathfir* (June 27 B).

**cathir, cathair** Feminine. **city, monastery**, Epilogue 149; singular genitive: *cathrach* (Epilogue 236); dative: *cathir* (Prologue 180, Epilogue 544); plural nominative: *(sen)chathraig* (Prologue 205); genitive: *cathrach* (Epilogue 460). Welsh: *cader*. <note>In early Ireland, a "city" often referred to a large monastic settlement.</note>

**cathlaic** from Latin *catholicus*, singular dative feminine: *cathlaic* (August 28).

**cathmíl** **battle-soldier**, October 21, Epilogue 262. Singular genitive: *cathmíled*, *Lebor na hUidre* (LU.) 88b, 129a. Welsh: *cadfilwr*.

**cé, cía** Conjunction. **though, if**, page 3, line 14, Prologue 101 (*cérod*), 230, 241, 257, Appendix 27, November 6, Epilogue 27, 125, 146, 397. Combined with the substantive verb: *cit* ("though they are," Prologue 245, Epilogue 81); *cíat* (Prologue 153, should be read as *cit*); *cérbo* (Prologue 93, November 7); *céptar* (Prologue 74); *cíaptar* (Epilogue 14); *césu* (Epilogue 133).

It explores the linguistic roots and usage of pronouns like "every," ecclesiastical terms for "church" and "celebration," and concepts of "suffering" and "music."</meta>

**GLOSSARIAL INDEX**

**cé** Pronoun: **this**. Used in the phrase "for this world" (*for bith ché*), Prologue 103. It is related to Latin *cis* <note>original Latin: "cis", meaning "on this side of"</note>, the Gothic pronominal stem *hi-*, and Lithuanian *szis*. A related word *ci*, meaning "hither," seems to appear in the phrase "Come hither, O Maive" (*tair-chi a Medb*) in the *Book of Leinster* (LL) 250a; however, this might be a copying error for *cé*.

**cech** Pronominal adjective: **every**. (References: page 4, line 12; Prologue 110; Epilogue 289).
Masculine singular genitive: (September 11).
Neuter: (Prologue 160, 228; Epilogue 21, 33; Appendix 13).
Masculine or neuter: (Appendix 23; July 22; October 22).
Feminine: *cecha* (Epilogue 510).
<note>The Middle Irish neuter form *cecha* found in Prologue 275 and Epilogue 510 F. should be corrected to *cech óen*.</note>
Neuter singular dative: (May 27, December 12, Epilogue 35).
Neuter accusative: *cech-n* (Prologue 39; January 24; April 4; July 15; September 28; October 29; Epilogue 206, 215, 345, 546).
Ablative: (April 22).

**cech-ae** **each of them** (Epilogue 43).

**cech-óen**, **cach óen** **every one** (Epilogue 5, 157).

**cechaing** 3rd person singular perfect form of *cingim* (see that entry).

**céim** Neuter noun. (Derived from the root *kngmen*; Welsh: *cam*, plural *cemmein*), **a step**. (March 20, November 30, December 31).

**céin** **so long as, while** (Epilogue 298).

**céle** Masculine noun: **a bondservant** or **companion**. (March 3; Epilogue 307, 426, 554).
Nominative plural: *céli* (Epilogue 14, 239).
Compound: *sóir-chele* (glossed as Latin *libertus* <note>original: "libertus", meaning "a freedman"</note>), from the Würzburg Glosses (Wb.) 10a 43.

**celebrad** The verbal noun of *celebraim*.
Singular dative: (August 26).
Accusative: (February 15).
"Celebration of Nones" (*celebrad nona*), page 70. <note>Nones is a traditional time of prayer in the church calendar, usually observed around 3:00 PM.</note>

**celebráim** **I celebrate** (from Latin *celebro* <note>original: "celebro", meaning "I celebrate or honor"</note>).
2nd person singular imperative: *celebair* (September 12, November 14, 17).

**célén** **little vassal**, a diminutive form of *céle* (see above). Singular vocative: page 226.

**celim** Matches Latin *celo* <note>original: "celo", meaning "I hide or conceal"</note>.
1st person plural present indicative: *-celam* (Prologue 142).
Future: *-célam* (Epilogue 86).
3rd person singular present indicative passive: *-celar* (February 20, August 11).
Future participle: *clithi* (December 9, Epilogue 306).
Welsh: *celu*.

**cell** Feminine noun. Welsh: *cell*, derived from Latin *cella* <note>original: "cella", meaning a small room, store-room, or a monk's cell</note>.
Singular genitive: *cille* (March 1, 26).
Dative: *cill* (October 16).

**céilliu**, **céilliu** (Prologue 316): the line appears to be corrupted; read it as "blind reason for people" (*dall-chíall do dóinib*).

**cellóir** **cellarer** or **steward** (from Latin *cellārius* <note>original: "cellārius", meaning a steward, butler, or someone in charge of provisions</note>).
Singular accusative: page 224.
Plural dative: *huanaib cellorib* (glossed as Latin *ex promptuariis* <note>original: "ex promptuariis", meaning "from the storehouses or larders"</note>), in the Milan Glosses (Ml.) 144a 1.

**cen** Preposition used with the accusative: **without**. (Page 4, line 13; Prologue 42, 63, 207, 291; January 13, 17, 22; February 10; April 28; May 11, 17, 26, 30; July 8, 29; August 7, 17; September 15, 17; October 10; November 8, 19, 28; December 8; Epilogue 167, 221, 247, 375).
Related to Old High German *hina* and Anglo-Saxon *hin*? Or perhaps a shortened form of *cían* (according to scholar Zimmer).

**cen mair** Read as **céin mair**: **long remain! long live!** (June 10).

**cén**, **cían** **remote** (Latin *remotus* <note>original: "remotus", meaning "distant" or "far removed"</note>), **long in years**.
Dative: "long ago" or "far away" (*i céin*), Epilogue 110.
*céin mair* (June 10); see *erchian*.

**cenn** Neuter noun: **head** or **end**. (February 1, 25; July 24; November 29; Epilogue 8).
Singular genitive: *cinn* (February 27, April 7, July 9, August 10).
Accusative: (April 23, Epilogue 8).
Locative: *cinn* (September 17).
Welsh: *penn*.

**ceól** Neuter noun: **music** or **melody**. (Derived from the root *kiuplo*; related to Gothic *hiufan*, meaning "to wail," just as *teól* ["thief"] comes from *tiuplo*, Gothic *þiubs*—more correctly *þiufs*—and Anglo-Saxon *þeof*).
Nominative: *a ceól* (Book of Leinster 288b 25).
Accusative: (November 27).

**ceóldae** **melodious**. Feminine singular accusative: *ceóldai* (January 22).

**cepach**, **Ceppach** Feminine noun: **a plot of tilled ground** or **garden**. Accusative: *cepaigh*, page 92.

**cé-ro-d** (Prologue 101).

**cert** **right**, **just**, or **correct**. (Page 4, line 10).
Comparative adjective: *certu* (**more right**), Epilogue 148.
Compound: *ceirt-gním* ("right-deed"), plural genitive, page 114.
From this comes *certaím*, meaning **I adjust** or **I correct**.

**céssad**, **céssad** Masculine noun: **passion** or **suffering**. This is the verbal noun of the verb *céssaím* (related to Lithuanian *kencziu* <note>original: "kencziu", meaning "I suffer"</note>). (January 23, February 20, May 31, June 26, August 5, November 23).
Singular genitive: *césta* (August 25, Epilogue 270).
Dative: *céssad* (May 23, November 22).
Accusative: *céssad* (February 15, 27, 28; March 4; April 20; July 10, 23, 27; August 29; September 14; October 4, 14; November 15, 20).
Plural accusative: *céstu* (Epilogue 320).

**césu** **though it is**, Epilogue 133. See *cia*.

**cet** **permission, leave**, page 4, line 14; page 46, line 3. (Glossed as "let it be done" <note>original Latin: *fiat*</note>), *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 240. Related to the Latin *cedo* <note>meaning "to yield" or "go"</note> from the root *kezdo*.

**cét** Neuter noun: **a hundred**. (Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *cant*). 
Singular genitive: *céit* (March 12, July 24, Epilogue 188). 
Dative: *cét* (Prologue 151). 
Accusative: *cét* (July 4, October 5, *Leabhar Breac*). 
Plural nominative: *cét* (September 1, October 10). 
Dual nominative: *cét* (June 30). 
Dative: *cétaib* (April 3). 
Plural genitive: *fo chét cét* <note>"under a hundred hundreds"</note> (Prologue 151); *da nocht cét* (June 22). 
Dative: *cétaib* (Prologue 212, 328; May 12, 13; August 7; *Leabhar Breac* September 8; October 9, 16).

**cétach** **Centenary** <note>original Latin: *centenarius*</note> (relating to a hundred). Singular masculine genitive: *cétaig* (November 10).

**cét-áin** **Wednesday**, literally "first fast." It is contrasted with *áine diden*, the "last fast," which is Friday. *Dia cétáin* (page 2). The prefix *cét* comes from *cintu*, as seen in the Gaulish name *Cintugnatus*.

**cétal**, **cétol**, **cétul** **song**, June 1, Epilogue 150. Plural genitive: October 1. Compounds: *saerchetul* <note>"noble song"</note>, *cetul na Canoine* <note>"song of the Canon"</note>, *Cetul na Cosáite* <note>"song of the complaint"</note> (pages 4, 10). From the root *cantlo-n*. Welsh: *cathl*, *centhiliat*; Breton: *kentel* ("lesson").

**céte** Feminine noun: **path**. O'Clery's glossary <note>original: *O'Cl.*</note> defines *céide* as *conair* (a path). Dative: *céti* (December 20 and page 222). Perhaps related to Latin *incedo* <note>"to step" or "march"</note>?

**cethir** **four**, September 1, October 16, 25. Old Welsh: *petguar*; modern Welsh: *pedwar*.

**cethorchae** **forty**, April 3, November 16, 19. Genitive: *cethorchat* (March 9). Dative: *cethorchaib* (October 24).

**cethramad** **fourth**, page 78.

**cethrur** **four persons**, January 20, October 26.

**cétnae** (following a noun) **the same**, Prologue 244. Singular masculine genitive: *cétnai* (Prologue 202).

**cía** Conjunction: **although**. See *cé*.

**cíall** Feminine noun: **reason, sense**. (Welsh: *pwyll*). Genitive: *céille*. Accusative: *céill* (Epilogue 52).

**cían** **long**. See *cén, erchían*.

**cíarbu** **though it was**, Prologue 125. *Ciarsan* (page 52).

**cíat** **though they are**, Prologue 153. A Middle Irish corruption of *cit*.

**cicul** Masculine noun (from Latin *cyclus*): **a cycle**. Genitive: *cicúil* (page 98); *ciccaíl* (*Annals of Tigernach*, 1063). The Welsh *cylch* is identified by Joseph Loth as coming from the Latin *circulus* <note>meaning "circle"</note>, but it seems more likely to be a rearranged loan from *cyclus*.

**cid ná** **why not?** (Prologue 201). Literally, **"what is it that [is] not?"**

**cím** **I weep** or **I bewail**. Present indicative singular relative: *cías* (Epilogue 350). Related to Latin *queror* <note>"to complain" or "lament"</note>.

**cil** **wrong**, *rád nad cil* <note>"a saying that is not wrong"</note> (page 86; Cormac's Glossary 13).

**cimbid** Masculine noun: **a captive**, April 26, August 14. Genitive: *cimbedo* or *cimbetho* (*Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* I. 741).

**cin** **a crime, sin**. Singular accusative: *cinaid* (January 17, August 17). Plural nominative: *cinaid* (Epilogue 387). Accusative: *cinta* (Milan Glosses 74a 1).

**cing** Masculine noun: **champion, warrior**, July 24, August 20, 24. Singular accusative: *cingid-n* (September 13). Plural genitive: *cinged-n* (February 14); *cíñgeth* (P. manuscript).

**cingim** **I go, I step**. 3rd person singular perfect: *cechaing* (January 25, March 20, May 22, June 13, July 23, October 9). Related to the Sanskrit root *khañj* <note>"to limp"</note>, German *hinken*, and Welsh *rhy-gyngu* <note>"to amble"</note>.

**cingthecht** **championing**. See *do-chingthecht* and *cing*.

**cinnim** **I determine**. S-preterite 3rd person plural: *ro cinnset* (Epilogue 108). Verbal noun: *cinniud* (*Saltair na Rann* 967). Compare with Welsh *penodi*.

**císsucán** **a little tribute**, page 44. A diminutive of *císs*, which comes from Latin *census* <note>meaning "tax" or "assessment"</note> (pages 112, 188). Plural accusative: *císsu* (page 52). Compare the diminutive name *Isucán* <note>"Little Jesus," from a famous poem by St. Íte</note> on page 44.

**cit** **although they are** <note>original Latin: *quamvis sunt*</note>, Prologue 245, Epilogue 81.

**claideb** Masculine noun: **sword**, Prologue 101. Singular genitive: *claidib* (Epilogue 484). Welsh: *cleddyf*.

**cland** Feminine noun (Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. plant*</note>, from Latin <note>original: *planta*</note>): **offspring**. Singular genitive: *clainde*; plural: *cland* (December 18).

**clandach** **Prolific** (a derivative of *cland*). Dative singular feminine: *clandaig* (January 12); accusative singular masculine: *clandach* (May 22). Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. plantog*</note>.

**clandaim** **I plant** (Latin <note>original: *planto*</note>). Passive present singular 3rd person: *clantair* (August 9); preterite: *ro clandad* (February 14). Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. plana*</note>.

**clandmar** **Prolific**, page 172. *clandmór* in the *Saltair na Rann*, 6802.

**clár-ainech** **Flat-faced**, October 12. Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. gwynebclawr*</note>. *clár* is related to the Doric Greek <note>original: κλᾶρος (*klāros*)</note> meaning "a lot" <note>in the sense of a plot of land or a share</note>. See *ainech*.

**class** Feminine noun: **a quire** <note>a choir or a group of singers</note> or **quire-singing**. *O’Mulconry's Glossary*, 213. Genitive: *claisse*; they used to sing them in a choir <note>original: *nos-gaibtis for clais*</note>. Plural nominative: *classa* (Prologue 181); dative: *classaib*, page 116. From Latin <note>original: *classis*</note>.

**cléir** Feminine noun: **the clergy**, **a train**, or **a company**. (November 8, Epilogue 287). Singular dative: *cléir* (January 3, 12; March 31; May 14, 27; July 5, 26, 29; August 16, 28; October 17; December 7, 15; Epilogue 43). Accusative: *cléir-n* (February 28; April 30; May 15; June 2; October 7). Plural nominative: *cléri* (March 14). Derived from Latin <note>original: *clērus*</note> and Greek <note>original: κλῆρος (*klēros*)</note>, with a change to the i-declension.

**clérech** Masculine noun: from Latin <note>original: *clēricus*</note> (**cleric**), June 21. Cornish: *cloirec*; Breton: *cloarrec*.

**clí** **A kingpost** <note>the central vertical pillar supporting a roof</note>. (March 8, August 6, September 10, October 6). *Cormac's Glossary*, 10; *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* i. 707.

**clíar** Neuter noun: **a train** or **company**. (January 22, September 28, November 16). Vocative singular: *á chlíar* <note>"O company"</note>, Epilogue 373. Plural nominative: *clíara* (March 14, May 19).

**clíarach** **Having a train** or company, October 27.

**clíthi** See *celim*.

**cloch** Feminine noun: **stone**. Genitive: *cloiche*; dative: *cloich*; plural nominative: *clocha* (Prologue 194). Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. clog*</note>.

**clochar** **Assembly**, August 15. Glossed as a gathering <note>original Irish: *coimhthionol*</note> in O’Clery’s Glossary.

**clóine** Feminine noun: **wrongness**, **iniquity**, or **partiality**. Singular accusative: *clóini* (Epilogue 424). The form *ní ro chluine* (possibly for *chlóinea*), page 6, may be a subjunctive from the same verb.

**clóithe** **Vanquished**, December 14. Participle of *clóim* ("I overcome").

**clotha** August 24. See *ro cluiniur*.

**clothach** **Famous**. Singular genitive masculine: *clothaig* (May 4). A derivative of *cloth*, which is related to Old Breton *clot* (glossed as Latin <note>original: *rumoris*</note>, "of rumor" or "fame"). Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. clod*</note> ("fame").

**clú** **Fame** or **renown**. Related to Greek <note>original: κλέος (*kleos*)</note>. (March 5, August 11, Epilogue 86).

**clúain** Masculine noun: **a meadow**. Singular genitive: *clúana* (Prologue 180, 184; January 15; February 17; April 4; May 16; June 13; August 21; October 6; December 12, 13, 19, 23). Dative: *clúain* (May 26, August 6).

**cluinte**, **clunter**, **cúala** See *ro cluiniur*.

**clúm** Feminine noun: **down** or **plumage**. (Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. pluf*</note>, from Latin <note>original: *plūma*</note>). Singular genitive: *clúime* (Prologue 126).

**cnedach** **Wounded**. A derivative of *cned* ("wound"). Teutonic <note>original: *hnītan*</note>.

**cnet** Feminine noun: **sigh**, **sob**, or **groan**. (Prologue 228). Singular accusative: *cneit* (Epilogue 314); plural: *cneta* (Epilogue 325). Scholar Zupitza, in *Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung* (KZ) xxxvi. 233, derives *cned* from *knēsd(h)* and compares it to Sanskrit <note>original: *kiknasa-*</note> meaning "grist" or "crushed grain" <note>original German: *schrot*</note>. See *rochnet*.

**1. co** Preposition with the accusative case: **to** or **up to**. (January 5, 6, 25; June 22). Before vowels: "to the high sea" <note>original: *co hollmuir*</note> (February 17); "to the angels" <note>original: *co hangliu*</note> (March 10). Before the letter *r*: "to kings" <note>original: *co rrīga*</note> (June 13). In June 22, we should probably read "to the king-son" <note>original: *co rrīgmacc*</note>.

**2. co** Preposition used for *co-n*: **with**. "With a clergy" <note>original: *co cléir*</note> (Epilogue 43); "with a reach" <note>original: *co saichi*</note> (Prologue 298).

**3. co** A prefix used to form adverbs from adjectives <note>equivalent to the English suffix "-ly"</note>: "truly" <note>original: *co fírbail*</note> (June 15); "fully" <note>original: *co-lleír*</note> (Prologue 332); "quickly" <note>original: *co luath*</note> (page 12). See *menic*, page 4.

## GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**coair** *Just, proper, fitting, meet*, October 26, Epilogue 432, 433, Milan Glosses 48ª 8; plural nominative: *corí* March 25; accusative: *corai* Milan Glosses 51ᵈ 3. Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. cywir*</note>.

**cobair, cobuir** Feminine noun. *Help, aid*, July 28, October 19, December 29; singular genitive: *cobra*, *Lebor na hUidre* 71ᵇ 46; dative: *cobair*, July 24, Epilogue 44, 271, 292, 293; accusative: September 28, Epilogue 381, 388, 400. ***combair***, Prologue 243, may be a scribal error for *cobair*. From this comes *cobrigur*, meaning "I help" <note>original Latin: *auxilior*</note>.

**cobra** *Help, aid*, accusative singular: *cobraid*, October 18.

**cocertad** *The act of correcting*, dative: Epilogue 95. This is the verbal noun of *con-certain*.

**cocrait** (*com-corait*) *A couple*, December 24.

**codail** Epilogue 386, *skinny*?

**codal** Feminine noun. *Skin, hide*, accusative singular: *coduil*, December 8. *Codal* from *cutilia*, that is, from skin <note>original Latin: *.i. a pelle*</note>, *O’Mulconry's Glossary* 231. *Codal*, that is, a hide <note>original Old Irish: *.i. seiche*</note>, *O’Davoren's Glossary* no. 442. "A new skin-boat with a red-hide covering upon the sea" <note>original: *curiusa curuch nua co nderg-codail for muir*</note>, H. 2. 16, column 388. Root *kudh*, from which comes the Anglo-Saxon *hosa*, meaning "husk."

**cóel, cóil** *Slender*. Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. cul*</note>. Dative singular masculine: *cóel*, Epilogue 386.

**cóem, cóim** *Loveable, dear*, accusative singular masculine: *cóem*, April 10, Epilogue 66; nominative plural masculine: *cóim*, September 2; feminine: *cóema*, March 14. Compound: *cóem-aite* (dear foster-father), August 24. Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. cu*</note>.

**cóemchlóither** See *con-imchlóim*.

**cóemdae** *Loveable, beloved*, May 12; accusative singular masculine: August 5, September 19, Epilogue 170; feminine: *cóemdai*, December 28.

**coemnae** See *bith-chóemnae*.

**coibse** (Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. cyffes*</note>, from Latin *confessio* <note>confession</note>). Genitive singular: *coibsen*, Epilogue 185.

**coibtel** Epilogue 100, see *caiptel*.

**cóic** *Five* (from the root *kvenkve*; Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. pump*</note>), Prologue 327; accusative: August 7.

**cóicae** *Fifty*, January 30, October 9; plural genitive: *cóicat*, Epilogue 179; dative: *cóectaib*, August 7; dual nominative: *cóicait*, October 25.

**cóicat** *Fifty*, December 10.

**coich** *Who*? page 6, line 16.

**coicsed** (from *com-céssad*) *Compassion*, Epilogue 393; *Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie* III. 449. *coicsath*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 246.

**coimmdiu** Masculine noun. *Lord*, *Ascoli's Glossary* 395, Prologue 90, 160, 229; singular genitive: *coimmded*, March 10; dative: *commdid*, Epilogue 218.

**cóimthecht** *Company*, dative: December 20, Epilogue 291.

**coimti** *Attendants*? *companions*? It seems to be the plural of *com-éte*, cognate with *téit*, meaning "he comes" <note>original Latin: *venit*</note>, March 11.

**coir** December 12. This may be the accusative singular of *cor*, "hand," as seen in *ten-chor*, a word for "tongs" <note>original Latin: *forceps*</note>, *St. Gall Glosses* 70ª 8. Sanskrit: *kara*, "hand."

**col** Neuter noun. *Sin*. Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. cwl*</note>. Epilogue 98; genitive: *cuil*, *Yellow Book of Lecan* 91ᵇ 8; dative: *cul*, page 226, line 2; plural nominative: *(mór)chol* Milan Glosses 91ᵈ 21; genitive: *inna col* or *inna cuilech*, glossing the word "wicked" <note>original Latin: *nefandorum*</note>, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 714. From this comes *culigur*, "I profane."

**colainn** Feminine noun. *Body*, genitive: *colno*; accusative: *colainn*, March 12.

**colbae** *Love*, singular dative (likely instrumental): *colbu*, Epilogue 74. Perhaps from *co-lubae*, cognate with the Latin *lubens* (willing/pleasing), Sanskrit *lubh* (to desire), and Gothic *lubo* (love).

**col-léce** *Meanwhile*, Prologue 239. Compare with *colléic* in Meyer’s *Contributions*, derived from *con-leci*, "until he lets go" <note>original German: *bis er lässt*</note> (according to Zimmer).

**colum** *A column*, page 66. Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. colofn*</note>, from Latin *columna*.

**1. com, comm** *To my*, January 21, Epilogue 46.

**2. com** *With my*, Epilogue 51, 52, 327.
