<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

3. **com-**, a prefix, as in *com-ainm* (namesake), *com-arbae* (heir), etc.

4. **com-**, a perfective prefix <note>indicates a completed action</note>, as in *as-com-art* (struck off), October 19, *do-coem-nagtar* (they washed), January 4 (from *to-com-nenagtar*).

5. **com-**, the form taken by the preposition *con-* (with) before a labial consonant <note>a sound made with the lips, like b, p, or m</note>.

**comainm** Neuter noun. *A surname or namesake* <note>original Latin: cognomen</note>, March 14; accusative case: November 11, *Leabhar Breac* <note>original: LB</note>, B. F. P. Welsh <note>original: Cymr. cyfenw</note> 'surname.'

**comarbae** Masculine noun. *Heir, successor*, singular genitive case: *comarbai*, December 15.

**comarbus, comorbus**, *heritage, succession*, page 50, genitive: *comarpsa*. *Tripartite Life of Patrick* <note>original: Trip.</note> 138, 13.

**comarc**, *commemoration*, accusative case: August 5.

**combair**, see *cobair* <note>meaning help or aid</note>.

**combert, compert** Feminine noun. (from *com-ad-b.*), *conception*, March 25, September 24; genitive: *comperta*.

**comét**, *preservation*, March 17; genitive: *cométa*, *Tripartite Life of Patrick* <note>original: Trip.</note> 868; dative case: *comét*, Epilogue 149.

**comghas**, page 136, line 1, *meaning obscure*.

**comgnás** Feminine noun. *Companionship*, Epilogue 379; dative: *comgnáis*, *Saltair na Rann* <note>original: Salt.</note> 1763, 7640.

**comiúir**, *equally just*, Prologue 229.

**comlán** (Welsh <note>original: Cymr. cyflawn</note>), *equally full, complete*, page 4; comparative form: *comlániu*, *Book of Leinster* <note>original: LL</note> 13ᵃ 21.

**comland** Masculine noun. *A conflict*, Epilogue 163; genitive: *comlaind*.

**comlín** Neuter noun. *An equal number*, Prologue 295; plural nominative case: *trí comlín* (three equal numbers), *Lebor na hUidre* <note>original: LU</note> 78ᵇ 5. Welsh <note>original: Cymr. cyflawn</note> 'a complement.'

**communn** Feminine noun. (Welsh <note>original: Cymr. cymmun</note>), *communion*, Epilogue 189; accusative: *commainn*, April 14; *comainn*, page 46.

**commur**, page 208, line 32, *great abundance*, a compound of *com-* and *múr* (see the entry for *múr* <note>original: q.v.</note>).

**comna**, *of sexual union* <note>original Latin: coitionis</note>, page 228.

**compert**, see *combert*.

**com-súathim**, *I mix together, I churn*, "was being mixed" <note>original: no chomsuaithed</note>, page 146. Verbal noun: *comsúathad*, *Book of Leinster* <note>original: LL</note> 273ᵇ 26.

**comsuide**, page 54, *sitting together*, dative: *in[na] chomsuidiu* (glossed as "of sitting together" <note>original Latin: consessionis</note>), *Milan Glosses* <note>original: Ml.</note> 127ᵈ 13.

**comul**, *union, assembly*, July 5; plural genitive: *comul*, Epilogue 446; *more correctly comol* from *com-ól* <note>originally meaning "drinking together" or a banquet</note>.

**1. con-, co-**, preposition *with*, Prologue 6, 154, 211, 212, 227, January 19, February 5, 6, 11, 23, July 14. Before *b* it becomes *com-*, Prologue 307, January 27, August 19, 27, October 7, 21. Before *r*, it becomes *cor*, Prologue 37. Before *l*, it becomes *co-l*: Prologue 19, 299, February 21, October 7, 13, 22, Epilogue 106. In combination with the possessive pronouns: *com* (with my), Epilogue 52, 327; *cona* (with his), Prologue 105, 254, January 24, July 26, September 19, December 3; *cona* (with her), July 5, August 30, September 20; *cona-n* (with their), January 23, July 28; before *b*, *cona-m* (with their), Prologue 34.

**2. con-, co-**, conjunction *so that, until*, in *con-ecmaingsem* (so that we happened upon), Epilogue 7, *con-id* (so that it is), September 26, *con-dom-roib* (so that it may be to me), Prologue 11; before *b*, *co mbad* (so that it would be), Epilogue 217; before *l*: *col-léce* (until a while or meanwhile), Prologue 39.

**con-berim** = Latin *confero* (I bring together): 3rd person plural perfect with infixed pronoun <note>a pronoun placed inside the verb</note>: *cotaruicset*, May 8.

**con-certaím**, *I amend*, 1st person singular preterite <note>past tense</note> with perfective *ad*: *con-acertus-sa* (I have corrected), *Milan Glosses* <note>original: Ml.</note> 2 and 3; with infixed pronoun and perfective *ad*: *con-idn-aicert* (he has corrected it) (derived from *ad-cert*), Epilogue 105. Verbal nouns: *cocert*, *cocertad*.

**conchenn**, *dog-head*, page 118. *Revue Celtique* <note>original: Rev. Celt.</note> volume 9, page 20. *Contributions to Irish Lexicography* <note>original: Contribb.</note> 462.

**con-di-eig** (from *com-de-šiag*), *seeks, asks*. From this comes *conesta* and *cuintesta* (which see <note>original: qq.v.</note>).

**con-éirgim**, *I arise*; subjunctive singular second person: *coméir*, August 26; verbal form: *conesta*, page 2, see *condieig*.

**con-étgim** (from *con-en-tiag-*), *I resort to*? subjunctive singular second person: *conétis*, July 16.

**con-gabim**, *I take, I contain, I set up*; present indicative singular third person: *congaib*, April 1, April 76, 279; preterite <note>past tense</note> singular third person, with perfective *ad*: *conacab* <note>original Latin gloss: *contenuit*, meaning "he contained"</note>, Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 100ᶜ 1; plural third person: *congabsat* <note>original Latin gloss: *continuerunt*, meaning "they contained"</note>, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* <note>original: Thes.</note> I. 496.

**con-icim**, *I am able, I rule*; present indicative singular second person: *conic*, Prologue 7, Epilogue 434; singular third person: Prologue 359; plural second person: *conicid*, Epilogue 381, 388; subjunctive plural second person: *coníssid*, Epilogue 393; past subjunctive plural third person: *-coemsaitis*, *Saltair na Rann* <note>original: Salt.</note> 519. The perfect tense is deponent <note>a verb with a passive form but active meaning</note>: *conanacuir*, Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 119ᵈ 7. Enclitic forms (such as *-cumai*, *-cumgub*, etc.) come from *com-ang*. Verbal noun: *cumang*, which see <note>original: q.v.</note>.

**conid**, *so that it is*, September 26.

**con-im-chlóim**, *I change*; imperative passive singular third person: *cóemchlóither*, Epilogue 420. Verbal noun: *coemchlód*.

**conn** (or *cond*?), *sense, reason*; singular dative case: *cund*, Epilogue 52.

**con-ocbaim** (from *com-ud-g.*), *I raise up, extol*; subjunctive plural third person: *co-tom-r-occbhat*, Epilogue 45; singular third person perfect: *conuargaib, conuargaib, con-n-uargaib*, Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 37ᵇ 15. Verbal noun: *cumgabáil*, Epilogue 208.

**con-óim**, *I preserve, I protect* <note>related to Sanskrit: *avate*, meaning "he protects or satisfies"</note>; present indicative singular third person: *conói, -comai*, Ascoli 109; imperative passive singular third person: *co-tam-r-óither*, Epilogue 69. For the deponent form, see Strachan, *Deponent Verb*, 51, 70.

**conolaim** (from *com-od-laim*), *I depart* <note>original Latin: *discedo*</note>; perfect singular third person: *con-r-úalae*, November 21, Epilogue 25.

**con-oscaigim**, *I move* (from *com-od-scag-*), Ascoli 290-1; s-preterite <note>a specific type of past tense</note> singular third person: *con-r-oscaig*, Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 45ᶜ 2; plural third person enclitic: *-cumscaigset*, February 6. Verbal noun: *cumscugud* <note>original Latin gloss: *commutatio*, meaning "change or alteration"</note>, Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 26ᵈ 12.

**con-ruidiur**, Prologue 277; the analysis and meaning are obscure. Mac Firbis <note>a famous Irish hereditary scholar</note> explains *conruidiur* as *co ro raidiur*, O'Davoren's Glossary <note>original: O'Dav.</note> no. 434.

**con-sádu**, *I set together*, January 23.

**contan** (Welsh <note>original: Cymr. cynhen</note>), *contention*? singular dative: *conton*, page 152, last line; *Book of Leinster* <note>original: LL</note> 284ᵃ 42; accusative: *contan*, *Tripartite Life of Patrick* <note>original: Trip.</note> 220, line 4.

**con-tulim**, *I sleep*; perfect singular third person: *conatuil* (from *com-ad-t.*), August 7; imperative singular second person: *cotail*, page 12. Verbal noun: *cotlud*, which see <note>original: q.v.</note>.

**con-úagu**, *I knit together*, January 20; *con-r-uaig*, Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 99ᵃ 2; *conóigset* <note>original Latin gloss: *consuerunt*, meaning "they have sewn together"</note>, Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 19ᵃ.

**cor** Masculine noun. *A stir, a movement*; plural accusative: *rolá in scrín curu de*, page 76, line 38, meaning *the shrine moved of itself*; *ní ralá cor de*, *Revue Celtique* <note>original: Rev. Celt.</note> x. 74.

**cor**, Feminine noun. *A hand*, see *coir*.

**corach**, *quireful*? *musical*? singular genitive masculine: *coraig*, February 21; derived from *cor*, which means music <note>original: *ceol*</note>, O'Clery's Glossary <note>original: O'Cl.</note>. Welsh <note>original: Cym.</note> *côr*.

**corad** (or *córad*?), genitive plural of *caur*, meaning *champion*, Prologue 167; singular genitive: *caurad*, *Lebor na hUidre* <note>original: LU.</note> 73ᵃ 9. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *cawr*.

**córaid**, *sinners*? Prologue 65; genitive plural: *fri tabairt corad 7 eccraibdech in tsaegail documm n-irse 7 cretim* <note>meaning "for bringing the sinners and the irreligious of the world to faith and belief"</note>, *Leabhar Breac* <note>original: LB.</note> 29ᵃ 19; *córaidh*, which is a bad person <note>original: *drochduine*</note>, O'Reilly's Dictionary <note>original: O'R.</note>.

**corann** Feminine noun (Welsh <note>original: Cymr. coron</note>, from Latin *corōna*), November 25; singular genitive: *inna corne* <note>original gloss: *cornae*, meaning "of the crown"</note>, Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 24ᵃ 6.

**corgas**, Masculine, *Lent*. Derived from the Latin *quadragesima* <note>meaning: "fortieth," referring to the forty days of Lent</note>. Found on November 15, January 7, and November 13. Genitive case <note>showing possession</note>: *corgais*. Dative case <note>indicating a location or object of a preposition</note>: *corgus*, Epilogue 562. *i corgus erraig* <note>meaning: "in the spring Lent"</note>, page 54. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *carawys, grawys*.

**corp**, Masculine, *body*. Derived from the Latin *corpus*. Welsh: *corff*. Found in Prologue 293, February 5, and Epilogue 297. Singular genitive: *coirp, cuirp* (see *tol cuirp* <note>desire of the body</note>). Dative: *curp*, Epilogue 52, 363. Accusative <note>direct object</note>: *corp*, April 14, Epilogue 442. Plural nominative: *cuirp*, Prologue 79. Accusative plural: *curpu*, January 4, Epilogue 435.

**corpán**, *a little body* or *a dead body*. August 3, Epilogue 347. Singular genitive: *corpáin*, April 19. Dative: *corpán*, January 24, August 10, Epilogue 10.

**corpdae**, *corporeal* <note>bodily or physical</note>. Page 2. Hence the adverb *in-chorpdid* <note>meaning: "corporeally"</note>.

**corp-lén**, *bodily ease*. Accusative singular, June 22.

**corr-chíchech**, *having pointed breasts*. Page 40, Book of Leinster <note>original: LL.</note> 210b 13. Welsh *cor* means "point."

**cos**, used for *cosa-n*, *unto which*. Epilogue 58.

**coscar**, *victory*. *Glossarium Palaeo-Hibernicum* <note>original: Asc.</note> 288. Genitive: *coscair*, Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 33c 13. Singular dative: *coscur*, Prologue 63, Epilogue 23.

**cosecrad, coisecrad**, Masculine, *consecration*. Accusative: September 15, November 18, 19. This is the verbal noun of *cosecraim*, from which comes *cutsecar*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* <note>original: Thes.</note> II. 242, line 8. Welsh: *cysegru*. Derived from the Latin *consecro* <note>to dedicate or make sacred</note>.

**cosin**, (from *\*com-sind*), *with the*. June 20, Epilogue 57 in the Laud manuscript <note>original: L</note>, while the Paschal manuscript <note>original: P</note> uses *cosind*.

**cosnam**, *the act of striving*. Singular accusative: Epilogue 221. This is the verbal noun of *con-sním*.

**cosóit**, *accusation*. Derived from the Latin *causātio* <note>a reason, pretext, or accusation</note>. Genitive singular: *cosáite*, page 4; better spelled *cosóite*.

**cotaruicset**, see the entry for ***con-berim***.

**cotlud**, *sleep*. December 27. This is the verbal noun of *contuilim*.

**crábud**, *devotion* or *piety*. Accusative: Epilogue 197. Welsh: *crefydd*.

**cráibdech**, *devout* or *pious*. March 24, July 11. Singular genitive masculine: *cráibdig*, January 16, March 30. Accusative: *cráibdech*, July 20. Plural nominative: *cráibdig*, Prologue 79.

**cráidim**, *I torment*. Passive preterite <note>past tense</note> plural third person: *ro cráite* <note>meaning: "they were tormented"</note>, Epilogue 269.

**crann**, Neuter, *tree*. March 10. Singular genitive: *crainn*, May 3. Welsh: *prenn*.

**crann-bríathrach**, page 96. The meaning is obscure. Found in the Book of Fermoy <note>original: Ferm.</note> 43b.

**cré**, *clay* or *mould*. Singular genitive: *críad*, April 19, where the word is pronounced with two syllables. Welsh: *pridd*.

**credal**, *pious, devout,* or *believing*. January 15, February 4, March 24, August 9. Singular genitive masculine: *credail*, June 12, Epilogue 291. Dative feminine: *credail*, Epilogue 43. Accusative masculine: *credal*, Prologue 111, April 4. Plural genitive: *credal*, November 16, Epilogue 188. Dative plural: *credlaib*, Epilogue 191. Welsh: *credol*.

**credlach**, *truthful* or *pious*. October 21, December 13. Singular genitive masculine: *credlaig*, February 25.

**creim**, *the act of gnawing*. Page 48. Also spelled *creimm* in Meyer’s *Contributions to Irish Lexicography* <note>original: Contribb.</note> 511.

**crésen, créssen**, *pious*. February 4, April 27. Plural genitive: October 24. Perhaps derived from the Latin *Christianus* <note>Christian</note>?

**cretar, cretair**, *something holy or consecrated*, or perhaps *a reliquary* <note>a container for holy relics</note>? Prologue 114, Epilogue 189. Accusative: *cretair*, April 12. The scholar O'Clery explains *cretar* as "a house containing relics," and this may be the meaning for the entries at April 12 and Epilogue 189. Welsh *crair*, meaning "a relic," seems related, though the exact connection is unclear.

**cretem**, Feminine, *belief*. Prologue 173. Genitive: *creitme*. This is the verbal noun of *cretim*. Welsh: *cred*.

**crích**, Feminine, *boundary, limit,* or *end*. Derived from the Latin *finis* <note>end or boundary</note>. Singular accusative: *crích-n*, February 28. In the Leabhar Breac <note>original: LB.</note>, feminine accusative, June 3. Dual genitive <note>referring to two boundaries</note>: *dá chrích*, August 15, October 6. Plural dative: *críchaib*, June 17. Accusative plural: *crícha*, September 9.

**críde**, Neuter, *heart*. Epilogue 194. Singular genitive: *cridi*, Prologue 228, September 27, Epilogue 68. Accusative: *críde*, Epilogue 383. Welsh: *craidd*. Greek: *καρδία* <note>original: kardia, meaning "heart"</note>.

## GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**crinner**, *a falling*. Singular dative: *crinniur*, Prologue 298.

**croan**, *valour* <note>meaning: bravery or courage</note>, Prologue 51. Glossed as *cródhachd* <note>meaning: "bravery"</note> in O'Clery's Glossary <note>original: O'Cl.</note>.

**croch**, Feminine, *cross*. Found on January 11, March 31, April 10, 30, July 10, 21, August 10, 19, September 27, and October 22. Singular genitive <note>showing possession</note>: *croiche*, March 10, May 3; *cruiche*, April 12, Epilogue 270. Dative: *croich*, August 17. Accusative <note>direct object</note>: *croich*, August 16. Plural dative: *crochaib*, Prologue 46. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *croes*, derived from an oblique case of the Latin *crux* <note>meaning: "cross"</note>.

**crochad**, Masculine, *crucifixion* or *hanging*. March 25. Singular genitive: *crochtha*, February 24, April 20.

**crochaim**, *I crucify* or *I hang*. Preterite active, 3rd person singular: *crochais*, March 8, 12, December 30. 3rd person plural with an infixed pronoun: *ro-da-crochsat* <note>meaning: "they crucified them"</note>, Prologue 73. Passive preterite, 3rd person singular: *crochthae*, February 5, 12, May 12. Present, 3rd person singular: *ro crochad* <note>meaning: "he was crucified"</note>, Prologue 89. Preterite participle: *crochthae*, October 21, 31. Singular masculine genitive: *crochthai*, May 6. Verbal noun: *crochad*.

**crochaire**, Masculine, *hangman*. Page 90, line 18.

**crossaire, croxaire**, Masculine. Page 202. *A cross-bearer*. A derivative of *cross*. Welsh: *croes*, from the Latin *crux*.

**crothaim**, *I shake*. Present indicative, 3rd person singular, relative form: *crothass*, September 9. Compare with the phrase *co fu-crothad*, meaning "that it might be shaken" <note>original Latin: *ut cassaret*</note> in the Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 23ᵇ 14. Old Breton <note>original: O.Br.</note>: *ro-credihat* (glossed on *uigricatus* <note>possibly a scribal error for "vibrated"</note>), read as *ro crediat* (glossed on the Latin *uibratus*, meaning "shaken").

**cruimther**, Masculine. *A presbyter* <note>meaning: a priest</note>. May 11, 27, August 9. Singular genitive: *cruimthir*, February 24, April 10, 20. Welsh: *pryfder*, derived from the Latin forms *prebiter* or *previter* <note>corruptions of *presbyter*</note>.

**cruth**, Masculine, *form*. Welsh: *pryd*. January 5. Genitive: *crotha*. From this comes the verb *cruthaigur*, "I form."

**cúairt**, Masculine, *circuit* or *sojourn*. Singular accusative: *cuairt*, January 22. Plural nominative: *chuartai*, glossed as "circles" <note>original Latin: *orbes*</note> in the Milan Glosses 39ᶜ 12.

**cúala**, *I have heard* <note>original Latin: *audivi*</note>. June 13. See the entry for *rocluinniur*.

**cuart**, *a fourth part* of an ecclesiastical offering <note>original: "oblation"</note>. Derived from the Latin *quarta*. Found in *Contributions to Irish Lexicography* <note>original: Contribb.</note> 544. "He gives the fourth to Lassrán" <note>original: *tidnaid do lassran in chuaird*</note>, *Revue Celtique* 52. See also *fírchuairt* <note>meaning: "true fourth"</note>, page 112, and *lánchuairt* <note>meaning: "full fourth"</note> in the *Annals of the Four Masters* <note>original: FM.</note> II. 894, 948.

**cubat**, page 90, line 1. *A grave?* Related to the Latin *cubo* <note>meaning: "to lie down"</note> and the Sabine word *cumba*, meaning a "litter" or "couch" <note>original Latin: *lectica*</note>.

**cubus**, derived from *com-fius* <note>meaning: "joint-knowledge"</note>. *Conscience*. Singular dative, pages 4, 10.

**cucut**, *unto you* <note>singular</note>. Prologue 280.

**cuibded**, *the act of harmonizing*. Singular dative, Epilogue 124. This is the verbal noun of *cuibdigim*.

**cuibsigeim**, *I cause confession*. Preterite, 3rd person singular: *ro-s-cuibsīgestar*, page 242, note 3. Derived from *cuibse* <note>meaning: "confession"</note>. Welsh: *cyffes*, from the Latin *confessio*.

**cuilche**, *a cassock* <note>a long clerical garment</note>. Pages 88, 222, 224. Also *cuilciu*, page 90. Related to the German *hülle* <note>meaning: "a covering"</note>.

**cuilenn**, *holly*. Singular genitive: *cuilinn*, May 21, July 6. Welsh: *celynen*. Anglo-Saxon <note>original: Ags.</note>: *holegn*.

**cuimbrigud**, *the act of abridging* <note>shortening a text</note>. Epilogue 123.

**cuimnech**, *mindful*. Masculine singular dative, Epilogue 363. From *cuimne* (Welsh: *côf*), meaning "memory" <note>original Latin: *memoria*</note>. From this comes *cuimnigur*, meaning "I remember" <note>original Latin: *reminiscor*</note>.

**cuimrech**, Neuter, *chain* or *bond*. Singular genitive: *cumrig*, February 25. Plural genitive: *cuimrech*, October 15. See the entry for *adriug*.

**cuindgid**, *the act of seeking*. Dative, Prologue 329. This is the verbal noun of *condieig*.

**cuintesta**, page 8. Also written as *conesta* on page 4. This is the "participle of necessity" <note>meaning: "must be sought"</note> for the verb *cuintig*, meaning "seeks" or "asks" (from *con-de-siag*). Compare with *comitesti* in the Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 1ᶜ 12 (for *comitechtī*), and the German form *nischts* used for *nichts*.

**cuiriur**, *I put forth*. Active present, 3rd person plural: *cuiretar*, *Bedae Carlsruhensis* <note>original: Bcr.</note> 32ᵇ 11. Passive present, 3rd person plural: *cuirter*, January 25.

**cúis**, Feminine, *a cause*. From the Latin *causa*. Page 8.

**cuit**, Feminine, *a portion*. Welsh: *peth*. Singular genitive: *cota*. Accusative: *cu*, July 29.

<term>cuitech</term>, *requital* (a payment or compensation), page 94, line 20; *cúiteach* in Coneys' Irish-English Dictionary, 1849; incorrectly written as *cuiteadh* in O'Reilly's dictionary <note>original: O'R.</note>.

<term>cuithe</term>, *pit*, derived from the Latin word for "well" or "pit" <note>original: puteus</note>. Singular dative <note>the grammatical case indicating the object of a preposition</note>: *cuithi*, Epilogue 500. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *pydew*.

<term>cuitid</term>, page 110, line 33, *share* or *portion*. This should perhaps be corrected to *cuitig* (see Ériu, volume 1, page 44), or to *cuitín*, which is a diminutive form of *cuit* (part).

<term>cúl</term>, Feminine, *corner* or *recess*. Singular genitive <note>showing possession</note>: *cúlae*, November 11. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *cil*.

<term>cumang</term>, *power*. The verbal noun of the verb *conícim* (I am able). Epilogue 9.

<term>cumce</term>, Feminine, *a strait* or *straitness* (a narrow or difficult place), Epilogue 385. Dative: *hi cumcai*, Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 33ᵃ 12. Derived from *cumac*, which is related to the Welsh word for "narrow" or "strait" <note>original: cyfŷng</note>. From this comes the verb *cumcigim*, meaning "I distress" or "I compress" <note>original: ango</note>, St. Gall Glosses <note>original: Sg.</note> 16ᵇ 9.

<term>cumgabáil</term>, Feminine, *an uplifting*, Epilogue 208; also written *cumgabál*, Milan Glosses 138ᵃ 2.

<term>cummuscrad</term>, *mixture*. Dative: *-raid*, page 92. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *cymysg*.

<term>-cumscaigset</term>, see the verb *conoscagim* (I move).

<term>cundu</term>, *relationship* or *friendship*, Epilogue 230. Mentioned in O'Davoren's Glossary <note>original: O'Dav.</note> number 435, and St. Gall Glosses 70ᵃ 17.

<term>cungnam</term>, see *congam* (I help).

<term>curach</term>, Masculine, *boat*. Genitive: *curaig*. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *corwg, curwca*. See Reeves' *Adamnan's Life of Saint Columba* <note>original: Reeves Col.</note>, page 442.

<term>curchán</term>, *a little boat*. Dative: February 13, December 8. A diminutive of *curach*.

<term>cutaim</term> (from *con-tuitim*), *a fall*. Dative: Epilogue 556. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *codwm*.

***

<term>d</term>, an infixed pronoun <note>a pronoun placed inside a verb</note> for the 3rd person singular masculine and neuter. Examples: *atgab* (ad-d-gab), Prologue 107; *atsluindi* (ad-d-sluindi), Prologue 111; *no-d-dlomaim*, Prologue 316; *fo-d-lugai*, June 6; *atglennís* (ad-d-g.), July 30; *no-d-bágu*, November 30; *fo-d-r²-uair*, Epilogue 97; *fo-d-fuasna*, Epilogue 102; *no-d-géba*, Epilogue 166, 180. Another *d* that has not yet been explained occurs in *mani-d* (June 13, July 19), *cia-d*, and *ma-d*.

<term>da</term>, an infixed pronoun for the 3rd person plural. Examples: *ro-da-crochsat* (they crucified them), Prologue 73; *cotaruicset* (coth-da-r².), May 8; *do-da-farnaic*, June 10; *atasníaím* (ad-da-s.), October 26; *ar-da-légfa*, Epilogue 216.

<term>dá</term>, *two*. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *dau*. Masculine and neuter: September 28, October 25, 30. Feminine form: *dí*. Welsh: *dwŷ* <note>original: Cymr. dwŷ</note>, May 31, September 27, December 9. Neuter form: *dá-n*, Prologue 324, June 22. Genitive: *dá*, Prologue 196. Dative: *díb*, April 3, June 14. Accusative feminine: *dí*, March 3. See also *díb-línaib* (both).

<term>dabach</term>, Feminine, *vat* or *tub*. Dative: *dabaig*, Epilogue 540. Cognate <note>related in origin</note> with the Greek words for "burial or trench" <note>original: τάφος</note>, "ditch" <note>original: τάφρος</note>, and "to devour or rend" <note>original: δάπτω</note>.

<term>dag</term>, *good*. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *da*. Found in compounds: **dag-ordan**, Masculine, *good ordination*, July 4; **daig-thech**, *a good house*, page 14.

<term>daille</term>, Feminine, *blindness*. Singular genitive: Epilogue 512. A derivative of *dall* (blind).

<term>daingen</term>, *strong, firm, or steadfast*, Prologue 130, Epilogue 210, 342. Comparative form <note>meaning "stronger"</note>: *daingniu*, May 23. From this comes *daingnigim*, meaning "I fortify" <note>original: munio</note>.

<term>daire</term>, Masculine, *oakwood*. Dative: *dairiu*, May 7.

<term>daith</term>, *swift*. Comparative: *daithiu*, March 31.

<term>dál</term>, Feminine, *assembly*. Old Welsh <note>original: O. Cymr.</note>: *datl*; modern Welsh: *dadl*. October 28. Plural dative: *dálaib*, Prologue 35, 211, 315, Epilogue 63. Accusative plural: *dála*, September 20. Hence:

<term>dálach</term>, *multitudinous* (or having many assemblies), Prologue 192, 196. Singular dative masculine: *dálach*, January 1, April 11, August 6. Feminine: *dálaig*, September 12. Accusative masculine: *dálach*, September 29, November 26. Neuter: *dálach*, December 13.

<term>dálaim</term>, *I allot* (or I assign), preterite active singular 3rd person: *dálais*, April 12. Future relative: *dalfas*, Saltair na Rann <note>original: Salt.</note> 3318. A denominative verb <note>a verb formed from a noun</note> of *dál* (division). Compare *fodáli* (he divides) and the Old Welsh word for "excluded" or "having no part in" <note>original: didaul, glossing the Latin "expers"</note>.

<term>dall-chéilliu</term>, *blind-guidance*, Prologue 316. Compare: "he was a fosterling with blind guidance" <note>original: ropo dalta co ndallcheill</note>, Book of Leinster <note>original: LL</note> 169ᵃ 10. See also *célliu*, page 308, above.

<term>daltae</term>, Masculine, *fosterling* or *pupil*. Singular genitive: *daltai*, May 2, August 22.

### GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

<term>dam-airecht</term>, *ox-herding*, page 48.

<term>damim</term>, *I endure, I suffer*. This is a deponent verb <note>a verb that is passive in form but active in meaning</note>. The past tense active singular (third person) is *dámair*, used on February 9 and 16. The plural (third person) is *damdatar* (though it should perhaps be read as *damnatar*?) on October 15. However, the form *ro damnatar* (Prologue 32, 53), like *fo-ro-damnatar* (Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 90, 96) and "as they suffered" <note>original: amal fo-nd-ro-damnatar</note> (Milan Glosses 105), shows an *n* sound that has not yet been explained by linguists.

<term>dána</term>, *bold*, May 25. The masculine genitive <note>possessive</note> form is *dáni*, December 10; the masculine dative <note>object of a preposition</note> is *dánu*, January 23. The comparative form <note>meaning "bolder"</note> is *dánu*, March 20, May 23, and November 30 (where it is used as a superlative, meaning "boldest").

<term>dar</term>, a preposition used instead of *tar* ("across" or "over"), February 13, March 5, 22, June 3, 12, August 14, and in the Epilogue 25, 164.

<term>darbile</term>, a (*sacred*) *tree*, page 258, line 15. See the entry for *bile*.

<term>darrála</term> (from *do-an-rala*), December 8, *he has come* (literally, "it brought him"). Compare to *do-t-rala*, meaning *you have come*, found in Reeves' *Columba* (page 266), the *Gaelic Journal* (1904, page 303), and *Revue Celtique*, volume 12, page 442.

<term>dath</term>, Neuter noun meaning *hue* or *color*. The singular genitive <note>possessive</note> is *datha*, November 15. For compound words, see *líg-dath* and *so-dath*.

<term>de, di</term>, the unstressed form of the preposition *do*. It is used with the dative and ablative cases <note>grammatical cases indicating objects of prepositions or origin</note> on January 8, May 21, June 25, December 22, and frequently in the Epilogue. Combined with the article, it becomes *dind* (Epilogue 26). Combined with personal pronouns, it becomes *dim* (from me), *dinn* (from us), *de* (from him/it), *dib* (from them), and *dii* (from her). It is related to the Latin preposition *de* <note>meaning "from" or "of"</note>.

<term>de de</term>, meaning "from him" <note>original Latin: ex eo</note>, Prologue 188.

<term>déac</term>, *ten*, July 15, September 22. It is pronounced with two syllables in both places. For various explanations of this form (which may be a singular genitive), see Brugmann's *Grundriss*, section 175, and *Indogermanische Forschungen* <note>original: Ind. F.</note>, volume 12, page 188.

<term>déacht</term>, Feminine noun meaning *godhead* or *divinity*, Epilogue 353. The genitive <note>possessive</note> is *deachte*. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *duwiaeth*.

<term>-déccaim</term>, *I see*. This is the dependent form of the verb *do-éccim*. The present indicative plural (second person, "you all see") is *-déccaid*, Prologue 201. The imperative singular (second person, "see!") is *décce* or *déiccesiu*, as seen in the Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 10 and 31.

<term>dech</term>, *best*, page 4, line 10, November 16. It is related to the Latin words *decus* <note>honor or ornament</note> and *decens* <note>fitting or decent</note>.

<term>dechaid</term>, *he went* <note>original Latin: ivit</note> (derived from *\*de-co-fáith*), May 4. Also spelled *deocháid* (see that entry).

<term>dechenbor</term>, *ten persons*. The dative form is *dechenbur*, July 14.

<term>décheng</term>, a *pair of persons*, March 7, September 6. The accusative <note>direct object</note> form is *décheng*, November 26. See also *trecheng* (a trio of persons).

<term>decimber</term>, *December*. The genitive <note>possessive</note> form is *decimbir*, December 1.

<term>decmaic</term>, *difficult*, Epilogue 172.

<term>dedblén</term>, Masculine noun meaning a *weakling*, Epilogue 396, 399. The plural genitive is *dedblén*, January 24. This is a diminutive of *dedbul*.

<term>dedbul</term> (from *de-adbul*), meaning *petty*, January 25, Epilogue 266.

<term>dédenach</term>, *final*, Epilogue 281.

<term>dedól</term>, Feminine noun meaning *twilight*. The dative form is *dedóil*, July 26. However, in the Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 136, the dative is *dedól*, as if the word were masculine or neuter.

<term>deg-feth</term>, page 146, a *goodly aspect*.

<term>deich-n</term>, *ten*, January 27, February 28, October 16, 25. The dative form is *dechib*, October 10. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note>: *deg, deng*.

<term>deilm</term>, Neuter noun meaning *noise*, Prologue 163, June 29. The singular genitive is *delmae*, April 7. The dative form is *delmaimm*, Prologue 154 and Epilogue 127.

<term>deismberecht</term>, Feminine noun meaning *example*, page 48. The genitive is *desimrechte*, Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 26. Derived from *\*de-es-sembr*...: perhaps related to the Italian word *sembrare* <note>meaning "to seem"</note>?

<term>deit</term>, a form used for *duit* ("to you"), September 14, and in several versions of the Epilogue including the *Leabhar Breac* <note>original: LB.</note> and others.

<term>deithbir</term>, *just*, Prologue 114.

<term>delbdae</term>, *shapely*. The singular accusative masculine is in Epilogue 354; the plural nominative feminine *delbdai* is in February 28. In Epilogue 354, the form *delbdae* stands for "seven-shaped" <note>original Latin: septiformis</note>, referring to the "grace of the Holy Spirit" <note>original Latin: gratia Spiritus sancti</note>. Compare this to "the coming of the seven-shaped Spirit" <note>original Old Irish: dí thetacht in spírto sechtnádelbich</note> in the *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* (I. 496). It is derived from *delb* (form or image), which is related to the Welsh word *delw* <note>original: Cymr.</note>.

### GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**deligthech**, *distinct*, page 46. This is a derivative of *deligud* (found in the Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 128a 9), which is the verbal noun <note>a noun formed from a verb, like "the act of differing"</note> of the verbs *deligur* or *deligiur*, meaning "I differ" or "I surpass."

**demin**, an adverb meaning *certainly* or *verily*, October 18. From this root comes *demnigur*, meaning "I confirm" <note>original: *firmo*</note>.

**demon**, Masculine noun meaning *a demon* or *the Devil*, February 16. The singular genitive <note>possessive</note> is *demuin* (Prologue 253; Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 9d 24); the accusative <note>direct object</note> is *demon* (Prologue 242, March 16, Epilogue 154). The plural genitive is *demnae* (February 24, October 17, Epilogue 198, 211, 520). In the plural, it follows the "i-declension" <note>a specific grammatical pattern for word endings</note>.

1. **dénam**, Masculine noun meaning the *act of doing or making*. The singular dative <note>object of a preposition</note> is *dénam* (Epilogue 88). This is the verbal noun of *do-gníu* ("I do").

2. **dénam**, (Prologue 317), the first-person plural imperative <note>a command or exhortation, "let us do"</note> of *do-gníu* ("I do" or "I make").

**denn**, *color*; see the entry for *glédénn*.

**deochoid** (derived from the reconstructed form *\*deco-fáith*), *he went* <note>original: *ivit*</note>, April 13. See also the related forms *dechaid* and *docuaid*.

**deochoin, dechain**, Masculine noun (related to the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *diacon*), *deacon*, April 13, May 5. The singular genitive is *deochain* (January 14, April 17, August 10); also spelled *deochain* (April 16) and *dechain* (May 4). The feminine plural nominative is *dechuín*, meaning "deaconesses" (Würzburg Glosses 28c 5).

**deodae**, *godly*, January 9, February 9, March 7, Epilogue 210.

**deórudán**, Masculine noun meaning *a poor exile*, Epilogue 366. This is a diminutive <note>a form of a word expressing smallness or affection</note> of *deórad*.

**dér**, Neuter noun meaning *a tear* (related to Old Welsh <note>original: O. Cymr.</note> *dacr* and Greek *δάκρυ* <note>original: dákry</note>). The plural nominative is *na dáer* (Milan Glosses 23a 13); the genitive is *dér* (Epilogue 400); and the dative is *déraib* (Prologue 24, Epilogue 174).

**deramrae**, Neuter noun found in the Epilogue, line 342, meaning *a great marvel*.

**derb**, *sure, true, certain*, January 3, May 25. The masculine singular dative is *derb* (February 2, April 11); the accusative is *derb* (July 8, November 26). In the entry for November 1, the word *derb* should probably be corrected to the masculine singular genitive *deirb*.

**derb-bráthir**, Masculine noun meaning *own-brother* <note>a full brother as opposed to a relative or spiritual brother</note>. The plural nominative occurs on June 27, where the manuscripts use a single letter for the softened <note>aspirated</note> *bb*.

**dergnaide**, page 44. The meaning is unclear, but it perhaps means *ignorant*. It is formed from the negative prefix *dí-* and *ergnaide*, which is a derivative of *ergnae* ("knowledge" or "understanding," see February 24).

**derg**, *red* (related to the Anglo-Saxon <note>original: Ags.</note> word *deorc*, meaning "dark"). Compounds include:
**dergmartra**, *red martyrdom* <note>the act of dying for the faith, distinguished from "white martyrdom" or asceticism</note>, pages 116, 144.
**dergór**, *red gold*, genitive *dergóir*, September 10.
**dergthuírenn**, page 134, *red wheat*.

**dermar**, *vast* or *huge* (related to Welsh *dirfawr* and Old Breton *dermorion*, which translates the Latin word for "enormous things" <note>original: *inormia*</note>). Occurs March 27, October 9, Epilogue 281, 288. The masculine singular genitive is *dermair* (May 15, September 14); the neuter dative is *dermar* (March 23). See also the entry for *már*.

**dermaire**, Epilogue 342. This seems to be a scribal error for *deramrae* (see above).

**dermet, dermat**, Neuter noun meaning *forgetfulness*, Epilogue 121; also cited by Ascoli <note>original: Asc.</note> on page 381. The accusative singular is *dermet* (May 11). This is the verbal noun of the verbs *dermaitim* or *doromoiníur*, meaning "I forget." The first-person plural past tense, "we did not forget" <note>original: *ni dermenmarni*</note>, is found in the Milan Glosses 64a 3.

**descipul**, Masculine noun (related to Welsh *dysgybl*), *disciple*. The plural dative is *desciplaib* (Epilogue 246).

**désérc**, Feminine noun meaning *charity*. The accusative singular is *déséirc* (Epilogue 389). This is a compound of *día* ("God") and *serc* ("love").

**désillabach**, *disyllabic* <note>having two syllables</note>, page 4. It is a derivative of *désillab*, which corresponds to the Welsh *dwysill*.

**des-mag**, Neuter noun meaning *southern plain*. The locative singular <note>showing place</note> is *desmaig* (Prologue 226). This word is related to the Welsh *dehou*, the Greek *δεξιός* <note>original: dexios</note>, and the Sanskrit *dakshina*, all of which refer to the "right hand" or the "south."

**détlae**, *bold*? Accusative singular masculine, Prologue 242.

**déud**, *end*, Prologue 220; also spelled *deudh* (feminine). Related to the Welsh *diwedd*.

**dí**, a preposition meaning *from*. This is a variant of the preposition *de* (see that entry).

**dí**, the feminine form of the number *two*. Related to the Welsh *dwy*. See also the entry for *dá*.

<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX</header>
<page-num>319</page-num>

**dia**, meaning *to his, her, or its*. Found in the entries for February 11, August 10, 26, and the Epilogue <note>original: Ep.</note> 95, 115.

1. **día**, a Masculine noun meaning *God*. The singular genitive <note>possessive form</note> is **dé** (Prologue 104, 215; February 11, 15; November 5; December 19). The accusative <note>direct object</note> is **día** (Epilogue 153, where it is pronounced as two syllables). The vocative <note>form used for direct address</note> is **dé** (Epilogue 312, 313). Related to the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word *duw* (meaning "God").

2. **día**, meaning *day*. The singular genitive is found in the entry for July 16 and Epilogue 166 (where it is disyllabic). The dative <note>object of a preposition</note> form is **indíu** (meaning "today," Prologue 220). The accusative is **dé-n** (Prologue 174) or **frídei** (found in the Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 9a 5). Related to the Welsh word *dydd* (meaning "day").

1. **dia-n**, meaning *to whom* (Prologue 146; March 9; July 10; September 10) or *from whom* (April 2).

2. **dia-n**, meaning *to their* (December 28). For example, **dia n-éiss** (Prologue 79, 252) means "after them" <note>literally "on their track"</note>.

3. **dia-n**, a conjunction meaning *if* (July 25; Epilogue 98, 171). In Prologue 143, 219, and October 24, *dian* stands for **dian-d-**, where the second *d* is an infixed pronoun <note>a pronoun placed inside the word</note>; see the explanation on page 316.

4. **dia-n**, meaning *when*, used on page 4 with the indicative preterite and perfect <note>past tenses</note>.

**dían**, meaning *vehement* or *swift* (Prologue 219; December 18). The plural dative is **díanaib** (Prologue 24). From this root comes the word *dianagím*, meaning "I hasten" <note>original: celero</note>.

**diand** (derived from *dian-id*), meaning *to whom is* <note>original: cui est</note> (April 22; June 12; September 10). When appearing before the letter *d*, it is written **dian dír** (page 4, line 13), meaning "to whom is due."

**dian-da**, meaning *to whom I am* <note>original: cui sum</note> (Epilogue 307, 426).

**diar-n**, meaning *to our* (Prologue 243, 323; January 14, 29; September 27; November 24; December 26). The phrase **diar-n-éis** (Epilogue 419) means "after us."

1. **días**, a Feminine noun meaning *an ear of corn* <note>original: spica</note> (November 24, where it is disyllabic). Related to the Welsh word *tywysen*.

2. **días**, a Feminine noun meaning *a pair* or *two persons* <note>original: duitas</note> (March 13, where it is disyllabic). The singular genitive is **désse**; the accusative is **díis-n** (September 13, 14).

**díib-línaib**, meaning *from two parts* or *on both sides* <note>original: e duabus partibus, utrimque</note> (June 14).

**díchell**, a Feminine noun meaning *neglect*. The accusative form is **díchiul** (Prologue 291), which seems to be used instead of *díchell* to create a rhyme with *díriuch* in the following line.

**díchmairc** (derived from *dí-comarc*), meaning *an unpermitted and therefore illegal act* (singular accusative, August 16).

**díchrae**, meaning *fervent* or *earnest* (January 10).

**díchracht**, meaning *fervor* or *vehemence* (singular accusative, page 94, line 13).

**dídiu**, a conjunction meaning *hence* or *therefore* (page 2; derived from *dí-suidiu*).

**dídnad**, a Neuter noun meaning *solace* or *the act of consoling* (June 8; Epilogue 191). The dative is **dídnad** (Epilogue 299). This is the verbal noun of **dodonaím** (meaning "I console"); from this comes the form **do-ro-n-donad-ni** ("we have been consoled") in the Würzburg Glosses.

**dígal**, a Feminine noun (related to the Welsh *dial*) meaning *vengeance* or *punishment*. The singular genitive is **díglae**; the dative and accusative are **dígail**. This is the verbal noun of **dofeich** ("he avenges").

**dígdde** (derived from *dí-guide*), meaning *a blessing*. The singular dative is **dígdi** (December 26). An example from the Book of Leinster <note>original: LL</note> reads: "to seek my blessing from the Greeks after my tormenting them" <note>original: do chuinncidh mo dígde o Grecaib iar mo cradh' doaib</note>.

**dígnáe**, meaning *reproach*. The genitive is **dígnai** (Prologue 254; July 29). The accusative occurs on January 22, February 9, March 7, September 18, and November 4.

**dígrae** (derived from *dí-goire*), meaning *impiety* (singular accusative, November 4).

**dígraiss**, meaning *excellent* (January 9, July 3). The masculine singular genitive is **dígrais** (December 16); the feminine singular accusative is **dígraiss** (February 2).

**díi**, meaning *to her, for her,* or *concerning her* <note>original: ad eam, ei, de eâ</note> (page 4, line 9).

**dil**, meaning *dear* (singular accusative neuter, December 13). The comparative form <note>meaning "dearer"</note> is **díliu** (May 7). Related to the Gothic word *tils*.

**díllacht**, meaning *sinlessness* or *faultlessness* (singular accusative, Epilogue 71). It can also mean *a sinless person* (plural genitive, November 19).

**díle**, a Feminine noun meaning *dearness* or *affection*. O'Clery's glossary defines it as "love or affection" <note>original: .i. gradh no annsa</note>. The singular accusative is **díli** (Epilogue 66).

**díle**, *flood, deluge* (derived from the Latin *diluvium* <note>original: diluvium</note>), found as **díle** in the Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 48d 17; the genitive <note>possessive form</note> is **dílenñ** (Martyrology of Oengus <note>original: Fél. Oeng.</note> clxxxi); the dative and ablative <note>forms used after prepositions</note> is **díle** (Epilogue <note>original: Ep.</note> 452).

**díles**, *possession, property*; the singular dative is **dílius** (January 29, September 27).

**dílgud**, a Masculine noun meaning *forgiveness* (Ascoli's Lexicon <note>original: Asc.</note> 175); the dative is found on October 29. This is the verbal noun of **doluigim**, meaning *I forgive*.

**dílis**, meaning *one's own* <note>original: proprius</note>, and therefore *dear* or *beloved* <note>original: carus</note>. The comparative form <note>meaning "dearer"</note> is **dílsíu** (Prologue 185, 262; January 7).

**dillacht**, see the entry for **dílacht**.

**dílmáin**, *free, a freeman* (meaning *unimpeded* <note>original: expeditum</note> in the Milan Glosses 81b 7); found on pages 4 and 200; the dative is in the Epilogue 180.

**dím**, meaning *from me* (Prologue 223).

**dímais**, *inestimable, invaluable* (February 2).

**dímór**, *enormous, huge* (October 28); see the entry for **mór**.

1. **dind**, meaning *from the* (Epilogue 26).

2. **dind**, a Neuter noun meaning *a height*; the dative is in Prologue 155 and May 17. Compare to the Phrygian mountain name *Dindymus* <note>original: Δίνδυμος</note>.

**dindgnae**, *a hill*; the plural accusative <note>direct object form</note> is **dindgnu** (Epilogue 120).

**díne**, *assembly, group, stock* (April 17, 24; June 5; Epilogue 79); the dative is **díníu** (May 27).

**dínert**, *vast strength, exceeding might* (Epilogue 154, 320); see the entry for **nert** (strength).

**dínn**, meaning *from us* (June 1).

**dínnis**, possibly means *reproach*? Found in the accusative on February 27 and July 25.

**díorad**, meaning *gilding over* (from the Latin *deaurare* <note>original: deaurare</note>, "to gild"). In the Epilogue 199, it seems to mean *adorning* or *enhancing*; compare to **díor**, which is a gloss for *pure gold* <note>original: abriza</note>.

**díor**, meaning *due* (page 4, line 12).

**dírech**, an adjective meaning *right* or *straight*; the comparative form <note>meaning "straighter"</note> is **dírgu** (March 20) or **dirgiu**.

**dírge**, a Feminine noun meaning *a right condition* <note>original: recta conditio</note> or *righteousness*; the dative is **dírgi** (January 21, September 1). It can also mean *straightway* (March 6, June 4). It is a derivative of **dírech** (*rectus* or "straight").

**dírim**, *countless, innumerable*; the masculine dative is found on July 15. Related to the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word *dirif*.

**dírimm**, a Neuter noun meaning *a multitude*; the plural nominative is **dírman** (October 11); the accusative is in the Epilogue 143.

**dís**, an adjective meaning *slight* or *despicable* (pages 168, 240).

**dísertán**, *a little hermitage* (page 44); a diminutive of **dísert** (related to the Welsh *diserth*), which comes from the Latin *desertum* <note>original: desertum</note>, meaning "a desert" or "wilderness."

**díth**, *destruction*; the singular accusative is **díth-n** (December 25). It is used to gloss the Latin word for *loss* or *damage* <note>original: detrimentum</note>.

**díth-ár**, *destructive slaughter* (Epilogue 104); see the entry for **ár** above.

**díthreb**, a masculine or neuter noun meaning *desert* or *hermitage*; the dative is **díthrub** (Prologue 98). Related to the Welsh word *didryf*.

**dítíu**, a Feminine noun meaning *protection* (March 17).

**díubairt**, found in the Epilogue 71; possibly means *an earnest prayer*?

**díultach**, an adjective meaning *given to denial* (Epilogue 371); a derivative of **díultud**, which is the verbal noun of **do-sluindim** (I deny).

**díxu**, *higher, nobler* (January 18, 21; March 19; May 1; October 23; Epilogue 54, 248, 439). This is the comparative form of **dígas**, which means *lofty* or *elevated* <note>original: edito</note>.

**dligim**, *I have a claim to, I deserve*; found in the present tense (January 6, March 7, April 25) and past tenses.

**dlomaim**, *I announce, declare, proclaim*; found in Prologue 305 and as an imperative <note>command</note> (August 7, September 13, October 12).

**dn-**, a spelling variation for **-nd-**, perhaps found in the word **nodnali** (January 19, July 9).

<vocab>díle, díles, dílgud, dílis, dillacht, dílmáin, dím, dímais, dímór, dind, dindgnae, díne, dínert, dínn, dínnis, díorad, díor, dírech, dírge, dírim, dírimm, dís, dísertán, díth, díth-ár, díthreb, dítíu, díubairt, díultach, díxu, dligim, dlomaim, dn-, Latin, Welsh, Phrygian, Milan Glosses, Martyrology of Oengus, Epilogue, Ascoli's Lexicon, Prologue, St. Gall Glosses, Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus, Würzburg Glosses, Saltair na Rann, Glossarial Index</vocab>

<page-num>321</page-num>
<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

1. **do** (pronoun), the unstressed <note>original: atonic</note> form of *tō*. This is equivalent to the Welsh <note>original: Cymr. teu</note> word for "your" <note>original: thy</note>. Found in the Prologue 13, 267, 269, 278, and Epilogue 4.
2. **do** (preposition), an unstressed <note>original: atonic</note> form of *to*. Found in the Prologue 318, March 6, April 26, and Epilogue 14. It is also an unstressed form of *de* (Prologue 52). See also the entries for **do-badim**, **do-éccim**, **doemim**, **do-gníu**, and **do-legam**.
3. **do-**, a prefix indicating something bad, difficult, or negative <note>original: pejorative</note>. See the entries for **dochingthecht**, **dogar**, **dóire**, **donae**, and **dolmae**.

1. **dó**, meaning *to him*. Found on June 16.
2. **dó**, meaning *two*. Found on September 28 in the *R¹* and *L. F.* manuscripts.

**doaib**, meaning *to them*. Found in the Prologue 17.

**do-áirbiur** (derived from *to-ad-renk*?), meaning *I bow down, I reduce,* or *I bring*. The third-person singular subjunctive form is **do-m-r-airbera** (Epilogue 65); the passive forms are **du-n-erbarar** and **du-arbartha** (Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 99ᵈ 1).

**do-áircim**, meaning *I cause* or *I effect*. The third-person singular preterite <note>past tense</note> is **do-r-araic** (August 1, *Saltair na Rann* <note>original: Salt.</note> 7193, 7216), **do-raricc** (Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 19ᶜ 23), and **durairric** (Milan Glosses 33ᶜ 20).

**do-airicim**, meaning *I find*. The third-person singular perfect form is **do-da-farnaic** (June 12); also found in the third-person plural.

**do-airicim**, meaning *I visit*. The third-person singular present indicative is **taric** (July 19). The third-person plural preterite is **hore do-n-arnactar** (Würzburg Glosses 7ᵇ 13). The second-person singular subjunctive is **tair** (page 12); the third-person plural is **do airset** (September 20); the unstressed <note>term: enclitic</note> form is **-tairset** (December 13).

**do-airissim**, meaning *I consist* (derived from *to-air-siss-*). The third-person singular present indicative is **doairis** (page 2). In Old Irish, it is a deponent verb <note>term: a verb that is passive in form but active in meaning</note>: **do-airissedar** (Ascoli's Lexicon 227). The verbal noun is **tairissem**.

**do-ascnaim**, meaning *I come to* (derived from *to-ad-com-sná-*). The third-person singular present indicative is **do-n-ascnaí** (May 12, October 25). The third-person plural preterite is **do-da-ascansat** (*Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* <note>original: Thes.</note> II. 334, 340).

**do-bádim**, meaning *I perish* or *I extinguish*. The unstressed <note>original: enclitic</note> third-person singular present indicative is **-díbdai** (April 9). The passive preterite is **dorodbad** (Prologue 96), used instead of **dorobdad** (*dí-ro-báded*), similar to how **bibdu** <note>original: q.v.; Latin: quod vide, "which see"</note> becomes **bíbdai** (see Strachan, *Particle*, page 117).

**do-biur**, meaning *I give, put,* or *bring forward*. The third-person singular present indicative active is **dobeir** (March 31, November 30, Epilogue 207); the first-person plural is **doberam** (Prologue 144). The third-person singular t-preterite <note>a specific category of past tense in Old Irish</note> is **dobert** (February 13, April 14, October 18, Milan Glosses 23ᵇ 10, 58ᶜ 4). The first-person singular perfect is **doratus** (Epilogue 112); the third-person plural is **doratsat** (Epilogue 113). The first-person plural of the second perfect is **-tucsam** (Epilogue 31). The verbal noun is **tabart**.

**doche**, meaning *confidence*. Found on August 4.

**dochingthecht**, meaning *evil combating* or *championing*. Found in the Prologue 241; see the entry for **cing**.

**do-coemnachtar**, see the entry for **donigim**.

**do-cuaid**, meaning *he went* or *he approached* <note>original: ivit, adiit</note>. Found in Epilogue 267 (derived from *to-co-fáith*). The third-person plural relative form is **dochuatar** (Prologue 279). This served as the perfect tense of the verb **tíagu** <note>original: q.v.; Latin: quod vide, "which see"</note>.

**do-chuissin**, a relative form meaning *which exists*. Found in Epilogue 443.

**do-díget**, found in Epilogue 24 (derived from *to-de-co-feth-sent*). This serves as the perfective third-person plural subjunctive of **dotíag**, meaning *I come*.

**do-donaim**, see the entry for **dídnad**.

**doe**, meaning *a rampart*. Found on March 2 and August 27, where it is pronounced as two syllables <note>original: disyllabic</note>.

**do-éccim**, meaning *I behold* (derived from *dí-en-kes-*). See the entry for **-déccaim**. The verbal noun is **déicsiu**.

**do-ecmaingim** (derived from *to-aith-com-ong-*), meaning *I happen* or *I chance*. The third-person singular present indicative (with an infixed pronoun) is **do-n-ecmaic** (December 24). The third-person singular subjunctive is **dondecmaí** (December 29). The unstressed <note>original: enclitic</note> form is **tecma** (January 10). The third-person singular perfect is **tec-com-nocuir** (Würzburg Glosses 10ᵃ 4), or **amaíl do-nd-eccomnuccuir** (meaning "as it happened," *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 247, lines 11, 12).

**do-ecraim**, meaning *I shelter*. The third-person singular subjunctive with an infixed pronoun <note>original: cum pron. inf.</note> is **do-nn-ecrae** (December 29).

**do-emim** (derived from *dí-em*...), meaning *I protect* or *I shelter*. The third-person singular subjunctive with an infixed pronoun <note>original: cum pron. inf.</note> is **do-n-r-ema** (April 13, June 23); the third-person plural is **do-n-r-emat** (February 3). Another form is **do-r-et** (Milan Glosses 16ᶜ 8). For other forms, see Ascoli's Lexicon, page 65. The verbal noun is **dítiu** <note>original: q.v.; Latin: quod vide, "which see"</note>.

**dóenacht**, a Feminine noun meaning *manhood*. Found in Epilogue 353.

## GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**dóer, dóir**, meaning "ignoble" <note>original: *ignobilis*</note>. Found in Ascoli’s edition, 265. This is the opposite of **sóer, sóir**, which means "noble."
*   **Compound words:** **dóer-athech**, meaning "a base clown" (page 44); **dóer-galar**, meaning "hemorrhoids" (page 44).

**do-érnaim** (derived from the roots *to-ess-ro-sní*), meaning "I escape."
*   **Grammar:** The dependent past tense <note>original: enclitic preterite</note> in the third-person singular is **térnae** (Epilogue 544), which relates to **ernae** in the manuscript *Lebor na hUidre* <note>original: LU.</note> 85ª.

**do-escaim** (derived from the roots *to-ess-sec*), meaning "I cut down."
*   **Grammar:** The past tense passive third-person plural is **ro tesctha** (Prologue 238). The subjunctive passive third-person singular is **do-esister** (O’Davoren’s Glossary, entry 787). This is related to the Latin word for "I cut" <note>original: *seco*</note>.

**do-forcaim**, meaning "I surpass."
*   **Grammar:** Found as **tarcai** on June 29. The present indicative third-person plural is **dofarcat** (July 15).

**do-farcim**, meaning "I encompass" or "I surround"?
*   **Grammar:** The present indicative third-person singular is **do-don-farci** (January 26).

**do-fedim**, meaning "I lead." Found in Ascoli’s edition, 317.
*   **Grammar:** The imperative third-person singular is **tóided** (Prologue 340, January 1). The past tense <note>original: preterite</note> third-person singular is **du-da-ru[f]-id** (Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 63ᵇ 12).

**do-forgabim**, meaning "I arise."
*   **Grammar:** The dependent past tense <note>original: enclitic preterite</note> third-person singular is **-túargaib** (March 9).
*   **Verbal noun:** **turcbáil**, meaning "rising."

**do-formaigim**, meaning "I increase," "I enlarge," or "I add."
*   **Grammar:** The present indicative third-person singular is **doformaig** (Epilogue 195, 206) and **do-n-formaig** (October 18). The passive participle is **tórmachte**. This is compared to the Old Welsh word for "he added" <note>original: Cymr. *diguor-mechis*</note>.

**do-fortaim**, meaning "I spill."
*   **Grammar:** Found as **dortaíd** on page 401. The past tense passive third-person singular (derived from *to-ro-fortad*) is **dorortad** (May 27).

**do-fuismiu** (derived from *to-ud-semiu*), meaning "I generate" or "I create."
*   **Grammar:** The past tense <note>original: t-preterite</note> is **do-ró-sat** (Prologue 91; Ascoli 244) and **doforsat** (St. Gall Glosses <note>original: Sg.</note> 31ᶜ 5).
*   **Verbal noun:** **tuistiu**, meaning "creation" or "generation." The letter *f* in the spelling is added by analogy. See Strachan’s *Selections*, page 69.

**do-gabim**, meaning "I take out" or "I select."
*   **Grammar:** The past tense <note>original: preterite</note> third-person singular is **dorogbus** (Prologue 18). The passive forms are **di-ro-gbad** (St. Gall Glosses 9ᵇ 16) and **dorogbad** (Milan Glosses 17ᵃ 13).

**dogar**, meaning "mournful" (February 20).
*   **Derivative:** **dograe**, meaning "lamentation"; the dative form is **dograi** (page 56).

**do-gaur**, meaning "I call upon" <note>original: *advoco*</note> or "I name" <note>original: *appello*</note>.
*   **Grammar:** The past tense <note>original: t-preterite</note> is **do-ro-gart** (Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 21ᵈ 2). The third-person singular subjunctive is **do-ro-gra** (Prologue 112) and **do-n-rogra** (March 28, December 14). The perfect third-person singular is **do-ro-gart**, and the perfect passive third-person singular is **do-ro-grad** (March 10, September 5; Würzburg Glosses 10ᵃ 12).

**do-gníu**, meaning "I make" or "I do."
*   **Grammar:** The past tense <note>original: preterite</note> forms include: first-person singular **dorignius** (Epilogue 111), second-person singular **dorignis** (Epilogue 506), and third-person singular **dorigni** (Epilogue 89, 100). The past tense passive third-person plural is **dorónta** (Prologue 139). The second-person singular subjunctive is **dogné** (November 13). Forms with the particle *ro* include: first-person singular **dorón-sa** (Prologue 268, 269) and second-person plural **d-a-rónaid** (Prologue 186). The third-person singular future is **dogéna** (from *de-gígnat*), and the future passive third-person plural is **dogénatar** (Epilogue 176).
*   **Verbal noun:** **dénum**, meaning "doing" or "making."

**do-goim**, meaning "I choose." Found in the *Tripartite Life of Patrick* <note>original: Trip.</note> 180.
*   **Grammar:** The second reduplicated future third-person singular is **dogegainnd** (page 6, line 10). The perfect third-person singular is **doróigu** (Würzburg Glosses 4ᵇ 31).
*   **Verbal noun:** **togu**, meaning "choice." See that entry.

**dogrés**, an adverb meaning "always" (February 3).

**do-icim, ticim**, meaning "I come to."
*   **Grammar:** The present indicative third-person singular is **tic** (July 9) and **to-t-ic** (May 25). The future third-person singular is **do-t-icfa** (July 16). The subjunctive third-person singular is **do-mm-í** (Epilogue 561) and plural is **-tisat** (Epilogue 23) and **do-mm-isat** (Epilogue 36). The perfect third-person singular forms include **do-n-ánic** (April 14), **do-mm-ánic** (Epilogue 93), and **tánic** (January 11). The third-person plural is **táncatar** (Epilogue 98). The passive is **tícht**.
*   **Verbal noun:** **tíchtu**, meaning "coming." See that entry.

**do-ind-nacim**, meaning "I give."
*   **Grammar:** The past tense passive third-person singular is **do-r-indnacht** (November 12; compare Würzburg Glosses 20ᵈ 15). The active and passive perfect forms, **doécomnacht**, are derived from the roots *to-en-com-n*.

**do-imthasaim**, meaning "I constrain" <note>original: *coarto*</note>.
*   **Grammar:** The form **do-r-imthas**, meaning "he constrained," is found on page 92 and in the *Saltair na Rann* <note>original: Salt.</note> 5973. Also found as **doimmthastar** (St. Gall Glosses 3ᵃ 3). This word is related to the Latin *taxo*, meaning "I touch" or "I rate," or perhaps the Greek word *tásso*, meaning "I arrange" <note>original: *τάσσω*</note>.

**do-ind-scannaim**, meaning "I begin."
*   **Grammar:** The second-person singular imperative is **tindscan** (November 14). The past tense <note>original: preterite</note> third-person singular is **tinscann** (May 1).

**dóire**, a feminine noun meaning "bondage."
*   **Grammar:** The dative singular is **dóiri** (Epilogue 532). This is a derivative of **dóir** or **doer**, meaning "ignoble."

<meta>This page continues the glossarial index of Old Irish terms, focusing on words beginning with "do-," particularly verbs involving destruction, estimation, and motion, as well as nouns for "church," "world," and "darkness."</meta>

<page-num>323</page-num>
<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

**do-legaim** (also *di-leg..*), meaning **"I destroy"** or **"I abolish."** 
*   **Grammar:** Third-person plural past tense <note>original: preterite</note> is **dolegsat** (November 6). Third-person singular perfect passive is **du roilged** (Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 2ᶜ 16). 
*   **Verbal noun:** **dílgend** (Ascoli’s edition, 159).

**dolmae** (Feminine noun), meaning **"slowness"** or **"delay."** 
*   **Grammar:** Accusative case is **dolmai** (Epilogue 151).

**do-luid**, see entry for **-tulaid**.

**1. domm, dom**, meaning **"to my."** (Prologue 25, January 21, 24, November 12, Epilogue 271).

**2. -dom-** (infixed pronoun), meaning **"me."** 
*   **Examples:** **con-dom-roib** (Prologue 11), **co-tom-rócbhat** (Epilogue 45), **co-tam-r-óither** (Epilogue 69), **con-dom-fil** (page 94, line 36).

**domain**, meaning **"bottom"** (page 244). 
*   **Comparison:** Perhaps related to the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word ***an-nwfn*** (the abyss or underworld)?

**do-menaim**, meaning **"I opine"** (page 6, line 10). This is a Middle Irish form for **domoiniur**; see **domuiniim**.

**do-midiur**, meaning **"I estimate"** or **"I measure."** 
*   **Grammar:** Third-person singular present indicative is **du-mmidethar** (Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 82ᵃ 3). First-person plural past tense <note>original: preterite</note> is **do-s-ruimdemar** (Epilogue 6). Third-person plural is **durúimdetar** (Milan Glosses 87ª 4). Third-person plural present indicative passive is **doimditir** (page 21). 
*   **Comparison:** Related to the Greek ***μέδομαι*** <note>original: medomai; meaning "to provide for" or "think on"</note> and the Latin ***metior*** <note>meaning "I measure"</note>.

**1. domnach** (Masculine noun), meaning **"Sunday."** 
*   **Grammar:** Genitive singular is **domnaig** (February 15, Saltair na Rann <note>original: Salt.</note> 8019) or **domnich** (Würzburg Glosses 14ª). Dative case is **domnuch** (Saltair na Rann 8023).

**2. domnach** (Masculine noun), meaning **"a church."** 
*   **Grammar:** Genitive singular is **domnaig** (October 27).

**domhnus**, meaning **"domain"**? (page 206, line 31).

**do-muinim**, meaning **"I opine"** or **"I think."** 
*   **Grammar:** Third-person plural is **dommuinet** (page 150). In Old Irish, this is **domoiniur** (Würzburg Glosses 14ª 10) or **domoinur sa** <note>glosses the Latin word *puto*, meaning "I think"</note> (St. Gall Glosses <note>original: Sg.</note> 209ᵇ 10). 
*   **Comparison:** Related to the Sanskrit word ***mányate*** <note>meaning "he thinks"</note>. 
*   **Verbal noun:** **toimtiu**.

**domun** (Masculine noun), meaning **"world"** or **"domain."** 
*   **Grammar:** Genitive singular is **domuin** (Prologue 83, 93, 145, 149, 220, June 16, Epilogue 329, November 11). Dative is **domun** (March 16, Epilogue 448). Accusative is **domun** (Epilogue 368).

**don**, meaning **"misfortune."** (page 198). Defined by O’Brien as **"mischief, evil."**

**-don-** (infixed pronoun), first-person plural, meaning **"us."** Found in **ar-don-sela** (June 23).

**donae**, meaning **"wretched"** (September 16). This is the opposite of **sonae** <note>meaning "prosperous" or "happy"</note>.

**dond, don**, meaning **"to the."** (Prologue 31, January 23, February 16, March 21, May 29, June 19). Before an ***s***, it becomes **dont** (Epilogue 104).

**do-nigim** (also *to-n.*), meaning **"I wash."** 
*   **Grammar:** Third-person plural perfect is **do-cóem-nachtar** (January 4), where ***cóem-*** comes from ***cómen-*** and ***com*** acts as a perfective prefix. For related Old Irish forms, see Ascoli’s edition, 359, 360. 
*   **Verbal noun:** **tonach**.

**do-ráluis**, meaning **"I have placed"** (Prologue 15). 
*   **Grammar:** Third-person singular is **dorale**, which is the perfective form of **docuiredar**. The singular past passive is **doralad** (Würzburg Glosses 13ᵈ 8). Regarding the 'a' in *doralus*, see Thurneysen’s *Keltoromanisches* <note>original: *Celtic-Romance Studies*</note>, page 34.

**do-ratus** (derived from *to-ro-dadus*), meaning **"I have given"** (Epilogue 112, Würzburg Glosses 8ᶜ 6). 
*   **Grammar:** Third-person plural is **doratsat** (Epilogue 113, Milan Glosses 115ᵇ 8). See Ascoli’s edition 191, 192; see also **dobiur**.

**1. dorchae** (Feminine noun), meaning **"darkness."** (Ascoli 203). Genitive singular found on December 25.

**2. dorchae** (Adjective), meaning **"dark."** (Ascoli 203). Masculine dative singular is **dorchu** (March 9).

**do-rega**, meaning **"he will come"** <note>original Latin: *veniet*</note> (Prologue 258). It serves as the third-person singular future of **do-tíag**, meaning **"I come."** 
*   **Grammar:** Third-person plural forms are **doregat** (Ascoli 199) and **doragat** (Epilogue 115). It is a present form used with a future meaning, similar to the Greek word ***εἶμι*** <note>original: eimi; meaning "I go" or "I will go"</note>. 
*   **Root:** The root is ***regh***, related to the Greek ***ἔρχομαι*** <note>original: erchomai; meaning "I come"</note> (Sarauw, page 97).

**do-rethim**, meaning **"I run to."** 
*   **Grammar:** Third-person singular present indicative is **doreith** (April 16). See **rethim**.

**do-rímu**, meaning **"I reckon"** (Epilogue 317, Ascoli 212). 
*   **Grammar:** Second-person singular (with an infixed relative) is **do-r-rími** (April 30). First-person singular secondary present is **do-rui-rminn** (Epilogue 128). Second-person singular subjunctive is **doríme** (September 5) and **do-ruirim** (Milan Glosses 50ª 6). First-person plural subjunctive is **do-ruirmisem** (Epilogue 228) and **do-nd-ruirmissem** (Würzburg Glosses 24ª 16). The b-future first-person singular is **dorímub** (Epilogue 232) and plural is **dorímfem** (Epilogue 232). Past passive: **nád ro thuirmed** (Epilogue 122). 
*   **Comparison:** Welsh ***dyrifo***. Old English <note>original: Ags.</note> ***rím*** meaning **"number."**

**do-rochrair** (March 26, November 17, St. Gall Glosses 29ᵈ 8). 
*   **Grammar:** Dependent form is **-torchair** (Epilogue 361). Third-person plural is **dorochratar** (Milan Glosses 36ᵈ 13). It serves as a perfect tense for **dotuit** <note>meaning "he falls"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical glossarial index of Old Irish terms, specifically focusing on words beginning with "do-" and "du-," including verbs of profit and understanding, and nouns for elements like "door," "dragon," and "dew."</meta>

<page-num>324</page-num>
<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

**do-ror-banim**, meaning **"I profit."** 
*   **Grammar:** Third-person singular subjunctive is **do-m-rorbae** (Prologue 25), **da rorbai** (St. Gall Glosses <note>original: Sg.</note> 203ª 18), and **do-rorbai** (Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 123ᵈ 5). See the entry for **ror** below. 
*   **Verbal noun:** **torbe**, meaning "profit" or "use."

**do-ruacht**, meaning **"he came"** (page 12). Derived from the form ***to-ro-socht***.

**dorus** (Neuter noun), meaning **"door"** (January 30). 
*   **Comparison:** Old Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> ***drus***, now written as ***drws***.

**do-sluindim**, see the entry for **díultach** (denial/negative).

**doss** (Masculine noun), meaning **"bush"** or **"thicket"** (March 16, April 6, June 17, Epilogue 250). 
*   **Comparison:** Latin ***dumus*** <note>meaning "thorn-bush" or "thicket"</note>.

**dot**, meaning **"to your"** <note>singular</note> (Prologue 12, July 24).

**dót**, meaning **"hardship"**? (page 238).

**do-uccim**, meaning **"I understand."** 
*   **Grammar:** Second-person singular subjunctive is **-tuicce** (Prologue 313). The past tense <note>original: pret.</note> is **ní tuccussu** <note>meaning "I did not understand"</note> (Milan Glosses 91ᶜ 1). See Sarauw's research, pages 119-122.

**draic** (Masculine noun), meaning **"dragon"** (page 190). 
*   **Grammar:** Accusative case is **draic-n** (September 29). 
*   **Comparison:** Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> ***draig***.

**drebraining** (derived from ***dru-eb-raing***), meaning **"he went"** or **"he approached"** <note>original Latin: *ivit, adiit*</note> (April 2, 17). The form **ro drebraing** appears on August 26. See the entry for **eb** below, and for the prefix **dru**, see Thurneysen in *Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung* (KZ) volume 32, page 563.

**drem**, see the entry for **mórdrem** (a great company).

**dric**, meaning **"wrathful"** (Prologue 221). 
*   **Grammar:** Masculine genitive singular is **dric** (Prologue 134).

**drobél**, meaning **"hardship"** or **"difficulty."** 
*   **Grammar:** Dative singular is **drobéil** (August 26).

**droch**, meaning **"bad"** (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> ***drwg***). 
*   **Compounds:** **droch-enech**, meaning **"inhospitality"** (page 198); **droch-impide**, meaning **"an evil petition"** (page 94, lines 31, 33); and **droch-rann** (Feminine noun), meaning **"an evil lot"** or **"bad portion"** (January 10).

**dron**, see the entry for **fírdron** (truly solid).

**drong** (Masculine noun), meaning **"a troop"** or **"a crowd"** (Latin ***drungus*** <note>meaning a military unit or group</note>). This word appears frequently (Prologue 199, August 27, November 7, and many times in the Epilogue). 
*   **Grammar:** Nominative plural is **druing** (Epilogue 285). Genitive is **drong** (Epilogue 305). Dative is **drongaib** (Epilogue 290). Accusative is **drungu** (Epilogue 232). It was also sometimes declined as a feminine noun: vocative singular **á drong** (Epilogue 291). A citation from the *Book of Leinster* <note>original: LL 221ª</note> describes how "the common people performed very great troops" <note>original: *daringiset in daescoršluag droṅga dermára*</note>. The Old Breton word ***drogn*** (interpreted as "whale" <note>original: *cetus*</note>) should likely be ***droṅg*** (meaning "assembly" or "group" <note>original: *coetus*</note>).

**druchta**, meaning **"dew"** (Epilogue 224, page 95). 
*   **Grammar:** Genitive singular is **banna druchta**, meaning **"a drop of dew"** (*Lebor na hUidre* <note>original: LU 86ᵈ</note>).

**druimm** (Neuter noun), meaning **"ridge"** (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> ***trum***). 
*   **Grammar:** The form **druim** rhymes with ***truim*** (page 224). Genitive singular is **dromma** (May 21, August 19, September 3, 18, October 10) or **drommo** (Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus <note>original: Thes.</note> II. 238, 239). Middle Irish accusative plural is **dromand**, meaning **"backs"** <note>original Latin: *terga*</note> (*Lorica of Gildas* 171).

**1. du-** or **do**, a **negative or worsening prefix** <note>original: pejorative prefix</note>. 
*   **Comparison:** Similar to the Greek ***dys-*** <note>original: δυσ-</note> or German ***zer-***. See entries for **duba** and **duthain**.

**2. du**, a preposition used instead of **do**, meaning **"to"** or **"for."**

**duadus**, meaning **"I have eaten"** (page 88). Third-person plural is **dofuatar** or **danuathair** (likely should be read as ***d-an-uatar***), meaning **"they ate it"** (page 128).

**dúan** (Feminine noun), meaning **"song."** 
*   **Grammar:** Dative case is **dúain** (March 7). Nominative plural is **gaibtir dúana**, meaning **"songs are sung"** (Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II. 295).

**dúas** (December 28), used for **túas**, meaning **"above."**

**1. dub** (Adjective), meaning **"dark"** or **"black"** (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> ***du***). 
*   **Grammar:** Masculine dative singular is **dub** (March 9). 
*   **Comparison:** Related to the Greek ***typhlos*** <note>original: τυφλός; meaning "blind"</note>. 
*   **Compound:** **dubšluag**, meaning **"a black host"**; dative form (Prologue 254).

**2. dub** (Neuter noun), meaning **"ink"** (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> ***du***). 
*   **Grammar:** Genitive is **duib**. Accusative is **dubh scríbind**, meaning **"writing ink"** (page 246). 
*   **Comparison:** Greek ***to melan*** <note>original: τῷ μέλαν; meaning "the black substance"</note>.

**dubae**, meaning **"grief."** 
*   **Grammar:** Genitive singular is **dubai** (Epilogue 377). It is the opposite of **subae**, meaning **"joy."**

**dubach**, meaning **"mournful"** (April 2). 
*   **Grammar:** Masculine dative singular is **dubach** (Prologue 98). It is the opposite of **subach**, meaning **"cheerful."**

**dúbart** (also written as **dúbairt**), meaning **"an urgent prayer"** (Epilogue 153, 418). 
*   **Grammar:** Accusative case is **dúbairt** (Epilogue 71). 
*   **Glossary definitions:** O’Davoren’s Glossary <note>no. 654</note> defines it as a **"prayer"** <note>original: diprecoit</note> or a **"great entreaty"** <note>original: adbulguidhe</note>. O’Clery’s Glossary defines it as an **"earnest prayer"** or a **"devout petition"** <note>original: dibear-goid no guidhe dhuthrachdach</note>.

**dúib**, meaning **"to you"** <note>plural</note> (Epilogue 391).

**dúil** (Feminine noun), meaning **"an element"** or **"a creature."** 
*   **Grammar:** Genitive singular is **dúlo** (St. Gall Glosses 76ᵇ 8). Accusative singular is **dúil** (Prologue 91). Genitive plural is **dúile** (Prologue 337). In Middle Irish, the genitive plural is **dúl** (page 2), and the accusative plural is **dúile** instead of the older ***dúili*** (page 2ᶜ 1).

II. *a fort, an encampment*, dative *dúnud*, page 40, O'Davoren's Glossary <note>original: O'Dav.</note> number 657. For the gender see *Lebor na hUidre* 63ᵇ 25, 65ᵃ 28.

**ecc**, *sin?* accusative singular page 4 (rhyming with *becc*), may be related to Latin *pecco* <note>meaning "I sin"</note> or *peccatum* <note>meaning "a sin"</note>.

**eter, etir**, preposition *with the accusative case* <note>original Latin: cum acc.</note> = Latin *inter* <note>between</note>, November 23, Ascoli 75, see *itir*.
**ethrach** (*aethrach?*) page 14, line 32, *ethereal?* a derivative of *ether* = Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *ether* from Latin *aether*.
**ethre**, *tail*, nominative and accusative singular *ethre -n* August 31, October 31.
**étidach**, *robe-maker*, page 42, a derivative of *étiud*.
**etlae**, (Feminine) *penitence*, March 24, genitive *etlae* January 8, Epilogue 193, *sét sír-etla* <note>the path of lasting penitence</note> *Saltair na Rann* 2086, *cen sí n-etla* <note>without this penitence</note> *Saltair na Rann* 7199, plural dative *iarna hetlaib athirgi* <note>after her penitence of repentance</note> *Saltair na Rann* 6876.
**étrocht, étracht**, *bright, lustrous*, February 10, Ascoli 76. From this comes *étrachte, brightness*.
**etsecht**, by metathesis from *estecht*, which see <note>original Latin: q.v., quod vide</note>.
**eu**, see *eo*.
**fáilid, blithe**, *joyous*, Ascoli 219, August 4, December 19, plural nominative *fáilti*, Prologue 49, 64, December 18. From this come *failte* "joy" <note>original Latin: laetitia</note> and *failtigur* "I rejoice" <note>original Latin: laetor</note>.
**fainne**, (Feminine) *weakness*, genitive singular *fainne* May 17, a derivative of *fann*.
**fairge, foirge**, (Feminine) *sea*, Ascoli 338, singular genitive *fairge*, Epilogue 536, accusative *fairgi* August 14.
**fairinn**, (Feminine) *a company*, indeed *foirinn* (glossing <note>explaining</note> "a faction" <note>original Latin: factio</note>) Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 33ª 8, singular dative *fairinn*, Epilogue 51, accusative *fairinn* August 18, Old Welsh <note>original: O. Cymr.</note> *guerin* (glossing "a faction" <note>original Latin: factio</note>) now *gwerin*.
**fairsiung**, *fairsing, ample*, Ascoli 300, October 28.
**fáith**, (Masculine) *prophet* (Latin: *vātes*) Ascoli 303, genitive *fátho, fátha*, plural nominative *fáithi*, Epilogue 13, genitive *fáithe-n* November 29, Epilogue 241.
**fall**, *neglect, failure* toward God <note>original Old Irish: fall fri Dia</note>, *Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie* <note>original: ZCP.</note> volume 3, page 25, line 21, genitive singular *faille*, April 25.
**fálte**, (Feminine) *joy, welcome*, singular accusative *fálti* June 11, a derivative of *fáilid*, which see.
**fann**, *feeble* (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *gwan*), Ascoli 302, see *immfann, fainne*.
**farith** (*fo-a-r.*), see *foirithim*.
**far-n**, *your*, Epilogue 394, Ascoli 300, from *\*svarom*, Gothic *izvar*.
**fáss**, *waste, desolate*, Ascoli 301, plural nominative *fássa* Prologue 68, 207. From this comes *fássaigur* ‘I devastate’ <note>original Latin: vasto</note>.
**fáth airicc**, *cause of invention*, page 2.
**feb** (*feib?*), (Feminine) *long life* (defined as "a long life" <note>original Old Irish: feibh i. saeghal fada</note> by the lexicographer O’Clery), dative *feib* January 3. From this comes *febhas* Ascoli 321–2, and *febdae, aged?* February 24. But *feib* and *febdae* may be cognate with *feba* ‘excellence,’ *Fiacc’s Hymn* page 24.
