**feth**, *aspect*, see <note>original: degfeth</note>, and compare Cornish *feth* ‘face.’

**fethem**, *contemplating*, the act of observing or attending, accusative singular *fethim* Epilogue 266, a verbal noun of *fethim*, which see.

**fethim**, *I attend*, Ascoli 320, preterite singular 2nd person, -*fethis*, June 24, August 7.

**fiachán**, (Masculine) *a little raven*, page 48, a diminutive of *fiach* (glossed as Latin <note>original: corvus</note> *raven*), St. Gall Glosses 29^b 4.

**fíad**, preposition with the dative case, *before*, Ascoli 323, Prologue 33; 36, 81, 153; 315, January 9, Laud manuscript 27, June 19, Epilogue 103. Welsh <note>original: Cymr. gŵydd</note> ‘presence.’

**fíada, féda**, (Masculine) *lord*, a name for Christ, Prologue 86, May 5, see Thurneysen, *Journal of Celtic Philology* <note>original: ZCP. i. 349 note</note>; *moéda* (= *mo-féda*, meaning "my Lord"), January 27, genitive singular *fíadat*, March 11, April 6, May 30, August 18, Epilogue 209 = *fédot*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* volume II, page 244, line 32, dative *fíadait*, January 14. The phrase *beth f[ía]do* cited in Ascoli 322 is a misreading of *beth feil do(i)b(em)* <note>original: 'that we should be'</note>, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* volume II, page 32, line 31.

**fíaduib**, *before them*, Epilogue 95.

**fíal** (Welsh <note>original: Cymr. gwyl</note>), *modest*, December 4, genitive singular masculine *féil*, December 15.

**fíam**, *virulence, bitterness*, Prologue 50, where it is disyllabic, from the reconstructed form <note>original: \*visamo-</note> cognate with Irish *fí*, Latin <note>original: vīrus</note> *poison/venom*, Sanskrit <note>original: viṣá-m</note>, and Greek <note>original: (F)ιός</note> *arrow/poison*.

**fiche**, *twenty, a score* (Welsh <note>original: Cymr. ugain</note>, Latin <note>original: viginti</note>), March 18, September 1, genitive *fichet*, dative *fichit*, January 16, September 13, plural nominative *fichit*, accusative *fichtea*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* volume II, 342, 338, Ascoli 328.

**fídrád cubaid**, page 14, *harmonious juncture*, the poetic rule (not mandatory) that the first accented word in a stanza should alliterate with the final word of the preceding stanza. This seems to be the *fídrád freccomail* <note>original: 'alliteration of connection'</note> described in Thurneysen’s *Middle Irish Versification* <note>original: Mittel-ir. Verslehren</note>, pages 29, 122.

**figill**, **figill** (from Latin <note>original: vigilia</note> *vigil*), is explained by the lexicographer O’Clery as ‘a prayer which one makes on one’s knees,’ accusative singular *figill*, December 8, plural genitive *figle*, Epilogue 199, accusative *figli*, May 26.

**figlech**, *prayerful*, genitive singular masculine *figlig*, February 17.

**fil, file**, see *feil*.

**find**, *white, fair, blessed* (Welsh <note>original: Cymr. gwyn</note>), Ascoli 327, January 9, 14, February 3, 24, March 2, November 29, December 12, 16, singular genitive masculine *find*, April 6, May 22, feminine *finde*, August 8, October 13, dative masculine *find*, November 12, accusative masculine *find*, June 18, 30, feminine *find*, October 8. *Winter*, Gothic <note>original: vintrus</note> ‘the white season,’ may be cognate. In the compounds **findbad** (Welsh <note>original: gwynfyd</note> *bliss*) and **findgein** (*Würzburg Glosses* 2^c 2, April 6, and July 22), *find* means *blessed*.

**finde**, (Feminine) *whiteness, fairness*, singular dative *findi*, August 27, Laud manuscript *finde*, October 7, Rawlinson manuscript <note>original: H.</note>.

**find-gein**, (Neuter) *blessed nativity*, July 22. See *gein*.

**find-slúag**, (Masculine) *a fair host*, May 23.

**fine**, (Feminine) *tribe, family*, page 14, genitive <unclear>gas</unclear> *fine*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* volume II, page 295, line 13. Anglo-Saxon <note>original: Ags. wine</note> *friend*.

**fíne**, (Feminine) *vine*, Ascoli 326, singular genitive *fíne*, October 10, dative *fíni*, April 6.

**findae**, *hair*, *finna malach*, page 206, *hair of eyebrow*, genitive *ind finnai*.

**fír**, *true* (Welsh <note>original: Cymr. gwir</note>, Latin <note>original: vērus</note>, Ascoli 323), occurs in the compounds:—

**fír-balc**, *truly strong*, genitive singular masculine *fírbaile*, April 14, May 16, Rawlinson manuscript, Leabhar Breac <note>original: R. LB.</note>.

**fír-bail**, *true goodness?* or adjective *truly good*.

**fírbráthair**, *a true brother*, page 186.

**fírchert**, *truly accurate*, Epilogue 156.

**fírchuarta**, *true tributes*, page 112.

**fír-dron**, *truly strong*, dative singular feminine *fírdruin*, December 3.

**gainne** (Feminine): hardship? dative form *gainni* October 7; a derivative of *gann*, which usually means "scanty." However, this cannot be the meaning in "scanty onslaught" <note>original: ruathar gand</note> in the *Book of Leinster* <note>original: LL.</note> 127ᵃ 6; "to your companion your combat was scanty" <note>original: dot gleo frit chomtach ba gand</note> *Book of Leinster* 150ᵃ 41; "they gave a scanty shattering" <note>original: gand combach ro fersat</note> *Book of Leinster* 403ᵃ 46; or "scanty deed" <note>original: gním gann</note> *Saltair na Rann* 3219.

**gair**: short, dative Prologue 59; see **gor**.

**gáir** (Neuter): a shout, October 20, December 6. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *gawr*. Greek <note>original: γῆρυς</note> "voice" or "sound."

**gaire** (Feminine): piety <note>original: pietas</note>, Epilogue 382, 402; dative *gairi* Prologue 225; Old Irish *goire*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 241, line 14.

**gairm** (Neuter): a call, dative *garmaim* February 11, accusative *gairm* August 14. See **togairm**.

**gal** (Feminine): valor, genitive *gaile* Prologue 54, January 11, December 17; dative *gail*, Epilogue 484, "(great) valor" <note>original: (mór) gail</note> June 15.

**galar** (Neuter): disease, grief (Welsh *galar*), November 16; singular genitive *galair* September 11, plural nominative *galar* January 15.

**gébend** <note>original: géhénn</note>: a chain, Epilogue 282, where it seems to be the nominative to the verb *forcenna* ("ends") and rhymes with *Érenn* ("Ireland"). It also appears in *The Vision of Mac Con Glinne* <note>original: AisL.</note> 69 (*Leabhar Breac* 217ᵃ): "it was a fair fetter, a lock, or a shackle, or a chain" <note>original: ba cáin gébend glas no gemel no géibend</note>; *Ancient Laws of Ireland* I. 110, 11; singular dative "under a ... chain" <note>original: fo gébind gibsig</note> *Book of Leinster* 5ᵇ 30; plural dative "in locks and chains" <note>original: hi nglassaib 7 gébendaib</note>, *Irische Texte* II² 92. Welsh *gefyn*.

**géim** (Neuter): a shout, Prologue 139; genitive singular *géime*.

**gein** (Neuter): birth, nativity, offspring; January 27, February 10, 22, March 2, May 1, 6, 30, August 16, October 3; singular genitive *gene* February 26; dative *genim*, Milan Glosses 85ᵇ 11; accusative *gein-n* Prologue 178, September 18, November 14, 21.

**gel**: bright, February 10, July 8, September 21; singular genitive masculine *gil* September 6; feminine *gile* Prologue 4, Epilogue 118; dative feminine *gil* November 1; plural nominative neuter *gela* May 19.

**gel-bán**: bright-white, Epilogue 287; accusative singular feminine *gelbáin* May 15.

**geldae**: fair, June 22, August 31; dative singular masculine *geldu* August 20; accusative singular masculine *geldae* June 25, December 22; dual nominative masculine September 28.

**gelgrian** (Feminine): a bright sun, vocative singular Prologue 5.

**gell** (Neuter): a pledge, a hostage, July 6.

**génair**: "was born," *ro génair*; see **gainiur**.

**genech** or **gened**: Epilogue 538, meaning obscure, perhaps "gaping," derived from *giun* ("mouth"), see below.

**genti**: heathens, the Gentiles (from Latin *gentes*, "nations"), Prologue 175; plural *gente* Prologue 61, 205. *Dub-gint* ("Black Gentiles") was a term used for the Danes, *Annals of Cambria* 866 = Irish *Dubgenti*. The Welsh *gwys* is derived from the Latin nominative singular *gens*.

**gentlecht** (Feminine): heathendom, Prologue 213.

**gér**: sharp (from the root *gegro-*, related to Latin *ferus*, "wild"), accusative singular masculine Epilogue 538. Hence:

**gérat** (Feminine): champion, Prologue 20, February 5, April 7, 13, June 16; accusative *géraít* June 15; plural genitive *gérat* November 19, Epilogue 72; accusative *gréta* (*gerta* in the L manuscript) Prologue 232; dual nominative "two champions" <note>original: dí géraít</note> May 27, September 27.

**gessed**, **gessi**, **gestae**: see **gudiu**.

**gíall** (Masculine): hostage; plural nominative *géill* January 9. Welsh *gwystl*.

**gile** (Feminine): brightness, dative singular *gili* February 5, Epilogue 222; a derivative of **gel**, see above.

**gin**, **giun** (Masculine): mouth, April 22; singular genitive *gena* April 13, September 16, October 3; dative *gin*, Epilogue 126. Welsh *genau*.

**ginol**: maw, dative singular Epilogue 472.

**glaine** (Feminine): purity, singular genitive *glaine* January 6, April 1, July 6; dative *glaini* Prologue 227, January 9, February 5, April 21, September 10, Epilogue 67, 174, 250.

**gléss** (**glésse**?) (Feminine) *brightness*, singular genitive *glésse*, Epilogue 454.

**glu**, see **rétglu** <note>Meaning "star."</note>.

**glún** (Neuter) *knee* (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *glin*), accusative page 12, from the root *gnûl*, related to Anglo-Saxon <note>original: Ags.</note> *cneo* and *cneowlian* (English *kneel*; see V. Henry, *Etymological Lexicon of Modern Breton* <note>original: Lexique etym. du Breton moderne</note>, page 134).

**gnás** (Feminine) *presence*, dative *gnáis-si* Epilogue 375; "in eternal presence" <note>original: i mbith-gnáis</note> Epilogue 316.

**gnáth**, *customary or usual* <note>original: usitatus, solitus</note>, Epilogue 171 (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *gnawd*). Hence **gnáthaigur**, *I become accustomed* <note>original: assuesco</note>.

**gníd**, singular imperative (third person) of the verb *gním*, page 4, line 12.

**gním** (Masculine) *a deed, a work* (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *gnif*), October 23; singular genitive *gníma*, December 17; accusative *gním-n* Prologue 54; plural dative *gnímaib*, Epilogue 203. This is the verbal noun of the verb **gníd** (does).

**gnúis** (Feminine) *face, countenance*, used in the phrase "before the face" <note>original: ar-gnúis</note>, January 9, Epilogue 398; plural accusative *gnúissi* Epilogue 339.

**gó**, **gau**, *false* (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *gau*), *falsehood*, Epilogue 27; genitive *gúe*; plural accusative *guá* Epilogue 167; *goa* in the Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 31ᵇ 20.

**gobae** (Masculine) (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *gôf*), *smith*; singular and plural genitive *gobann*, November 25.

**gobgér**, *sharp-beaked*, page 72, line 14; *gob* comes from *gobnó-*, related to Old Slavonic <note>original: O. Slav.</note> *zobati* (to eat <note>original: edere</note>) and Sanskrit <note>original: Skr.</note> *jabhate*. For **gér** see above.

**golaim**, *I wail, I weep*; present indicative third person plural (with the prefix *bith-*, "continually") *golait* Prologue 62.

**gonaim**, *I wound*; past tense third person singular *geguin*, October 23; third person plural *gegnatar* May 19; future first person singular *nit-gén-sa* from the *Book of the Dun Cow* <note>original: LU.</note> 68ᵇ 34 (*gén* from *gignâm*). Greek <note>original: θείνω</note> "to strike."

**gor**, *short*, neuter singular accusative Prologue 59; see **gair**.

**gorim**, *I warm*; present indicative third person singular relative form *guires* or *goires*. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *gwresu*.

**gorm**, *red*, glossed as *dearg* by O'Clery, in the compound *rúad-gorm*, Epilogue 260. Latin *formus* <note>Meaning warm or glowing.</note>.

**gorm**, *famous, conspicuous*, in the compound **gorm-ríg** (famous kings), Prologue 233.

**gortae** (Feminine) *famine*, singular genitive December 2; dative *gortai*, January 26.

**gortaigim**, *I embitter*? passive past indicative third person singular *gortaigther*, page 70, line 9.

1. **grád** (Neuter) *rank* (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *gradd*), genitive *gráid*; singular accusative Epilogue 207; plural accusative Epilogue 235.

2. **grád** (Neuter) *love*. Compound: **grád-gréit** (Masculine) *loveable champion*, March 18.

**grafand**, *a race or course* <note>original: cursus</note>, Epilogue 73. plural genitive *graffand*, Laws 273^b 12, from *graig-svend*, according to Henderson.
**greim**, *a bit, a morsel*, accusative November 15, from the root *gres-mi*, cognate with the Greek word for "to gnaw" or "to eat" <note>original: γράω</note>.
**gréit**, *a champion*, January 5; see also *congreit* and *grádgreit*.
**gréss**, *continuance*, February 11, Epilogue 266.
**gréssche** (possibly *gréssae*?), *constancy*, accusative *gréschi* (possibly *gréschai*?), Prologue 16; a derivative, compare *gréssach*, "continuous," from the root *grengs-*, similar to the Old Norse *kringr* meaning "round" (according to Strachan).
**grían** (Feminine) *sun*, Prologue 302, January 15, February 10, March 9, April 24, May 28, June 17, 25, 26, August 30, 31, September 3, 21, October 1, 3, November 4; singular genitive *gréne*, Prologue 4, 321, March 17, Epilogue 118. Vocative (*O bright*) *sun* <note>original: á gel grían</note>, Prologue 5; dual nominative *two suns* <note>original: dí gréin</note>, December 9.
**grét** (Feminine) *a champion*, plural accusative *gréta*, Prologue 232. See also **gréit**.
**gríanach**, *sunny*, dative singular feminine *gríanaig*, November 1.
**gríandál**, page 204, line 27; the meaning of this term is obscure.
**grinn**, page 100, *fine, pleasant*.
**grith**, *shout, cry* (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *gryd*), singular genitive *gretha*, June 29; plural nominative *grethae*, January 25. In Prologue 154, *gretha* should likely be *grethae*, the genitive plural.
**guide** (Feminine) *prayer*, Epilogue 420, 421; singular genitive *guide*, Epilogue 370; dative *guidi*, Prologue 16; accusative *gudi*, March 1, and *guidi*, Epilogue 412. If the reading *guidi-uili* in Epilogue 226 and 228 is correct, we have here the genitive singular of a masculine or neuter *io*-stem, from which the dative "at your praying" <note>original: oc du guidiu-siu</note> (Milan Glosses 22^a 5) is derived. This is the verbal noun of *guidim* ("I pray").
**guin** (Neuter) *slaughter*, accusative singular Prologue 58, genitive *gona*, St. Gall Glosses 37^b 20.
**gúr**, *grievous, sore* (glossed as *gér* "sharp" by O'Clery), November 7; plural genitive *gúr*, January 15, November 16. Cognate with the Sanskrit *ghorá* ("terrible" or "venerable").

---

->**The letter H is found in the *Martyrology* [Félire]—**<-

(1) In foreign names such as *Hirúath* (Herod), Prologue 105; *Hermes*, August 28; and *Helair* (Hilary), November 1.
(2) In native names and words: *Hériu* (Ireland), genitive *Hérenn*, March 17; *Hí* (Iona), May 25; and *haue* (descendant), February 8, April 11, June 21.
(3) *After the plural article "na"*: *na hóige* (of the virgins), October 4; *na hóga* (the virgins), September 20; *na huili* (all the things), Epilogue 486. The form *na hErenn* (of Ireland) in Epilogue 284 perhaps falls under category (2).
(4) *After the possessive pronoun "her"*: *a háine* (her fasting), Prologue 127; *a haithmit* (her commemoration), August 15.
(5) *After "ba" (meaning "it was" <note>original: fuit</note>)*: *ba hilmain* (it was wealthy), February 11; *ba hoén* (it was one), December 4; *ba hénirt* (it was weak), Epilogue 9.
(6) *After the prepositions "from, to, against, and with" <note>original: a, co, fri, la</note>*: *a hEgipt* (out of Egypt), January 11; *a hAfraic* (out of Africa), August 28; *a h rainn* (from a part), November 21; *co hangliu* (to angels), March 10, May 28 (but *co aingliu*, July 12); *co himbel* (to the border), February 16, Epilogue 343; *co hollmuir* (to the great sea), February 17; *co hIssu* (to Jesus), April 19; *fri hilchu* (against many songs/cries), March 9; *fri homun* (against fear), Epilogue 202; *la hAilill* (with Ailill), Prologue 178; *la híssu* (with Jesus), February 5, Epilogue 440; *la hestecht* (with the departure/death), May 2; *la hEre* (with Ireland), May 12; *la hingru* (with sorrows); *la haingliu* (with angels), May 23; *la hOsuallt* (with Oswald), August 5; *la hIacób* (with Jacob), June 22; *la hógi* (with virgins), September 26; *la hÉmene* (with Émene), December 22; *la hAirerán* (with Airerán), December 29; *la hAilbe* (with Ailbe), December 30; *la hEnoch* (with Enoch), Epilogue 448.
(7) *After the negative "ní" when the meaning is "it is not"*: *ní hattach* (it is not a prayer), July 3, August 8; *ní hane* (it is not splendor), Epilogue 97; *ní hespae* (it is not vanity), Epilogue 430.
(8) To prevent a <term>hiatus</term> <note>A break or gap between two vowel sounds in adjacent syllables.</note>: *álne hEuis* (the beauty of Eve), April 4; *áge húage* (the pillar of virginity), May 25; *Glinne huissen* (of Killeshin), July 18.

---

In the preposition *hi* (in), Prologue 157, January 4, etc.; the pronoun *hed* (it), Epilogue 217; and the adjectives *húag* (pure/holy), *húar* (cold), and *húasal* (noble) and their derivatives, the *h* often seems to be a matter of scribal preference rather than a grammatical requirement.

### GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**í**, **she** <note>original Latin: ea</note>, *is hí*, page 4, line 15; *is í*, pages 6, 14.
**i**, an affixed pronoun: *ro scáich-i*, Prologue 177; *arpet-i*, Epilogue 79; *berth-i*, Epilogue 196.
**íarair**, a Feminine noun meaning **search**, Epilogue 302 (where it rhymes with *íaram*); singular dative *íarair*, Prologue 290; accusative *íarair*, Epilogue 2.
**íaram**, **afterwards, then**, Epilogue 216, 304. In the glosses, this is always, I believe, written as *íarum*.
**íarfaigim** (derived from *íar-fo-sagim*), **I ask**; perfect tense *ro íarfaig*, page 7; *ro íarfaicht*, Saltair na Rann 3093; *nád r-íarfaicht*, Würzburg Glosses 2ᵈ 18; *íarfoacht*, Book of Leinster 65ᵃ 2; from the form *íar-fo-šacht*.
**íar-n**, a preposition used with the dative case, meaning **after, along, according to**, Prologue 27, 64, 247, 311; January 26; March 6, 26; April 19, 21; May 23; June 8; July 26; August 4, 26; September 30; October 9, 20; November 17, 22; December 2, 17; Epilogue 23, 305, 315, where all the manuscripts except Manuscript C use the accusative form of the article.
**íarn-a**, **after his (her, its)**, Prologue 225; Epilogue 119, 223. **íarna-n**, **after their**, Prologue 48, 69.
**íarraim**, **I seek**; plural second-person imperative *íar[r]aid*, page 78.
**íarsind, íarsin**, **after the**, Prologue 279; Epilogue 315, 488.
**íarthar**, **the west, the occident**, singular genitive *íarthair*, Prologue 195; November 11.
**icc-**, **to come**; see also **doiccim, imriccim, ro-iccim**.
**íccaim**, **I heal**; b-future singular third-person *íccfaid*, Epilogue 224; passive present indicative singular third-person *ícthair*, Prologue 228; subjunctive *ícthar*, Epilogue 369. Verbal noun **ícc**, Feminine; genitive *íccæ*, Ascoli 106. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *iachâu*.
**íccid**, a Masculine noun meaning **healer**, Epilogue 200.
**íd**, from the Latin *idus* <note>the "Ides" of the Roman calendar</note>; dative singular November 13; plural nominative *ída*, Prologue 305, where Manuscript L has *idæ* but the Leabhar Breac and Manuscript F have *ida*.
**id**, meaning **is** or **let it be** <note>original Latin: est, sit</note>, used for *did*; *con-id*, September 26; older Irish *condid*, Würzburg Glosses 2ᵃ 7, 2ᵇ 22.
**idan**, **pure**, accusative singular masculine, August 11.
**id-n**, an infixed pronoun of the third-person singular: *ad-id-n-gíalla*, February 23; *ar-id-léga*, Epilogue 178; *con-idnaiscert*, Epilogue 105.
**idnae**, **purity**, dative *idnai*, Epilogue 99.
**ídol, ídal**, a Masculine noun meaning **idol**, singular genitive *ídail*, Epilogue 548; plural nominative *ídail*, Milan Glosses 36ᵈ 16; accusative *ídlu*, Milan Glosses 14ᵇ 4, Ascoli 107. Old Welsh <note>original: O. Cymr.</note> *idol-te* (glossing **temples** <note>original Latin: fanis</note>).
**ídu**, **pang**, plural nominative *ídain*, Epilogue 387, Liber Hymnorum, Ascoli 107.
**iffern**, **hell** (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *uffern*), Ascoli 85; accusative, Epilogue 482, 538; from the Latin *inferna, infernum*.
**iffernach**, **having hell** or **a dweller in hell**, page 74, line 17; page 246, line 34.
**il**, **many**, Ascoli 79; plural nominative *ili*, Prologue 133; March 18; Epilogue 175. Gothic *filu*; Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *el-* in proper names; Greek **many** <note>original: πολύς</note>. For compound words, see **ilgresaib, ilmain, ilrathach**. From this also comes **ilar** (see below) and *ilaigur*, meaning "**I multiply**" <note>original Latin: multiplico</note>.
**ilach**, a Masculine noun (glossing **paean** <note>a song of praise or triumph; original Latin: paean</note>), *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 227, Ascoli 80; plural genitive *ilach*, Prologue 106; accusative *ilchu*, March 9; the phrase *nirpsat [m]airm[si] can ulaig* in the journal *Ériu* i. 72 indicates a change of gender. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *elwch*, which uses a different suffix.
**ilar**, a Neuter noun meaning **a multitude**, Ascoli 80; singular dative *ilur*, May 3; September 7, 19.
**ilgresaib**, plural dative, meaning **many illuminations**, page 90.
**ilmain**, **opulent, wealthy**, February 11; singular genitive masculine *ilmain*, June 30.
**ilrathach**, **having many graces**, accusative singular masculine, Epilogue 466.
**im**, **in my**, Epilogue 126.
**imb, imm, im**, a preposition used with the accusative meaning **around, about**, Prologue 182; February 8, 11; September 4, 28; Epilogue 197, 245, 251. Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *am-, em-, im-* ; Greek **around** <note>original: ἀμφí</note>; Latin **around** <note>original: ambi</note>.

**imbel**, **a circuit or border** <note>original Latin: ambit</note>, Prologue 131; accusative February 16, Epilogue 343. Welsh: *ymyl*. Old Breton: *immel*.
**imbed**, a Neuter noun meaning **multitude or abundance**; dative form *imbud*, Prologue 66, September 11.
**imbi**, **around him**, April 26.
**imbliuch**, **land bordering a lake**, dative September 11.
**imma**, **around whom**; *imma-roerad* (which was caused/wrought), Prologue 206; *imma mbí* (around whom is), April 7; *immal-luid* (around whom he went), August 23; *imma-slecht* (around whom they were slain), February 20, June 16; *imma-slechta*, November 5.
**im-cuiriur**, **I carry or I convey**; imperfect plural 3rd person with an infixed pronoun *imm-a-cuirtis* (they used to carry them), April 27.
**im-foferaim**, **I effect or bring about** <note>original Latin: efficio</note>; preterite passive *immaróerad*, Prologue 206.
**immechtraid**, page 72 = *imeactraigh*, defined by the scholar O'Clery as **the ox at the edge of the plowing team** <note>original Irish: damh imil na seisrighe</note>.
**immelach**, **a ledge**? page 48.
**immfann**, **very weak**, December 31; see also **fann**.
**immon**, **around you** <note>singular</note>, Prologue 22, February 12, Epilogue 566.
**immut-sa**, **around you** <note>emphatic</note>, Epilogue 331.
**imper**, **a ruler** (derived from the Latin word for **authority or empire** <note>original Latin: imperium</note>); genitive *impir*, December 15.
**im-rádim**, **I commemorate**, Ascension 187; present indicative singular 2nd person relative *imm-e-rádi*, December 20; plural 1st person *imrádam*, October 11; preterite singular 1st person *im-r-orduss* (I have commemorated), Prologue 20, 21, January 7, Epilogue 564, 565; singular 2nd person *imrordais*, November 13; plural 3rd person *immero[r]daisset*, Milan Glosses 90ᵈ 16. Verbal noun: **imrádud**. Compare with the Old Welsh *is amraud* (which glosses the Latin for **it is a thought** <note>original Latin: mens est</note>).
**im-riccim**, **I come**; perfect singular 3rd person relative *imm-e-ránic*, May 2.
**im-tíag**, **I go round or I depart**; imperative singular 2nd person *imthig*, page 12.
**i. i-n i**, the preposition **in**. (a) used with the dative case: **in**, Prologue 35, 46, 62; January 16; February 22; March 3, 9; May 10; September 11, 12; October 1; December 21; Epilogue 10, 15, 20, 375. (b) used with the accusative case, where the "n" is preserved, December 29, Epilogue 318.
2. **i-n-**, the locative singular form of the relative pronoun, Prologue 157, 161, 274; August 3; September 4; Epilogue 385.
**ind, int**, the article **the**; forms include *ind, in*, and the neuter *a-n*. In the *Martyrology* <note>the Félire</note>, it follows the strict Old Irish grammatical pattern except in two instances of the masculine nominative plural: *na trí maccáin* (the three youths), August 2; and *inna druing-sea* (these crowds), Epilogue 285. For the former, compare *na trí recte* in the Würzburg Glosses 29ᵃ 16 and *na testimni* in the Milan Glosses 38ᶜ 9ᵃ. For the latter, compare *inna leomain* in the Milan Glosses 80ᵃ 10 and *inna testimni*, Milan Glosses 38ᶜ 9.

**indás**, **than is**, Epilogue 367, 423.
**indber**, **wherein are**, September 4.
**indber**, a Neuter noun meaning **an estuary**, genitive *indbir*, September 13.
**indíu**, **today**, Prologue 220. Welsh: *he-ddyw*.
**indúa**, **a great-grandson**; nominative plural *inndúi*, page 158.
**ingen**, a Feminine noun meaning **daughter or maiden**, Prologue 129; January 5, 21; March 23; May 29; October 5; genitive *ingene*, June 5; dual nominative *dí ingein* (two daughters), December 9; plural genitive *ingen-n*, January 22, March 29. Compare the Ogham inscription in Pembrokeshire, *inígena*.
**ingenrad**, a Feminine collective noun for *ingen*, meaning **a number of maidens**, dative singular *ingenraid*, July 21.
**ingir**, **bitter**, December 21; Würzburg Glosses 4ᵇ 28.
**ingrae**, **bitterness or grief**; plural accusative *ingru*, May 23, Epilogue 119.

It provides linguistic roots, grammatical forms, and cross-references to dates and other texts.</meta>

<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>
<page-num>339</page-num>

**inis**, Feminine noun (Welsh: *ynys*), **island**. Genitive singular: *inse*, January 10, February 7, March 8, July 4, 7, 22, August 12, 31; dative: *inis*, March 15, August 8; accusative plural: *insi*.

**init**, Feminine noun, **shrovetide** (Welsh: *ynyd*, from the Latin *initium* <note>original Latin: beginning</note>), November 13.

**inmain**, **dear, lovable, or beloved**, Prologue 130, 339, February 11, March 7, 16, May 24, 25, 28, August 3, September 19, October 26, December 12; masculine genitive singular: *inmain*, June 30, July 27. In the entry for May 29, *inmain* may be a nominative singular agreeing with *ingen* (daughter). If so, translate it as "Allén’s lovable daughter," and compare it to the August 5 entry: *ardrí Saxan sóerdae* <note>original Old Irish: noble high-king of the Saxons</note>.

**inmall**, **zealous? wearisome? or sad?** Prologue 323, September 10, December 31 in the Laud manuscript.

**inna-n**, **in their**, Prologue 308, April 28, where the Rawlinson manuscript has *inda*.

**insce** or **indsce**, Feminine noun, **speech**, genitive singular Epilogue 123.

**intliucht** or **intsliucht**, Masculine noun, **sense or understanding**, genitive *intliuchto*; dative Prologue 298, 318.

**ír**, **he granted**, 3rd person singular perfect of a verb cognate with the Greek *περάω* <note>original Greek: perao, meaning to pass through or bestow</note>, July 5, September 23. Compare with "he granted to us" <note>original Old Irish: ro ír dún</note> from the Würzburg Glosses 17b 13, and "he granted us" <note>original Old Irish: ro-nn-ír</note> Wb. 20d 11, and *ro era*, Epilogue 427, 431.

**írach**, **wrathful**, accusative singular masculine September 29. Compare with the Welsh *ir-llawn*. This is derived from *ír* (wrath), a loanword from the Latin *ira* <note>original Latin: wrath</note>.

**íriu**, **land or earth**, dative singular *íre*, Epilogue 26, 450. Cognate with Gothic *fēra*, Pamphylian Greek *Πηρία*, and Thessalian Greek *Πηρεία*.

**irguis**, **a great boon**, Epilogue 561; identical to *aurgais*, November 13.

**i. 1.** **is**, a substantive verb meaning **it is** (Latin: *est*), August 4, October 24, 28, November 10, Epilogue 554. Example: *is tú*, "it is you," Prologue 14. Plural form: *it*, Prologue 60, 64, 151, September 28, Epilogue 335, 387, 558.

**2.** **is**, a conjunction meaning **and**, Prologue 210 in the Leabhar Breac, June 26, November 18, Epilogue 294.

**ís**, a preposition used with the dative case (Welsh: *is*), meaning **below**, November 20, Epilogue 378. Derived from an earlier form **\*ins-**, similar to the Latin *infra* <note>original Latin: below</note> which comes from **\*insra**. See also *tís*.

**ísel**, **low or lowly** (Welsh: *ísel*); masculine nominative plural *ísil*, Prologue 152. Comparative form: *ísliu*, Prologue 153, Epilogue 10. From this comes *ísligur*, meaning **I humble** <note>original Latin: humilio</note>.

**isind** or **isin**, **in the**, Prologue 272, 274, November 10. *Isinn* means **into the**, May 16.

**ísle**, Feminine noun, **lowliness**, dative *ísli*, Epilogue 391. This is a derivative of *ísel*.

**it. 1.** **it**, meaning **in your** [singular], Prologue 310, Epilogue 39, 334, or **into your**, as in the phrase "into your neck" (*is it médi*), page 64.

**2.** **it**, meaning **they are** (Latin: *sunt*), from the roots **\*seit** or **\*senti**. See the entry for **i. is**.

**iter** or **eter**, a preposition used with the accusative case, meaning **between** or **among** (Latin: *inter*), March 11 in the Leabhar Breac, November 23. Old Welsh: *ithr*; Cornish: *inter, yntre*.

**itge** or **itche**, Neuter noun, **prayer**, December 21, 22, Epilogue 337; accusative *itge-n*, Prologue 17, January 10, Epilogue 413; nominative plural *itge*, July 16.

**iún** or **iune**, the month of **June**. Genitive singular *iúin*, June 1, 30.

**iunaich** or **iunaige**, **eunuchs** (Latin: *eunuchi*), page 98. Hiberno-Latin: *iunuchus*.

**la**, a preposition used with the accusative case, meaning **with, among, or in the possession of** (Latin: *apud, penes, cum*), Prologue 30, 111, 132, 166, 178, 216, January 28, February 15, 17, 19, 22, 24, March 16, 11, July 4, 5, December 22, Epilogue 117.

**lá-**, **to cast or to put**. 3rd person singular preterite passive: *ro laad* (it was put); plural: *ro láithea*, Prologue 41. This verb serves as the past tense and subjunctive for the verbs *cuiriur* and *focerdam*.

**labrae**, Feminine noun, **speech or utterance**, February 8; genitive singular *labrae*, December 22; accusative singular *labrai*, Prologue 1. From this come *erlabrae* and *comlabrae*. Welsh: *llafar*.

**ladnae**, **dumbness?** accusative singular May 26.

**láich**, Masculine noun derived from the Latin *laicus* <note>original Latin: layman</note>. See also *athlaech*. Welsh: *gwr lleyg* (layman).

<sig>Z 2</sig>

<vocab>inis (island), init (shrovetide), inmain (beloved), inmall (wearisome), inna-n (in their), insce (speech), intliucht (understanding), ír (granted), írach (wrathful), íriu (land), irguis (boon), i (is/and), ís (below), ísel (lowly), isind (in the), ísle (lowliness), it (in thy/they are), iter (between), itge (prayer), iún (June), iunaich (eunuchs), la (with), lá- (to cast), labrae (speech), ladnae (dumbness), láich (layman).</vocab>

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

<term>laice</term>, **slackness**, accusative singular page 6, line 3. It is a derivative of *lac*, meaning **weak or sluggish** <note>original Latin: debilis, languidus</note>, Ascoli 150. Welsh: *yslac*.

<term>laigen</term>, Feminine noun, **a lance**, dative singular: *lágin*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 254; accusative plural: *laignea*, Epilogue 324, where it is misprinted. Welsh: *llain*.

<term>lainnech</term>, **scaly**, October 11. A derivative of *lann*, plural *lanna*, which is glossed as **scales** <note>original Latin: scamae</note> in *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* I. 497.

<term>lainde</term>, Feminine noun, **splendor**, dative singular: *laindi*, February 21, October 7. A derivative of *lainn* (better written as *land*), meaning **bright or shining** <note>original Old Irish: solus nó taithnemach</note>, O'Davoren's Glossary 1184. It is cognate with the Irish *léss* ("light") and the Latin *splendeo* ("I shine").

<term>laindrech</term>, **lucid or bright**, Prologue 197, March 4, 16, June 9, July 28, November 22, December 6, Epilogue 90.

<term>laithe</term> or <term>lathe</term>, Neuter noun, **day**, January 25, Ascoli 150. Genitive singular: *laithi*, Prologue 288, December 9, Epilogue 5, 33, 48; accusative: *laithe*-n, Prologue 283, May 5, December 13, Epilogue 26, 271; nominative plural: *laithe*, Prologue 301, 321; genitive plural: *laithe*-n, Prologue 296; dative plural: *laithib*, Prologue 23, 309; *lathib*, March 26.

<term>lam</term>, **with me** or **at my place** <note>original Latin: apud meum</note>, June 25, July 13, 22 (found in the *Leabhar Breac* and the Franciscan manuscript of the *Martyrology of Tallaght*), December 23, 24.

<term>lám</term>, Feminine noun, **hand** (Welsh: *llaw*, Cornish: *lof*), Ascoli 149. Dative singular: *láim*, Prologue 273; dative plural: *lámaib*, Epilogue 456. The phrase *gabáil láime* means **to expel** (literally "to take by the hand"), pages 94, 96.

<term>lam-</term>, **to dare**, Ascoli 148. 1st person plural imperfect: *lammis*, July 25. See also *rolaimur*.

<term>lán</term>, **full** (Welsh: *llawn*, Latin: *plenus*), February 22, 26, August 10, Epilogue 41, Ascoli 146. Dative singular masculine: *lán*, January 11. See also *comlan* and *forlan*.

<term>lán-bendacht</term>, **a full blessing**, Epilogue 61.

<term>lán-šúairc</term> or <term>lánuairc</term>, **fully gentle**, page 240.

<term>land</term>, Feminine noun, **an area or church** (Old Welsh: *lann*, glossed as **hall or courtyard** <note>original Latin: aula</note>, now *llan*). Dative singular: *laind*, March 30, June 18, September 26.

<term>láne</term>, Feminine noun, **fullness**, Ascoli 146. Dative singular: *láni*, February 3, December 10; *láini*, Epilogue 15.

<term>lann</term>, **a gridiron**, that is, a **griddle or roasting-iron** <note>original Old Irish: greideal no roistín</note>, O'Clery's Glossary. Dative plural: *lannaib*, Prologue 40. Compare the Old Welsh *lann*, glossed as **frying-pan** <note>original Latin: sartago</note>.

<term>lánomain</term>, Feminine noun, better written as <term>lánamain</term> from the root *\*lán-šamain*, **a married couple or a pair**, March 24, Ascoli 148. From this comes *lánamnas*, meaning **union or marriage** <note>original Latin: coniugium, matrimonium</note>, Würzburg Glosses 10ᵃ 15, 18.

<term>lassa-n</term>, <term>lasa-n</term>, or <term>las-n</term>, **at or with whom**, Prologue 65, 106, March 10, June 15, October 22, Epilogue 162. In the entry for February 16, *la sceith* stands for *lasn-sceith*.

<term>lassin-n</term> or <term>lasin-n</term>, **at the**, January 18, 19, May 22, August 2, September 13, November 25, Epilogue 40, 356; plural: *lasna*, Epilogue 409.

<term>lassar</term>, Feminine noun, **flame**, March 17, April 18, July 8. Dative: *lassir* or *lassair*, Milan Glosses 40ᶜ 2, 40ᶜ 5. Welsh: *llachar*.

<term>1. lat</term>, **with you** (thee), February 19 (manuscripts *I, LB, F*), August 9 (manuscripts *R¹, LB, F*), Epilogue 365, 425.

<term>2. lat</term>, **with your** (thy), Prologue 271, Epilogue 354, 357, 470.

<term>lathach</term>, Feminine noun, **a slough or puddle**, accusative singular: *lathaig*, page 150.

<term>láthrach</term>, **a house-site**, Prologue 208. Dative singular: *láthruch*, *Book of Armagh* (*Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 240, line 16).

<term>lébenn</term>, **a platform, surface, or sea-level**, November 29, rhyming with *Érenn*. Dative plural: *lébennib*, Ascoli 164, where the mark of length is wrongly omitted. For the phrase *leir lébenn*, compare the compound *ler-lébhenn* in the *Annals of the Four Masters*, A.D. 882. Welsh: *llwyfan*.

<term>lebor</term> or <term>lebar</term>, Masculine noun, **a book** (Welsh: *lyfr*, from Latin: *liber*). Genitive plural: *lebar-n*, Epilogue 141; dative: *lebraib*, Ascoli 164; accusative: *libru*, Epilogue 75.

<term>lebrán</term>, Masculine noun, **a little book** <note>original Latin: libellus</note>, Epilogue 90, 106, 130, 133. Nominative plural: *lebráin*, Prologue 289; dative: *lebránaib*, Prologue 310. Welsh: *llyfran*.

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

<page-num>341</page-num>

<term>léicim</term>, **I leave, I let go**, preterite plural 3rd person: *lécsit*, October 8. See *colléce*.

<term>lecht</term> Masculine, **a grave**, singular dative: *lecht*, Prologue 227; accusative: *lechtu*, Epilogue 146. Derived from Latin *lectus*, meaning **a small compartment in a tomb** <note>original Latin: loculus in sepulchro</note>. See *lige*.

<term>lechtán</term> Masculine, a diminutive of *lecht*, Prologue 116.

<term>léciud</term> Masculine, singular dative: *lécud* (more correctly *léciud*), April 21. This is the verbal noun of *léicim*, Ascoli 160; derived from the root *lank*, and cognate with French *lancer* and Gallo-Latin *lancea* (**a lance or spear**).

<term>légaim</term>, **I read, I study**, present indicative plural 3rd person: *-légat*, Prologue 81. Derived from Latin *lēgo* (**I read**), with an unexplained lengthening of the next-to-last syllable. See *arlégaim*.

<term>léghait</term>, **legate**, page 158; plural genitive: *legaite*, *Tripartite Life of St. Patrick* xxviii.

<term>légend</term>, **reading, study**, Ascoli 158; singular dative: *légiunn*, page 12; plural genitive: *légend*, September 26. Similar to Welsh *llen* and Cornish *lyen*; derived from Latin *legenda* (**things to be read**).

<term>léim</term> Neuter, **a leap** (derived from *Ingmen*; Welsh: *llam*), December 31, Ascoli 157. This is the verbal noun of *lingim*.

<term>léir</term>, **diligent, pious**, April 30, June 24; singular accusative masculine: *léir*, Epilogue 90; plural dative masculine: *lérib*, Prologue 310, 334; accusative: *léri*, November 14; adverb: *col-léir*, Prologue 312.

<term>leis</term>, **with him** <note>original Latin: apud eum</note>; *maith léir*, February 11.

<term>lén</term>, see *corp-lén*, *merblén*.

<term>lénaim</term>, **I adhere to, I follow**, reduplicated future singular 2nd person: *lili-siu*, Prologue 309, 311. Perfect: *lil*; plural: *leltar*.

<term>lénaim</term>, **I wound, I hurt, I weaken** (from *lakn-*, cognate with Latin *lacerare*, **to tear or mangle**). Active preterite singular 3rd person: *nachar-len*, *Saltair na Rann* 1726; passive: *ro lénad*, Prologue 253. A derivative of *lén*, meaning **sorrow or a wound** <note>original Latin: dolor, vulnus</note>, dative: *lén*, *Book of Leinster* 95a 19.

<term>leoman</term> Masculine, **a lion**, plural genitive: Epilogue 500 (but *inna leon*, Milan Glosses 75b 2); nominative: *inna leomain*, Milan Glosses 80a 10. Welsh: *llew*.

<term>ler</term> Neuter, **ocean, a great sea** (Welsh: *llyr*), March 21, May 14, June 14, October 30; singular genitive: *lir*, March 15, 22, August 14, November 23; *leir*, November 29; accusative: *ler*, June 12. Compounds: *ler-mag*, dative: *lermaig*, December 12; *ler-muir*, dative: December 12 (*Leabhar Breac*).

<term>lére</term> Feminine, **diligence, piety**, genitive: *lére*, Prologue 3, April 5, September 5, Epilogue 78, 350, 428, 429; dative: *léri*; accusative: *léri-n*, July 9, March 6, 25, June 28, August 29, October 22, December 20, Epilogue 106, 130, 138. A derivative of *léir*; plural nominative: *léri* (glossing **diligent ones** <note>original Latin: diligentes</note>), Milan Glosses 88c 6.

<term>less</term> Masculine, **a courtyard, a fort** (Welsh: *llys*), singular genitive: *liss*, June 25, December 3; plural genitive: *loig les* (glossing **a title of cities** <note>original Latin: titulus ciuitatum</note>), *Book of Armagh* 10b.

<term>léss</term>, **light** (from *splend-to-*, cognate with Latin *splendor*, **brightness**), March 4, 22, June 9. From this comes *lés-baire*, Milan Glosses 121c 23.

<term>lestar</term> Neuter, **a vessel** (Welsh: *llestr*), Ascoli 154; singular dative: *lestur*, Epilogue 22.

<term>1. leth</term> Neuter, **side, part** (a stem in *s*, identical to Latin *latus*, **side**), singular dative: *leith*, Epilogue 35; accusative: *for leth*, page 4, line 10; dual genitive: *dá lethe*, December 4.

<term>2. leth</term> Neuter, **half, one of a pair** (as in *leth-assa*, page 12; *leth-rann*, page 4; *leth-taeb*, page 44), singular genitive: *leith*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 236; dative: *leuth*, *Thesaurus* II. 10.

<term>lethan</term>, **broad, widespread** (Welsh: *llydan*), Prologue 214, December 11; genitive singular (masculine or neuter): *lethain*, June 27, November 23; plural nominative feminine: *lethna*, Epilogue 82. Comparative: *letha*, Milan Glosses 44c 27. From this comes *lethnaigur*, **I spread out** <note>original Latin: dilato</note>.

<term>lethet</term>, **breadth, width**, singular dative: *lethet*, October 13, Ascoli 163. Welsh: *lled*.

<term>lett</term>, **with you** <note>original Latin: apud te</note>, February 19.

<term>lex</term>, **a chant**, plural accusative: *lechsa*, November 14. Perhaps derived from *lesc*, cognate with the Greek *lasko* <note>original Greek: λάσχω</note> or *lekeo* <note>original Greek: ληκέω</note>, meaning **to shout or ring**?

<term>lia</term>, **with his** or **with its**, Prologue 95, 190, April 8.

<term>líath</term>, **grey** (Welsh: *llwyd*, Old Breton *loit*, glossing **white or grey-haired** <note>original Latin: cano</note>), April 30.

<term>lib-si</term>, **with you** <note>original Latin: *apud vos*</note>, Epilogue 397.

<term>lie</term> Masculine, **stone**, April 15, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 288; genitive: *liac*; dative singular: *liic*, October 5. At April 15 and October 5, it is pronounced as two syllables. At October 5, it is feminine.

<term>lígach</term>, **beautiful**, Prologue 197, March 24, April 18, June 21; genitive singular masculine: *lígaig*, September 12; dative singular feminine: *lígaich*, March 30, *lígaig*, June 18.

<term>lígdae</term>, **beautiful**, Prologue 214; plural dative neuter: *lígdaib*, Prologue 23.

<term>lígdath</term>, **beauty** (literally, **a beautiful color**?), Prologue 19, September 21.

<term>lige</term> Neuter, **a bed, a grave**, Prologue 113; singular genitive: *ligi*, Epilogue 224; plural nominative: *lige*, Prologue 76. Cognate with Gothic *ligan* and Greek *λέχος* <note>original Greek: *lechos*, meaning "bed"</note>. See *lecht*.

<term>lígflaith</term> Feminine, **a beautiful realm**, genitive: *lígflatha*, Epilogue 22.

<term>lígmar</term>, **beautiful**, accusative singular masculine: July 7.

<term>lim</term>, **with me** <note>original Latin: *apud me*</note>, Epilogue 494; *lium*, Epilogue 367.

<term>lín</term> Neuter, **a number, a multitude**; *lín catha* (**the number of a battle** or **an army**), August 23; dative singular: *lín*, Prologue 106, 115, 167, 296, Epilogue 31, 103; accusative: *lín*, Prologue 30, December 2; dual dative: *díblínib* (**in both**), June 14.

<term>línaim</term>, **I fill**, present indicative singular 3rd person relative: *línass*, *línas*, September 9, November 8; preterite singular 3rd person: *ro lín*, Prologue 140, 215. Compare with Latin *plēnus* (**full**).

<term>1. lind</term>, **a pool** (Welsh: *llyn*), dual genitive: *dá lind*, June 3.

<term>2. lind</term>, *linn*, **age, wisdom**, genitive: *linde*, October 13; plural nominative: *lindi*, Epilogue 82, rhyming with *findi* and *rindi*. Strachan (in *Revue Celtique* xx. 196, note 1) suggests the meaning is "pools" (of wisdom); however, O'Clery defines *linn* as "age" <note>original Irish: *saeghal*</note>. See also Windisch's *Wörterbuch*.

<term>líne</term> Feminine (Welsh: *llinyn*, from Latin *linea*): singular dative: *líni*, Prologue 308, October 2, 14; plural dative: *línib*, Prologue 311, 335. From this comes the adjective *línech*, **linear** <note>original Latin: *linearis*</note>.

<term>lingim</term>, **I leap, I spring**, perfect singular 3rd person: *rol-eb-laing*, March 5; see August 26, note 14. See *eb* above and *ror* below.

<term>linni</term>, **with us** <note>original Latin: *apud nos*</note>, September 6.

<term>líth</term> Masculine, **festival**, January 25, October 1, November 3, December 10; singular genitive: *lítha*, May 5; dative: *líth* (in the phrase **for a single festival** <note>original Irish: *for óen-líth*</note>), January 20, February 26, March 21, April 29, May 14, June 28, August 23, October 30; accusative: *líth-n*, January 18, March 29, September 25, November 8; plural nominative: *líthe*; genitive: *líth*, Epilogue 20 (which seems ungrammatical); accusative: *líthu*. Thurneysen connects this word with Middle High German *vlât* and Greek *πληθύς* <note>original Greek: *plēthús*, meaning "crowd" or "fullness"</note>.

<term>lium</term>, **with me** <note>original Latin: *apud me*</note>, Epilogue 367.

<term>liuss</term>, see *árlius*.

<term>lobaím</term>, **I decay**, subjunctive plural 3rd person: *-lobat*; future plural 3rd person: *-lobfat*, Epilogue 220; verbal noun: *lobad*. Related to *lobrae* and *lobur*.

<term>lobrae</term> Feminine, **weakness, sickness**, genitive singular: Prologue 223. A derivative of *lobur* (see below).

<term>lobur</term>, **weak, sick, infirm** (Welsh: *llwfr*); accusative singular: Epilogue 366. From this comes *lobraigur*, **I am sick** or **I grow weak** <note>original Latin: *aegroto, languesco, infirmo*</note>.

<term>loc</term> Masculine (from Latin *locus*, **place**), singular genitive: *luic*; dative: *luc*, March 9, *lucc*; plural nominative: *luicc*; plural accusative: *lucu*, *luccu*. Welsh: (*mynach*)*log*.

<term>locán</term> Masculine, a diminutive of *loc* (**a little place**), plural nominative: *locáin*, Prologue 209.

<term>loch</term> Neuter, **lake**, singular genitive: *locha*, February 7; dual genitive: *dá locha* (**of two lakes**), Prologue 196.

<term>lócharn</term> Feminine, **lamp**, February 7, April 15; singular genitive: *lócharne*, April 22; accusative: *lochairnn*. Welsh: *llygorn*.

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

<term>lóichet</term> Neuter, **luster, brightness, light**, Prologue 197, January 26, April 23, November 22, December 20; genitive singular: *déne lóichet*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 335. This is a word stem ending in *-ent*, similar to the word *dét* (**tooth**). See Thurneysen, *Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie* V. 20.

<term>locht</term> Masculine, **fault, defect**, Ascoli 177; plural nominative: *lochtae*, March 18.

<term>lógmar</term>, **precious**, April 15; dative singular feminine: *lógmair*, October 5. This is a derivative of <term>lóg</term> Neuter, **price, pay, reward**, page 8, Ascoli 176.

<term>logud</term>, **the act of obtaining or petitioning** <note>original Latin: *impetratio*</note>, Ascoli 175; accusative singular: Epilogue 370.

<term>lóid</term>, **a song or poem** <note>original: "a lay"</note>, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 290, line 7; dative singular: *lóid*, Prologue 323; plural dative and instrumental: *lóidib*, Prologue 314, 334, February 27.

<term>loimm</term> Neuter, **a sip**, Epilogue 42, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 225, line 23; dative singular: *lommmum*, *Leabhar Laighneach* (Book of Leinster) 167a. Compare with the Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> word *llymaid*.

<term>long</term> Feminine (compare the Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *llong*, Feminine), **vessel, ship**; accusative singular: *loing* (translated from the Latin <note>original Latin: *uas*</note> for **vessel**), *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 497, line 7; plural accusative: *longa*, September 9. From this comes the Old Norse <note>original: *O.N.*</note> word *lung*.

<term>longach</term>, **shipful**; genitive singular neuter: *longaig*, August 14; accusative neuter: *longach*, June 12.

<term>loscim</term>, **I burn**, Ascoli 170; preterite passive plural 3rd person: *ro loisccthea*, Prologue 39. Compare with the Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> word *llosgi*.

<term>loscud</term>, **burning**, dative singular: Prologue 62. This is the verbal noun of *loscim*.

<term>lothe, loithe</term> Feminine, **dumbness** <note>the inability to speak</note>; accusative singular: *lothi, loithe*, Prologue 287, *The Yellow Book of Lecan*.

<term>lua</term>, **a kick**, page 180; *lue* (translated from the Latin <note>original Latin: *calx*</note> for **heel**), *St. Gall Glosses* 50b 20.

<term>lúachthe</term>, **white-hot**, a compound of *luach* and *té*; plural dative: *lúachthetib*, Prologue 40, which Ascoli (page 176) would change to *luaichthithib*, meaning **shining** or **bright** <note>original Latin: *fulgidis*</note>. Compare with the Greek word for **white** <note>original Greek: λευκός (leukos)</note>.

<term>lúad</term> Neuter, **rumor, mention, talk**, August 23.

<term>luam</term> Masculine, **pilot, abbot**, December 3, where it is pronounced as two syllables. The form *luum* in the Würzburg Glosses 4a 14 seems to be a scribal error for *luam*. Compare with the Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *llywio* or *llywydd*. Derived from the Indo-European <note>original: *Idg.*</note> root *plu*.

<term>lúath</term>, **fleet, swift**, Ascoli 180; plural accusative feminine: *lúatha*, September 9.

<term>lucht</term> Masculine, **folk, people** (compare the Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *llwyth*), January 17, Epilogue 49; dative singular: *lucht*, Epilogue 48; plural accusative: *luchtu*, Epilogue 147.

<term>luchtlach</term>, **a crew**, Epilogue 21; plural nominative: *luchtlaige*, *Leabhar Laighneach* (Book of Leinster) 219a.

<term>luid</term>, **he went** <note>original Latin: *ivit*</note>, Prologue 128, January 1, April 19, 28, May 20, June 4, 6, 15, 19, July 13, August 24, 27, September 15, November 8, 19, 22, 25; plural 3rd person: *lotar*, December 20. The verbal noun is *dul*; see Ascoli 171, 179.

<term>luithe</term> (perhaps should be read as *lúaithe*?) Feminine, **swiftness**; dative: *luithi* (perhaps *luaithi*?), Prologue 287, 299.

<term>lúrech</term>, derived from the Latin for **breastplate** <note>original Latin: *lorica*</note>, Epilogue 78, 197, Ascoli 181. Compare with the Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *lluricogion*.

<term>lúth</term>, **vigor**, Ascoli 182, 183; accusative singular: October 8. Perhaps related to the Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *llid*, meaning **anger**.

<term>lúthige</term> Feminine, **strength, vigor**?; dative: *lúthigi*, Epilogue 134.

***

<term>m, mm</term>, **first-person singular infixed pronoun**, Prologue 3, 18, 25.

<term>ma</term>, **if**, Ascoli 364, Prologue 186, March 2, July 4, November 15, Epilogue 102, 128, 389.

<term>macc</term> Masculine, **son** (derived from the reconstructed form *\*maqqos*, just as the Old Welsh <note>original: *O. Cymr.*</note> *\*map* comes from *\*maqos*), Ascoli 372, August 14, 18; genitive singular: *maicc*, June 24, October 26, Epilogue 428, 429; dative: *macc*, Prologue 148; accusative: *macc-n*, Prologue 56, May 22; plural nominative: Prologue 134, March 15, June 18, November 28; genitive: *macc-n*, April 24, August 1, September 26; dative: *maccaib*, June 16; accusative: *maccu*, Epilogue 507. This is a "hypocoristic" or pet name, which explains the doubling of the *q* (c) sound.

<term>maccán</term> Masculine, **child**, a diminutive form of *macc*, Prologue 137, June 15; genitive singular: *maccáin*, July 16; plural nominative: *maccáin*, August 2, September 4, December 28.

<term>maccrad</term> Feminine, **children** (a collective noun), dative: *maccraid*, February 12; accusative: *maccraid-n*, August 22.

<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

## GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**oté**, **and they**, Prologue 34, singular 77ª 8; **ote**, Milan Glosses 130ª 3, Ascoli 231. Latin: <note>original: "revera sunt ii, eae, ea"</note> **truly they are** (referring to masculine, feminine, or neuter plural subjects), Ascoli 221.

**páirt** (Old Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *part*, *pard*, from the Latin *partem*), **a volume** or **book**, plural genitive <note>original: "pl. gen."</note> **partae**, Epilogue 136.

**páiss** (from the Latin *passio*), **Passion**, <term>undeclined</term> <note>the word form does not change based on its grammatical role</note>, January 14, 26; February 19, 24; March 2, 3, 25; April 24; May 9, 30, 31; June 11, 20, 26, 28; July 2, 21, 22, 26 (Rawlinson B 505, Laud 610, Brussels MS, Luxembourg MS, Franciscan MS); September 17; October 1, 2, 8, 18, 20, 22; November 5; December 1, 7.

**pardus** (Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *paradwys*, from the Latin *paradisus*), dative singular <note>original: "dat. sg."</note> **Epilogue** 39.

**pauperán**, **a mendicant** or **beggar**, Epilogue 408; a derivative of *pauper*, meaning <term>bocht</term> <note>poor</note>, according to O’Clery’s Glossary.

**peccad** (Masculine) **sin** (Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *pechod*, from the Latin *peccatum*), singular genitive <note>original: "sg. gen."</note> **pectho**, **pectha**; dative **peccad**, Epilogue 460; compare with **ecc**.

**pían** (Feminine) **pain** (Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *poen*, from the Latin *poena*), singular genitive **péne**, Prologue 118; plural nominative **píana**, Prologue 75, 88; accusative **píana**, March 28, May 5, October 19.

**píanaim**, **I punish**, passive present indicative, third-person singular, **-píantar**, page 198.

**pit** (Feminine) in **terc-phit** (meaning a "scant portion"); <term>pid</term> means <note>original: "proind bec"</note> **a small meal**, Leccan Vocabulary 537; genitive **pite**, Leabhar Breac 11ª 1.

**plág** (Feminine) **plague** (from the Latin *plaga*, while the Welsh and Cornish *pla* comes from the Low Latin *plaga*), singular genitive **pláge**, Epilogue 492.

**plágaim**, **I plague** or **I afflict**, preterite passive plural, third person, **ro plágtha**, Prologue 234.

**pleo**, used for **breo**, **a flame**, Epilogue 258, Rawlinson B 512, Leabhar Breac.

**pontecla**, **Pontine**, or **belonging to Pontus**, page 100, line 8; an epithet used for Gregory Thaumaturgus.

**popul** (Masculine) **people** (Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *pobl*, from the Latin *populus*), singular genitive **popuil**, Prologue 115; dative **popul**, November 26. For compounds, see **cáin-popul**.

**port** (Masculine) **port** or **place** (Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *porth*, from the Latin *portus*), dative singular **purt**, Epilogue 187 and page 44.

**praicept** (Feminine) **a preachment** or **sermon** (Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *pregeth*, from the Latin *praeceptum*), May 1; singular genitive **na precepte**, Würzburg Glosses 9ᵇ 19.

**praidchim**, **I preach** (from the Latin *praedico*), present preterite, third-person singular, **ro phraidchi**, Prologue 164 (rhyming with *saigthi*).

**praisch**, **pottage** or **broth**, genitive **praisce**; Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *bresych*, from the Latin *brassica* <note>meaning cabbage</note>, page 146.

**préchán**, **a scarecrow**, genitive **prechain**, page 112, line 15.

**prím** (Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *prif*, from the Latin *primus*, meaning **first** or **chief**) occurs in the following compounds:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímairec**, **first finding** (referring to the Discovery of the Cross), May 3.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímapstal**, **chief apostle**, page 49.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímchell**, **a chief church**, plural genitive, page 68.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímchéssad**, **foremost suffering**, October 15.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímfáith**, **chief prophet**, page 146.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímféil** (Feminine) **chief feast**, June 10; dual nominative **dí prímféil**, May 31.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímloc** (Masculine) **chief place**, plural nominative **prímluic**, page 2.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímmartir** (Masculine) **chief martyr**, October 18.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímslóg**, **prímslúag**, **a chief host** or **multitude**, February 12; dative singular, April 13.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímsollamain**, **a chief festival**, page 74.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímsuide**, **chief seat**, Prologue 117.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**prímthrécheng**, **a chief trio**, November 28.

**prímdae**, Latin: <note>original: "primarius"</note> **primary** or **excellent**, March 7; April 5, 15; November 2, 4; Epilogue 247, 258.

**prinnssa**, **prince**, page 52.

**prolach**, Latin: <note>original: "prologus"</note> **prologue** (Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *prol*), Prologue 144. There is also a Middle Irish form **brolach**, dative **broluch**, page 10.

<page-num>354</page-num>
<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

**promaim** (for *probaim*, from the Latin *probo* <note>original: "probo"</note> and Welsh *profi* <note>original: "Cymr. profi"</note>), **I prove**. First person plural conjunctive (*dian*): **promam**, Prologue 143. Third person plural future: **promfat**, Epilogue 219. Third person plural preterite passive: **ro promtha**, February 27. Preterite passive participle: **promthae**, February 12, May 9, October 21.

**pudar**, **evil or mischief**, page 4, line 28. Perhaps from the Latin *pudor* <note>original: "pudor", meaning shame</note>? Or, like the Welsh *pwdr* <note>original: "Cymr. pwdr"</note>, from the Latin *putris* <note>original: "putris", meaning rotten</note>?

**rachrad**, Epilogue 478. The analysis and meaning of this word are unclear.

**rád**, **the act of saying**, January 18. This is the verbal noun of **-rádiu**.

**-rádiu**, **I say, I mention**. First person singular: **no ráidiu**, Epilogue 358 (compare with *no radim*, Milan Glosses 47b 13). Second person singular: **no rádi**, February 18. Second person singular imperative: **ráid**, September 17, November 19. First person singular <term>preterite</term> <note>a past tense form</note>: **ro rádius**, January 29. Second person singular: **ro rádis**, January 9. Future passive participle: **ráti**, April 9. See **imrádim**.

**raith**, in the phrase **dia raith-sium**, meaning **for his sake**, Epilogue 165.

1. **ráith**, **he ran** <note>original Latin: "cucurrit"</note>. See **rethim**.

2. **ráith** (Feminine), **a stronghold**, Prologue 177. Plural accusative: **ráthi**, Book of Armagh 6b 1. In Prologue 200, **ráith** appears to be in the locative singular.

**rán** (*ro-án*), **very splendid**, January 6, April 20, August 15. Plural genitive: **ran** (read as **rán**), September 19 in manuscripts R1, F, and H. Accusative: **rána**, in the *Song of Caillech Bérre*.

**ránic**, **he came** <note>original Latin: "venit"</note>, May 2, Epilogue 17. See **ricim**.

1. **rann** (Feminine), **a part or share** (Welsh *rhan* <note>original: "Cymr. rhan"</note>), Prologue 258. Singular genitive: **rainne**, Ascoli 185. Plural dative: **rannaib**, Prologue 38. Compound: see **droch-rann**. From this comes **rannaim**, **I divide**.

2. **rann** (Masculine), **a stanza**, especially a **quatrain** <note>a four-line stanza</note>. Singular dative: **rand**, page 4 (more correctly **runn**, Lebor na hUidre 6b). Plural dative: **rannaib**, December 21. Accusative: **runnu**, Lebor na hUidre 40b. See **lethrann**.

**rath** (Neuter), **grace or favor** (Welsh *rhad* <note>original: "Cymr. rhad"</note>), May 15, November 11. Singular genitive: **raith**, August 18. Dative: **rath**, November 5. Plural nominative and accusative: **ratha**, pages 4 and 10. Also found with an intensive prefix as **ro rath**. From this come **rathach** (as in **ilrathach**, which see) and **rathmar**.

**ráth** (Masculine or Neuter), **guarantor or surety**, Epilogue 164, 165. Ascoli 190.

**ráthatar**, see **rethim**.

**rathmar**, **gracious** (Welsh *rhadfawr* <note>original: "Cymr. rhadfawr"</note>), page 46. Masculine singular genitive: **rathmair**, Epilogue 235. Masculine vocative: **rathmar**, Epilogue 457 (which rhymes with *cathrach*).

**recht** (Masculine), **law** (Welsh *rhaith* <note>original: "Cymr. rhaith"</note>). Genitive: **rechto**, **rechta**. Dative: January 1, September 10. Accusative: **recht**, page 4, line 13. Plural accusative: **rechtu**, Ascoli 195. From this comes **rechtaigim** (glossed as **I appoint by law** <note>original Latin: "lego"</note>), St. Gall Glosses 60b 16.

**recomarc**, **a disyllable** <note>a word with two syllables</note>, page 4. Cormac’s Glossary Translation, 56.

1. **réde** (Feminine), **smoothness**. Dative: **rédi**, Epilogue 132.

2. **réde** (Neuter?), Prologue 120, meaning **a plain**. This might be the accusative plural of **réid** (a plain), Lebor na hUidre 65a 10.

**rega**, **I will come** or **I will go**. First person plural: **regmi**, Prologue 291; Ascoli 198. See **do-ragat**, and compare with the Greek **erchomai** <note>original: "ἔρχομαι", meaning to come or go</note>, Sarauw, page 97.

**recles**, **a little cell** (perhaps from the Latin *reclusum* <note>original: "reclusum", a closed place or cell</note>?). Dative: page 10. Genitive: *Dunadach in reiclesa* (Dunadach of the little cell), Annals of Ulster, 1010.

**réid**, **smooth or easy**, Epilogue 133; Ascoli 204. Masculine dative singular: November 28. From this come **réidigur** and **réidigim**.

**réid-rinnard**, the name of a specific **meter** <note>a poetic rhythm or structure</note>, page 4.

**réil**, **clear**, November 18; Ascoli 194. Also found with the intensive prefix **roreil**. Derived from *regli*, which is related to the Lithuanian word **regiu** <note>original: "regiu"</note>, meaning **I see**.

**réimm** (Neuter, derived from *rengmen*), **course**, Prologue 107, 306; January 21, July 23, Epilogue 54. Accusative: October 16. See Ascoli 206. **Réimm** serves as the verbal noun for **rethim** (to run), but it originates from the Indo-European root *rengh*, from which the Irish word *dr-eb-raing* is also derived.

### GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**rélad**: A masculine noun meaning **manifestation**. Dative singular: Prologue 278. This is the verbal noun of **rélaim**.

**relic**: A **relic** <note>original: "relique"</note>. See **noebrelic** (holy relic). Comparable to the Welsh *rheliw* <note>original: "Cymr. rheliw"</note>, which is derived from the Latin *reliquia* <note>original: "reliquia"</note>.

**relic**, **reilic**: A **graveyard**, April 16. Cited in Cormac’s Glossary as coming "from the relics of the saints" <note>original Latin: "a reliquiis sanctorum"</note>.

**remain**: This word sometimes, as in January 1 and 31 and March 3, seems to be an adjective meaning **pre-eminent**. At other times, as in the Epilogue (line 6), it acts as an adverb meaning **heretofore** or **hereinbefore**. In the entry for September 19 (*raith remain*) and in the *Book of the Dun Cow* (57b 15), where it says "they were those who used to be ahead before the host" <note>original: "ité side nobitis remain resi[n]slóg"</note>, it seems to mean **ahead**, **in front**, or **forward**. Similarly, in the *Book of the Dun Cow* (72b 2): "the girl goes forward before them" <note>original: "teit ind ingen remáin remib"</note>, and in the *Book of Leinster* (68a 26): "Cuchulainn's portion always ahead before them" <note>original: "cuid Cúchulainn riam remain rempu"</note>.

**remsamaigthi**: Perhaps **prioresses**? Compare with *remsamugud*, meaning **anteposition** or **placing before** <note>original: "anteposition"</note> (St. Gall Glosses 212a 15).

**remthechtas**: **Precedence** or **placing before** <note>original Latin: "antepositio"</note>. Genitive singular: *remthechtais*, page 2.

**ré-n**: See **ría-n**.

**renga**: **Shreds**, page 74 (at February 14). Compare with the phrase "they would be shreds of [his] forearms" <note>original: "roptis do renga rigthi"</note> in the *Book of the Dun Cow* (68b 33).

**rerach**: An **ancestor** or **patriarch**. Genitive: *rerig* (*Book of the Dun Cow* 104b 13). Nominative plural: *reraig*. Genitive plural: Epilogue 237.

**rerthae**: **Which was taken**? December 20. Explained in version E as *ructha*. Both the form and meaning are obscure.

**resme**: Prologue 257. A 1st person plural <term>s-subjunctive</term> <note>a specific verb mood in Old Irish</note>, derived from either the root *reg* (see **rega**) or the root *ret* (see **rethim**).

**rét**: A **star** or **heavenly body** <note>original Latin: "sidus"</note>. Genitive: *réta*. Compound word: **rétglu** (feminine), **star**. Nominative plural: *rétglainn* (July 29). Dative plural: *rétglannaib*. Dual accusative: *dí rétglainn* (two stars), March 3.

**rethet daurthige**: The site of an **oratory** <note>original: "daurthige"</note>, page 64.

**rethim**: **I run**. Third person singular: *rethid* (**runs**). <term>Perfect</term> <note>past tense</note> singular 3: *ro ráith* (he ran), Prologue 28. Also *ráith* (January 6, September 19, October 16, November 22). Third person plural: *ráthatar* (they ran), September 18. Verbal noun: **rith** (running) or *ruth*. Cognate with the Welsh *rhedu* or *rhedeg* <note>original: "Cymr. rhedu, rhedeg"</note>.

**rí**: A masculine noun meaning **king**. Cognate with the Welsh *rhi* <note>original: "Cymr. rhi"</note>. Used in Prologue 93, January 1, and Epilogue 85. At March 11, it refers to an **abbot**. Genitive singular: *ríg*. Dative: *ríg*. Accusative: *ríg*. Vocative: *rí*. Plural nominative: *ríg*. Genitive plural: *ríg-n*. Dative plural: *rígaib*. Accusative plural: *ríga*. Derived from the Latin *rex* <note>original: "rex"</note>.
  **Compounds**: **ardrí** (high king), **gormrí** (splendid king), **ócrí** (young king), **ruirí** (over-king), and:
  **rígepscop**: Masculine noun, **royal bishop**, April 14.
  **rígféil**: Feminine noun, **royal festival**, November 29.
  **rígflaith**: Feminine noun, **royal kingdom**. Dative: October 23, December 14, Epilogue 334.
  **ríggein**: **Royal birth**, June 24.
  **rígmacc**: Masculine noun, **royal son** or **prince**. Genitive: *rígmacc* (August 16). Accusative: *rígmacc* (November 22).

**ríag**: Feminine noun, a **gibbet** or **instrument of torture**. Glossed as a **gallows** <note>original Latin: "patibulum"</note>. July 2. Dative plural: *ríagaib*. Accusative plural: *ríaga* (February 23, October 19).

**ríagol**, **ríaguil**: Feminine noun, meaning **rule**. Derived from the Latin *regula* <note>original: "rēgula"</note>. The Welsh word *rheol* <note>original: "Cymr. rheol"</note> is also from *regula*. Page 4, line 15. Dative: *ríaguil* (Epilogue 96).

**riam**: An adverb meaning **aforetime** or **formerly**, Prologue 52, where it is pronounced as two syllables.

**ría-n**, **ré-n**: A preposition used with the <term>dative</term> <note>a grammatical case often indicating location or means</note> case. Prologue 248, 340, January 1, March 12, Epilogue 64.

**ríana-n**: **Before their**, Prologue 31.

**ríar**: Feminine noun, **will** or **liking**. Dative singular: **fo réir** (**in subjection to**). Accusative singular: **réir**, page 4, line 13, and Prologue 269.

<vocab>**rélad**: manifestation. **relic**: a relic, from Latin *reliquia*. **reilic**: graveyard. **remain**: pre-eminent, ahead, or forward. **remsamaigthi**: prioresses or those placed before. **remthechtas**: precedence. **renga**: shreds. **rerach**: ancestor or patriarch. **rerthae**: possibly "which was taken." **resme**: a verb form from the roots for "to rule" or "to run." **rét**: a star or heavenly body. **rétglu**: a star. **rethet daurthige**: site of an oratory. **rethim**: I run. **rí**: king or abbot; cognate with Latin *rex*. **rígepscop**: royal bishop. **rígféil**: royal festival. **rígflaith**: royal kingdom. **ríggein**: royal birth. **rígmacc**: royal son or prince. **ríag**: gibbet or torture instrument. **ríagol**: a rule, from Latin *regula*. **riam**: formerly. **ría-n**: before. **ríar**: will or liking; *fo réir* means in subjection to.</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the glossarial index of Old Irish terms, moving through the letter 'r'. It covers terms for "heaven," "queen," and "king," as well as several definitions for "rind" (meaning point, star, or meter), and explains the grammatical particle "ro."</meta>

<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

**riched**: A neuter noun meaning **heaven**. Ascoli 203. Singular genitive: *richith*, *Thesaurus* II. 257, *richid* Prologue 120; dative: *richiud* February 23; accusative: *riched* Prologue 6, 120, May 22, July 7, September 18, November 6, Epilogue 54, 222, 466. Plural accusative: *riched*, Epilogue 341. See **ard-riched** <note>high-heaven</note>.

**richt**: **form** (compare to the Welsh *rhith* <note>original: "Cymr. rhith"</note>), Ascoli 216. Dative: *richt*, page 12. Old Irish: *riucht*, *Thesaurus* I. 490, line 32.

**ríchtu**: **reaching**. Singular dative: *ríchtáin* March 12, Epilogue 223. This is the verbal noun of **roiccim** <note>I reach</note>.

**rígaim**: **I make a king**, **enthrone**, or **crown**. Preterite passive third-person singular: *ro rígad* (he was crowned) Prologue 104, May 18, August 25, Epilogue 263. Third-person plural: *ro ríghta* Prologue 235.

**rígain**: A feminine noun meaning **queen** (compare to the Welsh *rhian* <note>original: "Cymr. rhian"</note>), Prologue 125, September 20. Singular genitive: *rígnæ*, July 11, 18; dative: *rígain* Prologue 105. Plural genitive: *rígnæ*, *Thesaurus* II. 295, line 15.

**rígdae**: **kingly** or **royal**. February 9, March 5, April 10, August 4. Singular genitive masculine: *rígdai* July 2, November 18. Accusative masculine: *rígdæ* March 4, Epilogue 260. Feminine: *rígdai* April 16. Plural nominative feminine: *rígdai* July 29.

**ríge**: **kingdom**, Prologue 158. Genitive: *rígi* February 6, October 8, 22. Dative: *rígu* January 23, Epilogue 359. Accusative: *ríge* Prologue 70, January 16.

**rígrad**: A feminine noun meaning **king-folk**, Prologue 13, 20, 82, 278, Epilogue 41, 229, 300, 564. Dative: *rígraid* Prologue 12, July 13, November 10, December 23. Accusative: *rígraid-n* Prologue 21, 271, Epilogue 301, 565.

**rím**: A feminine noun meaning **a numbering** (compare to the Welsh *rhif* <note>original: "Cymr. rhif"</note>), Prologue 268, Ascoli 210. Genitive: *rímæ* St. Gall Glosses 181^b 8.

**rímim**: **I reckon**. Preterite: *ro rím* *Saltair na Rann* 114. Passive present indicative third-person plural: *rímter* Prologue 286, Epilogue 46. Preterite third-person singular: *ro rímed* March 18.

**1. rind**: **a point** or **a headland** (compare to the Welsh *rhyn* <note>original: "Cymr. rhyn"</note>), Ascoli 210. Plural accusative: *rindi* April 26, August 27. Dative: *rindit* Prologue 37, 238.

**2. rind**: **the termination of a metrical line**. Plural accusative: *rindi* Epilogue 84. Regarding the terms *rinn* and *airdrinn*, see O'Molloy page 165, and O'Donovan’s Grammar page 417. See also O'Davoren's Glossary numbers 1342, 1352, 1430.

**3. rind**: A neuter noun meaning **a star**, January 30. Plural nominative: *rind*, *rinn*, Ascoli 209. **Compounds:**
*   **rindmas**: **star-beautiful**. Singular genitive masculine: *rindmais* page 154. Singular dative masculine: Epilogue 378.
*   **rindbalc**: page 134, **star-strong**.
*   **rindnem**: A neuter noun meaning **starry heaven**, May 29.

**rindach**: **starry**. Singular accusative masculine: May 22.

**rindard**: A feminine noun; the name of the **Félire-meter** <note>The specific meter used in the Martyrology of Oengus</note>, page 4. A compound of the second definition of **rind** and **ard** (high).

**ríngim**: **I torture**. Preterite passive third-person singular: *ro rínged* February 14.

**ríth**: **ruth** <note>meaning a run or a course</note>, **the act of running**, or **a course**. Prologue 28, Ascoli 205. Plural nominative: *retha* Epilogue 274. Dative: *ríthib* Prologue 69. This is the verbal noun of **rethim** <note>I run</note>.

**1. ro, ru**: A verbal particle equivalent to the Latin *pro* <note>original: "pro"</note>, the Greek *pro* <note>original: "πρό"</note>, and the Sanskrit *pra* <note>original: "pra"</note>. Before vowels, it is generally reduced to *r*. In the perfect tense of **dogntu** <note>likely "do-gníu," I do</note>, it appears as *ri-*.
*   (a) It changes preterite (simple past) forms into perfects or pluperfects: *ro rádis* (you have said) January 9; *ro sonnta* Prologue 33; *ro uctha* Prologue 45; *ro-da ort-som* Prologue 57; *ro-da-crochsat* Prologue 73; *ro-s-taurus* June 26; *dorósat* Prologue 91; *do-ru-rmius*, *do-rui-rmius* Epilogue 40, 229; *fo-m-ru-* Epilogue 28; *im-ro-rdus* Prologue 20, 21; *do-r-alus* Prologue 5; *as-r-éracht* Prologue 92; *ad-r-annad* April 5; *r-orta* Prologue 65; *do-r-indnacht* November 12; *do-r-ortad* May 27; *ad-r-eth* August 30, November 6; *fris-r-ócaib* May 5; *do-rí-gnius* Epilogue 111 (from *de-ro-gníus*); *do-rí-gnis* Epilogue 506; *do-rí-gni* Epilogue 106. Similarly, *arareilced* from *ar-an-ro-léced*.

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

(b) it occurs before old perfects <note>past tenses indicating completed action</note>: *ro gádsa* Epilogue 412, *ad-rói-thach* (from *ad-ro-tetach*) Epilogue 300, 301, *ro ráith* Prologue 28, *ar-ro-chiúir* Prologue 67, 127, *ro selgatar* Prologue 29: after a negative: *nad ro thuirmed* Epilogue 122.

(c) it gives a present tense verb the force of a perfect <note>completed</note> tense: *ro phráidchi* Prologue 164, *ro chruidí* Epilogue 136.

(d) it occurs with the subjunctive <note>the mood used for possibilities, wishes, or uncertain actions</note>: for example, *ro-mm-ain* Prologue 18, *ro-nn-ain* April 11, 22, etc. *dorónsa* (*do-ro-gn* . .) Prologue 268, 269, *ma d-a-rónaid* Prologue 186, *ro beosa* Prologue 273, *ro-n-bé* Epilogue 56, *ro-n-beth* Prologue 241, *ro ge* Epilogue 364, *ro fésser* February 4, *ro-p* January 24, *ropat* January 18, December 18, *ro ere-siu* Epilogue 427, 431, *ro-n-snádat* January 23, *do-n-ro-gra* March 28, December 14, *do-n-r-ema* April 13, *do-m-r-airbera* Epilogue 65, *co-tam-r-óither* Epilogue 69. After *con'*: *con-dom-roi-b* Prologue 11, Epilogue 359. And with an infixed personal pronoun before *bia*, meaning "it will be" <note>original Latin: "erit"</note> (which was originally subjunctive), *ro-n-bia*, January 13.

2. **ro-**, **r'**, intensive prefix: see **ro-chnet**, **roglach**, **rolaínd**, **romaith**, **romar**, **romuil**.

**roach**: Epilogue 129, an obscure word of two syllables, possibly from *ro-sech*, root *seq*: "verbose" is a mere guess. *The B. manuscript has roat, that is <note>original Latin: ".i."</note> rofot, meaning "great length."*

**rochnet**: **a great sigh, much sorrow**, Epilogue 171, accusative: *rochneit* August 28. See **cnet**.

**rochtain**: August 4. Leabhar Breac manuscript: **arrival**.

**ro-cluniur**: **I hear**, present indicative second-person singular: *no clunter* Prologue 282 (read as <note>original Latin: "leg."</note> *roclunter*), imperative second-person singular: *cluinte* Epilogue 314, 365, 425, *Milan Glosses* 136ª 10, present subjunctive third-person singular: *ro cloathar*, future third-person singular: *ro cechladar*, perfect second-person singular: (*manid*) *cúala* June 13: third-person singular: *-cúalae* (from <note>original Latin: "ex"</note> *cúalove*), preterite third-person plural: *ro clotha* August 24.

**róe**: A feminine noun meaning **battle** (compare to the Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *rhae*), singular genitive: *roe* April 26, August 27 (where it is two syllables): *tri roe rinde*, that is <note>original Latin: ".i."</note> *tria rinde roi*, that is <note>original Latin: ".i."</note> **battles** <note>original Irish: "catha"</note>, P.

**róen**: **road**, plural accusative: *róenu* May 27, June 19, Epilogue 322.

**ro-fetar**: **I know**, Ascoli 328-9, subjunctive second-person singular: *ro-s-fésser* February 4, *dian-fésser* October 24: preterite passive third-person singular (used with the meaning of a present tense): *ro fess* Epilogue 17, *ní fess* Prologue 113, *ní con fess* Prologue 135: past passive participle nominative plural: *ní fessa* Prologue 76: participle of necessity: *fissi* Epilogue 335 and May 20 in the Leabhar Breac version.

**rogdae**: **chosen**, Prologue 221, related to *rogu* "choice," *Würzburg Glosses* 9ª 23.

**roglach**: (from *ro-galach*) **very valiant**, Prologue 94. See **gal**.

**rogrinn**: **very fine, very comely**, page 46. See **grinn**.

**rói**: A feminine noun meaning **a field or plain** (compare to the Latin *rus* <note>meaning "countryside" or "field"</note> and the Avestan <note>original: "Zend"</note> *ravañh*), dative: *rói*, February 14.

**ro-iccim**: **I come, I reach**, present subjunctive first-person plural: *-rísam* December 17, past subjunctive: *-rísed* Prologue 284, future: *roicfa* Epilogue 55, perfect third-person singular: *-ránic* May 2, Epilogue 17, *ro-b-ánic-si* *Würzburg Glosses* 16ª 40, third-person plural: *ráncatar* Prologue 78, passive perfect third-person singular: *rícht*: verbal noun: **ríchtu**, which see <note>original Latin: "q.v."</note>.

**rolaínd**: **vehement, zealous**, March 12, May 21: *laínd* (glossed as <note>original Latin: "gl."</note> **sharp/keen** <note>original Latin: "acer"</note>), Cormac's Glossary.

**ro-laimur**: *rulaimur*, *Würzburg Glosses* 17ᶜ 21, imperfect first-person plural: *ro-lammis* February 27, where there is a <term>tmesis</term> <note>a grammatical term where a compound word is separated into parts by other words</note>: see **lamiur**, from which comes *dia lammis* July 25.

**roléir**: **very pious**, August 26. See **léir**.

**romaith**: **excellent**, April 10, Epilogue 161, feminine accusative: September 17. See **maith**.

**romar**: *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 241, line 8, masculine singular genitive: *romáir* Epilogue 235 (rhymes with *sobáil*), feminine singular dative: *romoir* January 31. See **már**, **mór**.
