<header>GLOSSARIAL INDEX.</header>

**romuir**: **a great sea, a spring tide**, singular dative Epilogue 42; accusative November 3, 11, December 8; genitive **romra**: *is tond romra bhádes* <note>original Irish: "it is a wave of the spring tide that drowns"</note>, Book of Leinster 98^a 40. See **muir**.

**rop, rob**: **may it be, let it be** <note>the subjunctive form of the verb "to be"</note>, January 24, March 17, October 19, December 19; plural **ropat**, December 18.

**ropam**: **I was**, page 54, line 2; a Middle Irish formation, like *ropsat* or *rapsat* in the Book of Leinster 208^a.

**ror**: (equivalent to the Greek *προσπρο* <note>prospro</note> and Sanskrit *prapra*), **a verbal particle**; *do-m-ror-bae* (see **dororbanim**), Prologue 25, and see *Zeitschrift für celtische Philologie* III. 471; *fo-ror-cennta*, Prologue 85; *fo-ror-bairt*, Prologue 173 (standing for *for-ror-c-* or *for-ror-b-*). Before the verb *eb-laing*, the second *r* of *ror* is assimilated to the *l* of the root: *rol-eblaing*, March 5. Compare with *fo-r-rul-eb-langtar* (glossed in Latin as *subsiluerunt* <note>original Latin: "they leaped up"</note>) Milan Glosses 129^d 21, and *eibh-ling no ro eibh-ling .i. do ling* <note>original Irish: "leaped or has leaped, that is, he leaps"</note> in O'Clery’s Glossary.

**rorath**: **great grace**, dative Prologue 99. See **rath**.

**roréil**: **very clear**, August 26, R^1, Leabhar Breac. See **réil**.

**ro-sagim, ro sechim, ro sochim**: **I reach**, third person singular *ro soich*, page 12, Ascoli 246; present subjunctive second person singular *rois*, Epilogue 146; preterite <note>past tense</note> *roacht*, *Saltair na Rann* 6466; perfect third person singular *rosiacht* (from the earlier form *ro sisegt), page 40; third person plural *ro šiachtatar*, Prologue 70.

**ross** (Masculine): (1) **a wood**, (2) **a promontory**, singular genitive *roiss*, January 30, April 28, 30, September 6, 17; dative *russ*, April 10. Related to Welsh *rhawd* and Sanskrit *prastha*.

**rót** (Masculine): **a road**, plural accusative *rótu*, Prologue 29. Related to Welsh *rhawd*, Latin *via rupta* <note>original Latin: "a broken way"</note>, and French *route*.

**ro ucc, rucc**: **the perfect third person singular of "berim"** <note>meaning "he/she has carried" or "brought"</note>, August 6, December 14; passive third person plural *ro uctha*, Prologue 45.

**rúad**: **red, ruddy** (related to Welsh *rhudd*), Prologue 94, 221; feminine singular dative *rúaid*, October 16.

**ruad-gorm**: **fiery red**, masculine singular accusative Epilogue 260.

**rúam** (Feminine): **cemetery**, Prologue 192, October 28; plural nominative *rúama*, Prologue 71, and perhaps Prologue 211. The singular nominative (originally the singular dative) is *ruaim* on page 206, line 31. This word was borrowed from **Rome** (*Róma*) because it was the burial place of many confessors and martyrs (*Tripartite Life of Patrick*, 656).

**rúamach**: **possessing cemeteries**? March 5. In July 20 and August 6, *rúamach* may mean **Roman**.

**rúamdae**: **Roman**? **roomy**? The H manuscript glosses this as *catharda no uasal* <note>original Irish: "civic or noble"</note>; however, the meaning remains quite obscure.

**rúanaid**: **strong**, Prologue 256, meaning *laidir* <note>strong</note>; masculine plural nominative *tri ánraith rúanaidi rodana* <note>original Irish: "three strong, very bold champions"</note>, Book of Leinster 225^b 24.

**rucc**: see **roucc**.

**rudhrach**: page 182, line 18, **gloom**?

**rudrad**: Prologue 206, seems to mean **the acquisition of ownership through long use** <note>a legal term known as prescription</note>. In Epilogue 129, the reading of *rudrad* or *rudrach* is uncertain.

**ruidiud**: **a reddening, blushing**, singular accusative Epilogue 145; singular nominative in *ruidiud tic isin gruaid* <note>original Irish: "a reddening that comes into the cheek"</note>, Cormac's Glossary under the word *nare* <note>original Latin: "modesty/shame"</note>.

**ruidiur**: see **conruidiur**.

**ruiri** (Masculine): **a sovereign**, Prologue 14; singular genitive *ruirech*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 327, line 16; vocative *á ruiri* <note>O sovereign</note>, Prologue 285. Derived from the form *rorix; see **rí**.

**rún** (Feminine): (related to Welsh *rhin*) **mystery**, Ascoli 218; singular genitive *rúne*; dative *rúin*, April 22; plural dative *rúnaib*, July 30, November 20; accusative *rúna*, January 12. Related to Gothic *rūna* and Anglo-Saxon *rūn*.

**rúnach**: **mysterious**, masculine singular accusative November 6.

**rúndae, rúnde**: **mysterious**, Ascoli 218; masculine singular vocative *rúndai*, Epilogue 458; plural nominative *rúndai*, Epilogue 274.

**s, sn**: **infixed personal pronoun**.
I. **her / it** <note>original Latin: "eam"</note>: *ní-s-tarcai*, June 29; *ro-s-taurus*, June 26; *do-s-ruimdemar*, Epilogue 6; *ro-sm-bé*, Epilogue 56 (in manuscript *L*).
II. **them** <note>original Latin: "eos, eas, ea"</note>: *ní-s-gegnetar*...

<meta>This page continues the glossarial index of Old Irish terms, moving from the letter 'R' into 'S'. It focuses on emphatic pronouns and various nouns related to social roles, time, and labor.</meta>

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

May 19, *no-s-túirfem* <note>meaning: "we will search them"</note>, Prologue 289; *no-s-molammar* <note>meaning: "we praise them"</note>, January 17; *fo-s-dáil* <note>meaning: "he distributed them"</note>, July 15.

I. **sa, se**, emphatic pronoun <note>original: "emphasizing pronoun"</note>:
*   **Singular 1:** -sa, -se.
*   **Singular 2:** -su, -siu.
*   **Singular 3:** masculine and neuter *som*, *sium*; feminine *si*.
*   **Plural 1:** -ni, -nai.
*   **Plural 2:** -si.
*   **Plural 3:** som, seom.

**Examples:**
*   **Singular 1:** *am rath-sa* <note>I am grace</note>, Epilogue 165; *am triamain tróg-sa* <note>I am weary and wretched</note>, Prologue 26; *ro béo-sa* <note>may I be</note>, Prologue 273; *dorón-sa* <note>I have done</note>, Prologue 268, 269; *frim-sa* <note>against me</note>, December 18; *mo dér-sa* <note>my tears</note>, Epilogue 400; *mo chneit trúiag-se* <note>my wretched sigh</note>, Epilogue 314.
*   **Plural 1:** *ar-ríg-nai* <note>our kings</note>, Prologue 256; *álmi-ni* <note>we pray</note>, January 10; *úan-ni* <note>from us</note>, January 28; *sluindfem-ni* <note>we will declare</note>, Prologue 287.
*   **Singular 2:** *trit-su* <note>through you</note>, Epilogue 438; *duit-siu* <note>to you</note>, Epilogue 335, 338; *do réir-siu* <note>according to your will</note>, Prologue 269; *fort láim-siu* <note>on your hand</note>, Prologue 273; *i imbí-siu* <note>in which you are</note>, Prologue 274; *ro ere-siu* <note>you have granted</note>, Epilogue 427, 431.
*   **Plural 2:** *lib-si* <note>with you</note>, Epilogue 397; *i bar gnáis-si* <note>in your company</note>, Epilogue 375.
*   **Singular 3:** *a mind-som* <note>their diadem</note>, *a rann-som* <note>their part</note>, Prologue 257, 258; *tim-som*, 259; *ann-som* <note>in him/it</note>, 260.
*   **Plural 3:** *it sóir-seom* <note>they are free</note>, *it cóim-seom* <note>they are dear</note>, September 2; *a rrúam-som* <note>their Rome/city</note>, *a slúag-som* <note>their host</note>, October 28; *ro-da-ort-som* <note>he killed them</note>, *a-nguin-som* <note>their wounding</note>, *iarna saethur gair-som* <note>after their short labor</note>, Prologue 57.

**-sa, -sea, -se**, meaning **this**, used after a noun with a definite article <note>original: "after an articulated substantive"</note>, or an adjective agreeing with it, or a noun governed by such a substantive: *ind rígs-a* <note>this king</note>, Prologue 27, Epilogue 405; *na slóga-sa* <note>these hosts</note>, Prologue 28; *na slóga-sa*, *in maith mór-sa* <note>this great good</note>, Prologue 266, 267; *na mís már-sa* <note>these great months</note>, *in grian búana-sa* <note>this lasting sun</note>, *in slúaiged n-án-sa* <note>this noble hosting</note>, *an núall-sa* <note>this cry</note>, Prologue 301-304; *ind rí nélsa* <note>the king of these clouds</note>, Epilogue 398; *asin tsním-sa* <note>out of this grief</note>, 407; *in pauperán trúag-sa* <note>this wretched little pauper</note>, Epilogue 408; *tarsin báig-se* <note>over this battle/contest</note>, *in tslúaig-se* <note>of this host</note>, Epilogue 315, 316.

**sab** is defined <note>original: "glossed"</note> as an adjective meaning **brave** <note>original Irish: "calma"</note> by O'Davoren, entry 1433, and as **firm or strong** <note>original Irish: "sonairt no láidir"</note> by O'Clery. This may be the meaning in July 1, October 17, and Epilogue 272, where it governs the genitive case. However, in April 12, June 23, September 21, November 10, and December 14, **sab** seems to mean **ruler** <note>original: "dynast"</note> or **champion**; plural nominative *sabaid*, Laws i. 54, l. 7; O'Davoren entry 1415; and *saba*, Laws v. 458, 20. See Ascoli 236.

**sacart** Masculine noun, **priest** (derived from the Latin *sacerdos* <note>original: "sacerdos"</note>), Ascoli 234; singular genitive *sacairt*, accusative *sacart*, Epilogue 548; plural genitive Epilogue 269. It appears as *sacard*, *sacardd*, and *sacart* in the Old Irish glosses.

**saegul, saigul**, **lifetime** or **age** (derived from the Latin *saeculum* <note>original: "saeculum"</note>, from *saeclum*, *saitlom*, which is related to the Welsh word *hoedl* <note>original: "hoedl"</note>), Ascoli 223; singular genitive *saeguil*, Epilogue 204.

**sáer, sáir** Masculine noun, a **craftsman** or **wright** (related to the Welsh *saer* <note>original: "saer"</note>), Ascoli 222; singular genitive *sáir*, August 14, September 9.

**saeth**, **tribulation** or **suffering**, Ascoli 223; singular genitive *saítho*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 296; plural genitive April 3; dative *saethaib*, Prologue 69; accusative *saéthu*, Prologue 32.

**sáethar**, **labor** or **toil**, Epilogue 227; genitive *sáithir*, Armagh 184^b; dative *sáethur*, Prologue 59; accusative *sáethar* (should likely read *sáethar*), Epilogue 298. From this comes *sáithraigur*, meaning **I labor** <note>original Latin: "laboro"</note>.

**sáethrach**, **laborious** or **toilsome**, page 14, line 31.

**saiche** Feminine noun, **badness** or **evil**, dative *saichi*, Prologue 298, 318; a derivative of *saich*, Ascoli 234, *Lebor na hUidre* 17^a 23; related to the Latin *sequior* <note>original Latin: "sequior", meaning "following" or "inferior"</note>.

**saidbir** (from *so-adbir*), **wealthy**, May 15; plural nominative *saidbri*, Prologue 162. The opposite of *daidbir* <note>meaning "poor"</note>.

**saidbre** Feminine noun, **wealth**, dative *sadbri*, November 9. The opposite of *daidbre* <note>meaning "poverty"</note>.

**saigthi**, Prologue 162; the meaning is obscure, perhaps a mistake for **saichthi*, related to *saiche*, see above.

**sailm-chétlaid**, *psalmist*, p. 86, l. 4.
**sair**, *eastwards*, Nov. 11 Leabhar Breac <note>original: "LB."</note> *Félire*.
**sairde**, *eastern*, accusative singular neuter, March 5.
**saithe**, *sathe* (masculine) *swarm, multitude*, Jan. 25, May 28, July 23; singular dative *saithiu*, accusative *saithe* Aug. 6; plural nominative *in tsathi* <note>meaning: "the swarms"; original Latin gloss: "examina"</note> Milan Glosses 90ᵇ 7; dative *saithib* Sept. 30: Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *haid*.
**sál** (neuter) *brine, sea*, accusative *sál* March 5, Aug. 25, Sept. 10 (Latin *sal* <note>original: "sāl"</note> [salt], Greek *hals* <note>original: "ἅλς"</note>, genitive *halos* <note>original: "ἁλός"</note> [salt or sea]). Compound: *sálmuir* (see below).
**sále** (masculine or neuter?) *sea, salt water*, genitive *sáli* July 9; *R¹* uses this for "the wave of the sea" <note>original: "tuind in tsaili"</note>, Petrie's *Tara* 111: Welsh *heli* [brine].
**sallad**, *the act of singing*, Prologue 322; *sallann* Dec. 31 *R¹*. Latin *psallo* <note>original: "psallo"</note> [I sing or play the harp], Greek *psallō* <note>original: "ψάλλω"</note> [I sing].
**salm** (masculine) (Welsh *salm*), *psalm*, Prologue 218, Sept. 11, Epilogue 155, Ascoli 224; plural dative *salmaib*, Epilogue 190. Compounds: *salm-chetal*, *psalmody* <note>the singing of psalms</note>, p. 130, l. 8.
**sálmuir** (neuter) *salt sea, main sea*, plural genitive *sálmuire*, Epilogue 237.
**samail**, *samuil* (Welsh *hafal* [equal]), *a simile, similitude*, June 16, Nov. 11, Ascoli 228. From this comes the deponent verb *samlur* [I compare]. See the unstressed form *amail* [like].
**samain** (feminine) *assembly, All Saints' Day*, Nov. 1, accusative singular Nov. 1: Sanskrit *samana* [gathering].
**-sa** (-n, -s, -s-), the relative pronoun: *for-sa-torchair* <note>meaning: "on whom fell/died"</note>, Epilogue 361; *la-s-r-orta* <note>meaning: "with whom were slain"</note> Prologue 65; *la[s]-sceith* <note>meaning: "with which he vomited"</note> Feb. 16.
**sanas** (feminine) *whisper, muttered prayer*, accusative *sanais* March 15; *sanasa saeba*, p. 204, *seems to mean "bad stories"* <note>literally: "false whispers"</note>: compare Welsh *hanes* 'history.'
**sanct** (Welsh *sant*, from Latin *sanctus* [holy or saint]), June 12, Nov. 11, p. 182.
**sár** (neuter) *outrage*, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* I. 484, l. 7, accusative singular Jan. 6. From this comes *sáirigur*, meaning "I violate" <note>original Latin: "violo"</note>. Welsh *sarháu* [to insult].
**scarad** (masculine) (Welsh *ysgar*), *separation, severance*, Epilogue 368, 424. This is the verbal noun of *scaraim*, *I separate*, Ascoli 286; related to *scorim* (see below) and Old Norse *skeran*, German *scheren*, etc. (Zupitza 154).
**sceithim**, *I vomit*, preterite singular 3rd person, *-sceith* Feb. 16. Welsh *chwydu*.
**scél** (neuter) (Welsh *chwedl*), *tidings, a tale*, Ascoli 292–3, Feb. 10, March 27, May 9, July 12, Dec. 21; plural nominative *scél* Aug. 24; (*mór*) *scél* [great tidings] Prologue 24; dative *scélaib* Sept. 24.
**scíss**, *fatigue, weariness*, Ascoli 294, dative singular Epilogue 38; accusative *scél cen scís* <note>meaning: "a story without weariness"</note> *Thesaurus* II. 293, l. 18; derived from *scíth* (see below).
**scíth**, *weary*, Ascoli 294, Dec. 31 *R¹*. From this comes *scíthigur*, meaning "I grow weary" <note>original Latin: "defitiscor"</note>; related to Sanskrit *kshitá* 'exhausted' (Strachan).
**scor**, *a herd, a multitude*, plural dative *scoraib* Prologue 81: Old High German *skara*, now *schar* [a troop or host].
**scorim**, *scuirim, I unyoke, I desist*, preterite active plural 3rd person, *scorsit* May 17. Verbal noun: *scor*, Würzburg Glosses 12ᶜ 46. See *scarad*.
**scothad** (more correctly *scathad*) *imthechta*, *shortening a journey*, p. 40.
**scret**, *a scream*, plural *screta na nóiden*, p. 180, *the cries of the infants*.
**scríbaím**, *I write* (from Latin *scribo*), Ascoli 295, preterite active singular 3rd person, *ro scríb* May 6. Verbal noun *scríbend*, St. Gall Glosses 3ᵇ 28. Welsh *ysgrifen*.
**scríbnid**, *scríbnid* (masculine) *a scribe*, Ascoli 296, July 8.
**scrín**, p. 76, *a shrine*, from Latin *scrinium* [a chest or case], from which also comes Welsh *ysgrin*.
**scrútaím**, *I search out, investigate*, Ascoli 296 (from Latin *scrūtor* [I examine]), preterite active singular 1st person, *ro scrútus*, Epilogue 109; subjunctive singular 3rd person, *ara scrúta*, Würzburg Glosses 31ᵇ 10.

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

<term>schuchaim</term>, *I depart, pass away, vanish*; third-person singular perfect, *ro scáich*, Prologue 121, *ro fir-scáich* <note>meaning: "it has truly vanished"</note> Prologue 84. With an attached pronoun: *ro scáich-i*, Prologue 177; *roscaich-e* Prologue 193 in the *Félire* of Oengus <note>original: "F. LB." refers to the Franciscan and Leabhar Breac manuscripts</note>. Verbal noun: *scaichsin*, *Saltair na Rann* 2904.

<term>sé</term> (from the root *sveks*, Welsh <note>original: "Cymr."</note> *chwech*), *six*, May 13, Sept. 18 in the *R¹* manuscript; nominative dual *dá sé* <note>meaning: "twice six"</note>, July 10; *da sé ndéc ndaglaech* <note>meaning: "twelve goodly heroes"</note> in *Lebor na hUidre* 67ᵃ 19, where *sé* and *déc* <note>meaning: "six" and "ten" (sixteen)</note> are treated as neuters.

<term>secal, segal</term>, *rye*, p. 112, from Latin *secale*.

<term>sech</term>, *preposition with the accusative case: past, beyond*, March 28, May 5, Oct. 19, Epilogue 119, Ascoli 250. Welsh *heb*.

<term>sech</term> *conjunction: since, yet, although*, July 30, Epilogue 195 in the *Leinstermanuscript* <note>original: "L."</note>, Ascoli 250, 251; *sech ní mór ní becc* <note>meaning: "neither more nor less"</note>, p. 4, l. 15.

<term>secht-n</term>, *seven*, undeclined, Prologue 2, April 9, June 27, Epilogue 120, 125. Welsh *saith*.

<term>sechtae</term>, *septenary* <note>a group of seven</note>, *or of the seven things*; masculine genitive singular *sechtai*, May 15.

<term>sechtanach</term>, *septenary*; masculine genitive singular *sechtanaig*, p. 132, l. 5.

<term>sechtmoga</term>, *seventy*, April 3 in the *Leinstermanuscript* <note>original: "L."</note>, Nov. 19 in the *Franciscan* and *Leabhar Breac* manuscripts. Ascoli 272.

<term>seimle, semle</term>, *see soimle.*

<term>séis</term>, *thought, notion* (from Latin *sensus*), Epilogue 138, where it is the title of a book by Saint Hilary; accusative singular *séis*, Würzburg Glosses 14ᵈ 2; but accusative plural *sésu*, Milan Glosses 37ᵃ 10, Ascoli 240.

<term>sell</term>, *eye?* dative plural *sellaib*, July 4, where the commentator <note>original: "glossator"</note> interprets *sellaib* as a verbal form meaning *you have seen* <note>original: "vidisti"</note>, Ascoli 237. What is the meaning of *re srethaib seall*, p. 68? <note>likely "with ranks of eyes"</note>

<term>sen</term>, *old* (Welsh *hên*, Sanskrit *sána*, Greek *enos* <note>original: "ἔνος"</note>, Latin *senior*, Gothic *sinista*). Compounds: *sen-argat*, *old money*, p. 185; *sen-chathir*, *an old city*, nominative plural *senchathraig*, Prologue 205; and see below *Sen-Phátric* <note>Old Patrick</note>, *Sen-Phól* <note>Old Paul</note>, *Sen-Sinchell* <note>Old Sinchell</note>.

<term>senad</term> (*senud* in the Würzburg Glosses 9ᶜ 28), Welsh *senedd*, from Latin *synodus* <note>synod or assembly</note>, Prologue 110 (*cáin-senad* <note>law-synod</note>), Epilogue 93; genitive singular *senaid*, July 12, Nov. 3, p. 116. The scholar Vendryes would derive *senad* from *senatus* <note>senate</note> and *senud* from *synodus*.

<term>sénaim</term>, *I sign with the cross, I bless* (from Latin *signo*), Ascoli 242; second-person singular imperative *sén*, Prologue 1; Welsh *swyno*, meaning "to charm or cast a spell."

<term>sennad</term> Prologue 46: found in the adverb *asennad* <note>at last</note>.

<term>seol</term>, *a course*, Prologue 43. Welsh *heol*.

<term>-seom</term>, Sept. 2. See the entries for *i, sa, se* <note>emphatic pronouns</note>.

<term>serb</term>, *bitter, sour* (from the root *svervo-*, Welsh *chwerw*): Ascoli 239. Compounds: *serb-charcar* (feminine), *a bitter dungeon*, dative plural *charcraib*, Oct. 15; *serb-chroch* (feminine), *a bitter cross*, dative plural *chrochaib*, May 13; *serb-gábud* (masculine), *bitter danger*, dative plural *gáibthib*, Dec. 2.

<term>serblinn</term> *(-lenn?)* 134, meaning obscure.

<term>serc</term> (feminine), *love*, Prologue 148, Epilogue 12; genitive singular *serce*, dative *seirc*, Prologue 186, accusative *seirc*, Feb. 11, May 8. See *mór-serc* <note>great love</note> and Ascoli 238, 239. From this comes *conásercim* (interpreting the Latin *condilector* <note>I delight in</note>), Würzburg Glosses 3ᵈ 9. Welsh *serch* (masculine).

<term>sercach</term>, *loving, amorous*, Jan. 14; masculine genitive singular *sercaig*, Sept. 25. Welsh *serchog*.

<term>sernim</term>, *I declare or arrange*; third-person plural present indicative *sernait*, Aug. 31, Oct. 31 [dependent form *ní sernat*, meaning *they do not express*, interpreting the Latin phrase *neque... conserunt uerba* <note>meaning: "nor do they join words"</note>, Milan Glosses 31ᵃ 19]; second-person singular imperative *sern*, March 15; third-person singular past passive *ro sreth* <note>it was spread/arranged</note>, Aug. 25; plural second-person *ro sretha*, Prologue 138.

<term>*sertim</term>, *I strengthen*; third-person singular preterite *ro-n-sert*, Epilogue 11; a verb derived from *seirt*, meaning "strength," according to the O'Clery Glossary.

<term>sescae</term>, *sixty*; genitive *sescat*, Prologue 328, Oct. 30 (*sescot* in *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 254, l. 15); accusative *sescait*, Dec. 23.

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

<term>seser, sesser</term>, meaning a board of six men <note>original Latin: *seviratus*</note>, May 13, Ascoli 236.

<term>séssilbe</term>, feminine noun, *tumult*, Ascoli 240; accusative singular *séssilbi-n* Prologue 183; dative *o sésselbi ádbuil* <note>meaning: "from a great tumult"</note>, *Leabhar Breac* 6ᵇ.

**1. <term>sét</term>**, *likeness*, June 15; *séd* meaning *samhail* <note>meaning: likeness or similarity</note>, O’Clery's Glossary. From the roots *semto, *semti, *semtu*, cognate with the Latin word for "at the same time" <note>original: *simul*</note> and the Greek word for "together with" <note>original: ἅμα</note>. Compare: *ní pu séit samil 7 ind líthe* <note>meaning: "it was not a likeness or similarity of the festival"</note> in the *Old Irish Thesaurus* I. 495; and *in fáinne . . . co ngéim do na fríth sét na samail do gemaib in domain riam* <note>meaning: "the ring... with a gem of which no likeness or similarity was ever found among the gems of the world before"</note>, *Leabhar Breac* 138ᵃ 12.

**2. <term>sét</term>**, masculine noun, *way* (Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *hynt*, Gothic *sinþs*), Ascoli 253; plural dative *sétaib* Prologue 326, April 3, May 13, September 8, October 9. Hence <term>sétaigim</term>, *I travel* <note>original Latin: *vio*</note>, and <term>sétaigte</term>, glossed as *travelers* <note>original Latin: *vianttium*</note>, Milan Glosses 82ᵈ 4.

<term>sethir, sethraib</term>, *sisters*; see <term>siur</term>.

<term>sex</term>, from the Latin word for "sixth" <note>original: *sextus*</note>, March 27.

<term>sí</term>, *she* (Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *hí*); *is sí* Prologue 147 (or perhaps this is *iss í*?).

**<term>-sí</term>**, pronominal suffix, 2nd person plural, as in *n-gnáis-si* <note>meaning: "your company"</note> Epilogue 375, *lib-si* <note>meaning: "with you"</note> Epilogue 397.

<term>ro síachtatar</term>, *they have reached*, Prologue 701; see <term>ro sechim</term>.

<term>síanach</term>, *noisy*; dative singular feminine *síanaig* Nov. 1. *sían* meaning *glór* <note>meaning: noise or voice</note>, and *síanaigh* meaning *gloraigh* <note>meaning: noisy</note> in O’Clery's Glossary. Perhaps related to the Welsh word for "sound" <note>original: *sain*</note>?

<term>sían</term>, adverb, *west*, Nov. 11 in the *Leabhar Breac*, *Franciscan*, and *Brussels* manuscripts. Meaning *backwards* on page 154.

<term>síd</term>, neuter noun, *peace*, July 5; accusative singular April 2, July 18, Sept. 21 in the *R1* and *Leinster* manuscripts. *sith* in the *Franciscan* manuscript, Ascoli 261. Hence <term>síedaigim</term>, "I pacify"; compare the Welsh word for "peace" <note>original: *hedd*</note>.

<term>side</term>, genitive *sidi* Sept. 10. The meaning is obscure; perhaps a *swelling*, from the root *svidio*, cognate and synonymous with the Welsh word for "tumor" <note>original: *chwydd*</note>. Or perhaps it means *brightness*, compare the Lithuanian word "to shine" <note>original: *svidėti* / *glänzen*</note> or the Latin word for "star" <note>original: *sidus*</note>. It is unlikely to be the modern word *sidhe* meaning "blast."

<term>sídflaith</term>, feminine noun, *peace-kingdom, realm of peace*; accusative singular May 10, July 13. *sídflaith* meaning "of heaven" <note>original: *nime*</note>, manuscript H. 3. 18, page 249.

<term>sidit</term>, found in the phrase *for sidit*, meaning "swiftly," April 16. *sidid* meaning "swift" <note>original: *luath*</note>, manuscript H. 3. 18, page 289.

<term>síll</term>, neuter noun, *seed, race* (Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *hil*), Prologue 131, Epilogue 439; singular genitive *síl* page 14, Nov. 10, Dec. 25; dative *síl* Prologue 340, Jan. 1; accusative *síl*, Ascoli 255. Also found in Prologue 340 and July 15. Hence <term>sílaigur</term>, "I sow" <note>original Latin: *sero*</note>.

<term>sillab</term>, feminine noun, *syllable*, Ascoli 255; plural nominative *síllæba* pages 4, 14; Old Irish *sillaba*, Ascoli 255; Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *sillaf*.

**<term>-sin</term>**, *that*, Ascoli 260. Used after nouns preceded by the article: *cosin buaid-sin* <note>meaning: "with that victory"</note> June 20, Aug. 2, Oct. 12; *gair-sin* <note>meaning: "that cry" or "that short time"</note> Oct. 20; *réim-sin* <note>meaning: "that course"</note> Oct. 16; *lín-sin* <note>meaning: "that number"</note>, *sluag-sin* <note>meaning: "that host"</note> Epilogue 31, 32. It also follows adjectives agreeing with such nouns: *cosin dúnud már-sin* <note>meaning: "with that great encampment"</note> June 20; and see *án-sin* <note>meaning: "that splendid"</note> June 20; *moir-sin* <note>meaning: "that great"</note>, *maith-sin* <note>meaning: "that good"</note> Aug. 2; *cáin-sin* <note>meaning: "that fair"</note> Oct. 12; *búan-sin* <note>meaning: "that lasting"</note> Epilogue 30.

<term>sinnad</term>, *the act of reviling* or *railing*; dative singular Prologue 47. A derivative of *sin(n)*, meaning "mockery" <note>original Latin: *irrisio*</note>, Milan Glosses 44ᶜ 10. Compare the Welsh word for "reproach" or "scolding" <note>original Latin: *senn / jurgium, objurgatio*</note>. Also compare the Old Norse *Loka senna*, meaning the "railing of Loki."

<term>sír</term>, *long* (Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *hir*); plural dative *síraib* May 13. Comparative form: *sía* <note>meaning: longer</note> (Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *hwy*), Ascoli 256, *Book of Leinster* 69ᵃ 5.

<term>sírecht</term>, accusative singular Epilogue 332; *melody*? *music*? Perhaps equivalent to the Welsh word for "longing" <note>original: *hiraeth*</note>.

<term>sithbe</term>, a *pole*; metaphorically a *chieftain* or *leader*, Aug. 19. The marginal note <margin>.i. druim talman fota</margin> <note>meaning: "a long ridge of land"</note> on page 186 refers to this.

**<term>-siu</term>**, an emphasizing pronoun for the 2nd person singular. See entry **I. sa, se**.

**<term>-sium</term>**, Epilogue 165. See entry **I. sa, se**.

<term>siur</term>, feminine noun, *sister*, July 6, Dec. 14. In both places it is pronounced with two syllables. Plural nominative *sethir* Sept. 30; dative *sethraib* Aug. 30. Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *chwaer*, plural *chwiorydd*.

<term>slán</term>, *safe, whole* <note>original Latin: *salvus, integer*</note>, Ascoli 274, Jan. 6, March 2, Aug. 10, Sept. 30, Epilogue 172. Derived from *salán-*, which is cognate with the Latin word for "safe" <note>original: *salvus*</note>.

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

<term>slánaigim</term>, *I heal*. 2nd person singular imperative: *slánaigthe* (glossed as "hosanna" <note>original: *osanna*</note>) Milan Glosses 25ᵇ 2; 2nd person plural: *slánaigid* Epilogue 383, 403.

<term>slán-chotlud</term>, masculine noun, *sound sleep*, December 27.

<term>sláne</term>, October 30; seems to be an adverb meaning *in full* or *completely*.

<term>slechtaim</term>, (from the Latin *flecto* <note>meaning: to bend or bow</note>), Ascoli 276. 3rd person singular preterite (past tense): *slechtais* page 12. Verbal noun: <term>slechtan</term>.

<term>sleman</term>, *smooth, perfect* (cognate with Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *llyfn*), July 5; plural nominative *slemna*, meaning "smooth" <note>original Latin: *lēves*</note>, St. Gall Glosses 10ᵃ 8.

<term>slíab</term>, neuter noun, *mountain* or *upland*, Ascoli 277, November 11. Genitive singular: *slébe* July 6, Epilogue 556; dative: *sléib* April 7, July 26, October 20; plural nominative: *mórslébe* <note>meaning: great mountains</note> Prologue 237.

<term>slicht</term>, *a track* or *a trace*. Plural nominative: *slechtae* September 7.

<term>slige</term>, feminine noun, *a slaying, cutting down,* or *clearing*. November 7. Dative: *iar sligi cét* <note>meaning: after the slaying of hundreds</note>, *iar sligi na slúag* <note>meaning: after the slaying of the hosts</note> *Lebor na hUidre* 97ᵇ 22, 114ᵇ 41. Compounds: <term>all-slige</term>, *a second clearing*; <term>nua-slige</term>, *a new clearing*, Milan Glosses 2ᵃ 6.

<term>sligim</term>, *I cut down* (from the root *sleg*), *I slay*. Reduplicated perfect 3rd person singular: *ro selaig* (from *ro sešlaig*) Prologue 101; 3rd person plural: *ro selgatar* Prologue 29, *ra selgatar* *Lebor na hUidre* 58ᵃ 10. Conjunct preterite passive 3rd person singular: *-slecht* February 20, June 16; plural: *-slechta* (perhaps read as *-slechtai*?) November 5. Absolute preterite passive 3rd person singular: *slechtae* February 12. See <term>ar-sligim</term>. Root *slek*. Cognate with Gothic <note>original: *Goth.*</note> *slahan* <note>meaning: to strike</note> and Sanskrit <note>original: *Skr.*</note> *srká* <note>meaning: spear or missile</note>.

<term>slis</term>, masculine noun, *side* (cognate with Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *ystlys*). Genitive: *slesa* page 244, line 40. Compound: <term>slis-gel</term>, *bright-sided*, September 29.

<term>slisiu</term>, *a chip*, page 204, line 21. Cognate with Old English <note>original: *Ags.*</note> *slípan* and German <note>original: *Germ.*</note> *schleissen* <note>meaning: to split or slit</note>.

<term>slóg</term>, masculine noun, *host* or *army*, Ascoli 281 (cognate with Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *llû* and Gaulish *slógos*). Found in: Prologue 28, January 26, 28, February 2, March 6, April 3, June 15, 16, July 31, September 7, October 7, 22, 28, 29, November 20, December 17, 30. Singular genitive: *slóig*, *slúaig* February 15, March 29, 31, July 27, August 24, Epilogue 316. Dative: *slóg*, *slúag* January 31, March 4, April 16, June 1, July 12, 15, 16, September 15, December 11, 29. Accusative: *slóg-n*, *slúag-n* Prologue 132, July 17, 30, August 10. Plural nominative: *slóig*, *slúaig* Prologue 47, 63, November 1. Genitive: *slóg-n* Prologue 266, Epilogue 32. Dative: *slógaib*, *slúagaib* Prologue 33, June 19, Epilogue 62. Accusative: *slúagu* November 30.

<term>slógach</term>, *hostful* or *troopful*, March 5, May 10, June 14, 21, September 21, 29, Epilogue 262.

<term>slógad</term>, *a hosting* or *a thronging*, Ascoli 281, May 17 (in the R¹ manuscript). Genitive: *slógaid* December 19; dative: *slógud* July 28, November 15; accusative: *mórslúagad* <note>meaning: a great hosting</note> July 7.

<term>slógdae</term>, *hostful*, March 21, July 11.

<term>slóged, slóiged, slúaged, slúaiged</term>, *a hosting* (referring to a warlike expedition) or *a multitude*, February 3, *Leabhar Breac* May 17, July 18, Epilogue 33, 141. Dative: *slúaghiud* June 30; accusative singular: *slúaiged-n* Prologue 303.

<term>slondud</term>, masculine noun, *appellation* or *naming*, June 12. Identical to *slondod* in the *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 292, line 2; see also <term>asslondud</term> above.

<term>slondim</term>, *I denote* or *I name*. A derivative of <term>slond</term>, Ascoli 280. Present indicative 3rd person singular relative: Epilogue 155. 2nd person singular imperative: *sluind* January 31, February 19, March 4, 30, May 26, July 10, November 3, December 1. Future active 3rd person singular: *sloindfith*, *sluindfid* Prologue 300, 320; 1st person plural: *sluindfem-ni* Prologue 287. Cognate with Old Welsh <note>original: *O. Cymr.*</note> *istlinnit*, meaning "he speaks" <note>original: *loquitur*</note>, and <term>glan-stlinnim</term>, glossed as "with a holy utterance" <note>original Latin: *famine sancto*</note>.

<term>snádim</term>, *I protect* or *I convoy* (cognate with Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *noddi*), Ascoli 284. 3rd person singular: *ro-snáda* February 23, March 13, 14, May 10, 28, July 14, September 20, October 19, December 17. 3rd person plural: *ro-n-snádat* January 23, 29, March 6, May 29, June 9, September 27, Epilogue 563; *rom-snáidet* Epilogue 27. Future forms: *no-da-snáidfén* Epilogue 160; *snáidfíd-i* Epilogue 160. In the forms with an attached pronoun, *snáid-s-iunn* and *snáid-s-ium* (July 12, September 21), the second "s" appears to be due to the regular *s*-conjugation found in words like *ains-iunn* (Hymn of Saint Sanctán 14). See Thurneysen in *KZ* xxxi. 101, and the *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 300, line 9; 352, line 4.

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**snádud**, *protection*, dative singular January 21. Verbal noun of *snádim*.

**snámach**, *buoyant*? <note>Reference: Ascoli 284</note>, October 27, accusative singular masculine August 6, feminine *snámaig* September 12. A derivative of *snám* (swimming), page 228: compare Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *nawf*, *nofio*.

**snigim**, *I drop, drip*, present indicative 3rd person singular relative *sniges* <note>Reference: Milan Glosses 89ᶜ</note>, reduplicated preterite *senaig* (from *sesnaig*) May 15, Middle Irish t-preterite 3rd person plural *snegdatar*, <note>Reference: Saltair na Rann 2521</note>. Greek *neíphei* <note>original: *νείφει*, meaning "it snows" or "it rains"</note>.

**sním**, *sadness, sorrow*, dative Epilogue 407, accusative Prologue 223, page 56, line 8.

**so-**, *laudatory prefix* <note>a prefix indicating "good" or "well"</note>, see **su-**.

**soas**, *science* or *knowledge* (from *so-fís* <note>literally "good-wisdom"</note>), November 12, Epilogue 89, genitive singular *sois* April 4, *mór sóis* <note>meaning "great knowledge"</note> <note>Reference: Book of Leinster 117ᵇ</note>, dative *soas* March 13, Epilogue 124, accusative *soas-n*, Epilogue 132.

**sobail**, *holy*? Prologue 218, June 16, Epilogue 234, the opposite of *dobail*.

**sobarthan**, *good luck, prosperity*, Epilogue 57.

**sóbis**, **súabais**, *good, gentle* (*cheerful*?), January 13, dative masculine July 16, vocative *sóbis*, Epilogue 502 (where it rhymes with *Farōnis*), genitive plural February 2.

**sochor**, page 44, *profit, better contract*, opposite of *dochor*.

**sochlae**, **sochla**, *famous*, Prologue 163, January 13, April 24, May 9 (rhymes with *promthae*), June 21, 23, Epilogue 262, genitive singular masculine *sochlai* August 12, dative *sochlae* December 29, vocative *sochlai*, Epilogue 502.

**sochlach**, *famous*, January 14, dative singular neuter April 19.

**sodan**, *prosperous, happy*, August 10 <note>Reference: Rawlinson B 505 manuscript</note> <margin>meaning: *sona* (happy)</margin>, <note>Reference: O'Clery's Glossary</note>.

**sodath**, *well-colored, beautiful*, August 10, November 27 <note>Reference: Laud 610 and Paris manuscripts</note> (*sodad* in Rawlinson B 505).

**soee**, adjective, *sage* or *wise*? Epilogue 126, *ar súi soi* <note>Reference: Saltair na Rann 2692, where *sui soi* (wise sage) rhymes with *dúi doi* (ignorant person)</note>.

**sóer**, **sóir**, *free, noble*, <note>Reference: Ascoli 264</note>, April 12, July 20, October 26, 27, November 11, 27, December 31, dative singular feminine *sóir* December 7, accusative singular masculine April 2, August 10, genitive plural December 4, dative *sóeraib* November 30, Epilogue 286. Opposite of **dóer**, **dóir**. Compounds:
*   **sóerchul**, *a noble triumph*, July 8.
*   **sóerchaindel**, *a noble light*, accusative plural *-chaindlea*, Prologue 288.
*   **sóerdeochoín**, *a noble deacon*, nominative plural April 18, *-deochaíne*, page 116.
*   **sóerbúaid**, neuter, *a noble nativity* or *victory*, October 3.

**sóeraim**, *I ennoble, I free, I save*, present indicative 3rd person plural, *sóerait* April 1, November 1, 2nd person singular subjunctive, *re sóerae*, Epilogue 435, *rom-sóerae*, Epilogue 441, etc. 3rd person singular, *ron-sóera* March 14, October 19, 2nd person singular preterite, relative form *soérsai* Epilogue 447 etc., *ro sóerais*, Epilogue 486; 3rd person singular, *soérais* September 25, *ro saer*, page 4, passive preterite 3rd person singular, *ro sóerad*, Epilogue 440, plural *ro sóertha*, page 10. Verbal noun **sóirad** <note>Reference: Ascoli 265</note>.

**sóerdae**, *free, noble*, August 5, accusative singular feminine *sóerdai* July 13, neuter *sóerdae* July 18.

**soimle**, **seimle**, July 4, meaning obscure.

**soinmech**, *prosperous*, May 28, <note>Reference: Ascoli 297</note>, opposite of *doinmech*.

**solad**, *profit*, Prologue 11, November 27: opposite of *dolod*, *loss*.

**solus**, *bright*, January 30, <note>Reference: Ascoli 266</note>, opposite of *dolus*, <note>Reference: manuscript H. 3. 17, column 848</note>.

**som**, see **sa-**, **se-**.

**són**, demonstrative pronoun, *that*, <note>Reference: Ascoli 267</note>, Prologue 124, 172 (where *són* is misprinted as *som*).

**sonae**, *happy, prosperous*, June 23, September 16, October 3, dative singular masculine April 13, opposite of *donae*.

**sonirt**, **sonairt**, *strong, firm* (Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> *hynerth*), Prologue 261, <note>Reference: Ascoli 351</note>. Hence **sonairtnaigur**, *I am strong* or *I recover* <note>original Latin: *valeo, convalesco*</note>.

<vocab>snádud, snámach, snigim, sním, so-, soas, sobail, sobarthan, sóbis, sochor, sochlae, sochlach, sodan, sodath, soee, sóer, sóerchul, sóerchaindel, sóerdeochoín, sóerbúaid, sóeraim, sóerdae, soimle, soinmech, solad, solus, som, són, sonae, sonirt, sonairtnaigur</vocab>

### GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**sonnaim**, *I impale*, passive preterite plural 3rd person *ro sonnta*, Prologue 33. This is a verb derived from the noun *sonn* (Welsh <note>original: *ffon*</note>), meaning "a stake" or "post" <note>original: *i. cuaille*, as noted in O'Clery's Glossary</note>.

**sorchae**, *luminous*, December 25, 26 <note>Reference: Ascoli 203</note>, accusative singular feminine *sorchai* September 12, comparative *sorchu* March 9: the opposite of *dorchae* (dark). See **riched** <note>heaven</note>.

**soréid**, *easy*, Prologue 30 <note>Reference: Ascoli 205</note>: the opposite of *doraid* (difficult).

**sorn**, masculine, *furnace* (Welsh <note>original: *ffwrn*</note>, from Latin <note>original: *furnus*</note>), singular genitive *suirnn* <note>Reference: Milan Glosses 121ᶜ 14</note>, dative *surn* April 24, plural accusative *surnu*, Prologue 44.

**sossad**, *a position, a station, an abode* <note>Reference: Ascoli 269</note>, accusative *sossad-n* February 26, September 21 <note>Reference: Würzburg Glosses 4ᵇ 18</note>.

**sostan**, *rest, repose*, July 10 <note>Reference: O'Davoren's Glossary 1459</note>.

**sotlae**, feminine, *vainglory*, Epilogue 135, accusative *sotlai* April 28, September 15, plural nominative *sotli* (glossing "animosities" <note>original: *animositates*</note>) <note>Reference: Würzburg Glosses 18ᵃ 20</note>.

**sothnge**, **soithnge**, *well-tongued, eloquent*, January 13, Leabhar Breac. Compare *suithnge* in the Metrical Glosses 111.

**spirut**, **spiurt**, masculine, *spirit* <note>Reference: Ascoli 297</note> (Welsh <note>original: *ysbryd*</note>, from Latin <note>original: *spiritus*</note>), genitive singular *spirto* May 15.

**sreth**, feminine, singular genitive *sreithe*, *stratum* (a layer) <note>Reference: Ascoli 238</note>, or *rank*, December 4, accusative *sreith* August 24, plural accusative *sretha*, Epilogue 238. From this comes **srethaigim**, "I arrange." Compare the Welsh *rhês* (a row).

**sroiglim**, *I whip* <note>original Latin: *flagello*</note>, present passive plural 3rd person *sroiglithea*, Prologue 43. This is a verb derived from *srogell* (a whip), genitive *sroigill* <note>Reference: Würzburg Glosses 17ᵈ 3</note>, which, like the Welsh <note>original: *ffrewyll*</note>, comes from the Latin word for a whip <note>original: *flagellum*</note>.

**srúaim**, neuter, *a stream*, April 4, November 27 <note>Reference: Würzburg Glosses 11ᵃ 19</note>: related to Old High German *stroum* or *strôm* and Greek *rheuma* <note>original: *ῥεῦμα*</note>.

**srúamach**, *streamy, multitudinous*, November 26, accusative singular neuter August 25, feminine *srúamaig* December 7.

**srubán**, *a cake of barley* <note>original: *eorna*</note>, page 88 <note>Reference: Irish Glosses 143</note>: perhaps compare with the Latin *sorbeo* (to suck in)?

**sruith**, feminine, *old, venerable, an elder, a sage* <note>Reference: Ascoli 283</note>, Prologue 97 (in the "L" manuscript), November 2, genitive singular *srotha* January 5, August 24, plural nominative *sruithi*, Epilogue 47, genitive *sruithe* May 28. The comparative form is *sruithiu* (glossing "older" <note>original: *antiquior*</note>) <note>Reference: Milan Glosses 59ᵈ 5</note>. Compare Old Welsh <note>original: *strutiu*, glossing "ancient people"*</note> and Lithuanian *strujus*, meaning "an old man" <note>original: *Greis*</note>.

**sruithe**, feminine, *antiquity, wisdom* <note>Reference: Ascoli 283</note>, genitive singular July 1, Epilogue 272, and perhaps also in Prologue 167, July 23, and December 4. It is often difficult to distinguish between *sruithe-n* (the genitive plural of the noun *sruith*) and *sruithe* (the genitive singular of this noun).

**1. -su**, *an emphasizing pronoun*, see **sa**.

**2. su-**, **so-**, *a laudatory prefix* <note>used to indicate something "good" or "well"</note> <note>Reference: Ascoli 272</note> (Welsh <note>original: *hy-*</note>, Sanskrit <note>original: *su-*</note>). See **subae**, **súi**, **suilbir**, and **suthain**.

**súabais**, February 2. See **sóbis** (gentle); the opposite of **duabais** (gloomy).

**súas**, adverb, *upwards*, August 6, October 9.

**subae**, **sube**, masculine (possibly neuter), *gladness*, January 6, 11, April 1; also *sube* December 17 and *subai* April 21. Seen in *suibi* (glossing "of jubilation" <note>original: *iubelationis*</note>) <note>Reference: Milan Glosses 47ᵈ 2</note>, dative *subu* <note>Reference: Milan Glosses 67ᶜ 10</note>. From this comes **subaigur**, "I rejoice" <note>original: *gaudeo*</note>, which is the opposite of **dubae** (sorrow).

**subach**, *happy, joyful*, April 10, accusative singular neuter April 2.

**subaid**, April 10 in manuscripts R¹, B, and L; written as *subaich* in the Leabhar Breac (perhaps intended to be read as *subaith*?). It is synonymous with **subach**.

**súi**, masculine, *a sage* (derived from a root meaning "good-seer" <note>original: *\*su-vet-*</note>) September 10, 30 (where *súi* is pronounced as one syllable), plural nominative *súid*, Epilogue 81 (where *suid* is two syllables, and the manuscripts have *súide* or *suide*). This is the opposite of **dúi** (an ignorant person <note>original: *\*du-vet-*</note>), genitive *dúad*.

**suide**, neuter, *the act of sitting, a seat* (Welsh <note>original: *sedd*</note>) <note>Reference: Ascoli 269</note>, see **prímšuide** (chief seat). From this comes **suidigur**, "I place" <note>original: *pono*</note>.

**suidiu**, dative singular anaphoric pronoun (referring back to someone already mentioned), "him," Prologue 122; dative plural **suidib**, "them," Prologue 84. Except in the phrase *ol-suide*, the Old Irish nominative is **side** <note>Reference: Strachan, *Ériu* volume 1, page 5</note>.

**súil**, feminine, "eye" <note>Reference: Ascoli 272</note>; singular genitive **súlo**, **súla**; dative **súil**, Prologue 218. Compare to the Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. haul*</note> meaning "sun."

**suilbir**, see **sulbair**.

**suilge**, feminine, "ease"? Let it be read as <note>original: *leg.*</note> **soilge**, the opposite of **doilge** (difficult)? Leabhar Breac 151a; dative **suilgi**, November 8.

**suilgind** (or **suilginn**?), meaning obscure; dative Epilogue 126.

**suirge**, "wooing," Epilogue 135. "Every wooing and every concubinage that is in the world is from her [namely <note>original: *scil. Uenir*</note> Venus] it comes" <note>original: *cechlsuirgi 7 cech lennanacht fil isin doman is uaidhi [scil. Uenir] ata*</note>, Book of Leinster 401a. Hence **suirgech** (glossing "suitor" <note>original: *procus*</note>), Irish Glosses 618. Compare to the Greek words for "affection" <note>original: *στοργή*</note> and "to love" or "cherish" <note>original: *στέργω*</note>.

**súithe**, feminine, "wisdom"; accusative singular **súithi**, November 12. A derivative of the t-stem **súi** (a sage or scholar), see that entry.

**sulbair**, **suilbir** (from *su-labair*; Welsh <note>original: *hylafar*</note>), "eloquent," August 21. Hence **sulbirigim**, "I am eloquent" <note>original: *eloquens sum*</note>.

**-sum**, see **-som**.

**sund**, adverb, "here," September 6, Epilogue 378, 391, 395.

**sunnraid**, adverb, "specially" or "particularly," page 6. Old Irish **sainriud**.

**suthain**, **suthin**, "lasting" or "perennial," March 11, May 14 <note>Reference: Ascoli 273-4</note>.

**t'** (from *to*), "your," used before a vowel. Examples: **t' aiccept** (your lesson), page 12; **t' Eolis**, February 25; **t'ordan** (your dignity), Prologue 276; **t' Assach**, April 14; **t' ferta** (your miracles), Epilogue 558.

**-t-**, an infixed personal pronoun for the 2nd person singular. Examples: **to-t-icfa** (it will come to you), May 25; **do-t-icfa** (it will come to you), July 16; **no-t-guidhiu** (I pray to you), Epilogue 37.

**-táa**, **túsa**, Epilogue 385, "I am." **-tá**, "is," with affixed pronouns; see **táthum**.

**-táam**, present indicative plural 1st person, Prologue 157, 161. Weakened forms of the 3rd person plural are **con-dat** and **in-dat**. For other forms of the substantive verb (the verb "to be"), see **bíuu** and **feil**.

**tabair**, "put," page 12. Imperative singular 2nd person of **dobiur** (to give or put).

**tabart**, **tabairt**, feminine (see **fírthabart**), "giving" or "putting." The verbal noun of **dobiur**.

**táde**, masculine (or Neuter?), "stealth" or "concealment"; accusative singular Prologue 71, October 10. **táide** in Metrical Glosses 112. Compare to the Greek words "to be deprived of" <note>original: *τητάω*</note> or "to be in want" <note>original: *τατάομαι*</note>.

**tadlech**, "affliction"? Plural genitive October 15. **tadlach** is glossed as "difficulty" <note>original: *.i. documal*</note> in manuscript H.

**taimthiu**, "death" (specifically from sickness), June 30, July 2, 27, August 17. Cognate with **tathaim** ("he died"), Book of Leinster 131b 37; deponent form **tathamair**, Book of Leinster 199d 60.

**táinsem** (from *to-áinsem* <note>Reference: Ascoli 352</note>), "accusation" or "censure"; dative singular Epilogue 524.

**1. tair**, "in the east," Epilogue 70 in manuscript L (**thair** in manuscript B).

**2. tair**, "come you," page 13. This serves in Old Irish as the 2nd person singular imperative of **dotéit** (to come). **tairset**, "may they come," December 13, which is the same as **doairset**, September 20—subjunctives of **doairicim**, see that entry.

**tairic**, **taric**, "comes," July 19.

**tairngertaid** (manuscript reads **-taig**), page 12, "a prophesied one"?

**tairthim**, "death," accusative Prologue 166.

**taissi**, "relics," Epilogue 220; accusative plural Epilogue 336.

**taistel**, "a voyage," "journey," or "visiting"; singular dative page 52, line 32.

**taithlech**, neuter, "amends" or "satisfaction," September 19. Genitive **taidliuch**, Milan Glosses 23a 9; dative **taidliuch**, Milan Glosses 32a 24.

**taithmet**, "commemoration," Epilogue 131 <note>Reference: Ascoli 381</note>. The verbal noun of **doaithminiur**.

**taitnem**, "radiance" or "brightness," Prologue 331.

**tál**, "adze" (a carpentry tool), genitive **táil**, June 11. Derived from the root **tákslo-**, which is cognate with the Church Slavonic **tesla** ("axe").

## GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

<term>talam</term>, the earth or land, Prologue 108. Singular genitive: **talman**, Prologue 245, March 27; dative: **talmain**, May 20, June 6, July 27, Epilogue 294, 444; short form: **talam**, Prologue 136; accusative: **talmain-n**, Epilogue 434; short form: **talam**, Prologue 216.

<term>talcae</term>, feminine, strength or starkness. Dative: **talcai**, April 28, June 7, September 15.

<term>álgud</term>, a quieting. Singular dative: "they saw the boy in his quieting" <note>original: *conaccatar in mac inna thalgud*</note> <note>Book of Leinster 117b</note>. Accusative singular: **álgud**; dative singular feminine: **tálgaim**, October 29. This is the verbal noun of **tálgaim** (I quiet or soothe).

<term>talland</term>, a natural inclination or talent, December 31. Derived from the Latin <note>original: *talentum*</note> "talent." See Ascoli, *Supplementi periodici*, sixth issue, 1898, page 31.

<term>tan</term>, time; used as an adverb meaning "when," Epilogue 470, 561. **ind-ara-tan** . . . **in tan ele** (the one time . . . the other time) <note>Liber Hymnorum</note>. "Whenever the eye of the king does not visit it, it smiles" <note>original: *nách tan tosn-aidle súil ind ríg tibid*</note> <note>Lebor na hUidre 96b 38</note>. See also **suthain**.

<term>tánic</term>, he/it has come; see the entry for **doicim**.

<term>tar</term>, **dar**, preposition, "over," April 10, September 9, 10, November 3, December 8, 11, Epilogue 66, 238.

<term>-tarcai</term>, surpasses, June 29; see the entry for **dofarcim**. In the *Saltair na Rann* 161, 7002, **targai** and 7163, 8174 **tarcai** appear to be the third-person singular preterite (past tense).

<term>tarcenn</term>, nominal preposition, "on behalf of" or "for the sake of," Epilogue 414.

<term>-tarlam</term>, "may we come" or "let us approach" <note>original: *adeamus*</note>, Prologue 319 <note>Leabhar Breac version</note>.

<term>tarmbreth</term>, feminine, "translation" (referring to the ceremonial transfer of a saint's body or relics), July 3. Accusative singular: **tarmbreith**, June 4.

<term>tarmchruthud</term>, masculine, transformation or transfiguration, July 26.

<term>tarm-thucad</term>, was transferred, page 166.

<term>tasc</term>, report, rumor, or tidings, January 18. Found in manuscripts R¹, B, L, and F.

<term>tasse</term>, moist. Dative singular feminine: **tassi**, May 20. **tais** means wet, moist, or dank; **taise** means moisture according to O'Brien.

<term>tathchor</term>, removal or return. Accusative singular, June 24.

<term>táthum</term>, "I have" (literally "there is to me"). "I have a cause of grief" <note>original: *tathum domna broin*</note> <note>Book of Leinster 192b 48</note>. **táthunn**, "we have," Prologue 217; **táthus**, "she has," February 5; **táthut**, "you have," July 24.

<term>-táu</term>, **-too**, **-tú-sa**, "I am"; the enclitic (dependent) form of **attóo**. See the Würzburg Glosses 17d 24, 32a 10 and the Milan Glosses 92b 8.

<term>té</term>, hot (related to Latin <note>original: *tepens*</note> "warm"). Dative plural: **(luach)thétib**, Prologue 40.

<term>tech</term>, see **teg**.

1. <term>techt</term>, feminine, a going or a coming, Epilogue 561. Genitive: **tachtae**; dative: **techt**. See Ascoli 104, Prologue 31. This is the verbal noun of **tíagu** (I go). Compare with the Welsh <note>original: *Cymr. taith*</note> "journey."

2. <term>techt</term>, a messenger. Accusative plural: **techta**, Epilogue 560.

<term>téchte</term> (from the root *tenktio*), fitting or right. Dative singular feminine: **téchti**, Epilogue 390. Compare with Lithuanian <note>original: *tenkù*</note> meaning "it falls to my lot" <note>original: *falle zu*</note>.

<term>techtaim</term>, I have or I possess. Present indicative second-person plural: **-techtaid**, Epilogue 389.

<term>-tecma</term>, January 10; see the entry for **doecmangim**.

<term>teg</term>, **tech**, neuter, a house. Compare with Welsh <note>original: *ty*</note> and Greek <note>original: *τέγεος*</note> meaning "of a roof." Genitive singular: **tige**, Epilogue 94.

<term>teglach</term>, a household. Genitive: **teglaig**, Epilogue 550; accusative: **teglach**, Prologue 95. Compare with the Welsh <note>original: *teulu*</note>.

<term>teidm</term>, neuter, disease. Genitive: **tedmae**, Epilogue 200, 518.

<term>téit</term>, goes, Prologue 248. This word supplies the third-person singular and second-person plural of **tíagu**.

<term>temel</term>, darkness or gloom. Dative singular, page 166. It can also mean "death" <note>Metrical Glosses 113</note>. Compare with Welsh <note>original: *tewyll*</note> and Latin <note>original: *temere*</note> "darkly/blindly."

<term>tempul</term>, a temple. Derived from the Latin <note>original: *templum*</note>; compare to Welsh <note>original: *teml*</note>. Singular genitive: **tempuil**, April 8, May 10, December 15; dative: **tempul**, February 2.

<term>tendalach</term>, fiery, page 6, line 9. A derivative of **tendal**, meaning a firebrand or torch, which is now spelled <note>original: *teandáil*</note>.

<term>tend-ri</term> (perhaps **tennrí**?), *stern king*, page 6, line 9.

<term>tene</term>, *fire*, February 26. Genitive form: **tened**, Prologue 44, Epilogue 540. Compare with the Welsh <note>original: *Cymr.*</note> word **tân**.

<term>tenge</term>, *tongue*. Plural accusative: **tengtha**, Epilogue 125 (perhaps used for the nominative plural **tengaid**?). Compare with the Old Icelandic word **stinga**.

<term>tennim</term>, likely related to the Latin word meaning "I stretch" <note>original: *tendo*</note>? The third-person plural preterite passive is **ro tenntea**, Prologue 38, but the reading is doubtful. It might perhaps be **ro tenmtea**, from the verb **tenmim**, meaning "I cut" or "I divide."

<term>teoir</term> (compare the Welsh <note>original: *teir*</note>), the feminine form of the number *three*. On September 1, it is used as a two-syllable word, similar to **teuir** in the *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* (Volume II, page 291, line 6). It stems from the reconstructed form **tisores**, related to the Sanskrit <note>original: *Skr.*</note> **tisrás** and Avestan <note>original: *Av.*</note> **tisrō**.

<term>tercae</term>, feminine noun meaning *stint, scarcity, or scantiness*. Accusative singular: **tercai**, May 6.

<term>terc-phit</term>, *a scanty meal*, September 8. See the entry for **pit**.

<term>térnae</term>, Epilogue 544. The verbal noun (a noun derived from a verb) is **térnam** (escaping), found on page 128. See the entry for **doérnaim**.

<term>tert-íd</term>, page 114, *the third day of the ides* <note>a division of the Roman calendar</note>.

<term>tesctha</term>, Prologue 238. See the entry for **doescaim**.

<term>téte</term>, feminine noun meaning *comfort*. Dative singular: **téte**, Prologue 25. This is a derivative of **té** (warm or hot).

**1.** <term>tiachrae</term>, *affliction or soreness*, April 29. A derivative of **tiachair**, which is defined as "difficult" <note>original: *doiligh*</note> in *O'Davoren's Glossary* (number 1572). It is also a derivative of **tiachair**, defined as "bitter" or "sore" <note>original: *goirt*</note> in the *Archiv für celtische Lexikographie* (Volume I, page 97). It is glossed as "sharp" <note>original Latin: *acer*</note> in the St. Gall Priscian glosses (41ª 10).

**2.** <term>tiachrae</term>, masculine (or perhaps neuter). Meaning *shrewdness or prudence*. Genitive singular: **tiachrai**, November 12. A derivative of **tiachair**, defined as "clever" <note>original: *glic*</note> in *O'Davoren's Glossary* (number 441).

<term>tiachtain</term>, *a coming*, pages 40 and 42. This is the verbal noun of **tíagu**.

<term>tíagu</term>, *I go*. This is equivalent to the Greek word meaning "to march" or "to go" <note>original: *στείχω*</note>. Present indicative third-person plural: **-tiagat**, Epilogue 58. Present subjunctive third-person singular: **téis**, page 4. Relative plural: **tiastae**, Epilogue 470. Past subjunctive third-person singular: **-tésed**, April 27. The verbal nouns are **dul** and **techt**. For the forms that provide the various tenses of this verb, see the entries for **docuaid**, **luid**, **rega**, and **tét**.

**1.** <term>tíamdae</term>, *slow or weak*, Prologue 259. Found in *O'Davoren's Glossary* (210, 1571) and O'Clery's Glossary, where it is defined as "slow" <note>original: *mall*</note>.

**2.** <term>tíamdae</term>, *obscure*, Prologue 294. Defined in *O'Davoren's Glossary* (number 1571) and O'Clery's Glossary as "dark" <note>original: *dorcha*</note>.

<term>tiar</term>, adverb meaning *in the west*, Epilogue 70, *Book of Lecan*.

<term>-ticim</term>, see the entry for **doicim**.

<term>tíchtu</term>, *a coming*, Epilogue 394. This is the verbal noun of **doicim**.

<term>tim</term>, *soft or feeble*, Prologue 259. It is better spelled as **timm** in *The Vision of Adamnán* (page 66). "Be not too hard, be not too soft" <note>original: *nirbat rochruaid, nirbat rothim*</note> in the *Book of Leinster* (345ª).

<term>timnae</term>, neuter noun meaning *commandment or testament*. Dative plural: **timnaib**, Prologue 27.

<term>tinbúanad</term>, *the act of making permanent*, Epilogue 204.

<term>tinim</term>, *I vanish*. Reduplicated preterite (an archaic past tense) third-person singular: **rotetha**, Prologue 193.

<term>tindscan</term> or **tinscan**, *begin!* (imperative), May 1 and November 14.

<term>tindscetal</term>, *a beginning*, page 8.

<term>tinne</term>, *ingot*, April 25, page 132, line 19.

<term>tír</term>, neuter noun meaning *land* (compare the Welsh word **tir**). Prologue 161. Genitive singular: **tíre**, Prologue 160, May 24, November 2. Nominative plural: **tíre**, Prologue 161, from the *Leabhar Breac*.

<term>tirbaid</term>, *anguish*? Prologue 169.

<term>tís</term>, adverb meaning *below*, Epilogue 70. See also the entry for **ís**.

<term>tlacht</term>, masculine noun meaning *a robe or a garment*. Dative plural: **tlachtaib**. Accusative plural: **tlachtu**, January 4.

<term>tochuiruid</term>, masculine noun meaning *invitation*, Epilogue 212. This is the verbal noun of **docuiruir**.

<term>todiúscud</term>, masculine noun meaning *an awakening*, Epilogue 193. This is the verbal noun of **dodiuschim**.

<term>tóeb</term>, masculine noun meaning *side* (compare the Welsh word **tu**). Genitive singular: **tóib**. Accusative: October 23. Accusative plural: **tóebu**, Epilogue 324.

### GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

**tóebán**, a diminutive of **tóeb** (side), singular accusative: Epilogue 352.

**togae**, a *choice*, January 6, November 7; a variant of **togu**.

**togairm**, neuter noun. A *calling* or *summoning*, January 5. See also **gairm**.

**togu**, a *choice*, Prologue 123, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* Volume II, page 225, line 18. Derived from the root *gus* (to choose).

**toich**, a natural *right*, July 24. Also found in the Würzburg Glosses <note>original: Wb.</note> 9ª 13, 29ᵈ 13.

**toidecht do láim**, page 64, literally "coming to hand," referring to coming to receive the Eucharist. Compare with the phrase "to approach so that he might receive the Eucharist from the hand of the bishop" <note>original Latin: *techt do láim in epscuip* ‘accedere ut Eucharistiam sumeret de manu episcopi’</note>, cited in Hogan’s *Latin Lives*, page 84.

**tóided**, Prologue 340, January 1, *let him lead on*. See the entry for **dofedim**.

**tóiden**, a *troop* or *assembly*, July 7, August 13, September 23, Epilogue 142.

**tóidlech**, *shining* or *radiant*, September 21, 23. Accusative singular feminine: **tóidlig**, Prologue 78, February 22.

**toirm**, neuter noun. *Noise* or *din*, May 10. Compare with the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word **twrf**.

**toisc**, *wish* (derived from the reconstructed form *to-venski-*, related to the German word *Wunsch*). Plural accusative: **toscai**, July 19. See Zupitza 200.

**tol**, feminine noun. *Will, desire*, or *lust*, Prologue 267. Singular genitive: **tuile**, April 20, Epilogue 184. Nominative plural: **tola**, May 19. Dative plural: **tolaib**, Prologue 83. Accusative: **tola**, April 15.

**tol cuirp**, *male seed* <note>original: *semen virile*</note>, page 134, literally "desire of the body" <note>original Latin: *voluntas corporis*</note>.

**tolgdae**, *haughty*, Prologue 125. Related to the Old English <note>original: Ags.</note> word *stealc* (steep or high). See Zupitza 168.

**tond**, also spelled **tonn**. Feminine noun, a *wave*. (Compare with the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> feminine word **ton**). Singular dative: **tuinn**, Prologue 250; **tuind**, April 23. Accusative: **tuind**, June 3.

**tonnad**, *death, especially by poison*. Singular dative: **tonnud**, Epilogue 552.

**tonn-bláth**, *flower-swarded* (covered in flowering turf), page 226. Compare with the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word **ton**, meaning "sward" or "surface."

**topacht**, *was reaped*. This is the third-person singular preterite passive of the verb **dobongim**, page 56.

**tor**, masculine noun. A *tower*. (Compare with the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word **twr**), July 28, December 12.

**torbe**, neuter noun. *Profit* or *benefit*, Ascoli 313, Prologue 143, Epilogue 77. Genitive: **torbi**, Würzburg Glosses 11ᵇ 17a. Dative: **torbu**, Epilogue 76. This is the verbal noun of **dororbanim**.

**torc**, masculine noun. A *boar*. Genitive: **tuirc**, September 17. Compare with the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word **twrch**, meaning "hog."

-**torchair**, Epilogue 361. See the entry for **dotuitim** (to fall).

**tormach**, neuter noun. *Increase*. Accusative: **tormach-n**, Prologue 317. This is the verbal noun of **doformaigim**.

**toscélad**, the *act of ascertaining* or finding out. Dative singular: Epilogue 80. *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* Volume II, page 41. This is the verbal noun of **dosceulaim**.

**tossach**, neuter noun. A *beginning*, Ascoli 317, January 7. Genitive: **tossaig**. Dative: **tossuch** or **tossug**. Plural dative: **tossaichib**, page 14, line 30.

**tothlai**, April 15. Accusative plural feminine? Meaning *urgent* or *importunate*?

**traite**, *quickness*, page 6, line 4. A feminine derivative of **trait** (quick). Used as an adverb: **co trait** (quickly), page 64, line 8.

**tráth**, a *time*, especially a *canonical hour* (one of the set times for daily prayer). Accusative: Epilogue 411.

**tre**, also **tria**. (Compare with the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word **trwy**). A preposition used with the accusative case meaning *through*. Prologue 196, March 31, May 19, June 27, August 27, October 19, November 6, Epilogue 352. With suffixed pronouns: **triut**, meaning *through you*; **tria**, meaning *through his* (October 9, Epilogue 352); **trea-n** or **tria-n**, meaning *through their* (January 4, Epilogue 324). With the plural article: **trésna**, Prologue 44.

**treb**, feminine noun. A *homestead* or *household*. (Compare with the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word **tref**). Singular dative: **treib**, April 9. Accusative: **treib-n**, Prologue 78. See also **aittreb**.

**trebaim**, *I inhabit*. Third-person plural present indicative passive: -**trebtar**, Prologue 176. Compare with the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word **trefu**.

**trebar**, also spelled **trebair**. *Prudent* or *discreet*, August 11, Epilogue 142. Plural genitive: **trebar-n**, February 20. From this comes the verb **trebairigim** (<gloss>meaning: I am wise <note>original Latin: *sapio*</note></gloss>), St. Gall Glosses <note>original: Sg.</note> 146ᵇ 16.

**treblait**, also **treblóit**. A *trouble* or *affliction*. Derived from the Latin word *tribulatio*. Plural accusative: **treblaiti**, page 44.

**-trecheng**, **-drecheng** (spelled *trethenc* in the Würzburg Glosses 29c 5), a **trio**, September 16, and page 248. The phrase *trecheang breth Féni* in the Yellow Book of Lecan <note>original: YBL</note> 414b 24 refers to the "triads of the judgments of the Féne" <note>original: Féne — the ancient Irish free classes and the legal system associated with them</note>.

**tredan**, a **three-day fast** <note>original Latin: triduana</note>. Singular accusative: March 24, November 16; plural genitive: January 15, Epilogue 186. See Plummer’s edition of *Bede*, volume II, page 78, and the Book of Esther 4:16.

**trednach**, **abstinent**, October 21, December 13. Masculine genitive singular: **trednaig**, February 25; feminine dative singular: **trednaig**, October 18.

**trén**, **strong**, **bold**, or **valiant**, August 11, September 21, October 21, Epilogue 151. Masculine genitive singular: **triúin**, February 25; masculine dative: **trén**, December 11; feminine dative: **triúin**, October 18 (Laud manuscript). Comparative form: **tresa**, Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 19d 6. For the origins <note>original: etymologies</note> of Irish *trén*, *tress*, *tricc* and Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *tren*, see Strachan in *Beiträge zur Kunde der indogermanischen Sprachen* volume 20, page 9, and Zupitza, page 217. From this come the verbs **trénaigur** and **trénigim** (I strengthen).

**trénfer**, masculine noun. A **champion**, plural genitive: February 20.

**treoda**, **trinal** (relating to three), page 47. From this comes **treodatu** (the Trinity), genitive: **treodatad**, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* volume II, page 354; accusative: **treodatid**, Würzburg Glosses 26c 29.

**trét**, neuter noun. A **flock** or **herd**. Singular genitive: **treoit**; nominative plural: **tréta**, Prologue 230. Derived from the reconstructed form *tremto-*, related <note>original: cognate</note> to the Latin word **turma** (a troop or squadron).

**trethan**, masculine noun. The **sea**. Singular genitive: **trethain**, November 23; dative: **trethan**, April 22; accusative: **trethan**, Prologue 216, December 11; nominative plural: **trethain**, June 27. The forms found in the Rawlinson B 502 manuscript <note>original: R¹</note> and the *Book of the Dun Cow* <note>original: LU</note> point to an "n-stem" word (with a predicted nominative *trithu*), similar to the Greek sea-god **Triton** <note>original Greek: Τρίτων</note>.

**trethanglas**, **sea-blue**. Feminine dative singular: **trethanglais**, page 54.

**trí**, **three**. Masculine nominative: August 2; neuter: **trí chét** (three hundred), June 2; genitive: **trí-n**, April 24; dative: **trib**, August 7, September 8, October 9; accusative: **trí**, December 10 (Laud and Franciscan manuscripts).

**tríamain**, **weary** or **sad**, Prologue 26. Spelled *trémuin* in the Würzburg Glosses 17b 10.

**trícha**, **thirty**. Read as <note>original Latin: leg. (lege)</note> **trichae**, February 20; **trícha**, September 1 (Franciscan and Laud manuscripts).

**trírech**.

1. **trilis**, April 23. Masculine genitive singular or feminine dative singular. **Sparkling** or **brilliant**.
2. **trilis**, a **long head of hair**. Dative singular: March 15; "over the sea's hair" <note>original: dar trilis lir</note>, page 90.

**trírech** or **trilech**, feminine noun. A **song**. Accusative singular: **trírig**, page 10; **trilig**, page 8. For example, "the song of the birds" <note>original: trírech inna nÉn</note>, *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* volume II, page 290, line 8.

**triur**, a **set of three persons** or a **trio**. Singular genitive: **triir**, October 11 (where it is pronounced with two syllables); dative: **triur**, January 24 (two syllables), and December 14 (where it rhymes with **siur**, meaning "sister"); plural dative: **trírib**, Prologue 210 (where it is two syllables).

**triut**, see the entry for **tré**.

**tróethaim**, **I overwhelm**, **overthrow**, or **abate**. Third-person singular preterite (past tense): **troethais**, November 16 (Rawlinson and Leabhar Breac manuscripts). With an attached pronoun <note>original Latin: cum pron. aff. (cum pronomine affixo)</note>: **tróeths-us** (he overwhelmed them), November 16. In Modern Irish, this is **traochaim**. Compound form: **artróithaim**, Milan Glosses 38d 7, 121d 9.

**tróethad**, Epilogue 184. The verbal noun of **tróethaim**, see above <note>original Latin: q.v. (quod vide)</note>.

**tróg** or **trúag** (related to the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word *tru*), **wretched**, Prologue 26, 157, Epilogue 399, 408, 409. Feminine accusative singular: **trúag-n**, Epilogue 314. Diminutive form: **trógnat**, page 146. Compare with the Greek word **strephomai** (to be turned or twisted) <note>original Greek: στρέφομαι</note>, according to Windisch.

**tróige** or **trúage**, feminine noun (related to the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word *truedd*), **wretchedness**. Singular genitive: **tróge** or **trúage**, March 17; dative: **trógi**, Epilogue 482 (but the ablative case is **tróge**, Epilogue 512); accusative: **trógi**, February 3.

**tromm**, **heavy**, **grievous**, or **mighty** (related to the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> word *trwm*), Prologue 165, January 15, July 7, Epilogue 380.

1. **tú**, **you** (singular) <note>original: thou</note>, Prologue 14. Emphatic form: **tussu**. Related to Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *ti* and Latin *tū*.
2. **-tú**, **I am**. **-túsa**, Epilogue 385, a variant of **-táusa**, see above <note>original Latin: q.v.</note>.

**tuadhmhar**, page 78. Read as <note>original Latin: leg. (lege)</note> **tuaghmhar**, meaning **arched**? From the word *tuag*, meaning a "bow."

**túagaim**, **I cut with an axe**. Past passive: **ro tuagad** (he was cut/hewed), page 190. This is a verb derived from the noun **túag** (axe) and is related <note>original: cognate</note> to the Irish word *tocht* and perhaps the Sanskrit word **tujáti** (he strikes).

# GLOSSARIAL INDEX.

<term>túaith</term> adverb: **in the north**, December 11.
<term>-túarcaib</term>: **raised up** or **lifted**, see *doforgabaib*.
<term>túas</term> adverb: **up above**, December 28, Epilogue 70.
<term>túaslucud</term> masculine noun: the **act of opening or freeing**, dative: March 27.
<term>túath</term> feminine noun: **folk, tribe, or laity**. Singular genitive: *túaithe*; dative: *túaith* (Prologue 142, Epilogue 396); plural dative: *túathaib* (June 17); accusative: *túatha* (November 8, Epilogue 35). Compare to the Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *tud*, meaning "a region."
<term>túathach</term>: **lord**, May 24. A derivative of *túath* ("folk"), similar to the Gothic word *thiudans* <note>original: þiudans</note> derived from *thiuda* ("people").
<term>tuba</term> feminine noun: **a shelter? thatch?** Dative: *tubai* (June 6). The scholar O’Davoren (entry no. 1513) explains *tuba* (the verbal noun of *dobenim*) as *tochailt* (digging or excavation), as in <note>original Latin: ut est</note> *tuba tire*—that is, <note>original Irish: .i. foít do bhuain ás</note> "to cut sods out of the land."
<term>tuchtach</term>: **shapely**, feminine dative singular: *tuchtaig* (July 21). A derivative of *tucht* ("shape" or "manner").
<term>-tucsam</term>: **we have brought forward**, Epilogue 31; see *dobiur*.
<term>tudrach</term> masculine (or possibly neuter) noun: **incitement**, accusative: Epilogue 329.
<term>tugae</term> feminine noun (Welsh <note>original: Cymr.</note> *tô*): **thatch**, accusative: *tugai* (June 6) in the Rawlinson B 505 manuscript <note>original: R¹</note>. The Book of Leinster <note>original: B.L.</note> uses *tuighi*. From this comes *tuigiur* ("I cover") and its compound forms.
<term>tuicse</term>: **chosen**, masculine genitive singular: *tuicsi* (October 25). Superlative form: *to the most chosen* <note>original: du thuichsimem (read as thuicsimem)</note> in the Milan Glosses <note>original: Ml.</note> 71b 21.
<term>tuidme</term> (from *to-demia*): **a binding together or union**, October 17; accusative singular: Epilogue 355.
<term>tuile</term> neuter noun: **flood or abundance**. Singular genitive: *tuili* (Prologue 250); dative: *tuiliu* (Prologue 124, 247, Epilogue 310).
<term>tuillem</term>: **enhancement or addition**; see *fír-thuillem*.
<term>tuir</term>: **pillar**, April 8. Plural: *tuire rígthige* ("pillars of a king's house") in the *Lebor na hUidre* <note>original: LU.</note> 55a.
<term>tuirem</term> feminine noun: **a recounting**, dative: *tuirim* (Epilogue 231, 305, 390). This is the verbal noun of *dorímu*.
<term>tuirenn</term> feminine noun: **wheat**, dative: *tuirinn* (May 21, November 24), *tuirnn* (August 18), *tuirind* (pages 105, 134), or *tuirnd* in the *Leabhar Breac* <note>original: LB.</note> 106b.
<term>túirim</term>: **I scrutinize or I search** (from *to-fo-sírím*). Passive present indicative plural third-person: *túirtir* (Prologue 230). Active imperative singular second-person: *tuir* (Prologue 331). Past tense <note>original: preterite</note> singular first-person: *-taurus* (rhyming with *Paulus*), June 26. Plural first-person: *ro thúirsem* (Epilogue 75). Plural third-person: *rutúirset*, glossed as "they have scrutinized" <note>original Latin: scrutati sunt</note> in the Milan Glosses 44d 23, where it is treated as a simple verb. Future tense (b-future) plural first-person: *no-s-tuirfem* (Prologue 289).
<term>tuirme</term>: **ro thúirmed**, see *dorímu*.
<term>tuirpill luachrai</term>, page 180: **a clump or tussock of rushes**.
<term>tuissel</term> masculine noun: **a falling or a stumbling**, accusative: *tuissel* (July 8). This is the verbal noun of *dofuisliur* or *dofuislim*, glossed as "I slip or fall" <note>original Latin: labo</note> in the St. Gall Glosses <note>original: Sg.</note> 146b 1.
<term>tuluid</term>: **he came (or he went)**, July 12. Used for *doluid*, the past tense <note>original: preterite</note> singular third-person of *dotíag*.
<term>turscar</term>: **seaweed**, plural nominative: *turscair* (page 50). Also known as *turasgar*, **sea-ore** or **sea-wrack**, Latin *alga*. O'Brien and Dinneen define it as *turscar* or *troscar*.
<term>úabar</term> masculine (or possibly neuter) noun: **pride**, Ascoli 131. Singular genitive: *uabair* (Prologue 199).
<term>úacht</term>, **ócht** masculine noun: **coldness**, Ascoli 128. Singular genitive: *ind huachta* (the cold) in the Milan Glosses 94b 23; dative: *úacht* (April 19). Derived from *ógh-to-*; related to *úar* (cold).
<term>úag</term>, **úagdae**, **úage**: see *óc, ócdae, óce*.
<term>úaib</term>: **from you**, Epilogue 374.
<term>úainn</term>: **from us**, April 21, June 11, 13, December 20. With an emphasizing pronoun: *úanni* (January 28).
<term>úaitne</term> masculine (or possibly neuter) noun: **pillar**, April 29. See *uatne* in O'Donovan's edition of *Cormac's Glossary* <note>original: Corm. Tr.</note> 165.
<term>úallach</term>: **proud**, Prologue 189. A derivative of *úall* (feminine noun: **pride or arrogance**), Ascoli 1331. Genitive: *úaille* (Milan Glosses 33b 17). From this comes *ualligim*, glossed as "I claim or arrogate" <note>original Latin: arrogo</note> in the St. Gall Glosses 22b 2.

Comparative forms: **úasliu**, **úaisliu**, **húaisliu**, **úas** Prologue 351, 263, January 7, 18, 21, March 19, May 1, October 23, Epilogue 11, 15, 319, 295. From this comes **úaslaigim**, "I exalt," and **forúaisligim** ("I overwhelm" or "exalt over"), [Reference] Wb. 17ᵇ 7. Compounds:
> **úasalathair**, masculine noun: **patriarch** (literally "noble-father"), nominative plural: **-athraig** Epilogue 13, 243; genitive: **úasalathrach** [Reference] Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II. 355.
> **úasalnóeb**, masculine noun: **a noble saint**, plural genitive: Epilogue 277.

**úasucán**, a diminutive of **úas** (above), page 44; compare to **Ísucán** ("Little Jesus").
**úatíu**, a contraction of **úathatíu**, meaning **lonelier**, Epilogue 395; here the comparative form of **úathathe** (meaning **singular** or **single** <note>original Latin: singularis, singulus</note>), [Reference] Ascoli 131, is used for the superlative ("loneliest").
**ro-ucc**, perfect active 3rd person singular of the verb **berim** ("to carry" or "to bring"), **rot-ug** line 226; passive 3rd person plural: **ro uctha** Prologue 45.
**uile**, adjective or pronoun: **every** or **all**, Prologue 141, 147, [Reference] Ascoli 134–5; feminine genitive singular: April 20; plural nominative: **uili** Prologue 53, 201, 264; accusative: Epilogue 486.
**uiss**, **humble** or **obedient**, masculine nominative plural: **uissi** June 19. Alternatively, this may be the nominative plural of **uise**, meaning **fitting**.
**ulc**, used for **olc**, meaning **an evil**, accusative singular: Epilogue 478.
**-um**, **to me** <note>original Latin: mihi</note>; see **táth-um** ("I have") and **ains-ium** ("protect me").
**umal**, adjective: **humble** or **obedient** (Welsh <note>original: Cymr. ufell</note>, from the Latin <note>original: humilis</note>), [Reference] Ascoli 138; masculine genitive singular: **umáil** September 28, December 8.
**unga** (more correctly **ungae**) **úaige**, page 96, line 26: **ounce of virginity**. Compare to the Welsh <note>original: Cymr. wns</note>.
**-unn**, **to us** <note>original Latin: nobis</note>; see **táth-unn** ("we have"), **snáid-s-iunn** ("protect us"), and Thurneysen in *Kuhn's Zeitschrift* xxxi. 101.
**úr**, feminine noun: **earth** or **mould**, [Reference] Ascoli 137; genitive singular: **úre** or **úire** Prologue 128, Epilogue 219.
**uroibri**, page 54, line 37; used for **furoibri**, meaning **superfluous works** or **extra labors**, nominative plural of **furoipair** (from the Book of Leinster 285ᵇ 35); dative: **furopraib**. See **opair** ("work").
1. **-us**, **them (feminine)** or **her** <note>original Latin: eae, illam</note>; see **dlomth-us**, **táth-us**, and **mórth-us**.
2. **-us**, **them (masculine)** <note>original Latin: eos</note>; see **mórs-us**, **tróeths-us**, and compare to **fil-us** (Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus II. 246) and **boith-us** (Lebor na hUidre 128ᵃ 30).
**-ut**, **to you** <note>original Latin: tibi</note>; see **táthut** ("you have").

**Abann Liphe** (more correctly <note>original: rectius</note> **Liphi**), genitive singular, page 222; the river Liffey [Reference] *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 295, 340.

**Airec**, genitive **Airce**, January 2; name of a river in Leix, not yet identified.

**Airgéill**, page 190; anglicized as **Oriel**, comprising the counties of Louth, Armagh, and Monaghan.

**Airtech**, west of Crúachu in Connaught, page 76; the parish of Tibohine, county Roscommon.

**Alaxandria**, Epilogue 259, pages 118, 240; **Alexandria**, the Hellenic capital of **Egypt**. The Irish genitive form **Alexaindrech** occurs on page 98.

**Alba**, **Scotland** (formerly applied to **Great Britain** or **Albion**); genitive **Alban**, March 23, Epilogue 280, pages 92, 114, 465; dative **Albain**, pages 42, 118, 148, 156; **Alpain**, April 21; **Albae**, January 8, June 25; accusative **Albain**, page 148. In Fiacc's hymn [Reference] *Thesaurus Palaeohibernicus* II. 311, the accusative **Elpai** still means **Albion**.

**Allsaxain**, page 116; **Old-Saxons** <note>original Latin: Antiqui Saxones</note> [Reference] Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History* i. 15. In the *Annals of Ulster* (1038), the genitive plural **Allsaxan** means Germany: *Cuanu ri Allsaxan* means "Conrad II, King of the Germans."

**Altraige Caille**, page 132; near Tralee, county Kerry.

**Ambiani**, **Ambianenses** (manuscript: **Abinenses**), pages 230, 231; now Amiens, in the valley of the Somme.

**Andrianopolis**, page 226; for **Hadrianopolis** in Thrace, now **Adrianople**.
